items.title: An N.B.A. Player Got Hooked on Sports Betting. Soon, He Became the Bet

items.author: Nick Berardini
paragraphs: When Jontay Porter was ten, his father woke him up most mornings before dawn. He and his siblings piled into the family’s Sprinter van and drove to an empty field house off the highway. Then, while their friends slept, they ran basketball drills with their father. “All I remember is it still being pitch-black outside, and the two dreaded double doors on the side of the building that would always be left open for us,” Jontay told me recently. In the bleary moments just before one of his siblings tugged the field-house doors open, Jontay always secretly wished that they’d be locked. And, one morning, they were. Jontay smiled as he climbed back into the van and drifted off to sleep. But his brother Michael, Jr., who was seventeen months older, was furious. “Michael was the opposite,” Jontay said. “He wanted to go.”

Jontay grew up in Columbia, Missouri, the fourth of eight children. His father, Michael, Sr., worked in Christian ministry, and his mother, Lisa, homeschooled the children. Both had played college basketball—Lisa, as a high-school senior, had averaged a nearly impossible fifty-eight points per game—and they saw the sport as their children’s ticket to college. All eight of the kids eventually got basketball scholarships. By the time Jontay was sixteen, he was six feet ten. In most families, as a five-star high-school recruit, Jontay would have been the main attraction. But Michael was Mozart. In 2010, their father got a job on the coaching staff for the women’s team at the University of Missouri. The men’s coach spotted Michael shooting alone in the arena one night and offered him a full scholarship; he was still in seventh grade. When he accepted it, as a high-school senior, he was the top recruit in the country. His highlight reels had racked up millions of views on YouTube. N.B.A. scouts believed that he could be the next Kevin Durant. “He’s a game-changer,” a league executive told the New York Post.

Big state schools turn their best athletes into local celebrities, but the hype that followed Michael to Missouri’s campus on his recruiting visits was closer to Beatlemania. Fans asked for autographs and took selfies. Jontay, who came along, was seduced by the hysteria. “Frat houses are putting up posters, and he’s literally treated like a king,” he recalled. “I wanted to be a part of that circus.” He skipped his senior year of high school to join the team, too. The brothers were best friends. Still, it was sometimes hard to be one of the top players in the country but just the second best in his family. “He got all the attention,” Jontay said. “I was just kind of his biggest fan.”

For a time that first season, Michael was sidelined with a back injury, giving Jontay a turn in the spotlight. “He’s the best player I’ve ever been around,” Chris Hollender, then an assistant coach at Mizzou, told me. “I’ve always said I thought he was a more complete player than Mike.” At eighteen, Jontay led his team to the N.C.A.A. tournament. “For me to finally get a taste of stardom?” Jontay said. “I was the man. I controlled the narrative.”

Michael went to the N.B.A. draft that summer. Jontay planned to enter the following year. Then, during the final scrimmage before his sophomore season, he pushed off his right leg to explode toward the rim. “I felt, like, every crack in that moment, and just crumpled to the ground,” he said. He had torn the major ligaments in his knee. His teammates lifted him off the ground and laid him on a table in the training room. “He was beside himself,” Hollender said. “Couldn’t catch his breath, he was crying so hard.” It wasn’t from the pain; Jontay knew what his injury meant for the team’s chances that season. “The only thing he said to me was ‘I’m so sorry,’ ” Hollender said. “It was gut-wrenching.”

In 2019, while Jontay was in rehab for his knee, he injured it again. “Everybody’s telling me, ‘You’re going to be O.K.,’ ” he said. “I knew it wasn’t true.” By then, Michael was a rookie with the Denver Nuggets. (He went on to win a championship with the team, in 2023.) But Jontay, watching the N.B.A. draft in his parents’ basement, saw sixty picks go by without a team calling his name. Eventually, the Memphis Grizzlies took a chance and signed him to a contract as a free agent. He loved the N.B.A.—luxury travel, assistants to run his errands, last-minute reservations at Michelin-starred restaurants—but he felt that he was a tourist there. He had to take painkillers just to play, and after games he had to stick needles into his knees to drain fluid, in order to keep them from swelling. After just two seasons, he was cut from the roster.

In September, 2021, Jontay was in Memphis, living like any other twenty-one-year-old kid—except for the money. He’d made two million dollars from his N.B.A. salary, and had received an insurance settlement for another $2.7 million (the difference between his projected N.B.A. earnings before his injury and his actual deal). One Sunday, he invited some friends over to watch football. Sports betting had recently been legalized in several states, and apps like FanDuel and DraftKings, which previously hosted fantasy-sports contests, were suddenly the biggest sportsbooks in America. Jontay had always avoided them; it seemed improper for an N.B.A. player to bet even on other sports. But now he was out of the league, and had started dabbling in sports gambling. He opened up FanDuel and placed a hundred-and-twenty-five-thousand-dollar bet that the Kansas City Chiefs would beat the Baltimore Ravens. He put another ten thousand dollars on a parlay—a riskier bet that strings together multiple outcomes to increase the payout—wagering that the Chiefs would win, that their running back would rush more than his expected yards, and that the Ravens’ quarterback, Lamar Jackson, would run for a touchdown himself.

In the fourth quarter, the Chiefs were up eleven points, and Jackson raced along the right edge and into the end zone, clinching the last leg of the parlay. If the Chiefs held on to their lead, Jontay would win hundreds of thousands of dollars. His friends recorded a video of him jumping off his couch, hands in the air, shrieking, “Let’s go! Let’s go!”

But, in the final minutes of the game, the Ravens scored to take the lead. The Chiefs then fumbled while setting up what would have been a game-winning field goal. Ravens 36, Chiefs 35. Jontay slumped into his bed. “Literally, like, the party was over,” he said. That night, he stared at the ceiling, unable to sleep. How could he have been reckless enough to lose six figures on a football game? Then again, he had come so close to winning. In basketball, his body had betrayed him. But in sports betting all he needed was his brain. “That moment where I tore my knee is where everything that is on the news right now kind of started from,” he told me. “That point where I no longer had control.”

In 2015, amid a familiar flood of Bud Light and Allstate commercials, football fans were inundated with cheap-looking testimonials—men in jerseys holding oversized checks and spraying champagne. Some had taglines like “More sports, more winners, more millionaires.” The ads were for FanDuel and DraftKings, which had recently launched as fantasy-sports apps. That year, they spent a combined two hundred million dollars on TV advertising; in September, they ran a national spot every ninety seconds. The C.E.O. of DraftKings, Jason Robins, bragged that his business had signed up two hundred thousand new players in a single day.

The companies were taking advantage of a legal loophole. In 1992, sports betting had been made illegal almost everywhere in the country except Nevada, through the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act. But fantasy sports had been a staple of American fandom going back to the nineteen-eighties—a social activity that the comedian Joey Mulinaro once likened to a “book club for regular guys.” Traditional fantasy sports were slow and methodical. Friends and colleagues got together, forked over twenty dollars or so, and drafted an imaginary team of real players. Then they pored over newspapers and tallied up their players’ stats with pencil and paper. The person with the best record at the end of the season took home the pot. Eventually, leagues moved online so that computers could do the math, but the scrappy ethos remained. In 2006, lawmakers banned online gambling, but they exempted fantasy pools. They didn’t want the F.B.I. kicking down the doors of suburban dads on N.F.L. Sunday.

Nigel Eccles, a sandy-haired former McKinsey consultant, grew up on a dairy farm in Northern Ireland and knew nothing about American sports. But he saw that there was an opportunity to monetize the endless optimism of dudes who think they know ball. Eccles founded FanDuel out of his home in Edinburgh, in 2009, and began offering weekly, or sometimes daily, fantasy competitions. Pay an entry fee, draft a football team to compete against scores of strangers on the internet. If your team is good, you win some money; if it’s terrible, you can try again the next day. The action never stopped. “People love fantasy, and the idea that you could take something they love and make it faster, more exciting, give it real money, and they could play it on their phone was just, like, Yes, yes, definitely yes,” Eccles has said. (He left the company in 2017.) DraftKings launched soon after. In 2011, FanDuel had one U.S.-based salesperson, who worked out of a home office. Four years later, it had a forty-thousand-square-foot headquarters in the Flatiron district, with seats from the original Yankee Stadium. It also had a billion-dollar valuation.

The ad blitz brought in millions of new players, but it also drew scrutiny. To observers, the apps looked a lot like illegal sportsbooks. They collected entry fees that were essentially bets on a player’s performance, and kept a cut of around ten per cent. ESPN reported that FanDuel pitched investors on targeting players with a “higher preponderance to gambling.” In 2015, Jim Leach, a former congressman from Iowa who had co-sponsored the ban with the fantasy-sports carve-out, said he’d had no idea that it would “morph into today’s cauldron of daily betting.” By 2016, states were sending cease-and-desist letters to FanDuel and DraftKings, and both were facing bankruptcy.

That’s when they caught a lucky break. A couple of years before, New Jersey, hoping to revitalize Atlantic City, had attempted to legalize sports betting, eventually arguing in a lawsuit that the national ban violated states’ rights. In 2018, the Supreme Court struck down the ban, permitting states to decide for themselves. Jeremy Kudon, a lobbyist working for FanDuel and DraftKings, then started in on a plan called Project Aftermath. (“I’d just seen the N.W.A. movie, and that’s what Dre names his company after Death Row,” he said, laughing.) He went state to state, leaning into the similarities between sports betting and fantasy competitions. “I’d meet with legislators who were, like, ‘Didn’t we pass this already?’ ” he said.

Kudon had a powerful new ally. In the early nineties, major professional-league commissioners had testified in support of the sports-betting ban. “We should not gamble with our children’s heroes,” Paul Tagliabue, the N.F.L. commissioner at the time, said. The leagues even sued New Jersey to defend the ban. But by 2015 they had also cashed in on fantasy-sports deals. The N.B.A. became a direct investor in FanDuel, and M.L.B. in DraftKings. Twenty-eight of thirty-two N.F.L. teams formed partnerships with at least one of the companies. FanDuel, wooing the leagues, cited research showing that its customers watched forty per cent more sports after becoming members. The year after the Supreme Court ruling, the leagues were prepared to capitalize on the legalization of sports betting; the N.B.A. even advocated for it. “The data is clear,” Adam Silver, the N.B.A. commissioner, said at the time. “If someone has a bet on a game, even a small bet, they’re much more likely to engage in that match.”

Silver became the public face of the leagues’ flip-flop. The day after the N.B.A. closed on its deal with FanDuel, in 2014, Silver wrote an Op-Ed in the Times calling for sports betting to be legalized nationwide. He argued that Americans were already betting huge sums in unregulated markets. “Some estimate that nearly four hundred billion dollars is illegally wagered on sports each year,” he wrote. This figure was later debunked, but the idea allowed the leagues to appeal to the same sentimentality that they’d once used to argue against gambling—the purity of the games was at stake. Kudon began lobbying lawmakers with famous athletes by his side. “Everybody has a pennant for their favorite baseball team,” he said. “Nobody has a pennant for their favorite casino.” The effect was obvious. “We brought Joe Torre to the New York State Legislature,” he said, referring to the former manager of the Yankees. “And I watched grown men cry. I mean, people were weeping.”

Traditional casino giants like MGM and Caesars didn’t see what was coming. Sports gambling is typically a small slice of the betting pie relative to roulette and slots. The big casinos “were kind of almost patting us on the head: ‘What are you guys doing?’ ” Kudon joked. The casinos started building apps, but FanDuel and DraftKings were already on everyone’s phone. MGM and Caesars were like shops at the mall; FanDuel was Amazon.

By the end of 2021, thirty states and Washington, D.C., had legalized sports betting, many crafting legislation with substantial input from industry lobbyists. The companies launched another ad blitz. A study by McKinsey found that just five per cent of fantasy-baseball players were responsible for seventy per cent of the businesses’ profits. In a pitch to investors, according to ESPN, FanDuel noted internal data showing that twenty per cent of its customers would describe themselves as “a bit of an addict.” The companies spent a fortune on promotions, but it was nothing compared with the “customer lifetime value” of the guy who stuck around, day after day, to try his luck.

Strangers have always stared at Jontay Porter because of his height. Recently, I visited him at his brother’s house in Columbia, where he dipped under doorframes and moved through the living room like a parent navigating a child’s play fort. “There’s times where I wish I just lived a normal life,” he said. His size makes it difficult to find clothes that fit, or to squeeze into a commercial-airline seat. Still, he told me that he never once thought about buying a first-class ticket to get extra legroom. He saw himself as a frugal person.

Jontay had been fixated on money since childhood. In seventh grade, he started a side hustle fixing iPhone screens. At fifteen, he got hold of his mom’s driver’s license to create a Coinbase account, and bought bitcoin before most people had any idea what it was. He watched the price soar, and bought his first car with the proceeds. “I felt like, I’m better than these hedge-fund guys,” he said.

After his knee injury, he signed up for a Robinhood account and began day-trading stocks. In the N.B.A., ungodly money was the norm. “You’re just used to guys that are spending three thousand dollars on a bottle of wine at dinner,” he said. Jontay began to enjoy a reputation in the league as a market guru. He went “diamond hands” on meme stocks like Big 5 Sporting Goods and GameStop. This fuelled his belief that he didn’t need basketball to make what he called “N.B.A. F-U money.” (He rarely curses.) Soon, he and a partner were selling stock tips to subscribers on Discord through a company that he started called the Financial Cloud. “We couldn’t technically give financial advice, because we’re not licensed,” Jontay said. “We had automated algorithms that would spit out alerts of stocks to go buy.”

Robinhood’s interface was gamified: digital confetti exploded on the screen after customers placed a trade. “It looks like a casino,” Jontay said. “I’m not a scientist, you know. But that type of thing that gambling fed? Robinhood did the same thing.” He started playing a little blackjack on offshore-casino sites such as Stake, later made famous by the rapper Drake, who regularly streams six-figure bets. Jontay signed up for FanDuel two months shy of his twenty-first birthday. (His account couldn’t actually place bets until he turned twenty-one.)

For Jontay, there was truth to Paul Newman’s iconic line from “The Color of Money”—that money won is twice as sweet as money earned. He made a hundred thousand dollars on an unlikely ten-leg college-baseball parlay. But there were warning signs. He told me about his first big bet, on the Chiefs, yet he had memory-holed the fact that, the same weekend, he’d made a hundred and forty-three other bets for more than a million dollars. When I reviewed his transaction history and texted him about them, he replied, “Omg!!!! No way.”

Jontay’s family gave him the benefit of the doubt. He was bashful, but his brother Michael seemed to enjoy stirring up controversy. Michael had suggested that the COVID vaccine was a means of population control, and once warned that kids who attend public school might one day identify as “a cat.” He recently said that, when he’s dating women, he will “throw on some Andrew Tate and see how they react.” These takes, some offered on his own podcast, “Curious Mike,” have led fans to give him the nickname MAGA Porter, Jr. (More tragically, Jontay’s younger brother Coban, in 2024, pleaded guilty to vehicular manslaughter for driving drunk and causing a crash that killed a young mother. Two weeks after his sentencing, another brother, Jevon, got a D.U.I.) Jontay, by contrast, had never so much as stayed out past curfew.

Around the time Jontay started gambling, he began a long-distance relationship with a woman from Seattle named Kelli Kingma. She hadn’t initially been interested in him, because he played in the N.B.A. “I wanted a normal life,” she told me. But, she added, “I fell for how kind and humble and gentle he was. He seemed so innocent.” In 2021, he decided to sell his house. Kelli hoped to use the money to start a nest egg. What she didn’t know was that Jontay had taken out a five-hundred-thousand-dollar loan against the house, and then lost it all gambling. When he realized that she was sure to learn his secret, he panicked. “I’m instantly, like, I gotta make that five hundred thousand back real quick,” he said. While driving his Tesla from Memphis to his parents’ house, in Missouri, he put the car on Autopilot and spent the whole six-hour trip playing blackjack on his phone. By the end of the drive, he had lost another two hundred thousand dollars.

Later that month, Jontay holed up at his brother’s penthouse in Denver and opened FanDuel. He had discovered that his favorite sport to bet on wasn’t football; it was table tennis. It can take weeks to make money from a stock trade. But “a Ping-Pong match, it takes fifteen minutes,” he told me. FanDuel let players “live bet” a match while it was happening. Starting around midnight, he began repeatedly betting hundreds of thousands of dollars on Russian table tennis. “It’s exhilarating because, in your mind, your whole life rides on how good a serve this Ping-Pong guy has,” Jontay said. “It drives you insane, quite literally. Eyes bloodshot. Staring at the screen. I think you’re addicted to the thrill of the in-between, when you don’t know if it’s going to win or lose.” He bet for nearly three days straight, and won more than a million dollars.

Jontay called Kelli ecstatic. He told her that he’d earned the money trading futures. “I was super proud,” he said. “But she was equally, if not more, hurt.” Kelli was a financial adviser, and the story didn’t add up: what edge could her basketball-player boyfriend possibly have in commodities trading? She pressed him for details, but, ultimately, she backed down. “When you’re close to people, your own perspective makes you cling to things you want to be true,” she said. “I just wanted to get married. And I trusted that it was all O.K.”

Frank Cardenas started a job as a V.I.P. account manager at FanDuel a few months before Jontay began betting. At forty-two, Cardenas is a natural sportsbook host—classically good-looking yet weathered, like an aging frat guy. He had been working in casinos since he was sixteen, when he handled greyhounds at a dog track in Iowa. At FanDuel, part of his job was to scout big bettors. Poring over spreadsheets of fresh betting data, he quickly spotted Jontay. “I looked at his wagering history and I was, like, Damn,” he said. “I know that a guy making this many bets, betting every single game in the world right now, he doesn’t have some edge. He’s just a hard-core gambler.”

Online sportsbooks like FanDuel and DraftKings offer V.I.P. programs modelled on the perks that Vegas casinos provide for high rollers. DraftKings V.I.P.s can win the kinds of prizes one might expect (golf clubs, a Peloton) but also more exotic ones (a thirty-thousand-dollar crystal decanter of rare Cognac, a trip to the Pyramids of Giza). Cardenas regularly hosted clients in box suites for sporting events. He bought them steak dinners and took them to swank night clubs, where bottle-service girls in bikini tops lit sparklers and served alcohol under a banner that read “We bet on FanDuel only!” He took them to parties with Chris Rock, and to a track where they test-drove Porsches. The purpose of it all was to keep them betting.

The irony was that, to be a V.I.P., you had to be a loser. Unlike Vegas casinos, where hosts typically confirm the assets of their mega-rich whales, online sportsbooks don’t typically do so. Some of Cardenas’s clients were wealthy. But a V.I.P. could also be a “Taco Bell manager” who “was betting five hundred dollars a week, and then it goes up to two thousand,” he said. Bettors who show a propensity for winning often face restrictions on the apps, or are sometimes even banned. Isaac Rose-Berman, a professional tennis “sharp” and a gambling researcher, told me that, when he tried to place a bet on FanDuel predicting the winner of a tournament last summer, the app gave him a maximum wager of a hundred and ninety dollars. His friend, a V.I.P., could make the same bet for seventy-six thousand. “These are companies that want to make the most amount of money,” he said. “That’s their prerogative.”

Some pros will make dumb bets just to get V.I.P. status, so that they can unlock higher betting limits. It’s also now a common (though prohibited) practice to pay existing V.I.P.s for access to their accounts. I talked to two of these “straw bettors”—people who loved sports and jumped at the chance to let someone else bet for them as long as they could use the box seats. They expected a raucous atmosphere at the games they attended, with V.I.P.s living like kings. But both found quiet rooms of young men glued to their phones, placing bets. “Every other person in this box must be a gambling addict,” one told me. “It was profoundly joyless.” The other told me that, once his pro started winning, he never heard from his V.I.P. host again.

The real V.I.P.s, Cardenas said, are the people who “just can’t stay away.” I spoke with a former client of his whom I’ll call Chris. He told me that he had bet more than a billion dollars in two decades of relentless gambling, and that he’d tried “every modality of treatment” to quit. “My life’s been an absolute disaster for twenty-one years,” he said. “I’m getting evicted. I have a one-year-old daughter.” But nothing has worked. “I’m a zombie. Sex is whatever. Food is whatever. Everything is so mundane—unless I get a hundred thousand on a parlay.”

Jontay’s habits would have raised a red flag with any mental-health professional. One week, Cardenas told me, Jontay wagered more money than anyone else on FanDuel. Harry Levant, a counsellor and gambling-recovery coach who is one of the country’s leading experts on gambling addiction, and a recovering addict himself, told me, “Here’s a sentence that has never in the history of mankind been uttered. You ready? ‘I know what I want to do with my money for enjoyment purposes today. I’m going to go bet on Ping-Pong from the Czech Republic.’ ”

Cardenas wasn’t directly compensated for his clients’ losses, but, per a job posting, V.I.P. hosts were expected to use their clients to “drive revenue.” “These guys make all our money for us,” Cardenas said. When he first welcomed Jontay to the V.I.P. program, he sent him a bonus of ten thousand dollars to gamble with. For Jontay, it was a rush. He was used to offshore-casino apps in which he had to “beg for a bonus after losing” so that he could keep playing. When Jontay asked for another ten thousand the next night, Cardenas gave it to him. The following day, Cardenas got a call from a supervisor. “I got my ass chewed out,” Cardenas said. “ ‘Don’t you give him another dollar without our say-so!’ ” Cardenas was in trouble not only because he’d exceeded his discretionary-bonus limit but also because he’d given out the extra bonus while Jontay was winning. “Yeah, he might be up off ‘Monday Night Football,’ ” Cardenas said. “But we’re gonna get the money back.” The next day, Jontay lost six hundred thousand dollars. Cardenas’s bosses quit scolding him. Then the company gave Jontay another thirty-five thousand dollars in credit.

FanDuel didn’t ask Jontay for proof of his income. All he needed was his name. “It’s right away known that he’s a basketball player,” Cardenas said. “And it doesn’t take much of a deeper dive to find out he’s M.P.J.’s brother.” Michael had recently signed a contract extension with the Nuggets worth more than two hundred million dollars. “There was certainly a sentiment at some point, like, Well, what’s the big deal if M.P.J. has to break him off a million?” Cardenas said. Early on, the accounts team noticed that Jontay had made more than thirty million dollars’ worth of bets during his first two weeks on FanDuel, and when Jontay didn’t respond to an e-mail asking whether he was “comfortable” with his “level of spending,” his account was briefly suspended. Cardenas berated the employees, pointing out how much money Jontay’s brother had. Cardenas walked Jontay through replying, and FanDuel reactivated the account.

In fact, Cardenas said, the company had evidence to suggest that Jontay couldn’t afford his bets. Deposits from PayPal into Jontay’s FanDuel account were instant, but PayPal took a couple of days to actually withdraw the funds from a bank account. About a month after Jontay began betting on FanDuel, according to Cardenas, PayPal notified the company that Jontay owed half a million dollars in overdrawn deposits, and asked for help retrieving the funds. FanDuel decided to suspend Jontay’s account until receiving proof that he’d paid PayPal back. Cardenas said that the company could have used the incident to investigate how many V.I.P. players were betting with overdrawn deposits, though he speculated that the company didn’t want to know the answer. “A lot of these states don’t allow you to bet on credit,” he said. “But with PayPal you essentially can.”

A former FanDuel V.I.P.-program executive I spoke to defended the company’s actions, saying, of Jontay, “At no point when he was on FanDuel was he in such crazy debt.” When I suggested that FanDuel would have no way to know this without verifying Jontay’s finances, the executive agreed that there should be mandatory income checks and other safeguards, particularly for V.I.P. players. “It was never supposed to be twenty-four hours a day,” he said.

As one of the top V.I.P.s at FanDuel, Jontay was offered all kinds of perks: a new iPhone, courtside seats at N.B.A. games, tickets to the Super Bowl. Jontay and Cardenas became friends. They texted almost every day. Jontay called him the “goat of bonuses.” He told me that, while he was hiding his gambling from everyone else, it felt good to have someone who shared his secret. “Frank became why I stayed,” he said.

The anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll spent fifteen years studying how casinos developed electronic gambling machines such as slots and video poker. In her book “Addiction by Design,” from 2012, she wrote that executives said the machines were engineered to increase “time on device” by entrancing players into a kind of dissociative state that came to be known as “the zone.” The companies sped games up by increasing the lines in slots or the playable hands in blackjack and poker. They removed “frictions” like pulling levers or depositing coins. The machines flashed with bright lights and played rhythmic sounds. The zone was so hypnotic that some gamblers soiled themselves rather than leave their machines to go to the bathroom. A compulsive gambler named Mollie told Schüll, “The thing people never understand is that I’m not playing to win” but, rather, “to keep playing—to stay in that machine zone where nothing else matters.” One industry consultant admitted that the goal was to keep players so enchanted that they stopped only because they ran out of money: to “play to extinction.”

Traditional sports betting didn’t have much in common with machine gambling. The hypnosis of the zone shared characteristics with the Skinner-box effect. Beginning in the nineteen-thirties, the behavioral scientist B. F. Skinner discovered that, when pigeons were given a lever that dispensed food pellets at random, as opposed to in a predictable pattern, they began to unceasingly peck at it. Unlike slot machines, sports bets were not random. Games were narrative contests. There was a limited number of bets that a player could make, and matches took hours to resolve.
But FanDuel and DraftKings found ways to increase the speed and the volume of sports betting. They offered bets on everything from soccer to jai alai,

items.title: How an Unlikely Charles de Gaulle Bio-Pic Conquered France
items.description: In the summer of 1942, a cash-strapped William Faulkner signed on to work at Warner Bros. as a screenwriter, earning three hundred dollars a week. His first task was to whip up a biographical treatment of General Charles de Gaulle, leading the Free French gove
items.author: Lauren Collins
paragraphs: In the summer of 1942, a cash-strapped William Faulkner signed on to work at Warner Bros. as a screenwriter, earning three hundred dollars a week. His first task was to whip up a biographical treatment of General Charles de Gaulle, leading the Free French government from exile in London. Provisionally titled “The De Gaulle Story,” the project was intended as hagiography—explicitly so, as President Franklin Roosevelt had proposed the idea to Jack Warner, hoping to boost de Gaulle’s credibility with the American public. Faulkner gave the gig his best shot, producing some twelve hundred pages and entertaining fussy notes from French consultants. (A memo titled “Observations on Inexact Details” cautioned, “In a cafe in France one does not play dominos but cards or billiard.”) Ultimately, Faulkner found his protagonist so hard to pin down that he purged the bio from the bio-pic, instructing a colleague, “Let’s dispense with General de Gaulle as a living character in the story.” The script was soon relegated to oblivion.

Churchills and Roosevelts—not to mention Hitlers—abound in cinema, but, even in France, bringing de Gaulle to the big screen has historically been a fraught enterprise. As the British historian Julian Jackson has written, postwar filmmakers strove to emphasize the collective nature of resistance rather than focussing on a single great man; yet, when de Gaulle returned to power in 1958, becoming President after more than a decade’s retirement from politics, it was with such command that, as Jackson puts it, “to dare to ask an actor to portray de Gaulle himself would have been an act of lèse-majesté.” (The director Réné Clément solved the problem by using archival footage whenever the General’s presence was required.) Pierre Schoendoerffer and Bertrand Tavernier both tried to make de Gaulle films and failed, the latter surely unhelped by his producer’s insistence that the lead character be played by Gérard Depardieu. Then there was the challenge of de Gaulle’s distinctive physiognomy. Such were the sensitivities surrounding him and his myth that a single actor—the towering, schnozzy, serviceably chinless Adrien Cayla-Legrand—maintained an effective monopoly on the role for decades. It wasn’t until 2020 that the first full-scale feature film devoted to the General, Gabriel Le Bomin’s “De Gaulle,” premièred in French theatres. It closed just ten days later, with COVID-19 advancing like the Panzerjäger-Abteilung 187.

This is all to say that Antonin Baudry knew what he was getting into when he signed on to co-write and direct the most ambitious, improbable de Gaulle movie yet: “La Bataille de Gaulle”—a two-part, five-plus-hour epic, based on Julian Jackson’s nine-hundred-page biography “A Certain Idea of France.” (The book's title alludes to the opening lines of de Gaulle’s own memoirs: “All my life, I have had a certain idea of France.”) The film captivated France this summer, and the first part opened last week in the U.S. Its timing has certainly been fortuitous, with France facing a Presidential election that may put the far right in power for the first time since the Vichy regime. But when we met recently, at a café in the Luxembourg Gardens, Baudry told me he believes that the film has resonated largely because of its human element. He looked chicly rumpled in cream trousers, a button-down, and white leather high-tops decorated with red lightning bolts. He said, of the filmmakers who preceded him, “I understood the malediction—none of them had dared and managed to crack the character.”

Baudry, who is fifty-one, began his career far from the moving image, studying math before earning degrees in engineering and literature from France’s arch-prestigious grandes écoles. (He managed to slip in a film-studies minor, with a thesis on Wong Kar-wai.) After graduating, he entered the French diplomatic corps, where he worked as a speechwriter to the Foreign Minister at the time, Dominique de Villepin, and at least partially authored his famous speech at the United Nations, opposing the Iraq War. After that, he pseudonymously co-wrote a graphic novel called “Quai d’Orsay,” after the seat of the foreign ministry. The book—a juicy look at the inner workings of foreign-policymaking—was a hit, selling more than sixty thousand copies of its first edition. Having proved himself as a sort of beast of the French establishment, devouring the competition in every arena he entered, Baudry volunteered to co-write a film adaptation. Then he decided he wanted to be a director. Casual. So he wangled a meeting with Jérôme Seydoux, the chairman of Pathé film company, and persuaded him to finance a nuclear-submarine thriller called “Chant du Loup,” which premièred in 2019 to warm reviews and respectable takings.

For the de Gaulle project, Pathé gave Baudry carte blanche and an initial seventy-five million euros, an unheard-of budget for a French production. (The film was called “La Bataille de Gaulle” in France but is known as “De Gaulle” in the U.S.) It focusses on the critical years of 1940 to 1944, beginning, in Part 1, with de Gaulle refusing to join the collaborationist Vichy government and ending, in Part 2, with his triumphant return from exile during the Liberation of Paris. Baudry had a breakthrough when he and his co-writer, Bérénice Vila, who is also his wife, started thinking about de Gaulle as a figure spiritually not of the mid-century but of the Middle Ages. “I realized that de Gaulle was a modern Don Quixote,” Baudry recalled, citing the General’s “denial, his stubbornness, his readiness to die rather than admitting the unbearable reality that France had capitulated.” Once the notion of de Gaulle as a knight-errant had clicked, Baudry and Vila came up with a tactic to alleviate the pressure of his legend: as they wrote, they called their hero “Robert” instead of “Charles.” They emphasized the initial lostness of his cause: a mad band of marginals, holding on to France out of unaccountable faith, rather than a reasonable chance of wresting control from Vichy. By that point, Baudry recalled, “I had my character in my veins, and I was going to make these films.”

For the title role, Baudry cast Simon Abkarian, an actor best known for his work on the stage. The film took a hundred and fifty gruelling days to shoot, with reports of delays, quarrels, and a generally trying atmosphere leaking from sets in Paris and Cherbourg. Several months into filming, some twenty crew members quit, including the first assistant director and the director of photography. After filming finally wrapped, in 2024, post-production took more than a year, and Part 1 missed an anticipated release date in 2025. When it finally premièred, in May, at Cannes, reviews were mostly positive. Les Cahiers du Cinema criticized its formal “heavy-handedness” and its “idealized vision” of France, but critics in Le Monde and Le Figaro loved it. “De Gaulle” had won a battle, but it had not won the war.

The first installment hit French theatres in June, to dismal ticket sales. Baudry, meanwhile, was M.I.A., still editing the sound for Part 2. “I honestly didn’t give a shit about the noise outside the mixing room,” he recalled. The film’s producers, hoping for a turnaround, moved up the release of the second installment to coincide with la Fête du Cinema, a nationwide promotion offering discounted tickets. (The films’ full titles—“La Bataille de Gaulle: L’Âge de Fer” and “La Bataille de Gaulle: J’Écris Ton Nom”—were unwieldy enough to cause at least one moviegoer, yours truly, to accidentally see the second part first.) Executives overhauled the marketing campaign. Seydoux told me, “We had a crisis meeting, and I said, ‘We have a rifle with only two shots.’ ”

Then came a third, lucky blast—record-breaking heat, which sent people flocking to the cinema, one of the only reliable places to find air-conditioning. By its fourth week in theatres, “La Bataille de Gaulle” had seen admissions surge by seventy per cent. Word-of-mouth took over, and, suddenly, “La Bataille de Gaulle” was a sensation. I heard chatter about it, in the course of a few days, from both a government minister and my boxing coach. “It’s French panache!” Le Parisien crowed, heralding “a fiasco turned triumph.” The trajectory was almost embarrassingly de Gaullian: a crazy project, flailing and discounted, mounting a gritty comeback that would subsequently be treated as inevitable.

In late September, Jérôme Seydoux was sitting in an orange chair at a huge circular conference table on the top floor of Pathé Palace, his company’s Paris headquarters. He has piercing blue eyes and the plain confidence of a man born to industrial wealth—his mother was a member of the Schlumberger oil dynasty—who managed to conquer another field completely. (He is also grandfather to the actor Léa Seydoux.) At ninety-two, he is something of a cross between Louis B. Mayer and Willy Wonka, confecting France’s major films according to a proprietary formula of market savvy and personal conviction.

Seydoux and Baudry like to say that the “De Gaulle” project took shape out of serendipity: over lunch, they discovered that they were both reading the Julian Jackson biography. But in a way Seydoux has been preparing for much longer to make such a film. “I am an old man, and the story, to some extent, is the story of my life,” he admitted. Seydoux witnessed firsthand the Liberation of Paris, in August of 1944. “We tried to go to the Champs-Élysées, but we didn’t make it, because we were crossing the Tuileries and there were people shooting on the Rue de Rivoli,” he recalled. “The soldiers advised my mother to have us all go under a truck to be protected.” Another day, he and his sister were forbidden to go outside, but they snuck out and saw a German tank. “Kids were able to move because nobody would stop them,” he said.

Making a wildly expensive diptych about a long-dead, famously wooden statesman was a gamble, surely, but it conformed to a strategy that Seydoux has pursued to success in recent years,. This involves taking canonical French stories and turning them into “grandes fresques historiques,” the kind of lavish historical epics at which Hollywood once excelled in the nineteen-fifties and sixties. The movies are old-fashioned, and they are expensive, but they have proved adept at drawing big, cross-generational crowds to physical theatres. Pathé’s “The Three Musketeers: D’Artagnan” was the third-highest-grossing French film of 2023; the next year, its “The Count of Monte Cristo” took second place. “It’s this sort of instinctive I.P.,” the film critic Jordan Mintzer told me. “We have Marvel. They have Dumas.” The advantage of resurrecting a wartime superhero is that the world he saves is our own, though “De Gaulle” would have been a very different proposition if it had followed its protagonist into the years of the Algerian War, decolonization, and student revolt.

Baudry has said that he approached the film from another kind of decolonial perspective—that of a French director “breaking the Atlanticist taboo” and liberating his national history from the clutch of the American cultural empire. He spent years living in the U.S. (where he created Albertine, the French cultural center in Manhattan), and when he came back to France he found “a country that was mentally colonized,” as he told Le Monde. “I saw advertisements in public spaces written in broken English that even Americans wouldn’t have understood.” His de Gaulle is difficult, not because he is a comedy Frenchman but because he is a steadfast believer in the near-hopeless cause of maintaining the sovereignty of la Fraaaaaahnce. (Abkarian’s enunciation is the stuff of epic earworms.) “I embody everything the Americans detest,” de Gaulle once said. “I am weak, and I stand my ground.” In the film, he also says borderline delusional stuff such as, “Mosquitoes don’t bite General de Gaulle!” In the next scene, he’s in bed with malaria. Baudry explained, of the General’s almost mystical self-belief, “You have to be passionate. If you’re reasonable, you leave.”

Roosevelt, played by Campbell Scott, is a far more sour, transactional figure than the morally driven humanitarian we know from American history books. Churchill (Simon Russell Beale) waffles and feints as much as he blusters. Baudry told me, “This is the first time we’re seeing this full history through our own lens.” Call it a reverse Pepé Le Pew, flattening Anglo-American icons to give some space not only to de Gaulle but to his internal antagonists and allies and to the French people themselves. Niels Schneider’s sensational performance makes you long for a spinoff two-part, five-hour bio-pic of the Free French general Philippe Leclerc. Baudry’s dramatization of the Germans' violent crackdown on dozens of mostly young, civilian protesters on November 11, 1940, incorporating real live archival footage, is among the most moving set pieces I’ve seen. And nobody who has seen this film will ever forget the Battle of Bir-Hakeim.

There are many ironies to “De Gaulle”—a great-man bio-pic distinguished by its ensemble cast; an anti-American, or at least American-agnostic, film done in high Hollywood style. But its biggest contradiction might be the fact that it is both avowedly antifascist and profoundly patriotic, a film about resistance that could be seen as almost reactionary in its insistence on the purity of de Gaulle and his cause. During our coffee, I asked Baudry whether he’d had any reservations about making a movie that is so overtly, even unfashionably proud of France. He answered in a sidelong way, saying that he hadn’t anticipated the powerful frissons of pride that many moviegoers had reported feeling. Weeks later, I received a long text: “I keep thinking about our exchange in the Luxembourg Garden,” it began. “I don’t want to sound naïve on this,” Baudry wrote. Part of the problem, he said, was that “the far-right has managed to monopolize patriotism,” confiscating “our flag and our pride.” He brought up American exceptionalism, and said that “De Gaulle” does not try to argue for a French version. “It doesn’t say that the French are better than the Spanish, the British, the Americans,” he said. “It just shows people trying to save their country which is France and which they love.”

“Why now?” is an irksome question to impose on an artist, but with Europe struggling to assert itself against an increasingly aggressive American hegemon, and people all over the world searching for models of resistance against autocratic regimes, Baudry is not oblivious to the film’s broader resonances. “I thought to myself, It’s Trump-Zelensky!” he told Le Grand Continent, of a scene in which Roosevelt and de Gaulle face off at the Anfa Hotel, in Casablanca, in 1943. Baudry told me that the current political situation put him in mind of the words of Edward Grey, the British Foreign Secretary in 1914: “The lamps are going out all over Europe, we shall not see them lit again in our life-time.” He continued, “That was true, and that’s a little bit what we’re fearing now.” “De Gaulle” joins a slew of other recent French movies about the Second World War, including “Notre Salut,” a drama by Emmanuel Marre about his collaborationist great-grandfather, and a starry bio-pic of the French Resistance leader Jean Moulin. But “De Gaulle,” like its hero, stands out for its willingness to be true to itself, and even a little weird. Baudry brought up Don Quixote again. “A knight devoted to his lady isn’t necessarily convinced that she is technically more beautiful than, say, the king’s wife,” he told me. “He just thinks she’s perfect, and he’ll die for her any time if needed.” It’s a certain idea about a certain idea. ♦
An earlier version of this article inaccurately described the dramatization of the November 11, 1940, civilian crackdown.

items.title: What Is Biography For?
items.description: I had occasion, a year ago, to draft my mother’s eulogy. Unable to swallow, with advanced Alzheimer’s, she was being fed by intravenous drip. The end seemed imminent. Helpless and uncertain, I set out to write her life.
items.author: Kieran Setiya
paragraphs: I had occasion, a year ago, to draft my mother’s eulogy. Unable to swallow, with advanced Alzheimer’s, she was being fed by intravenous drip. The end seemed imminent. Helpless and uncertain, I set out to write her life.

My mother grew up in Hull, on the northeast coast of England, the youngest child of a large family. She took care of her mother, who lapsed into dementia; she married my father, quit her hospital job, and raised two children, my brother and me. The outlines of her life were clear but the insides dark, lit up by vivid memories here and there. I recall a newspaper cutting from before I was born, with a glamorous black-and-white photo of my mother as a radiotherapist, beside an impressive-looking medical machine. Later, there were trips to the local library, where I inherited her love of reading, and the speech she gave at my wedding, shaking but determined. My mother never liked to be the center of attention, and those around her generally obliged. If only I’d tried harder to push through her reticence, to ask her more about her life when she still remembered it.

As it turned out, my mother’s eulogy could wait. She recovered, as she had after a similar episode once before. But the biographical imperative rankled like an unpaid debt. Why did telling her story seem so vital and so fraught? And why did my inability to do so foster so much shame?

Clare Carlisle writes her mother into her new book, “Transcendence for Beginners,” three times over: once while teaching her daughter how to write; once as her mother is dying; and once to mourn and memorialize her. Like me, Carlisle is a philosophy professor; unlike me, she’s an award-winning biographer, the author of a life of Søren Kierkergaard that eschews chronology for thematic immersion, as well as a philosophical “biography” of George Eliot’s relationship with her romantic partner George Henry Lewes. If anyone could explain the value of writing a life—what I owed to my mother and why—it would be her.

“Transcendence for Beginners” is not a biography, though many lives are caught up in its weft. Instead, it’s a book about why life-stories matter. Both of Carlisle’s professions grapple with the value of human life, but philosophy veers toward the abstract, and biography toward the specific: a single individual with a mother and a given name. Whereas “Socrates went around Athens asking, ‘What is a human being?,’ ” Carlisle writes, “I want to know who this singular person is.” As a biographer, she attempts to create art, too, “to bring something new and singular into the world”—a world that “the philosophical part of us wants to declutter.”

Some philosophers will balk at that diminutive “declutter,” as though the great thinkers who built visions of the world were nothing more than metaphysical Marie Kondos. Not me. Carlisle is entitled to make fun of her colleagues for overestimating the power of rational argument and for preferring false simplicity to complicated truth. Her contrast is, in any case, provisional: she’s open both to moral philosophy that makes use of the individual and to art that does philosophical work.

But there’s a residual tension in Carlisle’s book, and it has to do with her touchstone, the seventeenth-century philosopher Baruch Spinoza. To those who know his ideas, the notion of a Spinozist biographer will seem about as logical as a vegan butcher or a pacifist contract killer. For Spinoza, there is one substance only, a depersonalized God, and everything else is simply a “mode,” or modification, of that substance, a ripple in the ocean of being. We are all ontological froth. As Carlisle argues:

On its face, biography is the genre of the integral subject—a person interacting with others but distinct from them, not dissolving in a sea of substance. For Carlisle, though, the “metaphysical selfishness” of a world composed of discrete human beings “reinforces moral selfishness, and vice versa.” Spinoza is an antidote to self-conceit. But what room is left, in his metaphysics, for the value of an individual life?

Carlisle finds an answer in the microcosm. If everything is an aspect of God, we can divine the value of the whole—the divine itself—within a single person. This way of looking at human life is radically democratic. Carlisle’s book begins halfway up a mountain in Dharamshala, India, in her twenties, when she meets a man who makes his home in a small cave, tending a stone shrine, selling concessions to tourists for a living. At sixteen or seventeen, he left the temporal world behind for a life of ascetic devotion. What moves Carlisle most is how ordinary he seems. “Over the years I’ve met a few people who exuded a palpable spiritual quality, some rare insight or depth or stillness you could feel in their presence,” she notes. “The man on the mountain was not like that.” Later in the book, we meet another ascetic, Ramana Maharshi, who spent his life on a sacred Himalayan mountain named Arunachala. Maharshi became a renowned spiritual guide, fictionalized by Somerset Maugham in “The Razor’s Edge.” Both lives are noble, both beautifully evoked: for the Spinozist biographer, it makes no sense to prize one over the other, the famous over the nameless, since they are merely different faces of a single peak.

Carlisle argues, then, for the value of unheroic lives. The argument is most overt in relation to works of art: George Eliot’s heroines, for example, or Celia Paul’s attentive portraits of her mother. Eliot, who produced the first English translation of Spinoza’s “Ethics,” lived in a time that idolized “great men”: in 1841, Thomas Carlyle wrote “On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History,” and Ralph Waldo Emerson’s “Representative Men” was published in 1850. Eliot’s riposte was “Middlemarch,” in which Dorothea Brooke devotes herself to her self-deluding husband Edward Casaubon, before discovering that his great work is a fraud. Dorothea lives a smaller life than she had hoped, but her life still matters, as the final lines of “Middlemarch” sing out: “For the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.”

Daringly, Carlisle reads even Eliot’s more morally ambiguous protagonists as “a manifestation of God. . . . a glimpse of something shining, perhaps not far away at all.” Carlisle guides us to a metaphysical summit from which we survey human lives “under the aspect of eternity,” in Spinoza’s phrase, filled with love for them as facets of a divine reality. It’s a breathtaking prospect, and “Transcendence for Beginners” is both moving and profound. But is its vision true? Or, to make this personal, how far does it illuminate the need I felt to write my mother’s life and the pain of being unable to do it well?

“Above all, Eliot was interested in the moral power of ordinary lives, like Dorothea’s,” Carlisle writes, “whose effects are ‘not widely visible’, though nevertheless ‘diffuse.’ ” My mother died soon after I tried, and failed, to write her eulogy. Like Dorothea Brooke, she lived an unhistoric life, and that things are not so ill with me as they might have been is at least half owing to her. I am grateful for that. Yet to value my mother in these terms, for her diffuse effects on me, or on other people, is not to value her for herself. For the Spinozist, the value of a life is the value of a sequence of events—waves in God’s ocean—not the value of the person living through them. “Even if the self dissolves, or never existed in the first place,” Carlisle insists, “the life remains vivid, its story compelling.” But my mother’s life—everything she did and everything that happened to her—only matters because she matters. The fundamental value of the subject: this is what the Spinozist cannot see.

If what we’re interested in are events, we will gravitate toward dramatic ones, and, though Spinoza reassures us that a small, flawed life is as much an expression of God as a heroic one, that doesn’t mean our interest is misplaced. It’s not an accident that Carlisle has published biographies of Kierkegaard and Eliot, not of her mother or mine: as a rule, we are more intrigued by bigger lives. There’s nothing wrong with that—unless we lose track of the fact that every person has a value independent of the life they happen to live. The “metaphysical selfishness” that Spinoza disdains—the world of discrete human beings—makes room for moral selfishness, true; but it makes room, too, for the dignity of the singular person.

For Carlisle, the artist Celia Paul’s repeated portraits of her mother celebrate the episodes in which they were created, “the beauty of those hours in which two human beings gave one another time.” But what is made in those beautiful hours is not a biography, nor the painting of a chapter in a life, but a picture of a person in time. Painting is not a narrative art in the way that life-writing is. The value of a portrait lies less in telling a life story, or part of one, than in sustained attention to a particular human being, the individual whose substance Carlisle and Spinoza dissolve. “My mother was never properly seen in her daily life,” Paul writes to Carlisle. “She found the attention I gave her healing in some way. She didn’t mind what I made of her, she just needed to be looked at.”

“I’ll see you when I see you”: the last full sentence my mother said to me, over the phone from the hospital, several years ago, before her power of speech fragmented. You could hear it as self-deprecation: I don’t matter so much, no need to rush to my side. You could also hear it as a vow of loving attention. We love people, first, and not their lives; but when we love them well, we look toward them, wanting to see them better. The shame of knowing so little about my mother’s life was not the shame of being blind to the value of a life story, but the shame of failing in love. ♦

items.title: In “The Heart” and “I Became We,” the Rise of the Hive-Mind Musical
items.description: The first image in the poignant, propulsive new E.D.M.-pop musical “The Heart,” at the Roundabout’s Laura Pels Theatre, is of a young surfer, Simon (Nick T. Daly), swaying in solitary bliss, like the only dancer left at a club. Behind him, a neon line pulses—i
items.author: Emily Nussbaum
paragraphs: The first image in the poignant, propulsive new E.D.M.-pop musical “The Heart,” at the Roundabout’s Laura Pels Theatre, is of a young surfer, Simon (Nick T. Daly), swaying in solitary bliss, like the only dancer left at a club. Behind him, a neon line pulses—it’s an ocean swell, an electrocardiogram, a musical beat. Just nineteen, Simon has slipped out early to catch a predawn wave, but on the drive home he’ll be critically injured in a crash.

And, in a flash, Simon is no longer the show’s protagonist—instead, his heart is. As bright grids fill up screens that frame the stage, the musical—smartly directed by the Roundabout’s new artistic director, Christopher Ashley, with lighting by Amanda Zieve, immersive video design by Lucy Mackinnon, and subtly gliding choreography by Mandy Moore (the auteur behind Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour)—becomes a thrilling, thrumming twenty-four-hour countdown to an organ transplant, tracing the path from one person’s tragedy to another’s miracle. We meet Simon’s powerhouse mother, Marianne (a moving Joaquina Kalukango, belting in denial by her son’s bedside); her prickly ex-husband, Sean (Jason Tam); Simon’s girlfriend, a d.j. named Juliette (Max McKenna); and also the medical team, including a warm, no-filter nurse (a fab Bre Jackson) and a cocksure surgeon (Drew Gehling, who, after playing doctors in “Waitress” and “Little Shop of Horrors,” may qualify for a medical degree). Later, we meet the recipient of Simon’s heart, portrayed with rueful glamour by Heidi Blickenstaff. These characters are distinct individuals, but there’s a fungibility to the whole enterprise: we meet each of them briefly but intensely, in passing, the way you do in a hospital. The cast juggles minor roles, so a patient might reappear as a doctor; Simon’s surfboard becomes an operating table.

The central concept, adapted by Kait Kerrigan from a poetic French novel, could easily go gooey or gimmicky, like a musical episode of “Grey’s Anatomy.” At first, there’s an almost bludgeoning pathos to what we witness, as Marianne resists the news that her son—brain-dead, but still with a beating heart—is gone. But, just as her grief becomes unbearable, a jarring image intervenes. At center stage, a fey stranger appears, warbling in a high operatic voice, with bright-blue gel patches under his eyes and a white towel wrapped around his head, diva style. Only after his phone rings do we learn who this person is: Thomas (Lincoln Klauss), the hospital professional assigned to persuade Marianne and Sean to donate Simon’s organs. “They might be divorced?” a colleague tells Thomas, filling him in on the case. “The divorce’ll be fun,” he responds, tartly.

It’s a tonic splash of detachment before Thomas’s mask of professionalism slides back up. Some of the production’s strongest moments feature this sort of tricky tonal pivot, as when a punkish gamer (a terrific Wren Rivera) is unveiled as the gleeful consultant who selects organ recipients using an algorithm. The show’s lyrics are often literal-minded, with rare outliers, such as a wry joke about Juliette becoming “a side piece to his nine-foot slab of fibreglass.” But did that blunt sincerity deliver emotionally? It sure did. Before long, my eyes stung; my chest got tight. If the critical part of my brain sometimes resisted an obvious turn of phrase—“You are my heartbeat,” say—the rest of my body was all in.

There was certainly no resisting the score, an audacious suite of electronic anthems and ballads co-written, with some help from Kerrigan, by the married pop-music wizards Anne and Ian Eisendrath, the latter of whom was an executive music producer for the banger-heavy “KPop Demon Hunters.” Broadway musicals have mined everything from rock and pop to hip-hop and folk. But there’s something bracingly logical about injecting the synthetic jolt of electronic dance music into a hospital environment, where vulnerable bodies are sustained by machines. The score has an exhilarating artificiality, from the breakneck “Keep Up,” which is punctuated by the beeps of hospital monitors, to the kinetic “Strike the Match,” in which layers of slick digital uplift thicken like shellac as the consultant homes in on her match. Any rhythm that repeats becomes fodder—the whoosh of the ocean, the boop-boop of video games. It’s an aural vocabulary that evokes both the cold, invisible workings of neural networks and sticky bodies losing themselves at a rave, united by a heartbeat.

“Was he generous?” is the question that Simon’s parents are forced to answer as they struggle over whether to let the doctors remove their son’s organs. The show itself feels generous, open to feeling as a source of wisdom. As one of the show’s lovelier lines says of surfing—and, implicitly, of nearly everything else in life—“You only get one wave, then you pass it on.” As anyone who has ever been in an emergency room knows, in a crisis some clichés ring true.

There is a ravenousness in midtown right now, after a frustrating few years, for Broadway to get behind some great new musical. Will “Galileo” break through? Lin-Manuel Miranda’s “The Warriors”? “Wanted”? In late October, a hot contender débuted: the London transfer “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button,” which had a celebrated run there. In New York, some critics found it twee, but I adored this small, oddball fable about a man aging backward. The production actually shared a lot with “The Heart,” even though it was scored with Celtic sea chanteys. It, too, is a countdown show obsessed with mortality, a stylized tale in which actors swap roles. It, too, had a lyrical directness that risked cliché in pursuit of elemental feelings.

But what felt most notable about “Button” was its structure, which, like “The Heart,” featured an ensemble telling an individual’s story in unison—in this case, down to the thoughts inside Benjamin’s head. Both plays are part of a cadre of hive-mind musicals, along with an earlier Ashley-directed project, “Come from Away” (which, like “Button,” has a Celtic-folk score). These shows are explicitly focussed on communities, not individuals—a hospital in “The Heart,” a fishing village in “Benjamin Button,” a rural Canadian town in “Come from Away.” They’re romances about systems, riffing off the choral storytelling of such classics as “A Chorus Line” and “Sweeney Todd” or the clever identity-flipping of “Operation Mincemeat.”

There’s another play in town that employs a similar technique, more austerely: the song cycle “I Became We,” written by Mona Pirnot, with soaringly lovely music by Jack D. Coen. At the Linda Gross Theatre, sixteen singers stand on risers, holding green choral folders. There’s a conductor and a piano. It felt like church until we heard the first line, which was sung as solemnly as Handel’s “Messiah”: “I saw a segment on ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live!’ called ‘What Do You Know About the Female Body?’ ”

What followed was the funny, philosophical narrative of a successful New York playwright in her mid-thirties. She’s got friends to dish with; she adores her mother, a math professor, and her “jumpy and nervous” husband; she is certain that she doesn’t want children. When she goes to a boring party in Brooklyn, a friend passes her a baby, who—as the chorus sings, in joyful, slightly frenzied counterpoint—starts “squirming, squirming!” and “screaming, screaming!” And then there’s a sudden, destabilizing shift in tone: a solo soprano begins singing mournfully, “She’s so small / She’s so small.”

It seems, at first, that this will be a story about fertility—or infertility. But the narrative never goes quite where we expect, its idiosyncratic turns intensified by the singers’ communal delivery, like a catechism or a shared consciousness. Nobody “plays” the narrator; nobody acts out her behavior. They just sing her thoughts, without comment.

Why did this pack such a punch? Maybe it was because of the tension between the elevated harmonies and the down-to-earth words. Maybe it was because the performance framed one person’s inner monologue—It is wonderful to see people love my talented mother! Why am I crying at this Adam Sandler movie?—as a grand, even sacred project. When the payoff arrived, it reduced the audience to sobs as heavy as any I’d heard at “The Heart.” I suspect that we were all thinking about our own lives. It was impossible not to. ♦

items.title: The Mothers We Pay
items.description: In a meeting of the British Psycho-Analytical Society, the psychoanalyst and pediatrician Donald Winnicott remarked, “with heat,” that “there is no such thing as a baby,” an observation he later qualified by saying that, although the infant’s existence is not
items.author: Jamie Hood
paragraphs: In a meeting of the British Psycho-Analytical Society, the psychoanalyst and pediatrician Donald Winnicott remarked, “with heat,” that “there is no such thing as a baby,” an observation he later qualified by saying that, although the infant’s existence is not itself in question, it is inescapably unindividuated—always dependent, always relational. “If you show me a baby,” he continued, “you certainly show me also someone caring for the baby, or at least a pram with someone’s eyes and ears glued to it.” Diverging from the Freudian understanding of selfhood, Winnicott insisted that the analytic unit was not the individual but the “nursing couple,” a psychically soupy dyad in which mommy’s and baby’s identities collapse into and become indistinguishable from each other, until baby progresses to transitional objects and, eventually, independent play.

Successful adult outcomes, Winnicott believed, are not the result of irreplaceable blood bonds but of consistent and well-managed care. Thus, his oft-cited figure of the “good-enough mother” was “not necessarily the infant’s own.” Winnicott saw his own childhood as one held together by an entire assemblage of women, among them his biological mother, two sisters, a governess, a nanny, and a house full of maids. Despite a spectral father (who “left me too much to all my mothers”), Winnicott—according to his second wife, Clare—considered his youth basically a happy one, marred by neither hampering nor neglect. It takes a village, we’re told, and Winnicott understood his own care to have benefitted from a bustling cluster of good-enough mothers.

But what of these other kinds of women, the intermediary mothers paid to occupy or accompany the role; do they, too, collapse into the nursing couple? When it’s an au pair’s eyes or a day-care employee’s ears glued to the pram, where does the rest of that woman go? Modern fictions of motherhood—Rachel Yoder’s “Nightbitch,” Torrey Peters’s “Detransition, Baby,” Kate Zambreno’s “Drifts,” and Olga Ravn’s “My Work” come to mind—are often energized by ambivalence about the decision to become a mother, fear of pregnancy’s bodily disturbances, and the eradication of ego inside the securities and satisfactions of maternal domesticity. Two débuts—Courtney Bush’s “Learning” and K Chiucarello’s “Nanny Nanny”—intervene in this canon by focussing, instead, on adrift young women who come to inhabit the not-mother mother role.

“Learning” tracks the events of a single Monday in a private Harlem day care, where thirtysomething Courtney manages a pack of four-year-olds. After her childhood best friend’s death and a divorce from a man she now hates, Courtney is surfacing from a “light nervous breakdown,” one that leaves her susceptible to, and even eager for, a surrender of self inside the demands of caretaking. On this morning, she lies in bed after her alarm sounds, lingering in “the few moments where I wasn’t yet anybody. Then came the parts of myself, the articulable variables that made up my life.” Echoing a scene from Virginia Woolf’s “Mrs Dalloway”—an unmistakable, wondrous antecedent—Courtney resists and then surrenders to what Clarissa Dalloway identifies as the “call on her to be her self,” “composed so for the world only into one centre, one diamond.”

Much of the day that follows is perfectly ordinary. Together, the children chant their daily itinerary: “Drop-off, Circle, Work Time, Bathroom,” and so on. The novel stretches time—granting notice, and so dignity, to what Woolf calls the “nondescript cotton wool” of experience, those routinized moments of “non-being” which make up everyday life. For Bush as for Woolf, identity is not a metaphysical fact but a style of attention or a social accumulation. This is, in part, what children’s education also works to engineer, and a process that “Learning” scrutinizes: assimilable personhood.

Against the backdrop of her unsettled connection with the past, Courtney experiences the job’s mandate of selflessness as a tool with which to establish her own center. In an almost Buddhist manner, she finds that escaping individual identity recalibrates her capacity to be in the world and with others. In the classroom, she imagines her role like that of the angels of Rilke’s “Duino Elegies,” “there to observe, to witness, to testify,” but exiled from “the experience of the humans.” For Courtney, the children, too, are angels—not blushing cherubs but Biblical seraphim, “armored beings covered in eyeballs . . . learning at a rate that is impossible to describe in something as structural as language.” The characterization of children in “Learning” is uncommonly complex; they are neither props nor narrative addenda but, rather, odd little people in perpetual motion, sensorily and imaginatively porous, “eating information with their entire beings.” Courtney is attuned to the singularity of each, their vocal tics and fixations and privacies, their fledgling channels of desire and uncanny knowledge of beauty. A petulant changeling girl, Quinn, refuses to say anything besides “mert”; hyperactive Sammy makes wild messes; Theo’s alienating intelligence keeps him friendless.

“Learning” extends recognition to all its characters, including even the day care’s “insane cunt” of a director, Elena, and her menacing, eventually violent boyfriend, the aptly named Mike Rott. Central to the novel’s buoyant, humane philosophy is a vision of the educational space as basically reparative, not particularly for the children—who have yet to make “bad” choices—but for the adults who enter its orbit, Courtney most of all. In the wake of tragedy and separation, she is lost, wary of the immensity and opacity of her desire; anger crouches inside her, too, a fact that her divorce made mercilessly clear to her. But her belief in the permeable and cumulative nature of identity enables Courtney to reckon with her mistakes as part of a process of learning, rather than immovable indicators of good or bad character. It’s a redemptive position, one that runs through Bush’s work. In a 2023 poetry collection, “I Love Information,” Bush writes that “the underworld / of learning which is not beautiful” is, instead, a “path of decimation,” one that veers between moments of embarrassment and revelation. In the novel, the children remind Courtney that learning is a “degrading experience,” one that requires “submission and humility and constantly admitting to yourself that you don’t know what the fuck” is going on.

This promise of redemption, we sense, is what draws Courtney to child care: not the desire to have a kid of her own, in any conventional manner, but a pull to the capaciousness and devotion that teaching asks of her. Courtney sees, without resentment or reservation, that to give love without anticipating any in return is the “fate of those of us who take care of other people’s children.” These children, she knows, will go on to other schools and other teachers; they will make bad decisions, and perhaps forget her. But it exhilarates her, this notion that care can be doled out without hope of repayment. “Unlike a parent,” she muses, “I do not cultivate the kind of love I want back later. I cultivate my own love, then pass it out like cut flowers.” Around the pleasures of self-sacrifice circles a perhaps familiar fear: What if she wakes one day to find that she’s given all her love away?

In “Learning” ’s conclusion, the peaceable kingdom of the school is interrupted by a sudden shock of violence, but brutality is the cornerstone of Chiucarello’s “Nanny Nanny.” The novel’s narrator is a career nanny whom we meet, like Courtney, in her mid-thirties and in the aftermath of a divorce. But she is on a rather different quest: to have a baby of her own. Though Chiucarello, like Bush, probes the labor politics and emotional weather of child care, “Nanny Nanny” presents, at its sharpest, a nauseating autopsy of marital abuse, one that likens the self-abandoning imperatives of parenthood to those that leave the narrator open to intimate harm. As is often true in such cases, a history of abuse precedes the marriage. The narrator, while navigating her father’s spells of anger and silence as a teen-ager, learned to coddle his moods, to seek approval—first from him, and later from everyone else. “It never occurred to me,” she confesses, “that one should not have to work to be loved.”

Indeed, for our narrator—who remains, notably, nameless—each subsequent relationship nestles into this groove, turning intimacy into a detachable skill set to be honed, and eventually, paid for. This malleability proves useful when easing into her employers’ families but contaminates the rhythms of her personal life. After a whirlwind courtship—“love-bombing,” we say now—the narrator weds Lucía, who, once infatuation has faded, mercilessly belittles, rapes, chokes, and hits her. For those of us familiar with domestic violence, the shape of their marriage appears unremarkable. Periods of paralyzing coldness are punctured by moments of passionate intensity; abject declarations of love and remorse follow savage explosions; then come the coercion, denials, gaslighting, and escalations. In a shocking exchange, Lucía commands the narrator to “consider the ways I had played a part in allowing her to rape me.” It’s classic abuser logic: to insist that the response to violence, and not the violence itself, is the problem at hand. But by repeatedly detailing the care with which the narrator tidies and disguises Lucía’s brutality—cleanups that bear uncanny resemblance to the tending she performs for the children she watches—both the narrator and novel refuse to flatly reject this logic. The narrator bristles against taxonomies of abuse that strip the victim’s capacity for agency: survivors are not, she thinks, merely dolls that “have things happen to them” but participants in their own lives.

This trauma shadows the narrator’s quest to become a mother. “I am very good at children,” she explains. “I am so good at children that it would seem like a waste of talent if I weren’t to have any myself.” Care work appeals to her, we sense, as a way to rewrite self-dispossession as an art form. One wonders who the narrator is beneath her devotion, this giving over of herself to the care of others. She doesn’t seem to know, an opacity that the novel disquietingly insinuates leaves her permeable to ever-compounding harms. Indeed, both “Learning” and “Nanny Nanny” suggest that care labor wields a consuming power to efface those who perform it. Like Courtney, Chiucarello’s narrator arrives at her vocation like a penitent, seeking salvation in dissolution. If she has done bad things, or feels shame, or fails to behave authoritatively, she can sidestep those regrets—at least for a time—by disaffiliating from ego.

But nannying is not teaching: it’s round-the-clock work, emotionally and physically intimate. Nor are mothering and nannying identical, though the narrator at times appears more enmeshed in the nursing couple than the biological parents that she works for, and questions a neat division between the roles. “Was mother a solo identity that couldn’t be shared?” she wonders. Her desire for her own child implies that she believes it can’t be, that there is a sui-generis quality to motherhood that’s impossible to approximate. In her paid capacity nannying for families such as the Millets, who pay her six figures and fly her around the world, this belief yields an anxiety that she is undermining the children’s mother. After a stranger misidentifies her with her young wards and insists on taking a family portrait, the narrator admits that “I never showed the photo to the Millet mother, too scared of what my boss would think if she learned that nearly every passerby confused her children for my children.” But this, we later learn, betrays only her projected sense of motherhood as a singular identity, one that competes for primacy in a zero-sum framework. The Millet mother, in actuality, holds a humbler perspective, one that accepts the fact that no mother can provide all things for her children alone. “I hired you,” she tells the narrator, “because everything I admire about you is everything I’m not. . . . My kids, they need someone total.”

Like Sheila Heti’s 2018 autofictional novel “Motherhood,” “Nanny Nanny” positions maternity as a philosophical “wrestling place” in which a reproductively capable woman must reckon with that singular refrain: to have a baby or not? And, if so, why? Much of “Nanny Nanny” is structured around an elaborate motivational account of her desire for a child, which the narrator gives to two friends, over drinks, at a bar. Only at the end does she admit to the reader—and, it would seem, to herself—that “the actual reason, is to exact revenge on Lucía,” with whom children were once a possibility but who will never now be party to this aspect of the narrator’s life. Once this realization crystallizes, every other line of reasoning looks like a diversion from what is, in fact, a post-traumatic response mechanism: a way “to break a long line of violence,” and “to simply witness a beginning.” The appeal of mothering, it would seem, is the promise of futurity after violence, a way to stamp out the miseries of her history.

Recently, I told my therapist that the women I know tend to speak of their aspirations for motherhood in one of two ways: there are those of us (I include myself here) who want to be mothers, and those who want to have kids. The split seems to hinge on a gap between action and achievement, identity and possession: Does one see motherhood as an orientation toward others or an opportunity to cement something about oneself? In “Learning,” although Courtney has no investment in “actual” motherhood, she is dexterous with its gestures in no small part because she understands children to be people.
