For the narrator of “Nanny Nanny,” her yearning for motherhood is aligned with a real capacity for care, but it’s nevertheless rooted in a sense that children may be understood as extensions of our identities and desires, that their lives in some crucial fashion might solve the problems of our own. Though she is not yet a mother by the novel’s end, she’s nannying a baby from birth onward, a stopgap resolution that deepens her nearness to the mother role while keeping her nonetheless outside of it. And yet she seems to have found a kind of peace. “It is calm here,” she thinks. “I am stretching my legs out in a home that is not mine and am listening for a baby that sometimes is.” ♦

items.title: FAA Lifts Crippling Ground Stop: Live Updates
items.description: Nationwide air travel was thrown into chaos on Friday after the FAA ordered the longest ground stop since 9/11, due to a systemwide telecommunication outage. The stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m., but thousands of flights were cancelled, it’s not yet clear when the
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: Nationwide air travel was thrown into chaos on Friday after the FAA ordered the longest ground stop since 9/11, due to a systemwide telecommunication outage. The stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m., but thousands of flights were cancelled, it’s not yet clear when the system will return to normal. Below are live updates on this developing story.

In the hours after the national ground stop was lifted, much of the air travel system remained in a state of semi-chaos. While some airports, like JFK, quickly began launching aircraft, others like Newark and LaGuardia took more than an hour to get back in operation. Others saw the imposition of partial ground stops, in which certain carriers were barred from certain airports, due to crew or equipment shortages.

Adding to the confusion, the Hawaii Department of Transportation posted on Facebook that “All west coast flight have been halted due to debris from SpaceX launch” — despite the fact that the Starship had launched successfully that evening and hadn’t even taken place in the vicinity.

According to the aviation analytics company Cirium, nearly a third of all U.S. departing flights were cancelled on Friday, more than 8,000 in total. At the low point in the crisis, at 8:30 p.m. ET, just 336 flights were in the air bound for U.S. airports, less than 10 percent of the usual figure.

By 10.30 p.m. ET more than five percent of Saturday’s flights had already been cancelled. That number is almost certain to climb, as the massive disruption to flight schedules has left aircraft and flight crews far from where they need to be for normal operation to resume.

Past experience can give some indication of how long things will remained snarled. The last national ground stop took place at 7:30 a.m. on Wednesday, January 11, 2023, lasted 90 minutes, and resulted in flights being snarled throughout that day and into the evening. Today’s lasted three times longer and took place during a busier part of the week, suggesting that disruptions could continue throughout this weekend.
Did the system just break on its own, was it somehow broken?

That’s one of the big questions tonight regarding the collapse of the FAA’s FTI network, which is what led to the nationwide ground stop. The FAA’s antiquated tech is a well known under-addressed problem, but this was an unprecedented breakdown and we don’t yet know if or how it was preventable.

Another big question is: will this happen again? “It’s going to continue to fail,” Transportation secretary Sean Duffy warned tonight. But what, other than asking for tens of billions of dollars for multi-year modernization projects — which may introduce additional risks — is the FAA going to do to prevent that in the meantime?
Trump speaks (to a congressman)

President Donald Trump in a phone call tonight with GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt pushed for Congress to pass legislation modernizing air traffic control, airport towers, terminals and other critical infrastructure as soon as possible, said a source familiar with the conversation.
Schmitt called the president before tonight’s briefing at the White House, the source said.

Schmitt, who serves on the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, introduced the Modern Skies Act in September, which would provide $30 billion in additional federal funding to update the nation’s aviation infrastructure. He is pushing for it to be included in reconciliation so the funding can pass sooner.
The Trump administration sent a letter to Congress this morning, hours before the ground stop, asking for the $30 billion in additional funding, the source said.
Sean Duffy unofficially upped that request to $50 billion tonight. And that would all be in addition to the $12.5 billion Congress gave the Transportation Department for ATC upgrades last year.
More details about the modernization efforts that may have triggered the crash
Wired reports on the system that seems to have failed:

The [FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI)] is the private communications backbone for the air traffic control system. The system is in the midst of a major, multi-year modernization project, which involves replacing a decades-old network of copper wire with high-speed fiber-optic cables. The FAA has said the update will reduce outages and outage-related delays, and make the system safer. …

The system is managed by the government contractor L3Harris Technologies. On its website, L3Harris says that its “team’s deep knowledge of the US national airspace allows us to upgrade systems without disrupting air traffic operations.” A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment.

In May, L3Harris said it had completed 50 percent of its modernization project. Seventy percent of FAA sites have been upgraded to fiber, the company said earlier this month. The Trump Administration has said it aims to overhaul the nation’s Air Traffic Control System by the end of 2028.

In August, the FAA tapped AT&T to upgrade the FTI, the private FAA communication network, to an entirely new system. That contract is worth $73 million, though its worth is likely to climb into the billions over the years. Previously, Verizon had been selected to build and operate this new system. L3Harris is meant to operate the legacy system until the upgrades are in place.
And at least one watchdog was worried:

A September report published by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) raised concerns that the FAA’s attempt to accelerate long-delayed modernization plans “could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruption.” It found that the FAA does not have a “well-documented” lifecycle cost estimate for its programs, and that, rather than a master schedule guiding the sprawling project, has 11,389 schedules that are not integrated.
Duckworth is not impressed
And Senator Brian Schatz has an idea:
According to the Athletic:
Many teams had already arrived at their respective destinations before the stoppage. But others were forced to consider alternate travel methods after being unable to fly as scheduled.

In college football, No. 2 Utah, No. 6 Texas, No. 8 Tennessee and No. 19 Ole Miss were among those whose travel for Saturday games was impacted, according to program sources and public updates from the schools. Those sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly. Amid the temporary uncertainty, teams like Auburn and North Texas decided to hit the road in buses.
Among NBA teams, the Brooklyn Nets were moments away from taking off from the New Orleans airport when the ground halt went into effect. They are scheduled to play in Memphis on Saturday.

It seems like most college football teams are expected to be able to play as scheduled. During tonights White House press conference, Transportation secretary Sean Duffy said any teams having trouble traveling should “call the FAA” and they would assist them.
The FAA’s latest statement
The agency reiterated that flying was safe about an hour after the White House press conference:

The safety of the flying public is always the FAA’s highest priority. The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming. Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable.
Passengers should contact their airlines for flight updates.
The Associated Press’ explanation of the Trump administration’s explanation
Per their updated main article on the crisis:

Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated systems and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps

But it’s still not clear whether anything could have been done to prevent the overloading, whether too much data was sent for some reason or whether there was some other trigger, and why this happened on this specific Friday afternoon.
Delta and United have resumed domestic departures
That includes some Friday night flights, per CNN, but everything is still a mess, passengers should expect ongoing disruptions, and it will probably take days for air travel to return to normal.
American Airlines released a statement about an hour after the ground stop was lifted:
American Airlines is focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening while positioning the airline for the strongest possible recovery tomorrow and in the days ahead.

For the remainder of the evening, we are prioritizing flights to non-hub cities, as well as international flying, to position aircraft and crew where they are needed to help restore our operation. We expect residual delays and cancellations tonight and into tomorrow following the FAA’s nationwide ground stop.

JetBlue cancelled all of its remaining domestic flights on Friday. Frontier says “we are working to restore operations.” Southwest says flights have resumed, but “customers may continue to experience delays and cancellations as we work to recover our operation.”
A mess of a press conference
Did they admit fault or not?

Duffy and Mullin went out of their way to blame the antiquated ATC infrastructure, and even more out of their way to blame Congress and everyone that came before them for not funding a complete replacement of the system. But they also seemed to say that the network upgrades made by Duffy’s FAA also played some role in the crash. “What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology…it was overwhelming the older system,” Mullin said. Duffy also said that routers were “overloaded with data.”
There weren’t many specifics and it wasn’t very clear exactly what went wrong.
This was Chris Cameron’s takeaway at the New York Times:

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy appeared to suggest that his effort to upgrade air traffic control infrastructure may have contributed to the outage, but he defended the upgrades by arguing that it had to be done.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said, adding, “I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this.”
It also wasn’t clear whether the contractor L3Harris was at all involved.
New patches overwhelmed the old system, or something
We’re obviously might need to wait for a more technical explanation from better public speakers regarding what actually happened.
And this was after practically no new information from the FAA or the Trump administration for hours.
A ‘legacy network problem’
It’s not my or Trump’s fault
That was the basic point of most of what Duffy said.
This was Duffy’s explanation
And most of it was blaming others, with some small amounts of useful information mixed in about this actual crisis:
And it wasn’t until almost ten minutes into the press conference when Duffy finally sounded like a public servant:
Next time maybe open with that instead of the DHS secretary joking about how it’s Friday the 13th and then complaining about stuff he read on the internet.
‘It doesn’t appear’ that a cyberattack or rogue AI were behind the outage
Mullin says they are investigating, and “there’s nothing completely certain right now.”
This was Mullin’s actual announcement related to the ground stop
Duffy is praising Trump and asking for money
He says today’s outage is why he should get the $50 billion in emergency funding he wants to build a new state-of-the-art air traffic control system. And he has praised Trump at least a dozen times.
Mullin and Duffy are giving a briefing
Mullin is again acting kind of weird. He didn’t announce anything about the ground stop at all. He seemed most interested in explaining how the conspiracy theories about the outage were not true.
The ground stop has been lifted
We’re still waiting for the White House briefing to start.
Jetblue cancels all domestic flights tonight
If you’re not in line, stay at home
You may remember L3Harris from such previous Trump administration deals as …
The Wall Street Journal and CBS News report that L3Harris is the contractor who manages the system which appears to have crashed today.

The company is the defense contractor who got the contract to retrofit the luxury Boeing 747 that Qatar gave President Trump and make it the new Air Force One (which Trump will probably try to keep when he leaves office).
It also got a billion dollar investment, in the form of a convertible preferred security, from the Pentagon in January for its Missile Solutions spinoff company that produces solid rocket motors.
For the Airplane! uninitiated, that’s this scene:
It appears some international departures are resuming, but not domestic
This right now may just be a software glitch, but …
From James Fallows’s New York Times Magazine story about whether or not air travel is now less safe under the Trump administration:

Over the past 22 months, the rate of airplane accidents and close calls has suggested a system under enormous strain. Here is an incomplete list of the incidents we’ve seen in the months since the Jan. 29, 2025, Potomac crash:

March 5, 2025: Debris from a failed SpaceX rocket launch affects civilian airliners. Nov. 24, 2025, Louisville, Ky.: An engine rips away from a UPS cargo jet on takeoff, killing all three members of the flight crew and 12 people on the ground. Dec. 12, 2025: A JetBlue flight diverts to avoid a military tanker that had turned off its transponder as part of an operation in the Caribbean, the first of several such episodes. Feb. 27, 2026, San Antonio: A police helicopter crosses the path of a plane cleared for landing. March 2, 2026, Burbank, Calif.: A TV news helicopter wanders into the path of another landing plane. March 22, 2026, New York: An Air Canada jet strikes a fire truck that was cleared to cross its path at LaGuardia Airport, killing the two Air Canada pilots. May 17, 2026, Idaho: Two Navy EA-18G Growler electronic-warfare planes collide during the “Gunfighter Skies” air show. July 15, 2026, Pensacola, Fla.: A Navy Blue Angels demo flight comes dangerously close to civilian spectators. Aug. 4, 2026, Washington: Marine One takes off toward the path of a departing regional jet. Sept. 6, 2026, Miami International Airport: A cargo jet subcontracting to Amazon overshoots a runway on landing and kills five airport employees in an airport van.

This is an extraordinary series of lapses, by any measure. Many of these could have been mass-casualty events, and three did involve fatalities. The Marine One incident was alarming for a different reason. The two aircraft didn’t come close enough to put them in real danger, but the helicopter was carrying President Trump — and, as the N.T.S.B. later found, its crew had taken off from the White House Ellipse before National Airport’s control tower received its required three-minute departure call. (The White House, the Department of Transportation and the Pentagon declined to provide specific answers to questions I sent them.)
All of this appears to be at odds with the cardinal principles that have made modern U.S. aviation so safe.
Overheard on a rerouted flight
Overheard at an airport: ‘We do not listen to robots’
And there is conflicting reporting!
Some pilots say they needed to use the emergency frequency
The FAA has asked multiple countries to halt their air traffic to the U.S.
Only the mainland U.S. was affected
The ground stop did not apply to regional flights in Hawaii and Alaska, according to Alaska Airlines:

Flights within the state of Alaska and Neighbor Island flights in Hawai’i are not impacted. Flights from the West Coast to Hawai’i can continue, and international flights from Honolulu have also been cleared for departure. Aircraft in the air are continuing to their destinations.
It may have been a software update
CBS News’ Olivia Rinaldi reports:
Multiple sources tell @CBSNews that an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot.
When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage.
The system is operated by L3Harris.
Now that are more than 2,400 flight cancellations and counting.
The sports world is probably gonna feel this too
Though the full extent of the impact is not yet clear. The Athletic has a liveblog devoted just to this topic, here’s what David Ubben wondered about college football teams:

I’m curious about the prospect of teams flying to games on the same day they’re supposed to be be played. A lot of these games have high stakes and a lot of potential money involved. And coaches are creatures of habit who have their own livelihoods at stake. I would expect schools to buck hard at any suggestion they could travel early tomorrow morning and kick off at night.
Utah and Tennessee say no discussions about contingency plans yet. They’re just waiting for word from the FAA and in the process of eating dinner.
The National Weather Service says it’s fine
Duckworth is demanding answers
We’d like some too, but she’s the ranking Democrat on the Senate’s Aviation, Space, and Innovation subcommittee:
The affected telecom network may be managed by a single company
The Wall Street Journal reports:

The outage appears to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to people briefed on the matter. The network handles crucial radio frequencies that air-traffic controllers use to communicate with pilots, the people said. It wasn’t immediately clear whether the outage also affected the radar feeds that controllers use to keep aircraft safely separated in the skies.
An L3Harris spokeswoman didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
1,700 cancellations and counting
Stuck streaming on the tarmac at LAX
Our colleague Devon Ivie says she was just stuck on the tarmac for 90 minutes in Los Angeles, but she was able to watch Minions and Monsters to pass the time.
The communication problems appear to have started in Chicago
Air Current reports that the problems originated at the Chicago ARTCC and spread quickly to other facilities:

The FAA’s Washington, D.C. command center was notified around 3:30 pm local time that multiple air centers around the country had lost communication, radio frequencies and radar, TAC has learned. The outages began with the Chicago air traffic route control center, with Boston, Washington, New York and Minneapolis verifying they had problems as well in rapid succession.

At that point the FAA decided to issue a ground stop for all aircraft flying to the east of the national air system. As that call was being made, more air traffic facilities began experiencing communications and frequency malfunctions and U.S. authorities extended the ground stop nationwide.
So about that SMART AI system the FAA just added

In September, the FAA announced the limited rollout of a $875 million software package called SMART, for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” that is aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” Initially, only flights in Washington, D.C. area were affected. Built by the Boston-based data company Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the new system use AI to process hundreds of data inputs and automatically plan aircraft routes. In one segment that aired on CNN, the system was shown routing a flight over a line of thunderstorms, instead of around them, saving 42 minutes of flight time.

On October 13, 23 Democratic members of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking it to review the system, given that that it could “hallucinate safety-critical information.” The lawmakers stated that “the use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits.”

Despite such concerns, the FAA decided to move forward to a full rollout. Three days ago, on November 10, the FAA released a statement saying that “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public.”
It is these Air Traffic Command Centers (ARTCC) that have been hit by today’s outage.
ASI says its system is not involved in the outage:
The skies are getting a lot less crowded
Apparently SpaceX rocket flights aren’t grounded
President Trump is posting about a congressional bill centered on the entertainment industry. At least people stuck in airports and airplanes will have something long to read:
Stuck on the tarmac in Chicago
The New York Times passes along one passenger’s experience from inside a grounded plane at O’Hare:

“I have no idea when or if they’re going to allow departures for today,” a United pilot told a flight bound for Rochester, N.Y., that sat on the tarmac for 45 minutes waiting to take off from Chicago O’Hare International Airport.
After an hour, the pilot tried to turn back to the terminal, telling passengers, “We’re definitely going back to the gate.”
But not even that was possible. There was so much congestion and confusion at the airport as planes jockeyed for gate space, some flights on the tarmac had nowhere to go.
“We were so close to getting out,” said Barbara Bullock, who was heading from Colorado to upstate New York on a college tour with her 17-year-old daughter. But not anymore. “Friday the 13th.”
The airlines are expecting this to last ‘for the rest of day’
In a statement, American Airlines indicated that it’s anticipating disruptions to its flights to continue throughout Friday.

“Flights already in the air can continue to their destinations. We expect disruption to our schedule for the rest of the day, depending on the length of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop. It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this ground stop,” the statement read.
‘This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age’
Explained an aviation expert to CBS News:

“This is absolutely unprecendented,” said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. “I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air at on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age.”
Thousands and thousands of flights impacted
According to FlightAware, there are now 1,195 cancellations and 9,917 delays for flights into and out of the U.S. today, as of 5:41 p.m. ET.

There were more than 4,000 airborne flights in the U.S. at the time when the ground stop was ordered. Again, they are all being allowed to land, and there is no indication that any of those passengers are in danger. Just after 5 p.m. the FAA announced that all inbound flights would be handled on a case by case basis.
More than a million passengers may be affected tonight
The aviation data and analytics company Cirium estimates upwards of 1.5 million passengers are scheduled to fly today from 4 p.m. ET onwards in the U.S.
This is going to be a while

Just heard over at ATC.com: a controller at North Las Vegas ground control tower told a private aircraft that “it’s going to be at least 8 hours for the indefinite ground stop, but no information besides that.”
Per the New York Times, passengers at multiple airports have already been told to go home if they live nearby.

Notably, Mullin kept referencing the most high-profile instance of the FAA ordering a complete ground stop — September 11, 2001 — hoping to reassure Americans that today’s stoppage was nothing like the aftermath of the nation’s deadliest terrorist attack.
“This isn’t another 9/11,” he said. “This is a communications outage.”
Never stop being you, Trump administration
Mullin says “no indication” that this was a nefarious attack

In a hastily-assembled press conference, Homeland Security Secretary Mullin tried to ease the public’s concerns about the cause of the ground stop. “There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack. It is just a telecommunication outage as of right now,” he said.

The secretary continued, “Everybody’s safe. There’s no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying or anything like that,” he said. “I just want to make sure everybody is at ease about that.”

U.S. national airspace shut down unexpectedly shortly afer 3:30 p.m. this afternoon, as aircraft waiting to take off at airports across the country were informed that the FAA had put in place a “national ground stop.” The shutdown hit air travel during one of the busiest times of the week, as business travelers return home from work trips and vacationers head out to their destinations. Inbound aircraft continued to land normally.

Over the air-traffic-control app ATC.com, controllers could be heard informing flight crew that they had received a message stating “all aircraft, all airports ground stopped until 22Z (5 p.m. EST) due to a nationwide equipment outage.”

At the site LiveATC.net, an American pilot could be heard saying that the company had told its aircraft to return to their gates, implying that they expect the delay to be prolonged. Other aircraft continued to line up on taxiways for eventual clearance to take off.

The outage apparently affected Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle aircraft during the cruise phase in between airports, but there was no indication of what might be causing the problem, and at time of writing it wasn’t clear if planes in this phase of flight were having trouble getting or receiving transmissions over the radio.

CNN reports that two law-enforcement officials said a cyberattack was unlikely to have caused the outage. There has also been speculation that a new AI system integrated into the FAA might be responsible, but that system, called SMART, is used for planning and scheduling, not for communication with aircraft.

Since the start of the second Trump administration, officials have come under increasing criticism for a raft of system failures and safety violations. On Thursday, the New York Times published a long feature by James Fallows titled, “Is Air Travel Less Safe?” which asserts that “Over the past 22 months, the rate of airplane accidents and close calls has suggested a system under enormous strain.”

Controllers said that they had been given no further information about the cause. As one controller at Dallas-Fort Worth put it, “we are not aware of a reason, all we know is that it’s indefinite and US-wide,” later adding: “there is no update.”
On flight-tracking software, planes could be seen lining up to land at major airports, but none departing, with clusters of aircraft growing on the ramp and taxiways.
At 4:16 p.m. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy tweeted that

“The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The system-wide outage occurred one day after a slew of Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams, Exchange Online, and Copilot, all suffered a major outage. None of these software packages are part of the system used by US air traffic control, and there was no known linkage at time of writing.

The first-ever national ground stop occurred immediately after the 9/11 attacks as a national security measure. The only other previous national ground stop was caused by technical malfunction that occurred on January 11, 2023, when an FAA system that distributes advisories to pilots crashed. That ground stop lasted 90 minutes.

items.title: Van Hollen Challenge to Schumer Raises Odds of Government Shutdown
items.description: Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has decided to fight Chuck Schumer for the position of Senate Majority Leader in the 120th Congress. The conflict is ostensibly about choosing the best strategist and tactician for the 55 or 56 Democrats who will spend the nex
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has decided to fight Chuck Schumer for the position of Senate Majority Leader in the 120th Congress. The conflict is ostensibly about choosing the best strategist and tactician for the 55 or 56 Democrats who will spend the next two years constraining the Trump administration and paving the way (they hope) for a 2029 Democratic trifecta regime. But it’s also going to have more immediate implications for congressional Democrats.

Van Hollen’s leadership bid seems partly ideological (he is the putative champion of Senate progressives despite his own mainstream background) and partly pitched to appeal to a widespread desire for novelty in light of Democrats’ massive midterm gains.

The 75-year-old Schumer has been in his position for a decade (as of January) and is generally considered a poor (and decidedly un-hip) developer and purveyor of the party message. Still, it’s more than a bit unusual to dump a leader immediately after so successful an election cycle, which is why Van Hollen’s challenge came as a surprise. He’s claiming “double-digit” support among old and new senators; so far only Bernie Sanders and senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan have publicly endorsed him, whereas Schumer has a growing list of loyalists backing his candidacy. Skeptical that he has any chance of success, most observers believe Van Hollen is seeking leverage for younger and more progressive Democrats. In that respect, the leadership fight will inevitably become conflated with a long-awaited “struggle for the soul of the Democratic Party” which will include a wide-open 2028 presidential competition.

Indeed, it’s very likely that the leadership battle (which will be resolved by a secret ballot among Senate Democrats at some point in early December) will be the opening act of the 2028 Democratic passion play for one simple reason: It will coincide with a December 11 congressional deadline for dealing with the expiration of a stopgap spending measure enacted in September to defer major budgetary decisions until after the midterm elections.

Normally you’d expect Democrats to kick the can down the road with another stopgap measure that would defer the real spending decisions until they are firmly in control of Congress after January, and there’s some reporting that Schumer and his Senate allies are inclined in that direction. But Van Hollen (joined by Sanders, Tammy Duckworth, and Michael Bennet) has already announced his opposition to any short-term spending deal that doesn’t include a cutoff of funds for continuation of the Iran War.

This blunt advocacy of a government shutdown just prior to Christmas (given the very low odds of Donald Trump agreeing to acceptable language on Iran) in conjunction with the leadership election will put enormous pressure on Schumer to take the same position. After all, Schumer’s current unsavory reputation among progressives and other Democratic activists dates back to his abrupt March 2025 decision to abandon a threat to shut down the federal government in the face of massive provocations from Trump, Elon Musk’s DOGE initiative, and power grabs by OMB Director Russell Vought. Another “surrender” by Schumer, even if it’s a temporary maneuver to get Democrats into a position of greater control over spending decisions, could give enormous impetus to Van Hollen’s challenge.

Right now restive progressives and other self-styled representatives of the Democratic “base” are spoiling for fights both with Trump and with establishment Democrats, and efforts to stop the Iran War are the most obvious flash-point. So unless Schumer can craft some sort of accommodation with his intraparty critics that heads off Van Hollen’s challenge, all hell could break out right away. Federal employees and contractors facing a hungry holiday season could become collateral damage in the first big post-election fight, even before its winners take office.

items.title: 20 Ways to Think About Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Mess
items.description: It’s been a roller coaster of a week for Nvidia and its now-departed co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It’s also been an overwhelming week for anybody trying to follow this fast-moving, multifaceted story of sex, espionage, White House intrigue, AI dominance, i
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: It’s been a roller coaster of a week for Nvidia and its now-departed co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It’s also been an overwhelming week for anybody trying to follow this fast-moving, multifaceted story of sex, espionage, White House intrigue, AI dominance, investor panic, and a growing number of ill-advised affairs. There have also been a lot of twists and turns and takes. Just in case you’re having trouble keeping up, here’s a collection of additional ways to think about this megascandal and its impact on, well, everything.
AI is helping us put Huang’s absurdly stupid situation in context
By which we mean AI-generated parodies:
Maybe these guys shouldn’t be masters of the universe
Gary Sernovitz writes about how Huang and the ten other tech emperors have proven they are not responsible enough to have so much concentrated power:

For years, there have been no consequences as the emperors’ lives got wackier, sometimes grosser, and always more known. Most of us can recite a few facts about each emperor’s love life without quite trying — or wanting — to. The impunity of the emperors’ carelessness and misdeeds coincided with a period in which they have become richer, louder, coarser, more visible, more Florida, and more right-wing. The emperors don’t all share the same politics, but they have grown comfortable with the sense of all of us as passive participants in their vision of the future. They like nothing more than to scold the scolds: the small thinkers, the enemies of progress, the pearl-clutching moralists. Theirs is the rhetoric of conquerors and commanders. It’s not the rhetoric of people in happy, committed relationships. They can do whatever they want.
Maybe, just maybe, the resignation of Jensen Huang is another sign that all of us have had enough of this rhetoric. And of the men behind it.
There may be some internal groundswell for Huang’s return
Wired notes that some Nvidia staffers don’t think Huang should have been ousted and want him reinstated, but it’s not clear from the report how widespread that sentiment is:

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.

One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
There’s probably more ugliness to come
At the New York Times, Huang’s biographer, Stephen Witt, explains why he knows the tech mogul’s humble public persona was all an act:

I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier this year, but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with the reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised. …

In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash.”
Nvidia’s downturn could be an investment opportunity

As of Thursday afternoon, the fallout from the Huang spy and employee affairs has erased about $500 billion of Nvidia’s market value, but that’s actually up from the roughly $1 trillion it was down after the company’s stock crashed 16 percent on Thursday morning, and really up from the $1.7 trillion it was down after news of Huang’s spy-lover news first broke.
Nvidia’s sudden downturn has also prompted a lively discourse among investors as to whether now is the perfect time to buy the dip, as CNBC notes:

“The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder,” says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. “It’s that they’re one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable.”

While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan’s fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia’s price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale, he says.

Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia’s prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price “happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor,” he says.
The take from JPMorgan analysts, per NBC News:
“We expect the [Nvidia] team to maintain its leadership in AI,” JPMorgan’s team said, while cautioning that “history has shown that one execution misstep often leads to more.”
“Maintaining flawless execution” will be critical to Nvidia and the sector going forward, they said.
The leather jackets were a tell
Our Cut colleague Emma Childs writes:

A $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution. That’s a man in a midlife crisis with an active Raya profile and a Harley in the garage. If someone had consulted me years ago, I’d have said Huang is clearly someone who drinks wine with his mistress in the middle of the day. (The Times uncovered a 2023 photo of Jensen appearing to do exactly that at a luncheon in Shanghai with Alice.)
But pity other leather-jacket lovers
At the New York Times, Anand Giridharadas decries how uncool Huang’s leather jackets have been for the leather-jacket-wearing community:

We may have undiagnosed issues with vulnerability (as reflected in our need for a supplemental dermis), but we’re not stupid. Did we acquire multiple jackets that our spouses smeared as “identical to the last one”? Yes. But a lot of our spouses don’t know the difference between a 1.5-ounce leather and a three-ounce leather, which is like not knowing the difference between Texas and cheese. This was our thing, OK?

Then Mr. Huang, with his own penchant for black leather jackets, had to go and become a household name, the pillar of artificial intelligence, and the man, we were told, without whom the future itself might vanish and the world regress to however it got things done in 2022.

It was annoying to watch a billionaire cosplaying as a rebel, perhaps in order to mask his extraordinary power. Here he was boasting in interviews of not even knowing where his jackets came from, saying his wife and daughter bought them for him, when we in the community could tell you what we ate for dinner any of those fateful days when a new jacket came into our lives. Leather jackets are for people with chips on their shoulders, not microchips in their palms.
And never forget what Charles de Gaulle probably never said
Per former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein:
(As Quote Investigator has concluded, there’s little to no evidence that de Gaulle ever actually said that.)
And never forget this was the beginning of the end
Or as SemiAnalysis posits:

We aren’t ones for conspiracy theories, but a few events around the same time seem to create a narrative that is hard to ignore. The intelligence community had much to gain. The second New York Times story on the topic explicitly states (five times) that the basis for its reporting is the U.S. intelligence community. Trump, Rubio and Lutnick have known about all of this since before their trip to China in May. What’s more is that there is reporting that Lutnick stalled the Chinese chip crackdown. Something has shifted in that relationship, and now the wind is blowing in the other direction.
Seriously, think about all the things we still don’t know
The Verge’s Elizabeth Lopatto wants to know how high it all goes:

Huang has insisted that Nvidia has seen “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” He’s been pretty emphatic on that point, actually. I am now wondering if that is even a little bit true. If the board is cutting Huang loose, there’s probably more on chip smuggling allegations coming. More substantively, Nvidia reportedly intervened in a 2025 Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips — halting the investigation. Since the scandal broke, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appears to have become the fall guy for this, with Axios reporting that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent “confronted” him about failing to note Megaspeed as a national security concern and Politico saying “more than half a dozen Republicans have demanded answers” from him. …

Come January, Elizabeth Warren will be able to send subpoenas in her role as the chair of the Senate Banking Committee. And wouldn’t you know, she seems to be pretty interested. Democrats will control both the House and the Senate. Their voters have given them a mandate to root out corruption. And boy howdy, does Nvidia look like a sitting duck right now. If Huang knew chips were being diverted — or had reason to know that — and tried to ensure their sales anyway, he may have committed actual crimes (bribery, espionage, smuggling, whatever) and, under a functioning legal system, could actually go to jail. Nvidia dispensing with its indispensable CEO is the company reducing its risk of getting roped into Huang’s drama.
And this saga has inspired a lot of overlong tweets
We won’t share any in their entirety because nobody should be forced to read a superlong tweet, but here’s how one begins:
Infidelity is obviously bad
But his contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated
We believe Jensen Huang is an irreplaceable part of Nvidia and the AI Revolution more broadly.
Once the dust settles, firing Jensen Huang would prove to be a costly mistake.
It is time to pause and consult your shareholders.
Huang didn’t just torch market value
Politico points out the terrible position Huang put his company in:

Trump has stuck with Huang. But the scandal is draining the company of the political capital that its CEO had accumulated during the Trump 2.0 era, according to more than a dozen lobbyists, executives, former administration officials and industry analysts who were interviewed for this story.

“If you have a personal brand that’s tied to the corporate brand, you have to think about: ‘What’s my bench look like? Who’s gonna be ready to step up into the spotlight?’” said Brett Bruen, a former diplomat and adviser to President Barack Obama who now runs the public affairs and crisis communications firm the Global Situation Room. “The fact that Nvidia apparently had none of this in place is both shocking and incredibly stupid.”
“Not only did they lose share value. They have lost and — in some cases — done irreparable harm to their relationship with the government, with clients and with investors,” Bruen added.
The second chances are already on offer
Professional scandal surfer Elon Musk is ready to give Huang one:
And armchair CEO Donald Trump is ready to give one to Tim Apple:
The scandal has (at least briefly) shattered a glass ceiling

Nvidia’s new interim CEO is the company’s longtime CFO Colette Kress, which instantly makes her the most powerful woman in tech, in the AI industry, and in the business world, overall, since she now runs one of the world’s three most valuable companies.
However, Huang overlooked Kress when Wired asked him to name the most powerful women in AI earlier this year:

Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure.

As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy.
Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls.
But beware the “web of financial dependencies”
The Financial Times warns that Huang’s resignation “threatens to unravel a web of financial dependencies that binds the AI ecosystem together”:

Huang has made Nvidia the AI industry’s backer of last resort — and he did much of the dealmaking himself. Despite having dozens of direct reports, he was personally involved in many of its investments worth billions of dollars, according to company founders who have received money from Nvidia.

When CoreWeave, the neocloud and prodigious buyer of Nvidia chips, saw its IPO falter last year, Huang led Nvidia to step in with an anchor order. When OpenAI needed support to build a massive data centre campus in Ohio, Huang had Nvidia guarantee up to $105bn of its lease and power payments.

He then worked with Wall Street groups on a plan to use Nvidia’s balance sheet to mobilise more than $500bn of outside capital for chip financing. Several deals are under way, people familiar with the matter said. Nvidia is planning to invest $10bn in Anthropic in a private placement alongside the Claude maker’s initial public offering next week.
And never underestimate the “dangers of lust”
YouTuber Asian Dad Energy’s takeaway:

I think what happened to Jensen over here, it’s a clear example of the dangers of lust. Lust is so dangerous that it can destroy the smartest, the most powerful of men. Yet despite the danger, it is so very appealing. And that’s because lust, it’s a part of man’s nature. …

I believe that most men, maybe even the vast majority of men, they have never experienced what it’s like to be pursued aggressively by a beautiful woman. It’s absolutely exhilarating, maybe even intoxicating to feel so wanted without having to ask.
Zuck is now big tech’s only remaining wife guy
Futurism’s Maggie Harrison Dupré makes her case, now that Jensen’s hidden life as an affair guy has been exposed:

[I]f there’s one tech industry wife guy to rule them all, it has to be Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The Facebook founder and his wife, Priscilla Chan, met as students at Harvard University. In 2024, to celebrate his love for his wife, Zuckerberg recorded a cover of T-Pain’s “Get Low,” which was apparently playing when they first met. Zuckerberg also built a 7-foot-tall statue of Chan, and implored others to join him in bringing back the “Roman tradition of making statues for your wife.” Chan, meanwhile, has stuck by Zuck through Congressional hearings, lawsuits, local jiu jitsu tournaments, and his blinged out fashion rebrand. They share two children and recently went as “burger night” for Halloween, which we have to admit was fun.
And maybe actions will have consequences again
This post has been updated.

items.title: City Leaders Press Google Over AI Schools Plan
items.description: City leaders are demanding answers from Google after the company recently suggested that school districts’ restrictions on artificial intelligence could result in students being unable to use Google Search. City Council Speaker Julie Menin and Shekar Krishnan,
items.author: Nia Prater
paragraphs: City leaders are demanding answers from Google after the company recently suggested that school districts’ restrictions on artificial intelligence could result in students being unable to use Google Search. City Council Speaker Julie Menin and Shekar Krishnan, the chair of the Council’s Committee on Oversight and Investigation, issued a joint letter to Google’s CEO Sundar Pichai, requesting more information on the tech giant’s planned AI restrictions on the school level and what they might mean for students and educators.

“No private company should have an outsized influence on the way our children are educated. Rather than giving more choice to our educators, as the company claims, this decision would force schools to embrace AI products in order to maintain access to the most widely used online search tool. The Council won’t sit idly by while decisions about our children’s education are effectively shifted from educators to the leaders of for-profit companies,” Menin and Krishnan said in a statement.

Last week, Google detailed new restrictions on its artificial-intelligence learning tools, revealing it will automatically turn off student access to its Gemini products as well as Google Search unless school administrators actively opt into those services. The company followed up with a social-media post, saying that schools can choose to turn off Gemini, Gemini Notebook, or Search individually, or any combination of the three. “We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control. That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning,” the post read.

But a subsequent comment from a top leader at the company has prompted concerns among parents and educators alike that the restrictions could go even further in some school districts that have implemented stricter regulations around AI use. In an interview with the New York Times last week, Google’s vice-president for education, Chris Philips, described search and AI as being “deeply integrated.” He added that if AI use was banned at a school that students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The remark, coupled with the company’s overall announcement, prompted swift backlash. Protesters gathered outside Google offices in Chicago and New York City this week, demonstrating against what they see as the slow creep of AI use into the classroom.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose administration rolled out a one-year moratorium on generative-AI use in the city’s public schools, suggested Google’s policy essentially pressures schools into embracing AI or risk losing access to key educational tools. “Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools. No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech,” he wrote Tuesday on X.

In their joint letter, Menin and Krishnan noted how deeply interwoven the use of Google products is into city school life, including the daily use of programs like Google Classroom, Google docs, and Google Search, as well as the use of Chromebooks. Among the questions they want answered are whether Google will allow city public-school students to use Search without having to opt into AI tools, and what safeguards, if any, the company has implemented to ensure schools have a choice when it comes to AI adoption, as well as queries on the accuracy of Gemini’s information and data collection.

“New York City Public Schools has made deliberate decisions about how technology should support classroom learning and protect students. Google must continue to respect those decisions, especially given New Yorkers’ substantial taxpayer investment in its products and services. Having secured a dominant presence in our schools, Google should not use that position to pressure districts into adopting AI tools they do not want for their students,” Menin and Krishnan wrote.

items.title: J.D. Vance’s ‘Will He, Won’t He’ Story Line Has Begun
items.description: In the aftermath of the GOP’s midterms catastrophe, J.D. Vance is going through a wrestling-with-his-future phase. That’s literally the headline of CNN’s new report, which reveals that the vice-president and supposed heir apparent to Donald Trump’s MAGA empire
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: In the aftermath of the GOP’s midterms catastrophe, J.D. Vance is going through a wrestling-with-his-future phase. That’s literally the headline of CNN’s new report, which reveals that the vice-president and supposed heir apparent to Donald Trump’s MAGA empire “has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028”:

While Vance has yet to make up his mind, interviews with roughly a dozen allies and advisers reveal a vice president wrestling with his political ambitions, the fracturing of the MAGA coalition and the demands of fatherhood. They described him as deeply committed to rebuilding the movement that won in 2024 but uncertain over whether he should be the one to lead it.

He’s also not at all sure he or any Republican can win in 2028, unnamed Vance insiders told CNN. And there’s more than one way to end up a loser that year, since he might not even be able to win the GOP nomination if people like Florida governor Ron DeSantis challenge him. Vance apparently realizes the only way to win would be to rebuild the change-election-focused coalition he and Trump won in 2024, and per CNN, “Vance’s allies and advisers envision that, if he runs, he would try to recapture the anti-Washington, anti-establishment message that propelled him to the Senate and then the vice presidency.”
The Washington Post, meanwhile, reports that he is in fact leaning toward a run:

Vance is still more likely to run for president than not, according to several close allies with knowledge of his thinking. In interviews, more than a dozen people with a view into the vice president’s orbit, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss his future, described Vance as keenly aware of the headwinds against the Trump administration — but also of the potential for those winds to shift as Democrats increase their power in Washington.

“Two years is such an eternity in politics, and people are very easily prisoners of the moment,” said one person close to Vance, describing the vice president as someone who is largely able to resist “panicky inclinations.”

In both reports, insiders and advisers say the Iran war is Vance’s most significant hurdle, but though Vance has clearly tried to take the lead on resolving that conflict over the past week, there’s little evidence that Trump thinks it’s anywhere near as big a problem as Vance and other GOP realists think — or any problem at all. And, of course, talking about the war in any negative light always risks backlash from the president, who tends to view contradictions of what he says as a betrayal. A day after reports surfaced that Vance had inserted himself into peace negotiations with Iran, Trump indicated that he had told him to bugger off. “I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States,” Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that “we don’t need a deal with Iran.”

Considering how critical ending the Iran war is to Vance’s 2028 chances, Trump might as well have said “we don’t need J.D. Vance, either.” If the vice-president decides he wants to replace Trump, he’s going to have get through him first.

items.title: You don’t have to be mean to get ahead. As it turns out, nice guys can have their cake and eat it too
items.description: I like an orderly queue. But this morning, the staff checking passports and tickets at the gate seemed keen to spice things up by starting a human stampede. Group-five passengers were allowed to shove in front of group-one folk (the injustice!). Seizing the op
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: I like an orderly queue. But this morning, the staff checking passports and tickets at the gate seemed keen to spice things up by starting a human stampede. Group-five passengers were allowed to shove in front of group-one folk (the injustice!). Seizing the opportunity, a group of older ladies with sharp elbows came out of nowhere in a bid to insert themselves in prime boarding positions. As another one of their troupe started pushing beside me, I edged my suitcase forward a few strategic inches to repel her attack.

“Oh, you’ll let everyone else in but not me,” she responded a little too vocally for comfort. “It’s like we are back in England already,” she said, trying to rally people to her cause. “Are you happy now?” she added like a child robbed of its inheritance by a wicked uncle. I assured her that I was, even if I might have begun to perspire just a little. Guess what? We were seat neighbours. Squeezed-in-economy-seat neighbours. Elbows-touching neighbours.

In future, I am going to try and be a little more James Talarico in my dealings with opportunistic queue jumpers. Because, while watching the campaigning and subsequent victory of the Texas senator-elect, I was struck not just by his youthfulness and integrity but the fact that he’s, well, a nice man.

“Nice” is a funny word. Indeed I remember our English-language teachers telling us to avoid its use, to search for richer, more evocative adjectives. “Nice”, we were told, hinted at something mediocre, pleasant but a little bland. I disagree. Nice is calm, enduring, welcoming, a safe haven. And after years of meanness and political egoism run amok, I would argue that nice is having a bit of a moment. Talarico certainly does nice very well; the new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, seems nice; Mark Carney is definitely nice. Let’s see – but I have a feeling that the nice guy might be back.

Recently, on The Urbanist, I interviewed Amanprit Arnold, an activist for deaf people who is campaigning to open Deafcity Hub, London’s first cultural and business centre for her community. I liked talking to her, listening to how she believes that good design can ensure that deaf people are not isolated (echoey restaurants, for example, cause mayhem for people who wear aids, while large computer screens in offices make lipreading impossible).

One of the reasons that her work resonated is because I had an aunt, long gone, who was in a building struck by a Luftwaffe bomb during the Second World War. She survived but, in the years that followed, her hearing increasingly deserted her. At first there were hearing aids that fixed things but, in old age, she struggled. She was surrounded by a wall of silence. And that’s when the dementia struck.

This is why I have long understood the dangers of such isolation and believed that rich friendships, conversation and community are key to defending our cognitive abilities. We are going to pick up this theme in Monocle’s December/January issue, where we meet a man who has researched this very link and found places where dementia is rare. Beyond community, he also believes that you need to eat a vegetable-rich protein diet to keep your brain running smoothly. And avoid processed food.

On Thursday, I had lunch with a woman who I have known all my working life and who was instrumental in helping me find the confidence to be a journalist. She’s unchanged: funny, sharp, editing a new magazine. She told me that she’s reading a recipe book on the very topic of brain health and that, apparently, we need to eat 10 different vegetables a day. It seems a lot, unless you are a pet rabbit. But after our little Scandi lunch, I saw her scanning the now-empty plates. “We might have done 10,” she said rather confidently. It seemed her forensic veg audit included the carrot in the delicious cake that we had devoured.

Being generous to pushy fellow travellers and hitting this new veg target feels like a lot of self-improvement targets to embrace. But I’ll try my best and my new daily rallying call is going to be: “nice guys eat cake”. Who’s with me?

items.title: Are we entering a new golden age of car design?
items.description: For the better part of a decade, cookie-cutter, identikit design and Chinese copycats have made the automotive market particularly bland. But in the past couple of weeks, off the back of major industry fairs such as the Mondial de l’Auto – or Paris Motor Show
items.author: Adam Workman; Chloe Lake
paragraphs: For the better part of a decade, cookie-cutter, identikit design and Chinese copycats have made the automotive market particularly bland. But in the past couple of weeks, off the back of major industry fairs such as the Mondial de l’Auto – or Paris Motor Show – has brought forth a glut of inspiring new designs. Are we entering a brave new era for automotive eye candy? The evidence suggests so.

Tesla grabbed headlines with its new Roadster that can (almost) fly – capable of performing short hops, leaps and mid-air manoeuvres. Whatever you think about the electric-carmaker’s enfant terrible in chief, Elon Musk, he’s rather good at a few things: namely putting on a show and turning out remarkable, narrative-shifting motors. The long-mooted Roadster’s space-age, wedge-like form variously brings to mind 1970s icons such as the Lamborghini Miura by Italian coachbuilder Bertone and the submersible Lotus Esprit piloted by James Bond in The Spy Who Loved Me. Almost 20 years on from its original pocket-rocket Roadster, it appears that Tesla has set another benchmark.

On the opposite shores of the Atlantic, the French have been hard at work bringing the nation’s trademark brand of idiosyncratic design back to life by drawing inspiration from decades past. Admittedly, two of the best examples, under the Renault umbrella, are in concept-car form. The new Alpine 310 Vision reanimates the original 310, an American muscle car-adjacent thing of brutalist beauty from 1971 and the last model conceived by the brand’s founder, Jean Rédélé. The result is a blueprint for how an electric car should look in Q2 of the 21st century. The Renault 8 Gordini Concept, meanwhile, is an electric two-seater that builds upon the 1964 model of the same name and continues a rich seam of aesthetically rear-gazing, technologically future-facing work.

Perhaps the most promising, however, is Citroën’s 2CV reboot, which drags the Gallic classic from 1948 into the modern day with an electric version. Yes, it looks like a Tonka toy model of what is arguably France’s greatest ever motoring export but the starting price is mooted to be similarly junior. At €15,000, it could be about to break the mould for electric-car pricing and usher in a new era of mass consumption for all – à la sea change created by its forebear.

Not to be outdone by its neighbour, the Italians also have some sleek new additions to the global garage. Alfa Romeo’s sumptuous Cuorerosso (for once, the English translation – Red Heart – doesn’t entirely ruin the mystique; we’re looking at you, Maserati Four-Door…sorry, Quattroporte). The sleek four-seater coupé is, again, only at concept stage for now but in terms of embodying Alfa Romeo’s design philosophy of bellezza necessaria (necessary beauty), it fulfils the brief and then some.

An honourable mention also goes to the Porsche Mission S, which injects charisma into the Stuttgart maker’s overarching visual language. And Jaguar’s mad, mega-bonneted Type 01 has been in the public domain for a while but it was only properly launched this month, warranting a hat tip. Nobody would argue that it looks like anything else, meaning that it’s a design that we’ll likely still be talking about in 50 years.

It has been almost a running joke that people who care little about automotive design can only differentiate cars by colour. But until now, the idea that tones had become the only identifying factors in a scene dominated by dull designs wasn’t that far off the mark. Thank goodness, then, that you will be needing more than a Pantone swatch to get to grips with the latest generation of automotive innovations as the industry forges ahead into 2027.

items.title: Who will be the next UN secretary-general? Ecuador’s María Fernanda Espinosa makes her case
items.description: Seven candidates are vying to become the next UN secretary-general at a time when the organisation appears to be in great peril. Trust is haemorrhaging among member states and the general public, and multilateralism is in retreat. The job of whoever succeeds t
items.author: Charlotte McDonald-Gibson; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Seven candidates are vying to become the next UN secretary-general at a time when the organisation appears to be in great peril. Trust is haemorrhaging among member states and the general public, and multilateralism is in retreat. The job of whoever succeeds the outgoing António Guterres, whose term ends in December, will be nothing less than to overhaul the entire institution.

Guterres is stepping down after a tenure that has seen huge global upheaval, including the coronavirus pandemic, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Hamas’s 7 October attack and the ensuing war in Gaza, and the re-election of Donald Trump. Though viewed as a competent administrator, he has lacked the global profile of predecessors such as Kofi Annan and Ban Ki-moon, and has chosen a low-key approach at odds with seismic geopolitical events.

The candidates to replace him must strike a delicate balance. Though US scepticism about the size, budget and role of the UN means that the new secretary-general will need to signal a willingness to change, too much reforming zeal will not be popular with the five permanent members (P5) of the Security Council – the UK, US, France, Russia and China – that jealously guard their veto power. To be elected, candidates take part in a series of straw polls, in which the P5 and the 10 non-permanent Security Council members cast ballots encouraging, discouraging or giving no opinion on the candidates. Once one of them has the support of at least nine Security Council members and no veto from a P5 member, they go to a full vote at the 193-member General Assembly, which traditionally backs the recommendation.

Conventional wisdom holds that a candidate from Latin America should prevail, given that just one of the previous nine secretaries-general, Javier Pérez de Cuéllar, has come from the region. There’s also a feeling that it’s time for a woman to take the helm. María Fernanda Espinosa, a former Ecuadorean defence minister and a former president of the UN General Assembly, is one of the four female aspirants. Monocle sat down with Espinosa to find out about her plans for the body.
What do people want from the next UN secretary-general?

As a citizen, you want to see the secretary-general up there sitting at the table – sometimes leading but sometimes supporting too. We have seen that this is perfectly doable. All of this will be possible with a renewed, strong leadership. It’s really an advantage to know the system well but not be captured by it.

I have full respect for the main asset of the organisation, which is the very committed, high-quality staff that it has. But you cannot continue to operate under 40,000 mandates [Since 1946, more than 40,000 resolutions, decisions and presidential statements have been adopted across key UN bodies] in times when, frankly, the UN will be getting not more money but less.
What differentiates you from other candidates?

I have touched on all of the spaces and places where the UN operates. I have seen it from the perspective of a high-level government official and also been on the receiving end, negotiating national co-operation frameworks with UN teams at the country level. But I have never worked for the UN so my impulse is not to preserve the status quo. It’s to change it. I was responsible for reforming the armed forces of my country. I had to make very structural, profound changes and wasn’t afraid to do so. I received the highest decoration that the Ecuadorian armed forces provide to a non-military person. I understood that it was best for them to modernise, to change the institutional culture.
Is multilateralism really in retreat?

If you look around, everybody wants more international co-operation. It’s inevitable: we are living in times of radical interdependence. We learnt that the hard way during the coronavirus pandemic and are learning it again with the Strait of Hormuz situation. It’s impossible to say that we are on our own. The national interest is connected to our common interest and everybody understands that, at some point, we need to co-operate with each other.
How important will receiving the backing of the US be for the next secretary-general?

Persuading the US to support – and not veto – your candidacy is not just a formality. I see America as a critical partner for the future of the UN. The US is a founding member. The country has contributed the most to the UN financially. It is responsible for 20 per cent of the overall budget and more than 20 per cent of the peacekeeping operations. So it’s not only about the US being the funder of the UN. It was there at the origins of the organisation and plays a very crucial role in the three pillars of peace and security, development and human rights. So it’s symbolically, financially and politically vital to have the trust and the backing of the US.
How would you rebuild trust among citizens?

It’s true that sometimes people don’t trust what the UN is doing or what its leaders are discussing or agreeing to. That is a response to a very divided, polarised world. When I say that I will be a leader who rebuilds trust, I understand that it isn’t just something that’s declared in a memo. You have to earn it. And I think that people will trust a leadership or a leader that is seen as impartial, as not having any alignments, as faithful to the UN Charter and to international law. A person who everybody can believe in is predictable. They abide by the rules and treat everyone equally. That is very important, especially in the present times.
Why do you want to be UN secretary-general at a time like this, when the organisation is facing huge challenges?

I have something to contribute when it comes to making the organisation better and more effective. I believe that the UN has a lot more to give and has a responsibility to modernise and to revitalise itself. And this is not done by magic. It is done by putting in some hard work and by having a deep knowledge of the organisation without being captured by it. My experience of it has been more from the member-state side, from the government side. So I know what the UN can do, the frustrations that it can create, and I understand very well what the role of the secretary-general should be. I’m a reformist. I like a challenge and think I can do it.
The other runners and riders
Rebeca Grynspan, Costa Rica

Taking special leave from her role as secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, economist Rebeca Grynspan emerged as an early frontrunner. The vice-president of Costa Rica from 1994 to 1998, Grynspan moved into UN roles and has held senior positions in trade and development. This gives her an insider perspective – her vision statement promises to make the world body “more useful, more agile and more accountable to the governments and people it serves”. With a strong track record in multilateralism, she’s seen as a safe establishment candidate and has the backing of senior figures.
Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana

Guyana’s current permanent representative to the UN and its former minister of foreign affairs, Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett has extensive experience in government and a deep understanding of the UN’s workings. She has also impressed in debates with UN staff and civil-society representatives. Though she has a relatively low international profile, this could work in her favour, because world powers are not looking for a big personality but rather a competent administrator and quiet reformer.

Once a leading contender, Rafael Grossi might have hurt his chances by not taking a leave of absence from his role as director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency while campaigning. With Iran’s nuclear programme in the headlines, he has been busy with global diplomacy, which might have affected his ability to travel and lobby for the UN position. But he has been at the heart of some of the most pressing issues today and, should there be a breakthrough with Iran, he could claim some credit. But Grossi was nominated by Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, whose recent sabre-rattling about the Falkland Islands could make the veto-wielding UK apprehensive.
The high-profile candidate

The president of Senegal from 2012 to 2024 and a former chair of the African Union (AU), Macky Sall is well versed in international diplomacy. Devolving some of the UN’s mandates to regional bodies such as the AU could be part of the streamlining process that many nations are demanding, so his experience will be an advantage. However, Sall’s vision might be at odds with those of some of the permanent Security Council members: he has called the body “the last vestige of a bygone world order”. While reforming the Security Council is a popular sentiment among the UN’s 193 member states, the prospect of a major overhaul is less welcome among the five permanent members, who prize their veto power.

A veteran of Ugandan politics who served as UN under-secretary-general for Kofi Annan, 76-year-old Olara Otunnu strikes a good balance between governmental and institutional experience. His candidacy has gained traction between the first few rounds of polling. He served as Uganda’s foreign affairs minister and its permanent representative to the UN, and is a respected diplomat with a good contacts book. He has campaigned on a promise of focusing on multilateral regulation of AI. If he can leverage panicked headlines about the technology into actionable talking points among the Security Council members, that could give his campaign added traction. But he could be foiled by his nominating government, which has faced criticism from UN bodies over its record on human and LGBT+ rights.

Another Ecuadorian candidate, Ivonne A-Baki also has Lebanese heritage and served as her country’s ambassador to the US, France and Qatar. She claims close ties to Donald Trump, a relationship that she traces back to 2004, when she helped him bring Miss Universe to Ecuador. Being a Trump whisperer could be useful, given his withdrawal of the US from 31 UN entities and his threats to the body’s funding. But touting a special relationship with any one government is a risky strategy – Russia and China also have veto powers and will not want to hand the role to anyone tied to a rival. A-Baki’s candidacy is also viewed as an anomaly because she was not nominated by her home country but by tiny Polynesian nation Tonga – and she has not performed well in straw polls so far.

items.title: Our ‘Design Directory’ 2026: The architects, studios and designers to know around the world
items.description: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the coun
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the countries where they work to produce objects and buildings that enhance our lives.

Europe’s architectural and design landscape has a rich history, from ancient castles and cathedrals to modernist masterpieces. Contemporary designers are using this as a foundation for cutting-edge adaptive reuse and the establishment of circular economies, setting global industry standards.
The country’s contemporary designers build on a foundation of secessionist art and early modernist rigour.
This Vorarlberg-based studio’s practice draws on the region’s timber-building traditions and exacting craftsmanship.

Innsbruck architect behind light-filled houses, schools and rooftop extensions, with a gift for breathing new life into existing buildings.

Schottenfeldgasse 62/2/22, Vienna
+43 1 890 8921, mostlikely.at
Tapping into a storied heritage of art nouveau and Flemish urbanism, modern Belgian design is a leader in minimalist creativity.
Landscape architect who designs with the climate and microclimates in mind, working with prevailing conditions to create welcoming, self-sustaining environments.

Hessenstraatje 1G, Antwerp
+32 3 290 62 73, wewantmore.studio
