- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.title: War Recap: Man on a Mission
items.description: Well, it had to happen: Johnny’s cover is blown, and he has no one to blame but himself. This week’s episode is aptly titled: It is the juicy bit, and not just where the divorce is concerned but in terms of the narrative structure of the season. This is the mo
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Well, it had to happen: Johnny’s cover is blown, and he has no one to blame but himself. This week’s episode is aptly titled: It is the juicy bit, and not just where the divorce is concerned but in terms of the narrative structure of the season. This is the moment the story has been leading to: The firms’ respective reactions to the mole reveal will define what kind of lawyers they really are. All season long, Taylor & Byrne was positioned as “the good guys” and Cathcarts as “the bad guys,” but, perhaps as a reflection of our screwed-up world, the firms turn out to be two sides of the same self-preservationist, unscrupulous coin.

The firms cut a deal: If Taylor & Byrne agree to forget about Johnny, Cathcarts will agree to forget about Flora and the honey trap. This way, everyone leaves this infernal trial with their reputations intact. The deal is good for everyone except Johnny, who is left in the worst position imaginable. It goes without saying that he should have thought of that sooner. For most of this week’s episode — until the deal is made — he still believes he might have a shot at securing that job with Cathcarts, his only opportunity not to get the British equivalent of being disbarred. I still think he should have double-crossed, but obviously he hasn’t watched The Departed as many times as I have, so he scrambles in vain.

This week’s episode opens where we left off, with Serena realizing that Johnny is the mole. She whispers as much to Nick as soon as she gets a chance, but by that time, court is already in session. Nick and Serena are distracted as Prudence delivers her opening statement, in which she emphasizes Morgan’s visionary status and Carla’s middling acting career, and soon Smallwood becomes distracted too: Johnny texts him from his burner that he has “been rumbled.” Smallwood texts back that the job offer still stands if he can produce proof of the honey trap. I’m still caught up on how this evidence could possibly, legally be admitted in court. (I would love to hear from our helpful, informed readers on this point — sound off in the comments!)

Meanwhile, Nick and Serena try to decide what to do. Serena’s first instinct is to stop the proceedings and alert the judge that the trial has been compromised. That’s what they should do, but this is television, folks, and this episode still has 40 minutes to go. As Budgie charms the room with her opening statement — in which she encourages the judge to remember that Carla is a creative professional as they debate the creation of Zephyr — Johnny runs to the Taylor & Byrne offices hoping to get a copy of the receipt for the construction of the conservatory with which they paid off Flora, charged to Bernard’s card. He uses his make-women-stupid spell on Cleo, but it fades as the walls close in: Cleo questions the purchase of the conservatory; the ever-watchful Molly questions Johnny’s urgency; Michael questions why he wasn’t notified if there was a document needed in court; Bernard questions why he is up in his finances without asking. All this questioning happens while Johnny is literally in the elevator, and Michael snatches the receipt from his hand before the door closes.

Johnny briefly loses it in a great short montage that sees him squirm under pressure. He proceeds to Flora’s house, and on the way, calls Bella to propose a midweek getaway, since he won’t be needed in court the next day. Bella correctly identifies this as a weird suggestion to make on a Tuesday. Johnny tries to convince Flora to “do what’s right” and go to Cathcarts to confess about the conservatory, the NDA, the honey trap, everything. He tells her she has been used by Taylor & Byrne, just as he’s been used. But his desperate demeanor is sudden enough to raise Flora’s suspicion. After seven episodes of women being too easily manipulated by Johnny, they finally wake up and smell the rat.

At this point, Nick is looking for Johnny. Still in court, Nick and Serena agree that they need to speak with Bernard, and by the time they get him on the phone during recess, all the stuff with the receipt has already happened. They decide not to alert Budgie to the mole problem because there’s nothing she can do at present, and there’s nothing Johnny himself can do for Cathcarts while Budgie cross-examines Morgan. They also immediately agree that they should not tell Carla, though they might reconsider if they knew she was sleeping with the mole. I thought Johnny might try to use Carla somehow, but at least for now, he’s ignoring her calls. I fear we’re in for a soapy how could you do this to me confrontation in the finale.

The firms race to find Johnny. As Morgan worries about his performance on cross-examination (we’ll get to the trial itself after we have surveyed the depth of Johnny’s snafu), Smallwood instructs Schill to get to Johnny before “Singer,” who has disappeared from court, and offer Johnny a job lest the other side tries to “turn him” (Smallwood is familiar with The Departed). But Schill is too late; Nick has a few hours’ head start and gets to Johnny first. He waits for him in his apartment, where he threatens Johnny with criminal charges for corporate espionage and promises to ruin his career forever. When Schill calls the burner, it’s Nick who picks up (Schill hangs up right away). Nick also tells Bella everything, and she is actually mad for once. She leaves and tells Johnny to be gone when she returns. Johnny weakly apologizes to Nick, but I think the show is banking on a stronger emotional reaction for next week. Archie Renaux embodies Johnny’s desperation well; I’m eager to see him bring this character to resolution.

Nick’s brief phone call with Schill leads to the deal between the firms. Serena and Nick meet with Beatrice, Smallwood, and Schill at the Cathcarts office. At first, Cathcarts plays dumb, but when Nick assures them they have proof, they get to business. If each side can overlook their opponent’s trespasses, neither firm’s reputation will suffer and no client will have to know about anything. They come to a settlement number in about 30 seconds that will hopefully bring this God-forsaken trial to a close, so everyone can forget about honey traps and corporate spies and go have tea and shoot clay pigeons or whatever it is they do for fun. It was that easy!

This is all done without the knowledge of clients or barristers, who might be a little peeved to see their hard work so easily dismissed. Prudence and Budgie spend the day with Morgan on the stand. He oscillates between tenderness and hostility toward Carla, though he brings up her diminishing relevance as an actress as many times as possible. Prudence’s goal is to show that Carla doesn’t have any real professional involvement with Zephyr, while Budgie labors to prove that Zephyr would never have existed without Carla. Under Prudence’s examination, Morgan explains that Carla wasn’t present for most of Zephyr’s development, which took place largely in Palo Alto. By way of illustration, Prudence introduces a photo of Zephyr’s American launch party, which Carla didn’t attend because she was at the premiere of a film she wasn’t even in.

What Morgan forgets — and what evades Cathcarts’ research — is that this launch party took place on the eve of Morgan and Carla’s wedding anniversary, and that Morgan set the party date himself. Budgie argues that, knowing Carla would be at a friend’s premiere, and that their anniversary was on the next day, and that every other Zephyr executive was bringing their spouses to the function, Morgan picked a date Carla couldn’t make to purposefully exclude her and take all the credit for himself. Losing his patience, Morgan scoffs that it’s ridiculous he should have to give away “half of [his] life’s work” because he forgot an anniversary date.

But that’s not Budgie’s main point, anyway; she is only course correcting. The core of her argument is that Zephyr couldn’t have existed without Carla because the idea for Zephyr emerged in reaction to something that happened to Carla, when she was the target of a social-media pile-on and became a viral laughingstock. That was the reason Morgan and Carla went to the cottage in Normandy for a needed respite. Maintaining that Carla was a passive muse, “the Jane to his Serge,” Morgan exploited his wife’s suffering for his own gain. The truth is, he can’t recite the poem that gave Zephyr its name, which we’ve seen Carla recite by heart. He can’t even correctly remember the name of its author. If I ever need a lawyer, I’m calling Budgie.

Budgie’s perfect rhetoric puts Carla ahead, but a string of Zephyr employees — including Gillian, Eric, and an unnamed front-desk receptionist — testify in Morgan’s favor that Carla was never professionally involved with the company. Despite Serena’s encouragement that they’re still in a good position, these testimonies make Carla nervous. Morgan is thankful for his colleagues’ contributions, but he notices that Gillain seems “off.” Carla notices the same thing a bit earlier, when Gillian stops her in the hallway to offer her sympathy for how things turned out and promises to call her.

The weirdness that Morgan sensed in Gillian was nothing less than the turning gears of machination. Gillian does call Carla, as promised, and they meet covertly in Carla’s car. Gillian tells Carla about Ancker’s offer and proposes a plan: If Carla changes her strategy to go after Morgan’s Zephyr shares, rather than cash, Morgan would no longer be the majority shareholder and they could force the sale to Ancker. As a result, Carla would become a billionaire. On the stand, Gillian hinted at her intention — she testified that her contributions to the company have been reflected in her shares. With Carla, she works the overlooked-woman angle, hoping she can convince her to act out of wrath and greed. But Carla has been notoriously wishy-washy when it comes to those cardinal sins. She has gone from honey-trapping Morgan to wanting only “what’s fair”; earlier that same night, sharing an umbrella with her soon-to-be ex-husband, she almost looked wistful. Maybe this final decision will invest Carla’s character with some actual complexity and humanity, though I fear, with one episode left, it’s too late.
Representations and Acknowledgments

• With Morgan on the stand, we finally get a definition of what Zephyr actually is: “A social-media platform with strict community guidelines designed to promote positivity rather than division.” Still sounds like word salad to me, though. I can’t envision what a platform like this would actually look like, especially when a couple of episodes ago, Carla got a lot of heat on Zephyr for bombing her late-night appearance.

• At the trial, the press is present both inside and outside the courtroom. Given the prominent place the media has had in the unraveling of Carla and Morgan’s marriage, I suspect the journalists sitting in on the proceedings will play some role in the finale.

• Taylor & Byrne’s eagerness to make a deal with Cathcarts seemed anti-climactic to me. I understand they’re nervous the stuff with Flora will come out, but isn’t employing a corporate spy a much graver transgression? Is anything that happened with Flora straight-up illegal, or as illegal as planting a mole in the opponent’s firm? As Nick said last week, the espionage plot could ruin Cathcarts forever, while Taylor & Byrne established deniability about the honey trap from the get-go. I wanted to see Nick and Serena coming in for the kill. I’m hoping this isn’t the end of negotiations!

• Let’s place our bets on what will happen in the finale. I think Carla will take Gillian’s offer but backtrack at the last minute, thereby ensuring some kind of dignified ending for herself. I also think Saeed will return to the Taylor & Byrne offices and that we will finally learn what actually happened in New York, though I have very high hopes we won’t have to sit through a flashback sequence. I think we’ve seen the last of Bella, and Johnny will end up as all greedy, selfish men do: lonely and friendless. And I think Carla and Morgan will reconcile. Will we see Gabe again at all? What about Flora? Cast your predictions!

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: Follow the Teeny Traitor
items.description: They got a Traitor at the last roundtable, and now the players are riding that high. It only took them weeks and weeks of blindly groping in the dark before chance finally gave them a win. That, and Victor’s incessant harping. Now we’re at the next roundtable,
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: They got a Traitor at the last roundtable, and now the players are riding that high. It only took them weeks and weeks of blindly groping in the dark before chance finally gave them a win. That, and Victor’s incessant harping. Now we’re at the next roundtable, and Victor is coming for Joe. Oh, Joe. You seem pretty good. I’m sorry about your fate.

Kriste kicks things off by accusing Wyatt. She thinks there’s someone young in the turret. Shane thinks it’s too on the nose for Abbey to have accused Wyatt and then get murdered, and Kriste calls out the men’s clique at the table. Yeah! How many women are left now? Three. Three women and seven men, and of the ten people left at the start of the episode, eight are white. Were players commenting on this and we’re just not seeing it? This is seriously so egregious and so embarrassing for the players. Now there’s a clique of men who sway all the votes, and no thanks, everyone can experience that in real life readily enough.

It’s not just that they’re a clique; it’s how they revel in both their in-group status and their voting power. You are grown men. Grow the fuck up, stop fawning over Victor, and stop acting like you’re in a fraternity. You’re making me prefer Jay. JAY.

At the roundtable, Victor starts coming after Joe. Joe doesn’t think he has anything but the fruit idea, which seems right? When Joe asks if anyone saw him interacting strongly with Tomica, no one has anything to say. And this is yet another reason this season is so infuriating. Based on this discussion, it seems really weird for people to vote for Joe, other than Victor having been right before. But when it comes time to vote, it goes: Joe (Wyatt), Wyatt (Joe), Jay (Joe), Shane (Kriste), Kriste (Wyatt), Katie (Wyatt), Victor (Joe), Abby (Joe), Clyde (Joe), Ben (Joe). So clearly, the men’s clique (plus Jay and Abby) agreed to vote for Joe beforehand, and/or there was more compelling evidence presented that we did not see. These votes are baffling because we’re missing so much context. Also, Jay cries when he votes for Joe, and everyone is suspicious of this.

Joe has the most votes, so he stands before them all and says, “My headstone will read: Here lies Joe, proud father, beloved husband, trrrrrrruly a great friend, and Traitor.” That “truly” was very fun, Joe. True dad energy.

So now it’s just Katie holding things down for the Traitors. She pulls Victor to chat since he has this huge voting bloc, and we learn that he is leaning toward Kriste or Jay. Wyatt and Ben are also thinking Jay, due to the crying. Okay, guys. With Katie right there, everyone speculates about her being a Traitor, just in case the Traitors have someone young. Ben asks Katie not to kill him tonight, which is kind of a joke, but also not, since Ben thinks it’s Katie. Before everyone leaves for the night, Victor pulls Shane aside and tells him he has a shield and he’s going to spread the rumor that Shane has one so Shane won’t get murdered. That’s a solid move, Victor.

Unfortunately, it’s recruitment night, and Katie has picked Shane. She debated choosing Victor, but there’s like a 90 percent possibility that Victor would turn on her. When Shane sees it’s Katie, he laughs really hard. He was totally set on Kriste and Jay! The visual of Shane and Katie as Traitors is excellent. They should cast more things by height difference. He’s so tall and she’s so wee! Shane accepts Katie’s offer and becomes a Traitor, making them (per Katie) the teeny Traitor and the mega Traitor. “Let’s hood up,” she says. I don’t know about that phrase, Katie.

Shane immediately has to help murder someone that night. He discloses that Victor has a shield (so much for trust, am I right, Victor?), and they decide that it’s between Ben, Clyde, and Abbey. I really thought Ben was out of the running since he’s been saying Katie’s name, but the next morning, who has been murdered but our Ben Platt look-alike, Rodeo Ben. Should I even mention the continued idiocy of trying to guess whether a knock is a “girl knock” or a “boy knock,” per Victor and Wyatt? And how they are consistently wrong about this? Players have also done this in previous seasons, and they were almost always wrong.

The mission today involves puzzle building. It’s a little Survivor-y, but with a Traitors twist. Every player has to search a trough for puzzle pieces to complete their own three-dimensional shield puzzle. If their shield puzzle is complete by the end of the mission, they are protected from that night’s murder. But the Traitors will also be completing a shield puzzle, only using pieces from other players’ puzzles. If their puzzle is completed, $26,000 will be added to the prize total. When the castle bells chime, everyone must pause, put on a visor, and the Traitors have one minute to steal pieces from other players’ puzzles. The mission ends when the Traitors’ shield is completed, or after four rounds.

Shane is rightfully concerned about stealthiness, as he is a friendly giant with a size-16 shoe. Victor hears floorboards creaking by him and tells us it can only be one person: Kriste. Amazing. Shout-out to Alan’s Victor/Victoria headpiece. Teeny Traitor and Mega Traitor creep around as best they can, trying to complete their puzzle. Clyde is getting suspicious. He was already suspicious of Katie, but he hears heavy footsteps, so he knows if Katie is a Traitor, there’s one more. When you look at the people remaining, he says, there are only a couple of people who could have such heavy footsteps. He hears Shane’s puzzle fall and now is considering Shane for the very first time.

It feels like the players are being given more opportunities to identify Traitors than in other seasons. Or maybe the Traitors aren’t great at this, but are saved by the players also being terrible at guessing. Except for Victor. Somehow. Can you imagine Lisa Rinna being given the fruit task? She would have crushed it.

Next week is the finale, if you can believe it. Really rooting for Katie and Shane, or at least Shane, if Katie can’t make it. Shane wants to support his family and provide some more financial stability for them! Which, again, should be a function of our government and not an NBC game show, but this is the society in which we live.

Who would I vote for on Traitors? It’s hard to judge what one would do without having the insider knowledge, because who knows the full context of what’s happening in that castle, but based on what’s presented, here are my picks:

No Insider Knowledge: I think I would have voted for Wyatt, but I’m interested in why Jay voted for Joe. We don’t really know why, which, again, is something aggravating about this season and its shortened format. If something compelling were brought up about Joe, then maybe! But Wyatt’s name has been thrown around long enough that I think I would go with Wyatt, due to building suspicions.
Yes Insider Knowledge: Victor has a shield, so I’m gonna also pick Wyatt here, if only because of him saying, “They’re clocking cliques. They know we’re boys.” How would anyone not know that, Wyatt?

items.title: The Lowdown Recap: Vote for Family
items.description: Alone together on Oklahoma’s wide-open highways, Lee Raybons Jr. and Sr. inch their way toward mutual understanding. The pair are heading to Frog’s old storage unit, the one he keeps in the podunk town where Frog and Lee Jr.’s mom, Helen Francis, grew up. Trap
items.author: Amanda Whiting
paragraphs: Alone together on Oklahoma’s wide-open highways, Lee Raybons Jr. and Sr. inch their way toward mutual understanding. The pair are heading to Frog’s old storage unit, the one he keeps in the podunk town where Frog and Lee Jr.’s mom, Helen Francis, grew up. Trapped in the small cab of Lee’s van for hours, their only options are music or conversation. Unsurprisingly, the men can’t agree on a radio station.

For all their idiosyncrasies, the fault lines between father and son are refreshingly obvious. Despite their estrangement, Frog believes that he understands his adult son — that what is essential about Lee Jr.’s character was knowable from birth and maybe even before. In our blood. Lee Jr. has committed a related fallacy — mistaking the story he’s been telling about his dad for his dad’s actual story.

Before they set out, Frog assures Lee that he’ll leave Tulsa if his son does him this one last favor. Maybe it’s the promise of his dad’s absence that allows Lee to meaningfully engage with the man he’s dismissed all season as a liar and a fake. There’s really only one question a neglected kid ever wants to ask their neglectful parent, and halfway through their road trip, Lee braves it: Why wasn’t I worth sticking around for?

“Well, we’re always leaving and coming back … aren’t we? I mean, that’s what we do,” Frog tells him vaguely. He is 80 years old, sitting in the diner where he wooed Lee’s mother when she was a 16-year-old waitress. All the versions of himself that ever existed are suddenly nearby again, and he still doesn’t know the answer to his only son’s simple question. Frog continues: “Isn’t that what you do? Leave, come back? Leave and come back?”

The first time I watched the diner scene, I heard Frog’s rhetorical questions as both a rationalization and an accusation against his son, who says nothing in response, just purses his lips and lightly shakes his head. The second time I watched it, though, I started to think Frog was sincerely confused about human nature. Isn’t everyone always leaving and coming back? No. Isn’t the inability to stay put a universal condition? Not really. But Frog has a tendency to locate the root cause of his bad behavior outside himself. Earlier in the episode, for example, Frog tells Lee that his love of chasing women is a heritable trait. But Frog doesn’t know anything about Lee’s love life. He’s talking about himself — the narrative he’s invented to justify his own habits.

Still, no one is wrong all the time. When Frog tells Lee his problem is that he wants to control the world rather than “adapt” to it, he’s onto something about his son’s self-righteousness. Later, he’ll direct Lee to pull over the van in front of a derelict white bungalow that Lee doesn’t remember. It’s the house he grew up in before the family moved to Tulsa. When the Raybons lived there, the house had a porch swing. Frog may have left, but he did not forget, and that’s worth something.

Eventually, the men make it to the storage unit. What did Frog, a sham preacher who was always coming and going, decide was worth holding onto? Not much. There’s a painted upright piano and a yo-yo. There’s a spring-suspended toy horse, not unlike the toy horse Lee couldn’t resist mounting at Jed Sallsman’s ranch. Frog doesn’t seem overly interested in the jetsam of his life. He finds the small gift he promised his granddaughter, grabs an ancient bag of weed, and heads back out. It’s Lee who lingers, discovering a Vietnam field jacket among the clutter; Lee always thought his dad was lying about his war service. Before he pulls the roller door shut on his dad’s history, Lee tucks one of Frog’s old journals in his back pocket.

The Lee Raybons share a joint against the fading light of a long day before getting back on the road. There is no big showdown between them. There are no tears and shockingly few recriminations. They figure out how to be quiet with each other. Over the course of season two, Lee has continually defended his decision to have Frog committed 20 years ago. When the men pull over for a final refueling outside Tulsa, Frog tells his son that his stay in the psychiatric hospital wasn’t that bad. Actually, when Frog thinks about it, he really did need some rest back then.

The signs that something is up with Frog’s health have been accumulating since the cops found him wandering in his red cap (like he’d just stepped out of the title sequence of the ultimate road movie, Paris, Texas). There’s his persistent, ugly cough. Occasionally, Frog seems confused, unable to recall what happened when. In “Leaving and Coming Back,” he falls asleep in the van despite the fact that it’s only mid-morning. He’s nostalgic for the past, as well as the present. He hasn’t taken off that “Grandpa” bowling shirt since Francis gave it to him. But the biggest clue that Frog is dying is that he’s boomeranged back to Tulsa at all.

He came to town wearing a trucker hat emblazoned with “Psalm 107:29.” In the truck stop mini-mart where Lee is paying for 15 bucks’ worth of gas — incidentally, a very teenage boy amount — we see the same hat for sale on the counter. He stilled the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed. It’s an appeal for divine comfort or maybe intervention. Frog crying for help.

With his son inside, the older Lee Raybon closes his eyes against the neon lights of the gas station and opens them to find kids playing with bubbles, bubbles climbing dreamily skyward. Yesterday, he took Francis to the movies (Tulsa’s Circle Cinema) and told her to live her own life, to go to college if she wants. Since we’ve known Francis, all she’s wanted was to be treated like a grown-up, and Frog is the one to finally do it. Today, Frog got to ride shotgun with his son, singing along to “Polk Salad Annie” and laughing.

When Lee gets back to the van, his dad has passed away, and the immensity of it is too much for his body to bear. He finds himself sitting on the sill of the passenger side, absorbing the loss of a father who was never around anyway. A man he thought he knew better than he ever did.

Other stuff happens in “Leaving and Coming Back,” all of it prior to Lee and Frog’s road trip. Judge Jed, currently running for reelection under the banner “Vote for Family,” chastises Vela for arresting the governor’s close, personal journalist friend, then assures the sheriff that he’s seduced Lee into submission. Not one to be cowed, Vela issues a warning of her own: Her and Bobby’s cut of the Fresh Start profits is starting to look pretty meager compared to what Jed is pulling in.

It’s no idle threat. We learn in this episode that without the cooperation of Vela and her cousin, Johnny McMann, Fresh Start couldn’t operate. See, when Jed told Lee that the prison diversion program didn’t employ guards, he was telling a half-truth. He doesn’t need to employ guards because, with the help of McMann, he’s been able to borrow violent offenders from Boontill who do the work for free. That’s what Mekko was doing at Fresh Start, at least according to spineless Lonnie, who Ginger is able to flip from her kidnapper to her co-conspirator over the course of a three-minute conversation.

Convinced that Vela and McMann will eventually turn on him, Lonnie helps Ginger escape from McMann’s cabin, where she’s been held for the last few hours since they abducted her. Lonnie accidentally hits McMann with his car as they flee, which should give the pair a decent head start. We don’t find out where Lonnie runs to, but Ginger heads to Lee’s place, where she feels safe enough to break down. She thought she knew Mekko, but according to McMann, Mekko showed the prison guard her sexts. According to Lonnie, the client she risked her career to be with is the same man who murdered Nathan Spence. Understandably, Ginger feels like a fool.

But Lee is there for her. He’s actually really good at making people feel safe. Heard. You can’t be embarrassed in front of Lee. You can’t make a mistake that he can’t top. After Ginger showers off the aroma of Vienna sausages, which is McMann’s signature scent, Lee breaks them into Sweet Emily’s in the middle of the night, where they raid the whiskey. They’re drinking to get drunk enough to make the “bad” decision they already want to make. Lee has been calling Ginger his girlfriend despite the fact they’ve barely touched. Ginger is eager to admit she’s into this kind and reckless man-child who uses sheets for window blinds, keeps a garden of empty liquor bottles, and likes the smell of his own toe jam.

After a few shots, they hook up at the Sweet Emily’s soda fountain, or maybe they do it in one of the booths; we can’t be sure. Ginger must leave in the night, but Lee is still asleep on the floor when Western comes in to open the diner. In fact, Lee’s on his walk of shame home from Sweet Emily’s when he runs into Frog, who asks him to take him to the storage unit. There’s something in there that he wants to give Francis for her birthday, and he needs his son’s help.

We never quite see the birthday present. It looks like a small wooden box, which Frog pops into the chest pocket of his Grandpa shirt. Presumably, it’s still in his pocket as Lee drives his dad’s body back to Tulsa. As he sits behind the wheel, “Oo-De-Lally” from Disney’s Robin Hood plays, a jaunty sing-along song that undercuts and enhances the gravity of what’s happened. Frog stole from the rich, but did he ever give to the poor? Across his life, he was a fake preacher, a cartoon hero, a Peter Pan dad. Born and raised in Oklahoma, Frog (maybe) ran away from home at an early age and (maybe) spent his teenage years in Mexico, working odd jobs. He answered the call to serve his country, including a deployment in Vietnam. After returning home, Frog started a family and moved to the city. He was always leaving and coming back, which he attributed to his fundamental nature.

Lee “Frog” Raybon Sr. was preceded in death by his wife, Helen Francis Raybon. He is survived by an adoring granddaughter (Francis), a befuddled son (Lee Jr.), and a rich legacy comprised of outrageous lies and true stories so wild they sound like lies.

items.title: Survivor Recap: It Takes Two
items.description: I know I do a lot of bitching about the New Era of Survivor (honestly, seven tenths of these recaps are just dick jokes and vitriol), but if we’re going to take one thing with us into the Open Era, I think it might be voting out a pair. It’s an innovation I do
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I know I do a lot of bitching about the New Era of Survivor (honestly, seven tenths of these recaps are just dick jokes and vitriol), but if we’re going to take one thing with us into the Open Era, I think it might be voting out a pair. It’s an innovation I don’t hate, but that mostly has to do with how this chaos-prone group of contestants decided to play the game. Yes, this episode convinced me. Let’s put one in the win column for Jeffrey Lee Probst.

The beginning of the episode expertly sets up everything about to happen, starting with everyone hating on Mike, a tray of sliced turkey club wraps at a shareholders’ meeting that no one ever bothers to take the cover off of. He sits down with Maggie and tells her the reason he flipped the vote to Brady last episode was that he was last in on the plan to get rid of Kristin, like he’s last in on every vote. She tells him exactly what he needs to hear, “If I was the last person to get information, maybe you should ask yourself why people don’t trust you.” Okay. Great. Now he knows. But what is he going to do about it?

The other consequential thing is Carter’s Salty and Sweet Alliance. He’s sick of all the plans going totally haywire, and he wants a group that is going to stick to a plan no matter what. Dude, don’t you realize you’re in the Open Era where Jeff’s motto is “No Fear!” Wait, that’s the wrong bumper sticker. Don’t you know his motto is, “[Calvin pissing on a Chevy logo.]” Nope, also the wrong sticker. Don’t you know his motto is “permanent uncertainty”? How are you going to stick to plans when everything is uncertain? Anyway, he gets together Kilby, Lewis, Cristian, Maggie, and Thien An and calls it the Salt Alliance because his favorite movie is the 2010 Angelina Jolie action-mystery film, Salt. No, it’s because they’re supposed to be the salt of the earth or something. To solidify this alliance with Cristian, he shows off his hidden immunity idol that he inherited from Rob, who quit on day six because he only got on the show so that his wife would be cast on The Real Housewives of Rhode Island.

As soon as the salt is on the pretzel, they get all twisted up. Everyone is going to be competing in pairs in the next immunity challenge. Yeah, how is that sticking to the plan? What I like about this is that they allow the players to decide what the pairs are going to be and don’t leave it up to chance. They are all unsure whether the pair will be voted out or will be fighting against each other, so they take a very interesting approach to forming the groups. Mike chooses Maggie, thinking that she’s well connected, so if they’re sending the group home, he might get spared because people don’t want to oust her. Carter and Cristian pair up because no one knows they’re working together. Devin and Jelly are bound together by a curse as ancient as the whale immunity idol that they dug up from the seabed. But other than them, most of the other pairs are unlikely and spread across alliances. Kilby and Kristin get together, as do Eric and Thien An and Lewis and Sharonda.

They get to the challenge, and Jeff shares some news. Our Brody Brady decided that he wanted to go home to tend to his thumb (which he partially cut off opening coconuts) and will no longer be on the jury. Are we sure that’s why? I don’t know; this whole stunt smells like the potent cologne of sour grapes. It’s like earlier this season when Jonathan had to leave because he had an owie. I would assume our Brody Brady is not used to losing and was like, “Brody. If this Brody can’t be the $1 million Brody, then this Brody is going home to Brody hospital to get his Brody thumb Brodied back onto his Brody body Brody. I mean, fuck this game, Brody. Don’t they know that I’m Brady the Brody?” And then they put him in the back of a van and drove him to the airport, where he just unceasingly said, “Brody” in different inflections for the entire ride.

Jeff tells everyone that they will be competing in pairs, winning immunity in pairs, and that a pair of players will be going home; however, everyone will be voting as individuals. He also says that immunity idols or other advantages, like Shots in the Dark, if played for one player, work on the whole pair, ensuring both players’ safety.

The challenge happens in three phases, with a pair of two being eliminated at each leg. The first challenge is to stand there and endure Eric’s incessant chattering about The Sopranos, spaghetti (which is the reward), and his fiancé the longest. At one point, Carter even says, “Can we focus up down there?” Kristin and Kilby are eliminated first, along with Maggie and Mike. There is also an advantage for the second part of the challenge for the people who listen to Eric the longest. (JK. They have to balance a ball on a plank.) Lewis and Sharonda make the only smart decision and throw the rest of the challenge, figuring that the energy they save by stepping down is better than whatever they might get from the advantage. This ends up being wise because, just as Carter and Cristian are about to win the whole damn thing by stacking a bunch of puzzle pieces, their stack falls to the ground, opening the door for Lewis and Sharonda to win. See, maybe if they didn’t stay listening to Eric for as long as they did, they might have come through when they needed it.

As they’re getting their necklaces from Jeff, Lewis tells Sharonda that he saw fire in her on day one, and when she was eliminated first in last week’s challenge, he knew that fire was back. Is this an unlikely alliance that is going to grow legs? I sure hope so, particularly because Sharonda has quite the week, as we’ll get to in a minute.

Lewis and Sharonda also have to send someone on a journey, and they choose Cristian. When the boat lands in the middle of the ocean, Cristian reads that he lost his vote, and if he gets a clue on the island, he might win it back but also win an extra vote for tonight. At first it doesn’t really make sense, but then he cuts a rope and a trough full of buoys empties out into the ocean. He soon realizes that some of them have letters on them and collects them all up to figure out what they say: “Dig Under Treemail.” He then leaves all the buoys and goes back to camp. Cristian comes back, tells everyone the truth, goes and digs up his vote and extra vote, with Mike watching over him like the corporate overlord he is.

Now the castaways have to select a pair who is going home, and this is where some deft selection comes into play. Everyone is tired of Mike for never saying anything of note and Eric for chattering more than a set of dentures on a roller coaster. However, no one wants Maggie or Thien An to go home, so both of those pairs are out, as are Lewis and Sharonda, who are immune, leaving only Carter and Cristian, Devin and Jelly, or Kilby and Kristen. Carter is whipping votes against Devin and Jelly for obvious reasons: they’re a close duo who everyone knows is working together. As Jelly accurately points out at tribal, it’s not like they win challenges or have lots of influence; it’s just that they’re clearly besties. Also, if Carter can get rid of both of them, then the Salt fan club has the majority and can coast the rest of the game. Devin and Jelly are going for Carter and Cristian, saying they’re both players no one has a problem with, and that is dangerous. When Carter hears this, he sits down with them and says that the vote is Kristin and they should just go for her. Jelly loves this idea because it means she can hold on to her extra vote and her idol for another week.

This is where our girl Sharonda comes in. She’s sitting down with Thien An and says, “We never talk game, but who are you voting for?” T&A Music Factory tells her Devin and Jelly. Sharonda has been working with both of them; she knows about Jelly’s idol, and she is skeptical of this plan. She doesn’t rat it out, but she tells Devin, “You need to come up with a game plan.” She asks Jelly who she is voting for, and Jelly tells her that everyone told her to vote for Kristin. Sharonda tells her, “That’s just a smoke screen.” This is what we would call on Real Housewives a “sniper from the side.” Sharonda is not trying to get into the mess, but she is trying to use a bit of influence to make sure exactly what she wants to happen happens. As we’re leaving camp for Tribal Council, the edit sets it up as Carter and Cristian versus Devin and Jelly, and whoever plays their idol is going to win.

At Tribal, it’s another live one with lots of whispers and gossiping and everyone not being sure what the plan is and who they can rely on. I usually hate a live tribal, but I’m kind of loving the vibes this season. Is it casting? Did they make this happen by getting us a bunch of nutcases who don’t know what they’re doing? Or is this Jeff’s “No Fear Chevy Peeing Constant Uncertainty” actually doing what it’s supposed to be doing? At one point, as everyone is chattering, he asks Maggie if she even hears the whispers anymore because they’re so constant. She’s basically like, “Jeff, STFU. I can’t hear the 14 different conversations happening around me.” The only thing of consequence that happens is that Christian goes to Eric and gives him his extra vote, saying he loses it if he uses his SITD and wants Eric to play it for Devin and Jelly.

The players are ready to vote, and Kilby, as he has at every Tribal, runs up to the voting booth with his arms outstretched like he’s just been cursed by the witch in Weapons. When Eric votes, he says that he knows this vote expires tonight, but they should have enough of a majority that he doesn’t need to use it. Dude! What is wrong with you? Use it! It’s like if you have a bunch of brown bananas on the counter that you know are going bad, do you just throw them away or do you make banana bread? You get out the walnuts, the chocolate chips, the Pam spray, and you Betty that M-er F-er Crocker. Why let a vote go to waste?

Before Jeff can tally the votes, a lot of advantages have to be played. Kristin tries her SITD, and it comes up “Not Safe.” Cristian was being paranoid all afternoon, and I was readying my whole monologue about how SITD is stupid, and he shouldn’t even think about it or waste his time going for it, and then it comes up SAFE, and he and Carter are protected. Monologue cancelled, I guess. Then Jelly plays her idol to everyone’s surprise, and it is on like Brody Kong. (That is the video game Brady played on the plane ride home while he sulked.)

Every vote comes up Devin and Jelly until the very end, with Jelly even cackling, “You tried it,” as Jeff keeps saying the votes don’t count. There is one vote for Carter and Cristian that also doesn’t count, and one vote left. It’s Kilby and Kristin, and that’s what Kilby gets for being possessed by a witch. We lose two excellent characters and one great player (no, Kilby, it’s not you) in one fell swoop. I feel kind of bad for them, but all in all it is an excellent episode, and that is much more important than keeping either of them around. As we watch the votes during the credits, a few things become clear: Sharonda, still sniping from the side, voted for Devin and Jelly just so she’d be in the majority in case Jelly was too stupid to play her idol. She got what she wanted and is still undercover. Also, Devin and Jelly were smart enough to split their votes in case one of the other pairs had some kind of advantage, which is exactly what happened, making sure that they were the ones choosing who went home no matter the outcome. A fantastic outcome for fans and a great night for the helicopter alliance, which is currently flying high over the rest of the competition.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City Recap: Swimming With the Sharks
items.description: If you thought last week’s exchange between Angie and Mary was painful, buckle up, because this show isn’t giving us a reprieve just yet. This week’s episode kicks off with yet another scene uncomfortable enough to make you crawl out of your skin, in which Bro
items.author: Tom Smyth
paragraphs: If you thought last week’s exchange between Angie and Mary was painful, buckle up, because this show isn’t giving us a reprieve just yet. This week’s episode kicks off with yet another scene uncomfortable enough to make you crawl out of your skin, in which Bronwyn introduces her fetal boyfriend, Brandon, to her mother, Muzzy, who has no interest in this sit-down whatsoever. And being that she’s Muzzy, she says that outright. Do you think if we banded together, there could be a class action lawsuit against Bravo for emotional distress for making us bear witness to this?

In all honesty, at the beginning of the season, when Muzzy seemed to be changing her ways after dealing with all the backlash she got as last season aired, I sympathized with her, because the ire of the Bravo fandom is no easy burden to bear. But this scene was a great reminder that she is, in fact, a nightmare. Before Brandon even arrives, she’s chiding him and expressing her disdain to Bronwyn at even having to meet him, and things only get worse when he gets there. Somehow she finds a way to blame him for the bad weather, tells him outright that she’s not happy about their relationship because she liked Todd (probably because they could reminisce together about FDR’s fireside chats), and says that she’s only there because she has to give him a chance in order to have a relationship with her daughter. Kudos to Brandon, because I would never be able to forgive or date anybody who would make me spend a single minute with this woman.

And why is this even happening so soon to begin with? Bronwyn notes that her daughter, Gwen, who apparently is the only sensible person in the family, said she won’t meet him until they’ve been dating for at least six months — so why rush to throw Muzzy into the mix? Well, Bronwyn notes in her confessional that she almost wishes the other women were there to see this because it would prove this wasn’t a publicity stunt. Ah, there’s our answer. This cursed meeting is a rebuttal to the PR relationship claims, but doing it on-camera kind of undoes the intended purpose and makes the whole thing seem even more fake. And speaking of falsities, as they leave, Brandon says to Muzzy, “You are such a joy; you are a fun time.” A damning lie that could only have been solicited via a hearty check or Zelle.

Meanwhile, Whitney and Justin have yet another sit-down about the state of their relationship without any real answers. Whitney says that sleeping apart has been an improvement but is still confused as to where she stands with the relationship, whereas Justin is simply standing by, waiting for a verdict. He says he’s very patient, but eventually needs her to make a decision because until then he’s just stuck in this odd marriage limbo. It’s not typical to see a marriage devolve like this on these shows, where there’s no one inciting event or tangible thing to point to, because as far as we’ve been able to tell, things between them are fine. We’re not seeing fighting or infidelity, or even Beador-esque tension. But the dissolution of a relationship doesn’t always come with all of that, and it’s compelling watching Whitney have to navigate and explain the intangible like this — all while planning a shark-themed Sweet Sixteen for her daughter.

Finally, we get to check in with Angie after last week’s blowup. She’s at the park with Heather and Lisa (who remain my favorite duo on this show, may the Good Weather never stop), and they’re both eager to chat with her now that the dust has settled and Angie has been able to process exactly how that fight played out.

“I said something that I will never be able to take back,” she says. “I regret it; I will never forgive myself, and Mary may never forgive me.” She admits to them that she’s been a ticking time bomb, and she now realizes that if she had been acknowledging her feelings rather than burying them, explosions like that wouldn’t have been happening. That was clearly Angie’s big error going into this season; she was hiding the diagnosis (her marital problems) while the symptoms were still on full display, and she repressed those emotions until they were uncontrollable. Learning from that, she’s now telling Lisa about her troubles with Shawn, and Lisa turns out to be the perfect person to confide in because she went through the same thing with John last season, and they ended up bouncing back. It’s not a guarantee that Angie and Shawn will, too, but Lisa is at least proof of that being a possibility.

As for Mary, Angie reached out to apologize, but she’s not responding, which doesn’t come as any big surprise. Mary will cut someone off for life over something as minor as stealing some flowers, so naturally something as big as this is going to be tough — if not impossible — to bounce back from. While Mary naturally deserves all the grace in the world this season, she hasn’t historically been a kind friend to Angie even in the best of times, so at this point I wouldn’t actually mind seeing Angie finally be freed from this roller coaster. They’ve long had this Gretchen Wieners and Regina George dynamic that can’t possibly be healthy for Angie.

We get to hear more from Mary at the tasting Meredith is throwing for her new lounge space, which looks like a desolate parking garage or a parody of an art gallery. If Meredith Marks invited me to an address and I showed up to that abandoned warehouse, I’d be certain she was going to kill me. I spent the entire event waiting for her to press a trap door button or shout, “Release the hounds.” But alas, it was just for caviar, and the event space will be named Perhaps, not to be confused with Premiere, which is Lisa’s event space across the street. All of the other women correctly point out that if this were anybody besides the two of them, these dueling lounges would result in a bloodbath.

Mary says that while she didn’t initially plan to do so, she ended up telling Robert Sr. — her step-grandfather and husband — about what Angie said, and naturally he didn’t take it well. The other women ask if she’s reached out, but Mary says she doesn’t know because she blocked her, which is a great representation of how Mary handles conflict with even the people closest to her. She also says that a big problem was that Angie didn’t realize what she said in the moment after she said it, which is a little confusing, because we did see Angie try to apologize right then and there, but Mary rebuffed it and stormed off. But the most shocking development is Mary saying that she’s now in a space to hear her apology, as long as it’s on her terms and face-to-face.

Quai has to leave early to head over to Bobbie’s birthday party, offending Meredith, who is apparently willing to have beef with a 16-year-old now, but who can blame Quai? Bobbie’s shark party is way cooler … and actually a party. Angie has an awkward encounter with Bronwyn there, but they both agree that it isn’t the time or place to hash things out. Something I do find promising is that Bronwyn isn’t reveling in or stoking the flames of Angie’s problems with Mary, but rather hopes to see the situation resolve. But speaking of awkward encounters, when Angie and Heather are chatting with and complimenting Justin, Angie jokes that he should call them up “if your wife ever dumps ya.” Heather recoils, since she’s the only one who knows that is exactly what’s happening.

Finally, Bobbie arrives, and they all surprise her before Whitney and Justin gift her with a brand-new car. But I don’t get any enjoyment from seeing children be surprised with cars in this (or any) economy, even children who seem totally great like Bobbie. The one exception to this is, of course, when Vicki Gunvalson surprised her daughter Briana with a car and excitedly told her that Briana was the one who was going to be making the payments. That is where this trope peaked, and we can leave it there.

The one positive of these two dueling events is having Quai zip between them like a carrier pigeon and filling in Angie about the conversation that happened over in Meredith’s abandoned garage turned lounge. She tells them all that Mary told Robert Sr. about the comments, that she blocked Angie and thus hasn’t received the apology, and that she rebuffed the suggestion that Angie loves her. The latter is what hurts Angie the most, but the good news comes when Quai informs her that she’s willing to hear her out in person. Normally, Mary is such a stone wall that it wouldn’t have been surprising if we never saw the two of them in the same room ever again, so this points to the potential of rebuilding some kind of connection. Now we just need to get Britani back into the mix.

items.title: Hollywood Still Faces Weekend Disruptions After FAA Lifts Flight Ground Stop
items.description: UPDATED: In the wake of a four-hour long flight ground stop, Hollywood can still expect a weekend of disruptions after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the shutdown Friday evening. Travel plans were thrown into question for talent, executives and buy
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: UPDATED: In the wake of a four-hour long flight ground stop, Hollywood can still expect a weekend of disruptions after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the shutdown Friday evening. Travel plans were thrown into question for talent, executives and buyers headed to and from Los Angeles and New York during one of the busiest stretches on the industry calendar.

The FAA says it grounded flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It marks the most extensive disruption to air travel in the U.S. since the federal government mandated a total shutdown of all activity after the 9/11 attacks in September 2001. Some flights resumed immediately, but hundreds of others were canceled while travelers scrambled to make new plans.

From the Motion Picture Academy’s Governors Awards to an array of premieres, screenings, concerts, among myriad other events, Hollywood’s plans as film award season kicks in to high gear were thrown into total disarray. The same is true for innumerable professional and college football and basketball games. CNN estimated that some 1.5 million travelers were left stranded in airports, on runways or on trips that inevitably had to be extended amid the ground stop.

The cause is not yet clear, but an FAA spokesperson says a communications problem affected the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle flights moving across the country. Preliminary reports indicate it is not a cyberattack, according to law enforcement officials and media outlets. The rare ground stop, which was announced just after 1 p.m. PT, led to more than 7,800 flights across the U.S. being delayed by Friday evening, according to the air travel tracking service FlightAware.

On Sunday, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences is set to hold its 17th Governors Awards at the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood, where honorary Oscars go to eight-time nominee Glenn Close, legendary Director Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman, Disney’s first Black animator. Killer Films producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, longtime champions of independent film, receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award.

The evening doubles as one of the season’s most important campaign stops, with contenders working a room filled with the Academy’s governors, three from each of its 19 branches, representing everyone from actors and directors to artisans and executives.
Variety has reached out to the Academy for comment.

The grounding will also affect buyers and sellers at the final days of the American Film Market, which runs Nov. 10-15 at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Century City. With international sales agents, buyers and financiers due to fly home this weekend, many of them could find themselves stuck in Los Angeles.
Numerous FYC events are also taking place around Los Angeles, with awards contenders frequently criss-crossing the country during the busy pre-Thanksgiving period.

On Saturday, Netflix will host the official Academy screening for AMPAS members for David Fincher’s highly anticipated “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” written by Quentin Tarantino, in which Brad Pitt reprises his Oscar-winning role from “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood” (2019). The

items.title: AFM Dealmakers, Talent Agents and Hollywood Stars Left Stranded by Nationwide Flight Stoppage
items.description: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a halt on all U.S. flights on Friday at around 1 p.m. PT and didn’t lift the order until approximately four hours later. With the American Film Market, the Governors Awards and numerous FYC panels scheduled over the n
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a halt on all U.S. flights on Friday at around 1 p.m. PT and didn’t lift the order until approximately four hours later. With the American Film Market, the Governors Awards and numerous FYC panels scheduled over the next several days, the stoppage left many Hollywood insiders grounded on one of the busiest travel weekends of the year.

AFM was hit hard by the standstill, and several events were canceled as dealmakers were preparing for their final days at the major sales function. Ryan Werner, president of global cinema at Neon, told Variety he was unsure if he could make it to AFM on Saturday for the studio’s party. He mentioned “our flights” when referring to travel plans, likely meaning several members of the Neon team were shut down on the way to Los Angeles.

One agency source told Variety that when the FAA shut down travel, their department broke out in a panic to see if anyone could still make their scheduled appearances at Saturday’s Governors Awards, which take place at the Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood.

“Once the news happened, everyone jumped on the phone to see if anyone is going to be able to make it to L.A. for the Governors Awards,” they said. “One agent has a client traveling through Europe with no idea how he will get back for his next things in the U.S., so they might have to hang out in Canada to at least be close.”

TMZ reported that “Baywatch” star Brooks Nader’s private jet was stopped in New York just before taking off for Louisiana. The outlet also shared a video of “Bachelorette” star Kaitlyn Bristowe stuck in an airport. Flava Flav and Morgan Fairchild both took to social media to share that their travel plans were affected. Variety also confirmed that the Sharpe Family Singers and actor Isaac Robinson Smith were all left stuck at the airport.

News of the flight stoppage broke around 1 p.m. PT. At the time, the FAA said the pause was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin later appeared on Fox News and clarified that it was a “telecommunications outage” that caused the backup and that there was no indication of a “nefarious attack” against the United States.
The FAA announced around 6 p.m. PT that the nationwide ground stoppage was canceled.

items.title: Amid Flight Halt, Trump Meets With Jon Voight to Talk U.S. Film Incentive: ‘Get This Done!’
items.description: As flights across the U.S. came to a halt Friday amid a rare nationwide ground stop, President Donald Trump was in a meeting with actor Jon Voight to talk about jumpstarting support for a federal film incentive.
items.author: Gene Maddaus; Pat Saperstein
paragraphs: As flights across the U.S. came to a halt Friday amid a rare nationwide ground stop, President Donald Trump was in a meeting with actor Jon Voight to talk about jumpstarting support for a federal film incentive.
Voight and his team, Steven Paul and Scott Karol, were at the White House to urge the president to push for the film incentive during the lame duck session of Congress.

“It was exciting to watch,” Karol told Variety, saying the president was getting updates on the flight situation and also the capsized boat in New Orleans. “He’s concerned with different things because he’s the president. He gave us attention while taking care of two emergencies.”
Voight made an impassioned speech in support of the Hollywood tax incentive bill, which would provide a 20%-30% rebate on domestic labor costs for films and TV shows.
“He was telling (Trump) he has a helpful heart and he feels this can get done,” Paul said. Voight “was great. He was crying by the end of the meeting. It was an Academy Award-winning speech.”
While Voight was still in the room, the president sent out a Truth Social post reaffirming his support for the federal incentive and urging Congress to pass it.

“Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE!” Trump wrote. “It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation.”

He also noted that he was working with Sen. Adam Schiff — “believe it or not.” Karol said the team had met with Schiff earlier in the day, and Schiff told them to tell Trump: “This is Tim Scott’s bill and I’m there to help.”
Schiff responded to Trump’s post on X, saying that the bill should not wait until the Democrats take over in January.
“President Trump and I agree: it’s time for Congress to pass a federal film incentive,” Schiff wrote.
Rep. Laura Friedman, a Democratic co-author, also responded, saying “there’s no excuse to wait.”
“A national film and TV incentive means jobs in California, Georgia, New York, New Jersey and every state across the country,” she wrote. “Let’s get it done.”

Karol said that the challenge is finding a legislative vehicle, in which to include the incentive bill. He said that momentum has not slowed since the Republicans’ defeat in last week’s midterm elections.
“There’s good energy on both sides,” he said. “There’s no indication from either side of the aisle that this is something that is not as important as it was before the election.”

Earlier on Friday, Politico published an article saying “Hollywood’s tax credit push runs into a post-midterm wall.” The story quoted Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., as saying chances were “pretty low” of passing any tax bill during the lame duck session.

Supporters of the incentive hope that Trump’s post will encourage lawmakers to make it a priority. Voight has served as Trump’s ambassador to Hollywood, and has met with the president several times to encourage him to back the tax credit. Those meetings paid off in August, when the president first endorsed the measure, leading to the introduction of the bill on a bipartisan basis in September.

Trump’s comment on the film incentive preceded any public statement on the nationwide ground stop. Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security, did address the public after the ground stop was called, telling the nation, “This isn’t another 9/11. This is a telecommunication outage.”
Read Trump’s Truth Social post below:

“I am working with Senator Tim Scott and, believe it or not, Senator Adam Schiff, and, additionally, Senators John Cornyn, Raphael Warnock, Steve Daines, Bernie Moreno, Tim Sheehy, Alex Padilla, Mark Warner, Thom Tillis, Chris Coons, Katie Britt, and Dick Durbin, together with Representatives Jason Smith, Nathaniel Moran, Brian Jack, Linda Sanchez, and many others, both Republican and Democrat, on the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act. The support and popularity of doing this, and bringing Entertainment back to the United States of America, has been unbelievable! Hollywood, and so many other places, have been virtually ’emptied out’ by the Tax Incentives, and much more, given by other Countries. Everyone feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry — and so do I, and we all want to save it. It was MADE IN AMERICA, and must STAY IN AMERICA. The Entertainment Industry has largely moved to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries, but the actors, producers, and all others involved want to come back home! Importantly, hundreds of thousands of Blue Collar Workers will be positively affected, BIG TIME, by the passage of this Bill. The amount of money spent on these Tax Incentives will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers. Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE! It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation. It can be done quickly, accurately, efficiently and, importantly, will benefit all of America. MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP”
Updated with remarks from Karol and Paul.

items.title: Margot Robbie to Star in A24’s ‘The Week of Pain’ From ‘The Drama’ Director Kristoffer Borgli
items.description: Margot Robbie will star in A24 and Square Peg’s “The Week of Pain” from “The Drama” writer-director Kristoffer Borgli, Variety has confirmed. A24 is set to produce and finance the project. Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg banner will also produce alongs
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: Margot Robbie will star in A24 and Square Peg’s “The Week of Pain” from “The Drama” writer-director Kristoffer Borgli, Variety has confirmed. A24 is set to produce and finance the project. Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg banner will also produce alongside Dilemma Films and Robbie’s LuckyChap.

Plot details for “The Week of Pain” remain under wraps, but considering Borgli’s previous works, which include “Dream Scenario” and “Sick of Myself,” it’s safe to assume it will be another squirmy drama with streaks of cringe-out humor. Square Peg and A24 recently collaborated with Borgli on April’s “The Drama,” which starred Robert Pattinson and Zendaya. The film, an intimate original dramedy about a wedding week derailed by a childhood secret, was a box office smash, grossing $135 million worldwide against a slim $28 million budget.

Robbie most recently appeared in the steamy literary romance “Wuthering Heights” for Warner Bros. Audiences couldn’t resist a big-screen affair between the “Barbie” superstar as Cathy and Jacob Elordi as her mysterious love interest, Heathcliff, and the film rocketed to $241 million worldwide. Coming up for Robbie is an “Ocean’s 11” prequel. She will star alongside Bradley Cooper, who is also directing, presumably as the mom and dad of George Clooney’s Danny Ocean. Robbie revealed at CinemaCon 2026 that the film will follow an “epic heist at the 1962 Monaco Grand Prix.” Clooney, in a completely separate sequel, is getting the band back together from the 2001 original for one last ride.
Robbie is represented by Entertainment 360, CAA, Narrative, Aran Michael Management and attorney Jeff Bernstein. Borgli is repped by UTA.

items.title: ‘The Bachelor’ Casts NFL Quarterback Sam Hartman as Season 30 Star
items.description: After two years off the air, “The Bachelor” is returning for its 30th season with a brand new face: NFL player Sam Hartman will be looking for love on the iconic ABC reality dating series beginning on March 21.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: After two years off the air, “The Bachelor” is returning for its 30th season with a brand new face: NFL player Sam Hartman will be looking for love on the iconic ABC reality dating series beginning on March 21.

Hartman is a quarterback for the Washington Commanders, who is also an alumnus of the Wake Forest and Notre Dame football teams, where he set the Atlantic Coast Conference records for most career touchdown passes and 300-yard passing games. He also made an appearance in Season 2 of the Netflix docuseries “QB1: Beyond the Lights.” Hartman is originally from Charlotte, N.C.

Hartman’s casting marks something of a relaunch for the “Bachelor” franchise. When Season 30 premieres, it will have been two years since the last iteration of the flagship series, which starred Grant Ellis, and once year since the failed return of “The Bachelorette,” which was pulled from the air last-minute amid a domestic violence scandal between star Taylor Frankie Paul and her ex-boyfriend, Dakota Mortensen. The most recent entry into the franchise was “Bachelor in Paradise” Season 10, which aired in the summer of 2025.

Also of note for “Bachelor” fans is the return of another scandal-wracked personality: Chris Harrison, who hosted all versions of “The Bachelor” until 2021, when he received major backlash for defending former contestant Rachel Kirkconnell from allegations of racism surrounding an antebellum plantation-themed party she had attended in the past. Harrison is now hosting a new dating series called “The Vow,” which follows contestants seeking a “traditional marriage,” on Fox Nation.
“The Bachelor” is produced by Warner Horizon Unscripted Television. Executive producers include Scott Teti, Jason Ehrlich and Andy Frank.
