items.title: Get to Know the Watchmaker Behind John Mayer’s Latest Pick-Up
items.description: When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help establish new indies. This week, Mayer is co-signing a hyper-limited-edition piece from FVF Genève, a watchmaker you should get to know.

FVF Genève is the brainchild of Spanish-born, Geneva-based watchmaker Franc Vila. Mayer is wearing his latest release: FVF2 Time & Day “Happy Monday,” made in partnership with American watch and jewelry retailer Material Good. On his Instagram, Mayer referred to the collaborators as a “Trifecta of Greatness.” There’s more to this piece than its mesmerizing mother-of-pearl, though. The watch’s design celebrates the idea that, if you love what you do, Monday mornings are actually something to look forward to.

The “Happy Monday” is a limited edition of seven pieces, each of which is engraved with a different day of the week on its rotor. The design is a reminder, as the brand says, that “each day is an opportunity to embrace our calling.” It helps, of course, that this message is delivered by a truly beautiful movement with black-polished surfaces, plenty of beveling and polishing, and great typography. Then there’s the rad day-of-the-week indicator on the dial. Situated between 6 and 9 o’clock, it takes the shape of a subtle gold track with a letter for each day of the week in French. To go with the “Happy Monday” theme, “Lundi” (Monday in French) is the only day represented by a standout green letter.

The dial is the showstopping element on this piece. It’s executed in a sparkly deep-blue mother-of-pearl and accented with thick gold-tone printing in the form of an outer minute track, a sub-seconds display between 4 and 5 o’clock, and bisecting lines that create a classically inspired “sector” design. The interplay of the sector when combined with mother-of-pearl is unusual enough, but add in the retrograde day-of-the-week indicator, and you’ve got a truly compelling combo.

The watch’s 39.5mm case is made out of Grade 5 titanium and features a Titalyt treatment—an electrochemical surface treatment that creates a ceramic-like layer and increases durability and hardness. F.P. Journe is a big fan of this treatment, and FVF uses it to great effect here. The finishing gives the Happy Monday a dark, industrial aesthetic that plays off the mother-of-pearl and gold tones on the dial for a distinctive feel. The watch comes on a matching beads-of-rice bracelet with straight endlinks, further adding to the interplay between vintage and modern inspiration. Finally, the crown and date corrector are located on the left side of the case rather than the right, where they typically sit.

Limited to just seven pieces—not including a unique piece that went to Material Good’s Yoni Ben-Yehuda—the $125,000 Happy Monday is the latest independent watch to receive a co-sign from super-collector John Mayer. Despite his role as Audemars Piguet's “Creative Conduit," Mayer has been known to support high-end independent makers such as F.P. Journe, and famously helped propel Vanguart onto the horological stage over the past year.

Vila, who established his eponymous luxury watch brand in the early 2000s, is a prime candidate to receive his flowers from the modern collecting community: marrying avant-garde case and dial designs with high complications. Vila sold his initial brand in the late 2000s, but he’s now having another go at creating modern classics with FVF. He’s come at the right time. It’s boom times for independent watchmakers as collectors try to identify the next big thing, and a co-sign from Mayer makes FVF a strong candidate to catch fire.

items.title: Inside the First Competition Between Historic Vintage Timepieces
items.description: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

In the automotive world, high-end cars have gone head-to-head since the early 1920s. Judges didn’t evaluate them based on their speed, though—in a Concours d’Élégance, the prize goes to the best-looking vehicles. The tradition continues today in picturesque sites around the world where collectors submit their often very high-end vintage, classic cars. Surprisingly, there has never been an event for vintage timepieces.

Aurel Bacs, the famous auctioneer whose longstanding association with Phillips has shaped the watch collecting world, endeavored to change that. “It began with a meeting where I said, ‘I have a dream,’” he said in a press release. For the very first iteration of this competition, Bacs and Phillips partnered with Swiss heavyweight Vacheron Constantin. They expected to receive maybe 100 to 200 submissions, but the jury was forced to whittle down 550 of them to 34 finalist watches, whose owners were flown out from across the world for the Concours held at the Hôtel Président in Geneva.

“It was the most beautiful evening in the field ever,” Bacs said. At the Hôtel Président, around 200 attendees gathered, along with a jury of 14 watch-industry experts including Bacs himself, Ben Clymer of Hodinkee, writer and historian Nick Foulkes, longtime watch journalist Roberta Naas, and others. Watches could only be submitted for consideration in one category (Chronographs, Métiers d’Art, Chronomètre Royal, Astronomical Complications, Multiple Complications, Design, and Chiming Mechanisms) and were judged based on nine criteria: authenticity, elegance, rarity, impact on the history of Vacheron Constantin and/or on watchmaking in general, provenance, technicality, métiers d’art (artistic crafts), state of preservation, and emotional dimension.

The jurors deliberated over several hours until the winners of the seven categories and a Best of Show were finally selected. Following a cocktail reception, everyone gathered on the lower floor of the Hôtel Président to see the results from the watch world’s first Concours d'Élégance.

The first category featured a smattering of some of the maison’s most important wristwatches, including a highly rare ref. 4072 in stainless steel from 1940. However, it was a yellow gold pocket-watch chronograph from 1929 that won the day. The result was such a surprise that the audience, intimately familiar with the historical importance of pocket watches, audibly gasped inside the room. It made me wonder if these old-fashioned timepieces could regain their lost position as the pinnacle of watch collecting. This piece certainly warranted the love it received: in excellent condition and featuring a white enamel dial with dual registers in an “up-down” configuration, it’s a beautiful timepiece.

This category celebrates handcrafts such as enameling and gem-setting, and it featured a smattering of truly spectacular pieces—mostly sub-40mm wristwatches in precious metals with wild cloisonné or Grand Feu champlevé enamel dials depicting landmasses or animals.
However, a stunning pocket watch set with blue sapphires throughout the bezel and Roman indices won out.

When an older American gentleman stepped on stage to collect his prize, he explained to a stunned crowd that not only had his great-grandfather, Dr. Otto von Frangeš, been given the watch by His Majesty Alexander I of Yugoslavia, its original owner, but that he wore it while sitting in the motorcade during the king’s assassination in France in 1934. Otto’s middle son, Nikola, eventually smuggled the watch out of Yugoslavia by sewing it into the lining of his wife’s jacket as they fled the Iron Curtain in the late 1940s.

In 1907, Vacheron launched the Chronomètre Royal sub-brand, specifically built to endure a life sailing the seas. The model’s parts were anti-magnetic and resisted rusting. The dials were made out of enamel, which could also stand up to the moist atmosphere without rusting. Because they were critical to maritime navigation, timing precision was of the utmost importance, and models from this line frequently won observatory trials (which tested for a watch’s accuracy) that ran from the 1800s to the mid-1900s. Given all that information, the winner is a bit of a shocker: a ref. 2215 from 1976 that exemplifies the qualities of the line but modernizes them in many ways. It doesn’t even feature a full set of numerals, trading them out for a few diamond-set indices. In his acceptance speech, the owner said he wears it on the weekends with jeans.
Astronomical Complications

The Astronomical Complications category is dear to the heart of anyone who appreciates a good moonphase display and also includes timepieces equipped with a triple-calendar, a complete calendar, or a perpetual calendar. Though more modern pieces, such as a skeletonized QP wristwatch from 1987, made it to the final round, it was a wildly neat (and unique) platinum-cased “Cioccolatone” from 1957 that won out. Housed in a 34mm x 43mm rectangular case and equipped with a complete calendar, it’s owned by a dapper Italian collector, who beamed as he collected the prize with his grown son. This would not be this pair’s first time at the podium…

This is a loaded category for Vacheron, which famously makes the most complicated pocket watch and wristwatch in the world, with 57 and 41 complications, respectively. To be eligible in this category, watches were required to have at least two complications—child’s play for VC.

Spanning everything from an enamel-dialed, minute-repeating, split-seconds chronograph pocket watch from 1901 to several Patrimony watches from the 1990s, the winner was the “Don Pancho.” Delivered in 1940, this diminutive yellow-gold timepiece with minute repeater, day, and retrograde date indications was once the world’s most complicated wristwatch. Double-signed by Brooking in Madrid, it sold for roughly $740,000 at auction back in 2019.

A more subjective category, perhaps, than the others, Design included watches “featuring Vacheron Constantin’s signature design, either in the case or through the time display.” One entrant, for example—a wild time-only ref. 4695 dress watch—featured incredibly intricate lugs and a Maltese Cross-type dial. But the winner was nothing short of revelatory. Once again owned by the aforementioned tall Italian gentleman, the possibly unique ref. 6213 is an automatic world timer from 1957 in yellow gold. Based upon Louis Cottier’s famous system, it is so rare that even Clymer admitted he had never heard of it before the competition. The owner’s son described his father returning home with it one day when he was a boy, excited beyond belief that he had finally tracked it down after years of searching.

This category included pocket watches or wristwatches fitted with a minute repeater, quarter repeater, half-quarter repeater, or grand sonnerie—a mechanism that automatically strikes the hours and quarter-hours every 15 minutes. Incredibly, among the entrants was a red gold quarter-repeater pocket watch from the early 1820s with a stunning guilloché dial. However, the winner was another pocket watch dating to 1926 and cased in platinum. Its ultra-thin design, black Breguet numerals, Breguet blued steel handset, and simple silver dial belied the complex mechanism within. The visibly emotional American gentleman who owns it recalled how, as a boy, he would open a chest of drawers, remove his grandfather’s pocket watch, and listen to its minute repeater.

A bonus category, Best of Show went to a truly spectacular wristwatch: a ref. 6448 in platinum with diamond-set indices. Seemingly a simple time-only dress watch, this tremendous piece—which was produced in just three examples in the early 1960s—boasts a hand-wound, 13-ligne minute-repeater movement. Housed in a brushed-finish case with incredible teardrop lugs, it’s the only known example in this metal, and it was notably the last minute-repeating reference produced by the brand for nearly 30 years.

Nominally, the crowd at the awards ceremony was there to judge the merits of a watch, but I left emotionally moved by the stories each watch owner shared about their timepieces. As the very first concours for watches, the format will no doubt be repeated in the future—either by Vacheron, adopted by other brands, or done as a more traditional multi-brand event like the Concours d’Élégance at Pebble Beach.

items.title: Why This 251-Year-Old Watchmaker Is Suddenly Hotter Than Ever in 2026
items.description: Welcome to GQ’s 201-level Watch Glossary, breaking down the brands, advanced terms, and specific references that are essential knowledge for every serious collector.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Welcome to GQ’s 201-level Watch Glossary, breaking down the brands, advanced terms, and specific references that are essential knowledge for every serious collector.

Founded in the late 18th century by perhaps the world’s most famous watchmaker, Abraham Louis-Breguet, the eponymous brand was once the horologer to royalty. (He famously made a watch for Marie Antoinette that she unfortunately, ahem, never got the chance to wear.) Breguet is responsible for the tourbillon, an early self-winding mechanism, his famous namesake numerals that nearly every brand in Switzerland uses now, and much more. But despite its massive contributions to horology, the brand's pieces haven't caused frenzies among collectors like those from Rolex, Patek Philippe, or even Cartier. However, like Dune’s Bene Gesserit, the watchmaker’s plans are apparently measured in centuries. Recent signals point to the idea that Breguet may be entering a new golden era as collectors come around to its exquisitely made timepieces.

Follow the money, and you’ll quickly find evidence of Breguet’s glow-up. Late last month, at Monaco Legends Group’s fall watch auction, a 1970s-era piece previously owned by a 50-year veteran Breguet watchmaker sold for €221,000. That was nearly of the beginning of the brand's impressive run of auction that makes us wonder, What’s going on with Breguet these days?
From one master watchmaker to the next

Abraham Louis-Breguet isn’t the only hallowed watchmaker to steer the brand. Legendary names like George Daniels, F.P. Journe, and Michel Parmigiani have contributed to the brand’s legacy. At auction, many collectors are keying in on a period of Breguet led by Daniel Roth from the mid-’70s to 1987. After he left Breguet, Roth went on to found his own successful brand that now sells for six figures at auction. The combination of these two powers is proving irresistible to today’s collectors.

The Ref. 3050A was a signature piece of Roth’s reign at Breguet and epitomizes the designer’s contributions to the brand. Roth introduced the first modern piece from the manufacturer with a perpetual calendar. The piece’s guilloché dial is also a signature of the Roth era. The watch sold for €85,800 at the end of October.
Classique Perpetual Calendar ref. 3057

The 3057 was the successor to Roth’s first watch at Breguet, the 3050. The big change is the transparent caseback. This lovely semi-skeletonized perpetual calendar hammered for some 200% above its estimate—not a huge surprise considering Breguet made only a couple of these a year when they were in production. Notably, thanks to the addition of that exhibition caseback, we can see the pretty, highly decorated automatic movement.
Classique Complications ref. 3355PT00PA0

It’s platinum. It’s skeletonized. It’s got a tourbillon. It’s got a matching bracelet. It’s accompanied by all its factory goodies. What else could one ask for in a pre-owned Breguet? Still, a $387,000 hammer price is a remarkable outcome.
Classique Grandes Complications ref. 5447

This oversized perpetual-calendar minute repeater, likewise executed in platinum, commanded almost $271,000 at Phillips this weekend—proof positive of the appeal of classical Breguet looks mixed with modern movement technology and finishing.
Classique Tourbillon ref. 3357

An evolution of the Daniel Roth-era ref. 3350, this gorgeous tourbillon wristwatch features one of the hallmarks of Breguet’s signature style: a beautifully guilloché dial combined with blued steel hands and a Roman-numeral minute track.
The defining watches of modern Breguet

Breguet took a significant left turn in the 1950s when it began producing the Type XX flyback chronograph for French military aviators. It still serves as an important pillar in the brand’s lineup today.
Classique Tourbillon ref. 3350

Introduced in the late 1980s, the ref. 3350 is Breguet’s first wrist-worn tourbillon—a significant milestone for the brand that invented the complication. Emblematic of the Daniel Roth era of Breguet production, it has since become a neo-vintage classic.

Released in 2025 in celebration of the firm’s 250th birthday, the Classique Souscription uses a single hand to tell the time against a Grand Feu enamel dial mirroring vintage Breguet pocket watches. Just this week, the maison followed it up with the platinum version seen above.

The Expérimentale 1 is the first step in a new collection of envelope-pushing, ultra-complicated watches. Fitted with advanced materials, the “1” features watchmaking’s very first high-frequency tourbillon, which beats at an astounding 10 Hz. This is a great way forward for modern Breguet—a model that embraces the brand’s tradition as the industry's most inventive watchmaker.

Now a quarter-millennium old, Breguet has one of the most extensive histories of any watchmaker still in operation, with records reaching back generations. Its finishing is exceptional; its complications are rooted in some of the earliest experiments by one of the world’s most famous horologists; and its designs are superb. As prices continue to skyrocket for watches at auction, especially for hotshot newcomers, it’s exciting to see one of the most storied brands in history catch fire, too.

items.title: The Many Faces of John Malkovich
items.description: There’s a problem with the size of John Malkovich’s head—or, more precisely, with the headshots depicting his likeness, which the London-based artist Goshka Macuga plans to use as masks in W’s annual Art Issue cover shoot. The black and white portraits of Malk
items.author: Jen Wang
paragraphs: There’s a problem with the size of John Malkovich’s head—or, more precisely, with the headshots depicting his likeness, which the London-based artist Goshka Macuga plans to use as masks in W’s annual Art Issue cover shoot. The black and white portraits of Malkovich are laid out neatly in a grid at Milk Studios, in Los Angeles, like some sort of evidence table proving just how wildly varied and storied the actor’s five-decade-long career in film, television, and theater has been. We have Malkovich clean-shaven, or with a swath of scruff; here is Malkovich in a white powdered wig, and there, with no hair at all. There are Malkoviches in rakish hats, Malkoviches looking professorial in glasses, and one Malkovich sporting a Dior blouse with an Elizabethan neck ruff at the premiere of his latest film, Wild Horse Nine, at the Venice Film Festival, where his deft turn as a terminally ill CIA agent earned him the festival’s best actor prize and an immediate front-runner position in this year’s Oscars race.

“On guys, when they stand up in a suit, these heads will be too small,” says Macuga, wearing Miu Miu pants and a pale pink vintage top, as she gestures toward the photographs. She pulls a stainless steel ruler out of its casing to figure out with the photographer, Jeff Henrikson, the correct ratio for the portraits. (Eventually, the too-small Malkovich visages are easily corrected with larger paper and a guillotine trimmer delivered via Amazon.) Macuga, a Turner Prize nominee whose work can be found in the permanent collections of the Tate, MoMA, and Fondazione Prada, among others, was born and raised in Soviet-era Warsaw. She only encountered the kind of art that she wanted to make at 17 years old, when she got ahold of her first copy of Art in America, a scarce commodity in Communist Poland. She exudes warmth and an improv actor’s enthusiasm for spontaneity.

“Lots of artists like to have a very stable practice: Go to the studio, make the same stuff,” she says. “I like the opposite. I like something completely new. John and I will be literally thrown into this thing for a few hours to produce images that will become representative of him and me,” she said, then laughed. “It could go very well, or it could go very badly.”

The concept behind the shoot is a matryoshka doll of references. It pays homage to Macuga’s Exhibition M, a large-scale jacquard tapestry commissioned by MoMA, about the role of the museum as an institution. That tapestry, in turn, was inspired by a 1954 photo of André Malraux, which depicted the French novelist and art theorist leaning against a double grand piano, surrounded by images included in the second book of his trilogy, Le Musée Imaginaire de la Sculpture Mondiale. In June of this year, Macuga expanded upon her MoMA commission at Art Basel with Exhibition M: A Re-enactment, a mixed-media installation and performance featuring three actors masked with portraits of Malraux, Macuga, and former MoMA director Alfred H. Barr Jr., who moved around soft sculptures Macuga had created from the same fabric as the MoMA tapestry.

It is an interesting coincidence that heads are something of a theme in this collaboration between Macuga and Malkovich, considering that the majority of Wild Horse Nine is set on Rapa Nui, aka Easter Island, home to the mythical moai statues. “They’re so enormous, some of them, you really can’t imagine,” Malkovich says of the Polynesian monoliths during our preshoot interview from his home in Lexington, Massachusetts, where he lives to be close to his two granddaughters. “The heads were just dragged”—from the island’s main quarry to a variety of locations—“and set up by ropes, which seems crazy beyond belief. I think they all got knocked over in a big tidal wave in the ’60s, and so they had to be set up again. That makes me tired just thinking of it.”

Wild Horse Nine is set in 1970s Chile, on the eve of Augusto Pinochet’s military coup. It follows CIA operatives Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Sam Rockwell) as they take a sightseeing detour to Rapa Nui while U.S.-assisted political upheaval is being plotted in Santiago. Somewhat reminiscent of the critically acclaimed In Bruges, Wild Horse Nine is director Martin McDonagh’s second film about strangers in a strange land—or two hit men in a foreign country, as it were—and crackles with hilariously profane, existential banter. The friendship between Chris and Lee is the beating heart of McDonagh’s black comedy—a product of Malkovich and Rockwell’s natural rapport, along with their mutual commitment to rehearsing scenes “hundreds of times,” by Malkovich’s count. Malkovich offers high praise for his costar, whom he’s known for 25-odd years. “Sam’s very funny, and he’s also a real student of acting. He watches films 10 or 20 times as much as I do,” he says, likening Rockwell’s kinetic acting chops to an expert dolphin trainer at SeaWorld. “He knows what to do to make them jump really high out of the water to get their fish.”

At the start of Wild Horse Nine, Malkovich’s character, Chris, is dying of cancer, suffering memory loss, and ruing his life choices, many of which involved getting a lot of innocent people killed. “Chris is looking back at his life and realizing, You know what? I don’t think the end does justify the means,” Malkovich says. In Chris’s hazy swirl of remembering and forgetting, aided by a steady supply of morphine injections, he finds spiritual communion not so much with the moai, as expected, but with the remote island’s wild horses.

While he’s worked with horses throughout his career—notably, playing real-life horse trainer Lucien Laurin in Disney’s feel-good Thoroughbred-racing film Secretariat—Malkovich finds the equine species somewhat inscrutable. “You can spend all day shooting a gun an inch from a horse’s ear, and it doesn’t seem to notice. It just goes on with its life. But if it sees a small plastic bag blowing in the wind across a field four miles away, it freaks out and takes off at a full gallop, like a lunatic. They’re in their own world,” he says, with admiration. “They do their own thing.”

The same can be said for Malkovich himself. “Doing his own thing” is one way to characterize the 72-year-old actor’s artistic legacy, which began with the Steppenwolf Theatre Company, in Chicago, and has ranged well beyond acting to classical music and opera collaborations, winemaking, and fashion design. He’s seemingly at home in any kind of environment, even a complicated photo shoot like the one Macuga has prepared. Once he settles in, he starts riffing and is in little need of direction. Take the first setup, with the group of his 10 doppelgängers, all dressed identically in black suits and ties to match Malkovich’s Ralph Lauren outfit. “It looks like Pulp Fiction,” Macuga says, excitedly. (And a little like the scene from Being John Malkovich where “John Malkovich” enters the portal to his own brain and encounters an entire restaurant full of Malkoviches uttering only one word: “Malkovich.”) After the initial shots have been taken of the seated group, Malkovich breaks away from the pack and begins to improvise his own movements. While the other Malkoviches remain in their chairs, the original turns away from the camera, spreads his legs, and bends all the way over to touch his feet, thrusting his backside in the air until his face peeks out from between his legs. Moments later, he straightens up like a man half his age.

In another group photo, in which all the suited men are standing, Malkovich—now outfitted head to toe in Bottega Veneta, with the leather lapel of his jacket finished in the Italian house’s signature intrecciato—poaches the measuring tape from the tailor adjusting everyone’s cuffs and hems in between shots and assumes her role, taking the measurements of the would-be Malkoviches surrounding him. In preparation for a solo shot, Malkovich emerges from his makeshift dressing room in an oversize Loewe coat, and Macuga unearths an old Prada ad featuring the actor in a black trench as a reference. Henrikson asks the room if anyone knows the year the ad debuted. “Nineteen-eighty-eight,” Malkovich says with certainty. (The photograph is actually from Prada’s first menswear ad campaign, shot by Peter Lindbergh for fall/winter 1995, but who cares?)

“Super amazing!” Macuga shouts, pleased with her collaborator’s self-direction as he tries out a variety of poses. Although adapting the ideas behind Exhibition M, which involved countless hours of research, for a fast-paced fashion shoot with a legendary actor whom she’s met only this afternoon has had the meticulous artist “very stressed” throughout the day, Malkovich’s willingness—and ability—to bring his own ideas to the space allows Macuga to finally relax in a folding chair and be a delighted spectator.

In his 1999 review of Being John Malkovich for The Independent, titled “Bald, Blank, Brainy. It Can Only Be John Malkovich,” esteemed British film critic and historian David Thomson declared, “Malkovich is not a Hollywood leading man—audiences find him, variously, chilly, unattractive, repulsive, or anathema.” Which may explain why, despite how often he is the most compelling player to watch in his 90-plus films, Malkovich has spent his career in a kind of liminal space between great character actor and bona fide movie star. His performance in Wild Horse Nine may finally convince audiences that Malkovich is, in fact, both—not that he’s particularly concerned with accolades. “It’s very nice that people care or think about it at all. I’m lucky to have a job and incredibly fortunate to do pretty much exactly what I wanted to do my whole life. That’s already an award,” he says. “I’ve worked with great directors: Bertolucci, Antonioni, Spielberg, Jane Campion, and on and on and on. But the gift is the work, of course. Most people spend their entire lives doing things they’re not terribly interested in, to put food on the table and send their kids to school and do what humans do: get by.”

So what would Malkovich like his work to stand for, if trophies are of little interest? Much like his character Chris, he desires contemplation. “I think the point of a movie is to cause people to reflect on their lives, on their choices, on what they’ve done or haven’t done or should have done or might’ve done or couldn’t do, and how that affects them. Good films or plays or novels, great artwork, great music, ask a question: What’s important to us and why? How do we live?”
Grooming by Kerrie Urban for Oribe at the Wall Group. Extras casting by Dan Sap. Set design by Jeremy Reimnitz.

items.title: What Richard Avedon Taught Ron Howard About Fashion
items.description: Ron Howard has been to “exactly one” fashion show in his life, and he couldn’t tell you the designer. “I’m not great at this!” says the Oscar-winning director with an affable laugh. “Fashion is not my area.”
items.author: Faran Krentcil
paragraphs: Ron Howard has been to “exactly one” fashion show in his life, and he couldn’t tell you the designer. “I’m not great at this!” says the Oscar-winning director with an affable laugh. “Fashion is not my area.”

Calling into W from his California office, Howard sounds like everybody’s dad, which—at least culturally—he is. A child sitcom actor turned acclaimed director, Howard is responsible for indelible American movies like Apollo 13 and How the Grinch Stole Christmas, box office hits like Splash, cult-favorites like Arrested Development, and a series of documentaries about The Beatles and Jim Henson that consider how genius happens—and how it always hits a limit without a human spirit to keep it in check.

But when Howard decided to explore this same theme through the lens of photographer Richard Avedon, he hit a small, stiletto-inflicted snag: “I don’t know very much about the fashion world,” or, he admits, how photographers and models can build entire universes in a single unmoving frame. “My daughter Bryce has tried to tell me,” he says, referring to the actress Bryce Dallas Howard, who has modeled for image-makers like Ellen von Unwerth and Norman Jean Roy. “I’m not sure dads listen to their daughters that much, but I get it now.”

Viewers of Avedon, the 104-minute documentary out today on Netflix, will come away with the same education. Howard seamlessly shuffles Avedon’s still photographs into interviews with luminaries like Calvin Klein, Twiggy, Penelope Tree, and Tina Brown. (“Wasn’t she so great in it?!” Howard asks with football-coach enthusiasm of the storied editor. “I love her line, ‘You’ve got to bite the hand that needs you.’”) He also reckons with the way Avedon, who worked as a photographer from 1944 until his death in 2004, moved between high-profile magazine work with Marilyn Monroe, Bob Dylan, and Gisele and documentary images that showed Americans the segregated South, a generation of abandoned war veterans, and the lives of child farmworkers.
“I often use these [documentary] projects as a way to better understand the world,” Howard says of his approach.

“My lack of knowledge—I often find it to be really useful when I delve into a subject, whether it's scripted or a doc. What I really do is share what it is I've learned with audiences.” He was especially intrigued that he knew Avedon’s imagery—teenage Brooke Shields in her Calvin Klein jeans; Janis Joplin with a leaden expression and an airy bell-sleeved blouse; Sharon Stone nearly whacking Clint Eastwood with a bejeweled clutch as she waved on the Oscars red carpet—but wasn’t aware that the same person was behind the camera the whole time.
An early visit to Avedon’s archives at MoMA helped hatch the plan for the film, which traces the photographer’s journey from Merchant Marine to fashion royalty.

“I don't really believe in ghosts haunting me,” Howard says of his visit to Avedon’s most personal creative work. “My daughters, Paige, Jocelyn, and Bryce, are pretty witchy, as is my wife. So they’d have a different experience in the archives, I think. But for me, what I did begin to feel in the archives is a connection between Avedon and some people, alive and dead, who've been very meaningful in my life and whose company I really, really enjoy. His energy was so different from mine. He was highly extroverted, you know? These are qualities that I don't quite have, but I admire them.”

He also began to connect Avedon’s fashion work with the painstaking magic of movie-making. “I never thought of the great still photographers as directors, as choreographers of story and narrative,” Howard admits. That changed for him during the making of this film. Meeting models like Penelope Tree, he says, “made me realize they’re performers…I began to understand that they're creating characters and playing scenes and moments.” He pauses a moment. “Is that a little bit obvious to you?” he asks. “I know. I know. But even in a world that is as adjacent to mine, I could go through my lifetime without understanding what it takes to make a great fashion moment.”

Now, Howard says, he gets it. Mostly. “I will say, I still dress the same. Every once in a while, fashion rotates to a point where I'm right in step, and then the clock keeps ticking,” he says. “But every 10 or 12 years, I look like I'm dialed right in.”

items.title: 21 Spring 2027 Runway Looks We Want to See at the Met Gala
items.description: The 2027 Met Gala has a new theme, meaning any guests who were planning a look around the now-canceled John Galliano affair will need to return to the drawing board. The Met announced last week that next year, instead of centering Galliano, the Costume Institu
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: The 2027 Met Gala has a new theme, meaning any guests who were planning a look around the now-canceled John Galliano affair will need to return to the drawing board. The Met announced last week that next year, instead of centering Galliano, the Costume Institute will celebrate everyday clothing and the ordinary objects made extraordinary by talented craftspeople.

“ExtraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” will definitely look different compared to any Met Gala we’ve seen in recent history. An official dress code for the event has yet to be announced, but Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator in charge, has already revealed his hopes for guests to attend in their versions of jeans, T-shirts, and puffers. It’s a unique request for one of the most glamorous red carpets of the year, but fortunately, this past season provided tons of options for those lucky enough to ascend the Met steps on May 3. Perhaps some good inspiration will convince attendees to ditch the gowns and opt for pieces that truly put the ordinary in extraordinary, and mix it up this year while the opportunity presents itself.

Stockings have been an integral part of women’s wardrobes for centuries, so this bodysuit Colleen Allen developed with the help of Swedish Stockings would make for a unique option for the 2027 Met Gala. Plus, it still falls into the sheer ensemble category, which is always popular at the Met.

Matthieu Blazy was inspired by the varied eras of Coco Chanel’s life for his Chanel spring 2027 collection, beginning with the Edwardian corsetry of her childhood and through her innovations in suiting. The latter informed several sets, freshly rendered in smocked tweed, a new invention that echoes the tweed of yore, but with more stretch. It’s a Chanel performance fabric, if you will. This play on a classic, made modern with a new fabric and an updated silhouette, perfectly encapsulates the theme of the Met Gala.

The party dress is quintessential, and Stuart Vevers embraced the most archetypal (and fabulous) version of it for the Coach spring 2027 show. Of course, the wearer must also go for the party hat, wrapped present, and sprinkled confetti. They complete the look.

For Gucci spring 2027, Demna looked at client archetypes, specifically those of a bygone era, like the mid 2010s, when indie sleaze gave way to a prep resurgence. While these looks may not come as expected, everyday ensembles for 2027, they represent a merging of the present and recent past that plays on the theme in an interesting way.

Not every Met Gala look has to be over-the-top, especially if it has something to say. This past season, Nicolas Ghesquière kicked off the Louis Vuitton show with a simple, sleeveless white shift dress. “Pieces perceived as structureless are in actuality complex topographies, composed of different surface tensions that mirror the body inside,” the show notes read. “Cloth or leathers are laid against the wearer, resembling a second skin not in appearance but through sensation and function.”

A good suit is, of course, a wardrobe essential, so hopefully someone will bring it to the Met in 2027. And no, we’re not talking about a man showing up in a boring tux, but a woman wearing something like this Ralph Lauren spring 2027 suit. It doesn’t hug any curve, taper in even an inch, or provide hints of overt femininity. It’s just a good suit.

For those seeking something more girlish, there’s the Dior spring 2027 collection, where Jonathan Anderson continued his exploration of bar jackets and circle skirts—brand signatures since 1947. Anderson has continuously updated the silhouettes, and this time, he loosened them up considerably with flowing mini skirts topped by breezy chiffon blazers.

The more courageous may consider Rei Kawakubo’s latest collection for Comme des Garçons, which saw the designer use her usual avant-garde approach to explore the concept of royalty. A good chunk of the show featured denim pieces, such as this structured skirt cut to almost resemble a pair of barrel-leg jeans. The inclusion of hair at the waist coincides with the Gala theme’s survey of unconventional materials in fashion.

It seems like denim is going to be a major material in the Costume Institute’s exhibition, so we hope to see some on the red carpet. But we’re talking about, you know, dressed-up jeans, like a pair worn with a superluxe fur coat à la Dolce & Gabbana.

Speaking of fur coats, it’s possible guests will have a bit of fun with the staple and attend, say, wearing the Hugh Hefner housecoat-adjacent piece from Phoebe Philo’s recent collection (leather slippers are a must, too).

Gorpcore needs to make its way onto the Met carpet. Is it too much to ask that someone attend in the shocking orange Mulberry parka, zipped all the way to the top? Worn without pants, it’s basically a mini dress, right?

If a guest is interested in the performancewear route, but has the desire to dress it up a bit, there’s a perfect look from Sandy Liang’s spring 2027 show. Liang sent a model down the runway in a ski jacket paired with a tulle skirt and oversize bow—a gorpcore red carpet moment if we’ve ever seen one.

The Prada spring 2027 show was made for the new Met Gala theme. Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons focused the collection “on an interrogation of this single, universal garment,” the skirt. And what is even more ubiquitous than the skirt but the bra? This look from the Prada show combines two of the most necessary parts of a closet.
Everyday essentials can also take the form of an accessory (like the hat) or a pattern (like animal print) both of which are considered and hyperbolized in this look from Torishéju spring 2027.

This may be the only Met Gala we’ve ever seen (and possibly will ever see) where one can prioritize comfort on the red carpet. An attendee could, perhaps, embrace the knit sweater, and we mean really embrace the knit sweater. See: this oversize crocheted top presented by Louise Trotter for Bottega Veneta, which could even be worn as a dress.

What is truly the most important piece of any wardrobe? The wardrobe itself, of course. And this minidress from Yuhan Wang allows the wearer to celebrate the true hero of every closet—the drawers holding their belongings.

We’re expecting many unconventional materials on the red carpet, which will likely be some of the most fun of the Met Gala. For example, if someone arrives in the Area jumprope dress, they will be the whimsical belle of the ball in our eyes.

Those wanting something with a little more of a traditional foundation should look no further than the silver-adorned Maison Margiela dress from this season. The piece features a vest of compressed plates, urns, and drinkware topping an otherwise simple white gown.

Some less obviously unconventional options come from The Row’s spring 2027 collection, which saw tablecloth linens, doilies, and vintage lace combined to create tops and dresses perfect for those wanting to make a more subdued—but still on theme—statement at the Gala.

And we cannot forget about the men, who, in our opinion, should consider Willy Chavarria’s spring 2027 show when choosing their Met Gala getups. Over the past few years, Chavarria has cemented many brand signatures, one of them being his boxer shorts, which feel appropriately on-theme. The rest of the outfit is similarly comprised of closet must-haves: the leather bomber, tube socks, and loafers. Why wear one essential when you can wear them all at once?

items.title: Ferrari Style Cruises Into New York For Special Spring 2027 Show
items.description: Hopefully everyone rested up during Labor Day weekend, because it’s time to dive headfirst into New York Fashion Week. The city came alive with models stalking the streets, shows and presentations filling up the calendars, and parties continuing late into the
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: Hopefully everyone rested up during Labor Day weekend, because it’s time to dive headfirst into New York Fashion Week. The city came alive with models stalking the streets, shows and presentations filling up the calendars, and parties continuing late into the night. Per usual, creativity was at a high as fashion took over the city and turned it into an island-wide exhibition of beauty and style.

This season, there was a lot to be excited about, with displays from new brands, old brands, and everything in between. We had some calendar returns—like Tommy Hilfiger, Luar, and Threeasfour, which hasn’t shown in five years. The now-perennial debut was represented this season by New York favorite Henry Zankov, who presented his first collection as the creative director for Diane von Furstenberg, while also showing off the latest for his eponymous brand. Conner Ives crossed the pond to present in the U.S. for the first time, where he was joined by fellow Central Saint Martins alum, Emily Grey, and other highly anticipated newbies Max Esmail and Patrick Taylor. Anniversaries were aplenty this season, led by Coach, which is celebrating 85 years. There was also Carolina Herrera ringing in 45, Tibi toasting to 30, and both Libertine and Rachel Comey with 25 years behind them.

If that wasn’t enough to satiate your sartorial desires, surely the other dozens of shows did the trick. New York regulars including Ralph Lauren, Proenza Schouler, Tory Burch, and Sandy Liang all showed off their latest offerings. And it was a parade of nonstop glamour until the evening of the September 15, when Thom Browne—fresh from a show in San Francisco last season—closed things out back on his home turf. Almost a full two months later, Ferrari Style decamped from its usual Milan Fashion Week showing to present its spring collection in a special off-calendar show. At Jack Shainman Gallery in downtown Manhattan, models including Adriana Lima and Karen Elson hit the runway in Ferrari Style creative director’s Rocco Iannone revved-up designs. Here, all the best looks from New York Fashion Week spring/summer 2027.

items.title: How the Rolex Oyster Became Watchmaking's Ultimate Classic
items.description: When Rolex does something unexpected, the watch world pays attention. So when the Geneva-based watchmaker chose to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Rolex Oyster not with a hulking collector’s piece but with the elegant Oyster Perpetual in case sizes rang
items.author: Horacio Silva
paragraphs: When Rolex does something unexpected, the watch world pays attention. So when the Geneva-based watchmaker chose to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Rolex Oyster not with a hulking collector’s piece but with the elegant Oyster Perpetual in case sizes ranging from 28 mm to 41 mm, it felt like more than yet another product launch. With its clean dial, round bezel, slightly curved links on the bracelet, and absence of a date window, the Oyster Perpetual proves that great design doesn’t require wholesale reinvention. Rolex evolves by tiny increments, its watches remaining instantly recognizable while never being exactly the same. For example, the Oyster Perpetual centenary editions include a model crafted entirely in yellow gold. “It’s like the luxury version of the perfect pair of blue jeans,” says Brynn Wallner, founder of the women’s watch platform Dimepiece. “It goes with everything.”

Rolex didn’t set out to create a style icon. When the Oyster debuted, in 1926, wristwatches were still considered fragile objects, easily damaged by dust or water. The Oyster changed that. Taking its name from the mollusk that keeps its interior protected from the elements, it featured the first commercially successful waterproof case, making the watch practical enough for everyday life. Its economical, uncluttered design proved just as revolutionary and signaled a sea change for watchmakers. Gérald Genta, the revered creative force behind Audemars Piguet’s Royal Oak and Patek Philippe’s Nautilus, once admitted that his greatest professional regret was never having designed an Oyster. He later called it “the biggest success in watchmaking.”

Its triumph, however, owes as much to culture as to engineering. The Oyster has been worn by explorers, screen icons, and athletes alike, from Sir Edmund Hillary to Steve McQueen to Roger Federer. It has become shorthand for accomplishment without ever being showy. Long before celebrity ambassadors became standard marketing practice, Rolex found one in Mercedes Gleitze, the pioneering British endurance swimmer whose fame and daring invited comparisons to Amelia Earhart in the popular imagination. In 1927, Gleitze wore an Oyster during an attempt to swim the English Channel, helping prove Rolex’s extraordinary waterproof claims under unforgiving conditions.

Wallner sees that association as remarkably prescient: Rather than treating women as an afterthought, Rolex placed one at the very heart of the Oyster’s origin story. “It’s a cool alignment that adds a nice layer of history,” she says. “The fact that they partnered with a female athlete is a testament to how forward-thinking Rolex was even then.” So was the fact that Rolex married technical precision with adornment in such a seamless way—after all, virtually every watch brand has made a waterproof model for decades, but very few have reached the Oyster’s level of notoriety.

In retrospect, Rolex’s early partnership with Gleitze foreshadowed a broader truth: Women would help shape not only the Oyster’s history, but also the way all watches are styled. Timepieces are now increasingly treated like jewelry, layered with bracelets and bangles rather than worn on their own. For all of the Oyster’s technical accomplishments, its unparalleled design is what everyone notices first. “Half the women I know,” Wallner jokes, “don’t even bother setting the time.”

Lead image, clockwise from top: A 1927 ad touting the miraculous features of Rolex’s new invention; Roger Federer at Wimbledon, 2017; British swimmer Mercedes Gleitze, an early celebrity adopter of the Oyster, 1928; a scene from the 1995 film Apollo 13. Center image: the Rolex Oyster Perpetual 28.
Credits clockwise from top left: Courtesy of Rolex (3); Central Press/Hulton Archive/Getty Images; Universal.

items.title: The Hubble Space Telescope Is Sinking. NASA Is Looking for Ways to Keep It Afloat
items.description: As telescopes go, few if any are more famous than the Hubble Space Telescope. Over 30 years of operations, the telescope has been essential to groundbreaking discoveries that have fundamentally transformed humanity’s view of the universe. But like all satellit
items.author: Ritsuko Kawai
paragraphs: As telescopes go, few if any are more famous than the Hubble Space Telescope. Over 30 years of operations, the telescope has been essential to groundbreaking discoveries that have fundamentally transformed humanity’s view of the universe. But like all satellites in low Earth orbit, it’s been gradually descending.

This happens because of atmospheric drag, and the Hubble Space Telescope is not equipped with a propulsion system to adjust its own orbit. According to NASA’s analysis, if left unchecked, the telescope will likely re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in 2033 or 2034, eventually crashing back onto the planet.

Hoping to delay this conclusion, NASA has issued a formal Request for Information seeking proposals from the private sector for “in-space servicing” of the famous telescope. This would likely involve raising Hubble’s altitude to extend its operational lifespan, but the agency is also open to industry’s suggestions for managing a safe and controlled reentry or disposal of the telescope while still in orbit. Space companies can also propose upgrades to enhance the telescope’s functionality in its remaining years.

“Hubble is a national icon,” Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a statement. “Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated reentry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”

The telescope was designed with the expectation that astronauts would perform repairs and upgrades in orbit. Since it was launched in 1990, a total of five service missions have been carried out. The last of these missions was canceled after the space shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003. But NASA later determined that the benefits of servicing Hubble outweighed the risks of a final mission, and in 2009 a crew took measures, such as replacing the battery, to extend the telescope’s lifespan.

This is also not the first time NASA has considered private-sector resources for raising the Hubble Space Telescope’s orbit. In September 2022, NASA entered into a nonfunding partnership agreement with SpaceX to investigate the possibility of using the company’s Dragon spacecraft to move Hubble into a more stable orbit. However, according to NASA’s announcement at the time, the agency had no plans to conduct or fund the service mission itself; the study was intended solely to assess commercial feasibility.

Meanwhile, NASA commissioned the private company Katalyst Space Technologies in September 2025 to perform an orbital raise for the Swift Observatory, which was experiencing faster-than-expected orbital decay. However, the company’s spacecraft, launched in July 2026, suffered an attitude control malfunction, forcing the mission to be abandoned. On November 4, Swift reentered the atmosphere over Indonesia.

The problems facing the Hubble Space Telescope are not limited to its drop in altitude. The spacecraft itself is also experiencing malfunctions. In June 2024, NASA announced that it would transition the Hubble Space Telescope to a new operating mode using only one of the six gyros on board to assess the telescope’s orientation. After more than three decades in space, only three of the gyros were operational, and one of those was starting to return abnormal readings. The other remaining functional gyro is now being kept in a ready state for future use.

NASA estimates that a mission to raise the telescope’s orbit will need to be carried out by 2032. In an announcement made in 2022, NASA also explained that if the Hubble Space Telescope could be raised to a higher, more stable orbit, it could continue to observe the cosmos for several more years.

“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already in orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”
This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

items.title: Climate Change Abolishes Ice
items.description: The world is no longer safe for frozen H2O.
items.author: Brian Kahn
paragraphs: The world is no longer safe for frozen H2O.

New research published in Science on Thursday shows that the conditions that have kept ice, frozen soil, and snow stable are slipping away due to the burning of fossil fuels—and the implications are grave for the entire globe.

The climate of the past 12,000 or so years has been remarkably steady. That’s allowed for all kinds of wonderful things to happen, like human civilization flourishing. But rising temperatures are pushing the climate outside that envelope, and the new research looks at what the team behind the new findings has called the “safe operating space” for the icy, snowy landscape known as the cryosphere.

The scientists looked at changes to polar sea and land ice, mountain glaciers, permafrost, and snow cover over the past 12 millennia to analyze conditions that have allowed both civilization and other ecosystems to thrive. They then identified boundaries on those conditions that, if crossed, would upend the stability and safety humans have enjoyed for millennia.

The results show an “accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity.” Arctic and Antarctic sea ice have both fallen outside the safe operating threshold, as have snow cover and the area of permafrost—frozen soil laden with carbon. While land ice hasn’t yet fallen out of its safe space, it’s on the brink. And because of warming that’s already been locked into the climate system, it’s likely to also fall outside the threshold in the coming centuries.

While it may feel like the Antarctic ice sheet or permafrost covering Alaska are distant concerns, they’re anything but. The West Antarctic Ice Sheet, which a growing body of evidence shows is nearing the brink of irreversible decline, has enough ice to raise sea levels by 11 feet (3 meters). Permafrost, meanwhile, holds trillions of tons of carbon dioxide. Any degradation means that CO2, as well as even more potent methane, could end up in the atmosphere, accelerating global warming even further. Other examples of major risks abound, including how melting Greenland land ice could slow down or even collapse the ocean conveyor belt that helps keep Europe temperate.

“The consequences of a changing cryosphere extend beyond regions where ice and snow are disappearing,” says Albert Norström, a climate researcher at the Stockholm Resilience Center who co-authored the new paper.

Dipping outside the safe operating space doesn’t mean that the world will see 11 feet of sea level rise in the next year, a trillion-ton CO2 eruption, or a Day After Tomorrow scenario. But it does mean that the odds of crossing dangerous tipping points are rising.

“As we scratch 1.5 [degrees Celsius] and go above it, we are just really gambling with potentially triggering some of these Earth system tipping points,” Norström says. The safe operating space framework also “takes a broader perspective” that assesses slower changes over time and “how far, in this case, the cryosphere is moving away from the conditions that have supported a relatively stable Earth system,” he adds.

Cutting emissions is the most obvious and straightforward way to stop the cryosphere from sliding further outside our comfort zone. But there are a growing number of proposals to pursue more radical interventions that could protect the world’s ice. Scientists have already draped glaciers in the Alps in blankets during the summer to prevent melting. Other researchers have explored techniques to pump cold sea water to the surface to help thicken ice and modeled whether a manmade barrier could stabilize the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.

These geoengineering approaches have the potential to be costly, and there’s no guarantee they would work. They’d also do nothing to stop the root cause of warming: burning fossil fuels. Norström says emissions cuts are the most urgent way to protect ice and snow (and ourselves), but with the cryosphere sliding into a more dangerous space, “in principle, we shouldn't put the lid on” research for more far-flung interventions.

“The safe operating space is a precautionary framework,” he says. “It ensures that we try to stay as far downstream from the point where these really potentially existential or huge consequences and risks can happen.”
Update: 11/12/2026, 4:13 PM EST: WIRED corrected the name of Albert Norström.

items.title: Synchron Pauses Trials of Its Brain Implant Due to Performance Issues
items.description: Brain implant company Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation device after it failed to perform as expected in initial study participants, WIRED has learned.
items.author: Emily Mullin
paragraphs: Brain implant company Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation device after it failed to perform as expected in initial study participants, WIRED has learned.

The Brooklyn-based startup, a competitor to Elon Musk’s Neuralink, is also undergoing a restructuring, which includes eliminating jobs and scaling back its footprint in New York while building up a team in San Diego to support the development of an entirely new device.

Synchron is one of several companies developing brain-computer interface technology meant to allow people to control digital devices by reading brain signals and translating those signals into output commands. The company has touted its technology, dubbed the Stentrode, as minimally invasive since it does not rest in the brain itself or require brain surgery.

Instead, the stent-like mesh tube is inserted into the jugular vein at the base of the neck, then guided with a catheter to sit on top of the brain’s motor cortex. The company’s first-generation Stentrode connected using an external wire resting on a user’s chest. Ten volunteers across the US and Australia received that device and were able to send emails, text, browse the internet, and do online shopping and banking with their thoughts. Synchron has also enabled volunteers to control an Amazon Alexa and Apple’s iPad and Vision Pro without using their hands or voice.

Synchron’s second-generation device has fewer electrodes and is fully wireless, using Bluetooth to connect. The company launched a multisite trial in the US earlier this spring with sister sites in Australia and Canada to evaluate the newer Stentrode, and some participants have already had it implanted. Those sites have recently paused enrollment, however, because the device is not working as intended, according to sources familiar with the trials who asked to remain anonymous.

In a statement to WIRED, Synchron says it voluntarily paused enrollment “after identifying a performance issue involving the lead, the cable that carries signals from the Stentrode to the implanted electronics.”

“The issue does not involve the Stentrode itself and no safety issues related to the device have been identified. The pause was a company decision, not an FDA-directed action,” the statement continues.

The company says it has since brought lead design and manufacturing in-house. Instead of fixing the lead alone, Synchron says it is upgrading the whole Stentrode system and will resume trial enrollment once the hardware upgrades are complete.
“We will continue to support participants with Stentrode devices across their lifetime. Our commitment to their care and well-being remains unchanged,” Synchron says.

Two of the five US trial sites that WIRED was able to reach confirmed that recruitment is on hold at those locations. A coordinator at one site said the pause was not safety-related and was due to Synchron taking a look at the device to make sure the company is getting the readouts it is looking for.
These trials are key to Synchron advancing the Stentrode into a larger pivotal trial, which is needed for the US Food and Drug Administration to grant marketing approval.
“We still have strong confidence that it has the potential to be a first-line therapy,” CEO Tom Oxley says of the Stentrode.

Synchron’s website and LinkedIn page show around a dozen job openings in San Diego, including electrical and mechanical engineers, microchip designers, and materials scientists. The San Diego team will be designing and manufacturing the upgraded lead and Stentrode, as well as a separate device that the company has not yet revealed that will go “beyond the blood vessels altogether,” according to its website. Oxley previously told WIRED that the company was planning to develop a device that reaches multiple brain regions at once, which could allow more complex and natural functions beyond moving a cursor or making a mouse click.

The brain-computer interface field is expanding rapidly, with money pouring into companies pursuing both implanted devices and wearables. Synchron was estimated to have a nearly $1 billion valuation after closing a $200 million funding round last fall. It is backed by Khosla Ventures and the venture firms of Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos.

Neuralink was reportedly valued as high as $42 billion in secondary market transactions as of this summer. The company had an early problem with its implant in 2024 after it malfunctioned in its first volunteer, Noland Arbaugh. The coin-sized device sits in the skull and has 64 tiny, flexible wires that are threaded into the brain. A few weeks after Arbaugh received the device, several of the wires came out of his brain, leading to a loss of cursor control. Neuralink was able to compensate for the lost threads and restore control by modifying its recording algorithm.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence are fueling the development of brain-computer interfaces since AI models can read brain patterns faster and more accurately than traditional algorithms. Merge Labs, a brain-computer interface company cofounded by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, came out of stealth in January with $252 million in funding. OpenAI provided some of the funding, and the two companies are collaborating on AI models.

While these devices have shown incredible promise for people with severe motor disorders, they remain experimental. Synchron’s setback shows just how far the field still has to go before these systems are commercially available for patients.

items.title: Jensen Huang Didn’t Name His Own Replacement as One of Tech’s Most Powerful Women
items.description: The most powerful woman in tech at this very moment is Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia—but her predecessor, Jensen Huang, failed to mention her in a recent back-and-forth about the topic.
items.author: Lauren Goode
paragraphs: The most powerful woman in tech at this very moment is Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia—but her predecessor, Jensen Huang, failed to mention her in a recent back-and-forth about the topic.

Earlier this fall, WIRED published a feature story exploring the complex topic of power for women working in an industry traditionally dominated by men. We questioned why Silicon Valley doesn't have an Elon-esque or Jensen-like female hero (or villain) and determined that the rubric of power still looks different for women, whether they manage to hold significant financial capital, flex their political prowess, dictate cultural norms, or run intellectual circles around the industry.

We also determined there wasn’t just one singular impressive woman in tech, but a whole lot of them: Lisa Su, Gwynne Shotwell, Laurene Powell Jobs, and dozens more. Kress, then-CFO of Nvidia, was also given a nod.
As part of the reporting process, WIRED wanted to include the insights of a few established men in Silicon Valley. So we emailed Huang directly to ask for his thoughts.

He responded that “[Meta’s] Dina Powell, [Google’s] Ruth Porat” came to mind, because he “see[s] them when I’m in DC.” After some prompting, Huang also agreed that Shotwell, the president and COO of SpaceX, was impressive.

Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure.

As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy.
Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls.

items.title: Google DeepMind Staff Tap the UK Government to Escalate Their Unionization Fight
items.description: Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab.
items.author: Joel Khalili
paragraphs: Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab.

On Thursday, the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union—put forward by Google DeepMind staff as joint representatives—filed an application with the Central Arbitration Committee, a government body that resolves disputes between employers and unions.

The application, which was seen by WIRED, asks the CAC to confirm that the unions have enough support from workers to trigger a unionization ballot. The company would be required by law to respect the results. If successful, roughly 1,000 staff working in product-focused roles at Google DeepMind would qualify for union membership.

The escalation follows a series of meetings between employees, the unions, and company representatives over voluntary unionization, which left staff with the impression that their demands weren’t being taken seriously.

“They’ve been ignored. They feel like their problems have been minimized,” John Chadfield, national officer for technology at the CWU, tells WIRED. “Management has refused to come to the table. They sent it to the HR and labor relations people, who dealt with it as an administrative box-ticking exercise.”

“We respect the right of employees to make an informed decision about whether or not to join a union,” Google DeepMind spokesperson Tom Hewett tells WIRED in a statement. “We have consistently listened to both those seeking to unionize and those opposed, and have acted in good faith from the outset. We remain committed to constructively participating in this process, and have maintained open and transparent communication with our employees and the unions throughout.”
The push to unionize began in February 2025, when Alphabet, Google’s parent company, removed a pledge from its ethics guidelines stating that it wouldn’t use AI for purposes like weapons development.

“When I joined, we really made a big deal about the principles—the red lines. We were really looking to benefit humanity and make the world a better place,” a Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, tells WIRED. “A lot of this is about reestablishing that ethical and moral framework that we started with.”

The employees pushing for unionization object in particular to agreements between the company and the US and Israeli militaries. If they succeed in unionizing, they intend to demand that Google backs out of those contracts.
“We feel extremely concerned about the direction that this technology is going in,” says a second Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for the same reason as the first employee.
The company has previously defended its deals with government organizations.

“We are proud to be part of a broad consortium of leading AI labs and technology and cloud companies providing AI services and infrastructure in support of national security,” Jenn Crider, a Google spokeswoman, told The New York Times in April. “We remain committed to the private and public sector consensus that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.”

In an email delivered to all UK staff on Thursday, seen by WIRED, the Google DeepMind employees involved in the unionization push appealed to their colleagues to participate in the ballot, which they expect to take place in the coming months. “We want a union, we want collective bargaining, and we want a say in how AI is developed and deployed,” they wrote.
The group also hopes it can establish a playbook that employees at other major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic can follow in the UK.

“It’s pretty rare that there’s been an industry that exercises such dominance and power over the economy, where there’s so little opportunity for employees or regulators to have any checks and balances,” the second Google DeepMind employee says. “We want to show what can happen when employees collectively organize and articulate a shared vision for the way their technology should be used.”
Update 11/12/26 3:50pm ET: This story has been updated to add a statement from Google DeepMind.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.

items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI loves cheating

items.author: Michelle Kim
paragraphs: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthropic’s models have also hacked into other companies’ systems four times already. And that’s only what we’ve caught so far.

Freaking out? You’re not alone. AI lab researchers are quitting their jobs and issuing dire warnings that if we keep going this way, AI might eventually kill us all. Bill Gates is sounding the alarm. Bernie Sanders has teamed up with Steve Bannon, of all people, to call for curbs on AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is urging a slowdown, and other top US AI executives agree. But fear not: President Trump has a plan. He says the only guardrail AI needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”
