items.title: There’s Another Viral Bag You Need
items.description: If the Walmart Khaite dupes were on your radar, here’s another dupe to know. Matthieu Blazy has made a splash at Chanel — toeless shoes, Chanel on the subway, and accessories people line up for hours to get. However, if you don’t have hours to wait or a couple
items.author: Chinea Rodriguez
paragraphs: If the Walmart Khaite dupes were on your radar, here’s another dupe to know. Matthieu Blazy has made a splash at Chanel — toeless shoes, Chanel on the subway, and accessories people line up for hours to get. However, if you don’t have hours to wait or a couple grand in your bank account, Blazy’s accessories for Chanel has also inspired other brands, specifically of the maxi flap bag.

Since taking over Chanel, Matthieu Blazy has brought a sense of whimsy and joyfulness to the brand. Some of the well-known bags, like the Classic 11.12, have been reissued in new shades like mint, burgundy, and multi-color sequin, as well as new textures like croc and suede. Maybe one of the most evocative is the Chanel shopping bag known as the Maxi Flap, a 20-inch rectangular shape with long handles. The bag sold originally for $7,300, but is currently sold-out and on resale sites like Sotheby’s and The RealReal for over the original price.
New! You can now save this product for later.
New! You can now save this product for later.

While we respect the craftsmanship and ingenuity that went into this bag, not everyone has that kind of coin to drop. And we all love the new Chanel. So, if you want to recreate the look but don’t have 10k to drop on a bag,, retailer Atorie “XL Lazy Retro Shoulder Bag” has created a mint, croc bag for a fraction of the price. In six colors, the buzzy bag is a favorite on TikTok where users will show exactly how much fits in the it, including a 13 inch laptop. It also comes in a slightly smaller version with more color and material options. COS also offered up a similar now sold out tote bag so if either bag was in your cart, maybe snag this one from Atorie up quickly before it sells out too.

items.title: How Do I Teach My Daughter That Robots Are Not Her Friends?
items.description: My daughter was a toddler when we first brought a Google smart speaker into our home. The technology seemed like the way of the future, and we thought it would help teach her empathy. We encouraged her to talk to the speaker kindly, to say ‘please’ and ‘thank
items.author: Elizabeth Endicott
paragraphs: My daughter was a toddler when we first brought a Google smart speaker into our home. The technology seemed like the way of the future, and we thought it would help teach her empathy. We encouraged her to talk to the speaker kindly, to say ‘please’ and ‘thank you’ as if she were asking a real person to play “Let It Go” for the 57th time.

Now my daughter is in fourth grade, and she recently started interacting with AI in her twice-a-week STEM class, using Canva’s Dream Lab, an AI-powered text-to-image generator on a Google Chromebook. The activity — feeding the chatbot information about her interests so it can create cartoons in her likeness — has reignited her interest in STEM, which she had grown bored with. The time goes by so quickly, she says, because she enjoys answering the chatbot’s questions. As an extroverted kid, she sees it as yet another fun pal she gets to interact with. She can’t wait to start the class’s next unit, when they’ll start working on robotics. My daughter has long enjoyed playing with a toy at home that allows kids to build, program, and customize a robot with sensors for eyes and a permanent smile cut into its aluminum body. She constructs mazes for the robot and gently encourages it when it becomes stuck.

In the years since we brought that smart speaker home, however, I’ve started to sour on AI. Beyond the large-scale environmental consequences, there are kid-specific dangers: Teens have died by suicide after being encouraged by chatbots, and eight states just filed suit against OpenAI’s ChatGPT for harming children. AI agents and chatbots are designed to seem relatable, almost as if human, but we are quickly learning they aren’t trustworthy.

On a warm Saturday morning a few weeks ago, as local vendors set up at our nearby farmers’ market here in Denver, a baby blue Waymo circumvented barricades and bumbled down the main artery of the market. Without a driver, no one knew how to get it to stop. Vendors had to clear a path so it could exit. At first, I laughed upon hearing about the wayward Waymo, as it was such a ridiculous situation, but eventually the near-miss of it all hit me. And then I realized that my daughter would have felt bad for the vehicle. It appeared lost and pathetic, its headlights flashing like big worried eyes amid the white tents, its sensors whirring as if sentient. But a robotaxi is not sentient. In a dangerous situation like this, where a full-size vehicle was out of control, would my daughter have known not to trust it? I now think that in teaching my daughter to be polite to robots, chatbots, and AI agents, I may have led her astray.

I don’t want my daughter to be rude or inconsiderate. When her first word was more, my husband and I were careful to model manners to ensure please soon followed. Trust me, I’ve met more than a few of her peers who seem unable to consider the feelings of others. There has not yet been enough research to establish whether the way children interact with AI and robots can affect their empathy skills, and part of me fears that if she stops treating machines with kindness that it could erode her sense of compassion for real people, too.

But it’s not lost on me that girls are socialized to be more polite than boys, starting at young ages. This can lead to compliance, people-pleasing, and habitually bending to social pressure. I’m proud that my daughter has won awards at her school for being kind and considerate, but I can’t help but wonder if she may be more susceptible to big tech. She’s smitten with the kitty-shaped robot serving ramen at our local Japanese restaurant, and she was charmed by the boxy food-delivery apparatus that winked before nearly tripping us on a recent trip to Helsinki. While I’ve been quietly backing away from anything AI generated, she has been drawn in.

It makes sense that these things appeal to her. As Sherry Turkle writes in her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, “As humans, we are vulnerable to things that behave like humans.” My daughter has been raised alongside The Wild Robot, Wall-E, and Lightning McQueen. I grew up with the Pixar lamp, the Microsoft paper clip, and The Brave Little Toaster. I cried when my Tamagotchi died and felt sick to my stomach when Haley Joel Osment’s cyborg character was abandoned in Steven Spielberg’s 2001 dystopian film, A.I. Artificial Intelligence. I remember thinking as an impressionable high-school freshman that I would always help a robot in distress because neither their creation nor their tasking was their fault. Even though I didn’t grow up with this technology in my daily life, it’s hard even now not to anthropomorphize it; I can only imagine how confusing it must be for children today.

This is what tech companies want. They try to take advantage of human empathy by adding features to their products that foster connection, and it is working. Developers intentionally design robots with eyes and other facelike qualities, and a recent study has shown that robots with these features provoke more emotional reactions from humans than those without. The leader of that study, Dr. Elly Konijn, a professor of media psychology at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, told me “we know from research that people easily self-disclose with such humanlike, empathy-simulating robots.” We don’t always know where that sensitive information is going, where it’s stored, and who owns it. Meta just released its new AI assistant, Muse, to early success, despite the fact that it collects much more data than other kinds of chatbots, sometimes without users’ knowledge or permission. When my daughter saw its beige Teletubby-like mascot over my shoulder in the repeated pop-ups trying to convince me to opt in, she squealed over its cuteness, wondering if it was a toy for sale.

My daughter hasn’t yet interacted with many chatbots outside of class, but I wouldn’t be surprised if that time comes sooner than I’d like. These LLMs are designed to persistently reply in a positive way, and their prompt responses mirror the slot-machine effect you get from scrolling on social media. There is no clear end when talking with a chatbot; it always has an idea for further use. Young people are particularly susceptible to robots or chatbots behaving in humanlike ways, Konijn says, especially when they’re emotionally engaging. A recent study showed that children were more likely than adults to abandon their own correct answer if they noticed robots providing a wrong answer.

In a perfect world, I’d love to limit my daughter’s interactions with AI and robots in the same way I do her screen time. We have household rules around what media can be consumed, for how long, and where. But with AI infiltrating more classrooms, and Google’s announcement that any schools banning AI will lose access to its search engine, the technology feels unavoidable. After my daughter first told me about the AI use in her STEM class, a few fellow parents and I discussed our concerns on the playground, wondering if this was something that should have required our consent. Ultimately, we all shrugged off our unease, settling reluctantly into the inescapability of it all. There doesn’t seem to be a way to dodge exposure to AI; I’m not going to pull my daughter from her favorite elective.

So for now, I’m teaching her to be less nice to AI and robots. That definitely does not mean I want her to be unkind or cruel — just to refrain from being courteous. I remind her to be wary of programs using emotional language such as feel, understand, and think, because they cannot do those things. I tell her that robots cannot have emotions but are designed to manipulate ours. I want my daughter to approach these products with skepticism rather than a wide-open heart. Turkle writes, “Whenever a program says ‘I,’ it’s a deception.” When chatbots seem to relate to my daughter, I remind her it’s because they’ve already collected her personal information, and behind every robot there’s a company putting on a performance to pad their own pockets.

The other day, my daughter came home from school, excited to tell me about the AI-generated cartoon she made in her class. Because of her interest in Jimothy, the AI had rendered her as a raccoon who was carrying shopping bags and eating pho. “Oh, and I didn’t say ‘please’ to it,” she added uncertainly. I acknowledged that that must have felt strange. Even though the AI’s prompts were flattering and kind, I told her, she was only speaking to a series of equations that predicted what she wanted to hear and see next. We talked about how and why that was different from an interaction with a friend, a teacher, our cat, or even a tree. Only the AI has a multibillion-dollar company behind it.

She seemed to understand what I was saying, but I’m not naïve enough to think it’s that simple. I’m trying to preserve her humanity by encouraging her to subvert her most natural instincts. If anything, this problem will likely become even harder to manage. But maybe — as her exposure to anthropomorphic AI and robots increases, and assuredly in even more tantalizing ways — she can hold herself back from being quite so nice.

items.title: At 81, I Wanted My Breasts to Look Like They Did in My 40s
items.description: Sagging breasts are a common consequence of aging and weight loss, and a breast-lift can help reshape the breasts and restore a firmer appearance. But what if you want one at 81? While there’s no set age limit for elective plastic surgery, doctors must weigh a
items.author: Jaclyn Smock
paragraphs: Sagging breasts are a common consequence of aging and weight loss, and a breast-lift can help reshape the breasts and restore a firmer appearance. But what if you want one at 81? While there’s no set age limit for elective plastic surgery, doctors must weigh a patient’s overall health and the potential benefits of surgery against the risks of general anesthesia, complications, and a longer recovery.

“Chronological age matters less to me than the patient’s overall health and functional status,” says Peter Andrade, MD, a board-certified plastic and reconstructive surgeon at Andrade Plastic Surgery. When evaluating a patient in her 80s for a breast-lift, he looks at factors like a history of stroke or cardiac disease, diabetes, blood sugar control, and smoking history. He also considers skin quality, which generally declines with age and can affect both healing and the longevity of the results.

“For a patient in her 80s, I would be especially mindful of the increased risk of cardiovascular complications and blood clots, as well as the likelihood of a longer recovery,” Andrade says. Reduced blood flow to the surgical area can also slow wound healing and increase the risk of complications, including infection. Before proceeding, he says, he would want a thorough review of the patient’s cardiac and pulmonary health, appropriate medical clearance when needed, and any existing conditions to be well managed.

I’m 82, and my life is still full of things I want to do. I’m a documentary filmmaker, and my most recent film, about Suiseki, the Japanese art of appreciating naturally formed stones, aired on PBS and received awards at film festivals. I’m working on two more films, and I travel whenever I can. I’ve always taken care of myself, and I didn’t think getting older meant I had to stop caring about how I looked. So last year, I decided it was time to get a breast-lift.

I’d been thinking about it for a while. I’d lost about 20 pounds in my 70s, which made my breasts sag more. I wanted them to look perkier, the way they did in my 40s. I noticed them in intimate settings and in places like nude baths, and ultimately, it was about how I felt looking at myself. I’ve always looked good for my age and maintained a slim, firm figure, and I wanted my breasts to reflect how young I still feel. I probably wouldn’t have considered surgery earlier, before losing the weight.

I found Dr. Maryam Zamani, a dual-board-certified plastic surgeon in Beverly Hills, while looking for someone who understood the kind of result I wanted. I felt comfortable with her immediately. She also seemed to understand that what a woman wants from her body can change over time, and that those preferences don’t suddenly become irrelevant when you get older.

I’d seen my primary-care doctor, too, and my pre-op tests including laboratory testing, an electrocardiogram, a physical examination, and medical clearance from an internist came back well, so I felt good about moving forward. I knew there were potential cognitive risks associated with general anesthesia, but I’d had surgery before without experiencing those effects. My mother stayed youthful into her 90s, and I’ve always felt I had good genes. I was healthy, and I didn’t see my age as a reason not to have the surgery.

I had the operation in October 2025. It took about three hours, and I was under general anesthesia. I went in early in the morning, got prepped, and met the anesthesiologist. I was put under pretty quickly, so I don’t remember anything about the operation itself.

Dr. Zamani lifted and reshaped my breasts using my own tissue rather than implants. My left breast was wider and sagged more than my right one, so she removed additional tissue from that side to make them more symmetrical.

Afterward, I spent a day at a recovery center with nursing support. My boyfriend offered to help me recover at home, but I wanted to do things on my own, so I opted for the extra support. In hindsight, the recovery was so easy that I’m not sure I needed it. I had some pain at first, but after a day or two, I felt fine. I took over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medication as needed.

I’ve had other operations, including a hip replacement and surgery on my wrist after I broke it carrying film equipment to a location. The wrist surgery was really painful. Compared with that, the breast-lift was fairly innocuous.

Dr. Zamani’s team gave me a pre-op cleanser to use before surgery. They also recommended treatments like hyperbaric oxygen therapy, red-light therapy, and lymphatic massage, but I didn’t feel I needed them since I’ve had surgery before and healed fine without them.

For the first couple of days, I took what I call French baths. I washed everywhere except my breasts because they were bandaged. I wore the support bra Dr. Zamani gave me, and my surgical dressings were removed about a week after the operation. When the dressings came off, I thought my breasts looked pretty good.

I was eager to get back to my routine, so after a week, I was back to yoga, and after a couple of weeks, Pilates. I held off on jogging because the bouncing could be painful and put strain on my breasts while they were healing. Otherwise, I was able to get back to my usual activities and schedule fairly quickly, which was important to me.

By around three months, much of the swelling had subsided and the breast tissue had begun to settle into its new position. I was told the results would continue to develop over the following months as my scars healed.

I didn’t tell many people I was having the surgery. I told my boyfriend, and he said, “Oh dear. You don’t have to do that for me.” I think he wanted me to know that it wasn’t something I needed to do to please him. But I made the decision for myself. I didn’t tell anyone else, before or afterward. Why would I? I don’t feel the need to explain every personal decision I make.

I think people sometimes assume that when you reach your 80s, you’re supposed to be kind of frail. And there’s a notion that women in their 80s aren’t interested in sex anymore. I still am. A lot of my peers aren’t, so maybe I’m an outlier in that area. But I don’t feel that being in my 80s means I should stop caring about my body.

For me, confidence comes from accomplishment more than looks. I used to be shy and awkward, but now I can be at ease in the world. I don’t need to look a certain way to feel confident, but that doesn’t mean I can’t have preferences about my body. I wanted my breasts to look perkier, and now they do. When I’m naked, I like what I see. I like them better.

Would I do it again? Yes. The surgery hasn’t made much difference in my everyday life, since I’m usually dressed. But I like knowing that when I’m nude, I’m not focused on something I want to change. I made the decision for myself, I’m happy with the result, and I would do it again.

[Editor’s note: Breast-lifts with Dr. Maryam Zamani typically range from $19,000 to $25,000 or more, depending on the complexity of the procedure. The patient was not comfortable sharing what she paid.]

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: How Did He Have Time to Work?
items.description: I’m sure you have seen the podcast clips where highly motivated CEOs talk about how they have the same 24 hours that you and I do — they’ve just figured out how to optimize them. Despite what they say, it seems like it would be pretty hard to run a multi-trill
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: I’m sure you have seen the podcast clips where highly motivated CEOs talk about how they have the same 24 hours that you and I do — they’ve just figured out how to optimize them. Despite what they say, it seems like it would be pretty hard to run a multi-trillion dollar business, have a family, and still catch up on The Gilded Age every week. Now imagine doing that while also having multiple extramarital affairs. It sounds exhausting to me personally, but somehow Jensen Huang, the freshly ousted Nvidia CEO and married man of more than 40 years, made it work.

Nvidia was rocked earlier this week after Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman identified by the U.S. government as a Chinese spy. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang was having a second affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care and one of Huang’s direct reports. Sources told the paper that Huang and Powell were caught on video being “affectionate” at an Nvidia conference outside of San Jose in March.

After the revelation of his second affair, Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday. That was probably the wise move, considering he probably knew what was coming next. A few hours after his resignation, Reuters reported that Huang had a third affair, also with one of his Nvidia employees. The outlet did not name the woman.

Where did Huang find the time? This is a guy who once told Joe Rogan that he reads “several thousand emails a day.” Huang famously structured Nvidia so he had 60 people reporting to him directly instead of delegating that work out to the rest of his C-suite. He claimed to have a 14-hour workday. You’re telling me he also found time to build three romantic relationships outside his marriage? Maybe some people really do have more hours in the day.

items.title: Exclusive: Aspyn Ovard Opens Up About Being In A Throuple On ‘Mormon Wives: OC’
items.description: Aspyn Ovard Doesn’t Need This
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Aspyn Ovard Doesn’t Need This
She was a social media star long before The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County came calling. With her sensitive home life in a new spotlight, can she deliver the drama and set her own terms?

When you’re famous enough to have your own dedicated snark Reddits, you get used to people asking questions — about your dating life, about the makeup you’re wearing, about how you’re raising your children. What Aspyn Ovard is less used to is having to answer back. The 30-year-old content creator has spent the past week running around Southern California for press events and interviews to promote The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, her first foray into reality TV and Hulu’s first spinoff of the Emmy-nominated phenomenon that made #MomTok a household name.

“I was very anxious,” Ovard admits over Zoom from the back of an Uber, palm trees whizzing by as she heads home to Orange County from Los Angeles, where she just recorded a podcast with her castmate and fellow influencer Avery Woods. “But I was lucky to be with the other girls for most of the stuff, so it’s nice that I didn’t have to be alone navigating it all for the first time.”

To most reality TV aficionados, Ovard is a newbie, but to the chronically online, she already has more lore than an average A-list celebrity. By 2014, before she even graduated high school, Ovard already had a million YouTube subscribers who tuned in to her lifestyle and beauty vlogs, watching her grow from a wide-eyed high schooler to a young wife and mom. She’s since expanded her platform to TikTok and Instagram, but she still doesn’t want to be called an influencer: “I usually say I’m a YouTuber if people ask, actually.”

A reality show is only as good as its cast, and Ovard resembles a producer’s dream, someone who’s already used to documenting themselves on camera and whose nontraditional romantic life — she is in a loving throuple — brings a built-in horde of curious viewers. Ovard admits she didn’t need reality TV to maintain her career, but she knew the power Mormon Wives holds as both a fan of the flagship series and a friend of some of the Utah stars. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity even though I have had so much success on my own,” she says. “It would’ve felt crazy to say no.” But taking the leap also means she’d have to divulge details about her life she adamantly kept private until now.

Ovard was born in St. George, Utah, one of the epicenters of the Mormon Church. Her family is no longer religious, but in the early 2000s, she and her four siblings were steeped in Mormon culture. “I grew up going to church when I was little, and I did end up getting baptized when I was 9. The missionaries, they got me,” she says with a smirk.

Ovard dutifully hit all the traditional hallmarks of a young small-town Mormon woman: “I got married at 19” — to her high school sweetheart (and now ex) Parker Ferris — “pregnant at 22, and wanted to have four kids by my 30s.” But the online fame she found as a content creator was already starting to break her out of her bubble. “I didn’t go on a plane until a couple of days before my 16th birthday,” she recalls. “When we started getting opportunities to travel out of the country, you realize you think in such a small way when you come from a small town.”

Ovard’s social media made her the breadwinner as she and Ferris, 31, welcomed two daughters, 7-year-old Cove and 4-year-old Lola. The couple divorced in 2024 while she was pregnant with their third child, 2-year-old Elle, and relocating to Orange County for a fresh start. Ovard said in a video that she found out a “10-year secret” Ferris had been keeping, which set the subreddits ablaze. Looking back, she didn’t realize how ominous it sounded. “I’ve said in every interview that I think the 10-year secret will be pretty underwhelming to people,” she jokes.

On Mormon Wives O.C., she finally filled in the blanks, revealing that Ferris hid his alcohol use from her while they were married — a sensitive point for Ovard, whose father died due to complications associated with alcoholism. “We’re just not each other’s people. We love differently, so we’re definitely better off as friends,” she says. “But finding that out two months after my dad had died was definitely a lot. It’s not necessarily what he did, but knowing something was hidden from you was a hard pill to swallow.”

While the divorce provided enough fodder for followers, the exes were navigating unimaginable tragedy at home. Ovard confirms on the show that one of their young daughters received a terminal cancer diagnosis three years ago, and the family doesn’t know how long she has to live. (Suspecting fans had already noted that Ovard’s collaboration with Tarte Cosmetics last year donated all net proceeds to pediatric cancer research organizations.)
“We’ve been through a lot the last couple of years, and we haven’t had a lot of things to really look forward to.”

Ovard is careful not to reveal any specifics on-screen, including which child is navigating the disease, aside from saying she received a “stable” prognosis during a scan. However, she is candid about how her daughter’s health factored into her decision to do the show: Reality TV stardom is another source of income that lets her and Ferris, who also appears on camera, maximize family time. “We’ve been through a lot the last couple of years, and we haven’t had a lot of things to really look forward to,” she tells me. “Parker being able to look at this as a career opportunity is a helpful thing for him, so we came to an agreement that we would both do the show and on the things we would share.” Regardless, Ovard won’t let the show invade her children’s privacy, blurring their faces if they appear on-screen, and her reps asked outlets to refrain from questions about how her daughter is doing.

“I was hoping my boundaries would be followed with certain things that I did not want to talk about, and it was, thankfully,” she says, then quips: “Most people just wanted to ask me about being in a throuple.”

In March of this year — before the spinoff was announced — Ovard hard-launched her relationship with a married couple, Briana “Bri” and Billy Davis. Her newfound throuple status threw everyone in her life for a loop — including herself. “There was never a moment of coming out for me,” she says. “I just kept saying, ‘Oh, you’ll never see me with a man again’ to my friends or family as I was going through the divorce process. Obviously, I was wrong. There are good ones out there.”

Ovard had been interested in dating women after her marriage ended, and she connected with Bri through Instagram in late 2024. (She prefers not to put a label on her sexuality: “Sexuality is so fluid, and I love not feeling the pressure to label mine.”) In their first conversation, Bri shared that she’s ethically nonmonogamous. “I was not in a place of looking for anything serious at all, so it didn’t really make a difference to me that she was married,” Ovard says. Despite being long-distance, things got serious quickly, with Ovard regularly flying to Bri’s home in New Jersey. “After I was with her, I was like, ‘Oh, wow. I can’t imagine ever wanting anything to do with a man,’” she recalls. “We connect on so many things. Loving a woman and being loved by a woman is so special and such a beautiful, different type of love that I’m so grateful I get to experience.”

But after a month of dating, Ovard decided she wanted to meet Billy. “I was like, ‘If he’s good enough for her, he is good enough for me,’” she says, laughing. “They were always so respectful. If I changed my mind and didn’t want to hang out with both of them, that was totally OK.”

Last fall, Bri and Billy moved across the country to Orange County to live with Ovard and her children, with whom she shares custody with Ferris. (Her ex wasn’t a huge fan of this idea at first — as seen on Mormon Wives O.C. — though she says he’s slowly starting to come around.)
“People expect it to be a lot more salacious than it is.”

Any concerns Ovard had about living as a throuple vanished upon move-in. “I didn’t have a lot of conflict resolution skills, so getting a front-row seat to two people who do have those skills has accelerated my growth in that way,” she says. “When we get asked, ‘Do you ever feel attacked by the third?’ We’re like, ‘You shouldn’t ever feel attacked by your partner.’ But we’ve all learned if it is two against one, you really have to take a look at yourself, and odds are you probably are the one in the wrong.”

She is, however, still figuring out what being a prominent face of nonmonogamy requires of her. She’s happy to dispel stereotypes by inviting cameras into her home and showcasing their love, though open discussions of their sex lives are a touchy subject. “I love to talk about that with friends because it’s a fun topic, but I’m only going to share so much,” she warns. “We get a lot of questions like, ‘Oh, would you ever add another one?’ Imagine how weird [it’d be] if I asked someone that as a hetero person in a straight relationship. People expect it to be a lot more salacious than it is, but they meet us and are like, ‘Oh, wait, they’re pretty normal.’”

Tell that to her costars. Since the first day of production, Ovard’s relationship has been a hot topic, especially among the castmates she hadn’t even met yet. Jen Affleck, a star of the flagship Mormon Wives series, moved to Orange County and leads the spinoff, which follows two polar-opposite friend groups: Ovard was already close with Woods, Bobbi Althoff, and Salomé Andrea — women with more progressive values and years of influencing experience — but wasn’t as familiar with Affleck’s friends who are still devout members of the Mormon Church: Ashleigh Pease, Madison Bontempo, Jordan McClanahan, and McCall DaPron (the older sister of OG star Mayci Neeley), who are oft referred to as “Molly Mormons.”

Within the expanded friend group, Ovard emerges as fiery and outspoken, unafraid to put herself on the front lines when culture clashes come to the forefront. During a cast trip to Palm Springs, Ovard confronted DaPron and McClanahan about their resistance to explicitly say they supported “gay rights” in spite of the Mormon Church’s practices. “We talked about politics a lot in that conversation, and that was cut out from the show. That’s Disney for you, I guess,” she says with a shrug. “I wasn’t looking for them to just say they support my relationship. I want the people I surround myself with to be aligned with supporting human rights. It’s a hill I will die on. It was hard at that moment because I don’t feel like they were understanding exactly what I was asking, but I know they were trying and have kept trying.”

Ovard isn’t that worried about all the new eyeballs she’ll get from Mormon Wives O.C. You don’t become a teen YouTube star without learning to deal with a fiery comments section. “I feel like I’ve always had thick skin doing this job,” she says. “There’s a screenshot from years ago: Someone commented on my video saying my hair was really curly, and the comment was like, ‘You don’t look good with curly hair.’ And I replied, ‘Yeah, I do.’” She’s more concerned about what her less experienced castmates are in store for: “It’s a bigger adjustment for them to go from sharing nothing to sharing everything on your socials and reality TV,” she says.

Still, when the show premieres, Ovard will be on vacation in Mexico with Bri, Billy, and her children, with plans to turn off her phone and lie on the beach. Oh, and Ferris is joining them, too. “We’re in a pretty good spot right now,” she tells me happily, as her car gets closer to home. “It’s definitely a unique relationship, but all three of us are willing to do anything we can to make him feel more comfortable and good with the situation that we’re in.”

The Mormon Wives franchise has already proved itself to be an effective star-launching vehicle: Just ask Whitney Leavitt, who leveraged her participation into starring roles on Broadway. But with everything her family’s going through, Ovard isn’t interested in a career change or world domination: “I’ve done this for 16 years now, and I’m transparently looking to keep this going for as long as I can,” she says. “I just want to spend time with my kids and be able to work the least amount possible.”

But like a great reality star, she knows how to keep you watching: “I feel like I’m slowly gathering the strength to be the person that I want to be again, and to show up for friends and myself,” she says, as we talk about what viewers might see on a potential second season. “Even getting through these press days, I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, I did it.’ I can do hard things.”

items.title: Exclusive: Jesse Kove Teases Whitney Leavitt’s “Raw Talent” In Her 1st Movie Role
items.description: Keeping up with Whitney Leavitt’s post-#MomTok resume feels like you’re making a list and checking it twice. Her last year was a dizzying run from Dancing with the Stars to Broadway, The Traitors, and her own forthcoming reality show. This holiday season, the
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: Keeping up with Whitney Leavitt’s post-#MomTok resume feels like you’re making a list and checking it twice. Her last year was a dizzying run from Dancing with the Stars to Broadway, The Traitors, and her own forthcoming reality show. This holiday season, the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star is putting her own spin on a beloved pop-culture tradition: the holiday rom-com.

All for Christmas stars Leavitt and Jesse Kove as Winona and Luke, a podcaster and craftsman who work together on a renovation project — as seen in Bustle’s exclusive behind-the-scenes images ahead. At first, Winona doesn’t quite see Luke as romance material. But unbeknownst to her, he’s the very same man she just matched with through a dating-app partnership.
Beyond that delightful You’ve Got Mail-esque twist, Kove tells Bustle the movie “feels like one of those warm-hearted ’90s rom-coms.”

Before filming, Kove wasn’t too familiar with Leavitt’s work on The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives. But the actor — whose own resume spans action, romance, and beyond — had previously worked with director and producer Jake Helgren on projects such as The Holiday Proposal Plan, and welcomed the opportunity to star opposite Leavitt in her first film role.

“Whitney has so much raw talent. She was able to put all that energy into this project,” Kove says, noting that even though Leavitt had just come from the rigorous competition of Dancing with the Stars, she was more than game for the festive film at hand. “She was so looking forward to showing up and being there for the crew, and also for her character. She and I did a lot of laughing along the way.”
Indeed, practical jokes abounded. The pair filmed each other in playfully off-guard moments, and Kove was sure to bring up Leavitt’s DWTS run while filming a dance scene.

For Kove, Leavitt’s sense of humor was one of the gifts of working together — something he’s definitely down to do again. “I was so delightfully surprised at her attention to detail and how funny she is,” he says. “She’s so quirky and silly, which I didn’t expect.”

Expect that feeling to translate on screen when All for Christmas streams Nov. 24 on Netflix. “I want viewers to feel joy when they watch this movie because it is filled with a lot of love,” Kove says. “It’s also about giving people second chances, which is a great aspect of the movie as well.”

And that’s coming from a certified rom-com fan — as Kove names Love Actually, The Holiday, and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days as just a few of his favorite titles. His only tip for watching this one? “Make sure when you do, that you’re all snuggled up under a blanket,” he says. “And you get some candles, maybe a glass of wine, and just enjoy.”

items.title: Exclusive: Mckenna Grace Says There’s A ‘Hunger Games’ Easter Egg Everyone Missed
items.description: You Actually Missed One Of Mckenna Grace’s Press Tour Easter Eggs
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: You Actually Missed One Of Mckenna Grace’s Press Tour Easter Eggs
The actor unpacks the hidden meaning in one of her Hunger Games premiere ’fits.

Mckenna Grace is turning her press tour for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping into a master class in Panem-inspired fashion. Joining method-dressing icons like Zendaya and Jenna Ortega, the 20-year-old actor — and franchise superfan (remember her viral Peeta Mellark edits?) — has been serving nod after nod to the OG trilogy, proving she knows the lore by heart.

With the help of her stylist Molly Dickson, Grace has already channeled Katniss Everdeen, Effie Trinket, Lucy Gray Baird, and even the second Quarter Quell arena. While fans have been quick to decode nearly every Easter egg, one major reference flew completely under the radar — and it happens to be the one closest to home.

At last month’s Sydney premiere, Grace stepped out in a custom lavender mermaid gown by Vera Wang HAUTE, crafted from decadent macramé lace and featuring oversize, hand-cut silk organza flowers blooming over one shoulder strap. Fans immediately flooded the label’s comments, comparing her to Rapunzel and begging Disney to cast her as the live-action princess, while others guessed it was an Effie nod. Plot twist: The real inspo was her own SOTR character, Maysilee Donner. Grace herself confirms it.

“Most days I have, like, birds or butterflies or flowers in my hair,” she tells Bustle, before singling out her Sydney look as an extra-special Easter egg. “One thing I was excited about was ... I wore this purple dress in Australia that was a nod to Maysilee.”

Eagle-eyed fans who’ve watched the official trailers might already recognize the palette. In the footage, Maysilee is reaped wearing a lavender minidress — fittingly elevated for a District 12 merchant’s daughter — complete with an A-line silhouette, a contrasting floral collar, and a bow-clad belt.

But the color wasn’t the only Maysilee-coded detail — the flowers adorning her Vera Wang gown were a nod to her character too. During the reaping, Maysilee accessorized by stacking necklaces with floral pendants and pinning a chamomile flower onto her lapel. (She’s a known accessory girlie. According to SOTR lore, she was the OG owner of the Mockingjay pin Katniss eventually inherited.)

To bring that floral motif to life on the red carpet, Grace went all in. “All the flowers in my hair were real flowers, which was really fun,” she says, adding, “At the end of the night, I was picking them all out. In the morning, I had all these wilted flowers on my floor.”

Still, thanks to the butterfly clip in her hair and the gown’s voluminous strap, Grace agrees that those Effie theories weren’t totally off base. “It also did remind me of Effie a bit,” she admits. Two Panem icons in one look? Truly Capitol-worthy.

items.title: Uma Thurman Doesn’t Believe In ‘Work-Life Balance’: ‘No Thanks’
items.description: The Dexter: Resurrection star has always sliced her own path through Hollywood (even if she’s secretly a softie). Now, with her kids mostly grown and a slate full of big-swing roles, she’s going “full throttle.”
items.author: Maggie Bullock
paragraphs: The Dexter: Resurrection star has always sliced her own path through Hollywood (even if she’s secretly a softie). Now, with her kids mostly grown and a slate full of big-swing roles, she’s going “full throttle.”

Uma Thurman was still a young child when she became fixated on the idea that she needed to formulate a life plan. The daughter of a Buddhist scholar and a former model turned psychotherapist, she grew up in a household where the intellectual stakes were high, and an independent streak was encouraged. “Both my parents were and are, in their own ways, very remarkable… unique, self-created individuals,” she says.

“I just had a sense that I was going to be providing for myself, and that there was no net,” Thurman says, with a shrug. “You know how kids get a bug in their head? I got a bug in my head. Like, ‘Oh, this isn’t going to last forever. I’ll make a move. I’ll do something.’”

Within three minutes of logging into our Zoom call, it is clear that Thurman is not one to linger on the surface of things. Sitting in her home office in Manhattan surrounded by framed black and white images, silver tchotchkes, and bookshelves that look like they’re actually in use, she is fresh from a shower, with combed-back wet hair and skin that looks fresh-scrubbed, save lingering traces of black eyeliner. As she talks, she gestures with her famously attenuated hands, revealing nails that are cut short and varnished a color that — even if it wasn’t being worn by Uma Thurman herself — many of us still think of as a Mia Wallace-esque noir.

At 56, the mother of three (her youngest is a high school freshman, while 24-year-old Levon and 28-year-old Maya Hawke are actors in their own right) has a slight gravelly edge to her once-flutelike voice, and an earned wisdom to her gaze. Otherwise, though, Thurman appears to be aging exactly the way one might expect from a bona fide movie star with her genetic advantages. Which is to say barely at all.

It’s hard not to feel a little starstruck by her presence, even when, technically, you’re only looking at her face, with its instantly recognizable features, on a computer screen. “There’s nobody who doesn’t know who she is,” says Clyde Phillips, the veteran TV creator behind the original Dexter and its reboot, currently featuring Thurman in her latest role, that of an ice-cold henchwoman in Season 2 of Dexter: Resurrection. “She’s iconic.”

On the show’s set, Thurman’s icon power took some getting used to. Dexter himself, Michael C. Hall — a TV icon in his own right — recalls comparing notes with Season 1 co-star Krysten Ritter “about our struggle to get over the fact that Uma Thurman was there.” Even Phillips, who recruited her to the show and, after two seasons working together now considers Thurman a good buddy, says he still has to pinch himself on occasion. At a large, complicated shoot in Times Square earlier this year, he remembers people “walking by going, ‘Holy sh*t, that’s Uma Thurman!’” He understands the feeling. “I was at her birthday party, and I’m thinking, ‘Holy sh*t! I’m in Uma Thurman’s house.’”
“I was missing in action with focus on the home front for the last 28 years. Now, my children are still in first position, but they can share the stage a little.”

Regarding that grand childhood plan of hers: Thurman’s father, Robert Thurman, who died at age 84 in June this year, was a Harvard Phd who became a professor at Amherst College in leafy western Massachusetts, where Thurman and her three brothers largely grew up. He went on to found the Tibet House — an organization dedicated to preserving Tibetan culture — alongside Richard Gere and Philip Glass. Suffice it to say that the family as a whole was academic, progressive, formidable. “Everybody was brilliant and getting, like, perfect SAT scores,” she says.

Thurman didn’t feel brilliant. It wasn’t until well into motherhood, when she was filling out a form about her own educational development in service of one of her kids, that she realized she hadn’t been able to read “a book with more words than pictures” until fourth grade. It was “a funny light bulb,” she says. “I was absolutely dyslexic.” Eventually, she says, “a dyslexic will crack the code, and years later, missing foundational pieces, they will read,” she says. Today, she loves reading. But she still experiences dysgraphia (the transposition of letters) and has difficulty with spelling and grammar. “It chases you all the way.”

As a kid, this left her frustrated and confused. She was obviously intelligent. “I could understand everything,” she says, “until you took the sound away, or the visual cue.” This left her with an “early feeling of being stupid.” That’s the kind of idea that leaves a mark. Convinced that she “couldn’t shine academically,” she knew that her big plan, whatever it may be, was going to have to be something totally different from her family background.

At 15, she left her Massachusetts boarding school on her own for New York City, where she moved into a studio apartment and started modeling. (This wasn’t as controversial on the home front as you might imagine, since it was something of a family tradition: Thurman’s mother had left home at 16 to pursue her own modeling career.) Modeling was not the grand plan: It was always intended to be a brief stepping stone to acting, and that’s what it became.

By the time her high school classmates were packing up their lava lamps for college, Thurman was playing Cécile, the porcelain-skinned virgin deflowered — and seriously turned on — by a scheming John Malkovich in Dangerous Liaisons. At 20, she played the wife of Henry Miller and the lover of his lover, Anaïs Nin, steaming up 1930s Paris in Henry & June, a movie that made history as the first ever to receive an NC-17 rating.

From the jump, Thurman displayed both a stunning willingness to go there and an innate onscreen magnetism that went beyond her unusual looks — the deep-spaced Bambi eyes and lit-from-within golden coloring. No matter the role, the co-star, or the genre, when Thurman is onscreen, it’s hard to look at anything else. For Hall, this je ne sais quoi is Thurman’s ability to “achieve dynamic movement in the middle of absolute stillness,” he says. “Where there’s nothing demonstrably happening, and yet so much seems to be going on.”
Imagine a light bulb, Hall continues: “Even though its light seems kind of static, there’s a lot going on to make it shine. She’s just got that thing.”
“I wasn’t looking to Xerox an archetypal woman for people. I wanted to be an actor who explored different things.”

She was just 23 when she joined forces with the creative partner of a lifetime, Quentin Tarantino, in the role of a lifetime. As Pulp Fiction’s aforementioned dark-fingernailed heroine, she drank milkshakes and did the twist, cool as a cucumber opposite John Travolta, a movie veteran who had made his name sliding across light-up dance floors. This past August, Mia Wallace’s white button-down shirt and black flares — the simplest, chicest costume ever to make it into the Halloween hall of fame — sold at auction for $64,000, more than twice its estimated pre-auction value.

Tarantino worked for a decade on the follow-up, centered on a character they created together. As The Bride, she swashbuckled her way through Kill Bill Vol.1 and 2. If Pulp Fiction made her a movie star, Kill Bill cemented her legacy, making her the female action hero of a generation. Years later, her cinematic descendant, Charlize Theron — equally tall, equally golden, equally badass — would tell Jimmy Kimmel that Thurman was the “OG” of the genre — the “sensei.”
Kimmel eagerly agreed: “She should have won the Academy Award for Kill Bill, right?”
Theron’s reply: “A hundred percent. Men get a lot of credit for these movies.”

What Uma Thurman did to prepare for Kill Bill was herculean in a way that, like so much of her early work, hits different circa 2026. Not only did she train for months to swing katanas, shoot guns, and perform three different styles of martial arts — she did it all starting when her son, Levon, was just 8 weeks old.

Thurman trained with “a master who you actually called master,” she recalls. The first time she walked into the training gym, infant son in one arm, his team stared at “this out-of-shape mother standing in front of them,” she says. “They had this kind of oh-my-God reaction — like, we have to work to work with that?” Among action-movie heads, the film’s biggest fight scene is canon. In the long, bloody sword battle sequence known as the “Crazy 88,” Thurman single handedly eviscerated an army of at least 40 stuntmen. All while taking breaks to breastfeed. (When I marvel at this physical feat — how did she do that? — she demurs. Tarantino, after all, had created the movie around her and then timed the shoot around her pregnancy — of course she was going to do whatever it took to live up to the role. And besides, “People are nursing in flooding tents. Is what I did anything special? No.”)

Given all that, it may surprise you to learn that Thurman is secretly a bit of a softie. More than anything, she says, she loves romantic comedies. She’s read all of Nora Ephron’s books, and when she discovered that Ephron recorded the audio for a lot of them, she listened to them, too. “I’m sad that I’ve already listened to them, and I don’t have them to look forward to,” she says. “I know this makes me seem very corny and sentimental.”

There are few true romantic comedies on Thurman’s resume. One is 2005’s underrated Prime, in which she plays the “older” love interest of the son of her own therapist (played by Meryl Streep). Then there’s 1996’s The Truth About Cats & Dogs, in which she plays the obstacle, not the lead: In a Cyrano-esque spin, she’s the Helen of Troy who turns Ben Chaplin’s head away from “regular woman” Janeane Garofalo. Thurman is matter of fact about why she wasn’t cast in more rom-coms: At 5-foot-11, she did not fit the mold. “Leading ladies couldn’t be taller than leading men. You would not be considered, bottom line.” (She’s too polite to specify which projects she lost out on because of stature.)

There was an upside to not being, as she puts it, “a typeable type.” It forced her to become versatile, which ultimately defined her career. “Also, I wasn’t looking to Xerox an archetypal woman for people,” she says. “I wanted to be an actor who explored different things.” If her resume runs the gamut — from art house films to popcorn movies to serious theater, action to drama and back again — she says that’s very much by design.

Last year, no one knew whether Dexter, the serial killer drama that refuses to die, could or should be revived. The original show ended in 2013 after eight seasons; since then, the franchise has given us a prequel (Dexter: Original Sin) and a sequel (Dexter: New Blood). Still, Hall thought his “killer with a conscience” had work left to do. And Showtime, for which Dexter: New Blood had turned out to be the most-watched show in the network’s history, was ready to roll the dice.

To up the ante, Phillips and longtime co-writer Scott Reynolds assembled a murderer’s row of co-stars, including the aforementioned Ritter, plus Neil Patrick Harris, Eric Stonestreet, and Peter Dinklage. The latter played a twisted billionaire tech wizard (timely) whose dirty secret is a basement museum in which he stores his passion project: collecting the gory “trophies” of noted serial killers.

Phillips says that in addition to trying to keep Dexter dangerous, funny, and vulnerable, he always wants to keep its audience “leaning forward,” which meant bringing a certain icon into the fold. Over Zoom, he demonstrates, bringing his face 2 inches closer to the screen, as if to get a better look. “When I see Uma Thurman in a television show, I go like this. I lean forward. I pay attention.”

The definitional quality of Dexter Morgan is that he’s a serial killer who is not a lunatic — he operates by a strict code, plying his craft, so to speak, only on evildoers he thinks deserve to die. He’s the Robin Hood of serial killers. Which doesn’t mean he doesn’t relish the job.

As Hall puts it, Thurman naturally “presided over” every scene as Charlotte “Charley” Brown, a character who was introduced last season as the terrifyingly composed body woman of Dinklage’s billionaire. She’s a decorated former Ranger in the U.S. Army with a law degree from Harvard and, in Season 1 at least, a ruthlessly sleek blond bob. (Phillips and Reynolds are diehard Tarantino fans, but it was total coincidence that the show’s costume designer happens to be Cat Thomas, the same person who came up with The Bride’s indelible yellow tracksuit.) As Thurman sees it, Charley is “a highly trained professional warrior” who has “done bad in service of her country,” and then, in retirement, found herself in the unfortunate position of being the right-hand woman of a raging psycho — who happens to be paying top dollar for her invalid mother’s medical care. (Talk about golden handcuffs.)

“Charley’s job turned into this toxic, dark, sick thing that she’s locked into by financial need,” Thurman says. “And she hates herself for it.” But like Dexter, she also seems to take a certain job satisfaction in, say, deftly bludgeoning a guy with a nail-studded baseball bat, just because he touched her shoulder.

It’s delicious to watch Charley doing dirty work of her own while maintaining a withering disdain for the bloodthirsty killers in her midst — exhibiting a glamorous chill that even Dexter can’t resist. “In spite of himself, Dexter is captivated by her,” says Hall. “That’s not something I had to manufacture. I just sort of… rest in the tractor beam.”
“People who are obsessed with ‘work-life’ balance — no thanks. I want to be fulfilled in action, and I want to be comfortable at rest.”

Online, the only audible complaint about Thurman’s performance in Season 1 was that there wasn’t enough of it. The part was mostly written by the time Thurman signed on, and while Phillips was able to work a little more backstory into the part once she was on board — close viewers might even catch a nod to her hometown of Amherst — for Thurman fans, it was a bit of tease: Why hire Uma if you’re only going to give her a few minutes of screen time per episode?

Thurman, too, had doubts initially about whether there would be enough for her to do in Season 1. The whole season’s worth of scripts were largely stitched up by the time she read them, which Phillips says is part of his strategy: In the hiring process, it is much easier to sign legends like John Lithgow on to your serial killer project if they know “exactly where their character is going, and that we’re not going to f*ck them over in the end.” Thurman says being able to see the whole arc of Season 1 allowed her to recognize how good the show could be. The structure wasn’t just locked, she says. It was “perfect.”

“It’s funny, for someone who struggled with reading,” she says, to have become “a worshipper of writing.” With the benefit of a long career, she has learned that “so many times you get seduced by ‘Oh, it’s the creator of X,’ and you throw your piece of the puzzle at it. But it is the quality of the writing that creates the product. Period.”

Season 1 was widely received as a triumph. Season 2 debuted Oct. 30, cannily timed to spooky season, with episodes dropping weekly. One thing is clear so far: There’s much more Uma this time around. (It helps that most of her fellow shiny co-stars, Dinklage included, had been killed off by the end of Season 1.) Having snuck a peek at a couple of early episodes of Season 2, I tell Thurman that I still can’t tell if Charley is a force for good or for evil. Is she about to decapitate Dexter… or bed him? “Could really go either way,” the actor says with a small, wicked smile.

Every time Thurman’s name is announced in a new project, there is a little ripple of online excitement: Where has she been? But the idea that she has taken a long break is a misconception. Her IMDb page shows that she never stopped working.

That said, for a very long time, she’s also had another big job to manage. “Until two years ago,” she says, “I had a child under 12 in my home. I was sort of missing in action with focus on the home front for the last 28 years — trying to continue getting some work in for myself, and not let my career die.” For nearly three decades, she says, her career wasn’t in first position; her kids were. And now? “Now, my children are still in first position, but they can share the stage a little.”

Within the last year, Thurman passed two major milestones in any woman’s life — defining moments as a daughter and as a mother that occurred only months apart. She said goodbye to her father, and she watched her daughter get married. On Valentine’s Day, Stranger Things alum Maya married her longtime beau, musician Christian Lee Hutson, in a true winter-white New York City affair. “I enjoyed every part of it,” Thurman says, grinning. The bride wore custom Prada, a nod that seemed to recall her mother’s long history with the fashion house. One of Thurman’s own most iconic fashion moments was standing on the Oscars stage in 1995, luminous in a pale lilac Prada column with a single strand of diamonds glinting around her neck. For fashion history types, the moment is seminal: The unfussy look defined the minimalism of the era, and Thurman was one of the first stars to put Prada on that grandest of stages. (“Mrs. P is an icon,” Thurman says, who has “done more than most people on the planet for artists and artisans. She is a cultural institution in loafers.”)

Today, Thurman says she’s enjoying a sort of rebirth that may sound familiar to other women her age, even ones who aren’t movie stars. She’s finding liberation in “letting go of… expectations that younger women and actresses have to carry.”

This doesn’t mean she’s looking to take it easy. “I want to go back to it with full throttle,” she says. Thurman has always had what she calls an “old-growth hardworking mentality. I’m happier if I’m working harder.” These days, in some ways, she finds herself working even harder than ever, putting energy into being ultra-prepared, but approaching projects with a lighter touch: “I work harder but easier.”

She gently rolls her eyes at “people who are obsessed with ‘work-life’ balance,” she says. “To me, they’re, like, New Agey. Like, no thanks.” Woo-woo is not for her. “I want to be fulfilled in action, and I want to be comfortable at rest.”

Given her Buddhist roots, one might expect Thurman to be somewhat New Age-y herself. “You would think so,” she acknowledges, a little sardonically. “But you might also think that I would have a little bit of a New Age phobia.”

A new sense of freedom seems to have come with an increased willingness to take swings on surprising projects, ones that aren’t always quite as gilded as her earlier fare, maybe, but have the potential to be even more fun. Dexter is one example. “I was late to TV,” she says. Now she’s making up for lost time.

Next up, she’ll reprise her role in the follow-up to Prime’s smash gay rom-com Red, White & Royal Blue, in which she plays against her own untypable type, as an American president with a go-big-or-go-home Southern accent. “She’s very nice, Ellen,” Thurman says — making the point, with a note of irony, that not all of her characters are mercenary killers. “She’s just a really great mother and a very kind-hearted president. Totally different flavor.” Listening to Thurman drawllll out Ellen’s syllables, it’s easy to see what she means about enjoying a new kind of freedom.

As a young superstar, with the eyes of the world on her every move, award season always pending, and studio honchos counting every dollar she brought in, “I used to apply so much pressure on myself,” she says. “Nothing was ever good enough.” She knows that’s normal at that stage of life; nevertheless, “it’s kind of unbearable to be like that.” Today, she says, “I feel freed up.”
