items.title: Hayley Atwell Of 'Much Ado About Nothing' On Her 4 Favorite Plays & Musicals
items.description: Callback With Hayley Atwell
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: Callback With Hayley Atwell
Ahead of her Broadway debut opposite Tom Hiddleston, the actor reflects on the magic of live theater and the performances that have made her fall in love with it.

Hayley Atwell is an accomplished veteran of the London stage, but now, the actor — perhaps best known for her portrayal of Agent Peggy Carter in the Marvel Cinematic Universe — is making her Broadway debut, and she’s ready to party. Or at least throw a damn good one.

“We’re here to essentially host the audience in having an amazing party,” the actor, 44, says of the Shakespearean comedy Much Ado About Nothing, which opens Nov. 19 at the Winter Garden Theatre after a successful West End run. “We get to do it again, but in this completely different environment and a different kind of audience, which I expect will be even more raucous than in London.”

Co-starring fellow MCU star Tom Hiddleston as Benedick, the play is directed by Jamie Lloyd, who has been praised for his reimagining of works including Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Sunset Blvd. and Evita, the latter of which moves into the Winter Garden after Much Ado wraps up on Jan. 10. Much Ado received accolades in London for its high-energy campiness (picture lots of pink confetti and strobe lights) — something Atwell is here for.

She describes the production as “visceral, juicy, and gorgeous” while remaining rooted in the text. “The way [Jamie Lloyd] pitched it to me when he first offered me the role was, ‘It’s a massive party,’” she says. “Everyone’s having a great time. Some people drink a little bit too much. They stay a little bit too long. They have some feelings. Someone takes things too personally. Arguments break out. Confusions occur. We flirt with the wrong person.”

She’s also heartened by what she sees as a growing desire for the collective experience that you can only get by attending live events like a Broadway play. “When you have human beings in a room, it feels different. We can get more of a sense of each other when we’re sharing body language and just the molecules in the room changing because someone new has walked in or walked out,” she says. “That makes plays a very visceral, kind of immersive experience.
“I want to feel more alive and more connected and less numbed out from the sort of content that can kind of bore into my eyeballs that I realize I didn’t really consciously consent to.”
Ahead, Atwell shares five plays and musicals that have done just that for her.
Her first selection is August Osage County, Tracy Letts’ 2008 Pulitzer-winning dark comedy. The play follows a fractured Oklahoma family that is forced to reunite when their patriarch goes missing.

“I love plays that have a really strong ensemble, and there is a sense of real company on stage that have worked together intimately, intricately over a rehearsal period to understand the heart of the play,” she says. “But also understand their own dynamics within each other and how you always have to keep the ball in the air, and that the performance is only as strong as the people that you play with.”

Atwell learned the power of a strong ensemble during a run of Dry Powder in London. Her character, a private equity partner, often had to interrupt her casemates. “I remember coming in really hot, beginning a monologue and then realizing within about the first three lines of dialogue that I’d skipped three pages. And my fellow actors are looking at me and the terror in their eyes,” she says. “I had to keep on going and get to the end of my monologue and then try and work out what we needed to then improvise to backtrack to make sure the audience were at the same place in the script that we were.”
Sunday in the Park with George

Her second pick is Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s 1984 musical Sunday in the Park with George, which follows a fictionalized Georges Seurat. Atwell first saw the play in the West End revival starring Daniel Evans and Jenna Russell nearly 20 years ago.

“That musical encapsulates the creative process, the struggle for an artist’s identity, the struggle to have an artistic career and to maintain personal relationships. You can be selfish and also generous and fully focused on a creative career, and yet the cost of that can sometimes mean that personal relationships. In this musical, that’s where they start to falter,” she says. “And I find the tension of that really beautiful.”

Her third show is The Rocky Horror Show, the 1973 cult-classic rock musical by Richard O’Brien. “I saw it first when I was a child, probably way too young, didn’t really understand a lot of the ideas behind it, but I just loved the energy and I loved particularly Tim Curry’s performance — so magnetic,” she says. “And for me, it was about freedom. And although it’s also like a homage to the B movies and sci-fi films of back in the day, it’s very camp and it’s ridiculous and it’s silly and it’s weird and it’s bizarre.”

Her fourth selection is Shakespeare’s Hamlet, which Atwell fell in love with during a 2018 Robert Icke adaptation starring Andrew Scott. “I saw Andrew Scott playing Hamlet four times — in a play I know very well! And yet when I saw Andrew do it, I felt like I was hearing it for the first time and I felt like I was hearing it made up then and there,” she says. “He talked so openly to the audience. He felt like he was talking to every single individual in the auditorium.”

Her final pick is Medea, which Atwell saw starring Helen McCrory at the National Theatre in 2014. The play, written by Euripides in 431 BCE, tells the story of Medea, a sorceress who sacrifices her children in an act of revenge against her husband.

“Medea I think is one of the hardest roles in the canon for women to play because I think it’s one of the major taboos of our world and our society,” she says. “The idea that a woman could harm her child or her children — and how to have that as your protagonist, how a woman has to portray someone who does the absolute unspeakable, unthinkable, and that we’re having to want to engage with that feels an impossible task.”

Atwell feels McCrory handled the responsibility of Medea with grace. “Helen had, for me, as an actor such formidable courage in exposing human failings and human pain,” she says, “and how great pain and things being done to an individual can have such a devastating effect on the psyche, that then they become capable of doing the unspeakable.”

items.title: Refinery29 Loves: Our Favorite Fashion & Beauty Buys From October
items.description: Refinery29 Loves: Our Favorite Fashion & Beauty Buys From October
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: Refinery29 Loves: Our Favorite Fashion & Beauty Buys From October
Cécred Temple Oud Hair Perfume

"As soon as I tried Cécred, I fell in love with how it made my hair feel, but what I loved even more was how it made my hair smell. The signature Temple Oud scent is this beautiful blend of bergamot, night-blooming jasmine, rich oud, and warm sandalwood. So when they launched it as a hair perfume, I was immediately sold. The lightweight mist refreshes my hair without weighing it down, and because hair naturally holds onto fragrance, the scent lingers throughout the day. It’s my favorite way to elevate my everyday routine with a spritz of fragrance that follows me wherever I go." — Brooke DeVard, Chief Content Officer
Stila All Fire Liquid Eye Shadow & Kajal Eye Liner Duo

"As a die-hard Hunger Games girlie, I'm already counting down the days until Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters. So when one of my longtime favorite makeup brands, Stila, unveiled a collaboration inspired by the upcoming film, I had to get my hands on it. My standout pick from the collection is the All Fire Liquid Eye Shadow & Kajal Eye Liner Duo, featuring a shimmery bronze liquid eyeshadow and a smoky black eye pencil. (Fun fact: The name is a nod to Haymitch's romance with his District 12 sweetheart, Lenore Dove.) Together, they make the easiest two-step eye look: I sweep a wash of bronze across my lids and tightline my upper waterline for an effortlessly pretty daytime look, then build up the shimmer and intensity for date night." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer
Bath & Body Works Worth Wanting Eau de Parfum

"I'll always have a soft spot for Bath & Body Works. While the brand usually scratches a nostalgic itch for me, its new Everyday Luxuries collection — a lineup of fragrances inspired by designer scents — has seriously impressed me as a perfume snob. Dare I say, some of these affordable alternatives might even beat their high-end counterparts? My favorite of the bunch is Worth Wanting, which has quickly become my signature scent for fall. With notes of juicy stone fruits, delicate lily, and whipped honey, it's fruity, cozy, and just the right amount of indulgent. Despite its decadent-sounding notes, the fragrance feels surprisingly fresh and airy, making it just as lovely worn solo as it is layered with something woodier for a more earthy, grounded vibe. Proof that smelling expensive doesn't have to be." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer
Lounge ContourSoft Cinch Zip-Up Jacket

"The weather is dropping below 70 degrees, which means I’m swapping my tank-and-shorts activewear for warmer sets. Right now, I'm reaching for Lounge's ContourSoft sets. The buttery-soft fabric of these fitted leggings keeps my legs covered but not constricted. Meanwhile, the cinch zip-up jacket allows me to cover up or remove layers depending on fall’s unpredictable temperature changes. I’ve been wearing the set in the shade of dark chocolate, but I’m seriously eyeing cherry lacquer, too." — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
Dr. Loretta Barrier Enhancing Milky Essence

"As someone with dry skin, I’m forever chasing that juicy, dewy glow, especially during the fall and winter months when my skin wants to drink up every ounce of moisture it can get. This milky essence from Dr. Loretta has quickly become my favorite part of my morning skincare routine. I love pressing it into my skin before sunscreen for an instant hit of hydration that leaves my complexion looking plump, bouncy, and deliciously dewy. It’s packed with skin-loving ingredients like niacinamide, ectoin, and glycerin to support the skin barrier, lock in moisture, and soothe irritation. It’s lightweight, layers beautifully, and gives me that fresh, hydrated glow I’m always trying to achieve without a drop of makeup." — Brooke DeVard, Chief Content Officer
Reformation Clara Cashmere Crew Cardigan

"If you haven’t heard, purple is trending right now, and I’ve jumped on the bandwagon with this cute cashmere cardigan from Reformation. I love Reformation’s sweaters, and this is the perfect layering piece dressed down with sweats and a tee or to add some color to one of my all-black outfits." — Lisa Dionisio, Homepage & Newsletter Director
Salon Perfect Chill Short Square Press-On Nails

"I've always had a love-hate relationship with press-on nails. In theory, salon-worthy designs without the appointment, dry time, or hefty price tag sound like a dream. In reality? I've had nails pop off within hours of application. (Opening a can of soda? Forget about it.) So when I didn't have time for a manicure before an out-of-town wedding, I tossed a pack of these champagne cat-eye Salon Perfect press-ons into my carry-on and hoped for the best. Not only did they survive a night of dinner and dancing, but they stayed put for nearly two weeks. I'm not exaggerating: It took a full 14 days for a single nail to jump ship, at which point I finally removed the set. Since then, I've tried several more designs — including a fall-inspired ombré set I'm wearing as I type this — and the staying power continues to blow me away. At just $8 a pack, consider me a press-on convert." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer
PS Goodnight Printed Ruffle Short Sleeve Pajama Set

"Walking into my home feels like I'm entering the set of my favorite period dramas, just with some Puerto Rican banderas sprinkled in. I've mixed second-hand, vintage trinkets with new furniture inspired by a previous epoch to curate a home that would belong to a Latina Jane Austen. Well, everything except for my jammies. I'm trying to change that, trying to have my nightwear reflect the mood I’ve set for other parts of my home life. And I'm starting with PS Goodnight's Printed Ruffle Short Sleeve Pajama set, a baby-blue printed lightweight woven fabric set with short puff sleeves and ruffled trimming. I’m loving it!" — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
Goldie Tees Audrey Cardigan

"Cardigan season is my favorite (it’s also a great Taylor Swift song!). What I love about cardigans is that they're timeless, so investing in quality styles won't just last for years to come but will look great however they're worn with changing trends. My black Goldie Tee’s Audrey Cardigan is lightweight, has some stretch, and is made from ribbed knit fabric, so it pairs beautifully with denim pants, fitted skirts, or just sweatpants during cool, cozy days indoors." — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
YSL Loveshine Plumping Lip Oil

"I first discovered YSL's Loveshine Plumping Lip Oil last year during a trip to Marrakech with the brand, where I got to see the chili peppers and ginger used in the formula growing in the brand’s own community gardens. Fast-forward to this fall, when YSL unveiled a coffee-inspired collection featuring new shades of the glossy lip treatment. My favorite? Cold Brew Craze, a sheer, caramel-brown hue that's basically cozy season in lip gloss form. You can definitely feel a subtle warming sensation from the peppers, but it's far from uncomfortable — and the plumping effect is noticeable without leaving your lips looking overly red or swollen. I've been layering it over my go-to nude lip liner for the ultimate cozy-girl lip combo, and suffice it to say, I'm obsessed." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer

"During a recent press trip to Germany, I was told a day before my flight that I’d be attending a ball and needed to pack a gown. Where was I going to find a dress after work that was appropriate for a European-style ball? Turns out there was one hanging in my closet. I was already planning on wearing JJ's House's Felia dress for my friend's wedding, but its floor-length, mermaid silhouette, ruffle chiffon slit, and deep burgundy shade made it equally perfect for a fancy dance. With some makeup and accessory changes, I felt beautiful and comfortable both days, in the same affordable gown, just styled slightly differently." — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
Anastasia Beverly Hills Genesis Eyeshadow Palette

"It’s been a minute since I’ve had an Anastasia Beverly Hills palette, but full glam is back and so is ABH. As I lean into my pale girl era for winter, I keep reaching for these soft taupes and dusty roses that don’t pull too warm on my neutral skin tone. They make for a gorgeous everyday blush-toned look, and the generous mirror is the cherry on top for travel. I keep getting compliments every time I pair it with a super cool-toned pink blush." — Taylor Loren, Social Media Director
Live Tinted Magic Blur Primer Stick

"As someone with large pores and texture, I’m a bit of a primer enthusiast, and I can honestly say this is the best one I’ve ever used. I don’t know what kind of magic makes it glide onto my skin like that (I’m not the beauty editor on our team!), but the application feels so nice, and my makeup looks so much better with it. Plus, the stick format just makes sense: no primer-covered hands, just a smooth, beautiful base. I’m obsessed and telling everyone!" — Taylor Loren, Social Media Director
Mario Badescu Hydrogel Under Eye Patches

"Okay, these eye patches aren’t new, but they were new to me, so I had to shout them out. I’ve never been a huge fan of eye patches because I thought they were all a scam, but these ones have been a lifesaver as the weather gets colder and my skin gets drier (in fact, I’m wearing them as I write this!). It always shocks me just how cooling they are. Plus, I love the thin jelly consistency. After use, I notice that my under-eye area is a bit less puffy, a bit brighter, and my fine lines aren’t as noticeable thanks to them being soaked in hyaluronic acid and niacinamide goodness." — Taylor Loren, Social Media Director
Charlotte Tilbury Exagger-Eyes Waterproof Eyeshadow Stick

"I’m someone who typically uses my bronzer and blush as my eyeshadow (because I’m usually lazy), but when I tried this eyeshadow stick at a Charlotte Tilbury masterclass, I was converted. The crayon shape and creamy formula make it so easy and quick to swipe over my eyelids. I have a few sparkly shades now, and they make the perfect no-muss, no-fuss eye (and highlighter if you have a shade light enough) for glam makeup looks. I’m excited to use them during the holidays for an extra festive touch." — Victoria Montalti, Senior Fashion Commerce Writer
Gola Classics Women's Corva Snake Sneakers

"I own a few Gola sneakers, and the newest addition to my collection is the green snakeskin print Corva shoes. I wear a lot of green and animal prints are basically neutrals at this point, so this pick was a no-brainer. They’re a great (surprisingly versatile) fall sneaker, but I can see myself wearing them cross-seasonally too." — Victoria Montalti, Senior Fashion Commerce Writer
Damson Madder Alphia Neck Tie Alpaca Blend Jumper

"Another Damson Madder piece has entered the chat. While I purchased a reversible Damson Madder jacket last month, I was gifted this sweater-and-scarf combo this month. The bright berry color is so striking and cheerful (and got me lots of compliments). I love that there’s a slit in the neckline for the scarf to slip into and stay in place all day, sans constant fidgeting. The wool is a bit more coarse than I had imagined because it looks fuzzy in photos, so I’ve simply added a short-sleeve top underneath for extra comfort." — Victoria Montalti, Senior Fashion Commerce Writer

items.title: 29 Holiday Gifts Refinery29 Readers Bought on Repeat in 2026
items.description: The Data Is In: These Are The Best Products To Gift, According To Readers
items.author: Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: The Data Is In: These Are The Best Products To Gift, According To Readers

This unisex robe has been a fan favorite, especially when it's been on sale. And luckily, with Refinery29's exclusive code REFINERY29, you can take 20% off the regular price right now! It's the perfect present for homebodies and those deserving of an at-home spa-like experience.
Coachtopia Alter/Ego Patchwork Small Slouchy Shoulder Bag

Back in June, we highlighted Coachtopia's first bag drop on resale platform Depop in our weekly collab coverage. And many readers clicked through this specific bag, hoping to cart it up. While it had sold out, it's back in stock on Coachtopia's Depop shop and ready to be gifted to any Gen Z giftee, handbag collector, or Coach fan.
Hermès 2 oz Barénia Intense Eau de Parfum

Fragrance expert Aamna Lone shared her favorite unique fragrances to stand out from the crowd. And the one that resonated most with readers was this Hermès perfume that Lone claims to be classy and head-turning. There are herbal and woody notes from oak, leather, and patchouli. And thanks to the "intense" formula option, one spray goes a long way and lasts a long time, giving you the most bang for your buck.
Maeve Imara Faux Suede Funnel Neck Jacket

It turns out many readers just needed this Maeve by Anthropologie suede jacket to upgrade their fall outfits. And we see this particular style as a top gift option to take giftees throughout the winter in style too. Find the chocolate brown option in petite and plus sizes too to cross more people off your list.
HigherDose Red Light Showerhead Filter

This showerhead came on top as one of the favorite luxury Valentine's Day gifts. But we bet that your giftee would love to receive it before February. I personally use the red-light ring on a shelf in my shower, but it comes with a shower head, which is meant to be combined to your spout for a luxurious, wellness-focused showering experience.
Free People Something Good Pull-On Barrel Pants

Bringing in over 40 sales, these trendy drawstring pants were one of the most-purchased products of 2026. And at under $100, they make for a great budget-friendly gift. The versatile pant can be dressed down to lounge around in or elevated with a button-down for the office. Pick between several colorways in the tiny pinstripe design before they sell out!
Charlotte Tilbury Matte Revolution Hydrating Lipstick

One of the most-purchased picks from Ulta's 21 Days of Beauty Sale back in September was this popular Charlotte Tilbury lipstick in festive packaging. While it may not currently be on sale, this hydrating lipstick and its sparkling case is sure to put a smile on your giftee's perfectly plump lips.
Old Navy x Altuzarra Knit Scarf

The top-performing collaboration of 2026 (among the many collabs taking over our feeds and shopping carts) was the Old Navy x Altuzarra collection by a long shot. The romantic, Gothic-inspired collection still has some styles left in stock, like this on-sale scarf, which allows you to cart up designer fashion for under $20.
Owala 32 oz FreeSip Stainless Steel Water Bottle

When we see Owala on sale, we definitely highlight it, and that's why these bottles were some of the top purchases from Amazon in 2026. While I own and love this burgundy color combo, there are tons of variations and sizes on sale on Amazon right now. And best of all, they're a practical gift that many types of giftees will actually appreciate receiving.
In Good Taste 2026 Wine Advent Calendar

Readers have been shopping for unique advent calendars since August, and this mini wine assortment has been a clear fan favorite. We also think it's a great gift for holiday hosts. The calendar features 24 mini wine bottles spanning red, white, rosé, and sparkling varieties to fit everyone's tastes.
Therabody TheraFace Mask Glo-LED Skincare Mask

Whether readers carted this editor-approved face mask at full price or while discounted for Nordstrom's Anniversary Sale, it's clear that the high-tech beauty tool was a luxurious gift for themselves or a very special someone. Beyond the red, blue, and infrared LED light treatments, there are also built-in vibration massage points to help relieve tension. It's the ultimate beauty-meets-wellness tool for your most deserving giftee.
Lululemon Everywhere Crossbody Bag 2L Metal Hardware

Aside from a few different Lululemon shorts, the brand's Everywhere crossbody bag (no, surprisingly not the typical Everywhere belt bag) was a top performer. If you need more convincing to cart this up, read Ruby Ford-Dunker's review of the crossbody bag, and why she thinks it's the perfect travel companion. Then, admire all the new colors and pick your favorite.
Damson Madder Reversible Jerry Crop Trench Coat

Last January, this versatile trench performed well with readers when shopping for winter coats, and somehow someway, it's still in stock! Your giftee can remove the triangle scarf or flip the jacket inside out to reveal an all-over plaid design. (I personally own Damson Madder's newer reversible barn jacket and can say it's worth every penny.)
Olive & June Builder Gel Kit

If you have a manicure enthusiast to shop for and a $50 budget to work with, consider this popular at-home gel builder. Hoshikawa reviewed the user-friendly kit back in 2025, but it continued to gain traction with readers after it was featured in our 2026 Beauty Innovator Awards. If your giftee already has an LED lamp at home, this is a thoughtful extension to their at-home mani collection.
Monica Vinader Alta Slim Huggie Hoop Earrings

You can never go wrong with gifting jewelry, and these hoops are reader-approved. We love that they're not your typical hoop shape but are still versatile enough for many people's aesthetics and that they can effortlessly go from everyday wear to special occasions.

Having sold nearly 1k times on Amazon, these Medicube toner pads were the overall bestselling product of 2026. The Amazon reader-favorite product never lets us down, and for under $20, it's worth trying if it's your first time hearing of it. Cart up the K-beauty gift for skincare obsessives or as a stocking stuffer for nearly anyone on your shopping list.
Comfrt Airplane Mode Travel Hoodie

From Senior Beauty Writer Karina Hoshikawa's review of Comfrt's travel hoodie to its subsequent features in several Carted roundups, readers haven't stopped purchasing it. Thanks to the unisex design, sleep mask attached to the hood, spacious front pocket, and extra hidden zippers on the sleeves, this style is an excellent gift for an avid traveler or a younger giftee. It's practical, comfy... and budget-friendly.
Calpak Polka Dot Evry Starter Bundle

Whether you're shopping for an avid traveler or younger giftee starting to embark on adventures, this bestselling suitcase bundle is an extremely thoughtful and practical gift. The set comes with a carry-on and a checked suitcase, plus several packing cubes and pouches in a sweet polka dot print. And at 50% off, it's hard to pass on.

If you're searching for something sexier, especially for a partner or to treat yourself, consider this Bellesa sex toy. After being featured in our best suction vibrator roundup, it's consistently convinced readers to cart it up month after month. The 4.8-star rating from over 1.8K reviews says it all. We also love the cute pink design and discreet, compact packaging that can easily slip into a holiday stocking.
Quince 100% Australian Shearling Earmuffs

Quince always finds itself as a top performer when it comes to gifts, and these shearling earmuffs were no exception. They're a luxe yet affordable find that's perfect for those who love outdoorsy winter activities... or who refuse to sacrifice style for warmth.
Nécessaire The Body Wash Duo Set

What's better than one Nécessaire body wash? Two! Yes, we love a backup. This duo set was a popular purchase after being featured as a Nordstrom Anniversary Sale beauty deal. But if you're looking for something even more gift-worthy, check out Nécessaire's new body sets (especially in the signature eucalyptus scent) on its website and at Sephora.
Cuyana Mini Heart Leather Case

If your love language is gift giving, what's more perfect than giving a heart? This heart-shaped pouch from beloved leather brand Cuyana is another Valentine's Day-coded gift to consider for the holiday season. This luxe under-$100 gift is great for holding toiletries and cosmetics, especially for travel, and the pebbled leather is easy to clean and keep pristine for years to come.
Adidas Originals x Asos Zebra Print Track Jacket with Peplum

Adidas Originals and Asos collaborated three times in 2026 alone, and the capsule collections have consistently resonated with readers. Lucky for you, the latest sporty-chic collab is still in stock, so you can cart up elevated track suits or athleisure sweaters for your most stylish friend.
Givenchy Very Irresistible Eau de Parfum

After diving into the fall fragrance trends predicted by master perfumer Alberto Morillas, readers overwhelmingly leaned towards one pick. From the fresh and outdoorsy "cool musks" trend, this Givenchy perfume with notes of roses, star anise, patchouli wood, and blackberry came out on top. And we promise it'll be a "very irresistible" present.
Frye & Co Miranda Patchwork Boot

After receiving these trendy patchwork boots myself, I included them in our weekend sale coverage for DSW, and readers seemed to like the boho-meets-Western design too. Inspired by the look of Frye boots, which typically cost around $500, this option is an on-trend, budget-friendly option for gifting season.
Viola Castellani Suede Printed Crocodile Belt Bag

Four years ago, I called out a leather coral variation of this bag as one of my most-used crossbodies, and today, it remains the truth. And readers seem to agree, because many have carted this style up. While several colorways have sold out, this suede croc-effect option is available, which is a luxe yet budget-friendly gift option.

If you're not sure if your giftee gravitates towards lip balms, lipsticks, or lip stains, may we present to you the bestselling Merit’s Lip Blush. Former Beauty Director Jacqueline Kilikita described it as a “sheer, matte lipstick with a moisturizing balm-like feel.” She enjoyed the muted terracotta September shade, but there are eight shades to choose from to complement your giftee's beauty aesthetic.
Avec Les Filles Hooded Drawstring Waist Jacket

When this jacket was previously featured in our Nordstrom sale picks, it quickly became a fan favorite. The versatile and adjustable Avec les Filles jacket originally retailed for over $200, but it's currently on sale again, meaning you may want to cart it up asap.
The Ordinary 120 ml Rice Lipids + Ectoin Microemulsion

Over 70. That's how many bottles of The Ordinary's milky moisturizer sold after it launched last January. While it can be tricky to gift skincare due to everyone's specific needs, Kilikita declared that this toner-like moisturizer "is for everyone." (This jumbo size is yet another great stocking stuffer design, but you can find smaller bottles at Ulta and Sephora!)

items.title: 15 Gifts For The Friend Who Collects Perfume Like Memories
items.description: 15 Gifts For The Friend Who Collects Perfume Like Memories
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: 15 Gifts For The Friend Who Collects Perfume Like Memories

At Refinery29, we’re here to help you navigate this overwhelming world of stuff. All of our market picks are independently selected and curated by the editorial team. All product details reflect the price and availability at the time of publication. If you buy or click on something we link to on our site, Refinery29 may earn commission.
Rare Beauty Rare Moments Eau De Parfum Rollerball Mini Duo

As a self-professed perfume snob, I was seriously impressed by Selena Gomez's fragrance debut last year. Then, IMO, she outdid herself with her sophomore release, Rare Beginnings. This adorable rollerball duo lets you experience both scents, each offering a completely different (but equally Rare-coded) fragrance mood: one fresh and fruity, the other warm and comforting. Plus, the miniature bottles are practically made for tossing into your bag for midday touch-ups.
Summer Fridays Sunlit Vanilla Set

Summer Fridays' fragrance debut was one of my favorite beauty launches of 2026, making this gift set a no-brainer for anyone on the hunt for their next favorite vanilla perfume. I'm particularly obsessed with the blend of caramel, coconut, and bergamot, which creates a warm, creamy scent that feels cozy without veering too summery. And considering the full-size bottle alone retails for $82, getting that plus a travel spray and cosmetic case? Girl math at its finest.
Marc Jacobs Daisy 4-Piece Mini Perfume Discovery Gift Set

If you know someone (or are that someone) who’s dreamed of frolicking in a field of wildflowers ever since first seeing Marc Jacobs’ Daisy ads, this festive set is a steal at under $100 — not that your recipient would ever guess. Inside, your lucky giftee will discover a mini garden of different varieties encased in Christmas cracker-inspired packaging.
Tom Ford Private Blend Deluxe Discovery Set

Who doesn't love a little Tom Ford under the tree? This impossibly chic discovery set brings together four of the brand's most iconic fragrances, spanning the decadent, cherry-soaked Lost Cherry, smoky-sweet Tobacco Vanille, beach-resort-coded Soleil Blanc, and bold, woody Oud Wood. Consider this the gift of smelling expensive.
Hermès Barénia Eau de Parfum Gift Set

I treated myself to a similar version of Hermès' Barénia gift set during the Nordstrom Anniversary Sale, but if you missed out, fear not. This duo includes a full-size bottle of the brand's addictive, skin-like Barénia, plus a travel spray for keeping your signature scent close, whether you're commuting, jet-setting, or simply refreshing on the go.
Cyklar The Bestsellers Perfume Oil Gift Set

Without a doubt, perfume oil is one of the most sensual ways to wear fragrance. There's the ritual of applying it, the subtle sheen it leaves on skin, and the bonus of using it as a base to help other fragrances linger longer. Cyklar is quickly mastering the art of the perfume oil, and this quartet of its bestselling scents — Sacred Santal, Vanilla Verve, Sex Musk, and Naked Neroli — offers a little something for every mood, from cozy to come-hither.
Miu Miu Mini Miutine Eau De Parfum Perfume Duo Gift Set

I not-so-secretly love strawberry fragrances, and Miutine is my current favorite. With warm brown sugar and floral gardenia rounding out the juicy fruitiness, it's playful yet ladylike in the most Miu Miu way possible. This duo includes two adorable minis — a travel spray and a Honey, I Shrunk the Kids-sized version of the brand's signature matelassé bottle. All for under $40? A luxury fragrance steal, if you ask me.
Ellis Brooklyn ISLA TIME Mini Perfume Duo Gift Set

We haven't even reached the dead of winter, but for the person who's already dreaming of an island escape, Ellis Brooklyn's tropical perfume duo is just the ticket. It includes teeny-tiny bottles of ISLA SIRENA, a mermaid-coded blend of coconut water, blue java banana, and lime, alongside my personal Ellis Brooklyn favorite, Miami Nectar, a sun-drenched cocktail of pink pineapple, coconut water, and vanilla. OOO mode: activated.
Sephora Favorites Holiday Women's Perfume Sampler Gift Set

I'll say it every year: Gifting fragrance can be tricky unless you're replenishing someone's signature scent or know their tastes really well. Enter Sephora's perfume sampler set, aka my favorite hack for giving someone a fragrance they'll actually love. With 20 scents to choose from, the odds are very much in your favor. The set includes a treasure trove of Sephora bestsellers in sample sizes (which, trust me, last longer than you'd think), plus a voucher to redeem a favorite for a full-size bottle online or in-store. The gift that keeps on giving, indeed.
The 7 Virtues Mini Amber Orchid & Vanilla Woods Eau de Parfum Duo Gift Set

This right here is your ultimate cozy-girl scent combo. Vanilla Woods is an all-time favorite in my fragrance collection, and I'm convinced newcomer Amber Orchid is her long-lost soulmate-slash-bestie — that's how beautifully they complement each other. Together, they're subtly sweet, warm, and inviting, with an airy, skin-like amber floral quality that gives off that "naturally smells good" energy.

Leave it to IYKYK lifestyle brand Sidia to reimagine portable fragrance as an endlessly refillable, keepsake-worthy object. Meet The Strike, a chic scent atomizer that lets you choose from three of the brand's signature fragrances: warm and cozy Braless, earthy Soaked, and sunny Midas. Consider it your new favorite way to take your signature scent everywhere — and make every reapplication feel like a little luxury.
Glossier Mini Glossier You Wardrobe Kit

I audibly squealed when I spotted this Glossier You perfume set in-store — that's how good it is. Perfect for the Glossier obsessive on your list, this quartet of ambroxan-based fragrances is a skin-scent lover's dream, offering four takes on that signature your-skin-but-better magic. (Plus, the tiny bottles are the ultimate beauty-girl keepsakes.)
Sol de Janeiro Cheirosa All the Way Mini Perfume Mist Gift Set

Spread some holiday cheer — or should we say, Cheirosa — with this set of six Sol de Janeiro fragrance mists. The lineup includes fan favorites like caramel-forward '62 and fruity-floral '68, plus the chance to discover a new signature scent in picks like nutty, gourmand '71 and juicy, plum-forward '40. Consider it a one-way ticket to smelling delicious.
Kylie Cosmetics Kylie Jenner Mood Stones 3-Piece Discovery Gift Set

IMO, Kylie Jenner has yet to miss when it comes to her growing fragrance empire. Her first foray beyond the Cosmic collection came in the form of Mood Stones, arguably her most elevated perfume offering yet. This discovery set lets you sample all three scents — Cashmere Muse, Blush Wood, and Velvet Brew — and mix, match, and layer to your heart's content.
NOYZ Only Human Layering Set

There's no shame in knowing what you like — especially when it's as good as NOYZ's Only Human. This set lets you wear the sultry-sweet scent three ways: as an eau de parfum mist, a moisturizing milky lotion, and a solid perfume stick for on-the-go touch-ups. Layer them together for a fragrance ritual that goes the extra mile, or wear each one solo. (The chic faux-leather mini purse is just the cherry on top.)

items.title: Everything We Know About Adults Season 3
items.description: Adults has officially been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu. That's not all: the studio has ordered 16 episodes for the next season. Seasons 1 and 2 only had eight episodes each, so this is a true blessing. We'll be reunited with Samir (Malik Essal), Billie
items.author: Simran Pasricha
paragraphs: Adults has officially been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu. That's not all: the studio has ordered 16 episodes for the next season. Seasons 1 and 2 only had eight episodes each, so this is a true blessing. We'll be reunited with Samir (Malik Essal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele) and Paul Baker (Jack Innanen).

Specific plot details haven’t been announced. For now, the premise remains five twenty-somethings living in Samir’s childhood home in New York, trying to navigate work, relationships, family and the delicate business of being in each other’s space constantly.

Main cast members Malik Elassal, Lucy Freyer, Jack Innanen, Amita Rao and Owen Thiele are coming back. No guest stars or recurring stars have been announced, but we will likely see Issa's new love interest, the librarian played by Mia Fowler.

n 3, according to Freyer. "[Fox]was like, 'I wanna come back next season, and the season you don’t bring me back is the season you’re gonna get cancelled,'" she told Refinery29 Australia. "And I was like, she put a curse on us, and I believe it. And now, she has to be in every season of the show for as long as it runs. And I'm like, 'OK!'"

Behind the scenes, Kronengold and Shaw remain the creators, showrunners and executive producers. Their statement about the new FX deal also acknowledged a particularly important figure in this whole operation. "We started working with FX over six years ago, back when Paul Baker was but a twinkle in all of our eyes," they joked.
Not yet, but we will update this article once there is.

The audience has grown, which is reassuring news for anyone who has been personally campaigning for their friends to watch. According to FX, Season 2 viewership increased by 60% compared with Season 1 across Hulu and Disney+ globally over its first five weeks. International viewership doubled. The network didn’t release actual audience totals, so we don't know exactly how many people joined the household.

FX Entertainment president Nick Grad also credited the show’s devoted following. "Ben and Rebecca have elevated Adults in every way, earning critical praise and a legion of devoted fans who have embraced the friend group as their own," he said in a statement.
There’s no announced release date for season three yet, but in the meantime, Australians can watch the first two seasons on Disney+.

items.title: 'm 25, I Make $145K & I Feel Like I Would Be A Child Bride If I Got Engaged Or Married Anytime Soon
items.description: A Week In New York, NY On A $145,000 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In New York, NY On A $145,000 Salary
This week: An associate working in finance who makes $145,000 per year and spends it on her $40 Spotify "family" plan.

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Editor's Note: This is a follow-up diary. Read the previous one here.
Joint Income/Financial Setup: My boyfriend, J. makes $80,000 per year, but we don't combine finances. I pay 60% of the rent, and we split everything else 50/50.
Assets: These are only my assets — I don't have a clear view of my partner's finances.
401(k) (mostly Roth, some traditional): $33,359.25
Brokerage account: $28,434.90
Debt: About $10K on my credit cards this month, which I will pay in full when they are due.
Paycheck Amount (monthly): $7014.72
Housing Costs: $2,500 (I live with J. in a studio and he pays $1,500)
Internet: $59.99 (split with J.)
Electricity: ~$100 (on average, split with J.)
Phone: $0 (my work pays for it)
Lifetime membership: $123.97
Healthcare copay: $15 (comes out of my gross paycheck)
Brokerage investment: $550
Roth IRA investment: $1000 (once I hit the cap, this is being re-directed to brokerage)
Renters insurance: $146 (split with J.)
Amazon Prime Young Adult: $73.14
Capital One Venture X: $395
Amex Gold: $325 (for the past two years, I've gotten $100 off for having a corporate Amex)
Chase Sapphire Reserve: $795 (in theory I have renewed, but I think I'm downgrading to the Preferred, which is $95 per year)
YNAB: $115.54 (I share with J. but I don't charge him).
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

Yes, 100%. Both of my parents have advanced degrees and were the first in their families to attend higher education, so it wasn't a question of whether or not I would attend university, but where. They attended school outside the US, so their ability to help me through the college application process was limited. Luckily, I attended an excellent public school and had incredibly pushy parents. My parents started saving for school in a 529 plan when I was born, and my university provided ample need-based financial aid. Since my parents made undergraduate education (at the best schools we could get into) an expectation in our house, they felt responsible for paying for our degrees after any scholarships and aid we received. If I have a family, I will do the exact same thing because it allowed me and my brother to shoot for the stars when it came to colleges. Both of my parents have PhDs, so their expectation was actually that I also get a JD, MD, or PhD of some kind. They were the ones who pushed me to do the Master's when I was on the fence about it, as I mentioned in my previous Money Diary.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

My parents have always been very frugal people, so most of our conversations about money revolved around saving money for emergencies. I didn't receive much of an education about finances directly, but I was aware that my parents had things like a mortgage, retirement accounts, and life insurance. I'm really interested in personal finance, so before starting college, I did an entire course to educate myself and be as set up for living on my own as I could be.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

My first real W-2 job was an internship within my state's judicial system. It was pretty basic office work, but I got to listen to a lot of podcasts and music on the job! Where I went to school, families were optimizing their kids' résumés from birth, so I got this summer job to improve my own résumé. My parents didn't actually give me access to any of the money I earned from my summer jobs until I got to college, which I have mixed feelings about, but this probably ensured I didn't waste all my money on fast food and clothes (which I did during undergrad anyways).
Did you worry about money growing up?

Yes and no. My father grew up in poverty, and that mindset was reflected in our household. He would always compare how much things would cost to how many loaves of bread he could buy with that amount (with one loaf somehow remaining constantly at $1 to this day). I was told “no” all the time for things like snacks and toys, though my mother would occasionally go shopping with me and hide purchases from my father. This kind of restriction, though, meant that when one of my parents lost their job during the recession, I didn't feel the impact. We would visit one of my parent's home countries every year, which I later found out was paid for by my mom's family during some difficult times. Ultimately, there was always money for necessities, school activities, and anything my parents thought would help my brother and I academically, so I never felt worried.
Do you worry about money now?

Not really. I opened a Roth IRA when I was 18 and have been pretty savvy with savings and things like credit card points. The problem for me is that I'm a big saver who also likes to spend, especially on little treats, and now that I have a big girl salary, the treats aren't so little. I always hit my savings goals every month, but I always think that I could and should be saving more of my salary for things like a wedding or a down payment on a house. This is mostly because I have friends already doing both of these things and other friends working at crazy startups and making a ton of money when they IPO. I know the mindset of comparison isn't healthy or reasonable, but it's hard to stop these pretty ingrained habits.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

I would say I became completely financially responsible for myself this year when my job started paying for my phone plan, and the last financial tie to my parents fell away. While I'm technically on their health insurance, I have been using my own insurance through work since I moved to New York two years ago. My parents will probably always be my financial safety net, and maybe even J.'s if we get married, but my parents would never think of making me feel bad about it. I think they know that if I needed their help, it would be because something truly bad happened rather than me being irresponsible with money given my saving habits.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.

In my last Money Diary, I was given a "loan" from my parents for my Master's degree. After half a year of payments, they decided to forgive the loan on the condition that I put the same amount of money monthly ($1,000) into retirement or other investments. They reasoned that my brother's undergraduate education cost the same as my undergraduate education, plus my Master's, and they wanted to be fair to us. They don't check on this, but I'm very diligent about it. I guess my parents "forgiving" their loan to me for my Master's program might count, but otherwise, no. It will hopefully be a long time until my parents pass, and any inheritance from any of my grandparents would go to my parents directly.

I definitely had some high-ticket items this week, but I think the other spending is pretty in line with regular weeks for me. Unfortunately, that's not a great thing because I always exceed the budget I give myself for dining out and groceries. I need to either learn to say no a bit more or be more thoughtful about buying snacks and drinks ahead of time, rather than making impulse purchases.
The first step to getting your financial life in order is tracking what you spend — to try on your own, check out our guide to managing your money every day. For more Money Diaries, click here.
Do you have a Money Diary you'd like to share? Submit it with us here.
Have questions about how to submit or our publishing process? Read our Money Diaries FAQ doc here or email us here.

items.title: What does motherhood look like without my best friend? | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: On page five of an eight-page letter dated 3 September 2019, my friend – whom I will call Naaz – wrote to me:
items.author: Ashwaq Masoodi
paragraphs: On page five of an eight-page letter dated 3 September 2019, my friend – whom I will call Naaz – wrote to me:

I always pray that nothing in this world may ever blur your vision of your own self. Not people, not your circumstances. One must not be delusional, but one should also never lose the grip of one’s essence. Never forget who you are, what all you have achieved, how hard you worked to be where you are today.

Naaz had never written to me before – not a note, not a postcard. We were on each other’s speed dial for as long as I could remember. But that August, the Indian state had revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status and, anticipating blowback, had throttled internet broadband, cable TV, landlines and mobile networks. Even postal services were disrupted; Naaz planned to hand-deliver her letter. Another letter tells me that on 11 August she knocked on my door for a long time. But I had already left for New Delhi, and would soon be halfway across the world.

In Kashmir, we are used to uncertainty but, in those days, it was dialled all the way up. When I left, I did not know when I would be able to speak with my parents again. We seemed to have collectively tumbled back in time to the 1990s, when separatist conflict was at its peak and, with it, the Indian state’s iron-fist policy to counter it. I was leaving for a year-long journalism fellowship at Harvard, and wracked with guilt and self-doubt: guilt over leaving when so many others could not, self-doubt over whether I would live up to the opportunity. Perhaps Naaz sensed my ambivalence, which is why she wrote those lines. She knew I might need the reminder.

Naaz first knew me as a bushy-browed teenager, travelling 110 km each day to study journalism in Baramulla, a small town in Kashmir. We met on a bus, in the spring of 2005. She was in a three-seater near the middle, in a white crewneck sweater with a Fair Isle pattern around the neckline. I took the seat beside her. I remember what she wore because my mother knit sweaters for me in that pattern, too. Within minutes, we were exchanging names, then places, then families. My mother was from the same area as her. My naanu had taught Naaz’s father. Her father had taught mine. Our meeting felt both serendipitous and predetermined.

She was seven years older than me, a science teacher, a lover of poetry. In a society steeped in existential despair, she took her vocation seriously. ‘We are the builders of Kashmir,’ she’d say. Growing up, I’d seldom encountered older people who weren’t in survival mode, always braced for the next loss or threat, who were able to support those dreaming of lives larger than the ones they’d inherited. Perhaps that’s why Naaz – thoughtful, curious, never infantilising – was so easy to like.
My friendship with Naaz quickly deepened into something closer to sisterhood

I dreamed of being a reporter. A few years after meeting Naaz, I would join a workshop led by one of Kashmir’s finest journalists. Every Sunday, at 9 am, a group of us – the youngest in their teens, the oldest in their 40s – gathered in his tiny apartment in Srinagar, thick with the smell of old books and cigarettes. We read Ryszard Kapuściński’s dispatches and watched The Battle of Algiers.
‘If we don’t tell our story, someone else will,’ he would often remind us.

My friendship with Naaz quickly deepened into something closer to sisterhood. Even when I moved away, for further studies or for work, we spoke almost daily. We would fall asleep on the phone, only to wake when the phones slipped and knocked against our faces. When I visited, we would take boat rides on Dal Lake, stroll aimlessly through the Mughal Gardens, go on long drives around Srinagar, never running out of conversation. Two young men might be construed as a security threat and attract state surveillance; a young man and woman might be seen as romantically involved and draw social scrutiny. Female friendship, on the other hand, could occupy public space more freely, without constantly defending its right to exist.

Naaz and I often joked that our ‘halal:haram’ ratio was almost identical, a way of saying we drew a similar line between the permissible and the forbidden, with many of the same compromises and contradictions. And yet we were utterly different in other ways. She would not undo what she had already done. If she left the house with her hair tied, she would keep it tied, even if it no longer made sense to do so. Whereas I agonised over everything. Naaz was surprised I could put myself in all sorts of situations as a journalist – interviewing human traffickers, reporting from conflict zones – and yet be so internally unanchored. I was driven but also anxious: I wanted professional success but, when it came, I knew only how to move past it, towards the next milestone. Naaz would shake me lightly, yanking me back to the present.
‘Can you be proud of yourself? Can you accept that you are good?’

When I returned to Kashmir after my fellowship ended, we met at her wedding. The happiest bride I have ever seen, when she saw me, she held my hands and pulled me into a tight embrace. Within months, I too was married. Despite our age difference, it felt as if something larger was aligning our lives. We became pregnant within months of each other, our conversations turning to baby names, nausea, exhaustion.
‘What do you want,’ I asked her once, ‘a girl or a boy?’
‘It doesn’t matter,’ she said. ‘I just hope the baby survives. I hope I survive.’

I remember feeling a flicker of irritation when she said that. Doom-mongering was what I did. And why would anything go wrong? Yes, she was in her late 30s, but she was healthier than most 20-somethings. Meanwhile, I fretted over how motherhood would alter the life I’d carefully built for myself, the five-year plans that I worried would now be upended. It didn’t help that my partner and I would be moving to Germany soon.
Each time I visited Kashmir, my heart clenched – that unmistakable giggle was gone

Naaz gave birth in September. Days later, she suffered an intracerebral haemorrhage – a brain bleed caused by a ruptured blood vessel, the risk of which is three times higher among women during pregnancy and in the weeks following delivery. She was the one who messaged to tell me. I should keep a tab on my vitals, she added, and not stress out over small things while pregnant. Soon after, she slipped into a coma.

A month passed before Naaz regained consciousness. Even though there were times when she seemed to be improving, the things that distinguished her began slipping away. Among the first women in her village to drive, she could no longer hold the movement of a car. A poet, she could no longer read or write. Each time I visited Kashmir, my heart clenched – that unmistakable giggle was gone, as was the way she tucked loose strands of her hair, behind her right ear specifically. Once, when I went to see her, I noticed how her dupatta, which she typically flung around her neck, was spread out over her chest. She would never wear it that way, I kept thinking to myself. As terrifying as it was to witness her suffering, so was the dissipation of things that make a person: language, memory, skill.

For more than two years, Naaz fought bravely. She passed away in March 2024 – typically, a month of birthdays in my family. That year, all through March and April, my toddler played Zum Geburtstag viel Glück in an endless loop on her music box – Happy Birthday in German, the soundtrack to my grief.

It was early morning in Berlin when I received the news. When I read the message – N is no more – I collapsed onto the prayer rug, crying into my breath so I wouldn’t wake my two-year-old. Later, when my daughter stirred, expecting me beside her as always, I moved toward her, my body performing the choreography of care as if nothing had happened. As if the mountain hadn’t fallen over me.

In Kashmir, we are used to untimely death. But how to grieve the loss of your best friend, so young, so vividly alive? And how to grieve with a two-year-old at close hand, amid meals NOW, baths NOW, nappy change NOW, tantrums NOW?
Grief, in a sense, has become intertwined with motherhood

I had known motherhood would unsettle my sense of self – what I never imagined was that it would also take away the person who held my story alongside me. In narrative psychology, identity is theorised as what Dan P McAdams calls an ‘evolving story of the self’ – an integration of one’s reconstructed past, perceived present and imagined future. This story has multiple authors. We come to know who we are through conversation, through shared recollection, through being witnessed: by our parents, our siblings, our partners, our best friends. Each holds a fragment of us, reflecting the person we are and the person we once were. Those shared memories become the story we tell ourselves about our own life. That story is never fixed. It changes as we change, and as the people who hold pieces of it enter and leave our lives. With Naaz’s death, parts of my past lost their primary witness just as motherhood began shaking the very roots of who I was.

Kashmir – my home, my muse – has changed, too. Since 2019, dissent of any sort is promptly quashed. The graffiti proclaiming azadi, freedom, has disappeared from the walls as has any public expression of separatist sentiment. Local journalists are asked to sign pledges vowing not to ‘disturb the peace’. Most of our writing group has drifted into PR or fiction; one of the youngest members was recently released after two years in prison. Like people, places also need someone to hold on to their stories. In Kashmir, bearing witness now comes at a cost.

Two years ago, I became pregnant again. As I gave birth the second time, memories from the days after Naaz’s death started playing on a loop. Grief, in a sense, has become intertwined with motherhood. It is there when I lift my son, when I chase him down the hallway. I hear his laughter and think of Naaz’s. She should have lived to experience this: the chaos, the beauty, the bone-deep exhaustion that is now my everyday.

Occasionally, in a note jotted in the margin of a book, on a walk by myself in the park, in the sheaf of letters that eventually made their way into my hands, I catch a glimpse of my earlier self: the journalist, Naaz’s best girl. I have taken to telling my daughter stories from that time, as if piecing together a self she has never known. For now, the only one she remembers is about the time a jellyfish stung me on a beach in Miami. ‘Once more… only one,’ she says, asking me again and again to act out the moment the jellyfish stung me. I oblige every time.

items.title: Shunning people who ‘look homeless’ is an aesthetic injustice | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Being homeless is an unjust social condition. Unhoused individuals not only lack the resources necessary to satisfy their basic needs, but they are also excluded from the rest of society. They have little access to healthy food, to security, to the requirement
items.author: Giacomo Floris
paragraphs: Being homeless is an unjust social condition. Unhoused individuals not only lack the resources necessary to satisfy their basic needs, but they are also excluded from the rest of society. They have little access to healthy food, to security, to the requirements of good health. They are unable to fit in and participate in the normal activities of society, such as getting a job, and they are pushed to live in dangerous and socially deprived areas. But material deprivation and social exclusion are not the only injustices suffered by unhoused individuals. They also face aesthetic injustice. This is a widely neglected source of harm associated with homelessness, which seriously impedes the ability of unhoused people to live a life of dignity and to better their circumstances.

To understand the nature of aesthetic injustice, it will be helpful to start with the more general notion of justice. Justice concerns how people should be treated, and political philosophers often say that justice requires everyone to be treated with equal respect and concern. ‘Each person,’ wrote the philosopher John Rawls in A Theory of Justice (1971), ‘possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.’ An injustice, therefore, occurs when an individual is treated in a way that is incompatible with the respect and concern that is owed to them as an equal. Harming someone is unjust because it fails to express appropriate concern for their wellbeing. Exercising arbitrary power over an individual is unjust because it violates the equal freedom that everyone is entitled to.

Aesthetic injustice is a specific kind of injustice: it consists in the wrongful treatment of individuals based on how they look. In our society, many people benefit or suffer from aesthetic injustice. As the economist Daniel Hamermesh argued in his book Beauty Pays (2011), individuals perceived as physically attractive typically command higher salaries and occupy more prestigious positions. He estimated that the best-looking people, over the course of their careers, make around $250,000 more than their less attractive colleagues. Similarly, as Sean Talamas and colleagues found, attractiveness is strongly correlated with perceived competence and intelligence – despite bearing almost no relationship to actual performance. And as the philosopher Kate Manne showed in Unshrinking (2024), fat people are often bullied, discriminated against and marginalised. These are all instances of aesthetic injustice: individuals are treated as more or less worthy of respect and concern by virtue of their outward appearance.

The outward appearance of unhoused individuals is often a reflection of their social condition. Due to the lack of sufficient resources and reliable shelter, unhoused individuals typically display signs of deterioration, such as unkempt hair and damaged skin. Their clothing is frequently dirty and ill-fitting. Additionally, many unhoused individuals exhibit visible signs of substance use disorders, such as track marks on the arms and dilated blood vessels. In the sociologist Erving Goffman’s classic study Stigma (1963), he names these aesthetic traits ‘stigma symbols’. A stigma, for Goffman, is ‘an attribute that is deeply discrediting’. By possessing these aesthetic stigmas, unhoused individuals are placed at the very bottom of the aesthetic hierarchy. They are regarded as disgusting elements of the urban landscape, whose presence in prime urban areas – areas that are desirable due to their location or historical significance – is unacceptable.

To appreciate this, consider the wide range of strategies that are adopted by many cities in order to exclude unhoused individuals from prime urban areas, such as anti-homelessness laws and ‘hostile’ architecture. Unhoused individuals are likely to be fined for loitering in commercial districts, while they are permitted to remain in socially deprived neighbourhoods. As the legal scholar Robert Ellickson put it, ‘[a] bum on a Skid Row sidewalk would never hear [“move along”] because he was exactly where the cop wanted him’ – that is, away from profitable business districts or valuable residential areas. Similarly, ‘anti-sleep’ benches and ‘ground spikes’ are widespread in parks and main commercial streets, whereas they are nowhere to be found in socially deprived areas. These measures illustrate how negative aesthetic judgments about unhoused individuals are institutionalised through public policy and urban design.

Aesthetic injustice against unhoused people is sustained and compounded by the fact that they are deprived of their capacity for self-presentation, that is, the ability to exercise reasonable control over how they present themselves to others. This is because unhoused individuals lack ‘aesthetic resources’: the materials, tools and conditions that either directly contribute to a person’s aesthetic properties or are constitutive components of them. Without access to showers, unhoused individuals are unable to maintain personal cleanliness. Without grooming products, such as soap and razors, they’re unable to keep tidy their hair, skin and facial features. As a result, unhoused people cannot shape how they present themselves to others. They cannot but look homeless.

The deprivation of the capacity for self-presentation is unjust for two reasons. First, it reinforces the social exclusion of unhoused individuals. Employers typically screen out candidates whose appearance departs from the aesthetic norms of a ‘serious’ candidate – unkempt hair, wrinkled or dirty clothing, the absence of basic grooming – whatever their actual qualifications. The injustice is therefore doubled: unhoused individuals are denied the resources needed to present themselves as employable and are then penalised for lacking a presentation they were never given the means to produce.
They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold

The philosopher Andrea Sangiovanni points to the second reason it is unjust. In his book Humanity without Dignity (2017), he contends that developing and maintaining an integral sense of self requires the fundamental ability to exercise some degree of control over how we are perceived. That is, we need to be able to manage ‘what is inner and what is outer, what is presented and what is hidden’. In intimate relationships, for example, we may choose to reveal personal vulnerabilities, while professional relationships usually demand a more formal, public-facing image.

It’s morally necessary that we have the means of choosing what to reveal, and to whom, and how to present ourselves. Wearing a suit conveys professionalism, while casual clothing indicates approachability. Wearing a kippah represents an individual’s affiliation with the Jewish community, while wearing a hijab is associated with Muslim identity. Due to the lack of adequate aesthetic resources, unhoused individuals cannot shape and control how they present themselves to others. They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold, as most people routinely do. The inability to determine one’s outward appearance is, therefore, a violation of unhoused individuals’ status as equal, self-presenting persons – in Sangiovanni’s words, ‘as beings who have a say in how [they] are to be seen by others’.

How should a just society address the aesthetic injustices suffered by unhoused individuals? To start with, the social norms of respectable appearance – that is, the aesthetic standards that determine what counts as an acceptable way of presenting oneself in public spaces – should be revised. This is not to say, of course, that all people must be regarded as equally beautiful. Rather, it is to say that no one should be excluded from prime public spaces based solely on their appearance (provided that they satisfy very minimal aesthetic standards, such as covering their genitalia). This would involve abolishing beautification projects aimed at removing unhoused individuals from public spaces. For example, in Ottawa, Canada, officers of the National Capital Commission (NCC) are authorised to remove unhoused individuals from parks and confiscate their belongings on the grounds that they are in violation of ‘beautification goals’. As one study reports, NCC conservation officers often ‘approach homeless people as garbage and do not distinguish between homeless people and their belongings as objects for removal from parks’. No one should be denied access to and enjoyment of public spaces because they are perceived as ugly.

However, revising social norms of respectable appearance is not sufficient. A just society should ensure not only that unhoused individuals have the right to live and exist in prime urban areas, but also that they have the resources necessary to exercise some control over how they appear to others. It is not enough to grant unhoused people access to public spaces independently of their appearance – it is also necessary to provide them with the opportunity to shape and control their appearance as a matter of respect for their status as self-presenting persons. In pursuit of this goal, there are many charities providing free haircuts to unhoused people and programmes offering new and gently used clothes, including business attire. These are the kinds of social initiatives that society should actively promote as a matter of justice rather than as a matter of charity, since everyone has the right to the resources necessary to determine how they appear to others, at least to some extent.

Hardly anyone denies that being homeless is an unjust social condition characterised by material deprivation and social exclusion. But this doesn’t capture the entirety of the injustice that unhoused people suffer. Part of the burden of being homeless is to be regarded as a disgusting element of the urban landscape whose presence in public areas is unacceptable. That burden is badly compounded by the denial of aesthetic resources. Without a shower, a razor, a change of clean clothes, unhoused individuals are denied what those lucky enough to be housed take for granted: a say in how to appear to the world. A just society owes the unhoused the right to be looked at without disgust, and the resources to decide, for themselves, how they wish to be seen.
