items.title: The ex-cop on a mission to see fortune-tellers arrested | Psyche Portraits
items.description: In 2008, Bob Nygaard sat on a stool at the Neighborhood Sports Bar and Grill in Boca Raton, Florida, just before 5 pm. It was Wednesday, a night with generous happy-hour deals and the possibility of taking someone home by last call. Nygaard, a tall and brawny
items.author: Shayla Love
paragraphs: In 2008, Bob Nygaard sat on a stool at the Neighborhood Sports Bar and Grill in Boca Raton, Florida, just before 5 pm. It was Wednesday, a night with generous happy-hour deals and the possibility of taking someone home by last call. Nygaard, a tall and brawny man with a disarmingly goofy smile, had the strongest New York accent for miles. He had recently retired from a 21-year-long career as an NYPD officer. At 46, he got out when his pension kicked in, and moved down to Florida to relax.
Except he wasn’t relaxed. He was bored.

Nygaard had been a high-energy cop who didn’t get along with fellow officers because of how doggedly he pursued arrests. He probably should have known that he wouldn’t adjust to sipping Mai Tais and sitting on the beach. Shortly after arriving in Florida, he got a private investigator’s licence, using it to track down missing money or catch cheating husbands. Neither was satisfying.

He ordered a rum and Coke. He had become friendly with the bartender, who introduced him to two women sitting at the end of the bar, a nurse and a doctor. They had dinner together, swapping stories about working in medicine and the police force. Nygaard gave both women his card. Ten minutes later, his phone rang. It was the doctor. Could they meet up nearby, on a street corner outside a Chevron station? Nygaard thought she was hoping to hook up.

When she pulled up and rolled down the window, her face was half-covered in shadows. ‘I’ve never been able to tell anyone this before,’ she said from the driver’s seat. ‘I’m a medical doctor and I fell for a psychic.’ She had given more than $12,000 to a woman she met through her hairdresser. The psychic said someone had put a curse on the doctor: it explained why she was having issues with her immigration papers, and why her love life was ruined. For enough money, the curse could be lifted. Now, the doctor realised she’d been had. Nygaard had arrested conmen before. Could he help her?

From that moment on, Nygaard was never bored again. He became a PI who specialises in helping victims of psychics. And he didn’t settle cases out of court – he went after arrests to get as much money back for his clients as possible. Through word of mouth, psychic victims all over the country have sought him out. Since his first case, Nygaard has helped recover more than $5 million.

I first heard about Nygaard around a year ago, through a news article about a psychic’s arrest he had orchestrated in Philadelphia. I thought of him as part fictional detective Sherlock Holmes, part real-life Harry Houdini, who spent his later years exposing mediums. When I initially reached out over email, Nygaard didn’t respond. But after I sent a follow-up, I got a call from an unknown number a few days later. It was Nygaard: ‘I like when people don’t give up,’ he told me. He started talking fast, recounting his recent cases. What drives a retired cop, someone who busted drug dealers and burglars, to focus only on this fringe sect of society – psychics? And why was he so good at it? We made plans to meet up in the city.

On a below-freezing day in early February, I turned a narrow corner in lower Manhattan and saw a figure wearing a beige trench coat and fedora standing under the granite arch of the historic Life and Trust Bank. In my memory, steam started to rise up from the sidewalk grates, and the deserted street became the spot for a clandestine midnight meet-up. In truth, it was a clear sunny morning and Nygaard was politely waiting for me outside, but every minute spent with him can make you feel like you’re acting out a scene from a movie set in old New York. The former bank now houses a coffee shop. We walked into the cavernous lobby and ordered drinks where the bank tellers once sat.

I expected to meet a hardened law-enforcement officer with a dark past. Maybe he, or someone he loved, had been wronged by a psychic, and he had a score to settle. Or maybe he was a rationalist – someone so dedicated to an evidence-based view of the world that he wouldn’t stand for anyone proposing they could break the laws of nature.

But as we settled down with our hot drinks, I learned that Nygaard hadn’t thought about psychics at all until later in life. He had a happy, grounded childhood, he told me. He was born in Queens in 1961, and moved to New Hyde Park, Long Island, when he was four. His mother was 20 when she had him, his father only a few years older. The family, including his younger brother, ate dinner together every evening.
‘Knowing how to deal with the raccoon also helps you deal with the person’

They were a hard-working and proud unit. The family would put on their best clothes to go to the Howard Johnson’s on Jericho Turnpike for fish and chips. Nygaard was taught to always be ‘squared away’. He made his bed in the morning. His hair was always combed. ‘You pay attention to the details, to the little things,’ he said. ‘You’re clean, well dressed, polite, you’re on time.’ Even though his apartment was just around the corner from the café where we sat, he had arrived nearly 20 minutes early to make sure he wasn’t late. (Nygaard now splits his time between Florida and New York, based largely on when the New York Rangers are playing; he has season tickets.)

His sense of justice also seems to have started early. If Nygaard came home and said that all the kids were picking on someone in the schoolyard – ‘knocking them on the ground, calling him four-eyes’ – Nygaard’s father would counter: ‘You didn’t sit there and watch, did you?’

Nygaard spent summers in northeast Pennsylvania, where his grandfather had bought an old farmhouse with no running water or electricity; it relied on kerosene lamps and a well. The property reminded his grandfather of Norway. When Nygaard brought out his friends, brothers called Tommy and Richy Gambino, they had never seen a cow before. Once, they tricked another visiting city kid by telling him that chocolate milk came out of the brown cows’ udders.

In the countryside, Nygaard fostered compassion for other living things. When he was around six, he had a BB gun to shoot at cans. One day, he saw a bird, aimed his gun at it, and shot it out of a tree. Nygaard looked at it up close, examining the pellet in its belly. It wasn’t dead, but it was suffering. He killed it, to put it out of its misery, and then felt sick. ‘I never killed again,’ he told me. Yet, he also gained insights into the animalistic side of humans. When he saw a raccoon trapped inside the barn, he later recognised similar responses in perps with a warrant on them, cornered on a subway platform. ‘Knowing how to deal with the raccoon also helps you deal with the person,’ he said.

It was Nygaard’s father who wanted him to be a police officer. When Nygaard was 17, he took the police test. The job came with a pension and healthcare, Nygaard’s father would say. Plus, he could help people. But Nygaard went to college in Texas, at Southern Methodist University, majoring in business – thinking he would join the family flooring company. Then he got called to the police academy at 23.
He asked if the psychic’s last name was Marks. Stunned, the doctor asked how he had known. ‘I’m psychic,’ he joked

Police work matched his philosophy of justice: when someone broke the law, there were consequences, and it was his job to deliver them. He became obsessive about making arrests, so much so that he chafed against the other cops. When he was an officer on Long Island, there were unspoken rules about how proactive or ambitious to be, he said. Others would accuse him of creating too much paperwork. Supervisors punished him by putting him on desk duty. Yet he still managed to make arrests without leaving the station, remembering passersby with outstanding warrants, and once discovering drugs in someone’s purse. He memorised the penal code, so that he could always justify what he was doing, including a New York State law that fortune-telling was a crime.

One of Nygaard’s few police mentors was the late Jon Grow, a detective at the Baltimore Police Department. Grow co-founded the National Association of Bunco Investigators, a non-profit that helped law-enforcement officers share information about fraudsters and scams around the country. Grow passed Nygaard names and photos of scammers who had hit nearby cities. But it ‘wasn’t until that woman in that bar [in Florida] … that all of that knowledge from those years came into play,’ he said.

When the doctor asked Nygaard to help her, he asked if the psychic’s last name was Marks. Stunned, the doctor asked how he had known. ‘I’m psychic,’ he joked. Actually, the psychic in question was Gina Marie Marks, a serial offender whose last name Nygaard remembered from his conversations with Grow.

Nygaard had one stipulation for taking the doctor’s case: she would pursue an arrest no matter how much money the psychic offered her to settle. Then he found four more women who were Marks’s victims, and gathered evidence from all of them. Eventually, Marks was arrested, and the doctor got her money back.

Marks was his first psychic arrest, and that was the moment the disparate pieces of his life clicked into place. ‘All of those years, all that aggravation … fighting with the bosses … having to know the law – I never understood what it was forging me for,’ he said. ‘It was forging me for this fight.’

In early March, Nygaard and I ate dinner at a corner table at P J Clarke’s in midtown Manhattan. He was telling me about another case: in June 2010, a young woman – let’s use the name Vivian – was walking in New York City when she was approached by a woman who called herself Sarah. Sarah said she sensed an energy from Vivian and that something bad was happening in her life. Indeed, Vivian had recently been discharged from Army Officer Candidate School after an injury, and was going through a divorce.

Sarah and Vivian exchanged numbers, and Sarah later told her that she needed $90 for crystals to figure out where the negativity was coming from. By the end of the month, Sarah said she had figured it out: someone had placed a curse on Vivian, probably her stepmother. Vivian should take out $2,700 and put the money, along with rose petals and tree leaves, under her mattress and sleep on it.

Later, Sarah contacted Vivian to confirm it was her stepmother who had placed the curse. To lift it, she would have to sacrifice the $2,700. Vivian needed to bring the money, a jar, and a pair of white underwear to her apartment. Sarah filled the jar with water, wrapped an egg in the underwear, and rubbed it over Vivian’s body. In the dramatic finale of the ritual, the egg cracked open, and a dead baby corn snake fell out. The water had turned a deep, bloody red.
Psychic tricks haven’t changed much, Nygaard said. Needles emerge from a tomato. An egg cracks, and blood or dead animals spill out

Over the succeeding months, Sarah asked Vivian to send more money. In October 2013, Sarah said ‘the church’ needed $10,800, and Vivian went to the bank and took out a $12,000 loan. Vivian followed instructions to send Sarah a Cartier watch and Saks Fifth Avenue gift cards, though she was unsuccessful in leasing a Mercedes. By the time Vivian contacted Nygaard, she had lost more than $30,000.

Nygaard took Vivian’s case to the NYPD, where he was turned away. But Nygaard knew that Sarah had asked Vivian to send a watch to her address in Florida. If any part of a crime happens out of state, the whole crime can be prosecuted in that jurisdiction. Nygaard flew there to speak to a detective who agreed to help. His accumulation of evidence led to Sarah’s arrest, and Vivian’s money was returned.

Psychic tricks haven’t changed much, Nygaard told me. Needles emerge from a tomato. Something ominous comes out of a grapefruit. An egg cracks, and blood or dead animals spill out. ‘A lot of the newer ones, they stay away from that stuff, but when they want to really go for it, they go old school,’ Nygaard said.
As Nygaard ate his burger, I shared a case of my own: I had gone to see Sarah, who now goes by Emma, a couple weeks earlier, for a psychic reading. Nygaard perked up: ‘Oh, you did?’

I had nervously walked down 12th Street in the East Village until I arrived at a storefront with a green sign. I had wondered if Emma would try to scare me with a curse or some other tactic to get more money from me. I asked for a full-life reading for $150. I didn’t want to lie to be a better mark, so I brought up the most vulnerable topic I had on hand: whether my husband and I should try to have a baby. Emma looked carefully at me while I sat somewhat awkwardly in a large, velvet throne-like chair.

She asked some leading questions about my family (‘there is one family member you’re not as close to, there’s some pain there’) and my husband (‘you’re not spending as much time together these days’). Her first insight was universally obvious, and the second was untrue. I tried to keep the conversation going, but we naturally petered out around 25 minutes later. Emma asked if I would like to have my aura cleansed, because she saw I had two dark spots; it would cost an additional $250. I had budgeted only $300. I declined. Looking a little bored, Emma ended the session.

I found the interaction unimpressive, and, as I left, my sympathy for Nygaard’s clients wavered. The experience didn’t feel like a film noir; I wasn’t caught up in a seedy underbelly world of conmen who were experts at deception. The storefront space had been dumpy, and I was embarrassed to be there. I was even embarrassed for Emma, who was barefoot, possibly wearing a nightgown, and had put no effort into the reading. There were clearly children hiding behind a curtain, attempting to be quiet while their mom worked.

As a journalist who writes about science, I have covered my share of health scams. Throughout my career, I’ve spent hours carefully explaining in articles why certain wellness products don’t work and are a waste of money. There’s no scarcity of psychic scams either. Recent surveys suggest that four in 10 US adults believe in psychics, and as of 2022 the industry makes around $2 billion a year. After a few years of debunking, I accepted that scams were like a hydra’s heads: cut one off, and two more grew in its place.
Walking down the sidewalk, I hardened against the people who could fall for what I’d just experienced. If people could get tricked by that, what good was it to help them?

Across the street from P J Clarke’s, at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, I had tickets to a one-night-only performance of Houdini Speaks to the Living, a play based on letters between Harry Houdini and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Nygaard and I crossed the street into a packed auditorium, finding two empty seats near the back. The lights dimmed, and two actors walked on stage, one representing Doyle, and the other Houdini.

Doyle had dreamed up Sherlock Holmes, the ultimate logician who solved crimes by piecing together clues in ingenious ways. But Doyle was an advocate of Spiritualism, the belief that mediums could communicate with the dead, while Houdini (who once brought tricks based on the idea to his performance) came to believe that the profession was poison. In 1926, Houdini testified before the US Congress for a law that would criminalise fortune-telling. Elected officials didn’t feel it was necessarily their responsibility to help those who were duped. (Did I relate?) Ralph Gilbert, the representative for Kentucky, said that Houdini was ‘taking the matter entirely too seriously’.

The play dramatised Doyle’s attempts to convince Houdini that some mediums were credible. Houdini rebutted with counter-Spiritualism screeds, revealing how the mediums’ tricks work. He was harsh, and came across as a self-righteous know-it-all. Doyle and Houdini’s friendship ended, and they never spoke again.

At the end of the show, Nygaard was animated. I expected him to align with Houdini, especially after my encounter with Emma. Nygaard had seemed like an obvious reincarnation of the magician and his undertaking. Others think so too – Nygaard was recently invited to the Society of American Magicians’ Paranormal Investigations Committee, and regularly speaks at sceptic societies.
‘When the right con artist comes along and uses the right techniques on you … It can be more powerful than a gun’

But Nygaard felt conflicted. ‘My investigations are really not about supernatural ability,’ he said. He doesn’t care whether people can see the future. ‘I’ve never gone after a psychic and said … they should be arrested because they say they’re psychic,’ he said. He busts people for lying about what they say they’re doing with their clients’ money: buying cars and watches instead of casting spells.

We left the theatre and walked through a cold wind towards the 1 Train. ‘I’m going to take you out [to] the left field,’ he said. Nygaard told me he’s had experiences that have made him wonder about the supernatural. Sometimes, when driving a police car, he felt like the universe was taking the wheel. Once, while searching for a stolen briefcase, Nygaard heard a voice that told him to look up. He was passing by a deli, and stopped to check if the briefcase was on the roof; it was. In another instance, he was at the Chinese restaurant Wo Hop in Chinatown at 2 am when he saw, written on a dollar bill stuck to the wall, the nickname of a person who was connected to a crime he was investigating. ‘I have asked for help, and I’ve gotten answers, and I know those answers came from the universe,’ he said.

Nygaard had deep empathy for Doyle, who had lost a son in the war and wanted to speak to him again. Doyle’s grief fuelled his myopia when it came to a medium’s tricks, and when Houdini showed him it was all an illusion, it served as a reminder that his son would never return. For Nygaard, it was a perfect example of how ‘all of that learning, all of that knowledge, could go right out the window when the right con artist comes along and uses the right techniques on you … that’s how scary it is, how words can be so deceptive. It can be more powerful than a gun.’

I suddenly felt ashamed of how I felt when I left Emma. My attention had been misdirected, I realised. In being so judgmental about how someone could succumb to a bad trick, I had forgotten how much power the deceiver had.

Even Houdini remained vulnerable to wondering what if. He told his wife Bess that, if it was possible to send a message from the beyond, he would do so. For a decade, she held a seance on Halloween (the day he died) and waited. On the last one, Bess announced:

I do not believe that Houdini can come back to me, or to anyone … I do not believe that ghosts or spirits exist. The Houdini shrine has burned for 10 years … I now reverently turn out the light. It is finished. Good night, Harry.
The final moments of the show played recorded audio of Bess’s shaky voice. My stomach had tangled up into knots.
In May, Nygaard and I sat outside the Fanelli Cafe in SoHo, sharing a plate of fries in the afternoon sun.

I asked about his future. He works mostly by himself and has more cases than he can handle. He doesn’t think he could train someone to do what he does. Others might have the same investigative skills, but no one else would give psychic victims their all. He flies to other states to see clients or track psychics at the drop of a hat. He pressures police officers and prosecutors, and isn’t afraid to get in their face. His forcefulness has had consequences: in 2019, the National Association of Bunco Investigators rescinded his membership after his criticism of police handling of psychic fraud.

His dedication has required sacrifices. ‘I always did want a family, but I think what I do came at a cost,’ he said. When he was a cop, he was once on call with an officer who didn’t want to pursue an arrest because he would be late to his children’s dentist appointment. Nygaard responded: ‘Well, I guess your kids aren’t going to the dentist.’
‘You can’t have that attitude and have a relationship,’ he told me.
‘I was sitting all by myself in Florida contemplating on whether I have chosen the correct path in life’

Had I seen the movie Heat (1995), he asked, with Robert De Niro as a thief and Al Pacino as a cop? The two men are locked in a cat-and-mouse game. Near the end of the movie, they sit in a diner, comparing their lives.
‘So you never wanted a regular-type life?’ Pacino asks. He himself barely sees his family because he spends ‘all my time chasing guys like you around the block.’
De Niro replies: ‘A guy told me one time, don’t let yourself get attached to anything you are not willing to walk out on in 30 seconds flat if you feel the heat around a corner.’
That’s how Nygaard felt: ‘You want it, but you want the other thing more.’

Around a month later, on Father’s Day, I thought about Nygaard. I wondered if comparing his life with film characters who had simplistic moral drives was masking a deeper, more complex loss. The next day, I got a text from him. After spending Father’s Day alone, he had pondered the same: ‘I was sitting all by myself in Florida contemplating on whether I have chosen the correct path in life,’ he wrote. Was it all worth it?

Then, he received a message from a former client. ‘I don’t recall if you have children, but today I wanted to honour you all the same,’ she wrote. ‘You came into my life at such a strange time and the strength you provided, the direction, and how much you believed in me really made a difference and a massive impact on my life.’ Her text felt like a divine signal, he told me. ‘I felt like, through her, God was telling me: “Don’t doubt for a minute the path you have taken,”’ he wrote, ‘“because it’s the right one.”’

items.title: Those forced to cross borders are imagining a radical new world | Aeon Essays
items.description: In 1986, I was 19 and behind bars in a small prison on the border between Iran and Pakistan. I had been arrested while attempting to cross the border irregularly into Pakistan. Everyone I met in that prison had been detained in connection with the border. It w
items.author: Shahram Khosravi
paragraphs: In 1986, I was 19 and behind bars in a small prison on the border between Iran and Pakistan. I had been arrested while attempting to cross the border irregularly into Pakistan. Everyone I met in that prison had been detained in connection with the border. It was a small space, the cells overcrowded and unsanitary, but it held an extraordinary diversity of people: local smugglers, large-scale drug-traffickers, undocumented migrant workers, and refugees; Iranians, Afghans, Pakistanis, as well as Baluch men whose communities had crossed these lands freely for generations but who were now being punished for violating the territorial order of the nation-state. Multiple languages were spoken at once. Different histories, geographies and ways of inhabiting the world converged within the same confined space.

Yet we all shared one thing. We had refused, for different reasons, to respect the border. The state saw us through a single imaginary: as criminals, trespassers or illegal bodies to be contained. We, however, were animated by different imaginations. Each of us had imagined a life that exceeded the border and acted upon that imagination. In that sense, the prison did not simply contain border-crossers; it brought together people whose aspirations had collided with the territorial imaginary of the nation-state.

That prison experience was perhaps one reason I became a scholar of borders. It remains, even today, the most important school of border studies I have ever attended. The conversations in the cells and during brief moments in the prison yard revolved around borders; how they operated, how they were enforced and, above all, how they might be circumvented. The prison became an unlikely site of knowledge-production: not simply the sharing of survival strategies but the enactment of an imagination that paid no heed to prison walls or state borders.

Many years later, in a prison north of Stockholm, I interviewed a human smuggler who told me he saw himself as an architect: ‘I design a journey, like an architect designs a building,’ he said. The comparison stayed with me. Architects imagine and design structures that do not yet exist. Their work begins with the capacity to visualise what is not yet visible. In a similar way, smugglers design border crossings that, from the perspective of the state, would be impossible. A smuggler’s work consists of imagining routes where borders appear closed, creating connections where states impose separation, and envisioning possibilities for mobility when people are immobilised by borders. A smuggler speculates on possibilities in seemingly impossible situations. Seen this way, the smuggler’s ‘architecture’ is an enactment of an imagination that refuses the state imaginary expressed through borders.

The parallels between human smuggling and architecture helped me understand the relationship between imagination, fugitivity and knowledge-production. While fugitivity and imagination are oriented toward the future, toward not-yet-realised possibilities, state power often relies on backward-looking imaginaries grounded in myths of shared blood, origin and belonging. States are hostile to this relationship because it exposes borders as political constructions that can be reimagined, negotiated and crossed. Like capitalism, the nation-state depends upon such imaginaries to stabilise its claims to totality, making it difficult to imagine a world beyond capitalism and the nation-state system.
Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat

All around us, across the world, people are being confined, displaced, silenced and rendered disposable, in service of imaginaries that seek to define the limits of life, mobility and freedom. We live in a conjunctural moment shaped by the convergence of two dark forces: borderless wars that destroy lives, produce death and generate displacement, and endless borders that deny mobility to those seeking survival. Together, they produce fugitive lives and fugitive bodies. But they also produce fugitive imagination, the irreducible capacity to envision and enact life beyond the worlds that seek to contain it.

Philosophers often define imagination as the capacity to hold present in the mind what is absent from sensory perception. It is also the capacity to envision alternative ways of organising social reality. Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat. The state-centric imaginary presents history as coherent, and intact through symbols, narratives and rituals. The capacity to disrupt the hegemony of state imaginaries is therefore criminalised, suppressed and persecuted. In this sense, fugitivity is inseparable from imagination.

A fugitive is someone fleeing harsh institutions and conditions. The fugitive is an outlaw: a person hiding from a hostile law. Historically, the term referred to enslaved people’s resistance to slavery, its dehumanising logic, and the political economy built upon the extraction of uncompensated labour to maximise profits from cash crops like cotton, tobacco and sugar. Fugitivity was a response to captivity and, as such, an act of liberation, not only from the brutal material conditions of enslavement, but also from the imposed image of the enslaved subject produced by racist ideology. Fugitivity is a way of escaping and a way of knowing.

When Frederick Douglass, one of the most important figures in the 19th-century struggle for African American freedom and civil rights, began learning to read, his enslaver Hugh Auld forbade it, declaring that, if Douglass learned to read, ‘there would be no keeping him’. Once capable of reading, Auld argued, Douglass would inevitably desire to write, and ‘this accomplished, he will be running away with himself.’

This phrase is striking. It suggests a distinction between the enslaved person and the enslaved body. To ‘run away with oneself’ is not simply to flee physically; it is to reclaim one’s imagination and humanity. Under slavery, where Black bodies were turned into capital, fugitivity was criminalised as theft. The fugitive was pursued by law because they were perceived to have stolen property from their enslaver: their own body. In reality, they were reclaiming what had first been stolen from them. If the captivity of the body depends upon the captivity of the mind, then the emancipation of consciousness becomes a precondition for bodily liberation. Such emancipation engenders new subjectivities and creates the conditions for imagining what previously appeared impossible: life beyond chains, borders and confinement. Auld’s anxiety over Douglass’s literacy reflected precisely this logic. His fear was not simply the loss of labour, but the emergence of a subject who would not obey the racial imaginary; ‘he will be running away with himself.’
Literacy was inseparable from emancipation, whereas pedagogy became fugitive

The condition of fugitivity emerged from a radical imagination capable of envisioning existence beyond oppression. As a refusal of captivity, it entailed an inner transformation – a reorientation of consciousness that makes escape conceivable in the first place. This is the transformative power of imagination: it enables subjects to perceive possibilities beyond the limits imposed by domination. As Frantz Fanon reminds us in The Wretched of the Earth (1961), resistance opens a path toward liberation through a radical transformation of consciousness. Fugitivity is therefore a refusal to be objectified, categorised and reduced to the singular identities imposed by colonial imaginaries. The passage from subjection to freedom, from a colonial imaginary to a fugitive imagination, is thus a process of self-actualisation and the cultivation of what might be called a consciousness of refusal.

Despite prohibition and danger, Douglass pursued literacy covertly. Reading and writing eventually enabled him to forge passes for himself and others and to flee bondage. Literacy was thus inseparable from emancipation, whereas pedagogy became fugitive in two senses: first, because it was concerned with experiences of flight, concealment and resistance; and, second, because it was itself practised under conditions of flight and opacity.

Knowing the emancipatory power of education, many enslaved people continued to learn despite violent restrictions and anti-literacy laws. In Fugitive Pedagogy: Carter G Woodson and the Art of Black Teaching (2021), the historian Jarvis Givens traces the history of criminalised Black education in the United States, documenting the struggles of Black educators and students against centuries of anti-literacy laws and racist policing. The struggle surrounding Black education did not end with slavery, continuing instead through the era of racial segregation under Jim Crow and into the present. Contemporary attacks on Black studies and critical race theory in the US are among the latest examples of hostility toward forms of knowledge that expose structures of racial subordination.

In recent years, operations by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to arrest undocumented migrants have often been conducted near schools, where parents drop off and pick up their children. Such practices have deterred many parents from sending their children to school for fear of detention and deportation. One of the consequences of these enforcement strategies is that they undermine access to education and disrupt the pedagogical conditions. A study of five California school districts found a 22 per cent increase in daily student absences following ICE raids conducted in early 2025.

The situation is not much different in Europe. Universities are increasingly shaped by hostile political climates in which curricula are regulated, funding is reduced, and critical fields of enquiry are delegitimised. In such contexts, critical knowledge itself becomes fugitive. For example, Sweden recently proposed a controversial law requiring state employees, including teachers and university professors, to report undocumented migrants to the police; following protests, the law was amended to exclude teachers and doctors, but tax officers and insurance agents must still ‘snitch’ on the undocumented.

Across different historical periods and geographical contexts, we see attempts to control or criminalise education in order to reproduce the state imaginary and suppress any stirrings of a fugitive imagination.

Palestine offers a striking example of the relationship between imagination, knowledge and fugitivity. Palestinian resistance is sustained by a fugitive imagination of freedom beyond colonial domination. Israel’s continued imposition of its colonial imaginary through occupation, genocide and scholasticide therefore targets not only Palestinian bodies and institutions but also the spaces in which alternative futures are imagined. (‘Scholasticide’ describes the systematic destruction of educational institutions and schools in Palestine by Israel.) This is why schools, universities and cultural institutions have repeatedly become targets of repression.

Since the start of the recent genocide in Gaza, more than 95 per cent of schools have been damaged or destroyed, disrupting the education of nearly 700,000 students. All 19 of Gaza’s recognised higher education institutions, including 12 universities, have been destroyed, and approximately 100 university professors have been killed. Yet attacks on Palestinian education did not begin with the current war.
Called ‘cells of illegal education’ by the Israeli authorities, underground schools were frequently raided

Systematic destruction of educational infrastructures has been part of the war against Palestine since the early 1970s when the first higher education institutions emerged. Birzeit University, one of the most important centres of Palestinian intellectual life, was repeatedly closed by Israeli authorities. Between 1973 and 1992, the university was shut down 15 times, including a closure of almost four and a half years during the First Intifada. Starting in 1987, this period saw Palestinian education literally criminalised; repression only intensified. All six universities, 13 colleges and approximately 1,200 schools were closed.

Yet the suppression of formal education also generated fugitive pedagogical practices. As schools and universities were closed, teaching moved into homes, churches and mosques. Called ‘cells of illegal education’ by the Israeli authorities, these underground schools were frequently raided. ‘Soldiers would throw teargas grenades into the room to force all the students out, then split up so one group could arrest those who fled while the other would destroy science equipment or photocopiers and, later on, computers,’ writes Gabi Baramki in Peaceful Resistance: Building a Palestinian University Under Occupation (2009). Students escaped through windows or across roofs. Teachers and students who got arrested for organising and attending ‘cells of illegal education’ were charged with a ‘public order offence’.

The Palestinian case demonstrates that education is never merely about knowledge. It is also a site of political struggle because it cultivates the fugitive imagination, the capacity to envision freedom beyond the colonial imaginaries that sustain occupation.

Since the Taliban regained control of Afghanistan in August 2021, they have systematically restricted the rights and freedoms of women and girls. One of their earliest targets was female education. In March 2022, the Taliban banned girls and women from attending secondary schools and universities. According to UNESCO, by August 2025 nearly 2.2 million Afghan girls were barred from education beyond the primary level.

The criminalisation of female education has, however, generated resistance. Across Afghanistan, underground educational initiatives have emerged to challenge these restrictions. In parts of Kabul, local networks have organised clandestine schools hidden from the authorities. Living rooms, basements and private halls have been transformed into classrooms where small groups of girls continue to learn, despite the risks involved. If fugitivity in relation to education was historically shaped by race in the US, in Afghanistan it is profoundly shaped by gender. The struggle over women’s education is about regulation of who may know and imagine otherwise. What the Taliban fear is not women’s education but the fugitive imagination it cultivates. The Taliban know that literacy transforms consciousness. It enables women to refuse the patriarchal imaginary and to imagine lives beyond the confines it imposes.

The Taliban’s fear echoes Auld’s reaction to Douglass’s literacy. Auld warned that if an enslaved person learned to read, ‘he would at once become unmanageable’. The Taliban’s concern follows the same logic: a woman who acquires knowledge runs away with herself.

The history of fugitivity is deeply entangled with the history of modernity itself, a modernity grounded in racial capitalism and constituted through colonialism and the nation-state system. This connection can be seen in the continuity between enslaved people fleeing plantations and refugees crossing contemporary state borders – indeed, the words ‘refugee’ and ‘fugitive’ share the same etymological root in the Latin fugere, meaning ‘to flee’. So, it makes sense that Moria Camp on the Greek island of Lesvos, once the largest and most notorious refugee camp in Europe, offers another insight into how fugitivity and imagination are interlinked.

Set up in January 2013, the camp’s harsh militarised regulation, spatial design and material conditions produced what might be called a camp imaginary, an expression of Europe’s border regime and its political desires, positioning refugees as unwanted, unfree and disposable subjects. Yet Moria was also a site where refugees created alternative spaces of learning, artistic expression and collective care. Through education, music, art and everyday acts of mutual support, they generated conditions that made survival possible. As Yannis Hamilakis demonstrated in his archaeological study of Moria, refugees created spaces for imagining precisely what the camp sought to render impossible: life beyond its spatial and political boundaries. In this sense, the camp was not only a space of confinement but also a site of fugitive imagination.

The final act of this fugitivity came in 2020: after years of overcrowding and unsafe conditions, the camp burned down. Yet the most enduring expression of fugitive imagination was not the end of the camp itself but the lives that emerged from it. Many former residents became filmmakers, musicians, poets, researchers and activists, demonstrating that, while the camp sought to contain people physically, it could not extinguish their capacity to imagine and create otherwise.
A fugitive imagination emerges through the practical and intellectual labour of navigating violence

Survival under conditions of violence requires an intimate knowledge of violence – its logics, structures and repetitions. Such knowledge is necessary not only to endure violence but also to resist the imaginaries that sustain it. Drawing upon the idea of ‘borderland thinking’ – a concept originating from the Chicana scholar and poet Gloria Anzaldúa, which centres knowledge produced through the lived experience of physical and cultural borders – I think of fugitive imagination as a form of situated knowledge produced by people who must survive systems of capture, confinement and bordering. Anzaldúa, who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas, on the US-Mexico border, conceptualised the borderlands as a space of imagination through what she called la facultad:

… the capacity to see in surface phenomena the meaning of deeper realities, to see the deep structure below the surface … When we’re up against the wall, when we have all sorts of oppressions coming at us, we are forced to develop this faculty so that we’ll know when the next person is going to slap us or lock us away.

For people of the borderlands, la facultad is both a method of knowledge-production and a vital survival skill; it emerges not despite conditions of vulnerability and violence but through them. In the same manner, a fugitive imagination emerges through the practical and intellectual labour of navigating violence, even as it envisions possibilities beyond it.

To gain access to imagination, to learn how to cultivate and enact it, is to break with the imaginaries that make every future appear the same. It is to create, within the present, the conditions for something that does not yet exist. Politics, then, is not only a struggle over power. It is also a struggle over images, imaginaries and imagination itself. It is a battle over what can be thought, what can be desired, and what can still be made possible.

Earlier this year, I received a WhatsApp call from a childhood friend. We had grown up together in a small village in southwestern Iran, and it was the first call I had received from Iran in more than three months. The latest dreadful period had begun in December 2025 with the violent suppression of public protests; initially sparked by frustration over an economic crisis, they’d soon developed into a broad uprising. The Iranian state’s response was brutal. Thousands of people were killed and many more arrested. The state had cut off not only internet access but also much of the country’s telecommunications infrastructure. Iranians were still in shock from the militarised crackdown when an intense US-Israel war with Iran began on the last day of February 2026, bringing even more death and silence.

When my friend’s name appeared on my screen, I hesitated before answering. I felt ashamed: I did not know how to speak to someone who had lived through so much violence while I remained safe. I called him back later that day, after collecting myself. The connection was poor and our conversation fragmented: a word here, a phrase there, only occasionally a complete sentence. But I was surprised – unsettled, in fact – by what I was able to piece together. Spring, I heard him say, had brought abundant rain. Alongside bombs and bullets, rain had fallen, more than in previous years. What arrived through his fragmented voice was not words but imagination.

I imagined the mountains saturated with water, the springs running full, the wheat fields nourished and waiting to be harvested. Even as US bombs materialised a colonial imaginary that sought to reorder the world according to imperial logics of domination, people continued to imagine rain, harvests, seasons. To look toward the sky and see rain falling alongside bombs was a refusal of the imperial imaginary – an imagination of life, despite everything, an imagination that cannot be killed, bombed, stolen or abducted, and from which the seeds of an alternative future might emerge.

From the plantation to the border, from the genocide in Palestine to the Taliban’s war on women, and from refugee camps to the war on Iran, we encounter recurring attempts to preserve regimes of truth and imaginaries that seek to define the limits of life, mobility and freedom. Yet these projects of domination continually generate their own negation. Wherever people are confined, displaced, silenced or rendered disposable, fugitive forms of knowledge, pedagogy and imagination emerge. This is why history never ends.
Author’s note: a version of this essay’s opening story appears in my book ‘Illegal Traveller’: An Auto-Ethnography of Borders (2010) and in The Funambulist magazine.

items.title: Sometimes, you ‘just know’ something’s off – but how? | Aeon Essays
items.description: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
items.author: Marc A Moffett
paragraphs: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?
We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical. Because we encounter them in their most dramatic forms, like runaway trolleys and fake barns, thought experiments seem exotic. But properly understood, these imaginative episodes are important tools for sharpening our grasp of key concepts. In fact, their functioning is continuous with something far more familiar: the way we routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life, wondering what might happen if we take one path rather than another in the proverbial fork in the road.

These imaginings are just thought experiments as they appear in everyday life. Imagine you are deciding whether to tell a friend that his husband has been unfaithful. You picture the conversation, the shock, the hurt that registers on his face. And in that imagined moment, you see that causing such pain is a reason to hold your tongue, even if it’s not a good or decisive one.

How did you determine that this was a reason against divulging the infidelity? It’s not as if you literally see that causing pain is a reason not to do something, nor do you infer it from other things. Rather, in entertaining the possibility, you apprehended his pain as a relevant consideration, as something that counts against disclosure. Its status as a reason emerged not from an argument, but directly from your understanding. It just seems like a reason to hold your tongue.
Intuition’s verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work

Notice that this phenomenon also occurs in the thought experiments discussed above. It just seems wrong to push the bystander from the bridge; similarly, it just seems false that you would know it was a real barn in fake-barn country. In both cases, the answer doesn’t arise from an argument. These intuitions arrive unbidden, prior to any deliberation.

These seemings have an unmistakable epistemic pull. Because your friend’s pain seems like a reason, we accept it as such: the seeming is the reason. What is striking is not simply that we have such seemings, but that we trust them. They are involved in shaping our deliberations, guiding our actions, and eliciting belief. They do not merely occur to us; they appear to reveal something about how things must be in the imagined scenario.

For all their ordinariness, however, intuitions remain puzzling. In perceptual experience, we at least have an established framework: the world impinges on our senses, and different perceptual modalities reinforce one another. In the end, we can trace the causal route it takes to produce them. Intuition offers no such apparatus. Its verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work and nothing we can point to that they make contact with. Consequently, we rely on them without a clear account of their nature or epistemic authority. But before we can understand intuitions themselves, we need to situate them within a broader epistemological landscape, one shaped by attempts to unify the justification of our basic beliefs.

We all have beliefs about the world, and we care whether they are true. We want to get things right. But we can’t step outside our own minds to check a belief against the world; the best we can do is to hold it for good reasons – for considerations that, from where we stand, speak in favour of its truth. That is what justification is.

Now suppose that beliefs could only ever be justified by other beliefs. Then, as the ancient Sceptics observed, no belief could ever be justified at all. Each belief would derive its support from further beliefs, which would themselves require further support, and so on without end. To foil this regress, we have three options: embrace an infinite chain (infinitism), allow the chain to loop back on itself (coherentism), or hold that some beliefs are justified independently of others (foundationalism). It is this final option, the view that there is a starting point or foundation for justification, that I will develop. But to do so, we must spend a little time explaining how a belief can be justified by something other than another belief.
If it visually seems to you that there is a tree, then you have a justification for believing that there is a tree

Perception is the simplest example. When I see a tree, my visual experience makes it seem as if there is a tree in front of me. I am presented with the tree. As the philosopher William Tolhurst once put it, perceptual seemings have ‘the feel of truth’, a sense of revealing how things really are (unlike mere thoughts, imaginings or desires, which lack this air of disclosure). But visual experiences are not themselves beliefs: I can have them without forming a belief, perhaps because I distrust my eyesight or suspect my drink has been spiked. Conversely, I can believe there is a tree without seeing it, perhaps because I am told there is one there. Nevertheless, the fact that my visual experience seems to reveal a tree to me is relevant to explaining why I come to believe there is one and why this belief is reasonable.

This is the set-up we need in order to stop the regress of reasons: a state – the visual experience – that is not a belief, but that can nevertheless justify my belief. One influential proposal, developed in different ways by Jim Pryor and Michael Huemer, is that when the world seems to us to be a certain way, we thereby have some justification for believing that it is that way – unless we have a reason to distrust it. More specifically, if it visually seems to you that there is a tree in front of you, then you simply have a justification for believing that there is a tree. The justification does not depend on possessing independent reasons to think that your perceptual system is functioning properly, or that you are not hallucinating, or that your environment is benign. The perceptual seeming itself carries justificatory weight. Of course, my justification can be defeated (for instance, by evidence that I have taken a hallucinogen). The point is simply that no further positive belief is needed for a perceptual seeming to rationally support the corresponding belief.

This provides the basic framework for solving the regress problem. Perceptual experiences are not themselves beliefs, yet they provide reasons for belief. And they do so without relying on antecedent justified beliefs and are not themselves in need of justification. Still, this leaves us with an important question: what is it about these experiences that allows them to justify belief in this way?

Perceptual experience in general, and visual experience in particular, have two familiar features. First, as we have seen, they seem to reveal the world to us, to present objects and properties as actually being out there in the world. Second, they have a vivid phenomenology, a distinctive what-it’s-likeness, as the philosopher Thomas Nagel put it. Many philosophers take these two features to be inseparable: perception seems to disclose reality because it feels the way it does. On this standard view, its phenomenology is presentational, and it is this presentational phenomenology that explains the epistemic force of perceptual experience.

It is at this point that intuitions re-enter the story. According to John Bengson’s concept of quasi-perceptualism, we should model the epistemic behaviour of intuitions on the epistemic behaviour of perceptual experiences: if perceptual seemings justify because they possess a presentational phenomenology, and if intuitions are to justify in the same basic way, then they must share that same kind of presentational phenomenology. When we have an intuition, it justifies a corresponding belief by virtue of exhibiting a felt quality analogous to the what-it’s-likeness of perception, a kind of intellectual seeming that presents its content as actual. For instance, think again of the stranger who gives you a seriously creepy vibe. Just as the tree visually seems green, so the stranger may simply seem untrustworthy. Something about him presents itself to you that way without you having worked out what exactly is making you uncomfortable.

On this view, the explanation for the epistemic force of intuition mirrors the explanation for the epistemic force of perception. Both states present certain facts as real (or present certain propositions as true) by virtue of a distinctive presentational phenomenology. Call this the phenomenal strategy. The difference between them lies simply in the character of this phenomenology. In perception, it is an empirical sensory experience of the external world; in intuition, it is an intellectual or conceptual experience that purportedly reveals the normative, modal or conceptual structure of the world. These are features of the world that we comprehend but can’t see – that gratuitous cruelty counts against taking an action (normative structure), that there could be no round square (modal structure), or that the lucky believer in fake-barn country still doesn’t really know (conceptual structure).
A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual

But this phenomenological theory of the epistemic significance of intuitions faces a serious difficulty, one pressed most forcefully by Timothy Williamson and Ernest Sosa. Many reflective people report that they do not experience anything like the intellectual phenomenology that quasi-perceptualism posits. For them, judging that a proposition ‘seems right’ involves no distinctive experiential quality at all. If intuition lacks the requisite phenomenology in these cases, then the quasi-perceptualist explanation of its epistemic force collapses. (It’s worth evaluating this in yourself: do you feel an experiential quality when evaluating the thought experiments?)

This is the so-called absent intuition challenge. The kind of robust, presentational phenomenology developed on the basis of quasi-perceptualism is something many people simply deny having. Consequently, either these individuals lack introspective access to their own intuitions (an uncharitable conclusion), or the epistemic force of intuition cannot depend on the presence of a special intellectual phenomenology. If intuitions are to justify in the way quasi-perceptualism claims, then something other than phenomenology must be doing the epistemic work.

This conclusion can be pushed further to call into question even the epistemic significance of phenomenology for perception. To see why, consider the phenomenon known as derealisation disorder. Individuals with this condition report that their perceptual experiences feel perfectly normal from the inside – the colours, shapes and sensory qualities are all intact – yet the world does not seem real to them. Their experiences lack any sense of disclosure or revelatory force. In this respect, derealisation is the mirror image of a perfect hallucination. In derealisation, the experience gets things right, but it doesn’t feel like anything is being revealed; in hallucination, the experience gets things wrong, yet it feels totally convincing. The implication is striking. Call this apparent disclosure of reality presentationality: a mental state is presentational when its content is apprehended as how things actually are, rather than merely as they are thought about or imagined. Derealisation shows that neither the information carried by a perceptual state nor the way that state feels are sufficient for presentationality. A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual. Phenomenology, then, cannot explain the epistemic force of perceptual seemings, let alone intuitions.

This suggests that defenders of quasi-perceptualism have been looking in the wrong place. Earlier, I noted that perceptual experience has two salient features: it has a rich phenomenology, and it seems to reveal the world to us. The phenomenal strategy seized on the first feature – understandably, given how vivid and conspicuous perceptual phenomenology is – and then treated it as the source of the second. But derealisation cases show that phenomenology can remain intact even when the experience loses its revelatory character. What matters for justification is not how we experience something, but how we apprehend it. On the view I defend, presentationality is a cognitive posture, a way of apprehending a content rather than a distinctive way the experience feels. And it is this posture, this way of grasping the world and not its phenomenological glow, that supplies perceptual experience with its epistemic force.

To see what this posture amounts to, it helps to contrast it with more widely discussed attitudes. Belief, for example, is assertive: it commits us to the truth of its content. Imagination, by contrast, is non-assertive: it entertains possibilities without treating them as actual. Presentational attitudes (that is, seemings) occupy a middle ground. This cognitive posture is what makes a seeming capable of justifying a belief: it presents reality without committing to it, offering us a direct but defeasible route to acceptance.

Once we understand presentationality in this way, the case of intuition falls naturally into place. A crucial feature of presentational states is that they are happenings, not actions. They occur in us; we do not perform them. So, when something intuitively seems true, we do not decide to have this intuition any more than we decide to see a tree. It arrives unbidden. This passivity is precisely what allows a seeming to present its content as actual. When an intuition strikes us, we are not making a judgment or forming a belief. We are apprehending the content as the way things are. The intuition presents the scenario as actual in a manner that calls for belief. In this respect, intuitive seemings share the same role as perceptual seemings.
Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure

Understood in this way, the absent-intuition challenge dissolves. The quasi-perceptualist assumed that intuition’s presentational force must arise from an intellectual phenomenology analogous to the sensory phenomenology of perception. But if presentationality is a cognitive posture rather than a phenomenological glow, then no special ‘intellectual experience’ is needed. A person may have no distinctive phenomenology when an intuition arises and yet still apprehend the content as actual in the relevant sense. And once a content is apprehended as actual, it is reasonable to form the corresponding belief. The quasi-perceptualist is right that intuition and perception share something fundamental, but wrong about what that shared feature is. It is not a proprietary phenomenology, but the nature of the apprehension itself.

Why should apprehending a content as actual have any epistemic significance? The answer, I think, is simple. Presentational states are the cognitive events that place us in contact with the world or, more precisely, that seem to place us in contact with the world. When something presents itself to us as being the case, our default cognitive response is to form the corresponding belief. When I turn the corner of a building and my eyes fall on a tree, the tree is simply there before me. Believing that there is a tree is not normally a conclusion I draw; rather I simply accept what my experience presents to me. This is not a matter of inference or deliberation; it is the natural way a rational mind responds to what it takes to be reality.

Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure. When the apprehension is accurate, this default response reliably produces true belief; when it is not, the response is still intelligible and reasonable. Presentational states are epistemically respectable because they are where the world shows up for us: the point at which reality makes its first claim on belief. Intuitions inherit this status. They are simply the presentational events through which we apprehend the conceptual structure of a situation as actual, and in doing so provide a rational basis for belief without the need for any further epistemic mechanism.

Intuition saturates our ordinary reasoning. Whenever we see what follows from something, notice that something counts in favour of some action, or recognise something as a possible course of action, we are relying on intuition. These moments rarely announce themselves. They do not arrive with phenomenological fanfare. They are woven into the background of our deliberation, operating quietly whenever we take in a situation and immediately apprehend its normative or conceptual contours.

In this sense, intuition is to cognition what perception is to our engagement with the physical world. Perception allows us to navigate our environment by revealing how things stand around us; intuition allows us to navigate the space of reasons, norms and possibilities by revealing how things stand within the conceptual landscape. When we deliberate, we constantly rely on intuitions to apprehend which considerations matter, how they bear on one another, and what follows from them. Intuition is the cognitive means by which the conceptual structure of a situation is revealed to us.

Seen in this light, the thought experiments with which we started no longer appear as philosophical curiosities. They are simply highly controlled instances of a capacity we rely on constantly. When we imagine a runaway trolley or a real barn surrounded by fakes, we are not invoking a mysterious faculty or peering into a metaphysical telescope. We are exercising the same basic capacity we use when we imagine telling a difficult truth to a friend or weigh up different possible courses of action. The only difference is that philosophical cases are crafted to isolate a specific conceptual relation. Their dramatic trappings obscure the fact that they depend on the same presentational attitude at work in more mundane reasoning.
Intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it

This brings thought experiments back down to earth. Their epistemic significance arises not from exotic subject matter or imaginary scenarios, but from the fact that they trigger intuitions that disclose how certain concepts hang together. To see what it means for concepts to ‘hang together’, consider a familiar principle of storytelling: show, don’t tell. When J R R Tolkien in The Lord of the Rings (1954-55) describes the creature Gollum leading Frodo into the spider Shelob’s lair, he needn’t pause to explain: ‘This is an act of betrayal.’ The narrator doesn’t mark the moment when Gollum’s loyalties shift, or when his intentions cross a moral threshold. We grasp it directly from the unfolding of events. The situation presents itself as a betrayal: the actions, motives and dangers align in a way that demands the application of the concept. That is what I mean when I say that intuitions reveal how concepts hang together. They disclose the otherwise unstated conceptual requirements of a situation.

Now, a sceptic might argue that what is doing the work here is not intuition, but simply our skill at applying concepts. On this view, we respond correctly to cases because we are good at classifying situations. But this misses something crucial about the rationality of these classifications. To apply a concept is to act; it is to make a classificatory judgment. And judgments of this sort are not self-justifying. Simply deciding, without any basis, that a character has betrayed a friend would be epistemically arbitrary. Such judgments must themselves be grounded in something. Intuitions occur in us prior to and independently of any judgment. When a scenario strikes us as a clear instance of betrayal, that intuitive seeming is not itself an act of concept application. It is the pre-judgmental apprehension that makes the resulting judgment (the resulting application of the concept of betrayal) reasonable. In this sense, intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it.

This same phenomenon of intuitive apprehension preceding judgment also shows up in ordinary perception. When we open our eyes, the world does not appear as a mosaic of colours and shapes. It appears as a scene populated with meaningful objects: a child reaching for a toy, a cat waiting expectantly for dinner, a car approaching too fast. As P F Strawson observed, if we try to describe what we see using only low-level sensory terms (patches of colour, shifting brightness), we falsify the experience. The world comes to us in perception already organised by concepts. What is presented is not bare visual data but things of certain kinds, situated in relations to one another.

And here, intuition enters even into everyday perceptual experience itself. Perception reveals not merely visual arrays but robust, three-dimensional situations that are concept-laden. This becomes particularly vivid in cases where expertise comes into play. Imagine walking through a field with a trained herpetologist. You both see a snake. Your sensory experience may be phenomenologically indistinguishable from hers – the same curves of the body, the same mottled pattern. Yet what is presented to each of you differs. To you, it is simply a snake. To her, it is an Agkistrodon contortrix. The difference is not in your visual apparatus per se but in the concepts at work within perception. Her grasp of the relevant distinctions generates a conceptually richer, even if phenomenologically identical, presentational state. And because intuitions are not phenomenologically robust, there is no need for any difference in how things look. This is why perceptual expertise can subtly transform experience without altering its sensory character.

Perception, then, is a perfect illustration of the broader point about intuitions. Because they lack any robust phenomenology, intuitions serve their function in plain view without our taking explicit notice of them.

The person who declines to get in the stranger’s car, or who flags the email as a phishing attempt, or who walks away from the deal – these individuals are not acting irrationally or on mere feeling. They are responding to a genuine presentational state: something is showing up as creepy, fraudulent or wrong. The situation is presenting itself as having a certain character, and that presentation carries epistemic weight – not because it is infallible, but because it is the same kind of state that grounds all of our most basic cognitive contact with the world.

This is precisely what philosophers mean when they talk about intuition. The difference between the person on the bridge who immediately senses that pushing the bystander is wrong, and the person who declines to get into a stranger’s car, is not a difference in kind. It is a difference in context and control. The philosopher’s thought experiment is a deliberately engineered situation designed to isolate and interrogate a single intuitive response. The everyday case is messier, embedded in a richer context, and rarely examined. But the underlying capacity, the presentational apprehension of how things are, is the same.

What has been missing in our theorising, until now, is simply the explicit recognition of this continuity. Philosophers have a well-developed account of why rational intuitions carry epistemic weight. They have been slower to claim that this account extends naturally to the intuitions we act on every day. Once we see this, ‘vibes’ and gut feelings are neither vindicated wholesale nor dismissed as mere noise. Instead, they are brought into the same framework that governs our most careful reasoning. The task of philosophy, then, is not to decide whether to trust intuition. It is to understand the role it already plays, from the thought experiment to the uneasy feeling about a stranger, in almost every act of understanding.

items.title: The politics of masculinity at the end of the Roman republic | Aeon Essays
items.description: What does it mean to be a man? In the early 21st century, masculinity is contested and fraught with anxiety; influencers offer models of manliness involving fast cars, sexual conquests, and building up muscle. Before the rise of feminism, they suggest, in some
items.author: Catharine Edwards
paragraphs: What does it mean to be a man? In the early 21st century, masculinity is contested and fraught with anxiety; influencers offer models of manliness involving fast cars, sexual conquests, and building up muscle. Before the rise of feminism, they suggest, in some supposed Golden Age, everyone had a shared sense of what it meant to be a man – and being a man was unproblematically good. The Roman Empire, in their view, offers men today an inspirational example of power, hierarchy and achievement, which is why men think about it so much – unlike women, who are too immersed in their feelings…

Manliness certainly was celebrated in the works of Cicero, republican Rome’s most eloquent statesman. In the mid-1st century BCE, his persuasive powers in the law courts and the senate were second to none; his speeches went on to inspire would-be orators well into the 20th century. He is often seen as the very embodiment of the Roman republic. The political world in which he flourished was a self-consciously masculine one; to be accused of acting like a woman was, for a Roman man, a grievous insult. Yet in Cicero’s writing we can find other strains too.

For Roman men, anything labelled feminine was necessarily to be avoided, something to be ashamed of. But what exactly did it mean to act like a man? Ancient Rome in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE saw the rise of a succession of military leaders who were promoted as masculine role models. The great general Marius won a series of victories in Spain, North Africa and on Italy’s northern frontier. For several years in a row, he was elected consul, one of Rome’s two chief executive officers. Unlike many other Roman politicians, he didn’t have an aristocratic background. One Roman writer imagines Marius fending off accusations that he was coarse in his manners:
elegance is becoming to women but toil to men. All virtuous men ought to have more fame than riches. Arms, not fine trappings, bring glory.
– from The War Against Jugurtha by Sallust
(All translations are adapted from the Loeb Classical Library.)
Here was a model of manliness forged on the battlefield.

Given the military might of ancient Rome, it is surely unsurprising that Romans often associated masculinity with courage in battle. The word virtus, a term cognate with the Roman vir (meaning man as opposed to woman), clearly means ‘courage in war’ when it is first recorded in the mid-5th century BCE. Courage in battle could be taken as the foremost manifestation of Roman masculinity. The historian Sallust, writing in the 40s BCE, praises earlier generations of Romans for their pre-eminent manliness in war: ‘whenever their virtus repelled dangers, they rendered aid to their allies and friends.’ And yet, while Rome continued to boast ever more notable military successes in the middle and later republic (from the 3rd to the 1st century BCE), the battlefield was by no means the only arena in which Roman masculinity might be put to the test.

When Cicero was 16, like others of his social standing, his transition to adulthood was marked by a special ceremony, most likely at the feast of the Liberalia in 90 BCE. This was the moment when he first put on the toga of manhood, a cumbersome length of woollen fabric worn by Roman citizen men, a garment associated with civilian as opposed to military life. Years later, as consul in 63 BCE, Cicero played a leading role in uncovering and suppressing a conspiracy against the Roman state, and boasted that this was a victory won by ‘citizens in togas’. It was his speeches that had convinced his fellow senators and the Roman people of the dangers posed by Catiline’s conspiracy, leading to decisive action against those involved. Cicero had used his voice as consul to save Rome, he declared in a speech a few years later. Throughout his life, he insisted his victory was comparable to those of Rome’s greatest generals. Masculine achievements weren’t confined to the battlefield; rhetoric and oratory could also conquer.

By the time he secured the consulship, Cicero was regarded as Rome’s top orator. Public speaking was highly prized by members of Rome’s governing elite. Its end result mattered hugely – winning over one’s listeners. But the way Rome’s politicians spoke and even how they dressed could also serve to demonstrate their manliness. Codes of civilian masculinity governed behaviour in public spaces such as the Forum, the law-courts and the senate. Markers of manliness in this sphere were subject to relentless public scrutiny. As the later expert on oratory Quintilian put it, the orator’s dress needs to be ‘resplendent and manly: for when it comes to one’s toga and shoes and hair, excessive care as well as negligence are equally blameable’. The toga, for instance, must be correctly draped; he notes a little later, ‘throwing back the fold from its bottom onto the right shoulder is foppish and effeminate’.

Orators were alert to the niceties of their own – and one another’s – masculine self-fashioning. In the cacophonous world of the Roman republic, politicians, advocates and those aspiring to a public role exchanged no-holds-barred insults. Often, they cast aspersions on one another’s masculinity, with disparaging comments on an opponent’s way of speaking, his gestures, the way he wore his toga – as well as his sexual behaviour. Orators would be praised for speaking in a ‘manly’ way. And they were robustly attacked for any ‘effeminate’ deviations in their style and manner of speech. Some orators favoured a more elaborate style fashionable in the long-established rhetorical schools of the eastern Mediterranean, the zone the Romans called Asia. Contrasts were drawn between ‘Asian’ style and the plainer style associated with Athenian rhetorical tradition. The Asian style was regularly denigrated as ‘effeminate’. Yet too ‘unpolished’ a style could seem old-fashioned, even coarse. Moderation was itself celebrated as a quintessentially masculine quality. But where to draw the line?
Quintilian criticised rhetoric teachers who encourage their students to show off

In the late republic, attempts were made to codify guidance to aspiring orators. An anonymous treatise on rhetoric addressed To Herennius promises to help its reader present himself as a proper man through training in public speech.
