paragraphs: For the latest issue of AnOther Man, Pieter Hugo photographs Grace Wales Bonner’s Autumn/Winter 2026 collection with Adidas Originals in Nature’s Valley on coast of South Africa. The cover launched last week with a celebration at Dover Street Market

Pieter Hugo was celebrating his 50th birthday the night he and AnOther Man launched their photo story, shot in South Africa with stylist Akeem Smith for the magazine’s Winter/Spring 27 issue. The event, which took place at Dover Street Market last week, was co-hosted by Hugo, and AnOther Man’s editor-in-chief Ellie Grace Cumming and art director Jonny Lu.

Continuing his longstanding exploration of place, identity and representation, for this story the artist honed in on Nature’s Valley on South Africa’s southern coast. Speaking to AnOther Man’s contributing editor Lucy Kumara Moore for the edition, Hugo reflected on the area’s personal significance: “[When I spoke to Ellie and Jonny about a shoot for the edition], I happened to be at a house my family has on the south coast of South Africa. It’s in the middle of a nature reserve. It’s incredibly wild, very small and quite isolated. I’ve been going there for many years, always thinking about photography – making mental notes of locations and what looks great at what time of the day. I’ve shot a lot of personal work there.”

Moving between the city and its surrounding landscape, Hugo brought his distinctive documentary-style approach to Grace Wales Bonner’s Autumn/Winter 2026 collection, including her collaboration with Adidas Originals. The casting brought together Cape Town-based models and individuals street-cast in nearby villages. Typical of his approach, the story offers a portrait of a place and the people who inhabit it, touching on the visual codes of cinema, fashion and documentary.

“A big part of my practice, even though it’s concerned with portraiture, is often responding to an environment,” Hugo said. “I was seeing how one could fit together these three components: Grace’s fashion, my portraiture, and the environment I’d proposed.”

More than 200 guests enjoyed the cover’s launch party, celebrated with an evening of drinks and food, provided by Rose Bakery at Dover Street Market. Attendees, intersecting the worlds of fashion, music, filmmaking and art, included Tallulah Harlech, Isaac Benigson, Ancuta Sarca, Birgita Toyoda, Jerry Stafford, Denzel Himself, Piotr Chamier, Ella Ezekiel, Casper Sejersen, Reuben Esser, SJ Todd, Liberty Joy, Simon Parris, Raphael Hirsch and Manu Loca.

Opening the celebrations to the public, AnOther Man invited readers and members of the wider Dazed audience to attend, registering through the Dazed Club app. Guests left with posters signed by Hugo – a limited-edition keepsake from the evening, and the issue.

items.title: The Other Room: Hanna Moon and Moffy Gathorne-Hardy’s New Creative Agency
items.description: As the photographer and writer launch their women-only agency The Other Room, they discuss the importance of transgression, financial freedom and rebelling against the system
items.author: Violet Conroy
paragraphs: As the photographer and writer launch their women-only agency The Other Room, they discuss the importance of transgression, financial freedom and rebelling against the system

Although photographer Hanna Moon insists she is averse to the term ‘female gaze’, much of her creative work focuses on what it means to be a female artist. After coming across an introspective Dorothea Tanning self-portrait at a Tate retrospective in 2019, Moon became “interested in how the social and physical status of being female affects female artists’ work.” Feeling inspired, she revived her student publishing project A Nice Magazine, releasing a third issue in February 2025 devoted to the work of women photographers including Jet Swan, Momo Okabe, Rosie Marks, Julie Greve and Moon herself.

It’s an ethos that carries through to her latest endeavour, The Other Room – a new agency representing exclusively women: photographers Sandy Kim, Leigh Johnson, Donna Trope, Moon herself, and artist Frances Waite. Co-founded with Moon’s best friend, the writer and model Moffy Gathorne-Hardy, The Other Room takes a radical stance in its mission to facilitate artists’ creative freedom through financial stability. Most talent agencies operating in the fashion industry do not have a tone of voice or perspective per se, and not many are female-only; The Other Room is a welcome anomaly. A concurrent editorial platform, The Other Times, will expound upon the founding principles of the agency, publishing interviews, essays, articles and show reviews.

The Other Room takes its name from Virginia Woolf’s seminal 1929 essay A Room of One’s Own, a feminist polemic about women’s need for financial independence and intellectual freedom. Meanwhile, the design of the agency’s website lifts from the DIY, Xeroxed aesthetic of the Guerrilla Girls and feminist publications and posters from the 1970s and 1980s, with artists’ work showcased in a purposefully non-hierarchical manner. So, is there a uniting aesthetic that binds the work of these female artists? “There’s an inherent quality of resilience in women’s work because you have to go through so much shit, like having kids or people patronising you,” says Moon. “If you manage to actually have a voice as an artist, that’s already a huge achievement.”
Violet Conroy How did you two first meet?

Moffy Gathorne-Hardy I was a model when I was younger, and Hanna was on set as a photographer’s assistant on my first ever modelling job. She wanted to shoot me for something, so she asked the photographer for my number.

Hanna Moon I’ve always been interested in this weird or extraordinary kind of beauty. I was interested in Moffy because she was so awkward, and she came in with this book under her arm. I probably sensed something real in her, and then it was also her crossed eyes. [Laughs]. It’s quite hard to come across someone who fully embraces themselves in a fashion context.
VC How did your creative relationship unfold from there?

HM As well as photographing her, I commissioned Moffy to write things for my student magazine, A Nice Magazine, and I realised how intelligent she was. A sense of rebelliousness is the common thing for us. I also loved that Moffy doesn’t care about being naked in front of the camera. We’re very aligned: there’s a sense of transgression in our work but at the same time, it’s not serious.
MGH It always felt like our primary aim was just to have fun, and be cheeky in our work.
VC When did you start thinking about launching an agency together?

MGH We really wanted to do something creative together that felt like more of a long-form project, instead of Hanna just taking photos and me writing about them. Initially, we wanted to write a semi-autobiographical film loosely based on our friendship, then we thought we’d do a gallery. Then we landed on the idea of an agency. It felt like a structure we could use to fuck about with pre-existing structures.

HM I know what the agency world is like, so it made sense. It’s a bit naive to walk into a completely new system, like the art world, that you don’t really know how to navigate. In our relationship, Moffy is about thinking, ideas and feeling, whereas I’m very practical, like a bulldozer. I make things happen and I’m very decisive. We work well as a duo in that sense – it’s all about balance. We can operate in the current system with a touch of rebelliousness. But we are very serious about the business side of this project.
VC Why did you decide to represent only women artists? It’s quite radical.

HM It means there’s a clear starting point. The third issue of A Nice Magazine was female-only. It was inspired by a self-portrait by Dorothea Tanning, which made me cry. I wasn’t specifically focusing on gender, but the things Dorothea went through as a woman artist really resonated with me. There’s also a humour and lightness to her work that I love, despite the fact that the world wasn’t fair to her as an artist.

I hate the term ‘female gaze’, so I didn’t want it to be about that. But there’s an inherent quality of resilience in women’s work because you have to go through so much shit, like having kids or people patronising you. If you manage to have a voice as an artist, that’s already a huge achievement.
VC Tell me about your roster of artists.

HM We represent five artists, including me. There’s Sandy Kim, Leigh Johnson, Donna Trope and Frances Waite. Donna is from the older generation, but there’s a contemporariness to her work. There’s a certain freedom, confidence and provocation there. I first saw Sandy’s work when I was a student, and it was her nude self-portraits. I was quite shocked that she was an Asian girl doing that kind of work. It was ballsy and powerful. There’s an emotional and human quality to her work. Leigh bridges the worlds of art and fashion on her own terms. She’s primarily interested in sex and death. Frances is a visual artist who does pencil drawings. I saw the potential of how that could work in a commercial fashion context. She didn’t only want to belong in a traditional art space, and doesn’t care about labels. Her mentality aligned with ours.
VC I’m intrigued by the branding and design of The Other Room. It feels more editorial and conceptual than most agencies.

HM We want to be rebellious, but at the same time, we have to navigate the system and survive. We added a green filter on everything, which is an aesthetic from feminist publications and posters from the 1970s and 80s. The design is almost like an Easter egg: if you know, you know. If you’re interested in the sort of activism or feminism that we reference, it will resonate. The website homepage presentation is non-hierarchical and democratic. We also don’t want a news page, because the idea of constantly having to produce new work is just another pressure for artists.
VC How else is The Other Room different from other agencies?

HM We want to tackle all these traditional ideas, and the artist bio is one of them. What is the role of the bio? When you read the bio, it should be personal and make you feel the urge to look at their work.

MGH The thing I noticed when I did my own research on agency websites was that the focus was always on gallery names or big designers artists had worked with. That really detracted from the artists themselves because it was borrowing hype from other institutions. We do have client lists at the end of our bios though, because you need to in order to survive in the current climate.
VC Tell me about The Other Times, the editorial platform that runs alongside the agency.

MGH It’s making room for conversations and ideas that are being generated by the work that we’re doing at The Other Room. We’re going to do interviews, essays, articles, show reviews. The Xeroxed effect on the homepage was also a nod to the Guerrilla Girls and the DIY aesthetic. Alongside digital articles, we’re going to make physical newsletters that people can subscribe to.
VC Hanna, you’ve spoken about the importance of financial stability for female artists in the industry. Tell me about your own journey as a photographer?

HM As a student, I printed the first version of A Nice Magazine in Brighton on the cheapest paper. But I printed the most recent issue [in 2025] in Japan. When you have more financial freedom, it opens doors. You can have more power, a bigger platform, and most importantly, freedom. I managed to establish stability for myself as an artist via my work as a fashion photographer, and do multiple things at the same time. Having your own platform gives you freedom of speech.
VC How do you navigate that relationship between your editorial or personal work and your commercial work?

HM I think there almost shouldn’t be a separation. But if you work more, you have less focus on your personal projects. I’m not trying to criticise everything because I think any industry in the world is like that. I love fashion and I want to stick with it. But to do that, I shouldn’t feel bored in it. That’s why I’m trying to do something more meaningful with The Other Room. For me to have more passion, I just had to think about my value system and what really works for me.
VC Moffy, could you talk about your relationship to modelling and writing?

MGH I’m lucky in the sense that my experience of being a model hasn’t traumatised or disturbed me to the extent that it has lots of other people. But it has inserted itself into my experience of my own femininity and my own body. The fashion industry does this thing where it forces us to project ourselves into potential future aspirational states of being, like being thin or finally owning a certain handbag. By definition, having to project yourself into that potential state makes the current version of you ‘less than’. There’s also this idea that when you’re 30, 35, 40 – if we’re being generous – your life as a woman is also seen to be over. The whole experience of being a woman and being allowed to experience pleasure is really bookended. Writing is the antidote to that. And this project with Hanna feels like an antidote to that.
Learn more about The Other Room here

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

items.title: Inside Amanvari, Aman’s extraordinary new Baja California hideaway
items.description: Amanvari means 'peace' and 'water' in Sanskrit. An ethos of seaside tranquility is woven into every aspect of the intimate, 18-key property. Unlike the sprawling resorts in nearby Cabo San Lucas, Aman’s exclusive new Baja California retreat is intentionally sm
items.author: Lindsay Cohn
paragraphs: Amanvari means 'peace' and 'water' in Sanskrit. An ethos of seaside tranquility is woven into every aspect of the intimate, 18-key property. Unlike the sprawling resorts in nearby Cabo San Lucas, Aman’s exclusive new Baja California retreat is intentionally small, with privacy, serenity and connection to nature of equal importance. The landscape drives the design, acting as both the inspiration and the backdrop for a place so at home in its surroundings it feels as though the land and sea might have given permission to build it.

Set within the exclusive Costa Palmas community on Baja California’s East Cape, Amanvari is positioned to escape it all. Aside from Four Seasons Resort Los Cabos at Costa Palmas, a 10-minute drive away, there’s not much around. And that’s exactly the point. The property is wrapped in nature, removed from tourist-trodden Cabo San Lucas, but accessible enough to venture to a buzzy restaurant or bar should the mood strike – though, speaking from personal experience, you’re not going to want to leave the premises, aside from, perhaps, a day trip snorkelling the ancient coral reefs of Cabo Pulmo National Marine Park or an off-road expedition into the Sierra de la Laguna.

The Baja California landscape – soft sand extending into the deep blue Sea of Cortez, swaying palms, towering cardón cacti, arid desert, an estuary and distant mountains – inspired Elastic Architects’ design. The award-winning firm, with initial contributions from Heah & Co., used local elements, embraced minimalism and spotlighted artistic expression – from contemporary Mexican art to ancestral crafts – to create an indoor-outdoor sanctuary with a deep sense of place.

At the heart of the resort is Casa Grande, an open-plan, atrium-like structure perfectly balanced by a restrained neutral palette with views of the ever-changing sky throughout the day and night. It’s also home to one of Amanvari’s most impressive commissions: an intricate, textured dome, inspired by the spiral chambers of an extinct marine microfossil, which took artists Abi and Luisa Calvete of Extra Neutro more than 1,000 hours to create.

To the left, the curved lounge bar is enveloped in earthy materials, still water and rounded edges, fostering a sense of softness and serenity that’s matched by sweeping Baja vistas. Descend the spiral staircase down to the lower level for the panoramic main pool crafted from Caledonia Black granite as well as three dining venues that follow the same nature-led principles.
Amanvari has 18 stilted casitas, which almost appear to float above the trees.

Contemporary rooms are anchored by white concrete, natural limestone and tropical hardwoods, complemented by bespoke furnishings, textiles in sandy hues and original works by Mexican artisans such as exclusive mixed-media pieces by Arozarena de la Fuente and sculptural ceramics by Tomás Díaz of Disciplina Studio.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
The alfresco living spaces are an extension of the interiors – generous terraces with seating areas for morning coffee, and below, heated pools and outdoor showers.

While all the accommodations are striking, the most soul-stirring views are found in those facing the estuary or situated directly on the sand. I stayed in Casita #4, a short stroll down the path from Casa Grande.

Entering through the large wooden door into the courtyard and through the floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors, the sightlines of the inlet extend, unobstructed to the generous, second-floor terrace, an extension of the white and wood interiors.

Below, the heated pool and outdoor shower served as a private holiday haven, an even quieter respite, devoid of other guests (not that I saw many during my stay), where the only sounds were the fish frolicking in the water and the birds chirping.

Back inside, clever choices such as thoughtfully positioned beds and a television that rises and hides at the touch of a button reinforce the idea that the best thing to watch is the outdoors. The bathrooms feature dual limestone vanities on either side, Vermont Beige marble floors and walls, a spacious shower and a soaking tub for the ultimate unwinding experience.
Staying for drinks and dinner?

The curved, open-air lounge bar, which faces the waves on one side and the Sierra de la Laguna mountains on the other, is the place for pre-dinner drinks (I recommend the Bartolo, a clarified concoction of raicilla, mango and habanero) with a soundtrack of soulful live saxophone and the gentle crash of the waves.

Sesui is a sleek Japanese concept, centred around a 10-seat wood counter, illuminated by loofah lanterns the shape of sea urchins. It’s here that Chef Masao Matsubara prepares his ever-changing omakase, spotlighting the culinary conversation between Japan and Baja California. When I dined, highlights included a stunning mix of raw oyster with uni and caviar, dashi broth with shrimp, tempura and nigiri.

Arva, the Italian restaurant, offers seating in the elegant dining room, complete with a full-wall temperature-controlled wine display, and on the fire-warmed terrace below the stars. The menu highlights seasonal produce in dishes such as heirloom tomato and burrata salad, yellowtail crisp with caviar and orange, linguine with clams and fresh catch of the day.
For something more casual, Luma, pairs coastal-influenced Mexican cuisine with an laid-back beachfront setting.

The entire resort. From the moment the car turns down the gravel drive, a sense of calm washes over. Of course, it’s not just the peaceful atmosphere that allows guests to switch off but the thoughtful amenities and services geared towards unwinding.

If you really want to relax, first head to the 600-square-meter Aman Spa, a sanctuary of wellness that leans into ancestral healing traditions from Mexico and across Asia (Aman originated in Phuket, Thailand). Facilities include a stunning white temazcal (sweat lodge) and hydrotherapy houses. Treatments range from purifying facials and body wraps to the signature Desert Damiana, a healing journey that combines reflexology, stretching and an aromatic oil massage that took the post-flight tension straight out of me.

There’s also a 24-hour fitness centre kitted out with the latest Technogym equipment, a movement studio and a yoga pavilion. Though, I would recommend joining the sunrise sessions by the gorgeous pool for a chance to flow with the soundtrack

The service goes above and beyond. Snacks, cold water and Starlink Wi-Fi in the car from the airport. An umbrella to block the midday sun when I emerged from the car. Fresh herb bouquets upon first touring the spa. Pre-breakfast coffee service available on your private terrace. Returning from paddle boarding to find a glass of ice-cold water alongside a tray of sun care essentials beside my beach lounger. Knowledge of my food allergies at every F&B outlet on the property without me having to say it. A personalised WhatsApp group for any additional requests.

Amanvari’s nature-led architecture and exceptional service make it a compelling destination for a restorative escape. If you’re looking for a true escape, a place that welcomes stillness but doesn’t demand solitude, a reset complete with spa treatments, delicious food and an unhurried pace, it’s worth every peso.
Amanvari, Eureka s/n esquina con Sta Maria la Ribera, La Ribera, 23570 Baja California Sur, Mexico

Lindsay Cohn is a freelance travel journalist with a decade of experience writing, editing and jet-setting, and bylines in Vogue, Travel + Leisure, W Mag, Bloomberg, Galerie, and more. In between trips to sunny islands, cobbled villages and bustling cities, you can find her in Los Angeles with her husband and two sons.

items.title: Inside Lunette, London's hottest table and Florence Knight’s vision in food, light and design
items.description: A bright but overcast afternoon in late September. Eleven floors up at the St Clement hotel – a new build near the river, looming over Temple Gardens at 180 The Thames – Florence Knight is holding court at her new 30-seat restaurant, Lunette. Flooded with earl
items.author: Tom Howells
paragraphs: A bright but overcast afternoon in late September. Eleven floors up at the St Clement hotel – a new build near the river, looming over Temple Gardens at 180 The Thames – Florence Knight is holding court at her new 30-seat restaurant, Lunette. Flooded with early autumn light, its off-white palette, swathes of pale wood, steel tabletops, artist monographs artfully arranged on a coffee table and an abundance of Jean Prouvé’s modernist ‘INSA’ panels lining the walls make it resemble a curated loft apartment as much as a dining room. Lunette is a deeply personal project for Knight and, though the space was a concrete shell when she first saw it, the potential was clear. ‘I could see it instantly; the kitchen here, the bar there. The light, the movement and the water, it feels like it's almost holding you,’ she says.

Knight is a quietly totemic figure in London's food scene; first leading the pass at Polpetto (a standalone spin-off of Russell Norman's game-changing Soho bacaro Polpo), and then at Clerkenwell’s Sessions Arts Club, the beautifully weathered palazzo of a restaurant she co-founded with artist Jonny Gent in 2021. In 2024, she departed Sessions with the intention of opening her first solo venture. Where Sessions was ‘a roaring beast’, Knight says, ‘I realised that I wanted a sense of intimacy, something smaller.’ Nearly three years on, Lunette – developed with 180 Quarter’s Mark Wadhwa, St Clement mastermind (and Soho House founder) Nick Jones, and interiors studio Eagle + Hodges – is the result.

Given Knight’s epicurean bona fides, it may seem disjointed to talk design before dishes. But Lunette – named after the arched windows of the nearby disused Aldwych underground station, and a word that ‘writes beautifully’ – is a full-service undertaking, and irrefutably dreamy to look at. Knight studied fashion before segueing into kitchens, and she has the vibe of an artist who just happens to be a dynamite chef, too.

All of Lunette’s sofas, dining surfaces, chairs and lighting (save a midcentury Pierre Chapo teardrop table, and a wooden service station fashioned by Southampton’s shipyard fabricators Calshot) are of Eagle + Hodges’ own design – as is the chic utilitarian staff garb, created by co-founder Alex Eagle’s fashion label. But Knight commissioned nearly everything else: from the steely open kitchen to ceramics by Tetsuya Otani and Michel François, sinuous blown glassware by Danish designer Alexander Kirkeby, and even the finely layered and weighted paper menus, the embossed double ‘t’ in Lunette resembling a Lilliputian table. The room’s speaker system was created by artist and audio engineer Devon Turnbull, a neat callback to his immersive listening room up the block at 180 Studios, while the Prouvés were drawn from the personal collection of real-life couple Wadhwa and Eagle.

‘Florence has got amazing taste,’ says Eagle, a longtime friend of Knight’s. ‘She cares about texture, about light, about feeling and space – which is what makes me and Sophie [Hodges] tick. The collaboration is people coming together and being inspired, rather than trying to elevate or change her.’

Fundamentally, Eagle says, the room functions as a ‘very chic blank canvas’ for Knight’s food – which is, naturally, the main draw at Lunette. Even then, says Knight, ‘it’s completely transmissible’ to the surroundings. The balancing of layers and textures, of hard and soft (not least in the curtains, which she insisted were translucent, ‘like a thin onion skin’), is integral to her identity as a chef. ‘I’m always seeing things from a visual perspective,’ she says. ‘I just think that food is my material.’

Knight’s cooking is precise, seasonal, ‘reasonably gentle in flavour’, and inspired by nature and art. It has developed over the years, but there are through-lines for those who’ve been following. Take the fêted Sessions dish of layered confit potato and eel cake – at Lunette, it’s reconfigured into a pomme soufflé with smoked eel, roe and nasturtium flowers. These things, she says, ‘just matured with my technical ability, and with where I am as a person’.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

There’s a painterly assemblage of raw, late-summer runner and yellow French beans with slow-cooked squid, dressed with tomato water; a sunny dish of rice cooked in crab stock, with a sauce of long peppers and tomato juice, egg-yolk jam and cock crab in crab-shell butter; a more autumnal plate of French guinea fowl with a hazelnut and celeriac sauce, beetroot purée, and a jus split with hazelnut and tarragon oils; and an edgeless chocolate tart, its super-short pastry crisp with rice flour and depth afforded by tea-soaked raisins. The full dinner menu will feature eight courses, plus sundries.

Even on a restaurant scene as punctilious as London’s, the presentation is impressive, but ‘the precision is not to intimidate people’, Knight says. ‘Food is about pleasure, right? It needs to be joyful and fun, and have those nods to nostalgia and the things that we love.’

It’s clear how meaningful an endeavour Lunette is to Knight – every facet of it is a crystalline evocation of exactly where she is, right now, as both chef and aesthete. ‘Everything I’ve done has been personal because of the level of care and attention I’ve tried to give it,’ she concludes. ‘This time round, it is so much more than just the food. From someone who’s a control freak, it feels even more special.’
Lunette is located at Level 11, The Thames, St Clement 180, 12 Temple Pl, Temple, London WC2R 2NF, United Kingdom

items.title: Sony’s new MDR-3R wired headphones hark back to the glory days of the Walkman
items.description: Followers of hi-fidelity fashion trends will know that wired headphones are making a quiet comeback. Considered by some to be the last and most inconvenient vestige of analogue-era sound – and therefore hardest to return to from the convenience of wireless – t
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Followers of hi-fidelity fashion trends will know that wired headphones are making a quiet comeback. Considered by some to be the last and most inconvenient vestige of analogue-era sound – and therefore hardest to return to from the convenience of wireless – the desire for a more analogue, hands-on experience has led to a modest revival.

Sony has a bigger stake in this movement than most. As the creator of the original Sony Walkman, the 1979 invention that defined a genre and re-shaped the listening habits of millions, the Japanese electronics giant knows a thing or two about making lightweight, high-quality headphones.

One of the most iconic examples from the early Walkman era were the Sony MDR-3 open-backed stereo headphones, introduced in the early 80s and manufactured for a couple of years as the ultimate portable audio upgrade. Original pairs still command a healthy price on collectors’ forums, even if their brightly-coloured foam earpads have long since disintegrated.

Every now and again, this teeming underworld of retro nostalgia, ‘newtro’ design and cassette futurism spills over into the mainstream. Unwilling to see their IP mined by imitators, Sony is keeping itself in the game with a new, old, product: enter the MDR-3R headphones.

Although the internals have been thoroughly revised and updated for the modern era, the MDR-3R are strikingly similar to the 80s originals, right down to the typography and the size, shape and colour of the packaging. The slender stainless steel sliders precisely mimic the construction of the lightweight MDR-3, with aluminium detailing and an identical patterned array of sound holes over the drivers.

What has changed is the connectivity. The MDR-3R uses a USB Type-C connector, so it slots straight into most modern smartphones and mp3 players, with an inline remote control for handling volume and playback. On top of that, there’s also an inbuilt microphone, so calls can be taken and, should you so desire, smart assistants can be queried, just as you would with a pair of earbuds.

In the box you’ll find two different coloured foam earpads, blue and orange. The drivers are 23mm, recreated from the original technical drawings with an upgraded bass performance that retains some of the analogue feel of the first MDR-3. And at 38g, these are the lightest over-ear headphones in Sony’s current line-up.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

And that’s not all. Mindful of the zeitgeist spikes that helped us reach this point of reconnection with the past, Sony has teamed up with Netflix to produce a Limited-Edition Stranger Things branded pair of MDR-3Rs. In place of blue and orange, you get moody red and black and unique packaging, all the better for escaping the demon-haunted world.
Sony MDR-3R headphones, £49 / €59, Stranger Things edition MDR-3R headphones, £59 / €69, Sony.co.uk

items.title: Outerwear is bold and brilliant this season
items.description: The latter months of the year prompt the inevitable wardrobe shift – whether unpacking wool sweaters from storage or embracing envelopment with scarves, gloves and hats. Though it is outerwear which often provides the greatest conundrum when it comes to winter
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: The latter months of the year prompt the inevitable wardrobe shift – whether unpacking wool sweaters from storage or embracing envelopment with scarves, gloves and hats. Though it is outerwear which often provides the greatest conundrum when it comes to wintertime dressing – and, indeed, the greatest investment.

As seen in the December 2026 issue of Wallpaper*, photographer Luca Campri and stylist Camilla Sossi take to the streets of Milan with a selection of the A/W 2026 season’s best outerwear – from a colourful quilted leather gilet from Maximilian Davis at Ferragamo (its intriguing fastenings are inspired by the house’s Gancini motif) to the ultimate shaggy shearling from Louise Trotter at Bottega Veneta (its teddy-bear proportions will help you face even the harshest of winter days).

Captured in a series of spontaneous portraits of model Annabelle Weatherly, the prevailing mood is one of nostalgic elegance – albeit with a contemporary frisson. A double-breasted overcoat by Michael Rider at Celine captures the Parisian house’s bourgeois roots (here teamed with a requisite roll-neck sweater), while a Miu Miu Harrington jacket is crafted from classic herringbone wool (worn with a pillbox hat and ladylike top-handle handbag).

Elsewhere, moments of texture and play enliven traditional silhouettes: a slouchy Chloé parka comes in slices of shearling and tartan; a caped Carven coat is trimmed with the tassels one might find on a blanket; while a super-chunky Louis Vuitton sweater doubles as outerwear. Like their menswear counterparts, each embraces the idea of ‘character dressing’ – ‘the changing of the fashion seasons gives one a chance to craft a new persona’, we wrote earlier this month of A/W 2026’s best men’s looks.

‘I think I’ll remember this story as the first time I truly made peace with the city I live in,’ says Campri, who is currently working on a book ‘celebrating everyday domestic moments’. ‘For years, I’d been photographing stories here without ever feeling completely at ease, but this time, it inspired me in a whole new way.’

items.title: This 1970s Biarritz apartment feels like an endless summer
items.description: Biarritz is known to some as the birthplace of surfing in Europe, the sport having been introduced there in the late 1950s, bringing with it a laid-back attitude to coastal living – and this, coupled with the classic French sense of style, is exactly what arch
items.author: Tianna Williams
paragraphs: Biarritz is known to some as the birthplace of surfing in Europe, the sport having been introduced there in the late 1950s, bringing with it a laid-back attitude to coastal living – and this, coupled with the classic French sense of style, is exactly what architects Patrice Gardera and Philippe Pastre drew on in Sunset, their newly renovated 1970s apartment.
Tour Sunset apartment, a 1970s surfer's haven in Biarritz

Perched on the Côte des Basques, the renovation overlooks the Atlantic Ocean and evokes the warming afterglow of a setting sun through rich materials, natural touches and soft sculptural forms. The clients asked for a home to feel like a stunning hotel suite, a place to relax, entertain and enjoy their collection of vinyl records and contemporary art, including works by Biarritz-based artist Mathieu Chavaren.

While surfing culture very much defines Biarritz, the architects were equally inspired by the history of the building itself, as they told Wallpaper*: ‘The Sunset apartment dates back to the early 1970s. Set at the foot of the cliffs overlooking the Côte des Basques, it is part of the setting where the Carlina Hotel and Le Carlos [restaurant and bar] first emerged, two places that helped shape Biarritz’s surf culture.

'There is a distinctive atmosphere here, with something of a laid-back Californian feel, almost like a Los Angeles motel transplanted to the Basque coast. We wanted to preserve that character rather than erase it with a soulless renovation.’
They decided to approach the project using simple lines and a way of living that embraces the outdoors, highlighting the daily ritual of watching the sun set over the ocean.

The apartment is just 57 sq m, which proved a challenge for the architects, as they explain: The original apartment was divided into a series of small rooms, with an enclosed kitchen, entrance hall and sleeping area, all of which turned away from its greatest asset: the view.

‘We opened up the layout to create a generous, 33 sq m living and kitchen space facing the terraces. The challenge was then to accommodate a bedroom, dressing room and bathroom within [the remaining space], making every centimetre count through bespoke joinery and furniture. All of this had to be achieved without compromising the spirit of the 1970s building, while navigating the practical constraints of renovating an apartment in a shared residential building on the oceanfront.’
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Bespoke details include a rounded bookcase that seamlessly leads into the living area, while a sliding partition allows the bedroom to open into the living space, where a mahogany table takes centre stage.

The living area is Gardera and Pastre’s favourite part, they explain: ‘The building isn't called Sunset by chance. From the sofa or the kitchen worktop, you can look out over the ocean and watch surfers coming in from the water, while the entire room takes on the warm tones of the evening light. It's in those moments that you understand what has made this building so appealing for more than 50 years.’
Sunset is undoubtedly a sophisticated coastal home that steers clear of cliché surfing memorabilia. Instead, it transports visitors into a story-like setting that balances past and present.

The architects conclude: ‘We hoped to capture something of the feeling of heading down to Le Carlos for a drink after a surf session: the golden light, the sound of the waves and that instinctive desire to slow down. A place that feels like being on holiday, but also gives its owners a sense of belonging to a rather iconic corner of Biarritz.’

Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. When she isn’t writing extensively across varying content pillars, ranging from design and architecture to travel and art, she also helps put together the daily newsletter. She enjoys speaking to emerging artists, designers and architects, writing about gorgeously designed houses and restaurants, and day-dreaming about her next travel destination.

items.description: Total cost of the membership is 16 euros per each billing cycle, shipping not included. Membership is billed automatically twice a year (every six months, timed with the issue release), and can be cancelled at any time before the renewal date.
paragraphs: Total cost of the membership is 16 euros per each billing cycle, shipping not included. Membership is billed automatically twice a year (every six months, timed with the issue release), and can be cancelled at any time before the renewal date.
*The delivery of your print magazine will start with our Autumn/winter 2027 issue #38, released on November 12*.

Memberships allow us to invest back into our editorial production as an independent publisher, free from commercial pressure. Your support means we can keep bringing you new stories and publications inspired by our community.
Members are the first to receive each issue of Apartamento magazine, delivered straight from the printer to your doorstep! All magazines are shipped express with tracking.
Earlier issues of Apartamento are rare and hard to find. All members receive exclusive digital access to the full range of interviews and stories in our archive.
In recognition of your ongoing support, all members receive an automatic 10% discount on books, magazines, and other products available at our online shop!

Apartamento was founded in Barcelona in 2008. Its namesake magazine, published twice yearly and widely considered one of the most influential interiors publications of the past two decades, is rooted in how people actually live: the spaces they inhabit, the food they cook, the work they make, and the conviction with which they build their lives. Known for its unfiltered, human approach, each issue brings long-form conversations with artists, writers, designers, and thinkers across disciplines, accompanied by photography that unsettles conventional categories.

The values of the magazine extend beyond print. Through events, collaborations, exhibitions, design objects, and a growing body of short and documentary films, Apartamento builds community in real spaces around the world.

Since 2015, Apartamento has published books across a range of formats: monographs, cookbooks, photobooks, architecture series, artist books, and even a graphic novel. The publishing programme extends the editorial curiosity of the magazine into longer, more sustained forms, spanning art, design, architecture, food, and visual culture.

Members receive each issue of Apartamento magazine at a special 20% discount, plus unlimited access to our digital archive—including every interview, essay, and story ever published in our previous issues. In addition, members receive an automatic 10% discount in our Shop, as well as a free Apartamento Tote Bag and one 60-day trial for MUBI.

Current issues of Apartamento magazine tend to sell out quickly, and all earlier issues are sold out and can be hard to find. Our digital archive preserves each and every issue of the magazine on our website, a place where members can read every interview, essay, and story ever published!

items.title: Apartamento Magazine Issue #38
items.description: In issue #38 of Apartamento magazine, isolation becomes grounds for imagination, encouraging the possibility of creating the worlds we want.
paragraphs: In issue #38 of Apartamento magazine, isolation becomes grounds for imagination, encouraging the possibility of creating the worlds we want.

On the cover, American artist Dozie Kanu, winner of the Hublot Design Prize, talks with writer Camille Okhio in the home and studio he has made in the Portuguese countryside of Azoia de Cima. Photographed by José Pedro Cortes, the story follows what took his practice from New York to Portugal, how ambition has emerged from his Nigerian heritage, and the existential pressures of Blackness. Dozie candidly recounts how his live/work space once caught fire just before a photoshoot with furniture company Knoll.

In Paris, Playboy author and provocateur to the French literati Constance Debré speaks with contributing editor Jina Khayyer about the contradictions of love and desire, and boredom as ‘a state where you develop the freedom to invent things’. Photographed by Osma Harvilahti, she shows us her minimalist apartment, which has no full bath, proving that showers don’t need to be in the privacy of the home.

Featuring: Dozie Kanu, Constance Debré, Anupama Kundoo, Julian Schnabel, Dave Baby, Peaches, Joey Arias, Martine Syms, Gerard Malanga, Rodney Mullen, Filip Pągowski, Go Hasegawa, Darina Allen, and Muller Van Severen.
Plus: Peter Hanley’s ‘The Culinary Academy of the Pyrenees’ with illustrations by Oscar Grønner, an ode to Inge Mahn by Anna Herms, and ‘Wei Xing Doesn’t Skate’, an essay by Jocko Weyland.
Members have unlimited access to the entire Apartamento magazine digital archive!

items.title: Peluquería, Ouka Leele
items.description: Peluquería is the first book dedicated to late Spanish photographer Ouka Leele’s formative years in Barcelona and her portraits of the city’s underground scene. Widely celebrated as a key figure of the Movida Madrileña, Leele settled in Barcelona one year befo
paragraphs: Peluquería is the first book dedicated to late Spanish photographer Ouka Leele’s formative years in Barcelona and her portraits of the city’s underground scene. Widely celebrated as a key figure of the Movida Madrileña, Leele settled in Barcelona one year before the country’s official turn to democracy. The improvised ‘hair salon’ referred to by the series’ title gathers legends of the counterculture movement at this moment of extraordinary freedom, marked by the playful, defiant objects on their heads. Peluquería’s electric colours, unique for the era, are achieved through Leele’s innovative use of watercolours, which she painted onto her black-and-white prints by hand. Original sketches that inspired the series, as well as previously unpublished writings by Leele are presented alongside contact sheets newly unveiled by the artist’s archive. Reflections by Javier Mariscal, one of the first artists photographed for Peluquería, and Rossy de Palma, an icon of Spanish cinema, honour Leele’s poetic vision, while essays by Pepe Ribas and Elisa Medde mine the radical landscape that informed Leele’s early work.

Ouka Leele (Madrid, 1957), born Bárbara Allende Gil de Biedma, is a Spanish photographer and a fixture of the Movida Madrileña. She is renowned for the distinct visual language she pioneered with her work, beginning with the Peluquería series, in which she transformed black-and-white prints by painting them with vivid watercolours. She was awarded the 2004 Culture Prize by the Community of Madrid and the Spanish National Photography Prize in 2005.

items.title: Written at Night, Ettore Sottsass
items.description: The third in our reading series, Written at Night is the fragmented autobiography of Ettore Sottsass, one of the most seminal figures of 20th-century radical design. Originally written in Italian and published posthumously in 2010 as Scritto di notte, it now a
paragraphs: The third in our reading series, Written at Night is the fragmented autobiography of Ettore Sottsass, one of the most seminal figures of 20th-century radical design. Originally written in Italian and published posthumously in 2010 as Scritto di notte, it now arrives in English for the first time, translated by one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English, Alastair McEwen.

As he recounts his upbringing in Trento and Turin, his conscription in WWII, his Milan debut, his dance with poverty, and his travels—from Cuba with Hemingway to a snowy Italian night drive with Ginsberg to the fever of India—Written at Night begins as a slow tide into the mind of one of radical design’s greatest figures, only to sweep you up in its storm. Digging through the debris of memory, he finds the precious metals of people and places, so that what he’s writing in the dark is a sweeping blueprint of love, lust, and survival. In his attempts to start from childhood and climb forwards, Sottsass produces a piece of art in and of itself—self-interrupting, self-critical, self-affirming, self-annihilating.
Written at Night joins our growing reading book series, following Essential and The Unimportance of Form.

Ettore Sottsass (1917–2007) was an Austrian-born Italian postmodernist designer and architect, considered one of the most seminal figures in 20th design, and hailed for co-founding the design collective known as the Memphis Group. Considered a polymath by many, he moved freely between furniture, glass, lamps, jewellery, objects for the home and office, as well as the design of many buildings and interiors, magazines, and publications. Alongside a significant canon of published books, his contribution to design has earned him four Compassi d’Oro. His works are exhibited in the permanent collections of museums around the world, such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Centre Pompidou in Paris, and the Victoria & Albert Museum in London.

Alastair McEwen is considered to be one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English. To date, he has published over 100 book-length translations, essays, articles, and poems, plus several feature film scripts and operatic librettos. He has translated some of the most important Italian writers of our time: Umberto Eco, Roberto Calasso, Antonio Tabucchi, Fleur Jaeggy, Alessandro Baricco, Aldo Busi, and many others.

items.title: The Selfies of Jonas Unger
items.description: The Selfies of Jonas Unger is German photographer Jonas Unger’s years-long investigation into how close a portrait can get to its subject. In this seductive photobook, Karl Lagerfeld, David Lynch, Rossy de Palma and dozens of others from the glittering corners
paragraphs: The Selfies of Jonas Unger is German photographer Jonas Unger’s years-long investigation into how close a portrait can get to its subject. In this seductive photobook, Karl Lagerfeld, David Lynch, Rossy de Palma and dozens of others from the glittering corners of fashion, film, and sport turn the lens on themselves, caught in ways you’ve never seen before. Handing his camera to his sitters and stepping out of the frame, Jonas tampers with the role of the photographer, surrendering the lens and some of its authority, while never wholly relinquishing his own.

Celebrity, honesty, and dramaturgy meet the defining photographic phenomenon of our time: the self-taken photograph. Moving through philosophical dives and detours, the photobook catches people shaped by the limelight at the moment control over their image briefly changes hands. Gathered over more than a decade, these self-portraits, known also as his ‘Autoportraits’, form a book about the puzzles of authorship and spectatorship. How close can a portrait get? And what are we really seeing when someone famous looks back at themselves?

The Selfies of Jonas Unger follows on from our growing photobook catalogue after Coincidence by American photographer Jeremy Liebman, shortlisted for the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards, and the quirky Birds of Paradise by Spanish photographer Ángela Suárez.

Jonas Unger is a German photographer living and working in Paris. He is known for portrait, fashion, and editorial photography with a direct, intimate approach. His editorial work has appeared in Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Vogue, W Magazine, Interview, and many more. Alongside his commissioned work, Jonas develops long-term personal projects. The best known is his series of celebrity self-portraits, begun around 2010, which was first shown as Autoportraits at Galerie Derouillon in Paris in 2014 and later included in Ego Update at the NRW-Forum Düsseldorf. His work has received the LeadAward and the Hansel Mieth Prize (2013).

items.title: ADRIEN BRODY - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star
paragraphs: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star

Twenty-two years after he became the youngest ever winner of a best actor Oscar, for ‘The Pianist’, Adrien Brody has gone and done it again, this time taking home an Academy Award for his deeply moving performance as Hungarian architect László Toth in ‘The Brutalist’. What makes it all the more remarkable is that only a few years ago Adrien had all but given up acting. The awards are much deserved, of course. Adrien, 52, is an intense and uniquely gifted actor, which also makes him entertaining company. He doesn’t do things in half measures. He’s all in, all the time, and not afraid to speak his mind. In the following story Adrien engages in some energetic verbal ping-pong and gets dressed up in fashion by his friend Thom Browne. It captures some of the essence of what makes him such an incredible performer.
From Fantastic Man n° 40 – 2025
Photography by ILYA LIPKIN

The instant Adrien Brody sweeps into the room, he begins to express what I will soon come to think of as his resting affect: a kind of intense but fuzzy gratitude. “I just got back from London yesterday night,” he tells me. “Feeling very blessed with all the love that’s been coming my way. It’s a really special moment. It really is.” Maybe it’s just for now, in these hectic weeks promoting ‘The Brutalist’ ahead of the Academy Awards, but it’s with words like these that Brody seems at his most comfortable, and throughout our conversation he will periodically return to similar sentiments, restating and expanding upon them with evident sincerity.

With other kinds of words, though, it will often come to feel as though there are fault lines everywhere. Seconds after this initial declaration, I ask Brody – my question intended as little more than small talk to fill the empty space between us as we greet each other and take our seats – whether it feels like he’s being carried away in a whirlwind. He responds – not just in his words but in his body language too – as though he’s being somehow misunderstood or as though something wonderful is at risk of being spoiled.

“No, it’s not that at all,” he says, correcting me firmly. “No, my feet are on the ground. I’m ultra-present. I’m ultra-present and able to reciprocate the love. It’s different. Being older gives you a degree of perspective. It’s been a very long time since I’ve had an opportunity to do the work that I’m yearning to do. And the work is completed. So this is just something magical.”

Brody will prove to be engaging, fascinating company, and a man with plenty to say. In our conversation there will also be moments where he exudes a sense – verbally, but also through a repertoire of expressions that seem to hover between saddened and harried – that the world doesn’t quite get him.

What I then find myself wondering is whether such a sensibility might be a consequence of setbacks and reversals he has faced along his idiosyncratic chosen path, or whether it’s such a sensibility which sends you down that path in the first place. Conversely, I also find myself wondering whether it’s exactly this kind of off-kilter mindset which, when everything comes together in just the right way, somehow fuels Brody’s singular ability to inhabit and transmit a role like ‘The Brutalist’s’ László Toth with such compelling, all-consuming mastery.

It was back in 2019 when Adrien Brody was first given the script of ‘The Brutalist’, the expansive tale of a visionary Hungarian architect who escapes the Holocaust and makes his way to America, where he finds a new life – one of opportunity, but also one with horrors all of its own. Brody read it in the apartment he and his partner, fashion designer Georgina Chapman, then had in Manhattan. “I found myself very moved by the writing and the breadth of the storytelling, the complexity, the flaws of the character,” he remembers. “The opportunity for me to play someone that is experiencing so much and contending so much in life [was] wonderful. And I did consider parallels of László’s lived experience with my mother’s and my grandparents’ journey.” Brody’s mother, whose maternal grandparents were rounded up and taken to Auschwitz, survived the war in Budapest. She escaped in 1956, at the age of 13, buried under corn in a horse-drawn cart as she and her parents crossed the Austrian border. In New York, Brody grew up around his Hungarian grandparents. “So that, too, definitely is evident to me in reading it – saying: ‘Wow, I’m quite right to play this character.’”

After reading, Brody met with the director, Brady Corbet, who had written the script with his professional and personal partner, the filmmaker and actor Mona Fastvold, for brunch downtown. “A very long meeting – conversed a lot about lots of things,” Brody recalls. Nonetheless, he learned in due course that another actor had been chosen. “The message comes from your agent,” he says. “It’s either you get the message or they hope you’ve forgotten.” That’s the pattern. “I mourned the loss of this one,” he says. “I did not have expectations that it would be what it is today – I still mourned the creative loss of what I wanted to pour into it.”

Brody makes clear that over his career he has learned that this will happen, and maybe even why. “As an actor, you may be right for certain roles and you’re not necessarily eligible for them,” he says. “Even if you are quite a well-known actor and quite a successful actor. Because there are all these factors that are out of your control. You know, there are lists, and lists are based on a number of things that one might deem as an indication of success. Right? You know, consistent box office earnings are the primary reason you would be on the top of a list. But if you do make experimental choices and interesting choices in an artistic pursuit in a business, it’s not met with the same appreciation as, you know, your mother might have for your varied tastes.”

Brody points out that he’s balanced experimentation with “big blockbuster movies,” and that he enjoys those too. “But I like the range,” he says, and his suggestion seems to be that too much range has consequences. “I’m aware of how it has made certain things, such as this even, challenging,” he says. “Where I’m probably the most right performer for the role, but I wasn’t deemed valuable enough.”

This time, thankfully, everything eventually worked out. The film’s shoot was delayed several times, in part because of Covid, and by the time the project fell back in place the actor previously scheduled to play László Toth, Joel Edgerton, was no longer available. Brody heard from his agent that the role was back in play. Even then, it wasn’t as though Brody simply got a call saying the part was his. “No, not at all,” he says. “Not at all.” In the end, though, it was. Finally given the chance, he threw himself into it. “I knew we were making something special,” he says. “I wish I knew why things come when they do. This moment is because we’re very fortunate – all of us who have been involved in this project – that every collaborative creative element lifted up the other.”

It’s around now, a few minutes into our meeting, when another question seems to throw Brody, though this time the person asking is not me. It is the waiter, asking what Brody might like to eat or drink. From Brody’s reaction, you could easily think that he finds such an inquiry – at a pre-booked table by the window in a high-end New York hotel bar – somewhat perplexing. He talks aloud through this latest dilemma. “I’m not sure what I’m needing,” he says, then considers one kind of option. “I’m happy to have a drink,” he weighs, “but I’m also not needing it just yet.” He expands this thought. “I don’t really need anything.”
After vacillating further, he orders an oak milk decaf latte.
“Not too much milk,” he adds. “Just nice and strong.”

That ‘The Brutalist’ would allow Brody such a remarkable professional and creative renaissance is all the more marked given the place he has described finding himself in in recent years: sufficiently dejected by the opportunities coming his way that he had, unannounced, more or less turned his back on movies. As he recently put it, “I didn’t announce I was retiring, but I stepped back.” For a time, he concentrated on other artistic pursuits that he found more fulfilling, principally painting.

“I’ve been doing this so long, since I was a boy,” he says when I ask about that period. “There’s an ebb and flow in everything, in your own creative connections and personally, professionally in life, right? So I also was not under any illusion that it should just flow. But I found it oddly challenging to be up against things like this. I feel that I’ve proven my range. I’ve worked. The reason it seems inconsistent is I’ve been consistent in trying to break out of the box of subjective perception of what I am capable of doing, or what I represent for a character, or physically. Whatever it is. Too specific, often. And they find that…” He pauses, considering his words. “There’s a safer option, basically.”
“It wasn’t being reciprocated, for whatever reason,” he says. “It wasn’t. What I had to give was somehow not understood or not of value. I didn’t feel that I was of service and of value.”
How did that lack of reciprocation make him feel?

“I didn’t feel like I needed to prove that I was worth it. If I wasn’t, I’m going to go do something else that makes me feel good. I work primarily to feel connected and to feel immersed in something creative. And I handle my side of the bargain.”
I ask him whether he feels like he does all this for the same reasons as his peers do it.

“I mean, I would think so,” he says. “Like what? Like what reason?” Then he supplies his own answer. “I think anybody who cares about what they’re doing, which is such personal work – you have to embody the role.
