items.title: The Midterms Made MAGA Hardliners More Powerful, Not Less
items.description: According to the ancient conventional wisdom, when a political party loses as badly as Republicans lost on November 3, its leaders are supposed to show some humility, smooth off some of the party’s rougher edges, and pay more attention to the opinions of swing
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: According to the ancient conventional wisdom, when a political party loses as badly as Republicans lost on November 3, its leaders are supposed to show some humility, smooth off some of the party’s rougher edges, and pay more attention to the opinions of swing voters. When in addition said party loses Congress while holding onto a lame-duck presidency, the obvious thing to do is to make conciliatory noises and open negotiations over some sort of at least minimally bipartisan agenda.
But the conventional wisdom hasn’t had to cope with a presidency like the 47th, or with a Republican Party like today’s MAGA GOP.

While Donald Trump didn’t claim victory on election night (the magnitude and national scope of the Democratic wave made that virtually impossible), and made noises about cooperating with an opposition party he had long treated as lacking any legitimacy, he was soon back in his old groove. First he blamed the defeat on his absence from the ballot, which is bizarre given how intensely he insisted on dominating the GOP’s midterm message. Before long he was vaguely but emphatically attributing the outcome to voting machines. And then he completed the 180-degree turn by suggesting, much as he did for months prior to the election, that the Senate’s failure to enact the SAVE America Act produced the Democratic win, presumably via tens of millions of illegal votes by noncitizens.

At the same time, Trump took every step he could to repudiate any interest in reaching accommodations with Democrats. His first post-election personnel move was to fire the resolutely sane Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff and replace her with every Democrat’s living nightmare, Stephen Miller. At about the same time, the president doubled down on backing his embattled defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, even as House Democrats sought (unsuccessfully) to impeach him. Trump also reportedly rebuked his vice president and heir apparent, J.D. Vance, for acknowledging the political damage wrought by his war of choice against Iran, even though it was clear that bringing that war to a speedy end was going to represent a nonnegotiable demand for congressional Democrats during the lame-duck session already under way.

On the second day of that session, House Republicans added their own punctuation mark to the president’s refusal to trim his pirate sails by choosing longtime House Freedom Caucus militant Jim Jordan as their new Leader, succeeding the mild-mannered (albeit Trump-worshiping) Mike Johnson instead of Johnson’s deputy Steve Scalise. Jordan’s only heresies from Trump-era House GOP orthodoxy have involved his hostility toward any compromises with Democrats and his almost religious zest for deep cuts in the popular domestic programs Democrats hold sacred.

Miller, Hegseth, Jordan: These are the men who have taken the GOP’s first steps forward after the midterm debacle, even as their leader works overtime to dispel any thoughts that defeat might have changed his ways. The next clue to the immediate future will be whether Trump and his Hill allies choose to rush a lame-duck party-line budget reconciliation bill through the Congress they will still control for a few weeks, furthering the MAGA agenda of mass-deportation, a massive defense buildup to support “warfighting,” and as much damage to the New Deal, the Great Society, and Obamacare as can be managed in a single piece of legislation. In the face of such provocations, it seems very unlikely that Democrats could be convinced to go along with another GOP-drafted stopgap spending bill to head off a December 11 government shutdown, if indeed Republicans even want to keep their own federal government operating.

It’s always possible, of course, that Trump can change his own mind about his strategy for winding up his last two years in office and what sort of Republican Party he wants to leave to carry on his strange and self-adulatory agenda. His refusal to countenance any sort of independent GOP message prior to the midterms suggests he may not even care if his party flourishes without him. If that’s true, the hardliners apparently in charge of the GOP at both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue may be on a kamikaze mission that will ensure another Democratic wave in 2028, with lots of collateral damage to the country along the way.

items.title: Jason Voorhees Is Back for More Blood: the 13th 'Friday the 13th' Film Is Coming
items.description: The 13th installment of the Friday the 13th film franchise has been announced on Friday, Nov. 13, marking the first scheduled release in the horror series in almost 20 years.
items.author: Larisha Paul
paragraphs: The 13th installment of the Friday the 13th film franchise has been announced on Friday, Nov. 13, marking the first scheduled release in the horror series in almost 20 years.

Jason Voorhees is back for more blood in a script from newcomer David Fliegel. The film will be directed by Friday the 13th veteran Steve Miner, who played a pivotal role in shaping the murderous character in the second and third installments of the franchise, released in 1981 and 1982, respectively. The machete and mask introduced in those early releases have become his most iconic identifiers.

“When I put the hockey mask on Jason for Friday the 13th Part III, I knew it would create a truly scary image that would work for that movie,” Miner said. “I had no idea that it would live on as one of the most iconic symbols in horror films. I’m thrilled to come back and continue the legacy.”

The upcoming film will be released in 2027. The most recent film, Friday the 13th, arrived in 2009 from The Texas Chainsaw Massacre director Marcus Nispel via distributors Warner Bros. Pictures and Paramount Pictures. This time around, Friday the 13th is taking the indie route. Cineverse will distribute the film in North America and Horror, Inc. has partnered with the production studio CatchLight Studios.

“For generations of fans, Jason’s identity is inseparable from the creative choices Steve Miner brought to the screen,” said Robbie Barsamian, Executive Vice President of Horror, Inc. “Reuniting with Steve under a fully independent model allows us the creative control to honor what makes Jason the greatest slasher of all time and deliver the definitive theatrical event that today’s audiences expect.”

“Jason is one of the most recognizable figures in cinema history,” said Chris McGurk, Chairman and CEO of Cineverse. “We have a proven track record of empowering uncompromising genre filmmaking and connecting it directly with passionate audiences, and are honored to be a part of bringing Jason back to theaters where he belongs.”

items.title: Dancing With the Stars Recap: The Boy Is Nine
items.description: Dancing With the Stars continues to be a fever dream of the highest order. Where else can you turn on the television and get an Argentine tango set to “Thong Song”; an adult human saying with her full chest, “Turning your sister into your lover for one night”
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Dancing With the Stars continues to be a fever dream of the highest order. Where else can you turn on the television and get an Argentine tango set to “Thong Song”; an adult human saying with her full chest, “Turning your sister into your lover for one night” in the first ten minutes of the broadcast; and also Sheryl Crow? Nowhere, okay. God bless America, and God bless Dancing With the Stars.

It’s “Grammy Night” and also the quarterfinals — we’re really getting so close to crowning a new Len Goodman Mirrorball Champion. Everyone’s dancing like it, too. I mean, did you see that opening pro number to “Just Keep Watching”? It’s one of the best performances of the season. Also, that bumper with Sharna and Brandon, in which they start in a lift position and he throws her up from there? I shrieked. Incredible. As the season hurtles toward its end, people are leaving it all on the ballroom floor, including — especially — the seven couples still in the competition. All of whom, by the way, have to learn two dances this week thanks to the Dance-Off competition later in the evening. But first, our regularly scheduled routines.
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach
Argentine Tango // “Crazy in Love,” by Beyoncé

Since the beginning, Daniella has wanted to highlight, not shy away from, showing off Ezra’s prosthetic, and she goes into the Argentine tango with the same mission. The sharp kicks and flicks of the Argentine tango are, admittedly, the first time I was genuinely worried there might be a mishap out on the dance floor. There is not! But Ezra does seem to have a lot of balance issues in this routine, and he seems less sturdy a partner than he has been in the past. But who can really concentrate on this routine when this is the moment Carrie Ann decides to make the “sister/lover” comment that will be burned into our brains for the rest of eternity?
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov
Paso Doble // “Bring Me to Life,” by Evanescence

You know when the guy is doing a no-shirt paso, it’s going to be serious. I’ve been waiting to see Amber take on this style because it feels really suited to her strengths — the drama, the power, the shaping. (Her arms! Her hands!) Amber and Pasha don’t disappoint. Those knee spins alone should have earned this an automatic perfect score. Both Carrie Ann and Derek marvel at Amber’s ability to have resistance and tension but do it so gracefully. And yet still, these two aren’t handing out tens. What does this woman have to do to get a perfect score around here?
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 10
Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas
Argentine Tango // “Thong Song,” by Sisqó

I’ve never been so concerned about rib health in my life. First Julia, now Maura. Maura looks like she is in so much pain every time Mark lifts her in rehearsal, which is a lot — this is Argentine tango, after all. But her injury doesn’t seem to have any effect on her performance — that final lift in which she’s upside down for so long? Flawless. This style, which features a lot of time in hold, does wonders for Maura. She gets to remind us of her great lines, her poise, and precision. She also has a sparkly thong coming out of her costume, and that kind of commitment to the bit should earn her 11s at least. It’s the best Argentine tango of the three we get tonight.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy
Jazz // “All for You,” by Janet Jackson

Jenna Dewan’s career began with Janet Jackson — in her videos and then on her All for You Tour — so I’m glad we’re finally getting to see Jenna celebrate that. Janet even calls in! DWTS has so much cachet at the moment — we’re getting video messages from Janet freaking Jackson? Obviously, Jenna crushes this jazz. (Or, as Val notes, a jazz-funk.) She could’ve danced the whole thing solo, to be honest. I’m actually shocked this doesn’t earn tens across the board. Bruno does say she looked in her “comfort zone,” so maybe it was … just … too easy?
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik
Tango // “Boom Boom Pow,” by Black Eyed Peas

My little sweeties are sweetie-ing again! It seems like Tatyana and Jan expect to get eliminated every week, so they are simply dancing with abandon. For the fun of it. And this performance is fun. Not to be dramatic, but Tatyana staring directly into the camera to lip-sync a portion of this did alter my DNA. The judges love this routine, praising Tatyana’s power and control and her ability to always draw us in. Their technique may not always look as sharp as some of the people on top of the leaderboard (Tatyana’s neck seemed extra tense this week — was it just the costume?), but they remain one of the most exciting couples to watch this season.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold
Argentine Tango // “SexyBack,” by Justin Timberlake featuring Timbaland

Listen, I love Connor and Rylee, but this dance was not it. His biggest critique last week was that he needed to look more like a leading man. This week, he still doesn’t fully sell it. He is a sturdy partner for Rylee to do an insane amount of tricks and lifts throughout, but he is lacking finesse here. Where are all my Argentine tango kicks and flicks? The footwork is a little too stodgy for me, but the judges love the power and control, and they are our lords and commanders, as we know.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson
Salsa // “Die With a Smile,” by Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars

Please give a raise to the editor who cut from Harry getting emotional about getting some closure and perspective on his childhood trauma of watching his family struggle while growing up in Costa Rica right into him doing some insane body rolls. This is the chaos we live for. With all seriousness, Harry really has worn his heart on his sleeve throughout this competition — he is insanely likable. But I don’t think that heart and emotion have always translated to these routines. This salsa is not their cleanest dance — it’s intricate and energetic, but at times it felt more chaotic than anything else. Derek points out that while Harry’s arms were incredible, his bottom half looked surprisingly “rigid.” They earn the best score of the night from the judges, but I’d easily put both Jenna and Val and Amber and Pasha over this routine.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 10

Honestly, I’m not a huge fan of the Dance-Offs. Couples are paired up and have to dance the same style to the same song (tonight, we’re getting all live performances from Brandy and Monica, Maren Morris, and Sheryl Crow, if you can believe it) side by side on the floor. The winner of each matchup will win two extra points to add to their score for the night. But the setup — while closer to actual ballroom competitions — makes it hard to really focus on what people are doing right (or wrong). Also, I get that DWTS is pairing up celebrities with similar backgrounds — the gold medalists, the actresses, the personalities — but the only fair way to really do this is by leaderboard points, no? Did everyone see Tatyana and Jan’s faces when Jenna and Val walked into the room? They immediately knew those two points were but a dream at that point. Harry and Jenna have the highest overall score of the season, so they have immunity from this mini-competition and automatically get their two extra points. Everyone else takes to the dance floor again.
Amber and Pasha versus Ezra and Daniella
Rumba // “The Boy Is Mine,” by Brandy and Monica

I may dislike the Dance-Off as a concept, but if it brings us performances like this, keep it coming. The Pashkovs and their Team USA partners said, Oh, you want us to compete against each other? That’s so cute. They turn this matchup into more of a team dance. By the end, they even switch partners so Amber can dip Daniella, while Ezra dips Pasha. It’s one of the best moments of the season.
Jenna and Val versus Tatyana and Jan
Cha-Cha // “The Middle,” by Zedd, Maren Morris, and Grey

At least no one is kidding themselves with what’s going on in this pairing. Both couples know that this is technique versus performance, and that’s exactly what we get. Jenna and Val dance the hell out of this cha-cha, and yet, my eye kept being drawn over to, as Bruno puts it, the sultriness of what Tatyana and Jan have going on. But maybe that’s just me!
Connor and Rylee versus Maura and Mark
Cha-Cha // “All I Wanna Do,” by Sheryl Crow

What I wouldn’t give for 20 full minutes of footage of Connor and Maura rehearsing together. A dream team. And the fact that they come out wearing the same fringe pants (just different colors)? The cherry on top. Maura and Mark have a leg up on technique, but I actually think what really does Connor and Rylee in is the bit of country line-dancing choreography they have in the middle of their routine. The judges were looking for pure cha-cha, and that’s not what was served up.

If you’ve been paying attention to scores tonight, the leaderboard is insanely close. Only nines and tens were given out (Derek gave every single routine a nine), and while the bonus points from the Dance-Offs move things around a little bit, this is really coming down to viewer votes.

It’s Jenna and Val who get the boot just shy of the semifinals. I’m actually not that shocked. It never seemed like people were going to hand the Mirrorball over to Jenna Dewan despite her consistently high scores and obvious technical prowess. She performed some great routines, but there was a bit of an emotional disconnect she never fully got past. Hey, the heart wants what the heart wants.

items.title: Netflix’s ‘Magic the Gathering’ Animated Series Drops First Look at ‘Planeswalker,’ Set for 2027
items.description: Netflix has unveiled the first-look image from its upcoming animated series based on “Magic the Gathering.”
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Netflix has unveiled the first-look image from its upcoming animated series based on “Magic the Gathering.”
The series, titled “Planeswalker,” is set to debut in 2027, with an exact release date to be announced later.
The official description of the series states:

“‘Planeswalker,’ an epic fantasy saga from the world of ‘Magic: The Gathering,’ chronicles the fierce clash between formidable mages known as Planeswalkers. At the center of this struggle for power and survival burns Chandra, a volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past. Confronted by an insidious force, Chandra and some of the most legendary Planeswalkers must harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence. As the line between victory and annihilation grows thinner, a single spark determines the fate of thousands of worlds.”

The show is produced in partnership with Hasbro Entertainment and Wizards of the Coast. Terry Matalas and Cindy Appel serve as executive producers and co-showrunners. Patrick Osborne is an executive producer and supervising director. Gabriel Marano will also serve as executive producer and Lauren Chavez-Myers will co-executive produce for Hasbro Entertainment. Daisy West is a producer on the series. Digic provides the animation.

The show has been in the works at Netflix for over six years at this point. Originally announced in 2019, the first iteration of the series was overseen by the Russo brothers of MCU fame. But then Jeff Kline was announced as the new executive producer and creative lead on the show in 2021 after the Russos departed over creative differences, with Brandon Routh being announced as voicing the series lead not long after.

There was then no news about the series until 2024, when Routh gave an interview in which he said he believed the show was “not happening” anymore. Not long after that, Matalas was named the new showrunner.

The “Magic: The Gathering” tabletop card game was created by Richard Garfield and first released in 1993. Since then, the game has spawned a digital game, esports league, comic book series, and a best-selling novel. It has been published in 11 languages in over 70 countries.

items.title: ‘Pluribus’ Promotes Samba Schutte to Series Regular for Season 2
items.description: Samba Schutte has been upped to series regular status for “Pluribus” Season 2, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Samba Schutte has been upped to series regular status for “Pluribus” Season 2, Variety has learned.
Schutte is known for playing Mr. Diabaté in Season 1 as a guest star. Like Rhea Seehorn’s Carol, the character is immune to the outbreak and lives a hedonistic lifestyle.

Schutte is also known for starring in the HBO Max pirate comedy “Our Flag Means Death” as well as the NBC sitcom “Sunnyside.” He previously worked on the Dutch version of “The Daily Show,” “De Nieuwste Show,” as a writer and correspondent.
He is repped by Innovative Artists and Established Artists.
Along with Seehorn and Schutte, the cast also includes Karolina Wydra and Carlos-Manuel Vesga.

“Pluribus” Season 2 is currently in production. The first season debuted on Apple TV in November 2025. The series was well-received by critics and audiences upon its launch. It was one of the most nominated series at this year’s Emmy Awards, raking in 18 total nominations for its first season.

It won six Emmys for its first season, including Seehorn’s win for outstanding lead actress in a drama series. Series creator Vince Gilligan also won the Emmy for outstanding writing for a drama series. Additional wins were for outstanding picture editing for a drama series, outstanding sound mixing for a comedy or drama (one hour), outstanding original main title theme music, and outstanding production design for a narrative contemporary program (one hour or more).
“Pluribus” is produced for Apple TV by Sony Pictures Television and executive produced by Gilligan, Gordon Smith, Alison Tatlock, Diane Mercer, Jeff Frost, Jenn Carroll and Trina Siopy.

items.title: Taylor Swift to Perform at CMAs for the First Time in 13 Years
items.description: Taylor Swift will perform on the CMA Awards Wednesday for the first time in 13 years, ABC and the Country Music Association announced Friday morning.
items.author: Chris Willman
paragraphs: Taylor Swift will perform on the CMA Awards Wednesday for the first time in 13 years, ABC and the Country Music Association announced Friday morning.

Swift had already publicly declared, upon getting a CMA nomination this year, that she would attend the show, but there was no indication until now on how or whether she intended on participating in the show beyond being an audience member.

No information was given about what Swift will perform on the show, although it’s a good bet it will consist partly or wholly of her nominated song, “I Knew it, I Knew You,” her contribution to the Disney/Pixar film “Toy Story 5.”
Her previous appearance as a performer on the show came in 2013, when she received the Pinnacle Award and performed the song “Red” with Vince Gill and Alison Krauss.

Swift’s last time attending or appearing on the show at all was in 2016, when, as a surprise, she came on stage in the program’s last minutes to present the Entertainer of the Year award to Garth Brooks.

This year marks the 20th anniversary of her first appearance at the CMA Awards, shortly after the release of her self-titled debut album. Her first win came in 2007, when she won the Horizon Award as the CMA’s choice for the best new artist. In 2009, she became the youngest artist ever to win the top prize at the awards, Entertainer of the Year.
With the release of “1989” in 2015, Swift declared she was picking a lane between pop and country, and pop had won out, although she did not burn any bridges with the country community.

The release of “I Knew It, I Knew You” marked her first brand new song in more than a decade to be marketed as a country song — and to make it to No. 1 at country radio format — although she had dabbled in the genre in the intervening years with album tracks like “Betty” and a vault track duet with Chris Stapleton, “I Bet You Think About Me.”
The show airs from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on Wednesday from 8-11 p.m. ET/PT on ABC and Disney+, with next-day streaming availability on Hulu.

Other performers already announced for the Lainey Wilson-hosted 60th annual CMA Awards include leading nominee Ella Langley, Cody Johnson, Miranda Lambert, Tim McGraw, Kacey Musgraves, The Red Clay Strays, Zach Top, Tucker Wetmore, Luke Combs, Vince Gill, Megan Moroney, Mumford & Sons, Chris Stapleton, Lainey Wilson and Stephen Wilson Jr. Additionally, Brothers Osborne, Luke Bryan, Halestorm, Hardy and Marcus King will take part in a tribute to Brooks & Dunn. A salute to Dolly Parton is also planned.

Beyond her picking up a nomination for a CMA Award for “I Knew It, I Knew You,” the song — co-written by Jack Antonoff — is also being campaigned for an Oscar for best original song, and was submitted in the category of song of the year for the Grammy Awards.

items.title: Stephen King Threw ‘Carrie’ in the Trash. Then It Changed Everything
items.description: In the early 1970s, Stephen King was a struggling and frustrated English teacher in Maine with a wife, two small children and a stack of bills that seemed to be growing much faster than his literary career. During the day, he taught teenagers at Hampden Academ
items.author: Chris Nashawaty
paragraphs: In the early 1970s, Stephen King was a struggling and frustrated English teacher in Maine with a wife, two small children and a stack of bills that seemed to be growing much faster than his literary career. During the day, he taught teenagers at Hampden Academy. At night, he’d pound out short stories and quickie tales of terror for lower-tier skin magazines like Cavalier and Adam. The pay wasn’t much, but it kept the lights on … barely. “Two hundred dollars,” says King of his typical fee at the time. “Once in a while, it was $500. That was a huge payday. That bought a lot of groceries.” Things were so tight that the Kings didn’t even have a telephone.

Then, in 1972, King began tinkering with an idea about a painfully awkward teenage girl who is mercilessly bullied by her classmates and terrorized at home by her religiously fanatical mother. When the girl discovers that she possesses telekinetic powers, she finally has a way to strike back. The story would reach its cathartic crescendo at her high school prom, where a horrifically cruel prank involving a bucket of pig’s blood turns what should have been the best night of her young life into an apocalyptic bloodbath. Her name was Carrie White.

Although he had no way of knowing it at the time, the book he had just begun writing would change the course of his life. And not just his. The 1976 movie adaptation of Carrie would turn Sissy Spacek into a bona fide star, give Brian De Palma his first box office hit and pull off something scary movies almost never did, then or now: crash the Oscars. It would also mark the beginning of one of the most prolific — and lucrative — pipelines in movie history, with King’s stories adapted for the screen more than 60 times. Fifty years, several remakes, a notorious Broadway musical and one brand-new Prime Video series later, Carrie White’s bloody fingerprints are still everywhere you look.

The inspiration for the novel that would become Carrie came from several places. Years earlier, while working as a school janitor, King had cleaned the girls’ locker room and noticed the sanitary napkin dispensers mounted on the walls. He began imagining a teenage girl experiencing her first period in the shower with no understanding of what was happening to her while her classmates responded with ridicule. He combined that image with his interest in telekinesis and his memories of two girls he’d known growing up who had been treated as social pariahs. “I wasn’t bullied,” King says. “I think that every kid feels a little bit bullied in school, but I had less of it than others.” The girls, however, weren’t as fortunate. “They were savagely bullied about their clothes, about their hair, just about their lack of social graces. They were country kids and they were really treated poorly.”

What stuck with King was the impossibility of escaping the roles that high school had assigned them. Even when the girls tried to improve their appearance, their tormentors wouldn’t let them. “If they tried to wear new clothes or something like that after Christmas, they were bullied twice as hard,” he says. “Nobody wanted to let them out of the box.” That heartbreaking observation would become the emotional foundation of Carrie. Sometimes the only way out is to burn the whole place down.

At first, King envisioned the story as another quick sale to Cavalier, which he calls his “go-to magazine” at the time. “I thought to myself, ‘Here’s an idea for a story: a girl who gets her first period and she’s telekinetic and she just gets back at these girls.’ ” But almost immediately, he ran into problems. For one thing, he wasn’t convinced he knew enough about the female experience to make the opening believable. “I didn’t know anything about girls’ locker rooms,” he says, beginning to laugh. “I didn’t know if there were coin-op machines for the napkins. I didn’t even know what the napkins were, for God’s sake.” Worse, the story was already growing beyond the magazine’s usual word count, and King feared it would end up being too long for a short story and too short for a novel. So he crumpled up the pages and threw them in the wastebasket.

That might have been the end of Carrie White, except that King’s wife, Tabitha, discovered the discarded manuscript, read it and recognized something that her husband hadn’t. “Tabby fished it out and said, ‘You know, this is really good, so push on with it,’ ” King recalls. He did, and over the next three months, the little story he had abandoned grew into his first publishable novel. Fifty years later, when asked how often he has thanked his wife for retrieving those pages, King doesn’t even pause to think it over: “A lot.”

King’s manuscript eventually landed on the desk of Bill Thompson, an editor at Doubleday who had already read several of King’s earlier, rejected novels. Thompson saw something in Carrie and invited the wannabe author to New York. King could barely afford the trip. His grandmother- in-law gave him the cash for a Greyhound ticket, and he traveled overnight from Maine, with no money for a hotel. Thompson took him to lunch, where several gin and tonics were consumed on the publisher’s dime. “I got pretty much blitzed,” King remembers. Afterward, he became hopelessly lost walking back to the Port Authority bus terminal. When he finally got home, Tabitha asked how the meeting had gone. “I think they might publish the book,” he told her.

In 1973, Doubleday bought Carrie for $2,500. The news arrived by telegram because the Kings still didn’t have a phone. Tabitha received the message through Western Union and had her husband paged to the principal’s office over the school loudspeaker. King immediately imagined two possibilities: Either one of his children had been hurt or he’d sold the book. He still has the telegram, framed on the wall of his office in the much nicer house in Maine he now calls home, bearing Thompson’s wonderfully prophetic message: “The future lies ahead.”

Carrie was published on April 5, 1974, with a modest first printing of 30,000 copies. It wasn’t an immediate sensation in hardcover (it sold about 13,000 copies), but critics were intrigued by the newcomer. The New York Times praised the novel’s assurance and imagination, recognizing that its mixture of supernatural terror and teenage cruelty marked the arrival of a distinctive voice. King, however, felt that Doubleday was too consumed with another one of its titles — Peter Benchley’s Jaws — to promote his book.

Benchley presumably got a much bigger advance as well — King’s $2,500 was barely enough to splurge on a new Pinto. He didn’t exactly rake in a fortune when he sold the film rights, either. Veteran producer Paul Monash, whose credits included Peyton Place and Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, offered a whopping $500 for the story rights. “And Doubleday got half of that,” says King. “So, $250. Big whoop. I could have made more from one of the Cavalier stories.” He took the offer anyway.

Luckily, after the hardcover release there was a windfall when a New American Library editor fell in love with Carrie‘s story and ponied up $400,000 for the paperback rights. Again, Doubleday got half, but it was enough for King to quit teaching and start writing full time. He also used a chunk of the money to help his mother, who was still working even though she was suffering from cancer. “I went to the place where she worked and I said, ‘You’re done,’ ” King recalls. “She cried. That was a great, great moment.”

The film was set up at United Artists with a budget of $1.8 million — a modest figure even by the standards of the mid-1970s. And the director the studio landed on was then-35-year-old Brian De Palma, the New Hollywood movie brat who’d helmed the Hitchcockian 1972 thriller Sisters and the deliriously bonkers 1974 rock-horror musical Phantom of the Paradise. De Palma’s reputation was that of a dazzling visual stylist with a sweet tooth for split-screen trickery, daredevil camerawork and sexual provocation. The director’s drawn-out suspense sequences seemed to delight in torturing the audience. Still, for the most part, box office success had largely eluded him.

De Palma immediately recognized Carrie‘s potential and thought that it might lead to the commercial breakthrough that Jaws had recently given his pal Steven Spielberg. For his part, King was thrilled with the choice. He’d seen Sisters and picked up on a simpatico sensibility. The studio tapped Lawrence D. Cohen, a relative unknown, to adapt King’s novel. Cohen streamlined the book, including its climax. In the novel, Carrie devastates much of her hometown after the prom. But in the movie, the destruction is largely confined to the school gymnasium and back at her house, where she finally confronts her overbearing zealot mother. The adaptation was less sprawling and more intimate.

When it came time to cast the film, De Palma and his friend George Lucas (who was looking for up-and-coming talent for his own in-the-works project, which he was calling Star Wars) decided to pool resources and hold auditions for both films simultaneously. “George and I were both looking for young actors at the same time, so we held our casting sessions together,” De Palma once told me. “We both really wanted Amy Irving. George wanted her for Princess Leia.” William Katt, who eventually snagged the role of Carrie’s handsome prom date, was also considered for Luke Skywalker. The two movies couldn’t have been more different, but for a brief moment, they existed in the same galaxy.

De Palma would eventually cast Irving as Sue Snell, the sympathetic classmate who tries to make amends for Carrie’s humiliation. Nancy Allen played Chris Hargensen, the spoiled, vindictive teenager who orchestrates the prom night prank. John Travolta, already familiar to television audiences as Vinnie Barbarino on Welcome Back, Kotter, played her dim-witted boyfriend. For the part of Carrie’s mother, De Palma recruited Piper Laurie, an Oscar nominee for 1961’s The Hustler who had spent much of the intervening period away from Hollywood. Laurie would approach her character’s religious hysteria with an almost operatic intensity.

The crucial role, however, remained unfilled. Maybe because it seemed unfillable. Sissy Spacek, a 26-year-old Texan who looked at least 10 years younger, had made an indelible impression as a teenage runaway opposite Martin Sheen in Terrence Malick’s Badlands in 1973, but she was hardly a household name.

Her husband, though, production designer Jack Fisk, was working on Carrie and encouraged her to audition for the role. Spacek was supposed to shoot a television commercial on the weekend that De Palma asked her to come in, but she canceled it and showed up for her screen test instead. Spacek arrived looking as though she’d been dragged through the worst day of her life. She had rubbed Vaseline into her hair and wore an old sailor-style dress her mother had made when she was in seventh grade. Rather than try to make herself attractive, she transformed herself into someone almost painfully uncomfortable in her own skin. De Palma was blown away.

Principal photography began in March 1976, with a 50-day schedule and a budget that left little room beyond the barest necessities. The production used an abandoned school in Hermosa Beach for many of its exteriors, while Fisk constructed the gymnasium on a Hollywood soundstage so it could be destroyed during the film’s climax: The sequence of slow-building, screw-tightening suspense set during Carrie’s high school prom — drenched in pig’s blood and supernatural mayhem — is arguably the greatest Hitchcock scene that Hitchcock never directed.

When Carrie opened on Nov. 3, 1976, critics were surprisingly divided on the question of whether De Palma had made a brilliant horror movie or just an exceedingly well-made exploitation picture. In The New York Times, Vincent Canby sniffed at the film’s excesses, arguing that De Palma had encouraged his actors to push their performances beyond plausibility. Yet even Canby couldn’t resist the film’s leading lady. “The marvel, though, is Sissy Spacek,” he wrote, acknowledging that despite the heightened emotions, she made Carrie’s suffering genuinely moving. But others, like the Chicago Sun-Times‘ Roger Ebert, were more enthusiastic. Ebert called the film “an absolutely spellbinding horror movie.”

Audiences sided with Ebert. Carrie earned $33.8 million at the domestic box office — an impressive return on its $1.8 million budget. It marked De Palma’s first real commercial success. It also earned two Academy Award nominations, for Spacek as best actress and Laurie as best supporting actress, an unusual achievement for a horror movie in any era. As for King, he remembers seeing the film for the first time at a preview screening in Boston. He and Tabitha drove down from Maine to an inner-city theater, where Carrie was playing on a double bill with Norman … Is That You?, a comedy starring Redd Foxx.

King recalls the audience being almost entirely Black, and he initially worried that the crowd might have little interest in his story about a white teenage girl’s traumatic adolescence. “I thought to myself, ‘Man, this audience is not going to care about this little white girl with her menstrual problems,’ ” he says. But as the film unspooled, the crowd became increasingly animated, shouting at the screen and really dialing into the film’s white-knuckle suspense.

Then came the final scene. Sitting behind King were two men the size of football players. When Carrie’s hand suddenly burst through the grave, both shrieked and grabbed each other in terror. King recalls one of the men saying, “That’s it, that’s it. She ain’t never gonna be right.” That was when King knew the movie worked. “I thought to myself, ‘Well, we got a hit.’ “

When asked why Carrie still endures, King suspects it’s the primal satisfaction of watching an underdog get payback. “I think that it has something to do with the bullied child striking back,” he says. But the movie’s power is more complicated than just simple revenge. De Palma understood that the audience had to love Carrie before it could fear her.

The movie’s most powerful moment isn’t the prom night massacre or even the final hand reaching from beyond the grave. It’s the expression on Spacek’s face when she realizes she’s been crowned prom queen and believes, for perhaps the first time in her life, that she belongs. For that one brief, beautiful moment, anything and everything seems possible. Then the blood falls, and the dream dies. And half a century later, we still can’t look away.
This story appeared in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: ABC Reveals NFL Quarterback as Next Star of ‘The Bachelor’
items.description: Sam Hartman is the next star of The Bachelor.
items.author: Jackie Strause
paragraphs: Sam Hartman is the next star of The Bachelor.
ABC made the announcement on Good Morning America on Friday morning, surprising fans of the long-running reality dating series after a hiatus for the franchise.
“I’m excited but also very nervous,” Hartman said in his first interview. “I have a tough time holding conversation with one girl — 30 is going to be pretty tough.”

The 27-year-old pro athlete is “changing the game” and “ready to find his forever teammate,” promised ABC in the announcement. His 30th season of the flagship begins with the March 21 premiere (8-10 p.m. on ABC, streaming next day on Hulu and on Disney+ for bundle subscribers).

The Bachelor last wrapped its 29th season, starring Grant Ellis, on March 24, 2025. The overall franchise took an extended break following that fall’s Bachelor in Paradise, however, due to the last-minute cancellation of Taylor Frankie Paul‘s 22nd season of The Bachelorette, which had been planned to premiere in March 2026 but was pulled from the schedule after videos resurfaced of an alleged domestic incident.

Hartman’s casting marks the fifth athlete to lead The Bachelor (Mel Owens also starred on The Golden Bachelor), but the first to be a current athlete while starring on the dating show. The Charlotte, North Carolina, native, plays for the NFL’s Washington Commanders and is on the practice squad. The Wake Forest and Notre Dame alum holds ACC records, including for most career touchdown passes and 300-yard passing games.
He’s also a fan-favorite from the Netflix documentary series QB1: Beyond the Lights and a “charismatic heartthrob who is ready to find a win off the field,” says ABC.
There is no news yet on the returns of The Bachelorette, Golden Bachelor(ette) and/or Bachelor in Paradise.
The Bachelor is produced by Warner Horizon Unscripted Television, a Warner Bros. Television Group company. Scott Teti, Jason Ehrlich and Andy Frank serve as executive producers.

items.title: Russell Brand Accused of Predatory Behavior by Several More Women: “I Begged Him to Stop”
items.description: Convicted rapist Russell Brand is facing allegations of sexual misconduct from at least six more women in a new report from The Times and Netflix’s Russell Brand: Open Secret documentary.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: Convicted rapist Russell Brand is facing allegations of sexual misconduct from at least six more women in a new report from The Times and Netflix’s Russell Brand: Open Secret documentary.

The disgraced comedian and actor is behind bars after being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday. He was found guilty of one rape and three sexual assaults, and cleared on three other counts, in a landmark trial. The Hollywood Reporter has taken a deep dive into the years-long work to expose Brand as a sexual predator and bring him to justice.
Upon his sentencing, the Met Police had confirmed Brand was under investigation for two more alleged rapes.

And then on Thursday, The Times revealed that he has been accused of predatory behavior and misconduct by another six women. This report has come from the two journalists who led the 2023 joint investigation into Brand by The Sunday Times and Channel 4’s Dispatches, which helped other victims of his decide to speak up and, ultimately, press criminal charges.

From Charlotte Wace and Rosamund Urwin, the investigation includes an accusation that Brand had sex with a woman without her consent, then apologized afterwards. Another woman said that he continued having sex with her after she asked him to stop because he was hurting her. She says he later told her: “Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn’t want to do.”

The Times added that these allegations “could not be reported until the criminal case against the former comedian and actor ended, to avoid prejudicing proceedings.” Wace and Urwin wrote that his lawyer said he would consider “injunctive relief” and demanded further time to respond, but the deadline eventually passed with no response — “despite prompts.”
Brand maintained through his trial that all of his interactions were consensual.

Wace and Urwin spoke to a woman called Vicky, who met Brand multiple times for consensual sex. On their final meeting, she says he initiated intimacy without any warning. “My body wasn’t ready for this and it was painful,” Vicky told The Times. “An uneasy wave hits me and I’m scared. And I say, ‘It’s painful,’ and he doesn’t stop. And then it gets worse and it’s really painful. And I say, ‘Stop,’ and he doesn’t stop.” She said: “It was like… he wasn’t present.”

Another woman, called Zoe, said during their 2013 encounter — after Brand had split from pop star Katy Perry — he “grabbed me and manhandled me around a little bit and he put his hand on my throat. […] And then he shoved his other hand down my trousers and penetrated me with his finger.” She told The Times she froze. “I didn’t resist. I just sort of let it happen.”

The final allegation from The Times‘ latest piece of investigative work is from 2015 — when Brand was in a relationship with his now-wife and mother of his children, Laura, who accompanied him every day to court. She told the jury that Brand is a “caring and kind” person and a “wonderful father” to their three children.

Louise, then in her late 20s, worked at a London venue that Brand frequented. One day, a woman approached Louise and asked where he was. “I thought it was just another obsessive fan… She told me she was his girlfriend, but others had said that too.” It was Laura Gallacher, who had dated Brand briefly in 2007 when she was 19 and he was 31. They rekindled their relationship in 2015.

Louise said on one occasion, one of Brand’s staff told her, “‘Russell wants you,'” and that he was in the disabled toilets. Brand tried to “entice her” to come to the lavatory door, and had turned the lights off when she arrived. When Brand claimed he needed toilet paper, she went to hand it to him and he grabbed her. “It was halfway up my forearm, and I tried to get away. When I stepped back, I realized his [member of staff] was standing right behind me,” she recalls. She feared Brand would sexually assault her and managed to slip away. She went into the next room and cried, because “I felt like a piece of meat.”

Both Wace and Urwin contributed to Netflix’s Friday release, Russell Brand: Open Secret, which also included allegations against the convicted sex offender. The film described the experience of an ex-girlfriend of his, under the pseudonym Emily. She said she “literally begged” Brand to stop after he refused to wear a condom during sex. “I said to him, ‘No, Russell, please, let’s just use protection,'” said an actress playing Emily in the film. “I kept saying ‘No’. I said, ‘Stop Russell, stop, please don’t, please.’ […] I literally begged him. I tried to kick him off, I tried to draw my knees back, to kick him in his belly, but he was too strong for me.” She says he “just pinned my hands back behind my head” before forcing himself on her.

Brand is likely to serve around seven years of his prison sentence. Questions have been raised across the industry about how he was able to evade punishment for as long as he did. On Tuesday, another of his ex-girlfriends, Jemima Goldsmith, accused Brand of “violence, coercive control and abuse” while they were together.

items.title: Savannah Guthrie Extends ‘Today’ Show Deal
items.description: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. Guthrie’s contract was set to expire at the end of the year.
items.author: Tony Maglio
paragraphs: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. Guthrie’s contract was set to expire at the end of the year.

Guthrie, the popular co-anchor of NBC’s Today show, has been the news as much as she’s reported the news this year. In the early morning hours of Feb. 1, 2026, Guthrie’s mom Nancy Guthrie was kidnapped from her Tucson, Arizona home. Nancy Guthrie is presumed dead though her remains have never been found. Nancy was 84 years old and in poor health. She did not have her necessary medication with her.
On Feb. 10, doorbell footage of a masked man approaching her home on the night of her disappearance was made public. No suspect was ever identified.

A pair of notes from the purported kidnapper(s) were sent to local news outlets. The first demanded Bitcoin for Nancy’s safe return; the second note did not demand money but stated that Nancy died shortly after her abduction.

The second note reads, in full: “Guthrie Family, We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related. She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you can all find peace. We are truly sorry.”
Savannah Guthrie returned to work at the NBC morning show in April. Craig Melvin is her Today show co-anchor.

Guthrie is set to co-host the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade with her usual collaborators Hoda Kotb and Al Roker. This Thanksgiving marks the 100th anniversary of the procession. The Macy’s march actually began in 1924, but it took a three-year hiatus during World War II.

items.title: Ease Your Mom's Anxiety and Wear a Scarf Already
items.description: Are any accessories as essential, yet mysteriously overlooked, as the best men's scarves? First, they warm your neck (and face, and chest) like nothing else. Second, they put a style-forward, cheery, colorful bow on pretty much any outfit. And yet, these soft
items.author: Ben Kriz
paragraphs: Are any accessories as essential, yet mysteriously overlooked, as the best men's scarves? First, they warm your neck (and face, and chest) like nothing else. Second, they put a style-forward, cheery, colorful bow on pretty much any outfit. And yet, these soft little miracles are all too often an afterthought in the menswear world. Even if you’re the type of guy to painstakingly lay your fits out the night before, chances are when it comes to your scarf game, you’re still reaching for one you picked up in a rushed pinch from Nordstrom Rack, or at a frigid college football game.

This is, of course, fine. But it’s also sort of a tragedy. Because when you pick up a truly great scarf, everything changes. Swaddling your neck in cashmere (or cashmere-emulating fabrics) doesn’t just provide a soothing all-day embrace through bracing winds. It also, like a necktie, creates an opportunity for a flash of personal style, right under your handsome face. Even better, because scarves use less fabric than coats and knitwear, they’re also a great way to own some of the best materials in our industry for far less scratch.

To help you pick the one you’ll soon be recognized by, I surveyed hundreds of scarves from across the fashion (and budget) spectrum, journeying from mall chains, to historic British manufacturers, to the buzziest makers today, and everything in-between. Below, the final 26 best men's scarves to knot up this winter—and next winter, and the one after that.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 13, 2026
items.description: Good news! Mercury and Venus (in Scorpio and Libra, respectively) both end their retrogrades today: first Mercury in the morning, then Venus in the evening. If it’s seemed impossible to move forward lately — maybe unexpected disruptions have interfered with yo
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Good news! Mercury and Venus (in Scorpio and Libra, respectively) both end their retrogrades today: first Mercury in the morning, then Venus in the evening. If it’s seemed impossible to move forward lately — maybe unexpected disruptions have interfered with your plans, or maybe you’ve been too preoccupied with old problems to even consider taking on new ones — that’ll change now. Now is the time to let the small stuff go so that you can focus on the future.

Not every rift in your relationships can be chalked up to miscommunication. Sometimes, very real differences in values are at play, and real harms need to be addressed. But you won’t know unless you sit down and actually talk about what’s bothering you. If you haven’t yet, today could be the right time to initiate these conversations. You might be surprised by how many conflicts turn out to be simple misunderstandings after all.

You strive not to burden the people around you with your problems. Everyone has so much to deal with already, and you want to avoid adding to their plates. But today, remember that it’s normal to rely on other people; in fact, it’s unrealistic to try to be totally self-sufficient. You can’t expect other people to fix your issues for you, but it’s reasonable to want their support here and there. Right now, everything in your life will get easier if you ask for help when you need it. Stop trying to manage it all on your own.

There will always be some people you don’t enjoy being around. Maybe there isn’t anything “wrong” with them — they just don’t mesh well with you. Maybe you find their personality a bit grating, or maybe your communication styles are at odds. You might occasionally get away with avoiding these people, but today that’s unlikely, so put forth extra effort to get along with them. You might never become best friends, but if you try, you can figure out how to work together effectively.

You’re an incredibly good listener — not, as some people imagine, because you possess some rare skill set but simply because you’re interested in other people’s inner lives. Still, make sure you’re not doing so much listening today that you never end up expressing your own ideas. It’s not fair to anyone if you only listen and never speak up: You deserve to make your voice heard, and your friends deserve to know what’s on your mind. You have valuable insights to contribute. Don’t keep them to yourself.

You don’t mind being blunt when the situation calls for it; you see no reason to be coy or withholding. But sometimes even you can’t find the right words to describe how you’re feeling. Your emotions are so strong, or so confusing, that you can hardly understand them yourself, let alone describe them in a way that’ll make sense to anyone else. In these cases, it might seem safest just to keep your mouth shut. But today, you might finally find the words you’ve been looking for, so don’t hesitate to use them.

You prefer to take on projects methodically, one step at a time. Recently, though, you might be struggling to stay focused. Perhaps your energy has been bouncing all over the place, making it hard for you to make any meaningful headway. Today, consider that these detours aren’t an impediment to your progress; they’re a necessary part of the process. You’re on the right track, so keep going.

Lately, you’ve been questioning things you once took for granted. Maybe certain responsibilities have always fallen to you, but now you wonder if you’ve been doing more than your fair share. Maybe you’ve stayed within your comfort zone because you thought you couldn’t handle a challenge, but now you’re starting to crave a risk. The way things are now isn’t the way they have to be forever, so if you’ve been mulling over big life changes, now is the time to do something about them.

You’re deeply self-aware. You spend more time than most people pondering your flaws and weaknesses. You never want to delude yourself into thinking that you’re perfect, or that your problems are someone else’s fault. But recognizing your flaws is only useful if you actually do something with that knowledge. So today, start turning your insights into action. Think about what you’d like to change, then do it.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You probably don’t feel particularly chatty today. There’s no specific reason for it — you’re not sulking or being secretive — you’re just in a quiet mood. But try to be aware that, in the absence of clear communication from you, other people might project their own ideas about what you’re thinking and feeling. So do your best to be as open as you can with those you care about. Taking an extra moment or two to tell your friends how you’re feeling can stave off unnecessary conflicts down the line.

When your friends enthusiastically share their ideas, it’s easy to get swept up in their excitement. It feels good to be part of something bigger than yourself! Sometimes, though, you lose yourself in their energy and forget about your own dreams. Today, make an effort to reconnect with your personal goals. You don’t need to break from the group to fulfill them, but be sure you save some energy for your own projects, too.

Today, you might have the feeling that your hard work hasn’t gotten you anywhere meaningful. You might feel frustrated that all your efforts have yet to pay off. But take a step back and consider that you’re playing a long game, and the rewards will come with time. For now, use this moment to rest and reassess your plans. Then you can start moving forward again.

You want to experience everything the world has to offer. But while this desire can motivate you to take chances and have more fun, it also means you put an inordinate amount of pressure on yourself to “do it all.” You fixate on all the things you might, hypothetically, be missing out on. Today, remind yourself that no one person can do everything. Instead, focus on living your actual life well, and let go of the roads not taken.
