items.title: “Paper Tiger” Views Family as Deadweight
items.description: There are no ticking clocks or flipping calendar pages in James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” but it’s nonetheless a drama of time implacably passing. Call it a September song: the story opens on Labor Day in 1986, in Queens, at the home of the Pearl family.
items.author: Richard Brody
paragraphs: There are no ticking clocks or flipping calendar pages in James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” but it’s nonetheless a drama of time implacably passing. Call it a September song: the story opens on Labor Day in 1986, in Queens, at the home of the Pearl family. Early in the morning, the jovial, still youthful paterfamilias, Irwin (Miles Teller), has his power tools going in the narrow driveway beside the house, waking his sons—Scott (Gavin Goudey), who’s about to turn eighteen, and Ben (Roman Engel), maybe five years younger—on their last day of summer vacation. As Jerry Lewis’s annual telethon blares from a TV in the kitchen, Irwin and his wife, Hester (Scarlett Johansson), tell the boys that they’re all going to visit Hester’s mother, Iris (Cindy Katz), at a country club near her home, in the prosperous and largely Jewish Long Island suburb of Great Neck.

From this banal beginning, Gray launches a tale of fear and violence, criminal conspiracies and paranoia. That night, after the family gets back home, Irwin’s older brother, Gary (Adam Driver), arrives with princely pomp, bringing a takeout feast from the venerable steak house Peter Luger. A former high-ranking cop now earning a grand living as a security consultant—and basking in the admiration of his former N.Y.P.D. colleagues—Gary, who drives a Mercedes and is seemingly sewn into sharply tailored suits, is as dashing as Irwin is staid. The fancy meal is the prelude to a proposition: he wants Irwin, an environmental engineer, to team up with him as a co-consultant to the owners of a grossly polluted site on the Gowanus Canal, in Brooklyn, which is about to undergo a federally funded cleanup. Gary is sure that the job will be lucrative and tells Irwin that the owners, recently arrived Russians whom he describes as scientists and engineers, are in need of Irwin’s regulatory and technical expertise.

At a preliminary meeting in Gowanus, little about the prospective clients’ rough manner and crude appearance bears out Gary’s claims. And a few days later, when the overeager Irwin, following his usual procedure, visits the site to take stock—proudly bringing his sons along to see the world of his work—he finds that he’s dealing with gangsters of rare ruthlessness and brutality. By this time, though, he and Gary are in too deep: the gangsters beat Irwin and menace Hester and the boys. To protect the family, Gary goes into heavy debt to the syndicate; the movie’s title comes from the description he offers of his gangland creditors to allay Irwin’s fears. “I’m N.Y.P.D.,” Gary says, adding, “They’re not gonna touch me.” “But they can touch me,” Irwin skeptically retorts. As the days until payment is due tick grimly by, Irwin and Hester grow increasingly fretful and angry, and their widening divisions wrench the family apart, to intimately catastrophic effect.

Such lovequakes are a through line of Gray’s directorial career, which began in 1994, with “Little Odessa.” Gray, one of cinema’s great homebodies, grew up in Queens, and most of his movies are set there or in Brooklyn and deal bruisingly with the financial tensions, thwarted dreams, and frayed bonds of middle-class Jewish families like the one in which he was raised—stressed, streetwise, and crime-proximate. His previous film, “Armageddon Time,” from 2022—to my mind, his hitherto most accomplished one—is, like “Paper Tiger,” set in his home neighborhood, Fresh Meadows. That film takes place in 1980, with frequent allusions to Ronald Reagan’s ongoing Presidential campaign, and it focusses on a family very similar to the one in “Paper Tiger”: a father named Irving, who is a contractor; a mother named Esther; and two sons, the younger of whom transfers from public school to a nearby private day school dominated by a wealthy local family—the Trumps.

Gray conceived “Paper Tiger” as a sequel to “Armageddon Time” but altered his plans when the actors who played the parents in the earlier film, Anne Hathaway and Jeremy Strong, were unavailable. The two works remain cognate, but their differences are crucial. Strong’s Irving was tougher, more abrasive than Irwin is; conversely, Hathaway’s Esther, a teacher, was relatively refined and educated, whereas Johansson’s counterpart sleeps with rollers in her hair, like a vestige of the pre-Beatles sixties; speaks in a Queens accent that could cut metal; and holds the family together with her life-worn smarts and iron will. Yet she’s as unworldly as the nerdy Irwin, looking up to him with his fund of “facts and figures.”

But fires of rage burn below the surface of “Paper Tiger,” exemplified in the opening visit to Great Neck. Iris wants Hester and her family to move there; Hester demurs, explaining that college tuition for the boys must come first, but Irwin openly scoffs: “Everyone here was born with a silver spoon in their mouth, or stole one.” Iris, seeing suburban luxury as her daughter’s birthright, thinks that Hester’s marriage has been a comedown. The Pearls aren’t poor, but they’re burdened by expenses and tantalized by comforts just out of reach, especially now that their sons’ heads have been turned by Gary’s flashy success. (Comparing his uncle’s Mercedes with his parents’ cars, Scott whines, “Why do we always have to buy crappy stuff and live crappy?”)

Irwin’s run-in with the Mob dispels the fantasy of easy money; instead, he packs suitcases and makes plans to get the family out of town for their safety. Yet “Paper Tiger” is far more than a tale of criminal violence piercing the domestic bubble. It’s a story of silences, ones that form a conspicuous contrast with its precursor. “Armageddon Time,” with its expressly political context, is a film of rich discourse, filled with rhetorical expositions of ideology and history, reminiscences and commentaries. In “Paper Tiger,” there’s plenty of talk throughout, but hardly any of it involves cultural context, broader observation, or deeper reflection; it’s not a film of ideas. Instead, the heated dialogue is an expression of the inner life of the family and its time.

Interviews with directors have become a familiar part of movie promotion, but Gray’s interviews are different, often less like conversations than like performances. He’s among the most publicly funny of filmmakers, a gifted impersonator; I’ve long hoped that he would direct a comedy (he hasn’t yet) and appear in it. But his talent for mimicry comes across thrillingly in the dialogue of “Paper Tiger”—Gray wrote the screenplay himself—which adds an extra dimension to the story’s autobiographical elements. Both in ordinary chitchat and in big confrontations, the dialogue plays like a musical score of language built from a trove of memories. The film’s wondrously street-lyrical patter, its emblematic phrases and inflections, amount to a vast act of world-building—a lost milieu brought back to life in bygone clichés.

Much of this evocative talk also proves evasive. Just as Gary’s forecast for the Gowanus venture turns out to have been misleading, the fallout from that calamitous misadventure quickly brings on further elisions and secrets, transforming a happy home and a stable marriage into a curtained stage of furtive designs, hidden agendas, and stealthy exploits. Gary’s Mephistophelian temptations break the façades of business, law, and marriage, revealing the profound and irreparable solitude that lurks beneath life’s fundamental bonds.

Gray has always displayed a probing visual style, boldly confrontational yet painfully tender. In “Paper Tiger,” he refines these tendencies into lapidary images—spare, taut, and precise—that evoke the fierce solidity of the family circle and the fearsome emptiness that’s left when it shatters. With a quietly dazzling repertory of shadows and reflections, fragmented glimpses, truncated vistas, and blocked perspectives, he conjures everything the film keeps hidden, the illusions and limitations that inhere in frank gazes and point-blank views. I’ve seen “Paper Tiger” on the big screen but am looking forward to its streaming release in order to rewatch it as a silent film. Amid all its chatter, Gray has found the space to let images be eloquent, too. And their eloquence is greatest when expressing the silence and solitude of Hester.

In this regard, Gray’s movie resembles a pair of recent classics by Martin Scorsese, “The Irishman” and “Killers of the Flower Moon,” both of which feature women who respond to betrayal by men with silences deafening enough to rend the films’ finely textured surfaces. In “Paper Tiger,” the cycle of tragedy finds its definitive voice in Hester’s reproachful silences, which turn out to be radical rejections of the tight little world she inhabits. Determined and relentless, Hester, as incarnated by Johansson, dominates the action and steals the film with a decisive form of passive aggression—one that Gray condenses into a breathtakingly rapid, boldly symbolic special effect. By the time September winds down, Hester is on a timetable all her own, out of synch with her family, detached from its cares, paradoxically and bitterly free. ♦

items.title: What Is It About Rock Music and Fascism?
items.description: Fifty years ago, Cameron Crowe interviewed David Bowie for Playboy magazine. The exchange is best remembered for Bowie’s proclamation of his bisexuality, but another section deserves more scrutiny than it often receives:
items.author: Alex Ross
paragraphs: Fifty years ago, Cameron Crowe interviewed David Bowie for Playboy magazine. The exchange is best remembered for Bowie’s proclamation of his bisexuality, but another section deserves more scrutiny than it often receives:

Playboy had no more follow-up questions until the very end of the conversation, when Crowe, who was nineteen at the time, asked Bowie whether he stood by what he had said. “Everything but the inflammatory remarks,” Bowie replied, without specifying what they were.

In later years, Bowie struggled to explain this interview and various other instances in which he dabbled in fascist rhetoric. He said that he had been “out of my mind totally, completely crazed”; that he had been thinking in mythological terms, not in political ones; that he had indulged in “glib, theatrical observations”; that the horror of the Holocaust had “completely evaded my extraordinary fucked-up nature at that particular time.” Critics and biographers took a similar line, proposing that Bowie had been suffering from “cocaine psychosis,” or that he had been speaking “at least partially tongue-in-cheek,” or that he had been dealing in “illogical irony.” The issue has periodically resurfaced in the years since Bowie’s death, in 2016, but it has hardly dented his reputation, which long ago attained the status of greatness and genius—a seamless extension of the old Romantic cult of the artist-hero.

What’s striking about Bowie’s flirtation with fascism is how commonplace it was. Such is the import of “This Ain’t Rock ’n’ Roll: Pop Music, the Swastika, and the Third Reich” (Akashic), a recent book by the British musician and writer Daniel Rachel. (The title is taken from Bowie’s song “Diamond Dogs,” which begins with the announcement “This ain’t rock ’n’ roll—this is genocide!”) Although Rachel devotes a chapter to Bowie, he touches on so many other semi-fascist or full-on-Nazi outbursts from rock and pop musicians of the nineteen-sixties, seventies, and eighties that the Thin White Duke, as Bowie called himself circa 1976, gets lost in the shuffle. In this light, Kanye West’s intermittent admiration for Hitler seems less an anomaly than an homage to a venerable tradition. Reading Rachel’s compilation, I stopped worrying about the moral particulars of any one case—can the art be separated from the artist?—and instead wondered about the art itself. Something in the pop ritual keeps inducing the same symptoms.

Rachel focusses on the British context, going back as far as the late fifties. When John Lennon was a Liverpool art student, he drew a picture of himself delivering a Hitler salute, with the legend “HEIL JOHN.” Lennon occasionally snapped such salutes in the following decade. When the members of the Beatles were choosing faces to feature on the cover of “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band,” Lennon suggested Jesus and Hitler, neither of whom is visible. The innocent explanation is that Lennon and others of his generation were mocking the patriotic solemnity that their parents had conferred on the Second World War. George Harrison later said, “We were the generation who didn’t suffer from the war and we didn’t want to have to keep being told about Hitler.” At the time, the war was viewed more as a stomping of the Jerries than as a contest with genocidal evil. This was also the era of Mel Brooks’s “The Producers,” with its riotous “Springtime for Hitler” sequence—although Brooks’s obvious satirical intent, not to mention his status as a Jewish war veteran, places him in an entirely different category.

A notable scene took place in Melbourne in 1964, when the Beatles greeted thousands of fans from a hotel balcony. Lennon raised his right arm and mimicked a Hitler mustache with his left index finger. Paul McCartney and George Harrison followed suit. One newspaper caption read, “Whenever the Beatles appeared on a balcony, they couldn’t resist giving Hitler-type salutes.” The Beatles clearly had in mind old newsreel footage of the Führer and the Duce greeting their hordes. You could ascribe a critical intent to the gesture—a subversive response to unchecked hype. For the most part, the band seemed wary of the unprecedented fame that had been conferred upon it.

Creepier tics cropped up among the Beatles’ successors. Brian Jones, of the Rolling Stones, was photographed wearing an S.S. uniform and crushing a plastic doll with his boot. Mick Jagger praised Leni Riefenstahl’s “Triumph of the Will” and modelled for the director. Keith Moon thought it hilarious to march through a Jewish neighborhood in London wearing Third Reich regalia. Sid Vicious did much the same in Paris. Malcolm McLaren’s infatuation with Nazi style meant that swastikas became a staple of punk culture. Metal exhibited similar Teutonic tendencies—umlauts, Fraktur type, Iron Crosses. For Nikki Sixx, of Mötley Crüe, umlauts were “German and strong,” evocative of conquering youth. Motörhead’s Lemmy amassed a storehouse of Nazi memorabilia. Sinister associations were inscribed in band names: supposed sexual-slavery operations in German concentration camps, in the case of Joy Division; the prison where Rudolf Hess was held in postwar Berlin, in the case of Spandau Ballet. A Nazi-curious playlist would include the Sex Pistols’ “Belsen Was a Gas,” Devo’s “Triumph of the Will,” and the Ramones’ “Blitzkrieg Bop.”

Many of rock’s ersatz Nazis were, like Bowie, subsequently embarrassed by their behavior. Rachel catalogues their various excuses, titling one section of his book “Never Mind the Swastikas.” Some opted for an aesthetic defense: everyone looks good in shiny black. According to McLaren, the Nazis had “the best clothes sense.” Their uniforms were deemed “great” (Eric Clapton), “just so pretty” (Dee Dee Ramone), and “the coolest” (Ace Frehley, of Kiss). Others insisted that they had just been larking about. When Lou Reed was asked why he had an Iron Cross shaved into his hair, he replied, “I was young. I was having fun.” Siouxsie Sioux, of Siouxsie and the Banshees, called Nazi antics an “anti-mums-and-dads thing.” Peter Hook, of Joy Division, declared that his band was “nothing more than a bunch of lads obsessed with the war.” Nick Cave said that his use of the swastika on two record covers in the early eighties was “deliberately moronic.”

All the same, the trend troubled many members of the rock community—those who had managed to be young and dumb without donning an S.S. outfit or collecting Wehrmacht daggers. In the late seventies, the Rock Against Racism movement in the U.K. mobilized in response to anti-immigrant diatribes delivered by Clapton, which echoed the far-right National Front. Billy Bragg, who contributes an introduction to Rachel’s book, was a youthful member of that antifascist wave. The Dead Kennedys sang, “You still think swastikas look cool? / The real Nazis run your schools.” The rock critic Lester Bangs diagnosed white-supremacist strains in the punk world: “Anytime you conclude that life stinks and the human race mostly amounts to a pile of shit, you’ve got the perfect breeding ground for fascism.” In the dishevelled grunge years, Nazi regimentation lost prestige, although it didn’t disappear completely. Carlos Dengler, of the early-two-thousands band Interpol, adopted Hitler Youth drag, which he later rationalized as a critique of his German heritage.

The final chapters of Rachel’s book turn to modern pop, showing in the process that fascist chic is not exclusively a white male problem. Michael Jackson’s teaser for the album “HIStory,” in which the star marched between rigid ranks of soldiers, was echt Riefenstahl. Madonna and Lady Gaga each dipped into S.S. kink by way of the 1974 film “The Night Porter.” Nicki Minaj alluded to “Triumph of the Will” in her “Only” music video. Last year, Kanye West released a song titled “Heil Hitler”; this year, he blamed a car accident and a bipolar condition for the misstep. For the most part, however, Nazi strutting belongs to the glory days of white rock and roll, alongside the decorative use of the Confederate flag and other gestures of reactionary rebellion.

Few authors have looked closely at rock’s swastika fetish, and Rachel deserves credit for his assiduous gathering of evidence. In an epilogue to “This Ain’t Rock ’n’ Roll,” he says that he grew up with the music in question, singing along to “Belsen Was a Gas,” and that writing the book was painful for him. Unfortunately, he doesn’t shed much light on the origins of the phenomenon. Although he is right to emphasize unrepentant antisemitism in Western societies, it’s clear that many rockers in the book weren’t viscerally anti-Jewish. Some, in fact, were Jewish themselves. Tommy Ramone, the principal author of “Blitzkrieg Bop,” came from a family of Holocaust survivors. So did Gene Simmons, who once said, “One word from Hitler and the masses would move in unison. It was the same with Kiss.” At times, Rachel’s framing becomes hazy, as when he cites the Scottish band Primal Scream, which has used Nazi imagery to excoriate Benjamin Netanyahu and the state of Israel. Whatever the merits of that approach, this is not a case of a band drawing a positive charge from fascist iconography.

The British-born media theorist Dick Hebdige offered a gentler interpretation in his 1979 book, “Subculture: The Meaning of Style.” Focussing on punk, Hebdige argues that the likes of Siouxsie and Sid Vicious aimed to jolt the establishment by aping history’s supreme bogeymen. One scenester justified the swastika look by saying, “Punks just like to be hated.” Hebdige then turns to post-structuralist theory: “The signifier (swastika) had been willfully detached from the concept (Nazism) it conventionally signified.” In other words, in a postmodern, end-of-history age, fascist symbols lose their specific menace. Likewise, Pamela Rooke, a Sex Pistols adjutant who sported a red armband during the band’s television début in 1976, later shrugged off the episode by saying, “There was no Nazi Party now.” Johnny Ramone claimed that “there’s no threat right now of any Nazi thing,” though he did perceive a “communist threat.” Alas, signifiers have a way of reuniting with their signifieds, and the Nazi thing is alive and well.

The source of the syndrome may ultimately lie in the theatrics of the pop spectacle: isolated figures receiving the adoration of a mesmerized public. Such ceremonies of idolatry go back into the deepest past, but mass communication empowered performers to an unparalleled degree, as it had empowered Hitler. In this sense, Bowie’s discussion of media manipulation in that Playboy interview offered a valuable bit of analysis. The Beatles recognized the new reality when they walked out on a Melbourne hotel balcony. Rapt throngs were materializing out of nowhere, summoned by signals that had circled the planet. Centuries of Anglo-American cultural imperialism laid the groundwork for the Beatles’ ascendancy: English was the language of hegemony. Sound reproduction put the entire globe within reach. Electric amplification enabled the band to perform for audiences of awesome size—fifty-five thousand people in Shea Stadium, in 1965. Without microphones, the Beatles and all their successors would have been inaudible.

Such a superhuman magnification of the individual is unsettling to behold at close range. I witnessed the internal mechanics when I followed Radiohead on tour in 2000. Members of the band were variously thrilled, unnerved, and scared by what they were unleashing—a healthily complex reaction. Narcissists, not uncommon in pop circles, have no such hangups. They have always been preparing to greet crowds from a balcony; they are not surprised to hear their thoughts echoed by tens of thousands of voices in unison. But fame at the stadium level can have a corrosive effect on formerly amiable personalities, as we know from watching countless rise-and-fall documentaries on VH1. The music alone cannot generate a Nuremberg-rally atmosphere: the crucial factor is the audience’s desire for collective submission.

That longing to become one with the throng is elemental. We humans love to discard our anxious selves and join a unanimous pack. If no sinister ideology is at work—and, usually, none is—what harm is being done? In a hyper-mediated context, though, the synchronization of thousands of bodies in a rite of glorification cannot avoid being political, and the politics in question is hardly egalitarian. This was a theme of Susan Sontag’s 1975 essay “Fascinating Fascism,” which was alert to darker trends in the pop realm. Sontag wrote, “The relations of domination and enslavement take the form of a characteristic pageantry: the massing of groups of people; the turning of people into things; the multiplication or replication of things; and the grouping of people/things around an all-powerful, hypnotic leader-figure or force.” Theodor W. Adorno went even further and denounced mass culture as inherently totalitarian.

Having had a few ecstatic experiences of my own at stadium shows, I resist such drastic judgments. When Prince performed at Madison Square Garden in 2004, he imposed nothing more, and nothing less, than his own staggering virtuosity. At the same time, I mistrust pop culture’s boundless faith in its own innocence. As a rule, its products are held to be hugely influential in fostering progress, but when things go awry they are reclassified as harmless fun. Thus, Bowie’s announcement of his bisexuality is said to have significantly boosted gay rights while his Hitler fantasies amounted to boyish tomfoolery. In the same way, we tend not to talk about pop’s relationship with monopoly capitalism. The concentration of media power in the hands of a small circle of ubiquitous superstars mirrors economic inequality. Tellingly, with some honorable exceptions, élite celebrities have been circumspect about the trashing of democracy in the MAGA era. Many of them may dislike Trump, but politics is divisive and eats into profits.

Although the twilight of the pop gods is probably a long way off, a counter-swing toward a more decentered, democratic marketplace is something to dream about, particularly as offshoots of quasi-socialism take hold here and there. We need something like a redistribution of cultural wealth. At some point, fans may tire of paying hundreds or even thousands of dollars to see, at the distance of a Hail Mary pass, Taylor Swift earning her second billion. Whether or not anything political hangs on the outcome, mass worship is irrational at heart, as pop’s wiser practitioners know. Bob Dylan once sang, “Never did get the message, don’t even know if one was sent to me / About the madness of becoming what one was never meant to be.” ♦
An earlier version of this article misstated the title of a song by Sid Vicious.

items.title: A “Good Populism” Rises in the United States
items.description: Since Donald Trump descended that escalator and ushered in a new geopolitical age, eleven years ago, the United States and Europe have each been conducting a similar—if not identical—conversation about the future of their politics and their societies. As an up
items.author: Ishaan Tharoor
paragraphs: Since Donald Trump descended that escalator and ushered in a new geopolitical age, eleven years ago, the United States and Europe have each been conducting a similar—if not identical—conversation about the future of their politics and their societies. As an upstart Republican challenger, Trump set himself on course for the Presidency by importing wholesale the language and the animus of the European far right, grandstanding over the threat of Syrian refugees and Muslim migration by drawing on security fears that had little to do with the realities of the United States. He saw the British vote for Brexit, in 2016—a thumb in the eye of an overweening liberal establishment—as a boon for his own incipient political movement. His victory in 2024 was celebrated by fellow-travellers across the Atlantic as a harbinger of things to come; his second term has dovetailed with a surge in support for European far-right parties, some of which want to carry out Trump-style campaigns of mass deportations. In early 2025, Spain’s far-right Vox party convened a gathering of European ultranationalists under the banner of “Make Europe Great Again.” It included some factions that either were already in power or seemed on the precipice of winning it. “Yesterday, we were the heretics; today, we’re mainstream,” then Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán announced. “People thought we represented the past; today, everyone sees that we are the future.”

In fact, everyone did not. Orbán’s tenure is, of course, now in the past. He was defeated resoundingly in an election earlier this year by a Hungarian opposition committed to unravelling his illiberal, autocratic legacy. The European leader whom Steve Bannon once described as “Trump before Trump” can model for the lame-duck President what it’s like to be out of office, and his ideological allies elsewhere have recalibrated their positions. Even before last week, when the U.S. midterm elections delivered a historic rebuke to Trump’s project, some in the vanguard of Europe’s new right—including the Italian Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, and France’s Marine Le Pen—were keeping their distance from him, aware of his profound unpopularity among Europeans and the ways in which their nationalist ambitions were better served untethered from MAGA’s gravitational pull. And their ascension proceeds: in France, rolling social unrest and a sputtering economy may catapult Le Pen and her party into power next spring, and, in the United Kingdom, an economic malaise compounded by anti-migrant xenophobia may cause the Labour Party to suffer major losses in local elections next year. Meanwhile, Germany’s AfD, a far-right party classified as an extremist organization by the country’s own domestic-intelligence agency, is already the largest opposition party in the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament; it could be poised to take power in an eastern German state by the end of this year, and is, state by state, growing at the expense of the increasingly unpopular center-right Christian Democrats and center-left Social Democrats, who are jointly running the country in a coalition government.

Then, there’s Spain, where Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, currently Europe’s longest-serving center-left leader, gambled on a snap election later this month in an attempt to strengthen his fragile coalition. Opinion polls still show right-wing parties favored to form the next government, after eight years of Sánchez’s leadership and a damaging set of corruption scandals involving figures within the Prime Minister’s inner circle. But after the Democratic Party scored its biggest series of congressional wins in half a century, Sánchez and his allies are feeling encouraged. Their platform centers on implementing significant progressive reforms to alleviate the country’s housing crisis, and they hope their compatriots will see events in Spain on a continuum with the recent victory of Brazil’s leftist incumbent President and the Democrats’ overwhelming popular mandate. After years of keeping right-wing populism at bay in Spain, they see themselves marshalling a left-wing populist response.

In a phone call last week, José Manuel Albares, Spain’s foreign minister, talked to me about his world view, which, he said, “puts forward dialogue and coöperation,” and “respect for international law.” It’s a vision in line with that of the new Democrats arriving in Washington, such as Michigan’s senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who has said that the United States “should be the first among equals to enforce international law.” Albares noted that the victorious progressives in the United States and Brazil focussed on addressing economic inequity and hardship (“the things that matter to the people”), a belief that redistribution has to accompany economic growth, and an explicit embrace of the diversity of their countries. The Democrats, after all, won on platforms that promised to bring down prices, tackle corruption, reckon with inequality, expand health-care access, reject nativism, and take on the wealthiest of the élites. They are, arguably, America’s true populists. “The winners are people that really think that there is a place for everybody in the society, and that everyone needs equal opportunities,” Albares told me. The alternative, he said, would be to “scapegoat” migrants as his party’s rivals on the right have done, and return to “the law of the jungle,” where “the strong can impose their will on the weakest.”

Earlier this year, the political scientists Pepper Culpepper and Taeku Lee identified two competing strains of populism, in an essay for the Journal of Democracy. There are the populist tendencies that come out of a narrative of political failure—the fury of the AfD over refugee arrivals, the rage of the MAGA base that wanted to “drain the swamp” and who demonized migrants. Then, there’s another tendency, which emerges from a shared sense of economic unfairness and which, as Lee, a professor of government at Harvard, told me, is pluralist in its ethos, “does not scapegoat targeted groups, like immigrants and marginalized minorities,” and puts the blame on big business and billionaires. This, in Lee and Culpepper’s formulation, is “good populism” and that is the populism that prevailed in the United States last week. “You can only go so far in blaming immigrants for your unhappiness before you have to start looking elsewhere,” Lee said. “The sheer scale and astonishing arc of this Tuesday’s elections in America bends in the direction of good populism.” In an interview with the Times, Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, explicitly embraced the tag of “economic populism,” arguing that “this has to be the politics of the moment to meet the challenges of the moment.”

For now, Europe still seems on a different trajectory. Economies like France’s are grappling with a growing public-debt crisis, while Germany’s powerhouse manufacturing industries are facing existential pressure from Chinese competition. Increased military spending is forcing hard conversations about outlays for existing social-safety nets, while, as in the United States, the energy-price shocks triggered by the war in Iran have contributed to spiked inflation. The appeal of nativist culture wars endures, while more establishment parties are being pulled to the right. Germany’s center-right Chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has stoked his unpopularity by attempting a raft of reforms and cuts on social spending, including to pensions. Isabella Weber, a German economist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and the author of a new book, “Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defense of Affordability, Dignity, and Democracy,” points to the irony of Germany “turning to old recipes of the nineteen-nineties” with a campaign of austerity and deregulation at a moment when the United States is “the closest we have ever gotten to the Democrats breaking with neoliberalism and market fundamentalism.”

The AfD has gained from dissatisfaction with Merz and his big-tent coalition with the center-left Social Democrats. But, beyond promises to cut benefits for migrants and foreigners, the AfD’s economic program is far from populist; the Party wants to slash corporate taxes and abolish inheritance and wealth taxes. Tellingly, it has become the darling of Elon Musk, whose huge investment on behalf of Republicans this cycle proved ineffectual, and likely fomented a backlash against billionaires’ interfering in U.S. politics. In Germany, though, Musk has been a conspicuous ally of the far-right, urging Germans to move on from their guilt over the Nazi past while sounding alarms about the perils that immigrants supposedly present to white Europeans. These demographic anxieties pervade the Continent and seem to drive political calculations. Some centrists have pointed to the pragmatism of the so-called Danish model—the precedent set by center-left governments in Denmark, in the wake of the 2015 European migration crisis, that remained progressive on many social and economic issues but tacked hard to the right on questions of immigration. That approach kept the center left in power for more than a decade, but it’s no panacea. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s Social Democrats suffered their worst electoral result in more than a century earlier this year, and remain in power thanks only to a four-party minority coalition. As Jan-Werner Müller, a political theorist at Princeton put it, they were unable to check the far-right even as they aped its demagoguery on migrants, while simultaneously losing younger voters, who reject xenophobic politics, to smaller parties on the left. “Never mind morality on any of this, but just electorally, it’s actually not such a great idea,” he told me. After the U.S. midterms, it’s the Democrats now who have a chance to bring Europe into their conversation. ♦

items.title: Changing Our Relationship to Technology Will Require Collective Action
items.description: At noon, at six-thirty, and at ten at night, before I shuffle off to bed, my phone automatically shuts off access to all social-media sites. If I want to restore my ability to mindlessly scroll, I have to walk sheepishly to my kitchen and press my phone up aga
items.author: Jay Caspian Kang
paragraphs: At noon, at six-thirty, and at ten at night, before I shuffle off to bed, my phone automatically shuts off access to all social-media sites. If I want to restore my ability to mindlessly scroll, I have to walk sheepishly to my kitchen and press my phone up against a little plastic square that sits on a high shelf. This humiliation device, called the Brick, limits my screen time to the apps that, in an earlier moment of clarity, I deemed essential: text messages and Apple Books, which, during these Bricked hours, I have been using to dutifully reread “The Brothers Karamazov,” prompted more by a sense of shame than by a sincere interest in revisiting the great novels. (If I’m still going to be on my phone, it should be for something ostensibly edifying.) In the past year, the Brick has represented the only real resistance I’ve mustered against the continual creep of the online world into my daily life. My screen time hasn’t decreased, but it’s better, I suppose, to read Ivan Fyodorovich’s rants about God than to watch endless reels about the latest revolution in shin-guard technology or whatever.

I have been thinking and writing about resistance to technology for a while, spurred by an unresolved alarm that Americans have not put up much of a fight against the sense of alienation caused by our growing dependence on screens. It’s increasingly clear to me that we will not survive as a society without some seismic intervention that separates us from our screens, our algorithms, and our little simulacra of social life. I believe that such a rupture will come—but what will it look like? Will it resemble the dropout movement of the late nineteen-sixties and early seventies, with waves of young people refusing to abide by convention? Or will we eventually see a government anti-screen initiative, one that “raises awareness” and issues stiff penalties against tech companies, similar to the ones levelled against tobacco companies in the nineties? Perhaps we will shed our phone addiction the way we have gradually shed cigarettes.

Whatever the solution may be, it feels, at the moment, impossibly far away. In the immediate aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, which had glued us all more tightly than ever to our phones, many people, I’m sure, crafted some limp armistice like mine, buying a Brick or muting notifications or stashing their phones in other rooms at bedtime, or even just leaving them on “Do Not Disturb” throughout the day. But, in most cases, that was about the extent of their protests. If there is a local initiative to ban the use of devices in their children’s schools, they will support it, but they will probably not do much to rip the phones out of their children’s hands. Most of us have settled into a persistent but passive discontent.

During the next few weeks, I’ll be exploring, in a series of columns, whether this malaise is finally breaking. There is some evidence that it is. For example: the American public has coalesced into what the election forecaster Nate Silver calls a “super-majority” against data centers. That opposition began in raucous protests at town halls and building sites, but it has metastasized into something of a national movement. (According to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project, there have been more than three hundred protests against data centers in the U.S. this year.) Data centers now feature in the electoral platforms of numerous officeholders and candidates, including the Democratic Presidential hopeful Ruben Gallego, who recently announced a tax plan that would shift the construction and energy costs of data centers away from the public and onto the tech companies that benefit from them. Gallego is a relatively moderate and somewhat heterodox candidate, and although his plan isn’t exactly a Luddite call to smash the robots, he might be seen as a bellwether for what the left side of the aisle will be thinking in the coming years. People in the streets and politicians in Congress aren’t the only ones demonstrating a tech backlash: the courts have handed down a set of billion-dollar rulings against tech giants, including in a recent case in New Mexico in which Meta was found guilty of forty-three million violations of the state’s laws.

These days, resistance to tech is typically framed in terms of individual choices: if we buy the Brick, limit our children’s screen time, delete the worst apps from our phones, stop doomscrolling, and refuse to use ChatGPT for anything other than the most mundane searches, we will be released from the grasp of Big Tech. Freedom becomes a question of your own will power. In 2022, the Times published a charming story about “Luddite” teens in Brooklyn who met up in Prospect Park once a week to draw, whittle, and read “The Consolation of Philosophy.” The teens, many of them inspired by the D.I.Y. punk scene and Jon Krakauer’s “Into the Wild,” had decided to drop out of digitized life and start noticing the world outside their phones. Like these kids, I usually think about tech resistance in terms of my own attention and that of my family. I worry constantly about whether the iPad is rotting my children’s brains; I celebrate every reduction in my weekly screen-time reports. But I think this individual focus has a lot to do with why we feel so helpless against Big Tech, and I wonder whether those of us who want to free ourselves from our phones might be better off thinking more collectively.

One of the longest-running and most significant ongoing political actions against A.I. has come from nurses, who, since at least the spring of 2024, have been protesting the technology’s incursion into their profession. Their concerns are numerous and rooted in both present practices and future possibilities. This past March, more than two thousand mental-health professionals at the health-care consortium Kaiser Permanente went on a one-day strike over concerns that they would eventually be replaced by artificial intelligence. Four months later, a story in CalMatters detailed new surveillance layers that had been placed on nurses at Kaiser, including an A.I. program that allegedly assessed their empathy and the tone of their voices when they answered calls from patients. Last year, HCA Healthcare, one of the largest hospital providers in the country, released a joint program with Palantir called Timpani, which promised to streamline the scheduling of nurses by using A.I. to spot inefficiencies. This past August, the National Nurses United (N.N.U.) union led a day of nationwide demonstrations against Palantir.

Americans, in general, like nurses and don’t trust A.I. companies, much less Palantir, to make potentially life-saving decisions. And although hospital efficiency measures are nothing new—almost every labor fight in the health-care sector arises out of issues around head count and hours—A.I. represents a different type of invasion. The N.N.U. is not demanding a full removal of A.I. technology from workplaces, or suggesting a return to a time when all scheduling was done by hand and all consultations were aided only by a nurse’s hard-earned experience. Rather, the union is drawing a line at A.I. supremacy in staffing, decision-making, and clinical assessments. “What makes A.I. even more dangerous is the insistence of health-care companies and these billionaires to use it as a technology to override the judgment of nurses, and to override their clinical decision-making,” Puneet Maharaj, the executive director of the N.N.U., told me.

Maharaj said that A.I. has infiltrated many parts of a nurse’s workday. In the past, nurses’ schedules were partly automated but overseen by a human manager, who could be aware of, and responsive to, personal issues. Now schedules are run entirely by A.I., which, according to Maharaj, will always understaff nurses’ posts. When nurses arrive at their shifts, they may be asked to use A.I. tools that listen to their interactions with patients, and A.I. may also be used to evaluate medical records. These programs have been known to make mistakes in their automated assessments. For example, Maharaj said, in the course of describing the details of their day, a patient might mention battling pine needles in yardwork, and an A.I. might mislabel the patient as having an opioid problem. The listening machines also raise real questions about patient privacy. “With A.I., we don’t always know where that information is going and whether it will be protected or not,” Maharaj said. (A.I. phone-monitoring is of particular concern among mental-health professionals. This was another reason for the Kaiser Permanente strike in March.)

The ultimate concern, though, is that A.I. will replace the relationship between nurse and patient and turn medical professionals into meat puppets who do the machine’s bidding. “Maybe you can look at efficiency when you’re looking at widgets,” Maharaj said. “But when you’re talking about patients, and you’re talking about the relationship between a nurse and her patient—that is extremely important, and that is reserved for the judgment of the nurse, and not some technology that is going to override their judgment.”

The nurses’ protests are intriguing in part because organized labor has the capacity, the experience, and the public approval necessary to secure support outside of a single industry. And the N.N.U. protests go beyond the direct workplace concerns of nurses. Palantir was chosen specifically as a target of protest not just for its incursion into health care but for its role in surveillance and military technology. “A corporation that is invested in killing people should have no space in health care, where the goal is to keep people healthy and alive,” Maharaj said. She pointed out that Palantir was making inroads into a wide range of industries, and that this, in turn, presented a “great opportunity for allies, labor and non-labor alike.” The playbook, then, seems to be high-profile strikes and demonstrations that not only spotlight nuts-and-bolts questions about staffing but also address the more existential and perhaps still somewhat abstract fear that A.I. will become a replacement for nurses everywhere. A confrontation with Palantir, the mere name of which causes many Americans to recoil, can bring in other labor unions and also political activists who opposed Palantir’s more notorious work. Solidarity is easier when there’s a common enemy; there are few better ones than Palantir.

Is this a more productive path to resisting technology than our individual efforts? The sentimental lefty in me would say that the answer, obviously, is yes: rallying together against a powerful villain to address material and workplace harms offers both the clarity and the social support that we’ll need to beat back some of the most pernicious and anti-human excesses of the tech industry. Still, I’m not sure that such actions will entirely satisfy the Luddite teens who desire a separation from the digital world rather than worker control over inevitable technological change. Of course, that has no bearing on the merits of the nurses’ union’s actions—I only want to point out that the dissatisfaction with our screen lives is uniquely personal, for the simple reason that we mostly look at our devices alone, and whatever we bury inside them is generally accessed only by us. In the past decade, nobody, not even my parents or my kids or my wife, has looked upon my face more than has my phone’s camera, which, without comment, scans my features a hundred times a day. If that camera were always on, and someone were watching the feeds, what range of emotions would they witness passing through its narrow frame? Next week, I will write about this modern narcissism and what we might be able to do about it. ♦

items.title: Melania’s New Project: An Allegedly Pro-DEI Ivanka Rip-off
items.description: Melania Trump loves to show she’s her own woman. Previous First Ladies were constantly at their respective husbands’ sides and carefully coordinated with the White House to support their agendas. Melania skipped most of Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign events and
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Melania Trump loves to show she’s her own woman. Previous First Ladies were constantly at their respective husbands’ sides and carefully coordinated with the White House to support their agendas. Melania skipped most of Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign events and has been known to do things like throw a surprise press conference on Jeffrey Epstein in the middle of a tense international crisis.

The First Lady asserted her independence again this fall when she announced Imperia, a networking forum for female CEOs. Melania launched the project on September 23 by ringing the bell at the New York Stock Exchange while surrounded by female business leaders from major companies like Bank of America, IBM, and Prudential.

This whole thing, which Melania’s team described as “Davos for women,” didn’t really seem like something President Trump would be into. In fact, as Fortune noted at the time, it sounded an awful lot like one of those diversity, equity, and inclusion programs that the Trump administration was actively working to eradicate:

Trump’s anti-DEI spree has often focused on race in hiring and promotions, but it has impacted women too. Organizations that support women in tech and business have seen their funding evaporate, as companies fear getting close to anything that could even be perceived as DEI.
Back in September, Melania told Fox Business that Imperia actually isn’t DEI because “it’s all about the merit.” Plus she said, “DEI, we’re not talking about that anymore.”

But the New York Times has uncovered some evidence that Imperia is actually quite similar to programs that have suffered due to the Trump administration’s DEI purge. It turns out there’s already a company with a very similar name, Imperia Global, and the same mission: connecting female business leaders. The two projects are so alike that many confused the First Lady’s Imperia with the 11-year-old company, per the Times:

The day of the launch, Jennifer Forbes Iannolo, who started her own company, Imperia Global, in 2015, was startled by an unexpected flood of text messages and social media follows from people confusing her firm with the first lady’s forum. She said she had founded Imperia Global to contract with other companies to forge connections between female business leaders and innovators. “People were checking in to ask if I’d sold my company,” she said in an interview.
But Imperia Global isn’t operating in the U.S. anymore. It left the United States last year in response to Trump’s DEI crackdown:
After the re-election of Mr. Trump, the work ground to a halt as the administration focused on quashing D.E.I., [Forbes Iannolo] said.
She paused Imperia’s activities and moved to Scotland. Imperia Global is now registered in Britain, although it is not currently holding events.

Should the First Lady have known that she was launching a project with the same name and mission as an existing company driven out of the U.S. for its alleged wokeness? Probably. The website for Forbes Iannolo’s company is the first thing that pops up when you Google “Imperia.” Plus Ivanka Trump promoted Imperia Global’s work when she was girlbossing her way through her father’s first term, as the Times noted:

The Trump administration, however, did have reason to be aware of Imperia Global and its work. During Mr. Trump’s first term, the State Department invited Ms. Forbes Iannolo to speak on behalf of Imperia Global at events in Greece and Finland. They were part of a directive from Ivanka Trump, the president’s daughter who was then his adviser, to promote global female entrepreneurs.

Embarrassing! It remains unclear how the First Lady’s Imperia is funded and structured, or even what companies are committing to when they sign on to the initiative. So it shouldn’t be too hard for her to wind down the project and focus her energy on something a little more original. Hey, maybe Melania could channel her expertise in luxury properties and disappearing from public view into creating an island retreat for rich people. It’s hard to see how that could go wrong!

items.title: The Downfall of Jensen Huang and What’s Next for Nvidia
items.description: Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had a
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate.

On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO. Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day. According to The Information, Huang told colleagues in the past several years that he would run Nvidia until he is 120 years old. Which is all well and good if you’re planning to both (a) live that long and (b) not have an affair with an accused Chinese spy. Otherwise it’s pretty risky!

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump. On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month. In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

On Thursday morning, Trump — who spent the prior days telling reporters how wonderful Huang is — recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. Trump has gushed in the past about “Tim Apple,” who visited the White House last year bearing gifts. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote.
If you’re just catching up to the sex-spy-AI scandal, here’s everything that’s happened so far.
October 29: The Times reports Huang had a “close relationship” with a suspected spy

In a bombshell story, the New York Times reports that after concluding that Alice Huang (no relation), the chief executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, was a “Chinese intelligence asset,” U.S. intelligence officials made an even more startling discovery: that Huang “had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang.” The Times story also reveals that Donald Trump had been “briefed about the intelligence findings” a year ago and “chose not to do anything with the information.” In fairness, the president may have been preoccupied with ballroom renovations; at the time, he was fighting with his architect.
Later on October 29: Huang says there’s nothing to see here

In an interview with Bloomberg, the CEO insists his interactions with Ms. Huang were strictly professional. “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang says. He will regret this statement!
November 5: Republicans ask Huang to sit for closed-door interview

GOP representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford — who lead the House’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the Select Committee on Intelligence, respectively — send a letter to Huang telling him they want a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Ms. Huang. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” they write. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”
November 7: The likely new head of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee demands answers

Democratic senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee come January, writes on X: “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers.”
November 8: Huang admits to the affair, says company is opening an investigation

In a letter to Nvidia employees, Huang — who denied the affair less than two weeks prior — writes: “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He continues: “Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.” In a statement, Nvidia’s board says it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
Later on November 8: Trump defends Huang like a brother, repeatedly declares how awesome the guy is

Speaking to reporters the day Huang admitted to the affair, Trump says he would “certainly take” the CEO on an upcoming trip to China and that Huang “dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” (As a reminder, the president himself is an expert on affairs.) The president of the United States continues: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it … He’s done an amazing job for our country. You know, we have the hottest country anywhere in the world. We have the highest stock market.”
Also on November 8: The Times reports Marco Rubio circulated a big, flashing warning about Huang to administration officials

The Times runs a story reporting that last year, the secretary of State “oversaw the drafting” of a “highly classified memo” that warned top officials in the Trump administration that Huang “was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.” The memo was reportedly sent to officials prior to a trip the president took to China in May; according to the Times, it’s unclear if the warning played a role in Huang initially not being invited to join Trump. (After Trump saw coverage about Huang not being included on the delegation, he wrote on social media that he was honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” and other business executives “journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’ China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.” (Huang was picked up by Air Force One during a stop in Alaska.)
November 9: Trump tells reporters Huang is “suffering,” says he heard about the affair “not too long ago”
In fact, he was told about it a year ago and chose not to do anything.
Also on November 9: Report reveals that Commerce Department’s Nvidia investigation was abruptly halted

The Times reports that a “monthslong investigation” into Megaspeed, and whether it was “smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China,” was suddenly paused “after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.” Agents were reportedly alarmed when Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top Commerce official who reports directly to Secretary Howard Lutnick “had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case.”
November 10: Nvidia retains Wachtell to investigate

The board of directors announces it has hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation into Huang’s affair and whether company secrets were divulged or national security was breached. The probe will be run by Joon Kim, the former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District who was appointed in 2021 to investigate allegations of sexual harassment against then-governor Andrew Cuomo.
November 11: Oops, Huang had another affair

As it turns out, the Nvidia CEO wasn’t just having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, he was also cheating on his wife with a subordinate named Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times. And apparently he’d been hoping to keep that affair on the down low. Per the Times:

In March, Ms. Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology. Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr. Huang.

During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel. One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said.
Mr. Huang’s security workers witnessed the bystander with the phone and sequestered the person, the people said. The workers then asked the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement.
When asked by a reporter about the relationship by phone, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” and hung up.
Later on November 11: Nvidia’s board meets to discuss Huang, whose job security doesn’t appear super-solid
The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia’s board of directors “is preparing to oust” Huang. Of note, there is no successor in place.
November 12: Nvidia’s board announces Huang has resigned

After meeting for hours on Wednesday, Nvidia announces early Thursday morning that Huang has resigned, despite reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role.” Chief finance officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO with the search for a permanent replacement starting immediately. The board also says it has appointed its first-ever chairman, Harvey Jones, the former CEO of Synopsys.

items.title: The Black ‘Firsts’ Trap
items.description: On November 6, Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stood on the steps of the state capitol to announce her transition team. She listed a who’s who of Atlanta political and business leaders, and then one name that caused a collective double take. “Tyler
items.author: Zak Cheney-Rice
paragraphs: On November 6, Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stood on the steps of the state capitol to announce her transition team. She listed a who’s who of Atlanta political and business leaders, and then one name that caused a collective double take. “Tyler Perry,” Bottoms said, “an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community.” Perry is indeed a wealthy and charitable Atlantan, but as the force behind some of the most slapdash popular media of our time, his appointment to the transition team came off as unserious. “Why does that shit say ‘Tyler Perry,’” read a typical response to the list.

Few are likely to remember how silly this choice seems once Bottoms settles into office. But it allowed many people to use a kind of eye-rolling humor to convey a deeper skepticism. One of many ways the 2026 midterms were historic — beyond the sheer scale of their rebuke of President Trump — was the election of not just one but two Black governors in former Jim Crow strongholds. (A total of four were elected nationwide; Wes Moore was reelected in Maryland.) Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, will be the first Black or woman governor of Georgia and the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. In neighboring Florida, voters chose Byron Donalds, a Republican congressman from Cape Coral, as their first Black governor ever.

Each victory represented, on the most basic level, a rebuke of the racial caste system that has long dominated the region. But rather than uncritical jubilation of the kind that largely greeted then-President-elect Obama, the elections of Bottoms and Donalds have as often been met with wariness, scrutiny, and even dismay, most notably from Black voters. “A lot of these people Keisha Bottoms is hiring played a huge role in the gentrification, displacement, and funding a militarized police training facility in Black communities in Atlanta,” wrote one skeptic on X. “When them white folks in Florida said, ‘Slavery was a joyful time for us,’ Byron Donalds didn’t say a fucking word,” wrote another.

Some of this is likely because the instinct to glorify pathbreaking “firsts” in their own right — what some critics would call trafficking in “identity politics” — has greatly diminished. On MS NOW, a network known for applauding Democratic victories in such terms, panelists were quick to emphasize policy. “She didn’t run on making history; she ran on the issues,” Symone Sanders-Townsend said of Bottoms. “It is no small thing that Keisha Lance Bottoms will be governor of Georgia during the next presidential election … who will make sure the election is certified.” The fact that this was the main response on the network you’d expect to be the most unreservedly celebratory of a Black political “first” was a reminder that we are no longer in 2008 or even 2016. Acknowledgments of such history being made have become perfunctory, a departure that partly reflects a growing consensus — even among many liberals — that crowing about glass ceilings is not a winning electoral strategy. But it also signals a shift toward a truer marker of equality than Black people simply winning higher office: our freedom, as the governed, to regard Black “firsts” as we would any other disappointing politician.

The least-impressed reactions were reserved for Donalds, a MAGA Republican who — once the racial breakdown of the votes is made public — will almost certainly have lost Black Florida voters in a landslide. A St. Pete Polls survey from a week before the midterms showed just 18 percent of Black voters supported him, compared to 76 percent for his white Democratic opponent, David Jolly. Sanders-Townsend, who on MS NOW was openly pleased by Bottoms’s election, derided Donalds in the same segment as “skinfolk” but not “kinfolk.”

When I visited Florida in October, I went to a church service in Hollywood attended by Jolly, who, despite being white, clearly had the backing of the all-Black congregation. “Just because they’re your color don’t mean they’re your kind,” said one of Jolly’s surrogates, State Senator Shevrin Jones, to much applause. Angie Nixon, Florida’s Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, described Donalds to me as a “chameleon” — a craven opportunist who’d align himself with any faction to come out on top, even the anti-Black right. When Gainesville’s Black Democratic county commissioner, Cynthia Chestnut, broke with her party and most of her fellow Black Floridians and endorsed Donalds in September, her invocation of history reeked of defensive self-justification. “I want to see a Black governor of Florida in my lifetime,” she wrote on Facebook, “and I will not apologize for saying so.” Her reasoning rang especially hollow for backing a candidate who had remarked upon Trump’s 2025 inauguration, “Daddy’s back.”

Bottoms, in contrast, won the overwhelming majority of Black votes in her election. But it was not without some reservations. “I’m going to vote for Keisha,” C.J. Stewart, a youth-center leader, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution shortly before the election. “The truth of the matter is, I don’t know if she cares about what I care about.” Bottoms’s tenure as mayor of Atlanta — one of the birthplaces of the civil-rights movement — earned her a reputation as an unreliable steward of that legacy. When I profiled her in 2022, she was roughly 18 months removed from overseeing a brutal police crackdown on protesters. One Black civil-rights lawyer described her administration to me as part of “a political push to paint all of the protests as violent,” which became a core justification for Cop City, a police training facility that Bottoms urged into construction with deadly results: Amid a surge of law-enforcement efforts to clear the future construction site of protesters after Bottoms left office, police shot and killed an activist. When Bottoms was not facilitating their suppression, she was often blithely dismissive of dissenters. “That really wasn’t a Black protest,” Bottoms told me, untruthfully, of the 2020 George Floyd uprising. (The crowds were notably multiracial and largely Black.)

Critics to her left have long taken Bottoms to task for her alignment with the police. But those objections have been paired, since the midterms, with a chorus of confused grumblings about her odd political judgment. Besides naming Tyler Perry to her transition team, Bottoms attended, and was honored at, the Atlanta stop of the R&B Tour, one of whose two headliners was the recurrent assaulter of women Chris Brown.

For many years, the presence of Black Southerners in higher office was understood as a meaningful bellwether for Black equality. Writing in 1962, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. lamented how President Kennedy had devised a ten-year plan to put a man on the moon but none to “put a Negro in the State Legislature in Alabama.” Part of the logic was that Black officials were seen as a proxy for how far Black people had come toward attaining full citizenship. If Black Americans were allowed to vote in healthy numbers, a natural result, many thought, would be an influx of justice-minded Black elected leaders. Yet here we are 64 years later — with Black elected officials fairly commonplace and stark inequality very much persistent — and the presence of such Black leaders is still taken as synonymous with an inherently pro-Black politics that, while it may have been at least somewhat true decades ago, no longer is the case.

There’s something straightforwardly depressing about this state of affairs. It would indeed be a boon to American society if every Black elected leader was a staunch advocate for policies that uplifted everyday Black people. But it’s also a sign of improved civic health that more Americans seem able to look at Black officials in justifiably skeptical ways without assuming that their Blackness confers a preordained set of egalitarian politics. This is not equality at its fullest, to be sure — Black people vying for, or serving in, higher office will no doubt continue to be judged in purely racist terms. (As Obama, Bottoms, and Donalds all have been.) But it’s a version of equality that the U.S. needs much more of. If the past decade has taught us anything, it’s that we should be a lot more skeptical of our elected leaders. They should have to prove themselves to us, without the benefit of the doubt, even if they are Black and making history.

items.title: Why Didn’t Democrats Help Scott Colom?
items.description: The Associated Press and others have made it official: Democrat Scott Colom is going to become the next U.S. senator from Mississippi, and the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. The prediction markets had already been certain Colom won, b
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The Associated Press and others have made it official: Democrat Scott Colom is going to become the next U.S. senator from Mississippi, and the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. The prediction markets had already been certain Colom won, but it took a week for his victory to be called while some absentee ballots and provisional votes were still outstanding. Now there should be hard questions about why national Democrats did not see this result coming and didn’t do more than the very little they did to help Colom upset the evidently weak Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Yes, several leading Black politicians, plus Rhode Island senator Sheldon Whitehouse, offered Colom some hands-on assistance, which drew some needed national attention. And, yes, during the final two weeks of the campaign, the national Senate Democratic PAC bought some ads and threw some money Colom’s way. But compared to what the party was committing to other Senate races, it was sofa-cushion money. Early on, Democrats targeted national spending on races their candidates eventually won easily, like Georgia and North Carolina, and later, they focused on late-breaking opportunities like Kansas and even South Carolina while spending to shore up Democratic-leaning races in Maine and Michigan. They spent heavily on Ohio and Texas nonstop. A little more in Mississippi might have eliminated any doubt about one of the most remarkable political upsets in living memory. And even a little more effort in Louisiana, where Jamie Davis came within 25,000 votes of upsetting Republican incumbent Julia Letlow, could have produced an equally shocking result. And Florida Democrats believe more national help could have lifted Senate candidate Angie Nixon and gubernatorial candidate David Jolly to victory in races that wound up being very close.

So what was the problem? Colom understandably doesn’t want to blame Chuck Schumer and his likely future colleagues in the Senate Democratic Conference. But he’s clearly annoyed with the Beltway conventional wisdom and the institutions that help define it:

In defense of the Cook analysts, they typically base their ratings on polls, electoral history, and interviews with candidates, party leaders, and journalists on the ground in the places where the races are underway. So there may be some shooting-the-messenger in Colom’s complaints about Cook, which did move his race from “Solid R” to “Likely R” (a category where upsets are considered possible). But he’s right that Cook and most of the other experts, along with the national Democratic Party, underestimated the strength of their southern wing.

Perhaps there was an unconscious racial element in this myopia, since Colom, Davis, and Nixon were all Black candidates in red states that have not elected Black statewide candidates in living memory. But it seems to be more of a regional issue. White southern Democrats like the gubernatorial candidates in Alabama (Doug Jones), Florida (Jolly), and Tennessee (Jerri Green) were also written off and came very close to huge upsets. Meanwhile, the Beltway Establishment did not underrate Georgia’s Black Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms (whose race was rated a toss-up by Cook), despite her terrible fundraising disadvantage against billionaire Rick Jackson, for the simple reason that abundant polling showed her in a close race all along. So one very clear lesson of 2026 is that the national parties should do a lot more polling of states on the periphery of their vision, particularly in a “wave” election year. Even if the polling itself underestimated Democratic voting strength, as it did nationally by about 4 percent, it would have shown that a combination of strong Black turnout and swing-voter unhappiness with Donald Trump put much of the South within reach.

Perhaps the most difficult problem is that party strategists, like military strategists, have a strong tendency to fight the last war, basing their calculations on what happened in the last election. There is in fact no more reliable indicator of electoral outcomes in any given place than how that place has voted in the recent past. But there was abundant evidence throughout the 2026 cycle that the GOP’s 2024 coalition was falling apart. National Democrats (and the “prognosticators” they inform) should have been more open to the fresh opportunities Trump’s intense unpopularity presented for them. And strong “under-the-radar” candidates like Scott Colom should not have been forced to beg for attention and win an unequal fight on his own.
This post has been updated following Colom’s victory.

items.title: The Mystery of the 11 Vote-Missing House Democrats
items.description: Did Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth escape impeachment yesterday, or was he allowed to escape? The House voted 211 to 204 to send Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment to committee — all along party lines except for Massie’s crossover vote — effectively mothb
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: Did Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth escape impeachment yesterday, or was he allowed to escape? The House voted 211 to 204 to send Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment to committee — all along party lines except for Massie’s crossover vote — effectively mothballing the effort to remove Hegseth, at least until Democrats take control of Congress in a few months. But House Democrats might not have needed to wait that long. Seven Republicans weren’t there for the vote, which meant Democrats only needed seven more votes to defeat the maneuver. However, 11 Democrats were absent, and a number of their colleagues are pretty pissed about it. These are those lawmakers’ stories, broken down by category of excuse.
Sorry, I was stuck in traffic, but totally would have voted ‘No’ ( 3 )

The congresswoman said in a tweet: “I was stuck behind the same police escort blocking the Capitol when Republicans closed the vote. I would have voted no and believe strongly that Pete Hegseth should be impeached.”

Her team posted a statement to social media on Tuesday night saying she “was blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote. When she reached the chamber the vote had just gaveled out.”
Per the Washington Sun, her spokesperson said, “the Congresswoman was stuck behind a motorcade and missed the vote by 1 minute,” but “would have voted against the motion to refer.”

These excuses aren’t holding up very well a day later. Axios’s Andrew Solender reported Tuesday night that some of the missing members were caught in traffic on their way back from an Elect Democratic Women event a mile-and-a-half away. But, he adds, some other members did make it back in time:

Some members found other ways to get back to the Capitol because their cars were effectively stopped on the road. One got out and walked. Another got dropped off on the Senate side to avoid the traffic.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Democratic whip Katherine Clark, a founding member of Elect Democratic Women, left the event early after she heard about the traffic so she’d make it back in time for the vote.
I would have voted ‘No’ if I hadn’t been busy shooting a video right outside ( 1 )

Jackson said on X Tuesday night that “While en route to the floor to oppose that motion, a traffic incident and a police-escorted bus caused a delay that resulted in the vote closing before I, along with other Members, could reach the chamber.”

You’ll notice that this is actually a weirdly passive statement in which he doesn’t explicitly say that he, too, was stuck in traffic. Well, that’s because he wasn’t. TMZ DC’s Charlie Cotton later reported that Jackson missed the vote because he was busy recording a social media video about the Hegseth impeachment on the steps of the Capitol:
Cotton says Jackson got back to him and called the missed vote a “mistake.”
The Republicans ate my ‘No’ vote ( 2 )

It’s possible both of these lawmakers were also at the Elect Democratic Women event, as they both apparently tried and failed to make it to the floor in time. They mostly just blamed the GOP, however.

Brownley released a statement on Facebook in which she called Hegseth “one of the most incompetent, corrupt, and underqualified Secretaries of Defense in the history of our nation” — but “as I and many of my colleagues were rushing to the floor to support Hegseth’s impeachment, Mike Johnson closed the vote before we could.” She called it “a spineless political tactic” and vowed to continue to fight to get rid of the defense secretary.
