Pettersen put out a statement on X that though she “helped introduce articles of impeachment to remove the deeply unqualified and dangerous Pete Hegseth since April,” she was “denied the ability to vote on this motion while Mike Johnson worked overtime to shield him from accountability.”
Her office said she was at an as-of-yet undisclosed event and got stuck in traffic too.

It’s not fully clear what she means by “denied,” but an unnamed senior Democratic aide who spoke with the Washington Sun “disputed that the votes of members blocked by traffic from returning to the Capitol would have changed the outcome, arguing that Republicans had only two members unavailable and closed the vote even though they knew more members were en route.” (The House GOP pulled a fast one, so blame them, in other words.)
I would have voted ‘No’ but had to receive an award in San Francisco ( 1 )

The former Speaker of the House, who’s now serving her final months in office, bailed from D.C. for a Veteran’s Day celebration back home where she was being honored with an award. A spokesperson told the Washington Sun that though Pelosi “supports impeaching Secretary Hegseth and would have voted ‘No’ on the motion to refer,” she nonetheless “returned to San Francisco to join and honor local veterans at Swords to Plowshares’ 30th Annual Veterans Day Celebration tonight, an important and longstanding district tradition she regularly attends and will mark for the last time as a Member of Congress by receiving the Lifetime Advocate for Veterans Award.”
Wait, am I even a Democrat anymore? ( 1 )

After endorsing Republican Mike Rogers against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race and complaining the Democratic Party had left her out to pasture, Stevens’s political future and affiliation are not at all clear. The endorsement prompted her Congressional staff to quit, and on Monday her office at the Capitol remained closed and and she was at one point spotted hiding out in the GOP cloakroom. The lame-duck congresswoman still hasn’t said anything about the vote, so why she missed it and how she might have voted aren’t clear, either.
Nobody knows why I wasn’t there ( 1 )

The departing 83-year-old congresswoman has missed dozens of votes this year and in May announced she was suspending her reelection campaign and leaving Congress at the end of the term. She was, however, at a ground-breaking for a housing project for veterans in her South Florida district Monday.
The ‘Okay, What Can You Do?’ Duo
I would have voted ‘No’ but had a personal emergency ( 1 )
Horsford says he missed the vote due to a “personal emergency” for which he did not offer any details, but that he would have voted “No.”
“I take full responsibility,” he said Wednesday. “The accountability I demand of others applies to me, too.”
I have a doctor’s note ( 1 )

The California congressman told the Washington Sun that he is preparing for a medical procedure and that his doctor told him to avoid travel in the meantime. It’s not clear how he would have voted had he been there.
This post has been updated. It originally misstated the state Brittany Pettersen represents.

items.title: Sophie Monaghan-Coombs - Monocle
items.description: The filmmaker discusses his directorial style and his casting of Sandra Hüller in a drama that follows the Nobel laureate and his daughter on a journey through war-ravaged Germany.
paragraphs: The filmmaker discusses his directorial style and his casting of Sandra Hüller in a drama that follows the Nobel laureate and his daughter on a journey through war-ravaged Germany.
The opening of Frieze London is casting the world’s art market in a positive light – and catching the eye of eager buyers.
Forget the usual business books. If you really want to get ahead, take some advice from Cruella de Vil, Tom Ripley and other entrepreneurial characters from the world of fiction.
Part workspace, part residence, the communal facility by Jan Garde and Henning Weiss is bringing people in all stages of life together in style.
This month’s highlights include an irreverent novel about contemporary art, an exhibition of one of today’s most exciting fashion photographers and a Tom Cruise disaster movie.
To help you pick the right books for your summer reading list, we asked an array of cultural figures to share the titles old and new that have inspired them.
The preview week of the world’s most prestigious exhibition of contemporary art was an unruly spectacle – charged by political dissent, moments of beauty and works shining brightly through the chaos.
In recent years the art world’s largest commercial fair has painted itself into a corner. But satellite shows and new initiatives at this year’s event are helping to offer fresh perspectives.
The world’s biggest space dedicated to illustration has opened in London. Can it help to protect the art amid rising threats from AI?
There’s more to collecting than following markets and speculating on value appreciation. We meet the people at the heart of the action, from a veteran auctioneer to a design-fair director.

items.title: Madonna Really Does Love New York
items.description: There I was minding my business (by not minding my business) when I get the email of a lifetime: "What are you up to Thursday night? Wanna spend it with Madonna?"
items.author: Paper Magazine
paragraphs: There I was minding my business (by not minding my business) when I get the email of a lifetime: "What are you up to Thursday night? Wanna spend it with Madonna?"

You know me by now... and if you’re pretending you don’t: I’m Linux, New York’s premiere downtown it-girl. I spend my nights either attending or throwing Scene City’s hottest parties. This week in particular is madness, being New York Pride. It's the Thursday of NYC’s Gay Marathon and, "What are you up to Thursday night?", was a question I'm more than prepared to answer.
At the end of the day, I’m a human being on planet Earth. And around these parts, when Madonna calls... you answer!

So I did just that (after waiting about 30 minutes to respond, of course... I didn’t want to come off too desperate). They told me to meet at the Moxy in Chelsea at 10 PM. A bus would be there waiting to take me and a hundred drag queens to a very proud and very gay night with Madonna at Terminal 5.

My Uber pulled up to the trendy hotel to a Jean Paul Gaultier-emblazoned double decker bus already boarding the world’s hottest gaylebrities: Symone, GiGi Goode, Shea Coulee, Aquaria, Gottmik, Detox and Kylie Sonique Love all posed for photos as the Gaultier team smoked cigarettes on the sidewalk. The bus driver honked his horn and we all screamed, knowing that noise meant it was time to leave towards Hells Kitchen to party with Madonna.

A DJ on the bus blasted Madonna's deep cuts as we drove through Times Square — a moment when all of us asked ourselves, "Is this real life?" Once we pulled up to Terminal 5, the marquee with Madonna’s name in flashing lights made it all too real that we were really about to see the Queen MDNA herself. So, what was this Madonna event all for anyways?

Madonna, who has been a leader in the NFT space, partnered for another time with WoW (World of Women), a thriving community celebrating representation, inclusivity and equal opportunities. The entire event was sponsored by The Sandbox, who has partnered with WoW to create the WoW Foundation, which will invest $25 million over five years in education and mentorship through programs across the metaverse.

Finally Enough Love, Madonna's 16-track career-spanning remix compilation album, was also released on streaming at midnight. To put it in simpler terms: Madonna was doing God’s work for the LGBTQ+ and wrapped it all up into a sickening Pride party.

As I entered the venue, I was immediately welcomed by teams of artists from MAC Viva Glam, who were offering guests Madonna-inspired touch ups (MAC Viva Glam has raised more than a half billion dollars to end HIV/AIDS). My makeup was already flawless, so I didn’t need anything done, but it's always nice to kiki with a MAC girlie.

I scammed my VIP bracelet from Geordon Nicol of the Misshapes, who was helping produce the night, and ran upstairs to Terminal 5’s VIP rooftop. I needed a cocktail and, luckily, Belvedere was offering free vodka, keeping the kids all liquored up. Next to the bar sat boxes and boxes of pizza from Made in NY (so Italian). But we’re not here for Pizza, we’re here for Madonna! So I ran back downstairs to get a good spot for the show.

Bob the Drag Queen served as MC. The icon Laganja Estranja performed "Vogue," where she was joined by Jose Xtravaganza, one of Madonna's dancers on the Blond Ambition tour. After that, we were all blindsided by Saucy Santana appearing on stage to perform "Walk," before "Material Girl" started playing and Madonna came out to perform it with him. Girl, when I tell you the crowd went wild! Herstory in the making. Madonna then premiered a "Hung Up" remix with Tokischa, which ended with the two of them making out on stage... it was really hot.
Joined by all of the performers, Madonna ended the night with a show-stopping performance of "Celebration" while rainbow confetti flooded the venue.

It was the best way to celebrate Pride imaginable. There was only one problem: I didn’t want it to end! Luckily, Madonna didn’t want it to either. For those with VIP bracelets, the party continued on the third floor of Terminal 5, where all the Ru Girls, it-kids and fashion peeps partied until the early morning.
Photography: Ricardo Gomes

items.title: Sting Is Officially a Latin Grammy Winner
items.description: Sting has officially won his first Latin Grammy award. The rocker nabbed the award for Best Pop/Rock song for his feature on Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso’s song, “Hasta Jesús Tuvo Un Mal Día” from their latest album Free Spirits.
items.author: Maya Georgi
paragraphs: Sting has officially won his first Latin Grammy award. The rocker nabbed the award for Best Pop/Rock song for his feature on Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso’s song, “Hasta Jesús Tuvo Un Mal Día” from their latest album Free Spirits.

The former Police frontman was not at the awards ceremony to accept the award. Instead, Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso collected the Latin Grammy and made sure to thank him. “Sting was instrumental in helping us through this whole process,” Amoroso said of recording Free Spirits. “He gave us his warmth, his space. We have Sting to thank for this glory. We love him with all of our heart.”

It could be the first of many Latin Grammys for Sting tonight. “Hasta Jesús Tuvo Un Mal Día” is up for Song of the Year, and Free Spirits is also up for Album of the Year and Best Alternative Music Album.

Sting apparently played a pivotal role in the chaotic duo’s journey and the creation of Free Spirits, which acts as a reset of sorts. In detailed album promotion material for the album, Sting took to Instagram to explain how he “helped” Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso grapple with their newfound fame during a wellness retreat at a “secretive” holistic Free Spirits Center. While there, the duo underwent a “transcendent 12-step program” that helped formulate Free Spirits, an album “which confronts the twelve internal conflicts that pushed them to their breaking point,” according to a press release. If that sounds a bit ridiculous and over-the-top, it’s by design. Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso are Latin pop’s designated mischief makers, who are fully committed to the bit.

items.title: Pink Floyd's Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage
items.description: Roger Waters has filed for divorce from Kamilah Chavis after five years of marriage.
items.author: Charisma Madarang
paragraphs: Roger Waters has filed for divorce from Kamilah Chavis after five years of marriage.

The former Pink Floyd bassist filed the papers in New York Supreme Court on Tuesday, according to USA Today. The case is listed as “contested,” meaning one or more terms of the divorce remains unresolved. Additional details of the filing are not public.

Waters announced his marriage to Chavis in October 2021, posting images on Facebook including the two cutting a cake in a kitchen and standing on a bridge with their dog Sweet Georgia Brown. “I’m so happy, finally a keeper,” Waters captioned the post. In other captions alongside solo photos, he wrote, “a very happy man” and “a very beautiful bride.”

The divorce marks Waters’ fifth following his split from actress and director Laurie Durning in 2015 following three years of marriage. The British musician was previously married to Judith Trim from 1968 to 1975. He then married Carolyne Christie, with whom he shares son Harry and daughter India, in 1976 before divorcing in 1992. A year later, he tied the knot with Priscilla Phillips and welcomed son Jack before they went their separate ways in 2001.

Waters first met Chavis at one of his concerts, who was working in transportation at the time and drove the car that shuttled him between his hotel the show. In a 2018 interview with the Argentinian outlet Infobae, he said, “My bodyguard would sit in the front with her, and they’d talk, while I stayed in the back. I don’t know, something about her attracted me.” He added, “One day I said to her, ‘Excuse me,’ and she turned around. ‘Has anyone ever told you that you have beautiful cheekbones?’ I asked. I saw a small reaction, and that was the beginning.”

items.title: TV’s Biggest Salaries: Zendaya, Nicolas Cage, Selena Gomez and More Stars Earning Huge Paychecks
items.description: Peak TV may be over, but peak TV salaries haven’t gone away. The streaming revolution changed the game when it came to recruiting A-listers to appear in topline series on the small screen, and the biggest stars are still nabbing impressive paychecks.
items.author: Michael Schneider
paragraphs: Peak TV may be over, but peak TV salaries haven’t gone away. The streaming revolution changed the game when it came to recruiting A-listers to appear in topline series on the small screen, and the biggest stars are still nabbing impressive paychecks.

The downturn in original series production has tightened up the marketplace overall. But with the right project arriving at the right moment, marquee names are still making bank in TV. The film business, on the other hand, has been in a state of limbo for most of this year as the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger has unfolded. The recent shake-up of Netflix’s content leadership has also put a crimp in dealmaking, at least temporarily, even as the film sector celebrates the buoyancy of the box office this year.

Some of the eye-popping salaries for TV series have been well documented, including the packages that brought Jennifer Aniston and Reese Witherspoon to Apple TV’s “The Morning Show” at around $2 million an episode. More recent TV recruits include Sylvester Stallone, who’s believed to be clearing about $2 million an episode for his work on Paramount+’s Taylor Sheridan-produced drama “Tulsa King.”

Others who have negotiated a pretty payday are “Only Murders in the Building” stars Selena Gomez, Steve Martin and Martin Short, who are easily clearing more than $1 million an episode as the series enters Season 6. And popular faces who can immediately attract a fan base are also fetching top coin: Jennifer Garner, for example, crossed the $1 million threshold for Peacock’s “The Five-Star Weekend.”
“The need for stars that can anchor these television shows is bigger than it’s ever been,” says one talent agent. “It used to be unheard of that someone would get $2 million an episode.”

Stars who have perhaps aged out of marquee film roles have particularly benefited from the new marketplace. They’ve found a lucrative home in streaming, where their draw remains valuable. And as opposed to the 22-episode TV season required in the broadcast network days, they’re attracted to the less taxing commitment that comes with a 6-, 8- or 10-episode order.
“Every star now is looking at how to anchor a series,” says an insider. “If you’re No. 1 or No. 2 on the call sheet, it’s really never been better financially.”
Even as the conventional wisdom remains that Hollywood is struggling and the job market is challenged, agents in the TV talent field are perhaps the most optimistic folks in the industry right now.

“The TV actor salary game is still a really good business,” says one agent. “There’s still a lot of money to be made as an actor on television. Certainly for the starriest names, those people are still getting toward the upper limit of anything that anyone’s ever made on television.”

Says another rep: “It definitely feels like the opportunities are there. I mean, it’s not 2016 to 2019, when everyone was just blasting a fire hose of cash into the community, which was totally unsustainable. Comparing anything to that time, when the streamers were out there spending like drunken sailors, is not a fair comp.”

Of course, this is mostly the top stars on the call sheets, as the boom times aren’t for everyone. It’s still tougher than it used to be for the middle class of actors — the ones who made a nice living by bouncing from pilot to pilot or show to show in the broadcast age. Back then, even if you didn’t wind up on a hit show, you could still do OK.

Those days are gone — but so are the rigid exclusivity clauses that used to prevent actors from working on more than one TV series at a time. Because episodic orders are shorter now, limiting ultimate take-home pay, the networks and studios are more willing to let stars moonlight. (That’s especially true of those getting top billing: Just ask the ubiquitous Nicole Kidman.)

Eight years ago, when California banned the use of the “actor’s quote” — the rate an actor was paid for a previous role, which was used as that performer’s salary baseline in negotiations — more pay parity was brought to the business. “It’s leveled the playing field quite a bit,” an agent says. “Now the pay depends on the role.” Women and minorities, especially, who traditionally got paid less, can now demand more.

Among the major outlets, Apple is seen as the most competitive with salaries, with HBO and Amazon in the mix too. Even Peacock has shown a willingness to pay upward of $1 million an episode for talent like Garner. Paramount+, meanwhile, has attracted some top-tier talent (particularly on Sheridan and 101 Studios shows) by offering $1 million-plus an episode to some of its leads. Disney is seen as more spendthrift; FX, in particular, isn’t chasing as many high-salary stars as it focuses more on the power of the material with series like “Shōgun.”

If there’s any recent surprise, it’s how well the traditional broadcast networks are doing with their original scripted fare — and that’s attracting some major TV stars returning to the small screen, including Blair Underwood, Felicity Huffman, Peter Krause and Hope Davis. And those leads are getting paid as much as $250,000 to $350,000 an episode at the start, and more in success.

“It’s completely competitive with the top end of a hit show,” says one agent. “Obviously, in streaming, they’re going to pay you a hell of a lot more because they’re only doing eight episodes. But you can definitely still get paid in broadcast. It’s just without the obvious syndication windfalls that used to come with having those backend points.”

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns After Multiple Affairs, Including With Alleged Chinese Spy
items.description: Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned, the company’s board of directors said Thursday, ending a weekslong saga that revealed the executive engaged in several affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy — and drove the company’s stock pric
items.author: Corbin Bolies
paragraphs: Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned, the company’s board of directors said Thursday, ending a weekslong saga that revealed the executive engaged in several affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy — and drove the company’s stock price to eight-month lows over national security concerns.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement. She will remain the company’s CFO during the search, which will include internal and external candidates.
The board of directors also named tech executive Harvey C. Jones, a former CEO of the software company Synopsys and an Nvidia board member since 1993, its first chair of the board.

“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Jones said in a statement. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

Nvidia’s stock was down as much as 13% in premarket trading following the announcement; it closed regular trading Thursday down 4.3%, to $166.19/share, putting its market cap at about $4 trillion. The saga reflects how even the most human of all scandals — those involving sex and spycraft — can impact companies underpinning much of the AI boom capturing the world.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board of directors was weighing whether to oust Huang, who has led the company as CEO since he co-founded it in 1993. The decision came days after Nvidia’s board initially said it would launch an independent investigation into Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who the New York Times reported was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the executive and learn more about Nvidia’s AI chips. Nvidia hired former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim’s firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the investigation. The board at the time had said Jensen Huang would continue to lead the company, even as he also faced an FBI investigation over the affair with the alleged spy.

But the hits kept coming. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had a separate affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care who joined the company in 2008. Nvidia’s code of conduct prohibits employees from “situations where our actions might create a conflict — actual or potential—between our personal gain and our obligations” to the company. It also advises that “personal relationships” may pose a potential conflict.

The board said in its statement that Huang’s contributions to Nvidia were “profound.” “The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” it said.
Kress said she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”

“We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead,” she said in a statement. “Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

The stakes for what comes next for Nvidia — and the AI world — are massive. Huang co-founded Nvidia as a graphics chip provider for video games, though he later grew it into one of the world’s most valuable companies by producing chips that helped fuel many of the world’s leading AI companies.

Nvidia’s AI grip enveloped the entertainment industry. The company has invested in AI entertainment companies Higgsfield and Runway, and Huang posed with Higgsfield CTO Yerzat Dulat at an event in Kazakhstan last month. Nvidia on Wednesday also expanded its partnership with AI audio startup ElevenLabs, another company investment. The expanded partnership would see ElevenLabs try to make more voice agents available to governments worldwide — powered by Nvidia’s AI architecture.

Disney also announced a partnership with Nvidia and Google DeepMind last year to develop Newton, an open-source physics engine that lets robots learn how to handle complex tasks with greater precision. The robotics project, incorporating physical AI, included real-world robots of Star Wars characters like BDX droids and the “Frozen” snowman Olaf.

Nvidia’s entertainment entanglements also extend to the music industry. The company struck a deal with Universal Music Group in January to marry its AI technology with UMG’s catalog to develop “responsible AI for music discovery, creation, and engagement. The deal included enhancing Nvidia’s Music Flamingo AI audio model with UMG work and creating an artist incubator, an arrangement UMG CEO Lucian Grainge called “a shared mission to harness revolutionary AI technology to dramatically advance the interests of the creative community and the role of music in global culture.”

Nvidia’s heightened status made Huang one of President Donald Trump’s closest tech allies. Trump defended Huang in a news conference on Monday, saying he believed Huang’s assertions that he was unaware of Alice Huang’s affiliations, though the president confirmed the FBI was also investigating the relationship. The Commerce Department had also investigated Nvidia over whether it helped smuggle chips into China before it was moved to the Justice Department.
Trump offered his suggestion for who should replace Huang in a Truth Social post on Thursday: former Apple CEO Tim Cook, who handed the reins of the tech titan over to John Ternus in September.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

items.title: ‘Unlike Anything Else’: As ‘GTA 6’ Approaches, the Gaming Industry Braces the World for Its Pop Culture Takeover
items.description: There’s only so many times that gaming industry analysts can say “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be the biggest entertainment release of all time before the phrase seemingly loses all meaning to those who have never played a “GTA” game before.
items.author: Jennifer Maas
paragraphs: There’s only so many times that gaming industry analysts can say “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be the biggest entertainment release of all time before the phrase seemingly loses all meaning to those who have never played a “GTA” game before.

With just one week left until the Nov. 19 release of the most-anticipated video game release ever, everyone from the bystanders passing Vice City billboards and watching “SNL” sketches to Hollywood execs who’d seen Netflix’s “extended look” back in August knows the hottest topic right now is the Rockstar Games title. According to market research firm Newzoo, the game is currently estimated to bring in $3.25 billion to $5.2 billion in first week sales across PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S gaming consoles on a reported $1.5 billion budget.

“Even if you don’t play games, chances are you’ve heard it,” Netflix’s vice president of nonfiction series Brandon Riegg tells Variety. “Just like maybe you’ve heard of a famous athlete or you’ve heard a famous song. So I think they had that in their favor.”

But not everyone knows what it is about “GTA 6” that will take up pop culture’s collective attention (and money), and those who do are very likely already off in the massive echo chamber that has been waiting for the game for 13 years.

The simplest possible answer is that the “Grand Theft Auto” franchise created a new type of video game, the open-world genre, and that new kind of video game has steadily grown to become the most immersive form of entertainment we have today. In these games, you have almost limitless possibilities for how you interact with the virtual world, making the normally collective experience of consuming the same piece of narrative media a personalized one as well.

“Really, ‘GTA’ was the pioneer of the open-world game,” Game Awards creator, host and longtime gaming industry journalist Geoff Keighley tells Variety. “‘GTA 3,’ that’s really where Rockstar crossed over to do a 3D open-world game. So many games are so linear, where they are effectively scripts that you’re playing through and having a little bit of choice. But ‘GTA’ revolutionized the industry with a true open-world game that let you decide what journey you wanted to go on inside of this simulated environment. When ‘GTA 3’ came out, that was ahead of its time. And Rockstar has, with every game, the ambition has gotten bigger and bigger and bigger about what the density of the simulated world is. And that allows players to have a huge sense of agency to create the story that they want to create inside the world.”

Riegg, who collaborated with Rockstar Games studio director Jennifer Kolbe to launch the “GTA 6” extended trailer in what he says “wasn’t a monetary sort of deal,” says “the game itself is probably the closest thing to this full immersion in this video game world.”

“It’s ‘Ready Player One,’ maybe without the headset,” Riegg says. “There is a narrative to the game and objectives, but you can also just live in that world. You don’t have to do that stuff. I can have a relationship with somebody. I can text them. I can do crimes. It’s this immersive alternate universe that you can actually participate in in whatever way that you choose.”
Strauss Zelnick, the head of Rockstar Games parent company Take-Two Interactive, says he has “so many thoughts” about the game, but he’s at a loss for new words until it’s unveiled.

“It’s a nice question to ask,” Zelnick told Variety Monday when asked if there was anything specific that the Take-Two CEO feels he and the team at Rockstar haven’t said yet about “GTA 6” that they can say about the game before it’s out. “No, I mean I think our point of view has been well represented, and I think at this point, I put myself in the camp of cautiously optimistic.”

Zelnick, formerly the president of 20th Century Fox and head of BMG Entertainment, has done so many “GTA 6” preview interviews at this point that apart from recently defending Take-Two’s track record with hit franchises (“GTA,” “Red Dead Redemption,” “NBA 2K,” “Borderlands” and “Sid Meier’s Civilization”) in a conversation with the Wall Street Journal, not much has changed between Q&As.

“Everyone here is incredibly excited about the upcoming launch,” Zelnick says. “Pre-orders are running far in excess of our expectations, so that’s a good thing. That said, we never claim success before it occurs, so we’re just days away from beginning to see the fruits of our labor.”

“GTA 6” is a guaranteed hit (“Lord knows I need it,” Zelnick joked) so measuring the $80 game’s success is going to go well beyond analyzing financials and into hours played, time spent away from other forms of entertainment and the percentage of the workforce that takes the day off. And that last one is no joke.

“I honestly think hardly anyone in the gaming industry is going to be working that day,” says Christoph Hartmann, the former head of Take-Two Interactive’s 2K Games and currently the chief at Ubisoft’s Massive Entertainment.

“I actually downloaded it today, and I’m upset because the Wi-Fi went really slow in our house,” Hartmann told Variety Wednesday. “I think it was 212 GBs. And yes, I’m gonna take a day off, and then I have the challenge about my 14-year-old son insisting he can play as well, and I told him it’s mature, and I he said, ‘Yeah, but Dad, you worked on that game. Shouldn’t I know what it is?'”

“Grand Theft Auto 6” is the story of Jason and Lucia, a pair that “have always known the deck is stacked against them,” per Rockstar Games. “But when an easy score goes wrong, they find themselves on the darkest side of the sunniest place in America, in the middle of a criminal conspiracy stretching across the state of Leonida – forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive.”

Rockstar Games co-studio head Rob Nelson has said the game’s main narrative should take approximately 80 hours to play through. The title will have the largest open-world map in the franchise’s history and offer new ways for players to shape their gameplay, from deciding the level of romance between Jason and Lucia to what their physiques look like based on what they eat and how often they work out.

“‘GTA’ games have been unique in their ambition, and certainly this one. The scale of what they built over a decade is incredible,” Keighley says. “So I think that’s why players respond to these games, because there’s just so much possibility inside the world of how you play it. This is not a game that you play in 20 hours and finish. You continue to exist in this world and explore it. And obviously, ‘GTA Online,’ that’s been a big thing that continued to go on for a decade. So the ‘GTA’ experience is unlike anything else in gaming, much less entertainment. That’s what is so unique about the ‘GTA’ games, is that they really are peerless across all of entertainment because of the scale.”

Since its founding by brothers Dan Houser and Sam Houser in 1998, Rockstar Games has become the “largest American games publisher” and owns “the largest entertainment franchise” with “Grand Theft Auto 6,” according to SuperData CEO and NYU “Business of Video Games” professor Joost Van Dreunen.

On the massive success of “Red Dead Redemption 2” and “Grand Theft Auto 5,” “they’re not the underdog” anymore, Van Dreunen notes, meaning a big part of Rockstar’s counter-culture appeal has gone mainstream since its last hit released. “So can it maintain that character, and can it commercialize that?” Van Dreunen asks.

“GTA 6” will launch amid Rockstar Games workers’ continued efforts to unionize, now with public support from SAG-AFTRA. The timing isn’t a coincidence, with Rockstar employees aiming to call attention to their detailed work over the past 13 years while Take-Two Interactive is poised to make billions off their labor. The success of the game is likely to impact the gaming industry at large, as well as how the general public views the medium, which has long struggled to be taken as seriously as movies and TV despite the more than $200 billion in revenue games bring in each year.

“My hope is that they’ve taken the success of ‘GTA 5’ to manifest the creative vision that they had in their head this whole time, have really delivered on that,” Van Dreunen says. “And I think that will be its unique selling point, not the fact that it’s this sort of fringe form of entertainment and my mom tells me I’m not allowed to play this game. That was a big part of its selling point, its marketing. They used to guerrilla marketing. They would have stickers in Lower Manhattan and the East Village, these Rockstar stickers everywhere on lamp posts and on street furniture and all that stuff. They would take a very rebellious approach to marketing because it’s in line and on brand with the game.”

items.title: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Lists Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman Among 10 Writers
items.description: The chances that Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman could be back as Deadpool and Wolverine in “Avengers: Doomsday” may be getting higher.
items.author: Jordan Moreau
paragraphs: The chances that Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman could be back as Deadpool and Wolverine in “Avengers: Doomsday” may be getting higher.

Eagle-eyed Marvel fans combed through the Writer’s Guild of America’s directory and spotted the screenwriting credits for “Doomsday,” which lists Reynolds and Jackman among the 10 writers who contributed to the movie. Notably, Reynolds was one of the writers on “Deadpool 2” and “Deadpool & Wolverine,” while this marks Jackman’s first writing credit.

The main feature writing credits on “Doomsday” go to Marvel veteran Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron, creator of “Loki” and writer of “Doctor Strange Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.” The credits for additional literary materials (not on screen) go to McFeely, Waldron, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, Destin Daniel Cretton, Reynolds and Jackman.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” director Cretton had originally been tapped to helm the film when it was known as “The Kang Dynasty” with Loveness to write — but it was later reworked after Kang the Conqueror actor Jonathan Majors was fired by Disney. After Cretton had stepped down from the film, the Russo Bros. came on board with McFeely, McKenna, Sommers and Waldron to shift the focus to Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom as the main villain.
Variety has reached out to reps for Marvel, Reynolds and Jackman for comment. Reynolds also appeared to weigh in on the writing credits with a cryptic X post of a video from “Deadpool & Wolverine.”

The writing credits for Reynolds and Jackman certainly seem like they would be for writing dialogue for their “X-Men” characters, but it’s unclear if or how much they would appear in “Doomsday.” The website defines the additional literary material as “an official film credit introduced by the Writers Guild of America to recognize Guild-contracted writers who contributed writing services to a theatrical feature but did not qualify for a traditional primary writing credit.”

The WGA directory also has this caveat: “The information contained in the ‘Find a Writer’ database is the most current and accurate available to Writers Guild of America West (WGAW) and Writers Guild of America, East (WGAE). Some of the data is self-reported by writers and not independently verified by WGAW and WGAE. Users of the database accept the data as is, with no warranty of its accuracy stated or implied.”

items.title: Hollywood’s Next Big Deal: Will Netflix Make an M&A Play for NBCU?
items.description: David Ellison has knocked out Warner Bros. Discovery, merging it with Paramount into the new Skydance Corp. Now the chatter around town is about the industry’s next megamerger.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: David Ellison has knocked out Warner Bros. Discovery, merging it with Paramount into the new Skydance Corp. Now the chatter around town is about the industry’s next megamerger.

In the current landscape, only one media company of considerable size could be ripe for a takeover: NBCUniversal. Following its planned spinoff from Comcast in mid-2027, NBCU could fetch $60 billion from a motivated buyer, research firm Morningstar estimates. As for who that acquirer could be, industry sources uniformly point to Netflix as the leading candidate.

Netflix chief Ted Sarandos, after walking away from the streamer’s effort to acquire Warner Bros. and HBO, said his key takeaway was that “we really built our M&A muscle.” He hasn’t tipped his hand about what Netflix might pursue next, saying in April only that “we invest in the business both organically and opportunistically.”

Meanwhile, Comcast execs, in announcing the NBCU spinoff plans in June, said they weren’t splitting up the media company to ready it for a sale. But when pressed about the possibility of M&A after the separation, Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh, who’s set to become NBCU’s chief executive post-spin, suggested deals could be in the offing. As an independent company, it will “have the freedom now to explore adjacent businesses where we have the right to play,” he told Wall Street analysts.

Regarding speculation about deal scenarios for the independent NBCU, chief communications officer Jen Friedman said in a statement to Variety: “We have said from the beginning that we are not pursuing this spin for the purposes of M&A. Our plan for NBCU is to set the business up for growth, and we see a path to doing so given our industry-leading businesses in the most attractive segments of media, our differentiated strategy and our uniquely strong balance sheet.” Netflix declined to comment.

Over most of its 29-year history, Netflix shunned big M&A, preferring to stick to its knitting as it continued to enjoy strong subscriber and financial growth. But the calculus is different now: In the third quarter of 2026, top-line growth dropped to 11.8%, the lowest level in three years, and subscribers in the U.S. are spending less time with Netflix than they used to.

To jump-start its growth, “Netflix needs to make an acquisition,” says Terry Dugan, entertainment finance co-head of law firm Moore & Van Allen. “The only obvious suspect is NBCUniversal.” He says smaller players like Lionsgate, A24 or Neon on the movie side, or Starz or AMC Global Media on the TV side, simply wouldn’t be big enough to move the needle for Netflix in terms of boosting viewing on the service.

After Ellison’s capture of WB, “the pressure across the industry to be more scaled” — meaning assembling a larger collection of media assets and production firepower to compete on a global scale — “has never been higher,” says one senior studio exec. “People are feeling more pressure to consolidate. But it’s gotta be the right fit.”

Yes, Netflix is still turning a nice profit and delivering quarter-over-quarter growth. But the top brass became alarmed about the slowing pace. Sarandos and co-chief Greg Peters decided to overhaul its content leadership team, giving the boot to Bela Bajaria as chief content officer and to Dan Lin as head of film. The purge is a seeming concession by Netflix’s co-CEOs that the company is not delivering enough must-watch content — that the drop in U.S. engagement is not just part of the natural ebb and flow of viewing.

To replace Bajaria, Sarandos recruited veteran Peter Rice, who has a reputation as someone who “understands talent relations,” Sarandos explained to Wall Street after the streamer unveiled its Q3 earnings on Oct. 20.

But a revamp of Netflix’s content lineup might not be enough to turn things around, and that has fueled speculation that it could be eyeing a soon-to-be-independent NBCU — particularly as it faces Skydance in the market. That idea has been reinforced by how fast Netflix clinched a deal valued at $72 billion for Warner Bros. and HBO’s streaming and studios businesses before Paramount’s sky-high offer for all of Warner Bros. Discovery won out.

“When Comcast first announced that it was going to spin off NBCU, I immediately said, ‘Netflix is going after this,’ because they lost the crown jewel of Warner Bros.,” says Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester.

NBCU would for the most part fit in well with Netflix’s overall business. Peacock stood at 48 million subscribers as of the end of September, and fusing that with Netflix’s 325 million-plus subscriber base would be a win for both sides. It’s easy to see Bravo and its distinct brand of lifestyle shows becoming a tile on the Netflix app.

Universal Pictures’ library is home to more than 4,000 films and 130,000 episodes of TV, including enormous franchises like “Back to the Future,” “Jurassic Park,” “The Bourne Identity,” “Fast & Furious” and “Despicable Me” — not to mention Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” one of the biggest blockbusters of 2026. NBC has big sports rights deals, including pacts with the NFL, the NBA and Major League Baseball. And NBCU has a significant theme parks business, trailing only Disney in size. NBCU’s operations also encompass Sky, the satellite TV platform that serves about 20 million subscribers in the U.K., Ireland and Italy.
“Netflix is looking at sports, theatrical and experiences. NBCU ticks all of those boxes,” says John Conca, telecom and media analyst at investment research firm Third Bridge.

Adds Zach Darrow, chairman and CEO of business law firm DarrowEverett, who leads its private equity, capital markets and securities practice: “Netflix has money to spend. It didn’t get the Warner Bros. deal but it showed it was willing to make a significant investment. They walked away when they hit their limit — they are a credible bidder for a library or studio.”

For Comcast, the spinoff is mostly financial maneuvering. Brian Roberts, Comcast chairman and co-CEO, and the Roberts family will remain the controlling shareholder of both Comcast and NBCUniversal after the separation. Cavanagh will be CEO of NBCU, with top lieutenants including Donna Langley, chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment, and Matt Strauss, chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group (which includes Peacock). Nonetheless, it is a symbolic shift for the media mogul family that made its fortune as one of the first firms to wire the country for cable TV.

Comcast leaders say they’re unwinding their NBCU ownership after more than 15 years so that the slimmed-down company will be valued on its own rather than being lumped in with Comcast’s capital-intensive cable and wireless telco business. In other words, Comcast believes NBCU is worth more if it’s unshackled from the parent company’s core cable systems biz.

Comcast expects the spinoff to be tax-free to shareholders. But under IRS rules, to avoid incurring steep capital gains taxes, NBCU and Comcast have to wait two years before selling out to a third party. That means it could be mid-2029 by the time NBCU is in play. However, if Netflix wants NBCU badly enough, its bankers and lawyers can likely get creative with a deal structure to address the tax problem. The timeline might encourage Netflix to try to reach a deal with Comcast to snap up NBCU in the next six months or so, before the formal separation from Comcast is complete.

There are other complicating factors with a prospective Netflix-NBCU deal. For one thing, Netflix would certainly not want to own the Sky business, because it’s centered on pay TV and broadband, says Morningstar analyst Matthew Dolgin. Netflix also has disavowed interest in linear TV. But Reed Hastings used to swear Netflix would never get into the advertising business either — before the company did just that in 2022. The addition of NBC’s entertainment and sports programming, Dolgin says, “would make the Netflix service stickier and give them more pricing power.”

As for regulatory challenges to a prospective Netflix-NBCU merger, such a combo might see pushback such as a requirement that Netflix spin off the NBC broadcast TV operations. But the Justice Department this summer let the Paramount-Warner Bros. deal through without any conditions. An antitrust challenge launched by 12 Democratic state attorneys general to the Paramount-WBD deal — alleging the new entity would have undue power over theatrical movie releases and cable TV — ended with the AGs settling on a set of minimal behavioral conditions, ultimately letting the $111 billion horizontal merger close.

Instead of an outright M&A deal, Netflix could turn to other types of business deals like bundling partnerships to try to bulk up, says Prof. Tammy Madsen, a professor of management at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business. But, she adds, “If they want to move fast, it would be through acquisitions.” And again, NBC’s large stable of sports rights and other entertainment IP would give Netflix a wealth of new content to attract and retain subscribers.

Whether Netflix feels urgency to make a run at NBCU may depend on whether its investors are convinced Sarandos and Peters can stabilize the business without a big, transformative move. Netflix’s stock plunged after it signed the Warner Bros. deal — shareholders hated that the transaction would have loaded up $60 billion in new debt onto Netflix’s balance sheet. But perhaps NBCU will be the bullet Netflix needs to bite.
“Netflix is taking heat right now from Wall Street,” says a top Hollywood exec. “They are the streaming leader. And whatever happens, there will be the rationale for more combinations.”

items.title: “Evil All Along”: How Russell Brand Got Caught
items.description: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say ‘no’ and to demand justice from criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say ‘no’ and to demand justice from criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”

Those were the words that rang out across Southwark Crown Court as Justice Joel Bennathan sentenced the once-worshipped presenter, comedian and actor to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday. Hordes of journalists and paparazzi effectively set up camp for four weeks while the jury was taken through extensive allegations of rape and sexual assault. In total, six complainants accused Brand of frantic attacks from 1999 to 2009.

Here, the man who went on to carve out a career for himself in Hollywood films like Get Him to the Greek, Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Rock of Ages — a previously famed womanizer, sell-out stand-up and the ex-husband of pop superstar Katy Perry — was bleakly depicted in court sketches showing the now-devout Christian with his head bowed, rolling a rosary between his fingers.

And last week, after consistently denying any criminal wrongdoing whatsoever, he was found guilty on four of seven counts. Three were frenzied sexual assaults, and one was a violent anal rape that took place after a woman had consensual vaginal sex with Brand at his Hampstead home in 2009. Bennathan’s sentencing remarks capture the harrowing reality of the victim’s experience. He told Brand: “You flipped her over, removed the condom and, without asking, forced your penis into her anus, causing her great pain. She asked you to stop, then asked you again loudly. You replied, and I quote, ‘I want you to feel my cum.’ You ejaculated. She was distraught and in severe pain. The bed was heavily soiled by blood, sperm and faeces. You told her it was her mess, and made her try to clear it up. Shortly after, you went off to get ready, then went to work. She was driven to a nearby underground station by your driver, who for some reason had tissues ready to hand to her as she wept. She was left distraught, in pain and terrified she might have contracted HIV.” The courtroom was completely silent.

Over the last month, this trial has dominated the media, spawned entire podcast shows, and divided the British public. Brand admitted during the trial that no one would “touch him with a bargepole” and that he had failed to persuade anyone to testify on his behalf. Naturally, many of those familiar faces on the British comedy circuit distanced themselves long ago from the sex offender. Jonathan Ross released a statement this week saying he is “horrified” by Brand’s crimes and was “genuinely unaware” of his conduct; there are quite literally hundreds of others who have not — and won’t be — saying anything.

And as Brand now embarks on what looks like a seven-year stay at HMP Wandsworth prison, a number of questions remain unanswered. Is it true that his lurid behavior was “an open secret” across the British TV industry, and why were so many of these allegations about incidents in the workplace? Why had Brand’s defense, led by a barrister named Ian Winter, claimed that journalists “poisoned the well of justice” by publishing various investigations into Brand’s behavior? How, with the sheer brazenness of Brand’s actions palpable in each attack he was found guilty of, did this predator stay undetected for at least 17 years? And what message does his conviction send to others who still operate as he did?

Two sexual assault attorneys, a scholar of work, pay and insecurity in the creative industries at the University of Warwick, as well as the woman who spearheaded investigations at Channel 4 and Sunday Times that would kickstart a police probe into Brand’s crimes, talked to The Hollywood Reporter about how Brand’s conviction has changed the U.K. entertainment industry. They lay bare the specifics of a freelance-heavy industry that allowed Brand to evade punishment, how women were lured into spaces with him under the guise of flamboyant comedy, and the dedicated, years-long work of investigative reporters who helped bring a celebrity rapist to justice.

Dorothy Byrne was head of news and current affairs at Channel 4 when Jemima Goldsmith, Brand’s ex-girlfriend, came to talk to her in 2019. “People would say, ‘How did you get onto the story?’ And I would say, ‘Oh, well, somebody told me about it,'” Byrne begins to THR.

It is only in the last 48 hours that Byrne has been able to publicly name Goldsmith as that whistleblower. The TV producer, who dated Brand for around a year in 2014, took to social media after his sentencing this week to detail her own experience of “violence, coercive control and abuse” at the hands of Brand. “I didn’t know about Russell Brand,” says Byrne. “I thought he was creepy and sleazy — and we now know that massive numbers of people in the media industry knew what a terrible person he was.” (Brand scarcely attempted to hide it himself; one of his stand-up tours in 2006 included an entire section dedicated to Brand telling the audience he likes “blowjobs where mascara runs a little bit.” A former friend testifying for the prosecution said Brand bragged about wanting to sleep with 5,000 women.)

Byrne continues: “But I worked in news and current affairs. Not comedy and entertainment. [Goldsmith] told me of her experience and she said, ‘I think he should be exposed to protect other women.’ Even to have that conversation was, for her, difficult, and I really admire and thank her for it.”

This was the spark that would ignite a joint investigation between Channel 4’s Dispatches, The Times and Sunday Times, with two reporters — Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace — leading the charge into reports, and eventually interviewing hundreds of people on the topic of Brand’s behavior. Byrne left her Channel 4 role in 2020 and maintains she was only involved in the early investigation. But even then, she says, other national outlets were tracking the story. “[They’d] found it very difficult,” she tells THR. “In this case of Brand, women were particularly afraid to talk. Firstly, because he was just so famous. They felt he was so famous and powerful. He’s got loads of money. ‘If I speak, he’s got all the power.’ And nearly everybody who works in TV now is freelance.”

And so came one of the first major hurdles in this case against Brand — the enduring trickiness of temporary contracts. Dr. Heidi Ashton, an expert in work, pay, and insecurity in the creative industries, says of the freelancer-filled TV industry in which Brand preyed on women: “A freelancer’s future employment depends heavily on maintaining a good reputation with the individuals who hire them, rather than with the organization issuing their contract. Raising concerns about bullying, harassment or unsafe working practices can therefore carry substantial professional risks — who would they go to with these issues? Workers may fear losing not only their current role but also jeopardizing their career.”

Much has been said of the men around Brand who watched the attacks unfold and did nothing. One of the sexual assaults involved Brand grabbing a woman’s breasts in a busy Soho bar in 2004; another saw him pushing a victim up against a wall, kissing her body and squeezing her breasts and buttocks “aggressively” — in the Capital Radio office. Last week, a former associate of Brand’s, Jack Bayles, was accused of watching and laughing while the entertainer placed his head and nose in a co-worker’s “vaginal area,” one of the assaults Brand was found guilty of. It took place as they worked on a Channel 4 project. (Bayles, whose credits include Michaela Coel’s I May Destroy You and Kat Sadler’s Such Brave Girls, has officially been asked to “step back” from his producing role as head of comedy at independent TV production company Various Artists Limited.)

But this complainant did speak up immediately after Brand forced his head into her groin. “It was brushed under the carpet by senior management,” she explained in her victim impact statement on Monday. “This really affected me and had something similar happened again, at the time, I know I would not have had the confidence to speak up again. There was a culture, at the time, which meant I felt I had to just carry on and not talk about it anymore.”

“[Brand] was considered this treasure, and every time he got fired, he’d get promoted to another job. He kept moving around, and I don’t think it’s because he’s got a lot of talent,” says Dr. Ann Olivarius, a leading women’s rights attorney and co-founder of McAllister Olivarius, a law firm working across the U.K., U.S. and Ireland. Brand did indeed find himself bouncing between roles in British TV and radio: In the 2000s, he hosted Big Brother spinoff Big Brother’s Big Mouth and worked on The Big Fat Quiz of the Year, Russell Brand’s Got Issues and Russell Brand’s Ponderland. “His employers didn’t stop it,” Dr. Olivarius continues about his behavior. “It was all considered well and good. What is that old thing men say? ‘If you can get laid, then lucky you.’ I haven’t met a woman who’s told me that yet.”

Byrne, however, believes that the men in these offices were also frightened of how speaking up might affect their careers, with the risk of retaliation higher because of their freelance status. “These contracts are often so short that people’s fear is you just won’t get asked back, and it will get around that you are a complainer or a troublemaker.”

“But there was another thing as well with Brand — women described him as frightening,” she adds. “If you think of some of the evidence in the court … one minute he’s funny and sexy, and then in a moment he changes.”
“They Get to This Godlike State”

Women were routinely deceived by Brand’s status as a comedian. “The fact he was a comedian…” Byrne trails off. “This thing of when a man assaults you and he laughs. He’ll laugh and grab you. Brand treated it like a joke.” After Channel 4 began investigating, Byrne quickly became aware of how notorious Brand was among female comedians. “I discovered that female comedians warned each other about him,” she tells THR. His flamboyant nature and sharp wit — Brand himself also admits in his 2007 autobiography My Booky Wook: “I decided to act gay to attract girls” — allowed the shocking violence of his actions to be quickly diluted by that guise of drollery. “When a man laughs and grabs a woman, if the woman then complains, she’s regarded as having no sense of humor … In the world of comedy,” Byrne asks, “what could be worse than being branded as a woman with no sense of humor?”

New York-based sexual harassment and assault attorney Megan Thomas, of Megan Thomas Law, concurs. “I think he did a lot of things in the name of art and in the name of being a comedian and being in show business,” she tells THR. “People could laugh it off as ‘OK, that’s just part of his persona.’ But it isn’t real. He was really very derogatory towards women, and he had very little respect for them.”

It’s worth noting that Brand is not the first predator to have been brought to justice in the film and TV world, and he certainly won’t be the last. A fellow comic, David Walliams, is the subject of another bombshell investigation from The Guardian and ITV News on Tuesday that alleged he abused his power as a beloved comedy actor and Britain’s Got Talent judge to prey on teenage girls, some as young as 15, for sex. Walliams has vehemently denied he is a sexual predator and said: “I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to his reps for comment.

Walliams himself said in that same statement, “a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous.” It is a facet of these cases that arises time and time again, which makes women in the entertainment industry particularly vulnerable. “The element of fame really plays a role because when someone is so famous, it is easy to overlook red flags,” Thomas continues. “These women are maybe starstruck to a certain extent. … Everyone around this star is often creating a bubble and just constantly saying good things about them; they think to themselves, ‘No one will ever believe me,’ and this is why we see these cases happen so frequently with celebrities, because they get to this godlike state where they think they’re untouchable. And to an extent, they’re not wrong, right?”

Indeed, a couple of complainants in Brand’s case admitted to being fans of his. The anal rape victim met the disgraced star at his comedy gig at the Hammersmith Apollo (after which he saved her number in his phone as “T” for “tart,” according to Justice Bennathan). Not only was Brand able to exploit that sense of awe, but he also had the power — and money, as many of these male celebrities do — to put together a pretty intimidating legal team, who can advise their clients to resort to threats. “We have heard time and time again men using that threat,” says Thomas. “‘Oh, no one will ever hire you. I’ll tell everyone that you’re horrible.’ I don’t know that we’ve heard that in [the Brand] case. I didn’t read that specifically, but we’ve heard that repeatedly in cases involving actors and directors. And even if a woman’s not in show business, she realizes, ‘If I speak out because this person’s a celebrity, my name will get dragged through the mud too.'”

Dr. Olivarius says women fear retaliation in the workplace and can often lose their entire careers. “You lose your job, you can’t get hired, and then [your] whole future is destroyed. So the calculation is: ‘If I just keep quiet about this, and try to put it in a perspective that it’s a bad date as opposed to an actual rape and attack, then I can maybe live with this and I will still have a career,'” she tells THR.
“This Is Trump’s Playbook”

Even though the women testifying against Brand are entitled to lifelong anonymity, living through the trauma every day in court was clearly taxing. Some of them told the jury so themselves, and would fight back tears as they described how Brand forced himself on them.

Winter attempted to argue that these women were spurred on by the 2023 release of Channel 4 and The Sunday Times‘ investigation, in which Brand was accused of several attacks by a slew of women. Winter said Urwin, Wace and the team of journalists working on that documentary had “poisoned the well of justice” by prompting these complainants to reframe their encounters with Brand, decide they were nonconsensual and press criminal charges. Brand, says Winter, was denied a fair trial because of the media.

Though the jury was ultimately unconvinced by this line of reasoning, Byrne says Winter — who reportedly snarled at Urwin outside the court after Brand’s guilty verdicts came in: “Are you happy now? You f***ed it” — deployed a rhetoric imported by President Donald Trump. “This attempt to say that when journalists do an investigation, it’s criminal … That is new,” she says. “Where does it come from? Donald Trump. This is his playbook. You don’t just attack journalists. You don’t call them liars.” Dr. Olivarius makes a similar point — that the rise of Trump, who himself faces extensive allegations of sexual assault, has led the way, especially in the U.S., for a post-#MeToo dismissal of women’s experiences. “Are women really such liars?” Dr. Olivarius asks. “Can you not trust a woman with her testimony?” She cites the recent Cornell 7 case as an example of that trend.

Putting the other criticisms around Winter’s misogynistic and “shameful” defense aside, both Thomas and Dr. Olivarius maintain that it is extremely rare for women to lie about their rape and sexual assault experiences. “Who wants to brag about sexual interference? Nobody,” says Dr. Olivarius. “I don’t know those women, but there seems to be this image, these rape myths, that somehow women make it up. I’ve never had anybody in my thousands of clients who I felt had made it up.”

These women, now widely commended for their bravery, were indirectly found through the tireless work of investigative reporters at Channel 4 and The Sunday Times. Brand was brought to justice because of that work, no matter how Winter spun it in court. “That investigative journalism helped more victims come forward,” says Thomas.

Brand’s conviction and lengthy sentence have set a precedent — a warning — for fellow industry predators, who are likely still operating. “They should be very scared,” says Byrne. “One of Brand’s offenses was that he reached over and grabbed a woman’s breasts. That has happened every day in TV. Well, it won’t be happening now because he got several months in jail for that.”

Such was the media coverage around the trial — and the livestream of the firm, unemotional, victim-commending statement from Justice Bennathan — that Brand now serves as an illustration of what powerful investigative reporting and courageous victims can do: hold the previously unimpeachable to account. “Several women I know who work in TV said to me before the case, ‘He’ll never be found guilty,'” Byrne admits. “I said, ‘Why not?’ and they said, ‘Because they never get found guilty. They always get away with it.’ But the evidence was there … The coverage was massive, and the public reaction has been huge.”

With the confirmation from the Met Police that Brand is under investigation for two more alleged rapes, Byrne thinks there will be a change. “I think more women are going to come forward. Look at how long he worked in the industry, nearly 30 years, and look at how prolific he was. This man could have hundreds of victims. I think this is a turning point.”

Dr. Olivarius hopes that civil cases will allow the women to receive compensation for what they’ve been through. “With criminal cases, they get no money damages. They get no therapy costs. They get nothing. They just testified. They did the right thing.” She lauds the introduction of Britain’s Employment Rights Act, which introduces sweeping changes across 2026 and 2027 and is set to significantly strengthen rules around workplace harassment, whistleblower protections and nondisclosure agreements. The country remains in dire need of stronger law enforcement and funding for victims’ therapy, she adds as a caveat.

While sexual assault and rape remain “an epidemic” in British, American and Irish society, Dr. Olivarius concedes that Brand’s conviction is unusual. “It’s really rare that they’ve got this guy,” she says. “He was so flamboyant, so bragging, and even in the courtroom, he’s got his Bible, waving it in the air as if it were air freshener. And what this will do to his arrogance and sense of self-satisfaction, I [am] very curious to see.” Thomas believes it proves the existence of a harsher spotlight on male predators in our current climate. “I don’t know if anyone’s listening, but I think we are seeing a second wave of the #MeToo movement,” she tells THR.

And Byrne, who has been privy to Brand’s reign of terror longer than most, is simply just relieved that women across the industry now have proof of what’s possible. “You can do something about it, you can go to the police, you can report them to your employer, and your employer has to do something about it,” she says. She is content that the man now in prison is exactly the man those women said he was. “He’s been left wing, he’s been right wing, he’s been an atheist, he’s been a Christian, he’s been a conspiracy theorist. But he hasn’t been any of those really,” says Byrne. “He’s been evil, criminal Russell Brand, all along.”

items.title: Mike Myers Says He “Might” Be in ‘Shrek’ Spinoff ‘Donkey,’ Calls Film “Long Overdue”
items.description: As Mike Myers prepares to return to the swamp with Shrek 5 next summer, the actor is already looking ahead to the franchise’s future — and sharing his excitement about Donkey finally getting a movie of his own.
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: As Mike Myers prepares to return to the swamp with Shrek 5 next summer, the actor is already looking ahead to the franchise’s future — and sharing his excitement about Donkey finally getting a movie of his own.

“I’d love to,” Myers told The Hollywood Reporter Wednesday night at the Focker-in-Law premiere in New York when asked about continuing the Shrek films beyond their fifth installment. “It’s so much fun. It’s so well written. The filmmakers are so lovely and they’re so nice to me and I love playing the character. I love the messages in there and Cameron [Diaz]’s fantastic and Eddie [Murphy]’s a genius.”

In addition to Shrek 5, which will welcome Focker-in-Law star Skyler Gisondo into the mix as Farkle, one of Shrek (Myers) and Fiona’s (Diaz) teenage triplet sons, the franchise is also expanding with a standalone Donkey movie. Murphy is set to return to voice the beloved character in the DreamWorks Animation feature with a release date set for June 30, 2028.

While the Donkey movie has been described as a prequel exploring the character’s origin story, Myers isn’t entirely ruling out the possibility that Shrek could make an appearance. Regardless, he’s looking forward to seeing his longtime co-star get the spotlight.

“I wish Donkey lived in my house! I love that character so much,” he said. “I don’t think I’m in it. I might be. I’m not sure, but it’s long overdue. That character is one of my favorite characters of all time, and Eddie’s so great in it. I’m surprised it hasn’t come sooner, but I’ll be the first in line to see it. I love that guy.”
Myers even joked about just how much he loves the character, adding, “Honest to God, I have a cat named Pickles, and I love that cat as much as I love Donkey.”

Another long-awaited project Myers addressed was a fourth Austin Powers movie. Myers and filmmaker Jay Roach, who directed the 1997 original Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery and its two sequels, have previously teased the possibility of another installment in the James Bond-spoofing franchise. The last film, Austin Powers in Goldmember, hit theaters in 2002.
Though Myers was tight-lipped about revealing too much, he confirmed to THR that he is currently writing the screenplay for a fourth film.
“Yes, we are. I’m writing it right now; I’m having a great time,” he said. “I’m very, very secretive. He’s a secret agent, so I can’t really say too much.”

items.title: Next Gen 2026: 35 Rising Hollywood Executives Under 35
items.description: Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficu
items.author: Winston Cho; Aaron Couch; Caitlin Huston; Mia Galuppo; Ryan Gajewski; Katie Kilkenny; Borys Kit; Lacey Rose
paragraphs: Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficult to land, much less retain.

Such trends aren’t slowing the ascent of THR’s Next Gen class of 2026, who join such illustrious alumni as Donna Langley, Ari Emanuel, Kevin Feige and Peter Rice. In fact, this group is too busy forging new paths through the chaos — whether that’s bringing Gen Z back to cinemas (as indie producer Christian Vazquez did with both Primetime and You Can See Everything) or fortifying the streaming ecosystem amid endless churn (see Claudia Shin and Louie Hayes, behind the Apple TV Emmy darling Widow’s Bay and the Prime Video breakout Sterling Point, respectively.)
Meet the 35 executives and reps, each of them 35 years old or younger, who should be atop your call list, if they aren’t already.

- Alyssa Altman, 35 RK Films, senior vp LOGLINE Championing rom-coms like Anyone But You and Netflix’s upcoming 13 Going on 30 update. THE ARC Altman got a unique view of the industry when she would join her father, Steve, who rented out lighting, camera and grip equipment: “I grew up doing my homework in grip trucks, and I just loved being on set.” Her dad’s rom-com adoration rubbed off during their weekly trips to the movies, where films like Love Actually made an early impression. Altman studied journalism at Emerson but caught the producing bug while moonlighting on college TV projects. After time at Gersh, she became then-Universal exec Jeff Kirschenbaum’s assistant and followed him to RK Films. While the company focused on bigger IP plays, she endorsed the script for Anyone But You (“That was my baby”), Sony’s Sydney Sweeney-Glen Powell feature that became a rare theatrical comedy hit. Up next: Amazon MGM’s tennis rom-com Love Love and Netflix’s Millie Bobby Brown-led Just Picture It. PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Andy Cohen. My favorite way to de-stress after a long day is to watch and listen to the soothing sound of people fighting on Bravo.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “The fact that movies geared towards women do great theatrically. Every time it happens, people act like it’s an anomaly. Women are starved for content and it’s not a coincidence.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I was an assistant at Universal, we set up a screening for an A-list star who specifically requested popcorn from the Universal Studios theme park. I had to sneak into the park through the back lot and bring it back before he arrived.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Sally Albright from When Harry Met Sally. She isn’t afraid to speak her mind, is a hopeless romantic, and has strong opinions on how she orders her food.”

- Jenna Berger, 35 Marvel Studios, director of production development LOGLINE Berger is serving as co-producer, and Kevin Feige’s right hand, on Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars. ’Nuff said. THE ARC An L.A. native with industry parents, Berger grew up wanting to make movies. “I had this theory that everybody who didn’t want to make movies was lying to themselves and secretly did,” she says. So, shortly after graduating from University of Pennsylvania with a double major in English and film, she landed a gig at The Mark Gordon Co. Still, it was Marvel that was making some of her favorite films — she saw Spider-Man: Homecoming four times in the theater — but the company felt impenetrable … until it wasn’t. In 2019, Berger scored a position, rising to junior exec before finding herself the solo exec on the Marvel TV series Ms. Marvel, where she earned a supervising producer credit and honed her creative leadership, talent development and production expertise. “It was the best crash course in figuring out how this company worked and making something worthy of the Marvel name,” she says. The higher-ups took note, which is why Berger now oversees some of the studio’s most ambitious films. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kermit the Frog. Because my job is to bring amazingly talented people together to make something special amid total chaos … which sometimes means convincing everyone the show must go on before the set falls down around us.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “David Heyman. To get to work on Bond and Harry Potter?! A dream. Would love to trade places for a day … or forever.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Having a sneeze attack while leaving a voicemail for Aaron Sorkin on behalf of my boss.”

- Natalie Berkus, 35 LuckyChap, senior vp TV LOGLINE Developing (and producing) your future TV obsessions, including Andrew Garfield’sWild Things. THE ARC Rather than follow her agent dad and comedy writer mom into the business, Berkus arrived at University of Michigan eager to be a lawyer. “Then I rushed the law fraternity and didn’t get in,” she says. “I mean, I whiffed it and was like, ‘Shit, now what do I do?’ ” The answer, it turns out, was to parlay her love of TV into a series of PA gigs on shows like The Mindy Project before talking her way into a job as the writers assistant on Girls and, later, with Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s company. From there, she logged six years at Imagine Entertainment, where she was intimately involved in a slate that included The ’Burbs and the upcoming Siegfried and Roy series starring Garfield and Jude Law for Apple TV. But LuckyChap came calling a year ago, and the L.A. native and new mom to daughter Roonie jumped at the opportunity to work at the Margot Robbie-led hit factory. In that time, she has built a roster of 10 to 15 projects, including a Life Is Strange series for Amazon Prime Video. Still, Berkus doesn’t take herself too seriously. “If I had to brand myself, I’d say I like to bring a levity to this business,” she says, “because I think sometimes, especially now, things can get really stressful and we lose sight of the fact that ultimately this is just one big party.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Nina Rosenstein, who does all of the HBO comedy specials. We’ve never met, but Nina, girl, if you’re reading this, let’s link and get our Freaky Friday moment started!” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “That having unapproachable girlboss ‘I’m smarter than you’ energy is cool. It’s not, it’s lame! Normalize the quiet power in validating others and having a fun vibe.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Nowhere are you crazy!! No more of these!!”

- Mandi Brooksbank, 34 Netflix, senior manager, business affairs, scripted series LOGLINE Helps mold Netflix’s scripted slate, brokering deals with top talent like Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media. THE ARC As a kid in Reno, Nevada, Brooksbank figured she was destined for Broadway. While most her age were on the playground, she was busy with casino shows, doing dinner theater (and playing the harp) in vintage Hollywood glam. “It was entertainment or bust,” she recalls with a laugh. Later, she’d speedrun undergrad at USC and law school at Southwestern, finishing both in five years. Since then, she’s built a Hollywood résumé that includes stints at CAA, Donaldson Callif Perez and eOne. Now in her fifth year at Netflix, Brooksbank helps steer the streamer’s scripted series unit, striking deal after deal with TV’s biggest names. It’s a high volume affair, with Brooksbank managing a slate that includes The Altruists, Ransom Canyon and Sirens, among many others. “I’m the third child in a family of six,” she says of her negotiating chops. “They all have big personalities, so they prepared me well for Hollywood.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Miss Piggy.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Women directors’ second and third films. We talk about breaking through, but what about career longevity?” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “When I was considering law school, Patti Felker encouraged me to see being a woman as an advantage in negotiations, particularly the ability to read people, adapt and adjust your approach to the person across the table without losing sight of what you’re there to accomplish.”

- Barry Buren, 35 CAA, TV talent agent LOGLINE Makes deals for A-listers including Pedro Pascal, Matthew Rhys, Steven Yeun and Eddie Redmayne. THE ARC Hollywood has Orlando’s Central Florida Talent agency to thank for putting Buren on his path. After the New Jersey native graduated a semester early from nearby Rollins College, he picked up a gig at the model/talent agency to stay near friends who were still in school. Though he imagined he might become an engineer someday, he accepted an L.A.-based relative’s offer to live with her while giving Hollywood a try. As luck would have it, agenting stuck, and after a stint at Gersh, the avid golfer joined CAA in 2014.
