Today, the married rep is entrusted by actors including Josh Hartnett, Charlie Hunnam and Hannah Waddingham. Earlier this fall, client (and double Emmy winner) Rhys gave Buren a shout-out from the Emmy stage. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Serving coffee to people in an order determined by seniority and annual earnings. It was my first introduction to the Hollywood hierarchy, and I learned very quickly that even caffeine has a pecking order.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being on a call with 15 people to schedule another call with 15 people, only to discover that the one person who actually needed to be there wasn’t invited.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Lorne Michaels. To have spent five decades at the intersection of comedy, culture, and discovering talent is pretty remarkable.”

- Winnie Carrillo Montiel, 35 Amazon MGM, film executive, production & development LOGLINE Oversees films that range from bro-y actioners (The Wrecking Crew) to weepy love stories (Honeymoon With Harry). THE ARC Carrillo Montiel’s career in entertainment began with a clerical error. As an Emerson undergrad, she was mistakenly admitted as a screenwriting major instead of the literature and publishing program she had applied to. She ended up staying the course, eventually doubling down by attending graduate school at USC’s famed Peter Stark Producing Program. While there, she landed a temp job in MGM’s film group, which she did by day, leaving classes for night. Ultimately, it was the studio’s then-president Jonathan Glickman who helped push through the Guatemala City native’s visa sponsorship to land her her first full-time Hollywood gig. “He just made me promise that I wouldn’t get my green card and leave,” she remembers. “This was almost a decade ago and I’m still here. So, I really kept my promise.” Carrillo Montiel has since survived several regime changes, not to mention an acquisition, to land at her current spot on Amazon MGM’s film team, where she has overseen such films as The Sheep Detectives and an upcoming slate with projects from Dan Fogelman (Honeymoon) and Michael Showalter (a Serendipity reimagining). One of her proudest accomplishments is shepherding Angel Manuel Soto’sThe Wrecking Crew, explaining, “Latinos are often put in a very specific box, and we are only hired to tell Latino-specific stories. I’m always looking for opportunities to elevate talent that I think are just great filmmakers.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Unlimited budgets.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “I was advised to look for an American husband as I was told it would be impossible for me to earn a work visa in this industry.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Cold calling very specific animal experts in Russia and Brazil to attempt to track down recent sightings of extremely large species of bears and snakes.”

- Margaret Clark, 32 20th Television, director of development LOGLINE Manages a roster of overall deals (Liz Meriwether, Drew Goddard) and development projects, including the Hulu hit Furious. THE ARC Technically speaking, Clark was discovered at the Panera on South Beverly Drive. At least, that’s where a guy from APA overheard her during an informational coffee with a fellow University of Virginia alum and offered to pass along her résumé to his agency mailroom. She was hired the following week. “I treated it like my grad school,” Clark says of her agency stint. By late 2017, the Virginia native and onetime theater kid had jumped to 20th Television, where she eventually found her way to Dana Walden’s desk for three pivotal years. In that time, she gained both a high-level education and a top-tier mentor. These days, Clark’s back on the 20th team, punching above her weight as she manages a slate of projects and the studio’s IP pipeline. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jennifer Lopez in The Wedding Planner.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Buying a single old-fashioned donut for the CEO on Friday mornings. It had to be from Winchell’s. I wasn’t his assistant.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “The National Theater in London. Or the ABC Riverside Starbucks.”

- Sarah Colvin, 30 Neon, senior vp acquisitions LOGLINE Keeps Neon supplied with art house favorites and horror standouts, including The Secret Agent, Leviticus and All of a Sudden. THE ARC Colvin spends a good chunk of her year traveling to Sundance, Berlin, SXSW, Cannes and beyond in the name of supplying Neon’s film slate with titles that will soon be Letterboxd’s new obsession (see: Oliver Laxe’s Sirāt and the long-awaited doc Once Upon a Time in Harlem). Raised in New Mexico by artist parents, young Colvin would spend whatever free time she had with friends at Santa Fe’s one art house cinema. She laughs, “We thought we were so highbrow.” But she took that passion to NYU, where her professor, indie producer David Hinojosa, helped her land an internship at Neon, right as the then-upstart distributor was releasing its first success, I, Tonya. “There was no formal end date to the internship,” she says. “Eventually, Tom [Quinn] was like, ‘You should probably have a job here, then.’ ” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A blend of PeeWee Herman and Griffin Mill from The Player.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Wile E Coyote.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The great equalizer that is the valet stand after the Academy Awards.”

- Dylan Conklin, 34 Entertainment 360, manager LOGLINE Guides the careers of clients like Kaia Gerber and Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story star Ella Beatty. THE ARC Conklin was studying international business in China for a summer when he realized the path wasn’t for him. Fortunately, a TV class with guests from Breaking Bad and Mad Men opened his eyes to a career in the entertainment field instead. Following a stint as an assistant to producer Tripp Vinson and some good advice from mentor attorney Howard Weitzman, he landed at 360 in 2016. A decade later, the dad of two has an impressive roster of talent clients, including Costa D’Angelo, for whom he’s lined up back-to-back shows (East of Eden, The Sticks, We Were Liars), Ji-young Yoo, whose post-KPop Demon Hunters path includes a Paramount movie and Presumed Innocent season two, and Colin Woodell, who toplines as the title character in Myron Bolitar, a series based on the Harlan Coben books. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t chase hits. Champion exceptional artists, nurture their talent, and the hits will follow.” IT WAS FROM… “Mo Ostin.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Danny DeVito.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Making PB&J sandwiches in the office kitchen with Jennifer Garner.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Jerry Bruckheimer.”

- Kai Dolbashian, 33 1.21, Film & TV development head LOGLINE Identified filmmaker Michael Shanks and helped develop Together from script to splashy Sundance sale. THE ARC While attending Chapman’s film school, Dolbashian landed an internship at MGM TV. The problem: The job was an hour away on a good day, and he had no car. Though he racked up credit card bills renting Zipcars, the bet paid off. He scored a post-grad gig and found a mentor in producer Andrew Mittman. And when Mittman launched his own banner in 2020, he was there on day one. Now, as the company’s head of film and TV development, Dolbashian has a slew of projects in development, including Warner Bros.’ remake of Attack of the 50 Foot Woman with Margot Robbie and Tim Burton. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arno from Uncut Gems. We’re both impatient Armenians and both desperately want to do business with Adam Sandler.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The first time I had lunch with Christoph Waltz, he cut and ate his strudel exactly the way his infamous character Hans Landa does in Inglourious Basterds. Thankfully, unlike Hans, Christoph is one of the nicest human beings.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Bill Hader. There is literally no one else who could write and direct that epic motorcycle chase and shootout from season three of Barry, yet also perfectly embody the unhinged role of Officer Slater in Superbad.”

- Carly Elter, 32 Hidden Pictures, senior vp film and TV LOGLINE The architect behind The Housemaid is also behind lit-centric packages based on best-sellers from Rebecca Yarros and V. E. Schwab. THE ARC When Elter first walked into the house at the center of her 2025 movie The Housemaid, she cried. “It was such a surreal moment,” she says. “In my apartment, I read a book that I thought was a good idea for a movie, and now we have 100 people-plus employed making that movie.” Elter sold the film adaptation when it was self-published by author Freida McFadden; it would later land a publishing deal and sell 6 million copies, while the movie earned more than $400 million and quickly scored a sequel, which is in production. It’s not the married New Jersey native’s only claim to fame. While still an assistant — with stints at WME, Pascal Pictures and Mandeville — she also founded Women Wednesdays (now The Real Champions), where she’d screen films from women and nonbinary filmmakers for fellow assistants with the goal of getting the directors studio jobs. Later, Elter — who lives in Playa Vista with her husband and mutt Archie and also counts TV as a part of her remit with MGM+’s Robin Hood — started a mentorship program that’s helped place over 150 people into jobs. MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being approached by a famous actor on a red carpet who told me he was a huge fan of mine. Turns out he thought I was Alana Haim.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Amanda Seyfried. She has built a life where she makes incredible movies and TV shows and then goes home to her farm to hang out with goats and emus. She’s cracked the code.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “You have to work hard to build the version of Hollywood you want to be a part of.” IT WAS FROM “Sara Scott.”

- Anna Flickinger, 34 UTA, motion picture lit agent LOGLINE From Mary Beth Barone to Sterling Point producer Raffi Donatich, she gets funny women’s work to screen. THE ARC “I read these goddamn think pieces like, ‘Comedy’s dead,’ ” says Flickinger, whose response is often: “Really?! There’s always going to be a big theatrical comedy that gets people back in the seats.” She saw it happen firsthand when writer client Ilana Wolpert’s Anyone But You made over $200 million at the box office. Initially, the Chicago native and oldest of eight thought she’d pursue a career in politics, but after interning in the office of Sen. Dick Durbin (“loveliest man in America”) and a DC lobbying firm (“fucking depressing”), she realized her love of The West Wing was more about an interest in entertainment than government. After temping her way around L.A., she landed at UTA, where she ultimately found a home in the motion picture lit group. Now, Flickinger, who lives with her husband and their Rottweiler and Chihuahua, guides clients like Sammi Cohen (You Are So Not Invited to My Bar Mitzvah) and Barone, who’s writing and starring in her own rom-com. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “C.J. Cregg sun, Josh Lyman rising, Toby Ziegler moon.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “The public transit infrastructure of New York in L.A.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Why it takes women making their first, second, third and fourth movie to get the compensation and resources that men get to make their second movie.”

- Carly Frankel, 32 WME, digital agent LOGLINE Brokers deals for top podcasts, including Giggly Squad’s nine-figure pact with SiriusXM. THE ARC An L.A. native, Frankel got an early taste of agency life while booking comedy shows, including Chelsea Peretti’s, as an undergrad at UC Berkeley. It led to an assistant gig in UTA’s comedy touring department, then another at then-podcasting startup Wondery. But after greenlighting Wondery shows including Baby, This Is Keke Palmer, Frankel was called back to the agency side at WME, where she’s helped Maria Sharapova launch a podcast with Vox Media and brokered Tinx’s deal with SiriusXM and Dr. Mary Claire Haver’s deal with Audacy. As more and more people consider starting a podcast, Frankel advises talent about the hard work required, including recording a minimum of 45 episodes a year. “I think the number one thing is someone who is genuinely enthusiastic about it,” she said. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Chasing comedians down Melrose to introduce myself after their stand-up sets. Saying hi on behalf of the agency was my cardio.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Truly anywhere that offers a 16-ounce cup. The ‘default 10-ounce latte’ trend is killing me.”
BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Your reputation is your greatest currency. Work hard and be kind.”

- Katie Giarla, 35 Cut To, founding member/partner LOGLINE Building a slate of hot projects, including the upcoming Elle Fanning-Nicole Kidman legal thriller Discretion, for the A24-based company. THE ARC Raised by a psychologist and a lawyer in Pittsburgh, Giarla’s only link to the entertainment business was her childhood birthday parties at the local movie theater. “I thought I’d be a lawyer,” she says, “and then I did some internships in law and realized I could make money and I would hate my life.” Upon graduating from University of Pennsylvania, Giarla parlayed her love of reading into a gig in the books department at WME. The trouble, she’d soon learn, was that she was more interested in the books than the dealmaking. So, she shifted groups before segueing to Endeavor Content (later, Fifth Season), where she championed projects including East of Eden as a series for Netflix. Giarla would later jump with boss Joe Hipps to Cut To, a red-hot company that will soon have more shows than executives. Among its recent sales, all of which prompted frenzied bidding wars: the Joel Edgerton-led crime drama Trigger Point and a two-season order for a Gwyneth Paltrow drama. At press time, however, Giarla was more focused on her other major project, her newborn son, with whom she’s now home on maternity leave. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Lady Olenna Tyrell. I’ve been rewatching GoT on maternity leave. She’s inquisitive, sharp-tongued and loyal to a fault.“ MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I realized there was a typo on a deck that my boss was en route to present to Obama — at the White House. That was a crazy two hours.”
PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Andy Cohen. The writers’ strike was in full swing when Scandoval hit, which gave me way too much downtime to stumble into the Bravoverse.”

- Jordan Gorelick, 34 UTA, talent agent LOGLINE Steers the career of rising stars Odessa A’zion and Alien: Earth lead Sydney Chandler. THE ARC As an undergrad at Colgate, Gorelick had his sights set on a career in screenwriting. The dream shifted, however, once he stumbled upon HBO’s Hollywood show Entourage and David Rensin’s book The Mailroom: Hollywood History From the Bottom Up. Suddenly, agenting was the goal, which led to an early gig in UTA’s mailroom. It was everything Gorelick had hoped for: “Watching the agents, the intensity, being a 21-year-old kid and driving around Hollywood and seeing the billboards on the Sunset Strip — I loved being in it.” Eleven years on, he’s constructing a list of rising stars (Nicholas Braun, Ray Nicholson, Lili Reinhart) and helping craft the next stage for established actors (Lizzy Caplan, Adam Scott, Timothy Olyphant, Paul Bettany). He feels his abandoned writing ambitions are actually key to his success. “The way I analyze and interpret and discuss material, that comes from a writer’s perspective and has set me apart in the way I work with actors.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kevin McCallister eating that cheese pizza in the stretch limo.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Buddy from Air Bud.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Driving a young Chalamet to general meetings.”

- Angie Haney, 31 Netflix, director, film LOGLINE Supplies Netflix with rom-com hits like Voicemails From Isabelle and People We Meet on Vacation. THE ARC Haney was outside the Vatican on vacation when she saw two girls filming themselves doing a choreographed dance featured in her latest movie, Voicemails for Isabelle. “I was like, ‘There’s no way that’s what they’re doing!’” She approached the girls in St. Peter’s Square and that was exactly what they were doing. While Haney is now Netflix’s romantic comedy whisperer, she grew up envisioning a career in politics. In high school, the L.A. native and future Columbia poli-sci major was a congressional intern for outgoing L.A. Mayor Karen Bass. But a series of entertainment internships — not to mention a childhood watching classics like Singin’ in the Rain with her voiceover actress mom, theater director dad and screenwriter twin brother — prompted a change of heart. After a cold email led to a stint at Disney, she landed a job as the assistant to then-Lucasfilm head Kathleen Kennedy as the Star Wars series were starting to populate Disney+. She’d later jump to Netflix, where she has found success with rom-coms and coming-of-age films. Up next: a reimagining of 13 Going on 30. “I’ve heard it said before that we should all make movies for our 12-year-old self,” she says, “And that is very true for me.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Watching George Lucas meet Grogu on the set of The Mandalorian.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR “Nora Ephron to have written 20 more movies.”

- Louie Hayes, 35 LuckyChap, vp TV LOGLINE The on-set producer for the summer smash Sterling Point. THE ARC Hayes’ family moved half a dozen times before he left for college. The constant in his home growing up was TV, which he claims he watched “an unhealthy amount of.” Eager to put down roots after graduating from Northwestern, he settled in L.A. with some college buddies. “At the time, everyone started at a talent agency,” he says, so he dutifully lined up a gig at Gersh. And while agenting wasn’t Hayes’ calling, it was there that he’d meet his future wife (and fellow Next Gen honoree), Samantha Militante, who’d later follow him to FX. But after nearly a decade as a buyer — working on hits like Dave and Alien: Earth — he jumped to LuckyChap, where he’s built an impressive roster. In fact, one of Hayes’ very first projects at the uber-successful Margot Robbie outfit was the runaway hit Sterling Point, which he was intimately involved with every step of the way. Up next: series Sex Criminals, from Kumail Nanjiani and Emily Gordon, and an adaptation of The Retrievals from Molly Smith Metzler. PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Jeff Probst. I consider Survivor America’s fifth major sport, and I have some ideas.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arnold from Hey Arnold! An idealist with an oversized head and a compulsive need to help.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t date anyone in the industry. My wife is on this list.”

- Julia Iglesias, 34 Focus Features, VP LOGLINE Shepherds artistic films including Sense and Sensibility and Nosferatu, along with the upcoming Werwulf and the adaptation of The Bell Jar. THE ARC Growing up in South Florida, Iglesias would regularly make her little sister act in her home movies. It wasn’t until she landed at Boston University that she learned how to turn her passion for storytelling into a career. “I did tons of internships,” she says, “and took all of the screenwriting and production classes I could get my hands on.” After a brief, post-grad stint as an unscripted postproduction coordinator at Relativity Media, she landed at NBCUniversal. A job working for then-Universal Filmed Entertainment Group chairman Jeff Shell turned into a gig at Focus Features, where Iglesias has been ever since. Now, the newly engaged exec — her fiancé proposed at this year’s Sundance Film Festival — cherishes seeing projects through to the end with auteurs like Sarah Polley and Robert Eggers. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Pick your boss, not your job.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “The dog handler on Sense and Sensibility.”
THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Somewhere neither person has to valet.”

- Ben Iguchi, 32 Netflix, manager, original series, live-action comedy LOGLINE Champions buzzy comedies including Cobra Kai and Doozer Productions’ upcoming I Suck at Girls and Nick Kroll’s A Hundred Percent for Netflix. THE ARC Iguchi can’t remember a time when comedy wasn’t a central focus in his life. As he tells it, his Ph.D. dad had proposed to his dancer mom during an episode of The Golden Girls, and every memory in his childhood home seems to feature a sitcom of some kind. In fact, by the time Iguchi turned 13, Jewish comedy became his bar mitzvah theme. “It definitely was not cool,” he jokes as he recounts the Groucho Marx gla

items.title: JFK Jr.’s ’94 Saab Is Up for Auction. You Should Buy It
items.description: The late John F. Kennedy Jr., in addition to being the subject of countless menswear moodboards, a hit Ryan Murphy series, and, hey, a new coffee table book written by yours truly, was one of the most stylish guys in 1990s New York. Between his American-dynast
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: The late John F. Kennedy Jr., in addition to being the subject of countless menswear moodboards, a hit Ryan Murphy series, and, hey, a new coffee table book written by yours truly, was one of the most stylish guys in 1990s New York. Between his American-dynasty pedigree, chiseled good looks, and impossibly thick head of hair, not to mention his eclectic wardrobe of preppy classics, funky gorpcore, and Armani suits, it’s not hard to see why. It should come as no surprise, then, that he also had excellent taste in cars. Throughout the ’90s, JFK Jr.’s whip of choice was a 1994 Saab 900 SE Coupe, a quirky Swedish sports car that embodied everything that was great about ’90s style, down to its hunter green paint. Fortunately, for fans of oddball vintage autos and JFK Jr. alike, it’s currently up for sale via RR Auction, and the bids are rolling in.

Sporty, sophisticated, and eccentric, the Saab 900 was to JFK Jr. what the pink Cadillac Fleetwood was to Elvis, or the Porsche 935 was to Paul Newman. An consummate outlier in the American car market since the ’50s, Saab’s popularity peaked in the mid-1980s when its weird, angular designs and quirks(e.g., the ignition was next to the handbrake) found a following among design-obsessed American yuppies. Combining the Scandinavian sobriety of a Volvo with the postmodern flair of a Memphis sofa, Saab loomed large in ’90s culture: Jerry Seinfeld’s TV alter-ego drove one, as did Niles Crane, Dana Scully, and Clark Griswald’s humorless neighbors in National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation.

During the tail end of the decade, when JFK Jr. and his late wife, publicist Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, were fixtures of Lower Manhattan life, the couple was frequently photographed driving in the Saab near their Tribeca loft. With its sporty-yet-economical turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a sleek leather interior, and a custom set of aftermarket aqua-blue padded ski racks mounted to the roof, it embodied JFK Jr.’s characteristic blend of aristocratic, athletic, and bohemian to a tee.

According to Bobby Livingston, executive vice president at RR Auction, “what makes this lot so special is it's not some Maserati or something flashy like that—it's a practical car that was a part of his everyday life. For Kennedy, “the choice of this car, as opposed to a Mercedes or something, speaks a lot to his style.” This particular Saab—which JFK Jr. purchased new from Zumbach Sports Cars in Manhattan for $29,841.21 in the summer of 1994, and owned until his death in 1999—comes to auction via Kevin J. Hynes, a screenwriter and longtime friend of Kennedy’s who worked with him at the New York DA’s office in the early ’90s. According to the auction listing, the car had been left at Hynes’s Westchester home in the days following Kennedy’s fatal plane crash. In 2000, Hynes then bought the car from the Kennedy estate in 2000 for $6,000, and sold it for $12,000 two years later. Its third owner is said to have started up the car regularly, but judging by its overall condition and the looks of its odometer, which shows just 30,650 miles, it seems it hasn’t hit the road in a long time.

The Saab, which was listed with a minimum sale price of $15,000, is part of a RR’s Fine Autographs and Artifacts auction that also includes a tweed hat worn by the elder JFK and Lee Harvey Oswald’s overcoat. As of Wednesday afternoon, more than 20 bids have driven the price close to $30,000. “We’ve sold a Hummer that belonged to Tupac, and a Cadillac Escalade that was used by Tony Soprano in The Sopranos, but I didn't know there would be such an affection for John F. Kennedy Jr.’s Saab,” says Livingston. “It’s already exceeded our estimate, and there’s a lot of interest, so it could go for a lot more than where it is right now.”

Given its provenance and climbing auction price tag, whether JFK Jr.’s Saab ends up with a car collector, a Kennedy buff, or someone with a keen appreciation for peak-1990s style, one hopes that whoever buys it will be well-equipped to give it the treatment it deserves. That is to say, this is a car that deserves to be street-parked in Tribeca, driven to Vermont for ski trips, and otherwise treated like the ’90s style icon it is. A backward Kangol cap and an “I TOLD YA” tee are optional, but highly recommended.

items.title: Petra Fagerström Turns Fashion Discipline Into Something Unruly
items.description: At the Winter Olympics earlier this year, many of us found ourselves ensorcelled by young female figure skaters furiously spinning on ice. But designer Petra Fagerström’s gaze has always been rinkside. “Coaches are so often the supervillain in the media, but I
items.author: Claire Marie Healy
paragraphs: At the Winter Olympics earlier this year, many of us found ourselves ensorcelled by young female figure skaters furiously spinning on ice. But designer Petra Fagerström’s gaze has always been rinkside. “Coaches are so often the supervillain in the media, but I love them,” says the 28-year-old designer on a June afternoon. “That power dynamic has emotions that many women can relate to.”

Fagerström is serene among the organized chaos of her studio, located in London’s historic Smithfield meat market. Although the Swedish designer’s dark hair, pale skin, and all-black uniform give the impression of a Scandinavian noir protagonist, when she was a teenager in Gothenburg, her look was considerably sparklier. From age 14 to 16, she trained at a skating rink every day after school, even making Sweden’s national team for synchronized figure skating. Still, when she thinks back to that time, what comes to her mind is not girls in spangly costumes but the strength of the woman in charge. “My coach was this matriarch. She had power but perhaps hadn’t reached what she had wanted to for herself,” says Fagerström. “There’s something really vulnerable about where that presence comes from.”

For her most recent collection, Fagerström, who launched her label in February 2025, explored that duality through a tug-of-war between structure and softness. Take her signature double-fronted jackets with interior tailoring, or her lenticular-printed pleats, which create an optical illusion like an ice skater speeding by, as mediated by our screens. Although the collection, which marked her first time on the London Fashion Week schedule, happened to coincide with Alysa Liu fever, Fagerström is determined to “talk about fashion” with her garments. Don’t expect any leotards. (You may, however, find a floral print that pays homage to a coat once worn by the mother of 1990s Olympic figure skater Tonya Harding.)

While she was always interested in clothes—during her emo phase, at 13, she was influenced by the band Tokio Hotel—Fagerström truly decided clothes were her future after quitting skating at 16. “I found Nicolas Ghesquière’s Balenciaga and fell in love. I was like, I’m going to be a designer,” she explains. She studied at Parsons Paris, then completed stints at Acne Studios and Demna’s Balenciaga before heading to London in 2023 for Central Saint Martins’s MA fashion program. Her particularly wearable graduate collection laid out her distinctive point of view: distorted New Look–inspired tailoring, shimmering eveningwear worn over warm-up sweats. “Fashion, to me, is thinking about womanhood: how you want to present, and how you want to be perceived,” says Fagerström. “Looking at a lot of fashion now, it’s like: Where’s the agency? In clothes, the idea I usually come back to is breaking what is obedient.” Think of her designs as the flyaway hair in a gelled ponytail.

At a time when revisiting the tchotchkes of girlhood is trendy, Fagerström is more interested in maturity and all the friction that entails. When she designs, she asks herself: “How does this woman feel? Does she like music, food, and sex? You want to feel that there is a woman behind the fashion image.” In just a short time, those questions have resonated: Her brand is already sold at Dover Street Market Paris and 10 Corso Como, as well as on her own website, and she was a finalist this year for the prestigious LVMH Prize. “My course director at Saint Martins said to me, ‘Don’t feel like you’re only one year young, because you’ve obviously been creating this brand for much longer.’ When things happen, they happen.”

Fagerström has been at work on her new collection. Spring presents a challenge for the designer, given her penchant for dark colors and layers. She’s exploring an idea she’s long been interested in: “My next collection is about women’s relationship to sex,” explains Fagerström. “Conservative values seem to be back in my generation.” She’s been rewatching Michael Haneke’s The Piano Teacher, a portrait of repressed desires, and reading Gillian Anderson’s Want, a book of compiled anonymous sexual fantasies. “How do these things come out in other ways when you repress them?” asks Fagerström. In her designs, they emerge as controlled slippages: jackets that fall a little off the shoulder, or trompe l’oeil that pretends to reveal the body underneath.

The designer partly credits all those years on the ice for her single-minded drive. “Being disciplined enough to practice something repetitive is a good skill,” she says. “When I started studying fashion, I would perfect my pockets for days.” Whenever Fagerström’s head isn’t focused on the cutting table, she is researching, just as she did on the pre-algorithmic Internet when she was seeking out what Raf Simons listened to, or looking for archival Junya Watanabe runway images. “You had to do a lot of digging on Tumblr,” she says, explaining that the magic was in the effort. “If you remove the pursuit of something, it feels less exciting.”

Hair by Ali Pirzadeh at Streeters; Makeup by Abbie Nourse. Models: Belladonna Beeby at Storm Management; Jessie Craig, Khadijat Olafemiwa at The Squad Management; Astrid østergaard, Echo Zhao at Premier Model Management. Casting by Ashley Brokaw Casting; Photo Assistants: Emma Ercolani, Fiona Fitzpatrick; Retouching: SHE POST PRO; Fashion Assistants: Ella Bacon, Zaza McDonald; Hair Assistant: Krisztian Szalay; Makeup Assistant: Maho Moriyama.

items.title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
items.description: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.
items.author: Lily Hay Newman
paragraphs: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

“While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,” Ehren Kret, Signal's chief technology officer, says in a statement. “As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees.”

For critical services used in high-stakes settings, it would be a dream to be able to formally verify every code base and entire software supply chains. “If you can now verify the correctness of these implementations, then you can rest easy,” says Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind's vice president of research. “You can imagine banks, imagine all those other companies who rely on assurances and who worry about bugs who could now say, ‘I can prove these properties.’"

The open question across the tech sector, though, is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale—and whether it can do so at a workable cost. DeepMind conducted the Signal analysis free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to share the cost of the analysis. The company also declined to comment on whether it has plans to release a commercial formal verification product or service.

The researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written," Chaudhuri says. “There’s a middle ground.”

items.title: A Startup Wants to Fight AI Bioweapons With AI
items.description: Frontier AI labs have warned that their technology could help develop dangerous bioweapons.
items.author: Emily Mullin
paragraphs: Frontier AI labs have warned that their technology could help develop dangerous bioweapons.

Now, a startup says it has developed a defense. On Wednesday, Radical Numerics announced that it has developed a new edge model called Omnii Defense that is designed to flag natural and AI-engineered pathogens using a laptop and a USB gene sequencer. It can also run without an internet connection, allowing researchers in the field with spotty connections to use it. Though many scientists say AI-made bioweapons are a low-likelihood threat, Radical Numerics hopes its technology will help researchers and public health officials identify emerging biological threats.

Eric Nguyen, cofounder and CEO of Radical Numerics, says he sees a coming arms race in biodefense similar to what’s playing out in cybersecurity, where threat actors and security defenders are leveraging AI in an attempt to gain an edge.
“We felt that the biosecurity space was far behind on the defense side,” he says.

Nguyen and his cofounders were part of the research team behind Evo and Evo-2, open-source DNA foundation models they worked on during their doctoral research at Stanford University. They founded Radical Numerics in 2025.

The San Francisco–based company recently made waves after rolling out Omnii, a new genome language model built on different types of biological information beyond DNA, including RNA, proteins, and epigenetic signals. In October, Radical announced that it used Omnii to create custom bacteriophages, viruses that infect and kill specific bacteria, targeting a drug-resistant strain of E. coli. Its cocktail was used to treat a sick patient, with special permission from the Food and Drug Administration.

Another AI biotech startup, Tabula Bioscience, was also involved in that research, but Radical didn’t disclose the partnership in its announcement last month. The omission led Harvard geneticist George Church, who was an adviser to both companies, to resign from his role at Radical last week.

Omnii Defense, the company’s latest tool, makes multiple predictions about a sequence, including the odds of it being pathogenic or AI-generated and what taxonomic group it most closely resembles. The model assigns a genome a “threat score” between zero and one that combines the likelihood of unnaturalness with functional predictions. The higher the score, the higher the threat.

Earlier biodefense tools, such as the federally funded Finding Engineering-Linked Indicators, or Felix, can compare genetic sequences of interest against libraries of known organisms, essentially searching for cataloged matches. That can be helpful in a scenario where a bad actor has made a few tweaks to an existing pathogen. But they aren’t designed to make predictions in the way that Omnii is.

The benefit of AI models is that they can learn patterns in sequences associated with biological function instead of relying on exact sequence matches. That could allow them to recognize similarities between sequences even when their genetic spelling has changed. Christine Parthemore, Radical Numerics’ head of biodefense, says Omnii is a “step change.”

In one experiment, the company removed Bundibugyo virus—which is currently driving an Ebola outbreak in East Africa—from the training data, first at the species level and then its whole genus. “It was as if Omnii was operating in 1976,” Parthemore says, referring to the year Ebola was discovered. With just the species removed, the model still detected that 33 percent of the Bundibugyo sequences pushed to it were something pathogenic. Even with the whole genus removed, it flagged 22 percent of the viral sequences. Non-AI tools gave essentially no indication of potential risk, she says.

“We absolutely need to be vigilant about what AI is enabling, and if we can use technology to compete with it and hopefully get ahead of any kind of nefarious actors, that seems sensible,” says Bronwyn MacInnis, director of pathogen surveillance in the Infectious Disease and Microbiome program at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.
However, MacInnis cautions that detecting a signal is still a big leap from determining whether a pathogen has real consequence or whether a threat was engineered.

Access to Omnii Defense is currently limited to vetted external testers. Radical Numerics says it is working with national laboratories, government agencies, and other independent evaluators to assess the model’s performance.

items.title: A New Benchmark for De-Aging Comes From Slowly Turning Back Cells’ Clocks
items.description: Scientists have long known how to make cells younger—at least in the sense that adult cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells very similar to those found in embryos. While this capability has been foundational for biological research, these methods
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: Scientists have long known how to make cells younger—at least in the sense that adult cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells very similar to those found in embryos. While this capability has been foundational for biological research, these methods aren’t viable for anti-aging technologies, for a few reasons.
“You don't want to have a pluripotent cell in your body, because it can become all types of cells,” says Oliver Brüstle, a professor who studies stem cells at Germany’s Bonn University.

Additionally, the few key genes involved in the stem cell conversion process can drive the formation of cancer if left active. That’s why Brüstle and his team have looked for other ways of de-aging cells without going through a pluripotent state. In their recent study published in Aging Cell, the researchers started with blood cells from people of various ages, including an infant and a 101-year-old donor.

They guided these cells into a younger state but not all the way toward becoming embryonic-like stem cells. And as this transformation progressed, the chemical signals in the DNA that help estimate a cell’s age also changed. In less than two months of reprogramming, one biomarker in particular was set back as far as 60 years.

Aging continued to reverse even when the scientists drastically reduced the cells’ ability to multiply. Therefore, the apparent rejuvenation can’t be explained solely by the fact that the cells were dividing and producing new cells over and over again. However, the mechanism that did erase these signs of aging is still unclear.

“The hope is that you actually can do this systemically in the entire animal,” Brüstle says. “But if you think about applying it in a patient, then you want to be sure this is not a lab experiment, so it's about finding the mechanism.”

The researchers also shifted the blood cells specifically into a kind of cell that produces neurons. One caveat is that blood cells and neurons age on different timelines, so the extent of the reversal could be exaggerated by the use of a different measuring stick. The authors acknowledge this limitation in their paper, though this discrepancy couldn’t account for all the age-associated biomarkers that reversed course.

Blood cells getting brainy also would not be a desirable result if you gave a patient a de-aging drug, but it would be useful for other regenerative medicine purposes. However, what Brüstle sees as one of the most exciting outcomes of the study is the information gleaned about the process of de-aging.

Usually, making stem cells is quick. That’s useful for many experiments, but it doesn’t give researchers the chance to study cells as they shed the markers of age. In this recent study, since the scientists were able to slowly turn back the cells’ biological clocks, they could track each step of de-aging. “Now we can actually try to dissect the process much more easily than having an instantaneous event,” Brüstle says.

Scientists began converting adult cells back into stem cells two decades ago, but we’ve known very little about how the subsequent de-aging occurs. This means when clinical researchers test potential medical interventions for age-related conditions, they haven’t always had a reliable measure to compare against.
“Now we have a model” Brüstle says. “You can work along this, and now you can probe a zillion things. What impacts the process? This will lead you to the mechanisms. That’s our hope.”
Additional reporting from Anna Rogers.

items.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
items.description: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

items.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.
But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

items.title: Mercury and Venus Retrogrades Are Over But the Chaos Isn’t
items.description: Temp check: How are we feeling, hmm? The past several weeks have been nothing short of nutty, and the combo-platter retrograde has certainly been to blame. Both Mercury (the planet of communication) and Venus (symbolizing our values) have been going backwards,
items.author: Aliza Kelly
paragraphs: Temp check: How are we feeling, hmm? The past several weeks have been nothing short of nutty, and the combo-platter retrograde has certainly been to blame. Both Mercury (the planet of communication) and Venus (symbolizing our values) have been going backwards, wrecking havoc in virtually every aspect of our lives.

But on November 13 — yes, Friday the 13th (naturally) — both Mercury and Venus go direct, concluding their retrograde motions and entering the final phase: retroshade. So what does that mean? Is this hellscape finally going to freeze over? Are you going to be okay? Behold! Everything you need to know about the dramatic end to this very tumultuous season — and exactly what it means for you.
Wait, so Mercury retrograde is over?!

Yes, friend — finally. On October 24, Mercury went backward, beginning its three-week chaos-fest around communication, travel, transportation, technology, and basically everything we rely on for our day-to-day lives. Phew. From missed connections to technological malfunctions to conversations that escalated to flipping tables, Mercury retrograde has been keeping us on our toes.

Mercury goes retrograde approximately three or four times per year, so while it’s hardly a rare astrological occurrence, each backbend has its own unique characteristics. In this case, Mercury went retrograde in Scorpio, the zodiac sign associated with secrets, intimacy, power, and transformation, meaning that in addition to the usual logistical calamities, this retrograde had a particularly psychological dimension.

Scorpio is the detective of the zodiac, determined to uncover whatever is lurking beneath the surface. So over the past three weeks, even the most ordinary conversations may have revealed deeper layers: clandestine motives, power imbalances, and even ancient insecurities. It’s been a lot!
And Venus retrograde is over, too? That’s a thing!?

Oh, honey, is it ever! Exactly three weeks before Mercury went backward, on October 3, Venus — the planet of values, romance, and worthiness — began its own retrograde cycle, initiating a powerful period of reflection around love, desire, and, perhaps most importantly, confidence.Venus retrograde is considerably less common than Mercury retrograde, occurring approximately once every 18 months and lasting about 40 days. During this time, everything Venus governs becomes subject to reevaluation, from our romantic relationships, to our financial habits, to our personal aesthetics, and to our understanding of self-worth. You may have found yourself reconsidering relationships, questioning your professional arrangements, or even realizing that the version of self you’ve been presenting no longer matches the person you’ve become. And perhaps these revelations have been uncomfortable — especially as they’ve shifted our status quo. But that’s the entire point.

You see — from even an astronomical perspective — Venus undergoes a remarkable transformation during its retrograde, transitioning from an evening star (rising during sunset) to a morning star (rising before sunrise). And astrologically, this celestial metamorphosis mirrors our own emotional evolution: We enter the retrograde with one understanding of ourselves, venture into unfamiliar territory, and emerge with an entirely new perspective.

This particular Venus retrograde began in Scorpio before moving backward into Libra, two zodiac signs that explore relationships from very different angles. Scorpio is concerned with intimacy, vulnerability, and the complicated dynamics of trust, while Libra focuses on partnership, reciprocity, and finding balance. Together, these energies encouraged us to explore the intersection of our individual needs and our expectations of others. And as we prepare to wrap up this retrograde, it’s abundantly clear just how much has changed.
So… what does it mean that they were both retrograde together — and ending their retrogrades the same day?

The day Mercury retrograde began (October 24) was the same exact day Venus formed its “inferior conjunction” with the Sun — the exact halfway point of Venus retrograde — when Venus shifted her place in the sky and transformed from an evening star into a morning star. In other words, just as Venus was delivering some of the most significant revelations of her entire retrograde cycle, Mercury added an extra layer of intensity, asking us to investigate how we express these breakthroughs.

Of course, there have also been plenty of challenges along the way, both logistically (through delays, travel snafus, and technological meltdowns) and emotionally (via misunderstandings, strange disagreements, and even heightened suspicions). But this Mercury retrograde has also offered us the opportunity to examine situations from perspectives we may not have previously considered. When Mercury goes backward, we also find ourselves altering our point of view — and sometimes looking at something at a different vantage yields the exact breakthrough we’ve been searching for.

All in all, this Mercury-Venus retrograde combo-platter has shifted virtually every aspect of reality. Anecdotally, I’ve witnessed more breakups, career changes, and friendship shake-ups over the past six weeks than I’ve encountered during the rest of the year. People are standing up for themselves, reevaluating their commitments, and demanding more from their lives, which naturally means that certain outdated dynamics are beginning to fall away. And while these changes can be challenging, the past six weeks have also been tremendously inspiring, particularly because these pivots are rooted in a deeper understanding of personal worth.
And now, on Friday, November 13, both Mercury and Venus are ending their retrogrades on the very same day.
So now what? What’s “retroshade?”

Before you pop the bubbly, there’s one more important piece of the puzzle we need to discuss. Every planetary retrograde consists of three distinct phases: the pre-retrograde shadow, the retrograde itself, and the post-retrograde shadow. Before a planet stations retrograde, it travels across the section of the zodiac where it will soon go backward (the shadow period), introducing themes and circumstances that will become increasingly significant when the planet formally reverses. Then, as the planet flips (retrograde), and it retraces those same degrees, encouraging us to reconsider whatever unfolded during the initial passage. Finally, when the planet stations direct, it travels across that territory for a third and final time (retroshade), giving us an opportunity to integrate the insights we’ve gained along the way.

Although Mercury and Venus are both officially moving forward on November 13, they will continue traveling through their post-retrograde shadow periods, which means we’ll be revisiting some of the same themes that have been developing since early October. Fortunately, this final phase offers us an opportunity to approach familiar circumstances with a completely different understanding of ourselves.

Mercury’s post-retrograde shadow will last through November 30, during which time the planet of communication will retrace its steps through Scorpio, helping us revisit unresolved conversations, clarify misunderstandings, and make sense of the information we’ve uncovered. If you’ve been struggling to articulate something important, you may find that the words begin coming together more easily over the next few weeks.

Venus’s post-retrograde shadow, meanwhile, will go through December 15, giving us an additional time to integrate this bounty of revelations surrounding our relationships, finances, and self-worth. Venus will retrace the territory she covered through Libra and Scorpio, encouraging us to revisit the circumstances that initially prompted us to reconsider our priorities. Think of this retroshade as the integration phase: A gentle onboarding that teaches us how to adjust to our new reality and prepares us to step into this brand-new tomorrow.

First and foremost: movement! With Mercury and Venus finally going direct, conversations that have been postponed, decisions that have felt overwhelming, and situations that have been stuck in limbo will begin gaining momentum. We’ve spent the past six weeks discovering what we want, what we deserve, and what needs to change, and now it’s time to figure out what to actually do with that information. Whatever revelations have emerged, consider how you can begin making choices that put them into action. You’ll soon discover that the best part of the retrograde season is what happens next.
