items.title: The Nvidia Cheating Scandal Is Getting Messier
items.description: While we all wait around wondering which British hunk is going to be the next James Bond, might I interest you in some real-life espionage drama? On Sunday, Nvidia CEO and leather-jacket lover Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an affair with a woman suspec
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: While we all wait around wondering which British hunk is going to be the next James Bond, might I interest you in some real-life espionage drama? On Sunday, Nvidia CEO and leather-jacket lover Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The company’s board of directors announced on Sunday that it was initiating an investigation following reporting that Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” On Thursday, Huang resigned from Nvidia following a report of a second affair, this time with an executive at the company. Here’s what you need to know.
Remind me what Nvidia does, please.

Nvidia’s main products are artificial-intelligence chips, technology that powers nearly all machine learning in the U.S. The company is currently valued at $3.96 trillion (down from over $4 trillion earlier this week) and is one of the major tech companies currently bolstering the U.S. economy. The export of Nvidia chips has been intensely restricted since 2022, when the U.S. began to push for dominance in the AI race.
How did a spy get involved?

Last month, the New York Times reported that the U.S. suspected that Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), an executive at a Singapore-based data-center company called Megaspeed, had given intelligence to China and possibly sent Nvidia AI chips to the country. A week later, the paper reported that Alice had been recruited as a spy by China’s Ministry of State Security in order to get close to Jensen and learn more about Nvidia’s top-of-the-line AI chips. It’s unclear when exactly Alice was purportedly recruited, but according to the Times, part of her mission was to influence Nvidia to advocate for its chips to be made available in China.

The timeline of Jensen and Alice’s relationship is also murky. The pair were photographed sitting next to each other at a tech-industry party in Taipei in June 2024, around the same time her company began purchasing what would wind up being billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips. In May 2025, they were filmed dining together with other execs at a restaurant in Taipei, and the Times reported that she gave him a kiss on the cheek. Before Nvidia announced its investigation, company spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times that interactions between his CEO and Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected” and that she was merely one of the “thousands of customer executives” he speaks with every year.
One thing we do know is that Alice was kind of obsessed with posting photos of her and Jensen to her social-media feeds. Apparently, he was all over her WeChat and Weibo pages. Is that good spycraft?
What did Nvidia say about all of this?

On Sunday, the company announced an independent investigation into Jensen allegedly being targeted by a spy. The Nvidia board said it has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

In his own letter to the board, Jensen acknowledged having an extramarital affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he wrote. Huang said that he takes “full responsibility” for what he’s done and that he hopes he can “earn back” his family’s trust. He has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, and they have two grown children.

Huang also acknowledged the “national security concerns” in recent reports and promised that he is a good old-fashioned patriot. “I love our country and our company,” he said. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
Did President Trump know about this?

Yes, and he didn’t really care. Last year, President Trump — who has a close relationship with Jensen Huang — was reportedly briefed that Alice Huang was relaying information about Nvidia to Beijing but did nothing about it. This past spring, per the Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned Trump officials that Jensen was in a close relationship with Alice Huang. The memo arrived ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, where Jensen ultimately joined him, though the Times reported that he was not initially on the invite list. It’s unclear whether or not his exclusion was related to the memo.

Amid Jensen’s scandal, Trump is still riding for his pal. Speaking to reporters on Sunday night, the president said that the Nvidia CEO is an “honorable guy.” “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump said. The president added that Huang “probably had an excuse” and that he’s “done an amazing job for our country.” Of course, that was before the Times reported on a second affair.
What’s this about more cheating?

According to five sources who spoke to the Times, Jensen had a separate affair, though this one was less a matter of national security and more classically gauche. The Times reported on Wednesday that he had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care. Powell reported directly to Jensen. She is also married.
So is Jensen getting fired?

He can’t get fired, he quit! On Thursday, Jensen announced his resignation from Nvidia. In a press release, the company announced that executive vice-president and chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO. “Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a statement.
Does this mean I should scoop up some Nvidia stock?

Great question. The company’s stock took a nosedive following the news of Jensen’s departure, falling more than 10 percent at the NYSE opening bell. I am fairly certain that’s bad for them but maybe good for you? I don’t know; I zone out during the money parts of Industry.
This post has been updated.

items.title: ‘I Love My Boyfriend — But Is He Rich Enough?’
items.description: I’m 28, and I’ve been dating my boyfriend, who’s 38, for about a month. Somehow, I’ve already found myself in an inconvenient place where I genuinely love him (which I know is absolutely insane to say a month in, but let me explain) — while simultaneously wond
items.author: Amy Rose Spiegel
paragraphs: I’m 28, and I’ve been dating my boyfriend, who’s 38, for about a month. Somehow, I’ve already found myself in an inconvenient place where I genuinely love him (which I know is absolutely insane to say a month in, but let me explain) — while simultaneously wondering if I should walk away.

I recently went through aggressive cancer treatment. I’m in remission now, so thank God I’m back to man problems and not “am I going to live” problems. Still, I lost my hair and have a lot of residual health issues. He’s more understanding about them than I ever could have imagined. Also, he’s sweet, funny, affectionate, and very into me. He makes me feel cared for in a way nobody else has. The sex is out of this world. We have an incredible connection, and he’s been very clear that he wants a wife and children someday. I can picture a version of my future with him. But there are some things I can’t stop thinking about.

I’ve come to the extremely ugly realization that, while I love my boyfriend, I want to marry someone richer. I’m not looking for someone to fund my life. I’m ambitious and independent; I have my own money and career. But I want a partner whose financial situation makes me feel secure and whose lifestyle is closer to the one I envision for myself. My boyfriend has a normal income and is still living with his mother, partly because he helps care for her. (He’s also slightly shorter than me, which bugs me a little.) Even writing this makes me feel like the worst person on earth.

After my health scare, I told myself I would set extremely high standards, especially because my last boyfriend abandoned me during the hardest moments of my life. So that part of me thinks that I’m only one month into this relationship and I’m already doing an enormous amount of mental gymnastics to justify it when I barely know the guy. But I also don’t want to waste his time when I know, long-term, he’ll probably want to put a ring on my finger.

The most conflicting part: Despite all of this, I don’t actually want to break up with him right now, no matter what I ultimately decide. I want to keep dating him. I love him. I’m attracted to him. I have fun with him. I have great sex with him. I want to see where this goes. And I wonder whether the desire to be with a well-off man is actually mine, or whether I learned it in a previous relationship where money and financial security were constantly emphasized. But I also don’t want to stay because I’m afraid I’ll never find someone better. I’ve worked very hard to build the life I want, and after my cancer changed my perspective on life, I’ve become more determined not to settle.
Am I making a mistake by continuing to date someone who, on paper, makes me question whether I could marry him? Or is it completely reasonable to keep dating while I discover more about who he is?
Most important: Is “I love him, but I want someone richer” a legitimate relationship incompatibility? Or am I being an asshole? I’d love an honest answer, even if the answer is that I’m the problem.

Hey, Healthy Perspective. I’m so glad to hear you’re in remission, though sorry to hear you are such an asshole. Just kidding! I’m not shocked or appalled by anything in your letter. There’s nothing amoral in wondering, post-chemo at 28, how to reconfigure your newly updated understanding of stability. Nor is it wrong to wonder if your age-gap sweetheart is The One, even if it’s only been a calendar month, even if he only has a “normal income.” (I laughed. I like you!)

Still, and I hate to tell you this: I really tried to write a few answers that zeroed in on this 38-year-old newcomer’s place in your life. All of them ultimately struck me as dishonest. I don’t think your letter is about your monthlong boyfriend’s net worth, like, at all. It’s irritating to dwell on cancer when you’d prefer to move back to man problems, but they’re linked. I promise I don’t want to simper to you about how you’re a survivor and we’re going to hear you roar! Illness and treatment have changed your perspective. You’re figuring out how, next, to live. While this is never easy, it at least used to be semiautomatic.

Maybe getting into a relationship not long after such a major life event feels like nailing down the furniture before another big one hits. Especially considering you felt abandoned by your last boyfriend and you’re anxious — and that would be true no matter how lovely this new guy is. Life is an ambush. Of course you’re inclined to ask, Does this man have enough money to keep me safe? Even when you are safe, and you have enough money to support yourself. Writing checklists about your perfect husband can feel like protection against dread. But you’re wise to wonder, too, if it’s possible all you’re protecting yourself from is falling in love with a worthy person.

I hope I can stretch a hand back through the past few years for you to hold. I was diagnosed with cancer at 31. It’s well-managed four years later. We’ve doubtlessly had different experiences; all people do. I never went through chemo or lost my hair, and I’m sorry you did. But for all we don’t have in common, you and I still know things others can’t, including that sex and romance remain priorities for career women such as ourselves, even when you’re hanging out in the hospital a lot.

Early on, my oncologist told me the cancer I have isn’t environmental. I didn’t smoke too much or not eat enough blueberries, thus, bam, fatal outcome. Nor is what I have a hereditary family heirloom, passed down like my Italo-shtetl nose through an odd combo of recessive genes. “It’s random, like God took a little segment of your genome and pinched it,” the doctor said, making a twisting motion with his index finger and thumb. No one could have prevented it, there is no cure, it might get worse. Interesting. So what could I control? And how fast? This is my fight song!!!

Even though embracing nihilism was seriously right there, I instead became dictatorial about what would happen next. Pre-diagnosis, I thought marriage was insane. After, I was certain it was the rational next step with my boyfriend, with whom I shared an apartment and a profound, impossible-to-articulate mutual unease. I reasoned that relationships were about compromise. Time to be mature. Because what if I got really sick?

All the while, I was obsessive about employment in the signature key of Americans who need “yes, forever” medications. (Mine is an interferon that reduces the risk of my cancer progressing into leukemia. Its sticker price is $20,000 per monthly dose. I only recently stopped rationing injections, just in case.) I walked around my workplace and heard its noises differently. Did everyone overdoing the professional jargon secretly have cancer? Death’s call rang out in every desperate, assimilating “circle back.” No, yeah, this email does find me — for now! Ha ha ha.

I wasn’t going to panic out loud, though. I was seriously going to be so okay. I urgently searched for cancer’s big important lessons, then rushed to apply them. Possibly like you, I knew intellectually that the nobility and profundity of cancer was a fable about a notoriously complicated group of illnesses. Still, I preferred this interpretation to other popular favorites, including, “You die, horribly for you and everyone you love” or rubber bracelets stamped #BadAssSurvivorChica.

Unlike death’s vast morass and #WarriorBitchLikeAGirl, “I’m learning big beautiful lessons!” is a workable approach, aesthetically and practically, when you’re about 30. It’s similar to the script we’re already fed: You’ve reached the knowing age. You’ve figured out your ethical belief systems, not to mention what hairstyles actually flatter your face. Maybe you can afford to live on your own, given your diligence at work. Life is coalescing!

Healthy Perspective, nothing could have interrupted my self-actualization reverie. Was it like that for you? Oh, my body is overdoing it, to a potentially fatal degree, cell-division-wise? Just another story to pluckily locate a moral for! You’ve partially built the stability you have, I bet, through dogged optimism. Me too. It’s fab! But it can make me too hasty to decipher the promise in every heartbreak. Death is, by definition, not just another amazing new opportunity for your future.

Plus, cancer warps and rarefies time. It’s whiplash inducing. Out of nowhere, you maybe don’t have a future? Then you access treatment, and there it is, once more. You’re not going to idly take it for granted this time! You’ve Learned From Cancer. So you make lists about money. You will not be caught unawares again.

Treatment is only the start. From there, whenever I talked or wrote in my journal about what I wanted from marriage, it felt like repeating the promise that I was becoming healthier. It was not ever about love. More so, it was about worthiness and a sort of gameness toward what “rationally” came next in life. I insisted I wasn’t afraid. I was making a plan. I wanted to get wifed up by a heterosexual office job because I thought it would help, in some way, to keep me alive.

But I was already alive. The “survivor” mind-set is a boondoggle even if you’re positive you’re too smart for it, badass chica! When I came to my senses and broke up with my then-boyfriend because he was a broke bitch — I’m just playing; he was great, but we weren’t compatible, which got too sad to ignore — he thought I was out of my mind. How could I leave, given how nice he was to me about my cancer? He pointed out that he had been there for me throughout all the hard times.
“That’s absolutely true, and I’m grateful,” I said. “But shouldn’t there also be good times?”

You’re having them. You’re in your late 20s, excited by someone who’s been consistently kind for the 30 days you’ve known him. Incredible! You already know this is the answer, per the end of your letter. Yes, it’s fine to step back and see what happens now. (Especially when you’re still sorting out how you feel after your last breakup.) Keep your standards in mind, but don’t rule out revisions at the expense of your happiness.

Also? The “big lessons” of cancer are very, very boring in the end. Always the same texture-free bromides about strength and, also, the power of being strong. More interesting is individuated, ambiguous self-discovery. Great news, my diva: It seems like that means continuing to have hot sex with your short boyfriend, just for now, just to see.

I understand and think it’s fair if you’re annoyed that I made your new-boyfriend letter about cancer. I would have been. But my gut tells me that, thanks to your ex, you already know that money alone doesn’t fortify a relationship, unless that’s most or all of what you’re looking for. Either way, I trust your discernment.

You seem to need me, instead, to say: Even if — when! — life ambushes you again, you’ll know what to do. Real stability means not jumping to decisions out of insecurity, whether you’re feeling it about death or love or anything else. You’re capable of changing your mind, come what may with this boyfriend of 30 days.

Please actively try to reorient your sense of time. Feel your way through each arriving day, the only one like it. In “On the Shortness of Life,” Seneca wrote, “The greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which hangs upon tomorrow and loses today.” (Was Seneca a hot woman of about 30 with cancer? Historians of Roman Stoicism, weigh in.) Turning toward the present is about all there is to conclude, big lessons-wise. I think? Unless I missed the entire point of cancer? It’s possible! I have time to find out. Maybe. I’m choosing to think that I do.

You do too. When you get antsy, put $10 in your 401(k) and think, I throw my head back and laugh at Death! Read this poem about being 28 years old and observing the sunlight in your yard. The person who wrote it is now dead. Still, you can tell the warmth wasn’t wasted when the light washed over him. X ARS

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 12, 2026
items.description: The moon starts the day in Sagittarius, and you’ll benefit from a generally optimistic atmosphere until it moves into Capricorn in the afternoon, when your focus and discipline might suddenly snap back into place. You’ll understand that the universe won’t simp
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: The moon starts the day in Sagittarius, and you’ll benefit from a generally optimistic atmosphere until it moves into Capricorn in the afternoon, when your focus and discipline might suddenly snap back into place. You’ll understand that the universe won’t simply drop everything you want into your lap — if you want to make big things happen, you can’t count on anyone else to do the work for you. You have the power to make a real difference today, and it’s up to you to use it.

You know from experience that hard work doesn’t always get results. You can do everything “right” and still fail to get the outcome you wanted. Sometimes, the disappointment is enough to convince you it’s not worth trying at all. Today, though, don’t give in to your pessimistic side — because if you put in the work right now, it will pay off soon. The reward might not come about in precisely the way you envisioned, but trust it’ll be worth it all the same.

You try to assess problems with a practical lens. You need real, concrete solutions; you understand that wishful thinking won’t help you solve the issues in front of you. But make sure you’re not curtailing your imagination in your attempt to be pragmatic. If you don’t like the options available to you, see if you can think up a better alternative before you accept something less than ideal. There’s usually another way, if you’re willing to look for it.

Today, you might find yourself overanalyzing your interactions. People’s words will seem to hold deeper meaning; you’ll imagine that if you pay close enough attention, you’ll finally figure out how people really feel about you. It’s possible you will find some valuable insights by digging deeper in this way. But be careful not to get worked up over every little comment. Remember that people often speak without thinking and not all of their words need to be taken so seriously.

When you’re faced with a challenge, you attempt to figure it out on your own first before turning to anyone else. But sometimes you take your independence too far; you end up struggling with problems that could be easily resolved if you simply asked for help. Today, don’t be too proud to lean on the people around you. You don’t have anything to prove — everyone knows that you’re capable! — so don’t make things harder than they need to be. Let your people support you.

Sometimes you believe that the ends justify the means. Taking the occasional shortcut, or even putting your principles aside in the name of compromise, is sometimes necessary in service of a worthwhile goal. But right now, consider that the process is more important than the results. Take care today to carry yourself in a way you can be proud of, even if it seems like it’s slowing you down. In the long run, you’ll be glad you did.

You sometimes get the impression that nobody’s really listening to what you’re saying. Maybe they’re not purposefully ignoring you, but they’re so preoccupied by their own lives and problems that they fail to see yours. But today, don’t be too sure that others aren’t paying attention to you. Chances are, they’re aware of more than you think, and they’re taking your words more seriously than you realize. Your opinions carry real weight with the people in your life, and they’re likely to take your advice to heart, so try to be thoughtful about what you say.

You’re someone with a strong sense of duty. You feel you have a responsibility to change the world. So when you’re forced to deal with small problems rather than bigger, more significant ones, you worry you’re somehow wasting your potential. But this kind of thinking does more harm than good; it could trick you into thinking that small efforts don’t make a difference. Today, focus on solving problems within your own sphere of influence — your community, your friend group, even your own home. Realize that you can do so much good in your immediate circle. It might not feel like much, but the effects will ripple outward.

Maybe a normal, unexciting day sounds pretty great at the moment. You wouldn’t mind sitting back and relaxing for a bit! But don’t give into this urge just yet. If you seek out simplicity and ease today, you’ll ironically end up feeling restless and edgy. In order to feel happy and fulfilled, you need a challenge. Don’t take on more than you can handle, but don’t go too easy on yourself either. Facing an obstacle or two will prove to be invigorating, not stressful.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You try never to make things more difficult than necessary; you understand that the simplest solutions are often the most effective. Today, though, remember that some situations are genuinely complex, and the answers might not be straightforward. Your challenge is to stop wishing for an obvious solution or a single magic word that’ll solve everything; instead, deal with the complicated reality. Once you accept that you’re not going to find a quick fix, you can finally get serious about doing the slow — but useful and rewarding — work that’s required right now.

Sometimes you feel like you’re trying to prove yourself to others. You want to demonstrate that you’re cool and smart and interesting, that your ideas are worthy of consideration. But today, remind yourself that you don’t have to put on a show. If you’re tired of performing, you can decide you’re not going to do it any more: You are who you are, and there’s no point in trying to convince people otherwise. Some of them will recognize how much you have to offer, and others won’t. Either way, their opinions don’t have to be your problem anymore.

You’re likely to be more sensitive than usual today — and you might be inclined to hide it. You’ll imagine that carrying yourself with extra confidence, even a bit of bravado, will ensure nobody knows you’re vulnerable. But while your façade might manage to fool people, it could also make you seem arrogant and unapproachable. You’ll be better off letting people know how you’re actually feeling. That way, they’ll make an extra effort to treat you with the care you need right now.

Today, make a point of showing up for others even if you’d prefer not to. Sometimes, caring for some of the people in your life might feel like more hassle than it’s worth. But remember that a day will come when you’ll be the one who needs help. The more effort you put in to build your community right now, the stronger your support system will be in the future.
Buy Claire Comstock-Gay’s book, Madame Clairevoyant’s Guide to the Stars, here.

paragraphs: 25 Gifts For The Woman Who Has Everything & Wants Nothing
Lola Blankets Wild Moss Medium Lola Weighted Blanket

We're starting strong (and heavy) with one of Lola Blankets' weighted blankets. The beloved luxury blanket brand always has its praises sung with fans declaring that it's worth every penny. Your giftee may already own an original cozy blanket from the brand, so consider one of the weighted styles in a variety of sizes and designs if your budget allows for it.
Brighter Day Pigments DIY Watercolor Paint Set with Travel Pouch

2026 was the year of analogue hobbies, and we think the desire for hands-on activities will continue well into 2027, so why not purchase a sweet watercolor paint set? This one has a few Anthropologie-exclusive postcard prints and pouch designs to pick from. The neat watercolor pen and travel-sized paint tin are chef’s kiss for the friend who likes to get creative wherever they go.
Flamingo Estate Personalized Heritage Olive Oil

You've probably seen Flamingo Estate's iconic heirloom tomato candle in almost every gift guide (or have gifted one already), but the luxury lifestyle brand has so much more to offer. And its food, like the olive oil, shouldn't be slept on, making this personalized EVOO bottle an amazing gift for a mother, holiday host, or home chef. Write a short, sweet note and leave a long-lasting effect with your giftee.
Maison de Sabré The SABREMOJI Fruit Charm

Whether she’s a seasoned jet-setter... or a forgetful person, you can upgrade her AirTag game with these joyful fruit charms, intended to keep AirTags safe and stylish, personalizing everything from house keys to suitcases (I wear one on my work bag!). Pair it with a new AirTag for an extra thoughtful touch.
Free People Sunday Button Snood

A snood is the cozy solution to staying warm and stylish throughout the winter that isn't your everyday scarf (Because guess what? She doesn't need another one). This is a great option for your super stylish friend. She can wear it under her seasonal coat and oversized button-down top or over a cardigan for extra cozy coverage and dimension.
Shark ChillPill 3-in-1 Personal Cooling System with Fan

Shark's ChillPill fan was perhaps the most viral beauty tool of the year. And it is absolutely a little luxury, which many people say is worth the splurge. The portable fan stands out in price and quality because of the cooling plate and dry-touch mist for actually cold air. So if you're shopping for a giftee who runs hot, this is a gift they'll definitely need and want.

I've never met someone who doesn't love their Hulken rolling tote bag, including myself. While I use the large size for storage, others use it for laundry days, or opt for the smaller size for everyday commuting and grocery shopping. It's so versatile and practical, and with three sizes and multiple colors, you can pick the one that best fits your giftee's needs and lifestyle.
West Elm x Emma Chamberlain Pigeon Glasses Holder

Personally, I love Emma Chamberlain's quirky aesthetic, from her Architectural Digest home tours to her West Elm homeware collection. So if you have someone on your list with a similar aesthetic, check out the decor pieces for a gifting moment. This pigeon-shaped glasses holder is great for quirky decorators, sunglasses collectors, and NYC residents.
Bombas Merino Wool Blend Everyday Compression Knee High Socks

There's a high likelihood that your giftee already owns a pair of Bombas slippers or ankle socks. But the brand also offers compression socks that are perfect for the frequent flyer or avid hiker. And for an extra-luxurious touch, the merino wool options are extra comfy and warm.
MacKenzie-Childs Mocha Check Electric Salt & Pepper Grinder Set

Who doesn't love fancy salt and pepper shakers? These electric grinders from stylish hand-painted ceramics brand MacKenzie-Childs are an incredibly chic option to gift. Order and of the four checkered colorways to fit your giftee's space, then sit back, relax, and wait to receive shock and awe for the thoughtful present.
Ouai x Heaven Mayhem Fragrance Amulet Necklace

We can bet that even the woman who has everything doesn't have this new Heaven Mayhem necklace filled with Ouai perfume! The new collaboration consists of two vessel pendant designs and two fragrances (either warm and sensual Ibiza or floral & musky Rue St. Honoré) so that you can carry your favorite scent everywhere you go and reapply throughout the day in style.
LAnnodoMacrame Custom Hand Crank Photo Album

Especially when it comes to mothers and grandmothers, all they want is a simple, sentimental gift, like a photo album. But because you're trying to go above and beyond to impress them, consider this Etsy find, which is essentially a rolodex of your giftee's favorite memories and people. Customize the wood type, engraving, and number of photos you want, then send over a Google Photos link to the Etsy shop and they'll take care of the rest.
Miko Nest Towel Warmer with Aromatherapy

Upgrade something as simple as stepping out of the shower with a towel warmer for a not-so-expensive, spa-like environment. This bin can fit multiple towels or robes at a time, has adjustable timer and temperature settings, and releases a calming aromatherapy scent.
Big Night Aperitivo Spoons Set

For the hostess with the mostess or the girl dinner aficionado, check out Big Night's vibrant assortment of cutlery and serveware. This reusable tin set features three artsy spoons for scooping, smearing, and stirring. If you have an over-$50 budget, we also love the Snack Spreaders mini knives for a complete set perfect for charcuterie boards.
Checked Compression PackAway Closet

Travelers may not need another packing cube set, but they will appreciate a checked luggage organizer that holds their belongings and easily transforms into a hanging closet. The shelves and compartments help neatly organize an entire vacation wardrobe. Then just hook it into any hotel room to effortlessly see and pull your outfits without completely unpacking.
Granado Best-Sellers Perfume Suitcase

If you have a person on your list who loves experimenting with new fragrances or one who asks for a refill of their favorite scent year after year, go for something more unpredictable this time around. Brazilian brand Granado's tropical scents are a personal favorite (I'm still wearing the banana scent in the fall!). But if they're new to the brand, consider a suitcase full of mini perfumes so they can test and figure out their favorites before purchasing a full size.
Camp Snap Transparent Screen-Free Digital Camera

It's time to get nostalgic with a Y2K-inspired, colorful, jelly-looking camera. These Camp Snap options are like a hybrid of a digital camera and a disposable camera. While there's no screen (so you can't ruminate over getting the perfect shot), you can then connect a cable to your phone to upload the slightly grainy, retro-looking photos. It's a great companion for parties, concerts, and travels.
Quince Mongolian Cashmere Ribbed Wrap

Known for its luxe and budget-friendly cashmere, Quince needs to be on your radar when shopping for the woman who has everything. We’re thinking out of the box for your hard-to-shop-for giftee with this chic and versatile cashmere wrap.
Abbode Embroidered Dog Mom Small Croc Pouch

Abbode is a one-stop shop for the cutest and chicest personalized gifts. While there are so many styles to pick from, we've been eyeing this pouch for the dog moms in your life. This design can be personalized with several dog icons and text and used for everyday essentials, cosmetics, or travel must-haves so that your four-legged friend is never too far.

The woman who’s constantly traveling for work trips or vacations will appreciate this top-rated portable iron. The compact design — which comes in several cheerful colorways — quickly presses, steams, and irons six different fabric types, making it a practical, must-pack item.
Urban Outfitters Swan Shaped Metal Ring Holder

Sometimes we just need an unexpected design on an everyday essential, like a jewelry holder, to put a smile on our faces and make our daily routines a little less mundane. We can picture this swan ring holder, which can also hold stud earrings, elegantly perched on a bedside table or by a kitchen or bathroom sink to store rings while washing up.
Bobbi Brown x The Met Holiday-Exclusive Luxe Lipstick

Whether she's into makeup, art, or both since they often overlap, consider something from this new collaboration from Bobbi Brown and The Met. The festive holiday shades and whimsical packaging make everything — from the limited-edition eyeshadow palettes and the powder blushes to the creamy lipsticks — swoon- and gift-worthy.
Devyn Samara My Favorite Book Keepsake Necklace

You really can't go wrong with any gifts from Uncommon Goods, but these book locket necklaces stood out, especially if you're shopping for an avid reader. If you can't come up with a new book recommendation, consider this necklace, which highlights one of your giftee's favorite classic books, like Pride & Prejudice or The Great Gatsby.
Pura 12-Day Advent Calendar

While you may love carting up seasonal candles for yourself, we promise that the hard-to-shop-for woman in your life doesn't want another one. Instead, check out this unique advent calendar, which includes a Pura fragrance diffuser with 12 fragrances to unbox and try throughout the year. Then, she can keep the diffuser and re-stock her favorite scents to fill her space.
PalmRidge Custom Handcrafted Aluminum Matchbox Holder

At this point, you may have seen these custom matchboxes across many TikTok gift guides, and they're just so good that we had to include them here too! Pick from various embossed design options like cherries and butterflies or custom names and birth years. These are a sweet and unique gift (especially during the widespread matchbook obsession) to have lying around the house.

items.title: Why ‘patient influencers’ should come with a health warning | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Emily Miller was a 20-year-old university student in the UK when, shortly after a COVID-19 infection, she started having sensations that mirrored a heart attack. Other bewildering symptoms followed – dizziness, fainting, and uncontrollable muscle spasms. ‘By t
items.author: Zoe Cunniffe
paragraphs: Emily Miller was a 20-year-old university student in the UK when, shortly after a COVID-19 infection, she started having sensations that mirrored a heart attack. Other bewildering symptoms followed – dizziness, fainting, and uncontrollable muscle spasms. ‘By the time my classes ended I felt drunk, disoriented and my ears would ring,’ Miller wrote in a pinned post on her Instagram page, @thatgirlwithlongcovid_. ‘I couldn’t remember getting home from class.’

Miller is a ‘patient influencer’ – one of a growing number of people who share vivid accounts of their health experiences on social media. She first started posting about life with long COVID because her experience was incredibly isolating while her peers were still partying and going to classes like normal, and she hoped posting online would connect her with other young people in the same situation. Today, she has a small but engaged community of about 4,000 followers on Instagram and 3,000 on TikTok. Miller shares intimate details of life with long COVID, such as photo timelines outlining the onset of her symptoms and videos discussing everyday difficulties.

Patient influencers like Miller often build deeply personal bonds with their followers, many of whom live with the same condition. On a recent pair of Miller’s posts featuring the medical interventions that did and didn’t help her, followers have posted long comments detailing their own treatment experiences and thanking her for her advice.

As valuable as chronic illness content is for spreading awareness and building communities around stigmatised illnesses – maybe you too have found a sense of support and camaraderie from individuals whose experiences you identify with – there are also concerning aspects to this new trend. At the heart of it is the way social media serves up a distorted version of reality, drawing on selected content from patient influencers in ways that often don’t reflect the full range of chronic illness experiences people have in real life.

Patient influencers are often well meaning but can find themselves forced to choose between leaning into these narratives and losing engagement. ‘You’re not [posting] for followers or to get as many views as you possibly can,’ says Miller, ‘but you do want [your content] to be reaching the right people.’

Like Miller, Kaysie was in college when she first developed symptoms she couldn’t make sense of. Along with dizziness and sleepiness, Kaysie started falling down frequently. ‘It was super unclear exactly what the problem was,’ she says.

Hoping to alleviate her uncertainty, Kaysie turned to Reddit – another online environment where patient influencers share their stories and advice – where she saw her symptoms reflected in people’s posts about postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), an autonomic nervous system disorder that causes dizziness and fainting. Reading other people’s stories was comforting, giving Kaysie a framework to make sense of what was happening.

Diagnosis of a chronic illness can take years, particularly for conditions like POTS that aren’t well-understood, so it’s understandable why patients like Kaysie may be drawn to social media’s focus on diagnostic labels (a 2025 study led by the paediatrician Lindsey Daon analysed hundreds of chronic illness posts on Instagram and found that 87 per cent mentioned a specific diagnostic label). Yet this desire for the certainty of a diagnosis can lead to problems. Patient influencers with their own specific diagnosis often list the early signs of their illness that they originally overlooked – such as constant exhaustion, joint pain and dizziness. But symptoms like these can be associated with many different conditions, and followers who latch onto an influencer’s diagnosis often do so prematurely.
People become vigilant to body sensations that match their expectations, and filter out sensations that don’t

This is exactly what happened to Kaysie. Two years after being convinced by patient influencers that she had POTS, she was diagnosed by medical professionals with a different condition – narcolepsy. She learned that she was actually falling down because narcolepsy can cause cataplexy, a sudden, temporary loss of muscle control. ‘I definitely ended up on a weird path that wasn’t quite accurate,’ she says.

A related concern is that patient influencers can teach their followers to centre their own identities around a diagnostic label. ‘I’ve seen people that have ultimately felt a lot of grief because they really feel that they don’t have much left, other than their illness,’ says Sara Davin, a pain psychologist at the Cleveland Clinic.

Patient influencers could also be affecting their followers’ symptoms through a process called social transmission. Health researchers believe this phenomenon occurs because, when people develop expectations about what they should experience, they become vigilant to body sensations that match these expectations, and filter out sensations that don’t.

A 2023 study makes this process vivid. Participants observed someone else undergoing a virtual reality (VR) experience before undergoing it themselves. What participants didn’t know was that some of the people they observed were actors, who modelled the symptoms of cybersickness, a feeling of nausea and discomfort sometimes caused by VR.

Participants were told that the study was about online learning in VR, assessed through a series of memory-based questions, but the researchers’ real aim was to measure participants’ cybersickness. They found that those who viewed an apparently sick actor subsequently reported feeling more cybersickness symptoms themselves, compared with other participants who saw someone use the VR without getting sick. The study serves as a proof of concept confirming that seeing other people’s health experiences can shape our own.

Social media may be an especially fertile breeding ground for this kind of symptom transmission because of its ability to rapidly spread information across large populations. ‘In real life, you only have so much that you can actually observe,’ explains Winston Tan, lead author of the VR study. In contrast, he says that as soon as you go online, you can easily access thousands of people’s stories – and once you start engaging with them, the algorithm is more likely to keep feeding them to you, further heightening your expectations about having these experiences yourself.

None of this means that people’s health experiences should be dismissed just because they see themselves in patient influencer content – after all, the initial draw of the content is that it reflects what they’ve already been experiencing. In these cases, social transmission may be less about causing symptoms in people who were completely healthy and more about intensifying existing symptoms or adding new ones.

One of the most prominent social media-transmitted illnesses is the ‘TikTok tics’ of 2020-21, when neurologists began seeing increasing numbers of teenage patients with tics, or sudden, involuntary movements and sounds. Experts believe this trend was driven by the spread of videos from users with Tourette syndrome, and exacerbated by the anxiety of the COVID-19 pandemic (anxiety is thought to increase the social transmission of symptoms).
Repeated exposure to this highly medicalised content could prompt users to develop false beliefs

Unfortunately, social media algorithms tend to favour exactly those health-related posts that evoke fear and stress. Breonna Winfield (posting on Instagram as @healthywealthydivinesociety) coaches patient influencers and other content creators on how to build their followings. She explains that engagement is best when content is ‘drastic’ or ‘over the top’. She tells me about one particularly successful post that came from a client whose doctors repeatedly told her she just needed to lose weight – until, finally, the client learned that her symptoms were caused by a 30-pound fibroid lodged in her uterus. ‘People were shocked,’ Winfield says. ‘Personal stories that connect with their audience, those go the farthest.’

Daon’s study of Instagram posts backs up this idea. She found that posts featuring photos of invasive medical equipment tended to overperform, or receive more engagement, than other posts from the same account.

She warns that repeated exposure to this highly medicalised content could prompt users to develop false beliefs about the level of treatment their own condition requires. After all, research has shown that knowledge of other people’s personal experiences plays a key role in patients’ healthcare decision-making. Daon tells me she has even noticed patients asking for invasive treatments such as feeding tubes just because they’ve seen them online.

While this phenomenon may seem harmless in a world where doctors still need to prescribe treatments before patients can access them, research shows that patient requests have major influence over what physicians prescribe. (In one study, patients with sciatica symptoms who requested a strong narcotic were significantly more likely to receive one than those who didn’t – which is concerning, the study’s authors noted, because narcotic pain medications aren’t generally recommended for managing sciatica.)

Of course, most patient influencers want to help their followers, not hurt them – and when created with that intention, their content can be a source of comfort and patient education. Now that she has a confirmed diagnosis, Kaysie finds personal stories from Reddit much more useful than she used to. ‘You Google narcolepsy symptoms, and it’s always very general diagnostic information,’ she says. Reading about others’ experiences online has helped her figure out things that her doctor wouldn’t have known about, such as the fact that her cataplexy can be triggered by laughter.

Ella, a young woman who experiences chronic pain, says she finds social media useful for managing her symptoms even though she doesn’t have a specific diagnosis. ‘You don’t have to be diagnosed with something to treat yourself,’ she says. She’s also found ways to protect herself from the risks of harmful or misleading content by being more savvy online. She’s come across illness-related content that she found problematic at times – posts that seemed focused on stirring up emotions more than anything – but she’s noticed that avoiding engaging with this content has trained her algorithm to give her less of it. ‘I only interact with posts that are either educational, people being curious, or some kind of positive take,’ Ella explains. ‘I don’t want to just see people fight about things.’

Other ways to benefit from patient influencers while protecting yourself from the risks include deliberately seeking out people’s positive experiences (in the cybersickness study, researchers found that participants were actually less likely to experience cybersickness if they observed someone undergoing VR without these symptoms than if they didn’t observe anyone at all).
She wants her content to ease viewers’ anxieties, which means working against the algorithm’s desire for emotional stimulation

It’s also important to be wary of posts that centre on medical treatment, keeping in mind that one person’s need for a treatment does not mean everyone with the same condition will need it too. Other people’s experiences can be a valuable source of emotional support and lifestyle advice, but when it comes to the biomedical side of life with chronic illness, speaking to a doctor or finding reputable online sources is more reliable.

Meanwhile, even as the algorithm’s authority over social media content increases, there are still creators who refuse to tailor their content to its demands. ‘It’s important for me to be authentic,’ says Talia Cohen who as ‘Dr Talia PhD’ on Instagram provides chronic illness support to her 14,000-plus followers. ‘If I change myself for the algorithm, I won’t be attracting the people to my community who could really benefit.’

Cohen, who lives with chronic illness herself, wants her content to ease viewers’ anxieties, which means working against the algorithm’s desire for emotional stimulation. ‘I have a very calm tone,’ she says. ‘I don’t want to do anything that contributes to nervous system dysregulation when most people with chronic health conditions already struggle with that.’

Most of her posts are reassuring and involve either a video of her speaking or a line of text against a muted background. One from June contains a carousel of reminders that people with chronic illness may need, including sentiments such as ‘It’s allowed to be painful to think about what your body used to be able to do’ and ‘Compassion for yourself during flares is the best medicine there is.’

Refusing to conform to the algorithm doesn’t happen without consequences, of course, and Cohen has seen drops in engagement as the algorithm continues to shift its priorities. Still, she says: ‘My content will find the right people that it’s meant to find. Even if I’m helping just a few people, it’s worth it.’

items.title: A new answer to why there is something rather than nothing | Aeon Essays
items.description: Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the issue in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when
items.author: Andrew T Brenner
paragraphs: Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the issue in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when properly considered. This very obvious fact about the world – that things exist – can shift from seeming mundane and trivial to very surprising, even downright weird. Ludwig Wittgenstein expressed this astonishment when he wrote in his Tractatus (1921): ‘Not how the world is, is the mystical, but that it is.’ Arthur Schopenhauer in 1818 called the question ‘an unfathomable and always disquieting riddle’. And the Rigveda, one of the world’s oldest surviving religious texts, suggests that even the ‘overseer’ (adhyakṣaḥ) of the cosmos might not know the answer. Sheer existence is baffling.

Philosophers continue to discuss the question today, but there isn’t any consensus about the answer. Some have suggested that it’s the sort of question that couldn’t possibly have an answer. In 1973, the German philosopher Carl Hempel wrote:

But what kind of an answer would be appropriate? What seems to be wanted is an explanatory account which does not assume the existence of something or other. But such an account, I would submit, is a logical impossibility … No theory, no conceptual scheme, can explain the existence of anything without assuming the existence of something.

His idea is that if you were trying to explain why, for instance, any penguins at all exist, then you couldn’t appeal to a penguin in your explanation – after all, that penguin is one of the things you are trying to explain. Similarly, if we’re looking for an explanation for why anything at all exists, then our explanation cannot appeal to an existing thing, since that existing thing is one of the things we are trying to explain. But Hempel thinks that there couldn’t possibly be any other sort of explanation for why anything exists, since any explanation for why something exists has to appeal to some other existing thing.

One response to Hempel’s concern is to go ahead and do what he claimed can’t possibly be done: offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, an explanation that ‘does not assume the existence of something’. Many philosophers have attempted to do just that. But there is something wrong with these explanations.

Why might we expect there to be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing in the first place? Leibniz thought there must be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing because, as he put it, nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. It is this thought that lies behind much of the astonishment people have expressed at the fact that there is something rather than nothing.

A world in which nothing exists is how we should expect the world to be if it takes what would, by our usual criteria, be its most probable state. What I have in mind here is Ockham’s Razor. Simpler accounts of the world are more likely to be correct than complex ones. For example, consider all the traits shared among the species alive today. Whales and humans have similar bone structures, despite the fact that they live in very different environments. One of Charles Darwin’s key insights was that, while it might conceivably have been true that a creator just happened to want these various species to have similar traits, despite their different environments and lifestyles, it is so much simpler to suppose that they share those traits because those traits are derived from a common ancestor. And the simplicity itself of that explanation gives us an excellent reason to think that the common traits are derived from a common ancestor. We constantly rely on the assumption that the simplest account of the world compatible with our evidence is most likely to be correct. This is something we do in science as well as in everyday life.

Many of the proposed explanations for why there is something rather than nothing that have been offered in the past do not address the apparent fact that nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. The proposed explanations say that there is such-and-such a reason for why there is something rather than nothing, but they do nothing to address the thought that we should antecedently expect there to be nothing because, if there had been nothing, then reality would have been so much simpler.
There would have been a whole lot of non-ontological truths even if nothing had existed

What I’d like to do here is kill two birds with one stone: to offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, which simultaneously dissolves the suspicion that nothing would have been so much simpler than something. This also happens to be, as far as I can tell, a new explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, and new explanations are hard to come by given the antiquity of the question.

I would like to start with the important insight that there are truths that are not truths about existing things. Since they are not truths about existing things, we’ll call them ‘non-ontological’ truths. Contrast these with ‘ontological’ truths – truths that are about existing things, like the truth that Earth orbits the Sun, or that there are more trees in the world than there are dogs. The observation that there are non-ontological truths is an insight expressed by other philosophers puzzled by the question of why there is something rather than nothing. For example, in a number of publications, the philosopher John Leslie has argued that there is something rather than nothing simply because it is good for there to be something rather than nothing. Setting aside whether this is a successful explanation, note that it appeals to a non-ontological truth: even if there was nothing, then there would have still been the truth that reality was less good than it could have been. And that does seem plausible.
Once we notice that there are non-ontological truths, we can see on reflection that there would have been a whole lot of them even if nothing had existed. Here are a few examples:

- Negative existential truths, ie, truths regarding that which does not exist. A possible world in which nothing exists would have to have lots of these truths! This doesn’t exist, that doesn’t exist, and so on.
- Truths regarding what is possible and impossible. Even if nothing existed, it would still be possible for dogs to exist, and impossible for square circles to exist.

- Truths of logic. Even if nothing existed, we would still have what logicians call modus ponens, the logical rule that says that, if A is true, and it’s also true that if A is true then B is true, then B is true.

- Mathematical truths. Even if nothing existed, it would still be true that 2+3=5. Regardless of the existence of numbers or any other mathematical objects, it would still be true that if you’ve got two things, and you add to them three things, you’ll end up with five things.

- Moral truths. Even if nothing existed, all sorts of actions would still be morally better or worse than other actions. Even though Ewoks don’t exist, it’s still true that it would be wrong to pinch their fur. In fact, even if nothing existed, it would still be wrong to pinch Ewoks.

Again, these are just a few examples. I could list many others. Admittedly, it’s mysterious how we know about these non-ontological truths. Since they don’t concern existing things, it’s surprising that our cognitive faculties can ‘get a grip’ on them, in the way that they can get a grip on objects with which we can interact (eg, the dog in front of me that I can see with my eyes and pet with my hand).
There can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be

An immediate objection is that if there were truly nothing then there would not be any non-ontological truths either. A truly empty world would have nothing at all, including truths of any sort. The philosopher Tyron Goldschmidt expresses this thought when he writes in The Puzzle of Existence (2013) that the question of why any beings at all exist is:

the broadest question of all … The question amounts to a question about why any world obtains. After all, worlds are ways things could be, and without any ways or things – beings broadly construed – there can be no world.

But I don’t think this is right. This view assumes that, in asking why anything at all exists, we are asking why there are any truths at all (in Goldschmidt’s terms, ‘why any world obtains’). That is not what we are asking. We are looking for an explanation for existence specifically. We are not asking why there are truths rather than no truths. That would, as Goldschmidt himself notes, be a confused question to ask, since there isn’t any alternative to there being truths, not even an impossible alternative. ‘A situation in which nothing is true’ doesn’t describe a situation, not even an impossible situation, since descriptions of a situation tell us what is or would be true were that situation to happen. With the concept of non-ontological truths, we can also see that there can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be. In those empty worlds there would be truths, but no things.

Many non-ontological truths would still be true even if nothing existed because they are necessarily true, if true at all. For example, recall modus ponens. That logical rule couldn’t help but be true, whether or not anything exists. The same holds for many of the other non-ontological truths, such as truths regarding what is possible and impossible, mathematical truths, and moral truths.

Some of these non-ontological truths are more controversial than others. But you don’t have to buy into every non-ontological truth to see that a possible world in which nothing exists would be more complex than it seems at first glance. When we think of complexity we normally think of the complexity of things and their properties and behaviours. But there is this whole other sort of complexity that is more abstract: complexity with respect to non-ontological truths.

Even if a possible world in which nothing exists might be more complex than we initially thought, it doesn’t follow that Leibniz was wrong when he said that it is simpler for nothing to exist than for something to exist. After all, you might think that if something exists this would leave us with all those non-ontological truths cited above as well as ontological truths about the things that exist. But postulating something new can simplify our overall picture of reality if the new thing can explain a great deal that would otherwise remain unexplained.

A possible world in which something exists may very well simplify matters if one or more of the existing things could explain why the non-ontological truths are true. This is similar to how Darwin simplified our account of biological reality by postulating the existence of something we didn’t previously believe in: a common ancestor. So if something of the right sort exists, this might make reality simpler than if nothing at all exists, if the existing thing can explain why many of the non-ontological truths are true. The simpler that existing thing is, and the wider the range of non-ontological truths it can explain, the simpler our overall account of reality will be. But what sort of existing thing might do the trick? Three possibilities naturally suggest themselves, though I don’t claim that these three options are exhaustive.

First, God is a natural candidate. Here I have in mind the sort of God we find in the world’s major monotheistic religions, all-powerful, all-knowing and so on. The feature of theism most important for our purposes is the idea that God’s nature and decisions are supposed to ultimately explain many aspects of reality. It is God’s status as reality’s explanatory bedrock that makes God a natural candidate for explaining various non-ontological truths. For example, if there is a God, then God’s decisions would explain various negative existential truths. Mechagodzilla doesn’t exist because Mechagodzilla just isn’t one of the things God wanted to create, or allow to be created.

Divine command theorists such as William of Ockham (of Ockham’s Razor fame) explain moral truths in terms of God’s commands – an act is good or bad because God commands it to be. René Descartes notoriously claimed that God decrees which logical and mathematical truths are true. These truths could not be otherwise – they are necessary – but that too is only because God decided they can’t be otherwise. There is also a case to be made that God is a particularly simple being. If that’s right, then our overall account of reality might end up being simple if God explains why many non-ontological truths are true. There is the traditional doctrine of divine simplicity, endorsed by prominent Jewish thinkers such as Maimonides, Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas, and Islamic thinkers such as Ibn Sina. According to this view, there are no distinctions at all within God, either between God’s attributes, or between God and God’s attributes. Over the past several decades, the philosopher Richard Swinburne has argued in detail for a more modest way of understanding the idea that God is a very simple being, and so theism is a very simple hypothesis. The basic idea, which I don’t have the space to discuss in detail, is that many of God’s attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, etc) are ultimately derivable from one or two of God’s attributes, and those attributes fit together in a neat and tidy manner.

Here is a second option if the God explanation doesn’t appeal. Many of the non-ontological truths might be explained by a natural (that is, non-supernatural) object that explains why the Universe has many of the properties it has. Suppose that the Universe originated in a cosmic singularity, an object of infinite density. The state of the initial singularity would, given how the laws of nature dictate the Universe evolves over time, explain why various negative existential truths are true. This is because the Universe’s initial conditions plus the laws will result in the Universe’s history taking one course rather than another, one that either does or does not include the existence of various particular things in it. Even non-deterministic laws may dictate that the existence of certain things is very improbable, given the Universe’s initial conditions.
The actual world, though filled with existing things, may for all we know be the simplest possible world

Some philosophers think that truths regarding what is possible and impossible in the broadest sense are also explained by the properties had by an initial singularity. The idea is that what’s possible and impossible is grounded in which states of the Universe can result from the evolution of the initial singularity, given how the laws of nature say the Universe will evolve over time. If some state of the Universe can in principle result from the initial singularity and the laws, then it’s possible, but if it can’t result then it is strictly impossible, as impossible as a round square. In fact, on this view that’s what makes round squares impossible. But would an initial singularity give us a particularly simple explanation for various non-ontological truths? The philosopher Quentin Smith argued that an initial cosmic singularity is as simple as it gets, since an initial singularity would have had no spatial extension, no mass (at least on some models), and would not have been governed by any physical laws. So it’s certainly a candidate.

A third possibility is that we humans make many of the non-ontological truths true. And, with various degrees of plausibility, many of the non-ontological truths cited earlier have been attributed by some philosopher or other to our decisions, conventions, practices or whatever. For example, moral anti-realists such as Sharon Street think that there are moral truths, but that they are made true by our attitudes, conventions or practices (or the attitudes we would have in ideal conditions). Logical conventionalists such as Jared Warren contend that logical truths are a result of our linguistic practices. Mathematical intuitionists such as the mathematician L E J Brouwer think that mathematical truths are mentally constructed.

There are surely more possibilities than these three. But, confining our attention to these three options – God, singularity, human beings – is one of them clearly preferable to the others? It’s difficult to say. There are many non-ontological truths, and some non-ontological truths may be more plausibly explained by an existing thing than would other non-ontological truths. It is difficult to see how some of these explanations would work; I’ve never seen anyone claim that an initial singularity might explain which moral truths are true. And a full evaluation of the three options would require a detailed examination of the relative merits of the various explanations on offer. We would have to take a look at each of the versions of divine command theory and human-centred moral anti-realism on offer, and see if any of them seem plausible on closer inspection. That being said, the first two options (God, singularity) do seem to fare better than the third option with respect to simplicity. They propose to explain lots of non-ontological truths by appealing to one existing thing, an existing thing that might be very simple. By contrast, if we try to explain various non-ontological truths by appeal to human beings, we don’t seem to have a very simple explanation. Human beings are complex objects. There are also a lot of human beings. Are the non-ontological truths explained by some of them, or all of them? How would we reconcile conflicting human attitudes or practices that might result in contradictory non-ontological truths? It’s hard to see how we might come up with an elegant or simple way of accounting for how that’s all supposed to work.

We can leave further speculation regarding the details to another occasion. The main point is this: if we can posit some existing thing that is simple enough, and capable of explaining a wide-enough range of the non-ontological truths, we might very well end up with an account of reality in which one or more things exist, and yet which is simpler than an account of reality in which nothing exists. In fact, despite how counterintuitive it seems at first, the actual world, though filled with existing things, may for all we know be the simplest possible world, if it has a sufficiently simple explanatory foundation. In that case, Leibniz would have been incorrect when he said that nothing would have been ‘simpler and easier’ than something. If we found ourselves surprised that reality didn’t take its simplest and seemingly most probable state, one in which nothing exists, that sense of surprise should dissolve.

Suppose that if something of the right sort exists, then that would be simpler than if nothing at all existed. Would this fact explain why there is something rather than nothing? Presumably it would only if we think that reality is the way it is because of how simple it is. In other words, we would have to think that reality is somehow striving toward simplicity, so that, if the world is as simple as it can be, this is because it is as simple as it can be. You shouldn’t oppose this idea on the grounds that our world is very complex, since, as I’ve emphasised, that complexity might be accounted for in terms of a very simple explanatory starting point.

A more serious worry is that, even if our reason for thinking that something is true is because it is simpler (remember Ockham’s Razor), it doesn’t follow that the thing itself is true because it is simpler. The reason we think the various species have a common ancestor is because this hypothesis is the simplest explanation of the evidence. But that simplicity isn’t what makes it true that there is that common ancestor.

We should question this assumption that simplicity never explains why some state of affairs comes about. The idea that sometimes reality takes a simpler form because it is simpler is more defensible than it might first seem. It would have the benefit of explaining why simplicity is a guide to truth (that is, why we should accept principles such as Ockham’s Razor), a methodological practice followed in both science and everyday life, but which is notoriously hard to justify. What’s more, many of us follow Leibniz in being puzzled at the fact that reality didn’t take what seems at first to be its simplest form, wherein nothing exists. We tend to think that if nothing had existed, and if this would have in fact been the simplest way for reality to be, then nothing would have existed precisely because nothing was so much simpler than something.

My argument flips this line of reasoning on its head. We should expect reality to be simple, and for all we can tell that’s exactly what we find. There being something rather than nothing shouldn’t surprise us if that’s the simplest way for reality to be. That wouldn’t explain everything. Supposing that reality somehow strives for simplicity, for example, we might very well wonder why that’s the case. It won’t work to say that reality strives for simplicity because that’s the simplest way for reality to work, as that would be a circular explanation. So, even if my extremely speculative proposal is correct, we’d still be left with a lot of mystery. Out of the infinite number of ways for reality to be, why did it turn out this way? That’s still a baffling question, even if we conclude that one of reality’s features, that things exist, might turn out to be less baffling than it initially seems.

items.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays
items.description: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in a
items.author: Melanie Challenger
paragraphs: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.

Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.

Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.

We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.

This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.

Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.

By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock. Transhumanist thinkers then carried the machine comparison further, imagining technologies that could transfer a mind to a computer.

Machines now promised more than control. They offered a glimpse of immortality: the organism might be repaired, remade and ultimately replaced. The somewhat embarrassing body, with its impulses and eventual frailty, might then be cast aside. If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Today, we can see this fear writ large in the technological quest for a bodiless life. If a person is ultimately a pattern of information, that pattern might be restored or even uploaded. AI is only the latest iteration of this ancient impulse to escape the vulnerability of the body.

After all, the brain is itself a physical organ, continually shaped by what the body does and encounters. Once we decide that the mind is the real human and the rest of the body only hardware, it becomes easier to disregard the physical work, including the neurocognitive work of a biological brain, through which we move, find our way, put thoughts into words, and recognise our own needs. A machine may do some of that work faster, but each act it takes over is one that the body no longer performs and that the body, including the brain, no longer learns through. The irony is that a project motivated by the desire to overcome bodily fragility is helping to produce more fragile bodies.

On top of all this, we have little evidence that either thought or intelligence actually work like machines, and almost no indication that life is an abstract system that might emerge in silicon or mathematics. Instead, a substantial body of work, especially in systems biology, points to a quite different conclusion: that life and intelligence emerge from the unique qualities and organisation of our self-maintaining bodies, rather than from abstract models of information and algorithms.

For the past six years, I have been researching the latest science on what life is and how it works. As best as we can tell, the intelligent actions of organisms derive from the imperatives of a living body that must regulate and preserve its own conditions for existence. When cybernetics was ascendant, the molecular structure of DNA had only recently been discovered, and the emerging view of genes as information encouraged an oversimplified picture of the body as running on a program that could be made more efficient. Yet such confidence has since waned among biologists. While genes carry some of the information that shapes our bodies, many changes in how a cell or a body functions arise from the system as a whole. Genes cannot be understood apart from the living bodies in which they act.

First and foremost, life persists through physical plasticity. Consider how our bodies keep together. Living bodies do something unusual in the Universe: they perform work to preserve their own organisation. Life-forms use energy to remain discontinuous with the environment.
