WHAT HAS AND HASN’T CHANGED THE MOST IN MY LIFE ”I’m never really home, because I’m in Toronto filming Adults. And I miss my parents. You guys, come on the road! Get to Toronto. Everything else is exactly the same. I’m still doing my boyfriend’s laundry.”

MY MOST IMPACTFUL PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE HAS BEEN ”Working on Theater Camp with Molly Gordon directing. I grew up with her, we were in plays together. To watch her step into those shoes and telling me what to do was really, really fulfilling.”
RANDOM SKILL I PICKED UP ON A PROJECT ”I wrestle a raccoon to the floor in Adults. That’s a skill I didn’t know I had. So if you have raccoons in your backyard, call me.”
MY FAVORITE PLACE IN L.A. ”It’s cheesy, but my parents’ house. I love being on their couch.”
Owen Thiele was photographed Oct. 16 at Viceroy Santa Monica. Calvin Klein jacket, shirt, jeans; Thiele’s earrings.
Hair: Coree Moreno. Makeup: Shannon Pezzetta.

Creed-Miles never wanted to be part of Hollywood. She grew up watching her mother, veteran actress Samantha Morton, put herself through the wringer in service of her vocation, and she says she learned at a very young age not to covet fame. But at 16, her mother’s agent coaxed her into auditioning for the part of a young Ruth Wilson in the 2017 thriller Dark River. “Very quickly, I had this feeling of seeing what I was doing and that I was impressing them and having an emotional impact,” says the actress, who adds: “And I really liked feeling like I was good at something.” She was offered the job that day.

From there, Creed-Miles, now 26, began building the career she never knew she wanted. Before long, she was starring opposite Joel Kinnaman in the 2019 Prime Video thriller series Hanna. “As a kid, I was always with my mom on her jobs, so I understood exactly what it meant to be on a set,” she says. “I felt like such a grown-up on Hanna, even though I wasn’t.” But it was Creed-Miles’ turn as Marianne Dashwood — a more wild, nearly feral version of the lovelorn literary stalwart — in this year’s remake of Sense and Sensibility that has the town talking. Ironically, Creed-Miles almost didn’t audition for the role, having convinced herself that a project as lofty as a Jane Austen adaptation would call for a more extroverted actress. (“I’m not the best people person, so I didn’t think I had a chance in hell,” she explains.) In the end, Creed-Miles was drawn in by the cinematic bona fides of the production: a budding auteur in director Georgia Oakley and a mandate to shoot on 35mm. “It reignited my passion for filmmaking,” she says now.

Already, the film has sent her on her first global press tour and scored her her first major nomination — outstanding supporting performance — at the upcoming Gotham Awards. Still, she insists none of it has changed her outlook on fame: “It’s pretty unfair that women are expected to have this whole persona outside of their professional work, but men whose careers I’ve really obsessed over, like Daniel Day-Lewis or Joaquin Phoenix, are allowed to have very mysterious or even nonexistent public personas,” she says. “I just love the idea of showing up to be a weirdo in a movie and disappearing again.” — S.R.

MY FIRST AUDITION WAS … ”I’ve been doing this since I was 6, so I have no clue. I did a Harmony Korine film as a kid and I think I had dinner with him and my mom, so maybe that was an audition of sorts.”
THE ACTOR I LOOK UP TO MOST RIGHT NOW IS ”I’ll shout out Kristen Stewart, because I’ve worked with her a few times now and she’s an amazing filmmaker and always has really important things to say.”
RANDOM SKILL I PICKED UP ON A PROJECT ”I’m not a horse girl, but I did learn horseback riding for Sense and Sensibility. They’re so gentle and kind, and it’s very liberating to be on a horse.”
MY FAVORITE PLACE IN L.A. ”Honey Hi for brunch. They do this amazing bacon breakfast bowl and some really good gluten-free pancakes.”
Esmé Creed-Miles was photographed Oct. 7 at Viceroy Santa Monica. Tom Ford shirt, tights.
Hair: Cervando. Makeup: Kate Lee.

Like many young actors this year, Kalyn plays a hockey player on a buzzy television show. Unlike most actors playing hockey players, Kalyn actually grew up playing the sport. “Everyone is very comfortable in their skates now,” he says of his fellow actors, though it was clear his expertise made him the de facto captain of the Off Campus training sessions season one. Now, he jokes: “They’re all going to be ready to play beer league soon.”

This year has been a game-changer for Kalyn, who’d been building a résumé of recurring roles (on Essex County, Cruel Intentions, Gen V) before he landed the role of Dean Di Laurentis in Prime Video’s red-hot hockey romance. For the show’s upcoming season, set to premiere in April, the 28-year-old’s character (alongside Mika Abdalla’s Allie Hayes) will be at the center of the story, as his co-stars Belmont Cameli’s and Ella Bright’s characters were season one. “To watch them go through it was such a great learning lesson for me,” says the actor, who’s already seen his profile soar, as evidenced by his nearly 4 million new followers on Instagram. Once the first season dropped — reaching 36 million global viewers over its first 12 days — Kalyn’s phone began ringing in ways it never had before. In short order, he booked ad campaigns, brand partnerships and new Hollywood projects, including The Housemaid’s Secret, a follow-up to the 2025 film that has him starring alongside Sydney Sweeney, Kirsten Dunst and Paul Anthony Kelly. Having seen the first installment twice in the theater — once with his fiancée, once with his mom — he was admittedly nervous when he first got to set. But he’s since settled in, he says: “I’ve found my fitting in this story now.” — N.F.

MY FIRST AUDITION WAS … ”One of my first auditions would’ve been for a Pizza Pop commercial. I really thought I nailed it, and turns out I didn’t. I didn’t get a call back. I got a Tim Hortons commercial in Canada. They flew me to Mexico. I remember doing it, and I thought: ‘Once this comes out, I’m going to be huge. I’m going to be the face of Canada. It’s going to be unbelievable.’ That didn’t happen.”

RANDOM SKILL I PICKED UP ON A PROJECT ”I should have known how to do it, but I had to learn how to properly chop onions. There’s a technique to it. It’s not as simple as you think it is. This is for The Housemaid [2], the director came over and he’s like, ’You know how to cut onions, right?’ And I’m like, ’Yeah. Of course I do. Totally. Just one second.’ I went around the corner, I went on TikTok and I quickly found how to cut onions. When you see it on the big screen, you’re going to think, ‘That guy’s a really good onion cutter.’”

MY MOST IMPACTFUL PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE HAS BEEN ”As much as I would love to talk about a lot of them, it would’ve been doing season two of Off Campus. There are so many things and emotions and feelings that I had to discover.”
THE ACTOR I LOOK UP TO MOST RIGHT NOW IS ”I always grew up loving Jim Carrey. But then, as time went on, I’d say Leo DiCaprio.”
Stephen Kalyn was photographed Oct. 16 at Viceroy Santa Monica. Todd Snyder suit; David Yurman jewelry; Jacques Marie Mage sunglasses; stylist’s tank, belt.

”Career-wise, this is the busiest I’ve ever been,” says the Yellowjackets star. “It’s the first time I’ve not stopped for 10 months straight.” Nélisse got her start at age 11, with the French-language Canadian film Monsieur Lazhar. Now 26, Nélisse worked steadily through her teenage years and into her 20s, ultimately landing a lead role on the Showtime drama about a high school soccer team stranded in the woods after a plane crash.

But as Yellowjackets prepares to close out its four-season run, Nélisse has found herself in an enviable position with a slew of new projects on the horizon, including a starring role in Netflix’s adaptation of the Carley Fortune novel This Summer Will Be Different. It’s a 180 from Yellowjackets, she says, having quite literally gone from crying with dirt under her nails one day to flying to Prince Edward Island, where she immediately went into fittings, got hair extensions and a fake tan.

But the lion’s share of the heat surrounding Nélisse lately stems from a two-episode arc in last winter’s hockey juggernaut Heated Rivalry. Her character, superstar actress Rose Landry, dates Hudson Williams’ Shane Hollander and, in one of the show’s most memorable scenes, helps him come to terms with the fact that he’s gay. Nélisse is set to return for the show’s highly anticipated second season, which is filming in Toronto. She’s still making sense of the series’ outsize success — and her place within it.

“When articles come out and they say ‘star of Heated Rivalry,’ I’m like, ‘I have one scene!'” she jokes. The irony, she reveals, is that she didn’t prepare particularly hard for said scene, even if she’s immensely proud to be a part of it. It certainly wasn’t the “weeks of just sobbing and the most gut-wrenching scenes” she did on Yellowjackets. Instead, she recalls: “I came in, learned my lines and I was like, ‘All right, let’s do this!’ I didn’t think about it twice.” — N.F.

WHAT‘S CHANGED THE MOST IN MY LIFE IN THE PAST YEAR ”Wrapping up Yellowjackets. It had been this stability for the last almost 10 years of my life. Knowing that I was coming back and knowing there was going to be more than one season and also knowing that I was going to be reunited every year with these actors — that really felt like the end of an era and sort of closing a chapter of my life.”
MY MOST-PLAYED ARTIST THIS YEAR WILL BE “Noah Kahan. I’m dying to see him at a concert.”
THE ACTOR I LOOK UP TO MOST RIGHT NOW IS ”Kate Winslet is a big inspiration for me. Her career has been so diverse, and she’s chosen just beautiful characters.”

MY FAVORITE PLACE IN L.A. ”I’m so embarrassed to actually say my response. Now I need to say it. My favorite place, not to visit, but to go to would be the Erewhon hot bar, which is the most embarrassing answer ever. What can I say? I love it.”
Sophie Nélisse was photographed Oct. 27 at BOOM at The Standard, High Line, New York. Gabriela Hearst gown; Wolford underwear; Yvonne Leon rings; State Property rings.
Hair: Xavier Velasquez. Makeup: Leslie Ann Thomson.

The face that launched a thousand ships? Not exactly, but Tung was at the center of the internet’s hottest debate last year when social media took sides over who her character, Belly, should end up with on the hit Prime Video series The Summer I Turned Pretty. (Jennifer Lawrence recently admitted that when she publicly declared herself Team Jeremiah, “The level of hate that I got was bigger than any controversy I’ve ever been involved in in my life.”)

Tung, a 24-year-old New York City native and an alum of LaGuardia High School, led the show for three seasons in her professional acting debut. “I couldn’t have had a better first experience,” she says. She’ll return, alongside her co-stars Christopher Briney and Gavin Casalegno, for a feature film follow-up to the series, but she’s also working with Gracie Abrams and Connor Storrie in Halina Reijn’s upcoming A24 film Please and starring opposite Nicole Kidman and Nico Parker in Osgood Perkins’ horror The Young People. “Belly is such a huge part of me, so I was like, as this chapter is coming to an end, let’s dive into something super different,” she says. And although she’s not out to be the next scream queen — as an admitted “scaredy cat” — she emphasizes, “It’s really cool to be like, ‘Oh, this is how they do the blood and the grossness of it all.'” And when the blood and guts are washed off, Tung is busy becoming a fashion “It” girl, serving as a global ambassador for Coach and stepping out on the fashion show circuit. She’s also no stranger to the stage, having made her Broadway debut in 2024 with a limited run in Hadestown.

Looking ahead, Tung says she’d like to add to her already impressive list of female filmmaker collaborators, with Chloé Zhao at the top of her wish list, and hopes to write and direct herself one day — in a return to what drew her to the creative world in the first place. “I used to make music videos with my friends in elementary school, and I was always a really bossy director,” Tung recounts with a laugh. “It was always super fun for me — not fun for my friends, who were like, ‘We want a break, please!’ But I love every aspect of it, and it’s been really cool now to work with so many directors who are so collaborative and get a peek into what that world looks like.” — K.C.

MY MOST IMPACTFUL PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE HAS BEEN ”It’s funny because you learn something from every single experience that you have, obviously. But I was on Summer for the longest; that was five years of my life. Because of that, I learned so much as an actor and about myself.”
IF I COULD, I WOULD TELL MY FUTURE SELF ”I would like to tell future Lola that I love her and I hope she’s happy and I hope AI hasn’t taken over.”

THE ACTOR I LOOK UP TO MOST RIGHT NOW IS ”Renate Reinsve and Jessie Buckley. And, honestly, I think a lot of the people that I’ve worked with inspire me a lot. It’s fun because you get to watch them work up close and it’s so magical. Everyone on Summer is so fun to watch, and on Forbidden Fruits and The Young People. My friends Nico [Parker] and Lili [Reinhart] are so incredibly talented and special.”
MY MOST-PLAYED ARTIST THIS YEAR WILL BE “Probably either Lizzy McAlpine or Olivia Rodrigo. Those two albums have been on repeat for me.”
Lola Tung was photographed Oct. 27 at BOOM at The Standard, High Line, New York. Balenciaga gown, gloves; Ettika earrings.
Hair: Dana Boyer. Makeup: Misha Shahzada.

When Francis was starring in Sunset Boulevard on the West End and on Broadway, he says he approached the experience like a racehorse. “It was like I had those blinders on to block everything out,” he explains. “That was the only way that I could get through it and do the job that I wanted to do.” The strategy worked, of course. He earned an Olivier Award and a Tony nomination, and his performance as Joe Gillis — which included the much-talked-about title-song sequence in which Francis left the theater every night to perform to a Steadicam on 44th Street — caught the attention of big-time directors, including Peter Berg, who was so taken that he offered Francis a role in his new film The Mosquito Bowl. The movie, which centers on a real-life group of star college football players who enlist in World War II, marks Francis’ first major screen role.

The 27-year-old grew up in Suffolk, England, and graduated from drama school during the pandemic, falling quickly into a theater career — which he says actually gave him an advantage on the high-octane, occasionally chaotic production full of combat scenes. “I’m very used to being told, ‘You have to hit your light here every time.'” Berg also wrote in a singing scene just for Francis. “It’s factually incorrect because my character wasn’t a singer [in real life], but I figured Broadway fans might watch this movie,” Francis explains. “You’ve got to give the people what they want.” Next, he will be seen in a recurring role on season two of Benito Skinner’s Overcompensating — after that, he will play Richard Gere’s son in the Apple TV series Off Weeks. There was a time when Francis kept lists of his dream jobs, but lately he has simplified. He just wants to work with people who push him. “Benny definitely expected more of me than I thought I could give,” he says of the quippy Prime Video comedy, which he describes as the “most joyous” job he’s ever had.

It’s been a whirlwind year of firsts, but Francis says the most exciting thing to happen to him so far was his recent appearance at the Academy Museum Gala. “It was one of those moments where I looked around the room thinking, it’s filled with the most inspiring people to me,” he says of a crowd that included Taylor Swift, adding: “I’m a Swiftie now.” — S.R.
AN ACTOR MY AGE I ADMIRE IS ”Tom Blyth and David Jonsson. I watched Wasteman, and it’s so brilliant. I’d love to try and work with those two at some point in my life.”

RANDOM SKILL I PICKED UP ON A PROJECT ”In Rent, there’s a song called ’Light My Candle’ and we had to light the candles while walking at a perfect pace. The candle would go out all the time. I got really good at lighting matches.”

MY MOST-PLAYED ARTIST THIS YEAR WILL BE ”Deep sleep piano. I’ve recently gotten into going to sleep with this lo-fi music in the background. So that’s running the whole of the night. But after that, I’d say Matt Corby. I’m really loving his Rainbow Valley album at the moment.”
MY FAVORITE PLACE IN L.A. ”It’s my friend Ray Nicholson’s house. We call it Casa Mysterio because his nickname is Ray Mysterio. His house is very calming.”
Tom Francis was photographed Oct. 16 at Viceroy Santa Monica. Dolce & Gabbana shirt, pants, tee, belt; David Yurman jewelry.
Grooming: Shannon Pezzetta.

Hall’s collegiate years at Northwestern were primarily dedicated to the basketball team. But when the 6-foot-5 L.A. native realized a future in the NBA wasn’t in the cards, he turned his focus to his other passion — entertainment. It helped that he was already a film major. As was all but inevitable growing up with Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Saturday Night Live‘s Brad Hall as parents, he is a considerable talent and a major comedy fan. One of his first onscreen appearances was in a supporting role in the Amy Poehler-directed 2021 Netflix comedy Moxie, which boosted both his résumé and his confidence. “Amy would laugh occasionally at stuff I was doing,” he says, “and I remember thinking, ‘OK, if someone like Amy thinks I don’t suck, then maybe I don’t suck!'”

The next few years saw the now 29-year-old jumping from multi-episode arcs and supporting turns in series like Mindy Kaling’s The Sex Lives of College Girls, Ryan Murphy’s Monster franchise and, most recently, Apple TV’s Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed, where he starred opposite Tatiana Maslany. Up next is his biggest project to date: HBO’s The White Lotus, where his castmates will include Laura Dern, Steve Coogan and Ben Kingsley. “It was a really cool moment calling my family and telling them,” he says, laughing as he catches himself: “Even though I think you’re not supposed to do that. Whatever! They can’t fire me now!” Production on the series’ fourth season, which will be set in France, has already stretched well over six months. (“I’ve certainly had enough steak frites to last a lifetime,” he jokes.)

items.title: ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Gets a Creepily Effective Comeback Vehicle in Ti West’s Horror-Tinged Take on Dickens’ Yuletide Classic
items.description: Did the world need another cinematic adaptation of Charles Dickens’ classic A Christmas Carol? Not really, considering the myriad versions that have appeared over the years, which play with regularity on television screens every holiday season. But Johnny Depp
items.author: Frank Scheck
paragraphs: Did the world need another cinematic adaptation of Charles Dickens’ classic A Christmas Carol? Not really, considering the myriad versions that have appeared over the years, which play with regularity on television screens every holiday season. But Johnny Depp really needed a comeback vehicle, and he’s found an effective one in Ti West’s horror-tinged adaptation that allows the actor to deliver the sort of quirky theatrical performance for which he became famous. While Ebenezer doesn’t break any new ground, other than possibly being the first version of the story not really suitable for young children, it fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status.

Considering that the director’s oeuvre consists of such films as The House of the Devil, Cabin Fever 2: Spring Fever, and the recent acclaimed X trilogy, it’s not surprising that this version of the Yuletide tale features a dark Gothic tone. Indeed, Ebenezer feels essentially like a horror film for most of its running time, featuring jump scares, grotesque visuals, and enough ghostly creatures to fuel a season of American Horror Story. It’s no wonder a terrified Scrooge pees himself at one point.
Cast: Johnny Depp, Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman, Ian McKellen
Screenwriter: Nathaniel Halpern
Rated PG-13, 1 hour 56 minutes

Still, plenty of care has been taken for the movie, which features handsome visuals, excellent production design, and a stacked cast including Ian McKellen as Scrooge’s business partner Jacob Marley. Nathaniel Halpern’s screenplay expands upon the tale by providing more backstory than usual, with Marley still alive in the pre-credits prologue and demonstrating that he was just as irascible and nasty as Scrooge.

Cut to seven years later, when Scrooge is at his most Scrooge-like, uttering enough humbugs to satisfy those Dickens fans. (Another nod to them is that the film is divided into “staves,” as was the author’s novella.)

Soon enough, Scrooge is visited by the ghost of his former partner, who, besides carrying those infernal chains, looks decidedly worse for wear. Marley warns him that he’ll soon be visited by three ghosts who will … wait, why am I relating the story? You already know it.

First, of course, is the Ghost of Christmas Past, played by a wispy Andrea Riseborough made up to look like a corpse that’s been left out in the sun. She brings Scrooge back to his early days, when his younger self (Arthur Conti, Carrie) was in love with his fiancée Belle (Ellie Bamber), whom he subsequently lost due to his misplaced priorities. Then there’s the Ghost of Christmas Present, a surly figure played by Tramell Tillman (Severance), who physically decays as the visit wears on, eventually revealing horrific creatures trapped in his body. Finally, there’s the Ghost of Christmas Future (the appropriately named Robert Strange), an otherworldly apparition who introduces himself by having a crow fly out of his mouth.

Interspersed with all the creepiness, which includes numerous rampaging ghosts behaving like zombies, are some moments of genuine emotion. Depp provides moving glimpses into Scrooge’s underlying humanity, from his missing his deceased partner to his anguish over having lost Belle to his pity for Tiny Tim (Freddie Lee-Grey), his employee Bob Cratchit’s (Rupert Grint) disabled son.

Indeed, it’s when the film lets up on the frights and allows the story to breathe that it becomes most effective. The final redemption sequence, in which Depp gets to relax and show off his comic chops with the character’s newfound joyfulness as he visits nephew Fred (Sam Claflin) and his wife Clara (Daisy Ridley) with goose in tow, is a delight.

Depp, outfitted with prosthetic make-up and facial hair, delivers a performance that no one would call subtle. In style, it most closely resembles a heavily made-up Albert Finney’s broad take on the character in the now largely forgotten 1970 musical Scrooge. But the actor’s charisma and star power eventually come through.
Distributor: Paramount Pictures
Cast: Johnny Depp, Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman, Ian McKellen
Screenwriter: Nathaniel Halpern
Executive producers: Ti West, Adam Bohling, David Reid, Stephen Deuters, Jason Forman, Pete Chiappetta, Anthony Tittanegro, Andrew Lary, Molly Smith, Thad Luckinbill, Trent Luckinbill
Director of photography: Checco Varese
Production designer: Eve Stewart
Editors: Ti West, David Kashevaroff
Costume designer: Catherine George
Rated PG-13, 1 hour 56 minutes

items.title: ‘Love Trapped’ Podcast Coming to TV as Peacock Docuseries
items.description: Love Trapped is getting the TV treatment as a docuseries at Peacock.
items.author: Jackie Strause
paragraphs: Love Trapped is getting the TV treatment as a docuseries at Peacock.

The hit podcast from Glass Podcasts and iHeartPodcasts quickly became a sensation after first releasing in February. Love Trapped was initially a 10-episode weekly release; however the series expanded to 18 episodes, along with several mini “bonus” episodes, to track what has become a bizarre three-year ordeal chronicling the criminal case against Laura Owens, the Arizona woman who attempted to entrap former The Bachelor star Clayton Echard with paternity fraud.
The final episode released on Thursday timed to the announcement, with a bonus episode to the 18th episode, “The Bitter End,” teasing the doc.

After Love Trapped became a top Apple podcast of the year, The Hollywood Reporter reported in a feature that the audio story had become a hot Hollywood property, and that Glass Podcasts, which has had a string of recent podcast-to-TV adaptations, had been in talks about bringing Love Trapped to television.
Now the news is official: Peacock will adapt the story into a four-part docuseries titled Love Trapped: The Case of Laura Owens (wt).

Based on the podcast hosted by Stephani Young, the documentary will chronicle “the extraordinary story of former Bachelor star Clayton Echard and his tumultuous relationship with a woman named Laura Owens, which began with a brief encounter and, following her pregnancy claim, spiraled into a years-long legal battle that captivated social media and sparked widespread public fascination.”

Through exclusive interviews — including with Owens herself, speaking for the first time (she did not participate in the podcast) — the documentary brings together Echard, his legal team, Owens’ mother Jan Black, other men who were targeted by Owens, Young and the online detectives who helped unravel the story that shockingly extends far beyond one relationship.

The doc is executive produced by Glass Podcasts founder and CEO Nancy Glass, Emmy-winning documentarian Erin Lee Carr, and Keayr Braxton for Glass Entertainment Group, along with Danny Passman for Crybaby Media. Braxton is director.

The description continues: “Love Trapped: The Case of Laura Owens (wt) follows an astonishing story when Laura meets Clayton through a potential real estate deal and after their short connection, she tells him she’s pregnant with his twins. Their private dispute erupts into a nationally followed story fueled by citizen sleuths and social commentators that join the media firestorm that implodes into a shocking trail of deception, legal threats and public humiliation. The deeper the investigation goes, the more unbelievable the revelations become, while raising a disturbing question: when does the desire to be loved turn into an obsession?”

On Oct. 23, Owens, who pleaded guilty in August to four felony counts for falsely claiming she was pregnant with Echard’s twins, was sentenced to one month in jail and seven years of supervised probation. If she violates the terms of her probation, Owens could be sent to prison for more than 15 years.

In the Nov. 12 final episode of Love Trapped, Echard reflected on being disappointing in Owens’ sentencing, telling Young, “Does there always have to be a happy ending? Or maybe this is just one of these circumstances where there isn’t one, and that’s just life. This is where I think if you want a happy ending it’s, what do you do with that disappointment? I can let go of the pain and the anger and anything that doesn’t serve me because I ultimately won. And I did. I beat Laura head to head.”

Young concluded the podcast by saying that she “realized now that my questions are useless” and threw away the questions she had for Owens, who never participated on the podcast. “Even if I could ask them, I don’t think she’d be honest,” she said. “Laura will always be living in her own reality, but at least at the time I’m recording this, the truth is, that Clayton Echard finally gets to move on with his life. And Laura Owens woke up this morning in jail as a convicted felon.”

items.title: Remember When James Bond Was an Adidas Guy?
items.description: The search for the next James Bond continues. Over the weekend, Deadline reported that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had also screen-tested for the role, in addition to Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O'Connor. But once we've worked out who's gettin
items.author: Adam Cheung
paragraphs: The search for the next James Bond continues. Over the weekend, Deadline reported that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had also screen-tested for the role, in addition to Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O'Connor. But once we've worked out who's getting the tux, there's another question: What sneakers is he going to wear?

As it turns out, their predecessor Daniel Craig got that bit right, too. In 2012's Skyfall, 007 turns up for his MI6 fitness tests in a navy SIS tracksuit and Adidas Gazelle IIs. In the scene, Bond's trying to prove he's fit enough to get back to work, and it's not going particularly well. As a viewer, you'd be forgiven for missing the shoes.

But take another look. These were off-the-shelf Gazelles from Adidas's spring 2011 line, the sort that anyone could have picked up the year before the film came out. Bond is a guy whose wardrobe gets examined down to the last cufflink, and there he was in a regular pair of Adidas. His pair came in “dark indigo” suede with “Argentina blue” stripes, white rubber soles, and gold Gazelle lettering along the sides.

(There's a slight difference between the shoes a civilian could buy and the ones in the movie, though. The retail pair had a light blue heel tab, while Bond's appears darker. The fan website Bond Lifestyle suggests the costume department may have changed it, although that hasn't been officially confirmed.)

The Gazelle launched in 1966 as a multipurpose training shoe, and was the German sportswear giant's first-ever sneaker made from suede. The choice to put Bond in the shoe felt notable in more ways than one: In the training scene, the slim sole kept things nice and light underfoot, and the color combo went perfectly with his trackies. But there's also the Gazelle's place in British culture, from the football terraces in the ’80s to the Britpop crowd in the ’90s. So, it makes sense for a Gen-X British spy.

By 2021, Adidas had an official collab to go with No Time to Die. The collection featured all Ultraboost running shoes, with slight nods to Bond's tuxedos and Safin's porcelain mask. The “Q Branch” edition even had a hidden compartment in the lacing cage, handy if your gym shorts don't have pockets.

For a pair that came from a regular ol' Adidas collection, Bond's OG Gazelles are surprisingly difficult to find now. But if you fancy something similar without spending the next six months refreshing eBay, you can start with these.
A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

items.title: Our 11 Favorite Watches Coming to the Biggest Auctions of the Year
items.description: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.
items.author: Oren Hartov; Cam Wolf
paragraphs: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

This is the biggest weekend of the year for vintage watches. It’s the year-end watch auctions in Geneva, where many prestigious houses bring their very best pieces to market. And it’s never been a more enthralling time to keep a close eye on what happens in Geneva over the next few days. In the first half of the year, the number of million-dollar watches nearly eclipsed the total for the entirety of 2025. A couple of the pieces listed below, including a unique Rolex and a rare Patek Philippe in stainless steel, have estimates above a million bucks.
Writer Oren Hartov and I pored over hundreds of lots to bring you our 11 favorite watches plus one bonus selection. See them all below.
Rolex ref. 3830 Anti-Magnetique "Verga" (Estimate: In excess of $1,210,000)

You know a banger is coming up for sale when the house behind it doesn’t even bother capping its price range. Auction estimates are routinely and famously low to encourage bidders, and this watch’s starting point is still $1.2 million. Why? Well, have you ever seen a Rolex like this before? Before Rolex defined the look of modern watches with pieces like the Submariner, it operated similarly to many other manufacturers in Switzerland, willing to make one-off pieces and experiment frequently with its design.

This square beauty from the early 1940s is “most probably unique,” as Phillips auction house writes in its essay on the piece. This exact piece last hit the auction block in 2004, and no other example has come up for public sale since. It’s crazy to see how much this watch’s case shape resembles Heuer’s similarly blocky Monaco, which wouldn’t be released for another 25-plus years. Unfortunately, as cool as this watch is, it does not come with onyx prayer beads. —Cam Wolf
Patek Philippe ref. 1436 (High estimate: $4.8 million)

There’s Patek, then there’s complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples in insane condition. This watch checks all those boxes. A reference 1436, it’s a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph, meaning it can time successive intervals of a race or event. One of just two stainless steel examples known to the market, it has an estimate of $2.4-$4.8M, a testament to its rarity and importance. —Oren Hartov
A. Lange & Söhne Lange 1 (High estimate: roughly $365,800)

Yet another rare watch executed in stainless steel, this fabulous Lange 1 boasts a gorgeous two-tone dial in blue, with darker subdials contrasting against a cobalt-colored main dial. Dating to 1999 and first sold by the German retailer Oeding-Erdel, it’s one of approximately 30 pieces made in the most utilitarian of metals. Originally fitted with a more standard silvered dial, it received its current navy-blue dial as a replacement and is one of just two stainless steel Lange 1s known in this particular configuration. —OH
Urban Jürgensen ref. 2 (High estimate: roughly $121,940)

Renewed interest in Urban Jürgensen stemming from its recent relaunch under the directorship of Kari Voutilainen, who has since left the CEO position but remains on the company’s board, has seen watches such as this early-’90s ref. 2 garner more attention. A lovely perpetual calendar-moonphase, it’s housed in a classically inspired 37.7mm yellow gold case with cornes-de-vache-style lugs, a stepped bezel, and an incredible dial with the brand’s signature observatory-style hands. Someone tell Timothée Chalamet. —OH
Chopard L.U.C. Lunar One ref. 171927 (High estimate: $36,600)

Chopard has a hard-earned reputation for putting out some of the most finely made watches in Switzerland. It’s not just the nerds who are familiar with its work anymore, either. If we (the nerds, obviously) were sending a watch in a bottle to help share that message far and wide, this Lunar One, which looks like something out of Superman’s icy Fortress of Solitude, wouldn’t be a bad choice. This is Chopard’s first watch to combine a perpetual calendar and a moonphase, which is like shaving truffles on caviar. I love that the Roman numerals at 4 and 8 o’clock look like columns nearly buckling under the weight of the center of the dial. This watch also comes with several fun add-ons, like onyx prayer beads plus a ring and a pen set with diamonds. —Cam Wolf
Rolex ref. 3525 ‘Bariletto’ (High estimate: $609,000)

While many younger collectors are obsessed with the Cosmograph Daytona, true “Crown” heads know that other pre-Daytona chronographs sometimes present an even more compelling proposition. This ref. 3525 ‘’Bariletto,’ dating to the 1940s, is not only the first Oyster-cased Rolex chronograph, but it’s also the only known stainless-steel example carrying the signature on the dial of Proud’s, a Rolex retailer based in Sydney. Manually wound, paired to a handsome beads-of-rice bracelet, and measuring a compact 36mm, it comes from the collection of important Italian collector Pucci Papaleo. —OH
Patek Philippe ref. 2509 ‘School Watch’ (High estimate: $30,400)

While this stainless steel Patek may look like a normal ref. 2509—a beautiful hand-wound dress watch from the midcentury—it’s actually a “school watch” modified by a watchmaking student at the Geneva Watchmaking School. Dating to the 1960s, it’s housed in a 35mm stainless steel case and features a lovely dial with the ‘Ecole d’Horlogerie Geneve’ signature instead of Patek Philippe’s. Open it up, and the hand-wound movement is signed by Norbert Henry, the watchmaking student who assembled and finished it. While it may not attract the attention of more typical Patek collectors, its under-the-radar qualities make it a potential sleeper hit. —OH
Vacheron Constantin ref. 4072 (High estimate: roughly $48,777)

It’s tough to argue with the sheer beauty of Vacheron’s mid-20th-century output, much of which is vastly underappreciated compared to comparable pieces from the likes of Patek Philippe. This splendid yellow gold ref. 4072 with a two-tone multi-scale dial dates to the late 1940s—one of my favorite eras of watch design. Powered by the hand-wound cal. V 492 movement and featuring a lovely set of long, contoured lugs, its dial is in fantastic condition, with applied dart and Roman indices, sharp printing, a crisp signature, and legible tachymeter and telemeter scales. It will surely find its way onto the wrist of a collector with excellent taste. —OH
Universal Geneve pink-gold watch with cloisonné enamel dial (High estimate: roughly $36,600)

This watch’s dial depicts Saint George, who, according to legend, slew a dragon while on horseback. This is a perfect use for the rich, deep colors you get from enamel. The flames licking at Saint George are beautiful shades of orange and red. He triumphantly lifts his spear as his steed rears its front legs. It’s very cool how much story you can get from this little 35mm timepiece. —CW
F.P. Journe large stainless steel wall clock (High estimate: roughly $73,200)

Watch collectors might pony up a few thousand for one of independent watchmaker F.P. Journe’s used tissues at this point. However, they’ll have to settle for a host of accessories coming to auction instead this weekend. The maker is so in-demand that, in addition to his timepieces, houses are selling his empty watch boxes and a set of toys that resemble him. This lot is in the middle of those two extremes: a wall clock made to resemble Journe’s Octa Réserve de Marche. Although I’m not gonna lie, flipping this over and seeing the compartment where you stuff in the batteries is a bit of a buzzkill. —CW
Longines Lindbergh Hour Angle (High estimate: $2,500)

They used to make everything look more elegant. This original Longines design was developed in 1931 with famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. It is technically a pilot’s watch, but its elegant, icy-blue dial and Roman numerals would make it the fanciest model on many red carpets in 2026. This is a model from the ‘80s inspired by that original design, and it comes on an absolutely righteous beads-of-rice bracelet. Someone is going to get this guy for around $2,500 if the estimate is correct! —CW
Bonus: Rolex GMT-Master poster (High estimate: $4,900)

In Rolex world, even the advertisements sell for thousands of dollars. It’s hard to blame people when we’re talking about a rare poster of a GMT-Master wearing a snow-dusted Rolex beanie. Awwww. (Relatedly, imagine if Rolex sold that beanie!? Oh, boy.) —CW

items.title: Get Huge’s Director on How Looksmaxxing Is a ‘Trap’ for Men
items.description: Chasing physical perfection is a hobby now. This year, the community of men obsessed with climbing the ranks of society via square jawlines and hunter eyes, became a subject of widespread fascination. Once a term known in niche internet forums in the early 201
items.author: Tyler Chin
paragraphs: Chasing physical perfection is a hobby now. This year, the community of men obsessed with climbing the ranks of society via square jawlines and hunter eyes, became a subject of widespread fascination. Once a term known in niche internet forums in the early 2010s, the concept of “looksmaxxing” has gone mainstream. These days, even the casual scrollers among us have probably heard of techniques like bonesmashing and mewing.

But beyond a few self-appointed figureheads of the movement, the question of who is buying into these extreme self-improvement measures has loomed large. In Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death documentarian Stacey Lee gives viewers a deeper look into the lives of some of the looksmaxxing community’s more controversial figures. The three-part Hulu docuseries, out now, follows bodybuilding and biohacking influencer Dr. Tony Huge (whose real name is Anthony Hughes), controversial fitness personality, Connor Murphy, and a handful of other men.

Set largely in Thailand, the series tells the story of how these influencers decamped abroad and continued to post near daily videos of their body modification techniques. Lee also confronts the disturbing pattern of deaths among Huge’s inner circle, some of which have gone unsolved. Ultimately the series raises larger questions about the cultural, gender-driven motivations to push the limits of their bodies. GQ spoke with Lee about her nearly two-year immersion into a small corner of this community, the blurred lines between online persona and reality, and what it all reveals about a generation of young men who are seemingly searching for identity, connection, and purpose through increasingly unhealthy outlets.

These internet influencers create so much content, and there's a performance of masculinity that takes place within it. The topic is incredibly polarizing, but also very nuanced. We wanted to capture this world in a way that was more dimensional than what YouTube feeds allow, puncturing the veneer of performance to show who these people are beyond their online personas. I want audiences to see a more multifaceted view of this world and decide for themselves how they feel about these characters based on what they're seeing.

Looksmaxxing wasn't even a term when we started this project [in 2024]. We initially entered the bodybuilding, biohacking, and masculinity influencer community, which was still very fringe at the time. Tony had started making content nearly a decade ago, using shock value and radical transparency to build his brand. He was willing to do things on camera that others wouldn't, challenging social taboos. Ten years later, we're seeing a new generation of influencers who grew up watching Tony, [biohacking YouTuber Leo and Longevity], and Connor and are now using similar methods. But the algorithm has shifted the goalposts significantly since 2016, pushing the content into a much more extreme and nihilistic space.

I wouldn't necessarily say he was the godfather of looksmaxxing, but he was certainly influential in the biohacking and bodybuilding space. Connor Murphy was probably more directly connected to the origins of looksmaxxing, and Clavicular has referenced him as an inspiration. Tony was part of that same world, but represented a different generation.

Tony was a larger-than-life figure, but it was also a broader cultural moment. Around 2016, we were seeing the first Trump presidency, the post-Me Too movement, and the rise of Red Pill philosophy. There were several figures galvanizing these ideas, and Tony was among them.

I think what you're also referring to is this idea of legacy, right? He created something he believed was his unique gift to the world, but there's a sense that the next generation doesn't recognize him or understand his influence. That disconnect seems to drive some of his pursuit of the next big thing, which, in this instance, is looksmaxxing.

Look, Tony is incredibly charismatic and easygoing. Honestly, filming with him was a really respectful process. I think at times it was really discombobulating because he's always smiling in these videos, and he's presenting as this happy-go-lucky kind of guy, but then you're stopped in your tracks because he's doing and saying things that run against that.

The only other reference I'm thinking of is Andrew Tate, who presents in this very sinister way and has a darkness to him that's front and center. Tony doesn't present that way. For us, it was important to show that and to dimensionalize him. In his eyes, he didn't care if he was a hero or a villain. He just wanted to get his story out there. My approach was that I wanted to humanize him, but it wasn't about excusing what was happening.

It's important in this day and age to approach controversial subjects with an element of humanity while still maintaining journalistic independence. In this world, the boundaries are really slippery because people are performing so much. You really have to have your guard up about what's real and what's not. I don't think it's my job to tell audiences what to think of Tony. It's my job to provide a fuller understanding of who he is and allow them to make up their own minds. Discernment was something that was really important for us to communicate: What you see is not always what you get.

You see it in episodes one and two. [Editor's note: Tony lives with his wife and a group of other women he refers to as his girlfriends.] There's a very specific mentality rooted in Red Pill philosophy, where the role of a man is to control these women and provide for them, but also to assert himself. He's the leader, and they must follow. I think one of the things Tony is always battling is that he presents in such a nice way and isn't aggressive like [his friend and fellow biohacking influencer] Leo was, but there's still this desire to control the women. The women are very strong, opinionated women.

From conversations with Tony during the making of this documentary, I know a lot of the women didn't realize they were coming into a harem. They thought they were his one and only true love, and then they've entered this environment and suddenly they're in competition with one another.

That competition is part of the dynamic of how the harem works. The way Tony puts it is that if they're in competition with one another, they try harder to vie for his attention, love, and affection. That's an incredibly complicated way of pitting women against each other, and somewhat dehumanizing.

What I want to be really careful of is that these aren't a bunch of outrageous, crazy people doing crazy things from the start. It actually begins in a real human place, a place all of us can relate to. I want to be the best version of myself. Yeah, of course I do. That's very relatable.

What happens within this is that some of the needs, in Elon [Muscular, one of Tony Huge’s mentees and a content creator]'s case, a sense of belonging, a father figure, all of those kinds of things that he's craving, aren't solved by taking one pill. These are really deep societal issues that are complex and need to be approached with a multidimensional complexity.

Therein lies a lot of the challenges with this world, because the extreme and the attention keep pushing those goalposts further. You get a bigger jawline, a bigger penis, bigger muscles, and you're still not feeling happy. I think it creates this kind of trap that some men can get stuck within, because the original solution was never going to solve that problem to begin with.

Honestly, it was really important for me to make this. A lot of my prior work has centered on women and diverse perspectives, and it's such an honor and privilege to do that kind of work. But I also recognize I was existing in a bit of an echo chamber, so doing this project took me well outside my comfort zone.

I use this example with kids: When they're scared at night, you shine a light in the room. You look under the bed, you shine a light into it, and it makes the thing that's inside your head less scary. There was a little bit of that in making this documentary, of really looking at it and understanding it, witnessing how people come in, why they stay, and why they also can't leave, and using those things as what I need to teach my son. I need to teach him discernment. I need to teach him the difference between a YouTube influencer who's performing and one who's actually giving genuine, real tips.

In this day and age, where clipping culture and soundbites matter, there's no room for context. We're in a post-truth era, and no one's taking the time to provide context, human dimension, or other perspectives. I want my son to understand how the internet and influencer culture work so he can make his own decisions with more critical thought than what's often taught in the public space.

Yeah, of course. I never wanted to make something that was just another echo chamber. I want this documentary to reach people deep in the heart of the masculinity influencer space. I want them to see it. Everyone's going to have a different reaction, but most importantly, people are talking, and that's what I care about. I need the conversation, the depth of the conversation. That's what this is designed to have.

It's interesting because that question has come up a few times. There does appear to be a turning of the tides. Even within Tony's own universe, his sense of relevancy has shifted. He went from being the most masculine man he could be to wearing eyeliner. It's all become a lot more fluid and therefore a lot more interesting.

I think there's a time we're living through where the power structures that have existed for the last decade are starting to break down. People aren't feeling connected to them anymore, or they certainly aren't serving their needs.

I hope we're at a time of reckoning and change, where people are recognizing that this isn't working. There's so much more awareness about the issues men are facing, and there are specific influencers who are the opposite kind, who are speaking about this stuff more. There are some incredible voices in this space starting to counter the other perspectives out there.

items.title: The 11 Biggest Accessories Trends From the Spring 2027 Runways
items.description: The September (and October) shows were all about embellishment, which was especially true when it came to accessories. While bags and shoes typically capture the public’s imagination—and for good reason, this is luxury fashion we’re talking about—this season l
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: The September (and October) shows were all about embellishment, which was especially true when it came to accessories. While bags and shoes typically capture the public’s imagination—and for good reason, this is luxury fashion we’re talking about—this season lent a spotlight to major jewelry pieces worn in unexpected ways, like on shoes. Scarves were everywhere, as well as big-time belts worn two, three, or four at a time. Maximalism is back in style, with the quiet luxury mentality from just a couple years ago now on ice. Below, here are 10 accessories trends we saw on the spring 2027 runways that will be everywhere by the time the flowers start blooming again.

Chanel creative director Matthieu Blazy sent 83 looks down the runway at the Grand Palais, each with its own unique pair of shoes. The move was a pretty good indication of just how much attention designers paid to footwear for spring. Some of the biggest trends we saw were on shoes—from Burberry’s playful, face-covered paillette pumps to Valentino’s scenic sequin boots. Loewe’s beaded mules were made for folks looking to become great shoe collectors themselves.

Fashion magazines just can’t quit a “What’s in My Bag?” video series (yes, we are guilty of it). But designers this season weren’t asking that question so much as inquiring: What’s on your bag? The spring 2027 answer was everything—sequins, beads, pony hair, tweed, snakeskin, and more. The bag charm trend of the past couple seasons is still going strong as well.

Designers want you to put your money your feet are. From Saint Laurent’s charming sandals to Chanel’s pearly pumps, heels and flats this season were embellished with literal pieces of jewelry, like Loewe’s sandals decorated by a charm bracelet.
Designers also decorated their footwear with dainty ribbons (Prada), shoelaces (Miu Miu), and giant, sculptural bows (Loewe). At Moschino, each toe got its own individual loop.

Our third and final shoe trend shows more foot than ever. Michael Kors’s slides had barely visible, plastic straps; Bottega Veneta made delicate string sandals, and Area’s lace kitten heels were especially scantily clad.
Apparently, bags could also use a little fresh air. From Hermès to Prada and Chanel, designers put holes in their handbags. Wait, is this a recession indicator?

Scarves took center stage this season—and they took on new forms, with Dior’s flower-petal boas fluttering down the runway, while Saint Laurent’s scarves trailed dramatically behind the models. At Simone Rocha, a peach statement scarf was worn as a stole over one shoulder for added drama.

While we’re piling gems and chains onto our bags and shoes, we might as well pile on some actual jewelry, too. Shoulder-dusting earrings at Bottega Veneta and layers of pearls and beaded necklaces at Valentino proved it’s high time you invest in a bigger box for your baubles.

Mrs. Prada and Raf Simons may have ushered in the futuristic sunglass trend with their bug-eyed peepers from spring 2025, but the look has since taken on all kinds of new life—including at the house of Prada itself. The label debuted these mismatched sunglasses at their men’s show this summer, while Gucci and Miu Miu replicated the look of a fruit fly with their styles.

Belts for spring 2027 came in all shapes, sizes, and widths—and in multiples, too. Ferragamo designer Maximilian Davis stacked belts on belts for an extra cinch, while Valentino’s super-snatched waist came with a big gold buckle and two contrasting leather straps.

Sun protection is everything, every season—but especially in spring, when designers tend to have a little fun with toppers. From the chic and classic options at Ralph Lauren and Valentino to the ’70s-inspired, floppy versions at Chloé, there was something for everyone in the spring 2027 lineup.

items.title: Alex Karp Said He’s a ‘Progressive.’ OK! Here’s Some Other Stuff He’s Said Recently
items.description: When Palantir chief executive Alex Karp sat down with Politico this week, he reportedly used the word “progressive” eight times to describe both his political philosophy and his company.
items.author: Caroline Haskins
paragraphs: When Palantir chief executive Alex Karp sat down with Politico this week, he reportedly used the word “progressive” eight times to describe both his political philosophy and his company.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp told Politico, which noted that he called the Democratic Party “totally irresponsible” in the distant time of October 2025. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”

This isn’t the first time Karp has called himself a progressive. In 2018, The New York Times reported that Karp described himself as such. In the same article, he claimed to have voted for Hillary Clinton.

Karp has also donated money to Democratic candidates. In 2023, for instance, he donated $360,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. The next year, he donated $1 million to MAGA, Inc.

Palantir has a share of supporters from the Democratic party. However, it’s not necessarily clear how the products of Palantir—a company that built the technology that underpins much of the Trump administration's brutal arrest and deportation campaign, sold tools to the US military that can use generative AI to help plan and execute drone strikes, and partnered with the Israeli military to assist in its devastating war on the Gaza strip, among other things—could reasonably be seen as progressive.
It’s instructive, then, to look at what else Karp has said in recent weeks, and how it lines up with his idea of what’s “progressive.”

In his most recent quarterly letter to Palantir shareholders, Karp actually doubled down on his basic premise. In it, he argued that Palantir employees are “the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement.”

“We are all, in no uncertain terms, living through what John Lewis Gaddis, the professor of naval and military history at Yale, presciently described decades ago as the long peace,” Karp wrote, despite the fact that the US and Iran are currently engaged in direct warfare.
During Palantir’s corresponding earnings call on November 2, Karp was asked to clarify the statements in his letter.

“Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that in fact it's not worth going to war,” Karp said. He did not, however, address the relevant possibility that the US is the party that initiates war.

“I grew up as a lefty,” Karp continued. “I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I don't support wars.” But he said, “Sometimes they are necessary, and when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools.”

Karp went on to say that Palantir has both a “moral imperative” and a “mission reason” for having the “somewhat crazy aspiration” of dominating its market. That mission, Karp said, is supporting the war fighter. Conveniently, it’s also very profitable.
“We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money,” Karp said.

Karp’s recent comments in Politico could also be seen through the lens of convenience. Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and since about half of Palantir’s revenue comes from government work, it’s pragmatic to sow goodwill. Palantir has seen continued success, after all, across Democratic and Republican administrations.

However, Karp doesn’t care about cultivating favor with everybody. He pointedly excludes anyone who has criticized Palantir in what he calls “ridiculously stupid and malicious, incredibly hard to understand attacks.” (Karp didn’t name examples, although many critiques of Palantir have come from the American left.)

“What motivates me is helping to make sure we are fighting for you,” Karp said, addressing Palantir investors, “and quite frankly, making sure that the people that made fun of you and made fun of us are suffering.”

items.title: Duolingo, Strava, and Ticketmaster Are All Caught Up in EU’s New Digital Fairness Rules
items.description: The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media, or doing their Duolingo lesson.
items.author: Isabella Ward
paragraphs: The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media, or doing their Duolingo lesson.

Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns—practices that manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also ensure ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster, make tiered pricing transparent; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service.

The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference.
The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo.

Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act, which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.”

Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook. If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover.

The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act, says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds.

The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities.
Correction: 11/12/2026, 10:15 GMT. WIRED updated this article to correct that Ticketmaster does not use dynamic pricing in the EU.

items.title: A 13-Year-Old Asked AI About Suicide on Her School Laptop. It Didn’t Get Flagged for Weeks
items.description: A 13-year-old girl spent three months using her school-issued laptop to discuss depression, research suicide, and plan her funeral before self-harm-monitoring software finally prompted school officials to alert her parents, who intervened and stopped her, acco
items.author: Paresh Dave; Caroline Haskins
paragraphs: A 13-year-old girl spent three months using her school-issued laptop to discuss depression, research suicide, and plan her funeral before self-harm-monitoring software finally prompted school officials to alert her parents, who intervened and stopped her, according to a lawsuit filed this month by her parents.

The lawsuit alleges that Google and parent company Alphabet were negligent in their rollout of a Gemini model, claiming that the AI chatbot “coached” the North Carolina teenager to consider taking her own life. The case, which was previously reported by The New York Times, is one of several that allege harm from AI chatbot use, including claims of delusions and suicide. But it also illustrates the limitations of surveillance tools that thousands of schools have adopted in recent years, which are ostensibly designed to protect students from themselves when browsing and chatting online.

Andrew Liddell, a lawyer for the family, tells WIRED that, according to information the school provided to the family, the alert went to the personal phone of a former counselor who had left the school nine months before. The ex-employee was diligent in passing the alert along to current staff, who then notified the girl’s mother, he says.

As classrooms continue to rely on Google’s low-cost offerings, including Gemini, their ability to keep up with the potential risks is front and center. Just last week, parent and teacher groups across the country decried Google’s new requirement that schools must turn on generative AI features if they want to use Search. US senator Ed Markey cited Emma’s lawsuit in a letter to Google demanding the company let schools disable AI Mode and AI Overviews, writing that “Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage.”

According to the lawsuit, the North Carolina girl, identified as Emma Doe, descended into “a severe psychological crisis” after Google Search routed her to Gemini on her school-issued Google Chromebook. Though Emma’s school had blocked the stand-alone Gemini website, the lawsuit alleges that she was steered into interacting with the chatbot through AI Mode, which lets people ask follow-up questions about a query or begin an unrelated conversation.

Emma queried AI Mode about mental health issues starting last December. She asked about “severe depression” and “reasons to live,” and by late January she was asking about suicide, per the lawsuit. Over the course of two days around Valentine’s Day, she began writing a 1,500-word eulogy for herself with help from AI Mode in a Google Doc titled “Funeral.” The lawsuit says she worked on the document for more than four weeks while continuing to interact with the Gemini tool thousands of times.

After school on St. Patrick's Day, she deleted most of the file and restarted. But Liddell says the themes and thoughts the girl expressed didn't materially change. Around 7:30 pm, her mother allegedly received a message from the school indicating that her daughter was in “imminent danger,” the lawsuit states. Her mother used her phone to log in to Emma’s school account and “watched her daughter compose a suicide note in real time,” according to the lawsuit.

Google spokesperson José Castañeda says that the company is seriously “reviewing the claims in the lawsuit” and that its systems, including AI Mode, “aim to prevent users from engaging in harmful conversation.”
"We’ve worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources when they need it,” Castañeda says.

Lawyers for the family have sought to withhold the school's name to protect Emma's privacy. WIRED was able to identify the school, which did not return requests for comment. In recent months, the school added links to suicide prevention resources to the bottom of its website, according to WIRED’s review of the Internet Archive.

Liddell tells WIRED that Emma’s school only learned about her mental health crisis because it used at least one third-party student-activity-monitoring system. Citing information that was allegedly previously provided to the school’s parents, he says these may have included products from the companies GoGuardian and Gaggle. Liddell says that the family lacks a definitive answer because the school’s “window of cooperation” with them was brief.

GoGuardian spokesperson Natalia Switala tells WIRED that the company cannot “discuss any individual student or district” due to “student privacy obligations.” Gaggle did not immediately return WIRED’s request for comment.

The screening tools generally work by capturing keystrokes or scanning files and using algorithms and human review to identify potentially concerning content. It’s unclear whether the school’s third-party screening tools monitor AI Mode interactions or, if they do, how well they actually work. GoGuardian wrote in a July 2025 blog post that its flagship product monitors conversations with AI chatbots, including Gemini, but it didn’t mention AI Mode specifically.

Though it’s unclear exactly how effective student surveillance tools are at protecting students, studies show that educators perceive them as helpful. A 2022 white paper from the EdWeek Research Center found that in a survey of 1,000 American K-12 educators, 96 percent of Gaggle users believed that it helped to “keep students safe from suicide and/or self-harm.” While the study was sponsored by Gaggle, the findings were similar for teachers who reported using alternatives.

The allegation that Emma’s escalating interactions with Gemini went unnoticed for almost two months, after she explicitly asked about “hanging, suffocation, and overdosing,” appears to indicate that chatbot conversations embedded in Google Search may be a blind spot.

Civil rights groups have been critical of student surveillance tools, including calling out the marketing tactics and the invasion of student privacy. Experts have also worried that surveillance software undermines students’ ability to trust their teachers, the very people who may be able to help a child in crisis.

Benjamin Boudreaux, a policy researcher at Rand, which studies topics like student surveillance, tells WIRED that he fears that some schools have rushed to use tools without considering their limits and proper processes to act on alerts.

He expects Emma’s lawsuit to spark further outcry from parents, teachers, and students for instructional opportunities free of AI and surveillance and full of empathy. “It’s really only through that human connection,” he says, “that we can address the root issues.”

If you or someone you know needs help, call 988 for free, 24-hour support from the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline. You can also text HOME to 741-741 for the Crisis Text Line. Outside the US, visit the International Association for Suicide Prevention for crisis centers around the world.

items.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
items.description: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in settin
items.author: Grace Huckins
paragraphs: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

paragraphs: For more of The Cut’s favorite fashion, beauty, and home finds, sign up for the weekly Cut Shop Newsletter.

When I was little, my parents would always give my sister and me what I considered the best travel gifts: toys (remember Pixel Chix and Polly Pocket? Exactly — the best). As I’ve gotten older, though, I appreciate more age-appropriate and practical travel gifts, like new suitcases, hearty hand cream, and bluetooth eye masks. (Yes, that’s a thing. Keep reading.)

If you’re a frequent flier (or know somebody who never shuts up about their miles) whose love language is gift-giving, keep scrolling to find the best travel accessories that will make traveling (and gifting) easier.
