items.title: Amanda Seyfried Feared ‘You Can See Everything’ Could “Destroy” Her Career, Says Her Opinion of Billy Evans “Only Got Worse”
items.description: [This story contains spoilers from You Can See Everything.]
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: [This story contains spoilers from You Can See Everything.]

Amanda Seyfried is finally — really — opening up about her involvement in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, You Can See Everything, including why she feared the project could negatively impact her career and her tense confrontation with Elizabeth Holmes‘ husband, Billy Evans.

Following the A24 film’s release nearly a month ago, Seyfried has largely avoided directly addressing her surprise appearance in You Can See Everything. In the film’s third act, she reprises her portrayal of Holmes, the disgraced Theranos founder, whom she played in the limited series The Dropout — a role that earned her an Emmy in 2022.

In a new interview with Rolling Stone published Wednesday, Seyfried, Fielder and Oppenheim discuss the film’s full spoilers for the first time, including how the actress became involved in the project and her experience meeting Evans.

While filming the documentary, which chronicles Holmes’ life in the month leading up to her prison sentence, Fielder and Oppenheim began considering how to continue the film. That’s when they came up with the idea to bring Seyfried into the project. Fielder got the actress’ phone number through his The Curse co-star Emma Stone, and the pair eventually connected over Zoom, where he showed her footage from the film.

“I remember when [Emma] texted, and I was like, ‘Nathan Fielder? Ooh, I wonder if he wants to make something with me?’ My sister is a big fan [of yours, Nathan], and I know a lot of people are big fans of Nathan for You. I’d only seen The Curse. When you said you had 90 minutes of footage for me to see and help you work through, I was like, ‘Oh, he just wants some advice. He just wants us to know about my experience playing her and researching her and going into the mind of that quote-unquote character I portrayed,'” the actress recalled. “After the Zoom, I was totally game to do whatever you needed. It was just your energy [that persuaded me], and how much time you had spent [on this project], and that nobody knew this was happening.”

Seyfried said she wasn’t initially nervous about joining the project because she already had a “strange level of trust” with Fielder and Oppenheim. However, she acknowledged that agreeing to participate without first consulting her representatives wasn’t the typical process.

“I would say there was a lot of risk in the back of my head, and then when I told my agent and lawyer that I had already done it? Not the normal process,” she said. “But I go off and do my own thing sometimes, and nobody had any say or control over what I was doing with Nathan and Lance. My lawyer was like, ‘Well, now we have to retroactively set your deal in place because you need protection.’ We weren’t even considering reenactments at that point.”

Seyfried ultimately reprised her portrayal of Holmes through “muscle memory,” but the actress also worried about the potential professional consequences of participating in the documentary. Fielder emphasized that she had no creative control over the project or the footage that was filmed.

“No approval. Whatsoever,” she said. “There was always this vibration of risk and that sensation of: Am I going to destroy my career in some way? Am I going to get entangled in this, like, wasp’s nest with Billy? Am I gonna say the wrong thing? Am I gonna perpetuate negativity for her? Everything was scary.”
Seyfried also explained why she wanted to meet Evans after watching footage of his interactions with Holmes and the filmmakers.

“It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings. What he was doing and how he was in the footage that I saw, how you guys were interacting — it felt yucky to me,” she said. “I just wanted any information I could get on Billy. I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy. It was exciting to me, and it was scary, and it was questionable.”
Her opinion of Evans, however, “only got worse” after they met. “I do not like him,” she said.

The actress also met Holmes and Evans’ children during the documentary, in a scene that was interrupted by a phone call from Holmes herself, who was calling from prison. Seyfried recalled that the filmmakers weren’t expecting the call to come at that moment, adding that it really was Holmes on the other end.

Oppenheim also pointed to the tense dinner scene between Seyfried, Fielder and Evans, during which Evans criticizes the actress’ performance and they get into an argument over Seyfried’s criticisms of the late Charlie Kirk.
“The moment that I’ll probably be thinking about on my deathbed is the dinner scene between you and Billy,” Oppenheim said.

“There was no reason for him to get that aggressive,” Seyfried said. “That’s the word I’m going to use, as it’s more diplomatic. If my jaw wasn’t obviously on the floor, you could tell, like, it had come unhinged. I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off. Because this guy has disrespected me in such a way that I was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think so, buddy.'”

She continued, “I don’t like the way he’s using this human being, his wife — the person he says he’s ‘building monuments of love’ to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he’s behaving like he does not respect her. And not only am I protective of myself, I’m just trying to set the record straight in a way where I’m trying to defend myself, too, while maintaining some kind of rapport with him, so I can stay and he doesn’t kick us out, you know?”
Despite her concerns about the project, Seyfried said she has no regrets about participating: “I don’t regret it at all. I’m having the time of my life right now!”

items.title: ‘Exotic’ Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence
items.description: If you have been longing for a feature film about pole-dancing Poles, Exotic (Eksootika) is just what you were looking for! If you want to see a movie about self-discovery, body confidence, being exactly who you are and living life without asking permission, E
items.author: Georg Szalai
paragraphs: If you have been longing for a feature film about pole-dancing Poles, Exotic (Eksootika) is just what you were looking for! If you want to see a movie about self-discovery, body confidence, being exactly who you are and living life without asking permission, Exotic is also for you. Interested in a story about female friendship and belonging? Again, Exotic has got you covered. But even if you feel you would never care to catch a film about a writer’s attempt to master exotic pole dancing in a Polish beach resort, Exotic may well surprise you.

The feature debut of writer-director Sonja Orlewicz-Zakrzewska, who is also a visual artist and photographer, is full of humor, self-doubt and vulnerability. Adding authenticity, Exotic was shot during a recent edition of the Exo Stars Camp, a pole-dancing camp in a Polish beach town, and includes real participants and instructors.
The film will have its world premiere in the First Feature Competition of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) on Saturday, Nov. 14.

The filmmaker attended the camp herself and felt there was a story to tell. “I was fascinated by the clash of the fragile, intimate universes we carried within us around the camp,” she says. “It soon became clear that the camp itself was a perfect place to confront fears, leave one’s comfort zone and express oneself more than daily life ever allows.”

Exotic reflects that journey. It follows Mila, who is 30 and insecure. When her friend cancels on her, she reluctantly travels to a pole-dancing camp on the Polish coast alone, where she finds herself surrounded by confident dancers, skimpy costumes, high heels and a world that feels alien. But away from everyday life at home, her initial irony and unease give way to a journey of self-discovery.

Or as the PÖFF website teases: “Through demanding training, wild nights, awkward encounters, laughter, and intimate conversations, she discovers freedom, friendship, and a new relationship with herself.”

Mozaika Films is the main production company behind Exotic. The producers are Magdalena Sztorc and Anna Zajaczkowska. The cast is led by Jasmina Polak. The cinematographer was Adam Suzin, with editing handled by Tomasz Kajetan Naruszewicz. Pluto Film is handling sales.
Orlewicz-Zakrzewska talked to THR about mixing real-life experiences with fiction, how she made sure that her protagonist’s journey felt so believable and why pole dancing deserves a much better rep.

In case you don’t believe that real life inspired Exotic, just listen to the filmmaker. “I’m a pole dancer. I’ve been pole dancing for four years now,” she tells THR. “The main character in the film is played by Jasmina Polak. She’s actually a very good friend of mine in private life, and we went to pole-dancing classes together. After one or two months, we found out about the camp and decided to go together. But it was Jasmina who canceled at the last moment.”

So, Orlewicz-Zakrzewska attended the camp on her own. “Not everything in a film, but a lot of things you see are actually very much like my own experience and story,” she shares. “I did actually have those two roommates you see in the film, who were both kind of crazy in a different way. So, a lot of things there are inspired by reality.”

Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says she “fell in love with pole dancing right away.” And yes, she is aware that there still is a stigma attached to it. “There is a lot of it, and that’s why the pole-dancing community, all my girls, are really amazed by the fact that we shot this film,” she tells THR. “I did research about that and actually found out that it’s actually the first film that shows pole dance as a sport. There is no other full-length feature that shows the pole-dancing community as a sports community, as a hobby community rather than in a context of strip clubs.”

What does she love about it? “There are so many things,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says. “First, it’s an amazing workout. Your core strength is insane. For me, the gym is so boring. I also really like the femininity in this dance. And the more strength you have, the more effortless and, in a sense, more feminine and graceful you look. And then in your mind, the strength links up with the feminine.”

Exotic also shows the fun and party aspects that can come with the workouts. “I really love the fact that it has this entourage” and community spirit, explains Orlewicz-Zakrzewska. “The reason why I never explored it [before she started pole dancing] was that I was scared of judgment. I was scared of the patriarchal eye. There is a certain judgmental eye towards the pole-dancing community.”

How about the skimpy outfits? “You do often wear almost nothing, which actually makes a lot of sense because of the sweat and because you need your skin to hold on,” the filmmaker explains. “And the high-heeled shoes actually make a lot of sense when doing the spins [or jumps].”

And wearing these outfits and pole dancing opened her up to accepting a side of her that she was not willing to even consider before. “I have never been a girly girl,” shares Orlewicz-Zakrzewska. “I have always been a little bit intellectual and ran around with boys and climbed trees and so on. But I always had this other side in me, and [pole-dancing allowed me to] explore this more open form of femininity.”

Showcasing pole dancing and its community is something that excited the filmmaker and the folks at the camp. The writer-director actually knew right away that she would return to the post-Soviet hotel, where the camp takes place, with the camera. And she did.

But how did she approach the shoot and getting the people at the camp involved? “Before it started, I told the participants [and instructors] that I wanted to shoot the film. Is everybody okay with that? If anybody’s not, just please say no,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska recalls saying. “And imagine: nobody said no. Not a single person! Because they are performers, and most people in pole dancing are really open. So, they were really happy that we were doing this film and showing this community the way it really is.”

So keep your eyes open for non-professional actors in Exotic! “All is scripted, but we were just putting our actresses and actors inside the actual situations, inside the actual classes,” the director explains.

Exotic also features a 2007 clip of Jonas Mekas, the late Lithuanian filmmaker and poet who has been called “the godfather of American avant-garde cinema,” defending Paris Hilton. He argued that society has become too negative and skeptical to believe that people can actually change.

Which gets us to the question of Mila’s change in Exotic. Her transformation is neither instantaneous nor dramatic, and that is by design. The filmmaker recalls her experience at Exo Stars Campo. “It’s just really, really intense, you are outside of your everyday social bubble and you really have to confront the question of how you want to be perceived by others,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska tells THR. “It’s about both your relationship with yourself and also your relationship with the people you meet. So there are mechanisms that help you grow internally and reflect. But at the same time, nothing really happens because it’s just a sports camp. There are limitations to the massiveness of the internal journey.”
Her conclusion: “It’s not that a real revolution is going to happen there. But there is maybe the seed of the revolution that you are going to carry on with you.”

Exotic is Orlewicz-Zakrzewska’s first feature film, but it wasn’t supposed to be. “I was actually working on two other big projects before, but this one happened to get finished first,” she tells THR, adding with a laugh. “Maybe the reason why Exotic was produced as the first one is that it’s the most ‘normal’ thing I ever wrote. All the other things are much crazier.”
So, what’s next for her? “I’m working on two other feature films and a series,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says. “But all of these things are in development.”

It will be interesting to see if her next project has a short title, just like Exotic, or a really long one. After all, the title of her debut feature went through an evolution. “What’s funny is that with the titles for the things I write, it’s always either a full, super-long sentence or just one word. It’s never in between,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska explains. And she shares the first title she had for Exotic, and it is indeed long: If the World Is Round, I Don’t Know What It Means to Be Ahead.

items.title: Can Constantin Survive Its Own Parent Company?
items.description: In Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil, our plucky protagonist, medical courier Bryan (Austin Abrams), heroically fights his way through hordes of zombies, only to (spoiler alert!) be overcome by the mutant virus within him in the film’s final, controversial ending.
items.author: Scott Roxborough
paragraphs: In Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil, our plucky protagonist, medical courier Bryan (Austin Abrams), heroically fights his way through hordes of zombies, only to (spoiler alert!) be overcome by the mutant virus within him in the film’s final, controversial ending.
As a metaphor for Constantin Film, that might feel a bit on the nose.

The German production and distribution group, which holds the film rights to the Resident Evil video game franchise and produced Cregger’s reboot with Columbia Pictures, is coming off a triumphant year. But internal issues — specifically potentially toxic levels of debt at its parent company, Highlight Communications — mean its future may ultimately be beyond its control.

Resident Evil, at least, is a clear win for Constantin and its CEO, Oliver Berben. The global box office for Cregger’s reboot is $410 million and counting against a reported $75 million budget, making it the highest-grossing title in a franchise that now runs 12 features, including four animated films, and two Netflix series.

“I was discussing this with [Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group CEO] Tom Rothman,” says Berben, “and he pointed out how rare it is to take an intellectual property that has been around for so long — one that was arguably on the decline in terms of performance — and successfully reposition, revitalize and prepare it for the future. The fact that we managed to turn this IP around is remarkable.”

Berben, who took over as Constantin boss two years ago, sees this as evidence his strategy for the German mini-major is working. “Things have progressed faster than I had anticipated,” he says. “We have succeeded more quickly than expected in steering the company back onto a growth trajectory.”

Berben’s approach at Constantin has been to shift the company away from what he calls its previous “high-risk strategy” of investing in “large, very expensive productions” like recent flops In the Lost Lands, a $55 million fantasy starring Milla Jovovich and Dave Bautista, which grossed a fraction of its budget worldwide, and Momo, a family fantasy film featuring Martin Freeman and Claes Bang that cost upward of $35 million and has earned less than $3 million globally. “We need to rethink how we finance such large-scale productions moving forward,” he says.
Which doesn’t mean Constantin is going downmarket or putting a cap on its ambitions, budget-wise.
“This discussion about budgets is always somewhat misleading,” says Berben. “It’s rarely just about the budget itself. What’s actually at stake is the risk profile of a project, not the budget.”

Instead of relying primarily on in-house productions and shouldering most of the risk, Constantin is leaning into co-productions and projects with a clear, often hardcore fan base. That was the case with Resident Evil and Josh Boone’s Colleen Hoover adaptation Regretting You, a Constantin co-production with Harbinger Pictures, Frayed Pages Entertainment and Heartbones Entertainment that grossed more than $90 million globally on an estimated $30 million budget.

“It’s no longer about focusing on producing one major film every two or three years,” says Berben. “Our goal is to release at least one — if not more — films every single year. We have a wide range of filmmakers, and at Constantin, we’ve consistently brought in new talent — people who hadn’t worked with us before.”
The biggest uncertainty surrounding Constantin, however, has little to do with its films. It lies with its parent company.

Since 2009, Constantin has been wholly owned by Highlight, the Swiss media group chaired by Bernhard Burgener. And Highlight is in serious financial trouble. The group reported an operating loss of CHF 131.8 million ($165 million) in 2025 on revenue of CHF 412.1 million ($503 million) in 2025, and its balance sheet showed negative equity of CHF 3.3 million ($4 million). The damage came almost entirely from its struggling sports and events division, including broadcaster Sport1, which accounted for virtually all of the group’s operating loss. Constantin’s film division, by contrast, remained profitable. Constantin, which now accounts for roughly three-quarters of Highlight’s revenue, is the group’s most valuable operating asset.
The immediate problem is a CHF 74.5 million ($93 million) bank loan that comes due Nov. 30.

Highlight has pledged all of its Constantin shares, carried at about CHF 142 million ($177 million) on its books, along with other assets, as collateral for the loan. If it cannot refinance or repay the debt, the banks could enforce their claims against those assets, potentially putting Constantin’s ownership in play. Highlight’s annual report warns of significant uncertainty over the group’s ability to continue operating as a going concern.
Burgener has said Highlight is reviewing its options and has not ruled out selling Constantin.

At the same time, Constantin has taken steps that would make it possible to bring in a new investor. At an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting Aug. 21, the company authorized its board to issue up to 6.37 million new shares over the next five years, in exchange for cash or assets. That represents a potential one-third stake in Constantin after the new shares are issued. If all were placed with a single investor, Highlight’s ownership would fall from 100 percent to two-thirds. The authorization also allows Constantin to exclude existing shareholders from participating in the new share issue.

No deal with a new investor has been announced, and the authorization does not mean one is imminent. But it gives Constantin a mechanism to bring in fresh capital and potentially change its ownership structure.

In Resident Evil, Bryan ultimately cannot escape the infection inside him. Constantin may yet avoid a similar fate, but with its parent company facing a November debt deadline, the studio’s future is no longer entirely in its own hands.

items.title: 22 Killer Watches I Saw at One of New York’s Most Exclusive Collector Hangs
items.description: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.
items.author: Cam Wolf
paragraphs: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

I knew the watch collector meetup I was going to was legit when its organizer sent this text to the group: “We’ve engaged an off-duty NYPD detective to work security for our dinner. So, now really no reason not to bring your best!”

Last Wednesday night, at a fancy steakhouse in Midtown Manhattan, I was reminded why I love these enthusiast-organized events. This one was relatively small in comparison to blowouts like Rolliefest, but the idea was the same: A dozen or so collectors brought along their most prized timepieces and plunked them down on the table unattended (besides the off-duty NYPD detective, of course). When I asked one attendee if I could take his Breguet—similar to one heading to auction this weekend with a $73,000 estimate—across the room to take a photograph, he reacted like I’d asked if I could breathe oxygen: Of course! What a silly question. Events like these genuinely reflect the best of the hobby: deeply passionate collectors who really just want to share their watches with like-minded obsessives.

Between bites of miniature beef wellingtons and medium-rare steak, the guests passed around and ogled the dozens of grails on display. There were new classics on the table—including Vacheron Constantin’s Ultra-Thin, a leading contender for watch of the year—alongside plenty of old ones, including every flavor of vintage Rolex, from GMT-Masters to Daytonas to Explorer IIs. I was standing with one collector as he examined a pretty vintage Rolex GMT-Master. He stopped and looked around. So-and-so must be here, he muttered aloud. How did he know? Because he recognized the shade of the patina on the dial.

This particular group started getting together a couple of years ago, after the collectors @HorologicallyMinded, @s_h_lemon, @null_islands, and @jmsfisk (everyone at the event asked to remain anonymous) met at another watch-related retreat. @HorologicallyMinded, or HM, says that collecting was at one point something he did in solitude. “People generally judge when they learn how much watches cost,” HM tells me. “You paid how much for that!?” But he and the other three founders began meeting up for monthly dinners before eventually taking turns to organize these larger events. “This group has been the most rewarding part of this hobby,” HM says. “It’s been so great to have a group of people that have a common interest, but it’s not work-related and no one judges.”

Although the group has grown, the core four are still instrumental in making sure the functions go off without a hitch, with just the right spread of watches on the tables. “It is very deliberate and the four of us generally coordinate on it,” HM says. “We specifically make sure there is something for everyone.” That means ensuring there are at least a handful of watches worth less than $10,000—this time, that included several Rolex Datejusts, a Vulcain Cricket, and a gold Breitling from the 1940s. “We knew we were having some relative newbies and different people have different budgets, and we want everyone to be comfortable.” On the other end of the spectrum, some grail-level pieces were special requests from other members of the group.

All the watches wound up getting plenty of TLC. “I love the fact that we’re a group that can, and did, totally geek out about a vintage Longines Legend Diver, while a Doré dial Patek is on the same table,” HM says.
Below are some of the very best pieces I saw that night.
A Patek Philippe ref. 3970, part of the house’s historic lineage of pieces that combine a perpetual calendar with a chronograph. The dial on this one is so tasty.
A skeletonized Breguet Ref. 3355PT00PA0—maybe the watch of the night for me—on a show-stopping platinum bracelet.

A few years ago, MB&F started making more approachable versions of its sci-fi-ready watches and allocating them through a lottery system. This is the M.A.D2, with an outer ring on the dial that spins around very quickly. It’s really fun.
The aforementioned Rolex GMT-Master is a ref. 16760, a model produced during the ’80s that’s nicknamed the “Sophia Loren” thanks to its curvaceous profile.
Omega has incredible stuff in its archives. This is a chronograph from the ’30s that’s controlled entirely through that single button at 2 o’clock.

A couple of real bangers here. The Vacheron on the left is known as the “Cioccolatone,” because it resembles a square of chocolate. At the center is the Patek Philippe ref. 3417, an antimagnetic watch with just about the prettiest typography you’ll ever see on a watch. Zohran Mamdani should adopt that cursive for signs in the city, because it can make just about anything look nice: Warning: Rats. Or maybe, No Dumping Here.
A cloisonné dial from—of all brands—IWC! I am such a sucker for a cloisonné, which refers to the intricate images carefully fashioned from wire and colorful baked enamel.

A beautiful example of one of the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch from the ’50s through the ’70s, back when the latter was still a rugged outdoor outfitter. The shades of orange, yellow, and blue are dreamy.
A monochromatic take on the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar, which was produced in the ’80s and ’90s but looks incredibly modern.

Universal Genève finally relaunched last year after decades on the shelf, but it’s hard to beat the originals. This Polerouter comes on an extremely cool “wave” bracelet, which basically uses a repeating chevron pattern to make the slinky bit of metal appear to be in motion.

During World War II, a dozen watch manufacturers came together to make models following a strict set of specifications for the British Ministry of Defence. One of those brands was Longines, which produced this strapping piece.
You didn’t think we’d wrap this list up without a gorgeous yellow-gold Daytona, did you?
The ultimate fusion of sport and luxury watches. Heuer supplied this ’70s-era Carrera to Ferrari’s racing team, including legendary drivers like Jacky Ickx, Niki Lauda, and Clay Regazzoni.
This Patek is cool, but the bracelet is insane.

This isn’t your average Patek Philippe Nautilus. PP began producing this reference 3800 in 1981 as a smaller counterpart to the original. The few times I’ve gotten to try one on, I’m always struck by how perfect the proportions are. It’s nice and thin and looks just right on the wrist.
The United States Merchant Marines’ logo really punches up this Day-Date.
The ref. 6541 is the most beloved version of the Rolex Milgauss. It was produced in the ’50s and features a signature honeycomb dial. One sold for $2.5 million at auction in 2023.
Is there a better way to time your yacht race than with this Heuer Skipper? Probably not.

items.title: At the LACMA Art+Film Gala, Demna’s Gucci Steps Into the Spotlight
items.description: Stars from the worlds of art, film, music, and fashion came together Saturday, November 7, for the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala. Presented by Gucci, the benefit welcomed more than 600 guests to honor artist Vija Celmins and Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve,
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: Stars from the worlds of art, film, music, and fashion came together Saturday, November 7, for the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala. Presented by Gucci, the benefit welcomed more than 600 guests to honor artist Vija Celmins and Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve, raising a record-breaking nearly $7 million for the museum. The evening also marked the end of an era: Eva Chow, who has co-chaired the gala with Leonardo DiCaprio since its inception in 2011, announced that this would be her final year in the role.

Gucci artistic director Demna attended alongside house president and CEO Francesca Bellettini and Kering chairman François-Henri Pinault, with many of the evening’s guests dressed by the house. Among them were Kim Kardashian, Timothée Chalamet, Andrew Garfield, Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek Pinault, Parker Posey, Sarah Paulson, Sienna Miller, Emily Ratajkowski, and Viola Davis. Meanwhile a slew of top models fresh off the recent Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show—including Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Alex Consani, Vittoria Ceretti, and Candice Swanepoel—traded their angel wings for Demna’s designs.

After dinner, Paris Hilton introduced Blackpink sensation Rosé, who performed the live debut of her new single, “New Trick,” alongside “Number One Girl,” a cover of the Killers’ “Read My Mind,” and “APT.”

Before guests headed inside, photographer Myles Hendrik caught up with them beneath the glow of Chris Burden’s Urban Light, the landmark installation of 202 vintage street lamps that has framed LACMA’s Wilshire Boulevard entrance since 2008 and has served as the event’s red carpet, of sorts, for over a decade. See a selection of his portraits from the evening below.

items.title: Martine Rose, Beloved Cult Designer, Is Balenciaga’s New Creative Director
items.description: Designer Martine Rose may not be a household name, but many fashion insiders are celebrating the news that she has been appointed Balenciaga’s next creative director. The Jamaican-British designer’s eponymous menswear line not only has a cult following, she’s
items.author: Kyle Munzenrieder
paragraphs: Designer Martine Rose may not be a household name, but many fashion insiders are celebrating the news that she has been appointed Balenciaga’s next creative director. The Jamaican-British designer’s eponymous menswear line not only has a cult following, she’s also no stranger to the French label founded by Cristóbal Balenciaga. She served as a menswear consultant during the earliest year of former creative director Demna’s tenure, helping to establish many of the familiar codes that defined that era.

“It is a true privilege to be appointed creative director of Balenciaga, a house with an extraordinary heritage and a fearless creative spirit,” said Rose in a statement. “Balenciaga has been shaped by remarkable creative talents before me. I am committed to honoring this legacy and look forward to creating the next chapter in this rich and beautiful story.”

“Balenciaga has always been a house of radical creativity, challenging conventions, and redefining the boundaries of fashion,” added Kering CEO Luca de Meo. “Martine Rose embodies this spirit with a fresh, fearless, and deeply contemporary vision.”

Rose will succeed Pierpaolo Piccioli, who exited the house yesterday after just 18 months. Although a talented and respected designer, Piccioli’s romantic Italian vision often clashed with the generation-defining streetwear look that Demna established at Balenciaga during his 10-year tenure. Reports suggest that de Meo envisions the brand as a connector between those on the fringes of culture and Gen Z buyers. Notably, menswear sales—which rose dramatically under Demna—had begun to wane. Rose may be a more natural fit to cater to the Demna clientele.

Rose, born in London’s working-class neighborhood of Croydon, graduated with a degree in fashion design from Middlesex University. She established her own brand in 2007, which for years existed under the radar. In 2011, she won the support of Fashion East, London’s nonprofit fashion incubator program. News of her behind-the-scenes role at Balenciaga helped to raise her profile among fashion insiders.

Since then, her line has enjoyed something of a cult status. A pair of neon heeled sneakers from a collaboration with Nike could be classified as fashion’s favorite It sneaker. Hailey Bieber has often been spotted in Rose’s outerwear (husband Justin is a fan too). Kendrick Lamar wore a Rose-designed jacket to perform at the 2025 NFL Super Bowl halftime show. Dua Lipa, Kim Kardashian, and Rihanna have all been spotted in her designs, while the stylists of several K-pop stars often dress their clients in her wares.
Cate Blanchett wore a translucent Martine Rose trench coat on the cover of W’s Volume 5, 2018 issue.

Rose finds inspiration in her Jamaican-British upbringing, ‘90s rave culture, and the everyday clothing of the streets, though always with an unexpected twist. She’s staged fashion shows in markets, her daughter’s primary school, and directly on the streets, and has long taken pride in her niche status in fashion. “I feel really proud of it all,” she told W in 2018 of he growing success. “But then I remember, I like being under the radar.”

Still, her frequent collaborations with brands like Nike, Napapijri, Clark’s, and Supreme have been commercial successes, and Rose’s name has been floated as a candidate for bigger jobs (reports suggest she was considered to take over as Louis Vuitton’s menswear creative director before the job went to Pharrell Williams). Still, the future of Rose’s own line has been thrown into question recently. In 2023, Tomorrow Ltd, a fashion incubator aiding up-and-coming designer brands, acquired a 60 percent stake in the Martine Rose label. The company has faced financial hardship in the past year (just this week, Coperni, another former Tomorrow Ltd brand, announced it was shutting down), and was sold to The Level Group earlier this year.

Rose’s new job will ensure her voice continues to be heard in fashion—this time, on a much bigger stage. She will take up the job immediately, though the timing of her first collection has not yet been announced.

items.title: Here’s What We Know About the X-70 Fractal, NASA’s Experimental New Plane
items.description: NASA has unveiled a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated i
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: NASA has unveiled a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated images and some technical specifications regarding its capabilities.

Despite the secrecy, it is possible to get some idea of what the new vehicle is like. First of all, it’s not a spacecraft, meaning it is not designed to reach Earth’s orbit or operate outside the atmosphere. However, this crewed, subsonic aircraft is capable of flying far above commercial jets, reaching altitudes over 45,000 feet, well into the stratosphere. Other specs released include the plane’s max speed of Mach 0.75—about 575 miles per hour—and that it can travel nearly 1,700 miles in a single flight.

According to NASA, the X-70 Fractal will enable research into maneuver capabilities never before demonstrated in crewed aircraft, although the agency has not specified what types of maneuvers it intends to perform. The plane will also be capable of carrying up to one ton of experimental equipment and is expected to make its first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years.

One of the key features of the craft will be its modular design, allowing for the rapid installation and replacement of experimental equipment both inside and outside the aircraft. This is largely why it is referred to as an “experimental platform.” It will also feature reconfigurable flight control systems so that NASA can study different ways of steering an aircraft without having to develop a separate platform for each research project.

Although NASA is best known for its space missions, it’s long been dedicated to aeronautical research. That’s what the first A stands for. The agency also traces its origins to the creation of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which was founded in 1915 and was folded into the newly formed NASA in 1958.

Since then, the space agency has developed numerous experimental aircraft to test technologies that range from supersonic flight and propulsion systems to new aerodynamic configurations. Not all of these prototypes go on to become operational aircraft, but the knowledge gained contributes to the development of future commercial and military aircraft as well as space vehicles.

Among its most recent projects is the X-59, developed in collaboration with aerospace and defense company Lockheed Martin to investigate ways to reduce the noise produced by supersonic aircraft. The X-70 Fractal will join this tradition of pioneers in the sky.

The development of these technologies also has a strategic dimension. In its budget documents for 2027, NASA identifies aeronautical research as a tool for maintaining US technological leadership in the face of growing international competition. The agency also plans to collaborate with the Department of Defense to advance new flight capabilities, although it has not yet announced any military applications for the X-70 Fractal.

During the unveiling of the new aircraft, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman noted that the project represents only one part of a new era for federal aeronautical research and hinted that more announcements are coming. For now, the agency has not provided details on what those initiatives might be, nor has it specified when it will release more information about the X-70 Fractal.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
items.description: No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang. He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US–China relation
items.author: Will Knight; Paresh Dave
paragraphs: No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang. He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US–China relations. That now all stands in the balance.

Over the past few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia’s board of directors said the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance.

How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond.
“He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry.

Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang.

Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company.

But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.”

Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry.

“On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first.
“He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.”
Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.

The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The scandal also raises serious questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government’s strategy on China, Fedasiuk says.

Huang’s affair appears especially damning given how outspoken he has been in recent years against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China. His credibility on the topic could be permanently in doubt.

Both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration imposed export controls designed to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, as well as to technology required to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, however, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips; it was better to make China reliant on US technology, the argument went.
Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, says the Huang scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports.

“There was going to be more of an impetus to control what chips are getting sent to China anyway,” he says. “I expect there to be more scrutiny on what's going on, what's getting sent to China. I think there's also going to be more scrutiny from the Commerce Department.”

items.title: Jensen Huang Hired a PR Firm Known for Handling Sex Scandals Last Year
items.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handle
items.author: Lauren Goode
paragraphs: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handled Huang’s behind-the-scenes communications since at least October 2025, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Risa Heller, the firm’s founder, has built a reputation as a fixer for powerful men facing allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies, according to a 2023 New York magazine profile. Her past clients and people who have sought her advice include former congressman Anthony Weiner, chef Mario Batali, and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller also handles corporate communications and issues unrelated to personal controversies for its clients.

Heller’s public relations consultants were initially believed to be hired for matters related to Huang’s personal life, including his family’s philanthropic endeavors, according to people familiar with the arrangement. The firm frequently communicated with Huang and his daughter Madison, a product marketing director at Nvidia who has become an increasingly prominent figure within the company, sources tell WIRED. It’s not clear whether Heller’s early work with the Huang family involved Huang’s affair.

In 2024, Huang began appearing in public with a woman who goes by Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed, according to The New York Times. Megaspeed was created when it split off from a Chinese gaming and cloud computing firm in 2023, a few months after the US government began restricting exports of advanced semiconductors to China, including those developed by Nvidia. A subsidiary of Megaspeed later became a major buyer of Nvidia chips.

In early October 2025, Jensen Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed and his connection to Alice became public in a lengthy New York Times report, which alleged that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether the company was helping Chinese firms evade American export controls through its subsidiaries.

The report caused tensions to rise within Nvidia’s top ranks, and Jensen was rankled by the story, according to sources. By the end of that month, Nvidia’s internal communications teams had been instructed to include Heller’s firm on any press inquiries about Huang, whether personal or professional, according to people familiar with the matter.
When reached by email, a representative for Heller referred WIRED to Nvidia. John Rizzo, Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, declined to comment.

US intelligence officials have determined that Alice (who has no known relation to Jensen) is a spy working for the Chinese government, according to the Times. Nvidia initially said that Jensen’s interactions with Alice were part of routine business with clients. But on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that his relationship with her was romantic in nature. In an email to Nvidia staff, he said he owed them and his family an apology. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced it is opening an independent investigation into Jensen’s activities. It said it has no reason to believe that national security or confidential Nvidia information has been compromised.

Before founding her firm, Risa Heller worked for Jane Harman, then a Democratic congresswoman from California, and later served as Democratic senator Chuck Schumer’s New York City press secretary. Rizzo, Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, also previously worked for Schumer, serving as his deputy communications director.
Update 11/10/26 8:45am ET: This story has been updated to note that Nvidia declined to comment.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried Does Not Regret Fighting Billy Evans
items.description: Amanda Seyfried is finally ready to talk about You Can See Everything. In Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, Seyfried reprised her role as the convicted Theranos founder in several crucial reenactments and served as a much-neede
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Amanda Seyfried is finally ready to talk about You Can See Everything. In Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, Seyfried reprised her role as the convicted Theranos founder in several crucial reenactments and served as a much-needed sounding board for Fielder. She eventually got so involved that she flew to Austin to have dinner with Fielder and Billy Evans, Holmes’s partner, leading to an explosive conversation over Chinese food. Seyfried has remained mum about her involvement in the project until Wednesday, when Rolling Stone published a conversation among her, Fielder, and Oppenheim. Unsurprisingly, she has not warmed up to Evans since that meeting.

Seyfried told Fielder that she found Evans to be “yucky” when she first watched footage of him and Holmes in their San Diego rental home. Her immediate negative response to Evans’s whole deal was actually what fueled her desire to meet him in person. “I just wanted any information I could get on Billy,” Seyfried told Fielder. “I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy.”

As you likely already know if you’ve seen the film, Seyfried found that her feelings about Evans “only got worse” after meeting him. Apparently, she really did try to be on her best behavior while at Evans’s house — “I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children — with their children,” she told Fielder and Oppenheim. “I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of shit about him up until that point. Because look, I do not like him. But I’m coming into this man’s house.”

Despite her best efforts, things took a turn during dinner, when Evans attacked Seyfried for her portrayal of Holmes in The Dropout and for calling Charlie Kirk “hateful” on Instagram. “There was no reason for him to get that aggressive,” Seyfried said, a word she chose because it was “diplomatic.” She said that once Evans “disrespected” her, she felt as though “the gloves are off.”

“I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, ‘OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things,’” Seyfried said. “I don’t like the way he’s using this human being, his wife — the person he says he’s ‘building monuments of love’ to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he’s behaving like he does not respect her.”
After watching the three-and-a-half-hour documentary, it’s hard to disagree with Seyfried. But maybe the AI hologram of Holmes that hangs out in Evans’s dining room has a different opinion.

items.title: What to Buy for the Best-Smelling Person You Know
items.description: Everyone knows someone who gets stopped mid-conversation with the question “I’m sorry, but what are you wearing?” I’ve shamelessly asked people countless times, and I’ve been on the receiving end of the question, too. Those are usually the people who curate a
items.author: Asia Milia Ware
paragraphs: Everyone knows someone who gets stopped mid-conversation with the question “I’m sorry, but what are you wearing?” I’ve shamelessly asked people countless times, and I’ve been on the receiving end of the question, too. Those are usually the people who curate a fragrance wardrobe with the same intention that they curate their closet. They’re not just picking up the fragrance that everyone else is wearing or running to buy a gourmand scent because that’s the trend; they’ve developed a special nose for scent and a taste that’s specific to them. I know it sounds dramatic, but we can all think of one person we know like this — and they can be the hardest people to shop for.

But that’s where this list comes in. Consider it your guide to finding the next scent for your fragrance wardrobe or for the person in your life who always smells divine. These fragrances are some of my most-worn and most-complimented scents, the ones I’d gift to someone who wants to smell expensive and start a conversation this holiday season.
The Fragrances They’ll Love
New! You can now save this product for later.

For the person who likes a bit of mystery to their scent, consider this the intriguing smoky yet warm and intimate fragrance that leaves an addictive lasting impression. It’s the one I recommend to my friends for a first date because the scent trail makes you want to instantly lean in.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I’ve had multiple men stop me on the street to ask about this perfume, then purchase it for their wives on the spot — that’s how alluring the scent trail is! It’s a fragrance that’s meant to speak for you silently before you speak for yourself, hence the name. It’s sweet but not sugary because the vanilla notes are blended with peach, tuberose, orris, and more. It’s a striking balance of feminine and a warm addictive scent; what I consider the perfect signature.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Rose scents can be too flowery sometimes, but this is not your average rose. It’s a bright, unexpected floral with fruity notes like lychee and pear that soften the rose, plus a honeyed base that makes you want to smell it over and over again. I like to layer it with a softer rose, Parfums de Marly’s cult-classic Delina, for a balancing combo. It’s one that’s gotten me endless compliments, including from Jennifer Lawrence, who said she’s never smelled anything like it.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Mojave Ghost has become the white button-up of my fragrance wardrobe. It’s airy but soft and subtly sweet, the perfect everyday scent. Now picture that in silk: That’s what the absolu version of this scent smells like. It’s richer and warmer but still effortless with crisp pear notes contrasted by amberette.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Valaya Exclusif is a beloved Parfums de Marly scent. It smells clean, but it also has a creamy almond twist that takes it from powdery to a bit musky. If Mojave Ghost is your crisp white button-up, this is your cashmere sweater.
New! You can now save this product for later.

This is the fragrance for the person who likes a more unconventional scent, a far cry from your white button-up — more like the statement coat in the back of the closet that you rarely reach for. It’s a creamy and leathery attention-grabbing scent that’s a bit tart. The bottle itself is small, but I’d buy it over and over again for the intriguing looks I get when someone gets a whiff of the scent trail. It’s not for everyone, but those who like a mysterious, cozy scent will love it.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Fig is one of those notes that can be a bit polarizing in a scent. Korean brand Born to Stand Out finds joy in the challenge of taking a polarizing note and creating a scent that everyone would love to have in their fragrance wardrobe. Fig Porn is a fresh and green take on fig, but it’s balanced out with cedarwood and bergamot for a musky dry-down that’ll make you fall in love with fig.
New! You can now save this product for later.

If a smokier fig suits your taste, Bo’s Casa Blanca perfume adds a woody twist to a dry desert fig, and the result is transportive. It smells like you’ve just checked into the chicest villa with crisp sheets and a lovely view, but it can still be worn every day — not just when you’re on a dreamy holiday.
New! You can now save this product for later.

We love Baccarat at The Cut, but Maison Francis Kurkdjian has so many other great scents. Oud Satin Mood has been what I turn to when I’m in a sexy mood. It’s a rich oud with a hint of powder that enters a room before you do.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Influxious founder Funmi Monet created this with a vision of it becoming the berrylike scent you spritz on before heading out for a night on the town, and that’s exactly what it smells like. It’s a fruity floral scent that doesn’t smell like anything you’ve smelled before; the blueberry musk and patchouli notes challenge your average fragrance. I’ve never been into berry scents until I smelled this.
New! You can now save this product for later.

If you like floral scents but with a little edge and earthiness, this is for you. Barénia’s intense fragrance takes its classic chypre perfume a little deeper with leather and patchouli that smell luxurious on the skin. The bottle is a nod to the Collier de Chien bracelet, making it a vanity staple beyond what’s in the bottle.
New! You can now save this product for later.

You’ve never smelled cocoa like this. Dries Van Noten’s Soie Malaquais is another unexpected scent; it’s the one that makes you smell expensive but not predictable. The cocoa and chestnut in the fragrance is warm and indulgent, while the bergamot and rose is more romantic and sophisticated, making it a scent that needs no layering. It breaks all the rules and smells better throughout the day as it sits on the skin.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Yes, Balenciaga has scents, and they aren’t talked about enough. Usually, I’m opposed to discovery kits because they’re so small, but this cigarette-style box is a nice piece to keep in a purse, and the scents are great too.
New! You can now save this product for later.
More Scented Products for Your Consideration

If you’re buying a scent for someone who is particularly hard to please, you can’t go wrong with non-fragrance items — chances are they like their space to smell good too. So why not gift a scent for their home or even a perfume for their hair?
New! You can now save this product for later.

The chicest gift is a Loewe candle, and that’s a hill I’ll die on. It’s my favorite gift to receive and my favorite one to give. The brand’s take on the pistachio trend is a warm and nutty aroma that will make their home feel like a cozy gelato shop (probably not what you want in a fragrance, but a perfect wintry scent for their space).
New! You can now save this product for later.

Home scents don’t stop at candles; it also includes everyday essentials, like the hand soap you use. Adding Trudon hand soap to my bathroom was one of the best decisions I made, because guests are always smelling their hands after stepping out and asking what it is. Those same guests will be getting their own hand soap for the holidays.
New! You can now save this product for later.

For the person who keeps their scent essentials in their purse, a hydrating perfumed hand cream is the gift that keeps on giving. I love Le Labo’s Thé Matcha cream because it’s strong enough that the scent will linger, but not so strong that it overpowers whatever scent I’m already wearing.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Anyone who is serious about smelling good knows that it all starts in the shower. Cyklar’s scents have become some of my favorites this year, and the brand recently launched shea butter body scrubs. The santal in this scrub is subtle, and the post-scrub skin nourishment is intense. It’s a great gift when you don’t know what scent to give because it starts with a good base note.
New! You can now save this product for later.

And why not follow up a scrub with a fragrance oil? It has the lingering smell of a perfume with the nourishment of an oil and usually a price that isn’t as high. I wore this oil during a HYROX competition, and I was still receiving compliments on my scent after hours of running and sweating (and thankfully no pooping).
New! You can now save this product for later.

The secret to smelling good from every angle is to not stop at the fragrance you put on your skin, but you should never spray your perfumes directly on your hair because the alcohol can dry it out (ask me how I know). That’s where hair perfumes come in. Cécred’s classic jasmine-and-oud scent from its hair products was bottled into a hair perfume this year, and it’s a great addition to any scent wardrobe.

items.title: Gird Your Loins: A Heated Rivalry Monopoly Game Is Coming
items.description: Close your eyes for a second and think back to this time last year. Remember room 1410? The tuna melt? The way you screamed when you heard the words “I’m coming to the cottage”? If you’re one of the nearly 11 million people who tuned into Heated Rivalry, then
items.author: Hanna Flanagan
paragraphs: Close your eyes for a second and think back to this time last year. Remember room 1410? The tuna melt? The way you screamed when you heard the words “I’m coming to the cottage”? If you’re one of the nearly 11 million people who tuned into Heated Rivalry, then obviously you do. What a time to be alive! It was hard to move on from those six episodes, and some of us have been chasing the high ever since, doing whatever it takes to fill the void — obsessively reading fan fiction, buying the same skin-care products that Hudson Williams uses, watching TikTok edits over and over again, seeing Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody, even heading to our local Regal Cinemas to rewatch the final episodes in 4DX.

If all that is still not enough to quench your thirst (no judgment), you’ll be happy to know that Monopoly just announced a Heated Rivalry edition of its classic board game. It doesn’t officially launch until June 2027, but it’s available to preorder now on Amazon and Walmart and is set to ship next May. That means it’ll arrive on your doorstep just in time to cure your post-watch hangover from season two, which premieres in April 2027.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Whoever created this game is deep in the fandom, and it shows. Instead of buying streets, railroads, and utility companies, Monopoly: Heated Rivalry allows you to buy locations from the show, such as hotels, gyms, and the cottage. The themed tokens include a Straw+Berry smoothie, the MLH Cup, a hockey skate, a tuna melt, an extra banana, and a stupid Canadian wolf bird. The board itself also highlights key scenes from the show in chronological order, so you can relive Shane and Ilya’s love story from your living room, sans screen. Oh, and there’s one other very important detail: The game has an “ages 17 and up” rating. Immediately adding to cart …
More Heated Rivalry Merch We Love

Need a gift for your friend who still can’t be normal about Heated Rivalry (you know, the one you’ll need to check in on when season two drops)? We rounded up some ideas, below, since the Monopoly game won’t launch in time for the holidays. These products also make excellent White Elephant gifts or gag gifts if you’re shopping for a fellow chronically online person.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 11, 2026
items.description: The moon spends all day in Sagittarius giving you the optimism and can-do attitude to take on any challenge that comes your way. Even if you’re usually the sort of person to dwell on worst-case scenarios or get bogged down by self-doubt, you’ll probably still
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: The moon spends all day in Sagittarius giving you the optimism and can-do attitude to take on any challenge that comes your way. Even if you’re usually the sort of person to dwell on worst-case scenarios or get bogged down by self-doubt, you’ll probably still feel upbeat right now. There’s always the chance that you’ll make mistakes rooted in overconfidence, but try not to let any fears of messing up hold you back. Now is the time to err on the side of boldness: It could change your life, and at the very least, you’ll have more fun.

Although you aren’t afraid to take risks, you try to be smart about it. You don’t want to fail dramatically or embarrass yourself. If you’re going to take decisive action, you want there to be a reasonable likelihood that things will work out. But today, if you don’t make any mistakes, it probably means you’re playing it too safe. Trial and error is part of the process. You won’t learn without the occasional misstep, so today, make a point of taking chances and stepping outside your comfort zone.

You’re not the sort of person who’s quick to forgive and forget. When somebody wrongs you, you don’t see why you should be expected to pretend nothing happened. You may not make a big fuss about it, but you’re not going to brush it off and go back to “normal” either. There’s nothing exactly wrong with this approach, but keep this in mind: Nurturing grudges can take up a lot of mental space. Today, see what happens if you let old resentments drop so you can put more energy into the things you love.

As much as you enjoy being around other people, working with them is often frustrating. You want to be able to take your ideas and run with them; when you have a clear plan in your mind, you don’t want other people’s criticisms clouding your vision. But today, take it seriously when others challenge you. Maybe you’ll end up changing your mind, maybe not — but either way, working through the disagreements will make your own ideas stronger.

The more you lean into nostalgia, the harder it can be for you to accurately assess what’s going on in your life now. Maybe you keep working toward goals you’ve already outgrown or you hang on to old relationships even when they’re no longer healthy. Today, though, you’ll be able to assess your circumstances more clearly with less sentimentality getting in the way. Let go of fixed ideas about how things used to be and instead respond to them as they actually are.

When you suspect others are misunderstanding or underestimating you, your impulse is to set the record straight. You can’t stand the thought that anyone might think ill of you. You know your intentions are good and you have lots to offer, and you want to make sure everyone else knows, too. But today, try to let go of this worry. There will always be people who don’t like or understand you, and you’ll only stress yourself out trying to change their mind. Decide you’re going to live your life as you choose and nobody else’s opinions can get in the way.

When you have positive thoughts about the people around you today, share them. Compliment the people you admire, let colleagues know you’ve noticed their hard work, and tell your friends you care. You may assume these small comments won’t make much of a difference, but today especially, that couldn’t be further from the truth. Even the people who seem most confident feel overlooked and unappreciated sometimes. So if you have something good to say, don’t keep it to yourself.

If you already have a tendency to procrastinate, the habit’s likely to worsen today: You’ll convince yourself the tasks on your list can wait until tomorrow. But don’t offload all the boring work onto your future self. That’ll only make everything harder than it needs to be. Instead, make a point of taking care of the small stuff as soon as possible — ideally, as soon as it enters your mind. If it’s at all possible to do something right away, do it.

When other people are excited about a new plan or big change, you’re hesitant to voice your doubts. Even if you’re fairly certain things won’t work out the way others are hoping, you don’t want to be the one to dampen their enthusiasm. (In your experience, that doesn’t motivate anyone to rethink their assumptions; it only makes them mad at you.) But today, being willing to be the voice of dissent will prove rewarding. Others may not appreciate it in the moment, but they will in the long run.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

When you feel like nobody is listening, you may think the answer is to get louder and more dramatic. If you raise your voice, people will have no choice but to hear you; if you embellish your stories or overstate your opinions, others will sit up and take notice. There’s nothing wrong with presenting your thoughts and experiences in the best light possible — but take care not to be dishonest. Don’t prioritize getting attention over telling the truth.

If you suddenly start feeling insecure today, you’ll want to pinpoint a cause. Maybe some personal failing is making you feel bad about yourself, or maybe someone else’s unkindness has shaken you. You’re convinced that once you determine why you’re feeling so bad, you can fix the problem. But it’s likely that there’s no one reason for your feelings today, and they’re likely to blow over soon enough. So don’t put too much energy into coming up with solutions — chances are, all you really need to feel better is a bit of time.

Unexpected people may come to your aid today. Casual acquaintances could step in with the help you were too proud to ask for; strangers may offer a kind word exactly when you most need it. Try not to react with suspicion or assume they must have ulterior motives. You show up for your loved ones — why should it surprise you when they do the same for you? So focus on accepting these kindnesses with gratitude, then pay them forward.

Maybe you think the only way to get affirmation is to be “good” — to be capable and conscientious, the sort of person who makes only good decisions and follows all the rules. You imagine that if you can demonstrate you’re doing everything right, then everyone will definitely praise and admire you. But today, understand the people around you want to know the real you. They aren’t looking for perfection; they want to see your genuine personality, flaws and all.

items.title: Zazie Beetz Believes We Need The Bad Feelings, Too
items.description: In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.
items.author: Charlotte Owen
paragraphs: In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.

Zazie Beetz has been working as an actor for more than a decade, but she still gets nervous when starting a new project. Case in point: her new Apple TV thriller Nocturne, in which she stars as an undercover FBI agent opposite Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham. “On the first day I called my mom crying because I was like, ‘I’m so nervous. What if they don’t like me? What if I’m bad?’” the 35-year-old says. “I’ll never forget, she was like, ‘Zazie, just go in there with love in your heart and just spread love onto everyone. Just come in — your heart is open and just give love.’ I don’t know why it just resonated with me — like, ‘Yes, I’m not going to close in fear. I’m going to open and offer what I need.’”

For Beetz, who was born in Berlin and split her early childhood between Germany and New York before her family settled there when she was eight, the approach worked. Nocturne is a taut thriller, adapted from Lars Kepler’s book The Sandman, in which Graham turns in a terrifying performance as a serial killer who represents the worst of humanity. It’s Beetz’s character, Saga Bauer, who has to find ways to get through to him, and so she sought to find the shades of gray. “I’m always trying to kind of come at this — again, not excusing the Jurek character for killing people — but where is this coming from? What’s his mind around this? What’s the non-typical approach that I don’t necessarily understand that this character is experiencing and why?” she says.

It’s an approach she also took in far less contentious circumstances, such as when she played Van in Atlanta. Beetz’s character was pilloried by fans of the show in Season 3 when she abandoned her daughter to go on a trip to Paris, though Beetz has always defended the choice. “I’m always defensive of my characters,” she says. “People are human, and there are certainly things you don’t want to inflict on other people — or as a parent, you don’t want to let your emotions get in the way of creating a life or harming your children or something like that — but ultimately we are individuals first, and things happen. And for me, for Van, I’m like — Her child was safe and fine, and she needed a moment. And that happens whether or not we approve.”

Nevertheless, the work is still hard, and it’s her husband — fellow actor David Rysdahl, with whom she’s expecting her first child — who helps support her when that’s the case. “He’s made me a better performer,” she says. “Firstly, just by being my literal biggest fan, which is great. But then also, he’s just so talented and I think he’s very bold in his approach — I feel like when we are discussing a role, we question everything and try to get to the bottom of it all… He’s, I think, much better at character analyses than I am… I don’t think I would have as rich characters without him at all. And so I think he has really helped me with that and helped build my confidence and has literally picked me up off the floor when I felt so scared to go on set.”

Hard as it is, it’s this humanity in the work which continues to draw her to it. “Acting is extremely vulnerable, especially in the very blunt context of you're going on set, there are a hundred people there you’ve never met, and then you’re like, ‘All right, I’m just going to do something,’” she says. “And sometimes you look dumb or you make a bad choice and it’s bad and you’re bad. That happens. And the best actors in the world are sometimes just bad. And you have to accept that a hundred people saw that and thought that was really bad…How do you move through that and move on? And that’s been a huge part of my journey in this industry and in my career — not focusing so much on that sensation and how that would shut me down.”
Keep reading to discover four of Beetz’s favorite books.

Her first pick is John Steinbeck’s 1952 epic East of Eden. Despite the timing of the choice, she has yet to see Netflix’s adaptation. “I’m usually not one to like an adaptation,” she says. “You have such a personal relationship with these stories that I often am like, ‘You’re ruining what was in my head’ or, ‘You're veering off,’ and then I just get mad.”

Beetz has complicated feelings about the novel’s contentious female protagonist, Cathy. “I don’t think Steinbeck loves women but I think that they are the most interesting characters and extremely complicated and complex,” she says. “I don’t know if she’s an antihero really, but kind of this protagonist that you’re…I don’t know if you’re rooting for her, but you’re also just there with her. I think so much of what motivates her is also fear and I think that that can turn into aggression and rejection.”

She’s also drawn to those complexities in her own life. “I really do believe that context exists for everything and you’re a villain in someone’s life,” she says. “For me, as a person who’s not religious, I would say I have sort of spirituality in my own approach. I do think ultimately I will perceive things a certain way due to my cultural learnings, due to what I think is bad. I will perceive death as bad because I have emotional attachments and things like that.”

Her second choice is Sapiens, a digestible human history from history professor Yuval Noah Harari. “What I love about the book is it’s written for a lay person. It’s very accessible,” she says. “When works are available for people to read and enjoy and there’s pictures, it’s just a great read.”

The book, which she says shows how expansive yet personal humanity can be, also offered her valuable perspective on humankind as a whole. “I liked the idea that every creature on this planet has a special thing. A dog can smell, and a fish can swim,” she says. “I feel like for humans — and we’re animals and, to me, have the same value as any other creature — our special thing is our imagination and our ability to tell stories, which as a creative is very validating.”

At the same time, Beetz is worried about the future of human imagination. “I am a very black-and-white thinker on AI. I fall in the camp of [thinking] it’s devastating to our culture and our minds,” she says. “Obviously there’s so many things at risk — safety and all of that — but I feel like the greatest risk is our minds, our cognitive abilities and even just asking little questions. I keep thinking, ‘What am I robbing myself of if I’m not going out and seeking these answers in a different way?’”

Her third selection is The Giver by Lois Lowry, a Newbery Medal-winning middle-grade novel which follows a 12-year-old boy named Jonas living in a “utopian” society where emotion has been eliminated. Selected as the Receiver of Memory for his community, Jonas learns that in sheltering themselves from bad memories and emotions, the community has also deprived themselves of happy ones.

“It’s this book around literally what we’ve just been talking about — the fear of what the consequence is of choosing security, safety, comfort, and how it creates a life devoid of richness,” she says. “When I was younger, I remember I was speaking with a therapist and I just kept talking about all these bad feelings I was having, and it just felt very devastating to me at the time. And she was like, ‘These aren't bad feelings, you’re just having a richer experience. You’re just having richer feelings, and with depth also can come darkness.’”

That kind of vulnerability has been on her mind as she expects her first child. “I think about becoming a parent, I’m opening my heart to potentially the greatest heartbreak of my life if something happens to my child, which I hope of course never does,” she says. “But to open that chamber in my heart, that possibility of love and relationship that I would love to experience, I have to also open a chamber of potential pain.”

Her final pick is The Alchemist, Paulo Coelho’s 1988 philosophical novel that follows a young Spanish shepherd through the ups and downs of his journey to Egypt. The book advocates following your own personal journey and heeding your intuition. “I read it at a time when I just really needed it. It was very soothing for me,” she says. “It’s allowed me, I think, just a lot of acceptance and sort of surrender in general and being like, ‘I am here for this time and I’m just going to have my experience and I’m going to experience it, [and] also be OK to observe.’”

Beetz is a believer that everything happens for a reason. “I don’t fully believe in free will in a way because I think from the moment of the Big Bang, the moment that first atom went out in one direction [there was] only one series of events that can happen from that expulsion of energy,” she says. “Every single decision that I made in my life is because this dinosaur met that dinosaur, and then that dinosaur met that dinosaur. And then everything was just a domino effect from that first moment.”
