items.author: Ben Daitz
paragraphs: Six weeks after two open-heart surgeries in 12 days, Roshi Joan Halifax invited me for a visit. She was recovering, but feeling ‘weak as a kitten’. When I’d last seen her, three or four years earlier, her hair had been shorn in a Zen tonsure; now it hung in a lush, grey-streaked braid to the middle of her back. She was pale and short of breath.

As a physician and her friend, I was reluctant to press on with the interview, but she wanted to begin. She was staying with Wendy Lau, her close friend, an emergency physician and Zen priest whose home overlooks Upaya, the Zen centre Halifax established in 1990 in the foothills above Santa Fe in New Mexico. We sat on Lau’s back porch, drinking tea.

Halifax is a medical anthropologist, a Buddhist teacher and a caregiver to the dying, who has worked with the suffering of others for more than 50 years: in burn units and jail clinics, in remote Himalayan villages, at the bedsides of people for whom there was nothing left to cure. She learned that the qualities that drew her there could also pull her under, and more than once they did. When she found her way back, it was Buddhist practice that helped her remain steady enough to help.

Halifax had almost died. She had gone into the operating room at Stanford cheerful, she told me – upbeat, confident. Surgeons repaired her heart’s mitral valve. Coming out of anaesthesia, intubated, she was certain the tube was positioned incorrectly. She couldn’t speak, so she made writing motions until someone put a pen in her hand, and – stoned, half-conscious – she wrote glottis. Wendy Lau understood. They fixed it.

Then came what she called the worst 12 days of her life. The valve replacement was failing. Her blood pressure plunged; she bled internally; she had a dangerous arrhythmia, and had to be shocked to restore a normal heart rhythm. ‘Death is easier than this,’ she told Lau. She meant it. ‘I actually wanted to die,’ she said. ‘I just was so sick.’
She was still on a gurney from the latest resuscitative shock when the surgeon appeared in his scrubs and told her: ‘We have to take you back in.’
‘I had a moment of Yikes!’ she told me.

In the intensive care unit after the second operation, she awoke convinced she was hanging upside down against a wall of moss. A warmth enveloped her chest and expanded, and kept expanding, into utter bliss. Then a male voice said: ‘You’re not done with your work yet,’ and she found herself back against the moss-covered wall. The cycle began again. ‘My recognition was: this is death. It’s fine,’ Halifax said.

Halifax has spent much of her life crossing thresholds, sometimes knowingly and sometimes not, and in the process delivering a grittier, more hands-on and help-oriented form of Buddhism to the West. Now aged 84, facing her own mortality, she names the charnel grounds where she practised her art: refugee camps, prisons, cancer wards, war zones. To that list she adds one more. ‘My latest charnel ground was being hospitalised for this heart surgery,’ she said.

Halifax’s first encounter with illness had come 80 years earlier. Aged four, she woke one morning unable to see and partially paralysed on her left side. She remembers feeling her way along the wall into her parents’ bedroom. Later, when a doctor picked her up in his convertible, she knew the top was down only from the wind.

She spent much of the next couple of years in bed with polio, away from other children. ‘I discovered that I had a spiritual life, an inner life,’ she said. Even now, she can walk through a building in her mind, imagining its rooms and passages, ‘because that’s what I did when I was four.’

Her parents hired Lila Robinson, a local Black woman, to care for her, keep house and cook. The Halifaxes lived in Coral Gables in Florida, a restricted, all-white enclave where neither Jews nor African Americans were allowed to live. Robinson and her three daughters lived across the railroad tracks in West Coconut Grove, then known as ‘Coloured Town’, in what Halifax called a ‘concrete monster’ – one of the mould-filled, roach-infested semi-high-rises baking in the Florida heat. To Halifax, Robinson was ‘the most incredibly kind person in the world, a manifestation of unconditional love and brightness – the woman who raised me.’

As Halifax recovered, she sometimes rode with her father to pick up Robinson. The journey carried her between ‘two different universes’: one had a country club and an all-white school, and the other: understocked shops, tired cars, good music and warmth. She saw the gulf between the two but was not entirely convinced that hers was the better world. Looking back, she traced her attraction to places of suffering to that early collision of inequality and love.
‘You could be both contemplative and a social activist. I want to be like that’

At the H Sophie Newcomb women’s college of Tulane University in New Orleans, the disparity Halifax had registered as a child became something she could act on. It was 1960 and, with the civil rights movement gathering force around her, she joined protests and the fight for racial justice. ‘There was a whole cadre of us who felt that racism was abhorrent,’ she said.

Through that work, Halifax met Hodding Carter II, the progressive Southern newspaper editor who had established the Delta Democrat-Times in Greenville, Mississippi. Carter was going blind. ‘For a time, I became his kind of eyes and feet and hands,’ Halifax said – his assistant in civil rights activities. Carter and his wife supported her, but her activism put her at odds with Tulane. ‘I graduated early from Tulane with Tulane’s help, so to speak,’ she recalled. ‘They really wanted me out of the system.’

In 1963, she left for New York, where her civil rights work opened into a wider world of artists, musicians, filmmakers and political activists. There she met Alan Lomax, the folklorist and ethnomusicologist whose field recordings of folk, jazz and blues musicians had taken him around the world. His project studied music, dance and language across cultures. The work carried her from a huge computer in a university basement to field trips in Morocco, the Bahamas and rural Arkansas. ‘I was in anthropology heaven,’ she recalled. ‘I just wanted to learn everything about anthropology that I possibly could.’

Two years later, a different kind of encounter opened a path inward. Halifax heard the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh speak when he came to New York to urge an end to the bombing of his country through the calm of his Buddhist practice. Halifax was then ‘angry all the time’ – at the war, racism, the government and the suffering around her. She understood that ‘you could be both contemplative and a social activist. I want to be like that,’ she thought. But for almost a decade, she remained a ‘book Buddhist’, absorbing what she could from reading alone.

For now, her focus was anthropology. By 1968, she was in Paris, indexing ethnographic films at the Musée de l’Homme. There she met Germaine Dieterlen, a French anthropologist who had spent more than 20 years among the Dogon people of central Mali. Dieterlen told Halifax that the Dogon were midway through the Sigui, a seven-year cycle of ceremonies moving through 289 villages and held only once about every 60 years. Most Dogon would attend just one Segui in a lifetime. To Halifax, it was a rite of passage that ‘reconsecrated an entire culture’.

The attraction was also personal. Robinson’s family had roots in the Bahamas and, farther back, in Africa; her grandmother had been a slave. Halifax knew little more – not when the family had been taken, nor from where. ‘I really wanted to go to Africa,’ she told me, ‘to understand the cultural roots of this woman who had raised me.’

In early 1969, Halifax drove a VW bus, modified for desert driving, from Germany to Marseilles in France and on to a ship bound for Oran, on the Algerian coast. From there, she drove alone to Gao in Mali – including 1,600 miles of unpaved track across the western Sahara. There was no map. The route was marked by oil drums filled with rocks, like buoys set in an ocean of peach-coloured sand stretching to the horizon. She encountered only three transport trucks on the entire crossing; the drivers dug her out when she was stuck, and she rewarded them with oranges.

Three and a half weeks after setting out, she reached Gao, an ancient trading centre on the Niger River at the southern end of the Sahara. From there, she put the VW bus on a barge down the Niger, then drove on to the Bandiagara escarpment, a wall of sandstone cliffs extending more than 100 miles. ‘The Dogon villages were spectacular,’ she told me. ‘The ceremonies and incredible masks and dances were extraordinary. The ceremony began with elder women who had been alive and present in a previous Sigui cycle, 60 years before. These were powerful women, their torsos completely exposed, not big people, but very, very thin. Old, muscular women, marching out in front of all the men.’ She spent about five months interviewing Dogon spiritual leaders and photographing the Sigui with her Pentax. Among the Dogon, she found a cosmology in which death was a passage, one that bound the living to their ancestors.

In Bamako, Mali’s capital, she realised she had contracted hepatitis. ‘There was a war going on with Chad,’ she recalled, ‘and there were no hotel rooms, and I ended up sleeping in an iron bed in a whorehouse, listening both to the war and to people having sex, and I was so sick.’ She made her way to the train station. The manager saw how ill she was and arranged passage for her and a flatcar for the bus to Dakar. The US embassy and her parents helped her to fly to Miami for medical care. She doesn’t know what happened to the bus.

The hepatitis that sent Halifax home to Miami changed the direction of her work. The city had been remade while she was away. Hundreds of thousands of Cuban refugees had arrived after the revolution and, by 1969, the local healthcare system was overwhelmed – not only by the numbers but by the differences in culture. Mainstream medicine was often inaccessible or inadequate to Miami’s growing Latin American and Caribbean communities, and many people instead sought care from alternative, often unlicensed practitioners – a clínica, a storefront doctor’s office of uncertain legality, or a santero, a priest of the Afro-Cuban religion of Lukumí, or Santería.

Recuperating in her parents’ apartment on Key Biscayne, she met Emanuel ‘Manny’ Papper, a neighbour in the building and dean of the University of Miami School of Medicine. ‘That’s how I made it into the anthropology department at the medical school,’ Halifax said.

There, she joined the Miami Health Ecology Project, led by Hazel Weidman, a senior medical anthropologist in the University of Miami School of Medicine’s psychiatry department and a founder of the Society for Medical Anthropology. The project studied five ethnic communities surrounding Jackson Memorial Hospital – Bahamian, Cuban, Haitian, Puerto Rican and Southern Black – and asked what illness meant to the person who had it: what caused it, who could heal it, and what being made well would mean.
He believed Jose had been cursed, and recommended an exorcism. I called Halifax. She came immediately

Soon, Halifax was pursuing her PhD in medical anthropology and doing fieldwork in neighbourhoods, clinics and houses of worship. Because of her experience in Africa and the woman who had been her caregiver when she was first so sick, she was drawn to Dade County’s ‘co-cultures’. She began identifying healers, especially in Miami’s Cuban communities. In the cabildos – ‘cult houses’ devoted to different orishas (deities) – she watched ‘different qualities manifesting through the members who were possessed’.

‘It was just fascinating,’ she said. She became ‘a kind of cultural broker’, bringing Santería healers into the medical system at Jackson Memorial. That’s how I met her, in 1972, when, as a family medicine resident, I attended one of her lectures on the ceremonies, spells and healing traditions practised among South Florida’s Caribbean communities. Not long after, at the Dade County Jail clinic I’d helped start, a 20-year-old Cuban inmate named Jose – ‘normal’ when arrested for burglary the night before – sat staring and unresponsive in what appeared to be a catatonic trance. Needle tracks marked his hands and forearms. I wondered about schizophrenia or conversion hysteria. Ron, a former Navy medic and the clinic’s physician assistant, had apprenticed with a Santería priest. He believed Jose had been cursed, and recommended an exorcism. I called Halifax. She came immediately.

Ron pulled a beautiful king conch shell out of a grocery bag and smashed it into a hundred pieces on the floor. With a sharp piece of shell, he made a cut halfway up Jose’s forearm, blood oozing. With another piece of shell, he matched Jose’s cut on his own left forearm. Jose didn’t flinch, but Joan and I reached for each other’s hands and squeezed. Ron bound their arms together, palm-to-palm, with a red bandana, and spent the night in the clinic with Jose. The next morning, Jose began to speak.

He said he had used heroin since his early teens. After his mother threw him out and he consulted a Santería priest, he robbed a convenience store and returned to the family house to hide. A king conch stood beside the door; police waited in the bushes. To Jose, the shell embodied Elegua, the orisha of the crossroads, who had placed him under a curse. Only an exorcism could lift it.

Given permission by the warden, we all met the following morning in the jail laundry room, flanked by banks of industrial washers and dryers. I spoke and understood Spanish, but Ron’s incantations sounded like no language I had ever heard. I drew Jose’s blood, finding a vein despite his years of heroin use, and squirted it into a bowl. Jose’s hair and nails were clipped into other bowls and covered with red bandanas. Candles flickered in a semicircle; across the room, the glass door of a dryer gave back a distorted reflection of the ceremony. I could feel my pulse beating in my ears and shivers up my spine. At the end, Jose buried the red bandanas containing his hair and nail clippings in a grassy plot inside the jail’s security doors. The ceremony was deemed successful by all of us, most importantly, Jose. Looking back, I can hardly believe we exposed ourselves to one another’s blood – or that the warden had even allowed the ceremony.

When, over 50 years later, I asked Roshi Halifax, by now a Zen Buddhist priest, to reflect on the exorcism, she said: ‘By the time we first met, my life had been so intense and filled with challenges, this was just an interesting experience for me. It wasn’t a big deal. We were like characters in this strange drama. I felt a lot of compassion toward Jose. You could feel the pain in him, and I look at drug addiction as a way to cover pain; the whole thing was beautiful and bizarre. There was a suffering human being, and we did what he wanted and needed, and that was good.’

At Jackson, Halifax had encountered another kind of suffering as well. She worked in the burn unit and sat with dying patients, watching young clinicians confront an injury they could no longer cure. Many had entered medicine wanting to help, yet she felt conventional medical training was not grounded in compassion. ‘What does healing mean in our culture?’ she began asking herself. ‘What is the difference between healing and curing? … What is the relationship between compassion and equanimity? Can compassion be taught?’

Several months after the exorcism, at a meeting of the American Psychiatric Association in Dallas, Halifax met Stanislav Grof, a Czech psychiatrist who had pioneered LSD research and was studying its effects on patients dying of cancer at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center. They were married five weeks later in a volcanic crater in Iceland. Halifax wore a black Icelandic dress and a peaked crown representing a glacier; the world religions scholar Huston Smith officiated, and the mythology scholar Joseph Campbell gave her away. She had taken 600 micrograms of Sandoz LSD – what she called a ‘single overwhelming dose’.

‘There I was – married. All of a sudden!’ she recalled. ‘I was kind of in an altered state.’ The ceremony was ‘so archetypal’, she said. ‘And, needless to say, our marriage was a little bit like that.’

After leaving Miami, Halifax joined Grof’s research with dying cancer patients in Baltimore. The study was funded by the National Institute of Mental Health, and every patient knew the treatment would include LSD. The work began with preparation, including meetings with family members; on the day of the LSD session, Halifax might remain with a patient from 7:30 am until midnight, through the experience and the crucial period of integration afterward.

Aged 30, Halifax thought she was already somewhat experienced in medical settings and in being with suffering and death. She later wrote that she ‘was not prepared’ for the work or for the depth of the relationships she developed with people who were dying. Most were in extreme suffering, seeking relief from pain and fear and, as Halifax put it, the possibility of a ‘gentle death’. Death came to seem to her less like medicine’s failure than ‘the final developmental stage in a person’s life’ – one that called for attention even when curing was no longer possible.
Being a woman gave her ‘the permission and latitude to ride straight into a catastrophic mental and physical state’

At the same time, Grof had become her LSD therapist. She believed the drug might enable her ‘to know my mind completely. Talk about hubris. Oh my God.’ Instead, frequent high doses dissolved her defences and left her mentally fragile. The marriage approached a breaking point even as she continued the work. ‘It took me to the brink,’ she said. ‘Not only were these cancer patients suffering, but I was about to join the list of casualties as I plunged into the depths of physical and mental confusion. But it was also incredibly inspiring.’

In 1973, amid Halifax’s personal crisis, she and Grof went to Esalen, the experimental community on the cliffs of Big Sur in California, where psychedelics mingled with Zen and other contemplative traditions. There, she designed and produced ‘Buddhism in Mind’, a month-long gathering of teachers and scholars. During the programme, she confided to Jack Kornfield, a young American Buddhist teacher recently returned from monastic training in Asia: ‘I feel like I really need a teacher.’ Kornfield suggested Seung Sahn: ‘There’s this crazy intense Korean person. He might be a good match for you.’ Halifax invited the Korean Zen master to the gathering. ‘He and I connected,’ she said.

Halifax and Grof divorced in 1975. By then, she was experiencing what she described as extreme confusion and anguish, with full-blown hallucinations. She found herself ‘deeply identified with the so-called psychotics I had worked with in Florida’ – the people she had once approached as an anthropologist and could no longer regard from outside. Looking back, she thought her gender had made the descent possible: little was expected of her, and a man in her position would have had a harder time falling that far. Being a woman, she wrote, gave her ‘the permission and latitude to ride straight into a catastrophic mental and physical state’. She was, she said, ‘assigned and resigned to “my fate”’.
Her own summary of those years ran to four items: ‘A failed marriage, a failed career, my mind disordered, reputation lost.’

She looked for help in two places. The first was anthropology: Indigenous cultures have people who go crazy, and some of them go on to heal themselves and become healers. So she left the laboratory for the field. She went to Mexico several times a year, not to study the Huichol but to study with them, and ask for their help. There she met an old man named Don José Matsúwa: ‘No right hand, no teeth, Don José was dexterous and sharp in ways of the mind,’ she wrote. ‘With him, through him, and with the help of peyote, my humour was unearthed.’ All this helped her write the book Shamanic Voices (1979), gathering the testimony of shamans across more than a dozen cultures – accounts of initiation, of visionary journeys, of the healer who has first been broken, then healed.

The second source of help was Buddhist practice. LSD had opened Halifax’s mind without giving her a way to steady it. Meditation did. She described the essence of the practice as finding ‘the iron pivot in the spine that does not move even in the midst of great suffering’. A Buddhist metaphor.

For the next 10 years, Halifax travelled and practised with Seung Sahn’s community in the United States and abroad. One day, he casually asked how she had been spending her time. Halifax recited her recent ‘“good” deeds’. He paused and, as she later wrote, ‘growled: “You are a bad bodhisattva!”’

She felt like she had been ‘struck by lightning’. In Mahayana Buddhism, a bodhisattva dedicates her life to relieving suffering. A bodhisattva’s commitment requires humility as well as compassion. When Halifax recited her ‘good deeds’, Seung Sahn heard that she was keeping score. Her service had become tangled with a need for approval and with a habit of doing so much for others that she sometimes diminished their power to act for themselves. ‘I felt chagrined,’ she wrote, ‘but also grateful for the tough lesson he had given me.’

Halifax calls qualities such as empathy and altruism ‘edge states’. Altruism, the impulse that sends a person toward others in need, for instance, can curdle into its own kind of harm – resulting in helping that costs the helper great distress, or strips the one being helped of the power to act for themselves. So too with empathy, integrity, the drive to do good work: the qualities ‘without which we cannot serve, nor … survive’, she writes, are the same ones that can undo the server. She also argues that compassion can help restore the balance when those qualities turn destructive.
‘It wasn’t gritty enough for me. I always felt like a bull in a china shop’

Around 1980, she moved to California to develop the Ojai Foundation, where Buddhist teachers and their communities could gather and practise. Early each morning, a bell called the community to meditation, and through the day it called them back for meals and meetings. They sat in council, shared the work, and tried to work through the difficulties of living together. Seung Sahn returned each year to lead sessions in a tepee on the grounds. ‘I practised really hard under his aegis,’ Halifax said.

That same year, friends living in Nepal invited Halifax to travel into the Himalayas with some of her students. ‘What I saw,’ she said, ‘was really powerful because I had the medical school experience in my background and I saw so many sick people.’ In the remote mountain villages, illness was widespread and medical care nearly absent. The journey became the beginning of the Nomads Clinic, which has returned to the Nepalese Himalayas year after year.

By 1985, Halifax had reached the limit of what Seung Sahn could offer as a teacher. ‘He had real boundary problems, a serious crush on me,’ she said. ‘Because of his feelings for me and also … he wasn’t involved in social action, I just had to leave that community.’

That winter she went to Plum Village, Thich Nhat Hanh’s monastery in southern France, and met him for the first time – nearly 20 years after he had drawn her toward Buddhism in New York. For four days, she sat and walked with him, with Sister Chân Không and Richard Baker Roshi, ate silent meals of white rice and mustard greens, walked in fields of early jonquils, and talked about what a socially embedded, American Buddhism might look like. She studied and travelled with Thich Nhat Hanh for about 15 years and became a dharma teacher in his order, authorised to teach its practices.

But she ‘had some feelings of ambivalence in that community’ too. There was abundant loving-kindness and a stated dedication to social engagement, she said, but few projects involving the direct action she wanted. ‘It wasn’t gritty enough for me. I always felt like a bull in a china shop,’ she said.

Halifax had met Bernie Glassman in the 1970s, and their paths had crossed on and off over the years. Now, as her ambivalence about Plum Village grew, she encountered him again. ‘I realised, you know, I need to practise with a Western teacher,’ she recalled. She wanted a Zen that entered the places of suffering she already knew – someone ‘gritty’, she said, and ‘visionary, tough, open, radical’. She found that teacher in Glassman, a former aeronautical engineer who had turned Buddhist practice toward homelessness, poverty and AIDS. She became his student and told him she wanted to ordain as a Buddhist priest.

His training took her to Schoolhouse 86, an abandoned school in the Bronx, where they pulled on heavy gloves and cleared condoms and needles from the ground. Glassman also took his students to Auschwitz. On one retreat, some 150 people sat in the November rain on the railway tracks at the selection site, eating little more than soup and old bread as the names of people who had died there were read slowly ‘in the four directions’. In the museum, Halifax passed glass cases filled with children’s shoes and suitcases. Then she came to a case of human hair. ‘I felt like throwing up,’ she recalled. ‘And I almost passed out. I was just so horrified by the magnitude of the cruelty.’ Glassman called this ‘charnel ground practice’: entering places of suffering without averting one’s gaze.
His gesture made her see the pity within her grief – and that she had to let him go

Meanwhile, Halifax returned to a question she’d been asking since Miami: what could she offer someone when there was nothing left to cure? Toward the end of the Ojai years, her mother’s death made it personal. ‘If I were to die tomorrow, what would be left undone?’ Halifax asked herself. After leaving Ojai, and then spending time at a Zen centre in Crestone in Colorado, she retreated to a hermitage in Abiquiú, New Mexico. Each day, she sat alone beside the brown, churning Chama river. ‘Nowhere to go; nothing to do,’ became the refrain of her days. After a year, she knew one thing: ‘I wanted to be with people who were dying.’ She wanted to return to work that, for her, had begun at the University of Miami, now ‘more seasoned by age and practice’. ‘In being with dying,’ she wrote, ‘the true nature of the human mind and heart might be revealed.’

Halifax encountered that lesson again with Issan Dorsey, a Zen teacher and founder of Maitri Hospice in San Francisco. In a lecture at Harvard Divinity School, she described visiting him in the hospital near the end of his life. He was sitting up in bed in a simple cotton robe, ‘quite thin and transparent’. She sat beside him, looked into his eyes and began to cry. Dorsey reached over with a frail hand and touched hers. ‘Please don’t cry; it’s not necessary,’ he said, and smiled. Halifax had entered the room thinking of herself as the caregiver. ‘In fact, Issan was the bodhisattva,’ she later wrote. His gesture made her see the pity within her grief – and that she had to let him go.

In 1990, she moved to Santa Fe and founded Upaya. Four years later, she brought Being with Dying to the centre and invited me to join its faculty. There, clinicians and other caregivers examined what happened inside themselves when they faced catastrophic illness and death; neuroscience, ethics and communication were taught alongside contemplative practice. Most participants had no previous experience with Buddhism.

Anthony Back, an oncologist and palliative care physician who has worked with Halifax for more than 30 years, said her distinctive contribution was that she ‘brought contemplative care into palliative care’. ‘One of the words that comes to me is that she’s fierce,’ he said.

In the summer of 1996, Halifax sewed an okesa, a Buddhist robe made from clothing belonging to people who had died. Wearing that robe, she was ordained as a Zen Buddhist priest in an AIDS clinic in Yonkers, New York. Glassman later gave her dharma transmission – formal recognition as a teacher and an heir to his lineage. She remained his student until his death in 2018. As Halifax explains in Standing at the Edge, Glassman’s form of Buddhism – and hers – meant letting go of fixed ideas, attending to suffering and joy, and allowing that encounter to guide how one helped.

The Nomads Clinic kept bringing her back to that approach. Over the decades, the work had grown into a shared undertaking: Nepali doctors, nurses and dentists joined international clinicians, practitioners of Eastern and Western medicine learned from one another, and the clinic opened paths into medicine and nursing for Nepalis.

During a 2018 clinic journey, the limits of helping became the issue. The writer and conservationist William deBuys watched the team examine a young man paralysed by a stroke in infancy. ‘He moved across the ground by punching his calloused fists into the earth, one rigid leg stuck out,’ he wrote in his book The Trail to Kanjiroba (2021). The clinicians discussed Botox and physical therapy in Kathmandu, but the young man’s mother understood that such treatment could throw their lives out of balance. ‘Roshi cautioned us on the need to recognise limits, not just what is obtainable,’ deBuys wrote. Halifax raised the danger of pathological altruism: the desire to help could overwhelm the caregiver and disrupt the life of the person being helped.
‘It’ll be apparent after I’m dead, if I have any legacy at all. I haven’t tried to build one’
‘I was an altruist, and I went to the other side,’ she told me. ‘I became a pathological altruist.’ She had given beyond her capa

items.title: Does the principle of sufficient reason make panpsychism true? | Aeon Essays
items.description: When an explanation makes a fact intelligible, the mystery goes out of it. We understand it so well that we can hardly conceive of things being otherwise. Consider the simple mathematical fact that one plus one equals two. Once we understand elementary arithme
items.author: Sam Kimpton-Nye
paragraphs: When an explanation makes a fact intelligible, the mystery goes out of it. We understand it so well that we can hardly conceive of things being otherwise. Consider the simple mathematical fact that one plus one equals two. Once we understand elementary arithmetic, we no longer feel the urge to ask why one plus one equals two. That one plus one equals two strikes us as not merely true but unavoidable; we cannot even coherently imagine its falsity. Much of philosophy aims to bring other fundamental features of reality into a similar light, to make them appear not arbitrary but inevitable and, thus, intelligible.

This aspiration that philosophy render the world intelligible is best expressed by the German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and the Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza. According to Leibniz: ‘we can find no true or existent fact … without there being a sufficient reason why it is thus and not otherwise.’ And, as Spinoza wrote: ‘For each thing there must be assigned a cause or reason, both for its existence and for its nonexistence.’ What’s being expressed here, in the words of the US philosopher Michael Della Rocca, is the desire ‘to make the world and our place in it intelligible’. To grasp the kinds of reasons or explanations sought by Leibniz and Spinoza ‘is the perennial hope and promise of philosophy’.

The demand for intelligibility can lead to some extraordinary places. For Leibniz, the demand led him to propose that reality is ultimately made up of a multiplicity of monads: indivisible, infinitesimally small units of substance, each of which is a causally isolated, self-contained universe. Spinoza’s resolute commitment to universal intelligibility led him to conclude that reality is, instead, a single infinite substance that he called God or nature. As we will see, the demand for intelligibility can also lead into the strange and fascinating world of panpsychism.

Panpsychism is an increasingly popular view about consciousness. You are conscious, you feel pleasures, pains and all manner of other experiences. At every waking moment, and even when you dream, there is something that it is like to be you. The same goes for other humans and animals, and this accounts for moral status: thumping a fist on a desk in frustration is morally permissible in a way that hitting a conscious person or animal is not. Desks, chairs, rocks and so on are not conscious – and are therefore without moral status – whereas humans, bonobos, dogs and so on are conscious, and deserving of at least some moral recognition. But panpsychism rejects this division into conscious and non-conscious things. It is the view that consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, so everything from electrons and protons to tables and planets, and, of course, humans and dogs, has consciousness to some degree.

Panpsychism is a remarkable thesis, motivated by the ‘perennial hope’ that the world is ultimately intelligible. To investigate whether panpsychism truly can make the world intelligible, we will explore three different arguments, each of which is grounded in a principle that crystallises the ambitious aim of universal intelligibility: the principle of sufficient reason (PSR). This simple and plausible principle of philosophical enquiry – that there exist satisfying explanations for everything – can lead to a whole new understanding of the nature of reality. And, though I’m sceptical about the availability or even desirability of explanations that dissolve all the world’s mysteries, there is exceptional value in the mere contemplation of such projects.

If you come home from work to find a bouquet of flowers on your doorstep, there will be a reason for this. Maybe it’s a birthday present, a congratulations on a new job, a thank you for some good deed. If your car dashboard shows a warning light, you’d be wise to assume that there is some reason for this, such as a problem with the engine, fluids or tyres. The Chicxulub crater, 200 km wide and 1 km deep, in the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico, cries out for scientific explanation, which is precisely what the hypothesis of an extinction-level asteroid impact millions of years ago provides.

But is there really a reason for everything? The mass of a proton is 1.672 × 10-27 kg. What’s the reason for this? What’s the reason for a particular radioactive decay event to which our best scientific theory on the issue, quantum mechanics, assigns only a probability? According to the PSR, there is indeed a reason for everything. For any way the world is, from the flowers on your doorstep to the mass of a proton, there is some reason why it is this way and not some other way. All facts have a reason, and – according to the PSR in its strongest form, as defended by Spinoza – that reason makes them intelligible and necessary, and their contrary inconceivable.

Though the PSR found its fullest expression in Leibniz’s work – ‘The fundamental principle of reasoning,’ Leibniz wrote, ‘is that there is nothing without a reason’ – its lineage is far greater. As Della Rocca showed in his book Spinoza (2008): ‘Versions of [the PSR] go way back in philosophy and can be found in philosophers such as Parmenides, the Stoics, [and] Aquinas.’ And the principle is not restricted to Western European philosophy. It occupies a key position in the metaphysical system of the Islamic philosopher Ibn Sīnā (also known in Europe as Avicenna), who used it to argue that things that exist merely contingently – that is, things whose existence is not necessary – must have a cause outside themselves. Versions of the principle have also been defended in contemporary metaphysics and philosophy of physics. Shamik Dasgupta has argued that every substantive fact has a metaphysical grounding that makes it necessary. And Eddy Keming Chen has developed a physical model of the Universe according to which every single fact (from the number of hairs on your head at 2 pm this afternoon, to the mass of the electron) is entailed and thus explained by the laws of nature.

The PSR is so alluring because it would seem that the very activity of enquiry – whether philosophical, scientific, or the first ‘Why?’ question of a young child – is premised on there being an explanation, a reason, for everything. To endorse the PSR is to adopt an attitude of optimism that the world and our place in it are intelligible and infused with reason and meaning. If anything were unexplainable, there’d be a grave risk that human enquiry is ultimately futile. The falsity of the PSR would constitute a fundamental mismatch between our inquisitive nature and the world in which we find ourselves; it would imply that the world is unintelligible.
The optimistic attachment to intelligibility and reason comes at a significant cost

Intelligibility and meaningfulness are two sides of the same coin. When, on reflection, we can find no good reason for our personal and professional pursuits (lining the boss’s pockets won’t generally satisfy us!), when these things seem absurd or unintelligible, it’s natural to express the predicament in terms of a lack of meaning in life. Analogously, failure to uncover satisfying answers to questions about the nature of reality can lead to deep philosophical worries that the world itself is ultimately meaningless.

But this is not to say that the PSR is universally accepted among philosophers. It is controversial because it seems to entail necessitarianism – the thesis that everything is necessary. You are currently reading an essay about the PSR and panpsychism, but you could have been doing something else. If the PSR is true, however, then there is a sufficient reason why you are currently reading this essay, which makes it necessary that you are currently reading this essay and hence impossible that you could be doing anything else. Since the PSR applies to everything, it seems to entail the necessity of everything, and many find this unpalatable because it threatens free will and the seemingly obvious fact that all manner of things could have been different in all sorts of ways.

Contemporary philosophers who describe themselves as ‘Humean’, that is, as influenced by the Scottish Enlightenment philosopher David Hume, are explicit in their rejection of necessity and ultimate explanations. David Lewis, perhaps the most prominent Humean of the past century, maintained that ‘all there is to the world is a vast mosaic of local matters of particular fact, just one little thing and then another.’ That is to say, there are no reasons, and no necessity for what goes on in the world. In a similar spirit, the Dutch American philosopher Bas van Fraassen consistently challenges the need for a metaphysical explanatory structure. This manifests itself in the rejection of robust laws of nature that necessitate events in the Universe. Science, according to Van Fraassen, can get along just fine without deep explanations that make things necessary.

So, the optimistic attachment to intelligibility and reason comes at a significant cost: it demands a commitment to widespread necessity. There are, however, ways of mitigating this cost. Various authors, including Leibniz himself, have argued that the PSR is at least consistent with a sense in which things could have been different, and this will correspond to weaker senses of explanation. The strongest explanations, those that yield necessity, can be demonstrated in a finite number of steps; prime examples include mathematical and geometrical demonstrations. Other explanations are not finitely demonstrable, though they can be perceived by the infinite mind of God. But the fact that some explanatory connections cannot be grasped by our limited human intellect suffices, according to Leibniz, for contingency.

Alternatively, one could embrace necessitarianism, as Spinoza does, and see it as just another positive facet of the interconnectedness and intelligibility of all things – this seems the way to go if one is to maintain the courage of one’s conviction as a philosophical optimist. But necessitarianism is not the only controversial upshot of the PSR. It can also motivate panpsychism.

Perhaps the most elusive question in all of science and philosophy concerns the nature of conscious experience. Why are the arrangements of matter that constitute human beings and other animals accompanied by conscious experience? Why is there something that it is like to be you? Why are some physical states, but not others, conscious? However completely we describe the physical arrangements of matter that make up a conscious being, that description leaves out the very thing we’re trying to explain: what it feels like from the inside. This challenge to provide an explanation that bridges the gap between third-person scientific descriptions of matter and first-person conscious experience is what the Australian philosopher David Chalmers dubbed the ‘hard problem of consciousness’.

The question is so fiendishly hard because it does not seem amenable to scientific methods of enquiry. The operation of a mill, for example, can be explained by its components: water flow rotates a wheel, which drives gears connected to millstones, which grind wheat into flour. The whole operation of the mill and its output (flour) can be made intelligible to us. If we ask ‘Why does the mill produce flour?’ a fully satisfying answer can be given. No mystery remains.

The mill example is illustrative of scientific explanation in general. The boiling point of water is explained in terms of the hydrogen-bonding of H2O molecules, and the path of light around a massive celestial body is explained in terms of the curvature of spacetime described by Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity. These cases take more work to understand, but the principle is the same as in the mill case.
If consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, then the problem of explaining consciousness does not arise

However closely we look at the physical matter that makes up conscious beings, we get no closer to understanding how consciousness arises. Leibniz encouraged us to imagine increasing the size of the human brain to the size of a mill so that we can walk around inside it and observe all its working parts in meticulous detail. If we did this, at no point would we observe conscious experience. Conscious experience, by its very nature, is private, first-personal. Since scientific methods can yield knowledge only of the objective, third-person-accessible facts regarding matter in motion, there is an essential mystery concerning the origin of consciousness. The question of why some physical states, but not others, are conscious seems unanswerable.

Unanswerable questions do not sit comfortably with our inquisitive human nature. If consciousness cannot be explained in principle, this would be a particularly egregious violation of the PSR. However, it is worth considering our options for explaining consciousness and, thus, upholding the PSR once we accept that reductive scientific explanation is not up to the task.

One option is to understand consciousness in terms of a new substance entirely, one fully distinct from physical matter. On this view, reality is bifurcated into physical substance characterised by spatial extension, and mental substance characterised by thought, where the latter accounts for consciousness. This is called dualism. The most influential champion of dualism was the French philosopher René Descartes. But Descartes ultimately failed to uphold the PSR, since he couldn’t say why there are two substances as opposed to just one.

Alternatively, we could question the seemingly obvious assumption that fundamental physical matter isn’t conscious. The mystery arises because there is no way to understand how non-conscious physical matter, arranged in space and time, can give rise to consciousness. But why must we think that fundamental physical matter is not conscious? This assumption is not mandatory. If consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, then the problem of explaining consciousness, as formulated above, does not arise. So, in the interest of avoiding this in-principle obstacle to explaining consciousness, many are inclined to believe that consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, that panpsychism is true.

The hypothesis that fundamental matter is physical and non-conscious blocks the possibility of an intelligible explanation – in terms of the fundamental ‘bits’ of matter – of why creatures like us are conscious. If consciousness is absent at the fundamental level, there will always be an explanatory gap between the physical and the mental. What this means is that, for any arrangement of physical matter constitutive of a conscious being, it always seems possible that consciousness was absent; no arrangement of matter seems to be necessarily connected with, and hence able to explain, consciousness. But if consciousness is introduced at the fundamental level, this obstacle is removed. According to panpsychism, we no longer need to bridge the gap from non-conscious fundamental matter to consciousness at higher levels of organisation, since consciousness is present all the way down.

There is still significant work to be done to explain how fundamental consciousness combines to create human-level consciousness. But, at the very least, panpsychism offers a way of avoiding what would otherwise appear to be a potentially devastating violation of the PSR. If consciousness is already present at the fundamental level, there is no longer the same pervasive explanatory gap between wholly non-conscious matter and conscious beings at higher levels.

There is another route to panpsychism via the PSR. The Norwegian philosopher Hedda Hassel Mørch argues that fundamental consciousness is required to properly explain the basic motions of matter, documented by fundamental physics. Science tells us plenty about how matter behaves and what different subatomic particles such as protons, electrons and neutrons do. But it does not tell us what matter is. This is evident from the way in which science characterises matter. The electron, for example, is characterised in terms of its properties: mass, charge and quantum spin. And these properties, in turn, are understood in terms of how they dispose the electron to behave. What is absent from this scientific description of the world is an account of what physical properties are like in themselves, and hence why they have the power to dispose matter to behave in certain ways.

Why do the properties of an electron dispose it towards certain behaviours? How can this be rendered intelligible as per the demands of the PSR? Consider pain. If you are in pain, this mental property disposes you to avoid the thing that’s painful: accidentally touch a hot radiator, and you’ll instantly remove your hand. As Mørch puts it: ‘In the absence of any interfering motives, it seems pain always makes subjects try to avoid it, and [it is] difficult to conceive otherwise.’ If we ask why someone withdrew their hand from the radiator, it is a perfect explanation to say that the heat caused them pain. The explanation renders the action fully intelligible because part of what it is to be in pain is to try to avoid the painful source. Mental properties are special in that they are the only properties with this ability to provide intelligible explanations of behaviour. As Mørch writes:

The only fundamentally dispositional properties we know or can positively conceive of are phenomenal properties – in particular, phenomenal properties associated with agency, intention and/or motivation.

Other properties, such as negative charge, could, for all we know, have disposed things to behave very differently or in no systematic way at all. But it is inconceivable that pain disposed us to do anything besides avoid the source of pain. ‘It does not,’ Mørch writes, ‘seem conceivable that pain makes subjects try to do anything else than avoid it in virtue of its intrinsic character alone.’ This raises a fascinating prospect. In the interest of rendering the behaviour of matter intelligible, we should take those properties responsible for that behaviour to be conscious mental properties. That is to say: all paradigm physical properties such as charge, mass and quantum spin are conscious mental properties. This move provides an answer to the question of what matter fundamentally is, which, in turn, explains why matter does what it does. The fundamental properties of matter are properties of consciousness. By their very nature, they dispose the matter of which they are properties towards certain behaviours. This plugs the explanatory gap left by the scientific method alone. Again, the primary motive in this argument is the desire for intelligible explanations of the world, as per the PSR.
For Spinoza, if things depend on properties because properties individuate things, then it follows that properties are more fundamental than things

There is a third way that a commitment to the PSR leads us to panpsychism. Spinoza is perhaps most famous for his pantheism, the idea that God is nature. On this view, God is not a separate entity that is an external cause of nature; rather, God is coterminous with nature. It turns out that the argument for pantheism also works well as an argument for panpsychism. And, crucially, Spinoza’s argument depends on a truly unwavering commitment to the intelligibility of nature.

If asked ‘How many things exist?’ we’d probably say that there are a great many things indeed – a cat here, a house there, some protons, electrons, and so on – one might even think that there are infinitely many things. But Spinoza argues that there is just one thing. If we hold that there exists more than one thing, we must say something about what each of these things is like. So, we might say ‘This cat is black,’ ‘That house is made of brick,’ ‘Socrates is wise’ and so on. Crucially, for the advocate of the PSR, the different things that exist cannot have all the same properties. If two things, this table and that table, for example, are distinct, there must be some explanation of their distinctness that appeals to some difference between them, some difference in their properties (eg, one is square, the other oval).

Distinct things are individuated by their properties. But this relation of individuation is what philosophers call a dependence relation. For example, the fact that this is an essay on panpsychism, intelligibility and the aim of philosophy depends on the fact that there are words arranged in the appropriate way. This relation of dependence induces an ordering of fundamentality: the words are more fundamental than the essay because the latter depends on the former.

But, for Spinoza, if things depend on properties because properties individuate things, then it follows that properties are more fundamental than things. This result, however, is not acceptable. Things – or ‘substances’, as Spinoza would say – are supposed to be absolutely fundamental. What it is to be a substance, a distinct thing that exists, is to be independent of everything else, completely self-sustaining. It seems odd to say that properties occupy the fundamental level. Is the redness of an apple more fundamental than the apple itself? Surely not, since the apple, the thing, is required to exist before redness can be instantiated. So, we must find another way to explain why there are multiple distinct things. Doing so in terms of properties won’t cut it.

Instead of maintaining that different things merely have different properties, perhaps we ought to say that they are radically different in their essential attributes. What are ‘essential attributes’? Recall that, according to dualism, reality is bifurcated into mental substance with the essential attribute of thought, and physical substance with the essential attribute of extension. In other words, the mental and the physical have radically different essential attributes. But this raises a new question: why is mental substance not extended, and why is physical substance not thinking? The PSR demands an explanation. One might think that the nature of mental substance excludes being extended, and vice versa. But Spinoza objects that this violates the independence of substance, since it entails a mutual dependence of mental and physical substance to explain the fact that they exclude one another. Ultimately, Spinoza thinks there is no reason why substances would differ from each other and, since there is no reason, they do not differ. There is, then, just one substance, one thing, and this thing has all properties, and is both extended and thinking, because there is no reason that it should lack any properties or essential attributes.

A single thing with all properties and essential attributes fits the bill of both God and nature, hence Spinoza’s argument, that only one thing exists, is an argument for pantheism. But this can also be cast as an argument for panpsychism. The single existing substance is, according to Spinoza, both extended and thinking. Hence, thought is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of reality. There is, however, scope for debate about whether the fundamentality and ubiquity of thought amounts to panpsychism since there is reason to believe that not all thought is conscious thought, in Spinoza’s system. But, at the very least, mentality is a fundamental property of matter, for Spinoza, and many are happy to equate this with consciousness and, thus, categorise Spinoza as a panpsychist. The US philosopher Martin Lin, for example, writes: ‘Spinoza is a panpsychist. For him, mentality is a pervasive and fundamental feature of the natural world.’

This argument for panpsychism (and pantheism) results from leaving no stone unturned in the application of the PSR, and, in particular, from the demand to explain the idea that there are multiple distinct substances with different properties or attributes. Ultimately, Spinoza concludes that this demand cannot be met, which leads to the conclusion that there is a single fundamental substance with all properties and with both essential attributes of thought and extension. This conclusion can be cast in pantheist terms: to maintain that there exists just a single substance with all properties and attributes invites the identification of this substance with both God and nature. It can also be cast in panpsychist terms: the single fundamental substance is essentially a conscious, thinking thing. Hence consciousness is a fundamental property of reality.

Pursuing the demand for intelligibility leads to unexpected and thought-provoking places. If panpsychism doesn’t resonate with you, it’s worth asking if there truly is a reason for everything – if the world is ultimately intelligible after all. On the other hand, if you consider the PSR indispensable, panpsychism may seem inevitable.

But does this latter path offer a deeper sense of meaningful existence? I’m not so sure. In fact, uncertainty about ultimate meaning fuels the arts, which, at their most powerful, embrace and celebrate the unintelligibility and absurdity of life. On the other hand, it seems legitimate to criticise art when its meaning is too obvious, its message too on the nose. So, just as clear and unambiguous meaning is far from the supreme aesthetic goal, it’s not clear that rendering reality fully intelligible, providing the ‘meaning of life’, is a desirable or realistic aim for philosophy.

Dissatisfaction in life, a crisis in meaning, may originate when we can find no good reason for our personal and professional pursuits, and, analogously, philosophical dissatisfaction may stem from an inability to render the world intelligible. But it is far from clear that this sort of dissatisfaction can ever really be remedied by the provision of better reasons.
A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices

A more prestigious or better-paid job may constitute a reason to get out of bed in the morning. But deep questions about value and meaning will remain untouched. The absurd is not so easily vanquished. Similarly, the promise of a philosophical system built on the PSR, such as Spinoza’s, may appeal to the extent that we want to ‘solve’ philosophy by providing an answer to any possible question. But we may equally take an explanation of everything as an explanation of nothing.

Instead of seeking perfect reasons for all our pursuits, perhaps we ought to just embrace what we do, whatever it may be, for what it is. As the French philosopher and writer Albert Camus reflected, solace for Sisyphus can only come from positively embracing his situation: ‘The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.’

Perhaps it’s misguided to expect to render the world intelligible, and we ought instead to just enjoy the process of contemplating its messy unintelligible glory, of pushing our philosophical boulder up the mountain. One way of engaging with this contemplative project is in the development and exploration of systematic philosophical theories. A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices. But it would be a mistake to think these capable, even in principle, of definitively dissolving life’s mysteries. Philosophical theories such as panpsychism are better thought of as providing new and enriching perspectives on these mysteries, and we should remain open to the possibility of their collapse and replacement.

By giving up the all-encompassing demand for intelligibility and, instead, conceiving of philosophy as providing different perspectives on our condition, we can better understand what it is to make progress in philosophy. Widespread philosophical disagreement should not be taken as evidence that philosophy is degenerate compared with, say, the natural sciences. Rather, we should celebrate the fact that opposing views such as dualism, physicalism and panpsychism exist to provide us with richly diverse perspectives on life’s most tantalising mysteries.

Can panpsychism make the world intelligible? I’m not sure that anything can, or that it even makes sense to pursue supreme reasons. But there is still plenty of joy to be had in the contemplation of panpsychism as a response to the deep mystery of consciousness, and I doubt we could ask any more of a philosophical theory.

items.author: George Pistachio
paragraphs: Burberry keeps its most recognisable code in check this season – the pattern has long been associated with British weather after all

It’s autumn, when dressing in brown is an excellent idea. The leaves go tobacco, the parks turn olive and beige. Conveniently, Burberry has already put most of those colours into a rather famous check. For the new season, bowling bags, buckets and totes come in these autumnal shades. It is difficult to think of another pattern so immediately associated with British weather, which makes sense – the Burberry check began life in the 1920s lining raincoats. Among its later incarnations is Nova Check, a beige, black, red and white grid, ubiquitous around the turn of the millennium. Back in 1967, a buyer in Burberry’s Paris store, preparing a presentation for the British ambassador, pulled the check from a coat and used it to wrap luggage and cover an umbrella: the idea of making a bag in it was never very far away. Since arriving at Burberry in 2022, Bradford-born creative director Daniel Lee has set about reimagining the motif – with twists: the check has been turned on the bias, blown up, recoloured and worked into everything from kilts and bikinis to bags.
