items.title: Chiwetel Ejiofor: “Characters Have to Take Over a Part of Your Psychology”
items.description: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:
items.author: Hannah Lack
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:

On the sprawling Vancouver set of Kane Parsons’ liminal horror Backrooms, crew members regularly found themselves lost amid the 30,000-sq-ft puzzle of queasy fluorescent lighting and jaundiced wall-to-wall carpet. Maps were distributed each morning but even so, rescue missions were launched for those who’d taken a wrong turn. The A24-produced phenomenon, sprung from a 4chan image taken in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, via Parsons’ uncanny web series (it has hooked more than 224 million views to date), conjures an infinity loop of interchangeable, dread-submerged rooms that replicate and curdle memories like a malfunctioning photocopy machine.

It’s hard to imagine anyone better suited to interpreting Parsons’ mind-bending vision than Chiwetel Ejiofor, an actor feted for the kind of magnetic, deep-waters presence that keeps an audience tethered to his side whether he’s immersed in dystopian futures, comic-book universes or two centuries in the past. As Backrooms’ tragic villain Clark – the divorced owner of a cut-price 90s furniture store – a lifetime of disappointments ripple beneath the surface as he tumbles into the Escher-like underworld lurking in his store’s basement, his questionable decisions and self-delusion so messily human it’s as unsettling as the disorienting maze of drywall conjured by his fraying psyche.

The prodigious 21-year-old Parsons has said Ejiofor was the only actor he envisaged for the role – just as seasoned artist and filmmaker Steve McQueen could accept no one else to channel the quiet gravitas of Solomon Northup, the freeman forced into slavery played by Ejiofor in his unflinching 2013 masterpiece 12 Years a Slave. For two decades and more than 60 films (a couple of which he also wrote and directed, both centering on father-son dynamics), Ejiofor has excavated his life and emotions to play roles that contain multiplicities: conflicted radical militants, drag queens in thigh-high PVC boots, unravelling Los Angeles detectives, aliens from a dying planet, wayward heroin smugglers, and wry sorcerers – the latter a Marvel spectacle played by Ejiofor with Shakespearean undertones. That was perhaps only natural given Ejiofor’s award-heavy background on the London stage, where he has mastered Shakespeare, Chekhov, Ibsen and Césaire over the years. As a young teenager growing up in West Norwood, he remembers covering his bedroom walls with handwritten lines from Macbeth or Measure for Measure the way other kids might scrawl their favourite band’s lyrics.

Ejiofor was born to Nigerian parents who had escaped the Biafran war – his mother was a pharmacist, his father a successful musician and a doctor. At the age of 11, he survived the kind of unconscionable trauma that divides a life into before and after; during a family trip back to Nigeria, a car accident killed his father and hospitalised Ejiofor for 10 weeks, leaving a scar still visible on his forehead. His indefatigable mother went on to raise him and his three siblings singlehanded. Ejiofor’s discovery of acting aged 13 in his Dulwich school plays, brought what he describes as “a calming of the spirit”. By 18 he was playing Othello, by 19 he was on set with Steven Spielberg, and at 25, had the breakout lead in Stephen Frears’ Oscar-nominated Dirty Pretty Things, playing an undocumented immigrant confronting nocturnal London’s darkest secrets during night shifts at a seedy hotel. Today, on a busy Saturday morning in Soho, we meet the now 49-year-old at a considerably more pleasant hotel to discuss Backrooms’ looming tech-age anxieties, Ejiofor’s own psychological loops and thought patterns, the early obsessions that shaped him, and his forthcoming roles: as a ruthless tyrant in Gina Prince-Bythewood’s mythological fantasy Children of Blood and Bone and an ex-con turned priest opposite Scarlett Johansson in Mike Flanagan’s Exorcist adaptation.

HANNAH LACK: Horror films are said to reflect the fears of our times – the 50s atomic age in Invasion of the Body Snatchers, nature striking back in Jaws... What do you think Backrooms is saying about our current anxieties?

CHIWETEL EJIOFOR: I feel like it has a lot to say about our relationship to technology. My character Clark and his relationship to the Backrooms is so much about what brings you comfort in what might seem the blandness of the technological age. In the face of the complexities and difficulties of existing, the technological age offers all this comfort, simplicity, uniformity. And increasingly with generative AI, this idea of something having all the answers – being able to switch off from the much messier, unknowable, difficult business of being a human being: just turn to the machine for the answers to guide you through the process. That can be comforting, but the flip side is that it is completely horrifying.
HL: Were you familiar with the series before you met Kane Parsons? If I’d said ‘creepypasta’ to you...

CE: I would have guessed some sort of fusilli. Never heard of it. So I was astounded how big it was, how many people online had seen these shorts. But when I watched it, I completely understood why people had gone down that rabbit hole. Kane’s take on it was extraordinary in its scope and the developed science fiction aspects of it, and the capacity to involve and terrify an audience – not only with the fear factor, but psychologically to really put yourself in different worlds. His ability to surprise with some of the stuff he was achieving in Blender – you’re just not expecting the directions it goes in visually, which is so rare. And these concepts are severely pressure-tested by YouTube, an open platform where people are not shy about telling you what they think in the comments section – or they’ll just ignore you. Kane’s handle on the world was so complete at the point when I spoke to him. And he was really challenging himself to get underneath these characters in a rich way.
HL: Clark is so messily human, I found myself feeling a lot of sympathy for him despite some questionable decisions. What was your point of connection with Clark?

CE: I actually found Clark quite easy to relate to. I don’t know what that says about me! But his honesty and frankness and ways of looking at his place in life and evading his own culpability – that was relatable. The way we tell stories to ourselves about why we are who we are, and why we are where we are – it’s very human in the self-delusional aspects of it.
HL: So if you were in Backrooms, what loops do you think you’d find yourself in?

CE: Well all of us, as we travel through life, have relationships, friendships, that we tell ourselves the narrative of. And I think often we try to come out of those as the hero, which may be healthy to some degree. But how many of those stories would bear cross-examination? In the end, that is just part of the experience. Unfortunately, you’re never going to get through life completely clean. There will be things you could have done better, things that could have gone worse. So with Clark, the dynamics would be wildly different, but the capacity for self-delusion – I have that as much as anybody else.
HL: You’ve spoken in the past about being a perfectionist. How have you navigated that as an actor, because I imagine part of the process is trying things that aren’t necessarily going to work...

CE: Yeah, and I don’t think I’ve moved beyond perfectionism as much as I would have liked. Once you have that in you, it’s always going to slightly define your approach. I still approach roles with the idea that there is a correct way to play it, and my job is to find the correct way. And whether it succeeds or fails is based on how successfully I’ve achieved that. I don’t know if that’s healthy, but it’s the way my mind works. A lot of actors would say there isn’t a correct way of approaching artistic work. Which I do understand intellectually – I just don’t believe it emotionally. I sort of feel like there is the correct way, and it needs to be uncovered. But no matter how much you prep beforehand, the character teaches you so much in the playing of them – it’s always in the last week of shooting that you know the most about them.
HL: So when you know you’re going to play, say, King Saran in Children of Blood and Bone, where does the process of building him start?

CE: I think characters have to take over a part of your psychology. It’s the only way. It’s: where do I as an individual meet this other individual? Because whatever I end up doing is going to be a hybrid of the two of us.

It’s great when there’s time for that process to happen – in this case, it was a few months of allowing this character to sit in my psyche and Zooming with Gina (Prince-Bythewood). There are such complex family dynamics at play in this film, so I was keen on getting into that room as soon as the family unit was cast, to find the through lines for these relationships. The combination of Gina and shooting in South Africa was irresistible – in that area of Cape Town and beyond, the vistas are completely magical and give the film such a rich density, complexity, and there’s a human quality that is beautiful and deep. I love Gina’s detail and capacity to ground big stories. Early on she showed me all the artwork, the drawings they were working with. She didn’t need to convince me; I was already in – and the books are extraordinary.
HL: I read in your sister’s memoir that as kids your mother would give you books to read and report back on each week – did acting start with a love of language?

CE: It was English literature classes at school, being introduced to humanistic poetry and stories that weren’t about plot, but really intimate thought patterns, about the overall experience of living for its own sake. When you’re first exposed to Shakespeare, there’s the plot of Henry IV Part One – he does this and that – but the real point is, what does he think about life? That really captured my imagination as a young teenager. I ended up going to the theatre to try to get to the root of it. And that led to deciding to get on stage and inhabit it.
HL: What was the first role where something clicked for you?

CE: It was doing Measure for Measure when I was maybe 13, playing Angelo. I felt like I had gotten underneath this character. It wasn’t a choice after that. It was way beyond that. It was what I was thinking about when I’d wake up and all through the day. Everything else was in the margins for the main event, which was theatre at school. Then that extended into holidays with the National Youth Theatre or the Dulwich Youth Theatre – it just became part of my personality, that was it.
HL: Your late dad was a doctor but also a musician, do you think he opened a creative door for you when you were very young?

CE: I don’t know. I hadn’t really thought about art until I experienced it firsthand. And when that happened it was as if I didn’t think anybody else had ever travelled this route before. It was like I was the first to discover this code for living that no one else knew about. Art was this way of self-expression, but with this caveat that you didn’t have to expose yourself too much. You could be somebody else and still express yourself. The hybrid of two things – reading the text and you as an individual talking about your experiences – could create something even more compelling. And for me, within that there was a calming of the spirit. I found a way of communicating with people, not having to use my own words but still representing myself profoundly. I knew I would do this for the rest of my life. There was no doubt. Later, working on Joe Penhall’s play Blue/Orange, I was the younger of the group, 23 or so, and that was also a strong entry point into what the profession could be, dealing with these contemporary issues surrounding mental health.
“I wake up in a panic because I know at 7:30pm the show’s on. There’s no way I can have a normal day” – Chitewel Ejiofor
HL: Stephen Frears saw you in that play and cast you in Dirty Pretty Things, right? That was a big moment.

CE: Dirty Pretty Things was so ahead of its time in many ways, detailing a London that later on people would talk about more frequently, but at the time was as hidden culturally and in the media as it was in the narrative. I fell in love with film on that job. It was the extraordinary precision of Stephen Frears, but also Chris Menges as a cinematographer; understanding the poetry of filmmaking, the truthfulness that can be communicated, the silence of moments, and what drama can mean in film being very different to theatre. I’d always assumed I wasn’t a film actor. That film changed my perspective.
HL: Why had you assumed you weren’t a film actor? Is there a different energy required for film?

CE: I mean, there are people who can wake up in the morning and have a completely normal day and then go down to the theatre at 5:30pm, have a bite to eat and get ready for curtain up at 7:30pm. I’ve never been able to do that. I wake up in a panic because I know at 7:30pm the show’s on. There’s no way I can have a normal day. I remember in the play Everyman, my entrance was from the top of the Olivier Theatre on wires coming down onto the stage. I would be getting into a harness, watching the audience coming in like ants – they were so small beneath me. I had a harness on, but my hand was holding onto the rail and every night, I had to have my hand coaxed away from the rail by one of the stage team: “The show’s going up now, Chiwetel. You can let go now...” Once I landed, the business of doing the show felt much easier. But no, the rhythm of film and theatre is the same in that you live with the character all of the time until the show or the film is complete.

HL: You’ve worked with many incredible directors – Alfonso Cuarón, Spike Lee, Ridley Scott – and Steve McQueen, who brought you an Oscar nomination for 12 Years a Slave. He was absolutely clear he wanted you for the role of Solomon Northup – did he tell you what convinced him?

CE: Yeah, I mean he did. He would say that there was a quality of inherent integrity or something trustworthy about Solomon – that you felt you could be in his company and there were no sides to him. Not that he was naive or guileless, just that he was open, and so the audience could go on the journey with him and be carried by his experiences. I think for Steve it was around that – not charisma exactly, but an integrity or trustworthiness that he at least believes I exude – whether he thinks I actually have that, I don’t know!
HL: What did you take away from that set that you hadn’t discovered before?

CE: Steve would often talk about “catching butterflies” – the idea that you can set up an environment where something magical can happen. It could just be a question, or something completely unexpected that an actor who is immersed in a moment can produce, which could never be produced anywhere else. There’s a horrifying, extraordinarily powerful scene, the flaying of Patsey, Lupita Nyong’o’s character, where the camera movement, actors, the creation of that space, how the camera flowed in a sequence was mostly in one take. But as performers, we weren’t adhering to specific marks. It was everybody being open to where the scene would go.
HL: Did you take that idea of catching butterflies to your own sets? You’ve directed twice now, with The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind and Rob Peace...

CE: If you’re an actor-director, your relationship to performance is very different. What I get excited about is the silent communication between actors. I didn’t need language that much because I was already communicating so much about tone and style by the way I was acting in the scene, which other actors pick up on quickly. I was looking at stories, writing a little bit, kicking the tyres around directing. But when I read The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind, I could see it as I was reading. It was thematically aligning with so many things I had been searching for in ways I didn’t even know that I had been. Not just as a creative, but as a person – it was a story that meant so much to me, on so many different levels.
HL: You wrote both films as well. Have you always written, did you keep a diary as a kid?

CE: Yeah journals, diaries, all of that. Mostly day-to-day stuff and then during teenage years – actually not just teenage, into the turbulent 20s – it was a way of processing the world around me, trying to make sense of it. When I look back at the things I wrote, it’s fascinating because it does help identify patterns in behaviour, thought patterns. I think it helped me rationalise, compartmentalise the world that I was experiencing and some of the complicated emotions I was having.
HL: There’s a line in Rob Peace where he says he needed to “control the chaos”...
CE: Yeah exactly. It takes your feelings out of the chaotic world and creates something almost tangible, something that can hold it.
HL: I read that you’re a bit of a hoarder; what have you kept from your film roles?

CE: You know, since I mentioned that, it turns out there’s a hoarding community out there. There are support groups; there’s help if you need it. It has actually made me feel a bit better – declaring it has somehow alleviated some of the burden for me. But the thing is, it doesn’t have to be anything that holds value. That wouldn’t be a problem – a nice keepsake from a set or something with sentimental value – great! But it’s the stuff that doesn’t mean anything and I can’t explain why I’ve kept it; I just can’t get rid of it. It’s an ongoing challenge.
HL: Is it good then to find yourself often in hotel rooms without a lot of stuff?

CE: Where everything is out of sight? Yeah – but actually I found very early that living out of a suitcase and the constant travel didn’t agree with me. One of the reasons I started sailing was because I found that if I was in a new city and I could see that city from the water, it contained it. So that’s what I would do: land somewhere and immediately figure out how to get onto the water so I could see the city from a distance. And also, as a Cancerian – not that that’s really my thing – but I think I engage with water in a way that feels very grounded to me. Looking back at Vancouver or Los Angeles from the water allowed me to connect to the city in a different way. I don’t sail as much now, sadly, but when I can, I get on a houseboat and chase that feeling a little.
HL: You’ve been shooting a new adaptation of The Exorcist with Mike Flanagan. The original was famously cursed on set... has anything unusual been happening on this one?

CE: So far, so good. It’s one day at a time (laughs). But actually, it is always in the back of your mind because it’s dancing with certain... elements. I don’t know if I’m very superstitious, but if you’re doing The Exorcist, you lean into it a little more. I loved the original, the filmmaking is extraordinary and the last half of the film is so terrifying, but also so watchable, the characters and the depth of feeling you have for everybody in that house by the end is remarkable. Having worked with Mike on Life of Chuck, it was exciting to jump into the world with him. All I can say about it is, he’s created something so rich on so many levels – I can’t wait for people to see it.
HL: What’s the one film you’ve watched the most?
CE: Probably The Abyss – I actually love that film.
HL: Last question – what’s something thing you’d like to pass along to your daughter that you inherited from your parents?
CE: Well, my mother has always had a certain tenacity and an engagement with life that is electric. That’s what I’d pass on – but you know, I feel like my daughter has that already.

Photography OLIVER HADLEE PEARCH. Styling RAPHAEL HIRSCH. Grooming MATT MULHALL at Streeters. Set design ANDREW TOMLINSON at Streeters. Casting GREG KRELENSTEIN at GK-LD and Management Artists. Digital tech BELLA SPORLE. Photographic assistants ALBI GUALTIERI, THOMAS LOMBARD and STEFAN TURNER-POWELL styling assistants STORM FOSTER and ART O NEIL. Tailor JO O’CONNOR. Make-up assistant JO MEROLA. Production MIMI LOMAX at Partner Films. Production. Assistants THEA LEVINE and CELESTE MANDERS

items.title: Eight of the best high-shine men’s shoes for decadent winter dressing
items.description: There are few greater joys than a freshly polished leather shoe, an essential when it comes to a winter season of decadent dressing. For A/W 2026, glossy, patent and high-shine footwear appeared across the menswear collections, from the introduction of lustrou
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: There are few greater joys than a freshly polished leather shoe, an essential when it comes to a winter season of decadent dressing. For A/W 2026, glossy, patent and high-shine footwear appeared across the menswear collections, from the introduction of lustrous caviar leather at Church’s (a material as luxurious as the name suggests) to the elongated footwear at Saint Laurent, which saw Anthony Vaccarello reimagine traditional men’s shoes, from monk-straps to slippers, in glossy patent leather (continuing the wipe-clean mood, some were worn with black latex socks). Elsewhere, the Italian designer Brunello Cucinelli – a master of easy elegance and an expert in the men’s wardrobe – introduced these ‘glossed’ loafers, a minimal, round-toed style in highly polished leather designed to complement any evening-time attire.

They fit within a wider mood of dressing up which ran through the Autumn/Winter season, from Jonathan Anderson’s ‘aristo-youths’ at Dior Men (the designer imagined his partygoers dashing through the streets of Paris in riffs on the evening suit and tuxedo), to Prada’s reclamation of the cufflink – a largely abandoned accessory that recalls a bygone era of menswear. ‘We questioned: what should remain, from the past – and what can you build, from what you learn?’ said co-creative directors Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons.
Here, we select eight of the best high-shine men’s shoes befitting a season of dressing up.

The ultimate in evening attire, these Brunello Cucinelli shoes capture the Italian designer’s eye for easy – if impossibly elevated – elegance. Each pair is handmade in Italy from ‘glossed’ leather, lending them a gleaming shine that will likely look best on the dancefloor.

Church’s has been making footwear since 1617, meaning that when it comes to procuring a classic style – whether a loafer, brogue or Derby – you rarely need look further than the British shoemaker. These Maesteg loafers are one such example: made from soft calfskin designed to envelop the foot like a ‘second skin’, the fumé leather has been meticulously polished for an ultra-smooth finish.

There is an inflection of kink to these elongated, wipe-clean patent leather Oxfords, part of Anthony Vaccarello’s A/W 2026 menswear collection for Saint Laurent. Indeed, the Belgian designer – who recently left the house after a decade – describes the winter collection as one of ‘intimacy, vulnerability [and] eroticism’.

Jonathan Anderson’s menswear collections for Dior have riffed on the tenets of eveningwear – from morning coats and tuxedos to bow ties and brooches (albeit in the designer’s twisted, undone style). These Derby shoes capture a similar spirit: crafted from high-shine patent leather with an embossed Dior logo, they are called the ‘Timeless Derby’ – a nod to their enduring appeal.

Loewe has a 180-year history of working with leather – a landmark anniversary that the Spanish house celebrated earlier this year. Now led by Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, Loewe’s new ‘Bobine’ silhouette – currently used across loafers, derby shoes and Chelsea boots – shows off the house’s superlative skills in the material, seeing brushed calfskin cleverly moulded for a subtly sculptural finish.

Another traditional bootmaker, John Lobb has been crafting footwear for over a century (its eponymous founder walked on foot from Cornwall to London in 1851 to begin his apprenticeship in shoemaking). As such, craft remains central to the brand – which is now part of the Hermès group – as evidenced by these ‘Edward’ loafers, built on the slender 7000 last and constructed from lustrous panels of patent leather.

Eel leather, which is known a the ‘silk of the sea’ for its delicate texture and lustrous, luxurious finish, has become increasingly ubiquitous in recent seasons – collections from Saint Laurent, Proenza Schouler, Durazzi Milano and The Row have all featured eel-skin accessories in the past year. From the last, a pair of signature soft, ruched loafers, crafted from panels of brown eel leather in Italy.

Recent years have seen Junya Watanabe become a prolific collaborator, which each runway collection featuring an extensive list of the collaborative pieces which appear throughout (the Japanese designer has put his avant-garde spin on Levi’s, Carhartt and Brooks Brothers, among several others). These classic Tricker’s brogues are one such example, remade in glossy, high-shine leather.
A version of this article appears in the December 2026 issue of Wallpaper*, available from 5 November in print on newsstands, on the Wallpaper* app on Apple iOS, and to subscribers of Apple News +.

Jack Moss is the Fashion & Beauty Features Director at Wallpaper*, having joined the team in 2022 as Fashion Features Editor. Previously the digital features editor at AnOther and digital editor at 10 Magazine, he has also contributed to numerous international publications and featured in ‘Dazed: 32 Years Confused: The Covers’, published by Rizzoli. He is particularly interested in the moments when fashion intersects with other creative disciplines – notably art and design – as well as championing a new generation of international talent and reporting from international fashion weeks. Across his career, he has interviewed the fashion industry’s leading figures, including Rick Owens, Pieter Mulier, Jonathan Anderson, Grace Wales Bonner, Christian Lacroix, Kate Moss and Manolo Blahnik.

items.title: Head to Paris Photo 2026 as the city celebrates 200 years of photography
items.description: In 1838, just over a decade after Nicéphore Niépce captured the first surviving photograph (View from the Window at Le Gras, dated to around 1826/1827), Louis Daguerre pointed his camera at the Boulevard du Temple in Paris. The exposure lasted a few minutes, a
items.author: Cindy Parthonnaud
paragraphs: In 1838, just over a decade after Nicéphore Niépce captured the first surviving photograph (View from the Window at Le Gras, dated to around 1826/1827), Louis Daguerre pointed his camera at the Boulevard du Temple in Paris. The exposure lasted a few minutes, and nothing that moved left a mark on the image. Carriages, passersby, the whole traffic of the city, vanished. Only two figures stayed still long enough to remain: one man with his foot raised, and another shining his shoes. Often described as the first instance of people being photographed, they stand alone in an empty city.

In 2026, France marks the bicentenary of the invention of photography, and the 29th edition of Paris Photo returns to the Grand Palais from 12 to 15 November, with 246 exhibitors from 38 countries. After 200 years, photography seems to be pulling in two directions at once: towards images no camera ever took, and back to its origins of silver, paper and chemistry that Daguerre and his contemporaries worked with. Visitors to the fair this year can see both forms, sometimes in the same room.
Welcome to the Grand Palais

Inside the Grand Palais, a 36m retrospective wall of Thomas Ruff's work lines the entrance. Conceived as an 'open book', it moves through more than 40 years, from analogue images to digital simulations. Ruff joins Florian Ebner, head of the photography department at the Centre Pompidou, for a talk on his practice on Thursday 12 November at 2pm.

Further into the exhibition, the bicentenary is at its most literal. Hans P Kraus Jr brings works by Daguerre and Talbot, alongside Anna Atkins, whose cyanotypes of British algae, bound into volumes from 1843, are often recognised as the first photobook, a year before Talbot's The Pencil of Nature.

She's also a reminder of how selectively the history of photography has been told, and a good way into the ‘Elles x Paris Photo’ path, curated this year by Aldeide Delgado, founder of the Women Photographers International Archive. Since the ‘Elles’ path launched in 2018, the share of women artists at the fair has nearly doubled, from 20 to 38 per cent. Delgado’s selection, ‘An Oceanic Beginning’, takes the ocean as a starting point for retelling photography's history without a fixed centre

Among the selected works is Ous de granota (2025), Alba Yruela’s photograph of frogspawn suspended in murky water, each egg a dark pupil staring back. Yruela makes her Paris Photo debut with Barcelona gallery Chiquita Room in the ‘Emergence’ sector. Elle Pérez, who has a solo presentation at Public Relations, is also among the artists chosen by Delgado. Pérez works across photography, collage and film, and on Friday 13 November sits down with writer and curator Gem Fletcher for a conversation co-presented by Aperture and Fletcher's podcast, The Messy Truth. Its title poses a question: what is the work of photography today?

The ‘Digital’ sector offers one answer. Its new curator, Marco De Mutiis of Fotomuseum Winterthur, argues that we no longer 'see' through optics alone, but through layers of Photoshop, social media aesthetics, facial recognition and memes. He also contributes an essay to ECAL's ‘Soft Photography’, a research project led by the late Milo Keller, the school's head of photography, and this year the fair's educational programme. The project turns that idea towards emotion: images built to anger, soothe, or simply keep us scrolling, from rage-bait to ASMR (autonomous sensory meridian response). Rather than asking whether an AI-generated image looks real, it asks what it's designed to make us feel. De Mutiis discusses the project with the artist Charlie Engman on Thursday 12 November at 5pm.

Friday 13 November belongs to books. At 3pm, the Paris Photo-Aperture Foundation PhotoBook Awards are announced at the fair, and at 6pm, Palm* Studios launches Molly Matalon’s Lil Big Beach Book, a first look at a larger archive of beach pictures by the California-based photographer. But for many, the book’s real home this week is on the water. At Port de Solférino on the Seine, the photobook fair Polycopies opens on the Concorde-Atlantique boat, from 1pm on Wednesday 11 November. Polycopies has grown from around 35 publishers when founded in 2014 to nearly 100 publishers and booksellers, spread across the boat and the quay beside it.

Among the tables this year is Ciao Press, the Swiss imprint Nicolas Polli founded at the end of 2017, which he describes as a 'publishing playground'. Often photographer, designer and publisher on the same title, Polli last showed here in 2022, before a few years on the wider fair circuit. He's back with a launch in collaboration with Éditions Images Vevey, Dominique Teufen's Rays of Light – Reflected Realities, in which a reflective silver surface turns fragments of urban landscapes into something more painterly, with no digital manipulation. In an age of AI, it makes a quiet case for what light can still do on its own. Polli’s advice is to arrive as soon as the doors open. His Polycopies picks include publishers Skinnerboox, Yogurt Editions, Fraglich Publishing and Deadbeat Club. The last, based in Los Angeles, also makes its Paris Photo debut this year, with work by Daniel Dorsa, Cole Barash and Taylor Galloway, among others.

Beyond the fairs, the bicentenary extends across the city. Now in its seventh edition, Photo Days brings together exhibitions across Paris throughout November. In the Studio at the Maison Européenne de la Photographie, Nanténé Traoré's ‘pays des merveilles’, the artist's first museum solo show, is made from pictures shot in Brittany on expired film from the 1990s. At the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson, ‘Nicaragua, Histoire, Mémoire’ follows Susan Meiselas's photographs of the 1978-79 revolution long after she took them, onto T-shirts, stamps, matchboxes and murals, used sometimes to celebrate the revolution and sometimes to contest it. And at the Bibliothèque nationale de France's François-Mitterrand site, ‘Photographies japonaises’ draws on one of the first Western collections of postwar Japanese photography, begun in the late 1960s: around 250 prints and 50 rare books, including a section devoted to Japanese photographers looking at Paris.

Much of the week happens after hours, at openings, launches, and in bookshops across the city, and the first night is usually the busiest. On Thursday 12 November at 6pm, ECAL opens ‘Soft Photography’ at Espace Commines, a show that runs for just two days. Among the student works, Min Dai's Rate My Cake renders a mouth in glossy orange, sweetness pushed until it starts to repel. From 7pm, Francesca Allen launches ‘Hair’ at Cahier Central, her second volume on the significance of long hair. The first, shot in Lithuania at a contest for the world's longest hair, was shown at Paris Photo last year with Chloé Arts. This time, she follows 26 women who gathered in Las Vegas to compete for the first Miss Rapunzel title, photographing them away from the stage, their hair spilling across hotel beds and through the casinos. Later, the night moves to La Montgolfière in the tenth arrondissement, where Dans le Bain opens its first show, ‘Wild Ember Orchestra’, co-created with the independent imprint Pomegranate Press: a transatlantic exchange between American and French artists, Myles Loftin and Sarah Balhadère among them, open until 11pm.

By Sunday 15 November, after four days of looking, it's worth thinking back to the image taken on the Boulevard du Temple in 1838. The two figures are visible only because they stood still; everything else in the street moved too fast for the plate. Now that problem has almost reversed. Images are made faster than anyone can look at them, and this year's ‘Voices’ sector, curated by Zasha Colah and Francesco Zanot, takes disappearance as its theme. They look at photographs made to fade or destroy themselves, and AI images that look like photographs but no longer record anything. Across the week, the idea raised in Daguerre’s image keeps returning: what a photograph holds on to, and what it lets go.
Paris Photo runs 12-15 November 2026 at the Grand Palais

Cindy Parthonnaud is photo editor, agent and consultant, with a focus on fashion, portraiture, still life, beauty and interiors. Working across commissioning and artist representation, she has previously held photo editor roles at publications including The Times LUXX and WIRED. She is the founder of Sidelines Studio, a consultancy supporting photographers with strategic guidance and long-term career development.

items.title: A conversation with Eileen Myles for Apartamento magazine issue #37
items.description: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful w
items.author: Valeria Tusquets
paragraphs: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful wooden tray. That lives here’. Despite famously moving to New York City to become a poet in 1974, a metropolis which serves as the backdrop for much of their work, in this instance, ‘here’ is Marfa, Texas. Situated in North America’s largest desert with a population currently under 2,000, Marfa became a magnet for creatives after the artist Donald Judd moved there from New York in the ‘70s, and there has been an uneasy truce between outsiders and locals since then. Jokingly referred to as their ‘fortress of solitude’, Eileen’s Marfa home looks like many on their street, with a pickup truck parked outside a chain-link fence and little city blocks of prickly pear cactus dotted around their lot.

Eileen’s work has been translated into dozens of languages, and they have published more than 20 books across poetry, fiction, and nonfiction, earning them a Guggenheim Fellowship and an Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant. One of Eileen’s many superpowers as a writer is their ability to marry first-person narrative with more ephemeral truths, or, as they say, ‘trusting the mechanism of desire…[the] desire for certain language to sit over some curve of a moment’. This realness, coupled with writing about a character named ‘Eileen Myles’, has also led to being flattened by labels—another Charles Bukowski or Patti Smith—as they slid between poetry and prose. ‘I have a specific system that downplays grammar in a lot of ways’, they say, but their system of delaying any easy resolution is also grammatical; there’s a really tight thought, but they don’t let it resolve immediately. We are taken away, shown something new. The action is deferred until the text realises its necessary climax.

Inside their home, cut-outs between rooms create a flow where kitchen peeks into office peeks into bedroom peeks into living room. A big picture window in their office, paid for when the show Transparent bought some of Eileen’s poems and based a poet character on them, looks out into the yard towards their ‘writing shack’ which sports a clawfoot bathtub, a bench press and weights, and a desk facing double sliding doors out onto the porch where we sit and sip Topo Chico. While access to DC Comics’ original Fortress of Solitude is controlled by a key carved from super-dense dwarf star material weighing half a million tonnes—imagine lifting 100 elephants or the weight of a small cloud—Eileen’s own abode is guarded by three desert-coloured pups who sound an imposing alarm when we pull up.

items.title: Flau’jae Johnson Has Always Had Motion
items.description: Shirt PATCHES CATALOG, trousers STOFFA, belt L.L.BEAN, hat, jewelry, and watch AUDEMARS PIGUET Talent’s Own, shoes PUMA
items.author: Tiana Randall
paragraphs: Shirt PATCHES CATALOG, trousers STOFFA, belt L.L.BEAN, hat, jewelry, and watch AUDEMARS PIGUET Talent’s Own, shoes PUMA
Flau’jae Johnson isn’t the bashful type. “I’ve always had motion,” she asserts six times throughout our conversation (I counted).

Maybe it’s because she was Louisiana State University’s starting shooting guard her freshman year, helping the team win a national championship and signing a multi-year contract with PUMA. Maybe it’s because the next year, even while dominating at college ball, she maintained her career as a rising-star rapper, opening up for Rod Wave and making early morning practice the morning after. Or because her 2024 song “Came Out a Beast,” featuring Lil Wayne, went viral upon its debut, amassing 3.2 million views. Or it could be because, this past spring, she was the eighth overall pick in the WNBA draft.
Suit jacket and pants NANAMICA, jewelry Talent’s Own, shoes PUMA

To be clear, Johnson isn’t braggadocious. Rather, the 23-year-old possesses a deeply ingrained sense of self-confidence — one that was instilled in her from a young age by her mother, Kia J. Brooks, the self-titled “Black Kris Jenner.” “She had outfits made, she was doing my hair, she was doing my makeup, she was making me do photoshoots,” Johnson says with enthusiasm. “Because she already had the vision for me.”

Johnson pulls up a photo on her Instagram of one such shoot when she was 8. She’s standing before a studio backdrop in a custom purple-and-blue jersey, “Flau’jae” emblazoned across the chest with the number 01 beneath it. The caption reads: “This who y’all be cussing out when y’all parlay don’t hit.”

Flau’jae is a name you don’t forget. Maybe Brooks knew that when she gave it to her. But Johnson has given it a life of its own, building a presence that reaches well beyond the basketball court. As an athlete and an artist, she is part of a new generation of college-turned-W talent, showing that there’s room to pursue more than one dream.
Suit jacket and pants NANAMICA, jewelry Talent’s Own, shoes PUMA

Even over a Google Meet link — me in New York City, her in her home city of Atlanta — Johnson has the kind of extroversion that suggests the world hasn’t quite managed to sand her down. The longer she talks, the more I laugh. In watching her other interviews to prepare for our conversation, I noticed the same thing: the Flau’jae effect. When I point it out, she doesn’t offer a “Thank you,” but rather, “Facts,” as if to say, well, you’re not wrong. She shows off the quick wit and easy riffs of most Gen-Zers, but beneath all that energy she is composed — able to articulate even her most complex thoughts with care. Whether she’s speaking about her critics, referees, former partners, or friends, she rarely resorts to bitterness. There’s a grace in the way she describes those who may have wronged her: candid without being cruel. In an era when grievance can so easily become a personality, Johnson seems to have held onto something gentler.

You can see it in the way she interacts with her little brothers, Aydin and Nixon. Both are on set with her in Atlanta, popping in and out of view of the camera as she goes live on Instagram. On the night she was drafted, Aydin rushed the stage at her invitation, becoming a meme in the process. As Johnson stood there in a cutout mermaid gown, a fuzzy black shawl, and a jet-black bussdown, her younger brother was tucked beneath her in a purple Golden State Valkyries cap. It was a moment that belonged to both of them equally.

Family, to Flau’jae, is above all else. She speaks about them unprompted, weaving memories of them and their quirks into conversations that have seemingly nothing to do with family at all. Johnson grew up in Savannah, Georgia, raised by her grandparents and Brooks. “My mama used to do Uber before it was Uber,” Johnson says. “In Savannah, Georgia, St. Patrick’s Day, the parade is like a huge thing, right? She would rent a white van. She would drive all the drunk people to their hotels, and she would do it all night. She would come home with, like, wads and wads of money. She was always just a hustler and had this business mindset.”
Shirt PATCHES CATALOG, trousers STOFFA, belt L.L.BEAN, hat, jewelry, and watch AUDEMARS PIGUET Talent’s Own, shoes PUMA

Johnson’s father, Jason Akeil Johnson, known professionally as the rapper Camoflauge, was murdered before she was born, reportedly shot outside his recording studio. “I think I really struggled with that growing up,” Johnson says. “I was so angry at the world. I was a little bad kid.”

Although they never had the chance to meet, Camouflage’s legacy looms large in Johnson’s life, down to the way her name is pronounced (like “flauge,” the last part of his). She remembers listening to her dad’s album, Keepin It Real, when she was just six and feeling an inexplicable connection to it. “I’m talking about shit that I’m not supposed to know about. You listen to my dad’s music, he’s popping it,” she says. “I just connected with it, and it made me realize I wanted to do music. Like, I want to be able to tell stories like he did in that album. It really did change my life.”
Jacket and jeans 6397, shorts LITERARY SPORT, jewelry, and watch AUDEMARS PIGUET Talent’s Own

When she was 12, Johnson appeared on Season 3 of Lifetime’s The Rap Game, a reality TV show that features aspiring young hip-hop artists competing in a musical boot camp. She made it to the final round but ultimately didn’t take home the So So Def Recordings contract (or the chain).

As she got older and became more serious about music, she sometimes resented her father’s unshakable shadow. “My dad was my whole brand and identity as a rapper. I was Camouflage’s daughter,” she says. “And I was kind of irritated with it because I was like, I don’t want to just be known as the daughter of a famous rapper.”

Over time, though, she began to incorporate his experiences into her own. In 2005’s “Remember When ,” Johnson raps about the grief that preceded her arrival into the world: “My mama couldn’t smile when she had me/she had to mourn. They killed my pop while I was in her womb.” These days, Johnson sees her father’s legacy as a source of strength. “That’s my power. Like, all my dad left for me was his music and his name and his stories,” she says.

Both father and daughter come with impressive credentials. Camouflage inked a deal with Universal Records and Pure Pain Records at just 18. Johnson, meanwhile, achieved her own milestone, signing a distribution deal under Jay Z's Roc Nation in 2022. Two years later, she released her debut EP, Best of Both Worlds, following 4 Wave and 4 The Lovers.

Johnson’s remix of “Woah” with Monaleo will drop on November 6. She’s also working on an upcoming EP — or “mixtape,” as she calls it in true Southern fashion — although she’s keeping the details private. What she will share is how life itself has become her greatest writing tool. “My mama always told me, ‘Your music will get better when you experience more life.’ So I think just living and going through things and feeling emotions” has helped shape her process. “I make my best music when I feel everything I’m going through,” Johnson says. “It’s important for me to show, this shit ain’t all cake and ice cream.”

These days, the goal isn’t to supersede her father’s name, but to carry it forward. “Every time somebody hears a new song from me or hears a new story from me, in some way, my dad is going to be mentioned,” she says. “It’s building that whole Johnson line — making that name mean something.”

Johnson fell in love with basketball after her mother installed a hoop in their driveway when Johnson was 6. “I tried to get her to take ballet, and she was good at it, but she cried the day she had to perform,” Brooks says. “She really just wanted to play basketball.”

There wasn’t a girls’ team in their area so Johnson played with the boys. “I think that’s where she developed this dog mentality,” Brooks says. “She always wanted to be bigger and better than the boys so she worked harder, spent more time in the gym practicing so she could prove she should be there.”

Brooks moved the family to Atlanta because she saw Johnson’s talents as something to be taken seriously. Johnson played basketball throughout high school and was recruited by LSU’s head coach, Kim Mulkey. Mulkey was clear that Johnson could still pursue both her passions. “What do we sell this young lady…to get her to come and help us jumpstart this program? We sold her, ‘Hey, you can do your rap and also play basketball.’ A lot of people didn’t offer that to her. And they didn’t think she could do it,” Mulkey told WAFB last April.
Suit jacket and pants NANAMICA, jewelry Talent’s Own

It was in college where the world got to know and love Flau’jae. She was named SEC Freshman of the Year the same year that LSU won the national championship. By the time she graduated in 2026, she’d become the team’s second-leading scorer, starting in every game of her final season, according to the university athletic department.

That she would be drafted into the W was a no-brainer. But draft nights are a particular kind of nerve-racking theater. You wonder if you’ll land somewhere you don’t want to be, hear your name called lower than expected, or not hear it at all. For Johnson, the night took a turn few could have anticipated. After being selected eighth overall by the Golden State Valkyries, she was traded to the Seattle Storm 30 minutes later. Only a handful of players before her had experienced such a scenario, one of them being Kobe Bryant. “Everything happens for a reason,” she says, remembering what she told herself that night. “And one of my favorite players, Kobe, he got traded on draft night. The Charlotte Hornets traded him to the Lakers. Dumbest decision ever.”

Johnson played her rookie season with the Storm wearing the number 4 — “Big 4,” as she calls herself, emphasized with a Georgia accent. But it came to an early end; the Storm didn’t place for the playoffs. Still, she made new friends and learned new lessons. “I try to be intentional, especially with my teammates, about building bonds,” she says. “Even with the season that we had, a losing season, it kind of bonded us more together.”
Jacket and jeans 6397, shorts LITERARY SPORT, jewelry, and watch AUDEMARS PIGUET Talent’s Own, shoes PUMA

She speaks especially highly of one teammate, Spanish-born basketball player Awa Fam Thiam. “We have the same humor. We connect on such a crazy level,” she says. “It’s like, ‘Wow, I can’t believe basketball brought us together.’” Johnson says she has also formed friendships with WNBA veterans and legends, including Natasha Cloud , Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu, Caitlin Clark, and Paige Bueckers , to name a few.

Johnson talks about the legacy she wants to leave behind not as some far-off dream, but as something already taking shape. She often speaks in the present tense, sometimes even the past, as if the future she once imagined is already underway.

Her latest step toward building that legacy was purchasing land — 20 acres to be exact — in Atlanta. “Growing up, we had to move around a lot. Now, for us to have something that nobody can ever take from us, that’s the biggest blessing,” she says. Her mother is already planning to build a house on the property. “My brothers, they gonna grow up with a freaking football field, a basketball court, and a trampoline park in their backyard. I’ve never had nothing like that,” she says. There’s something particularly poignant about what the purchase means to her, beyond the acreage and the amenities. “We used to work on those same fields,” she says, “and now I have the chance to own them, take that back and have some of that pride back.”
Suit jacket NANAMICA, jewelry Talent’s Own

Still, beneath all the motion and the self-assurance, Johnson is only 23. Beyond her many roles as an entrepreneur, a basketball player, and a musician, she’s navigating some of the same questions that occupy many people her age, including finding a partner. “I’m in a great spot, romantically. I’m a lover girl. You know, I’m a Scorpio,” she says.

Johnson says she’s looking for someone who is “equally yoked.” Still, she’s quick to clarify: “I think that’s not really a priority in my life. I be trying to tell that to my friends: We need to build our life so that then, when love and marriage and kids come, we done did everything that we wanted to do.”

Looking at the life she has built, it seems like things just might work out — something Johnson would tell you herself. “I never worry because I have a whole bunch of prayer warriors on my side. I have a whole bunch of people that are conspiring for my dreams to come true,” she says. “I have a lot of people that want to see me win more than want to see me fail. And I feel my dreams are protected by that.”

В 2026 году фестиваль современного искусства «Норильские сезоны», проходящий по инициативе и при поддержке «Норникеля», вернулся в Норильск со вторым сезоном. Весной на сцене Заполярного театра драмы московский Театр имени Маяковского представил документальный спектакль Дмитрия Крестьянкина «Поиск продолжается», созданный при участии поисково-спасательного отряда «ЛизаАлерт», а осенью МТЮЗ привёз «Медовый месяц в “Кукольном доме”» Петра Шерешевского. Завершат сезон в октябре гастроли Санкт-Петербургского театра балета имени Леонида Якобсона со специально составленной для Норильска программой.

Но «Норильские сезоны» постепенно выходят за рамки гастрольного фестиваля. В апреле здесь открылась театральная студия Дмитрия Крестьянкина для подростков: в течение месяца с 60 участниками работали артисты и педагоги из Норильска, Москвы и Петербурга, а итогом стал эскиз спектакля «В твоих руках». В сентябре Алексей Нарутто и Ольга Тимошенко провели лабораторию современного танца, завершившуюся спектаклем «Север.Ок», созданным вместе с юными норильчанами. Так привезённое в Заполярье искусство становится поводом создавать собственное — и постепенно формирует в промышленном городе новую культурную среду.

Виноградники AYA расположены в предгорьях Крыма. Первый виноградник заложили в 2018 году и начали с пино нуара, высадив больше 10 тысяч лоз на гектар по плотной бургундской схеме. Сейчас виноградники занимают 116 га в сёлах Родном, Тенистом и Кировском; хозяйство выращивает 17 экологически чистых сортов винограда по строгим органическим стандартам.

AYA работает как винодельня открытого типа: посетители могут увидеть все этапы производства; формуле «от лозы до бокала» здесь следуют буквально. Белые и розовые вина выдерживают в стальных ёмкостях, красные — во французских бочках. Помимо классических линеек, проект выпускает небольшие серии без культурных дрожжей. В долине между морем и горами рождаются самодостаточные, элегантные, гастрономичные вина.

items.author: Анна Вострикова
paragraphs: Ресторан «Машенька» — лауреат премии «Сноба» «Сделано в России — 2026»

В феврале 1926 года Владимир Набоков подписал договор на публикацию своего первого романа «Машенька». Ровно сто лет спустя, 5 февраля 2026-го, Александр Раппопорт открыл на Варварке одноимённый ресторан современной русской кухни.

За меню отвечает Игорь Гришечкин — один из главных российских шефов, работающих с локальными продуктами и национальным кодом. Знакомые вкусы он разбирает и собирает заново: миниатюрные «голубчики» из брюссельской капусты готовит с крабом, икорным соусом и картофельным муссом, а тирамису дополняет кориандром — отсылкой к бородинскому хлебу. При этом привычных оливье и котлет по-киевски в меню нет: русское происхождение блюд здесь считывается не по хрестоматийным названиям, но по ингредиентам, их сочетаниям и вкусовой памяти.

Эту идею продолжают напитки. В барной карте Александры Водницкой появляются свёкла и запечённая тыква, а её оформление отсылает к увлечению Набокова бабочками. Отдельное место занимают самогон, хлебное вино и полугары. Винная карта Елены Капанелли полностью состоит из российских напитков: больше ста этикеток от небольших независимых хозяйств до крупных производителей из разных регионов страны.

Интерьер Archpoint тоже работает с русскими культурными кодами без буквального цитирования. Одной из доминант стала шпалерная стена с портретами реальных «Машенек» разных эпох, написанными московскими художниками специально для ресторана. Рядом — переосмысленные мотивы народных промыслов, коллекционные самовары, русская коса как графический элемент и настоящая печь в центре кухни.

items.title: Проект «Алупка. Возрождение исторического города» — лауреат премии «Сноба» «Сделано в России — 2026»
items.description: Проект «Алупка. Возрождение исторического города» — лауреат премии «Сноба» «Сделано в России — 2026»
items.author: Анна Вострикова
paragraphs: Проект «Алупка. Возрождение исторического города» — лауреат премии «Сноба» «Сделано в России — 2026»

С 2024 года Сбер и курорт «Мрия» в партнёрстве с городом реализуют программу комплексного развития Алупки. Стратегическая цель — превратить исторический город Южного берега Крыма в современный культурно-туристический кластер, объединяющий историческое наследие, искусство, общественные пространства и событийную жизнь. Проект направлен не на точечное благоустройство, а на формирование единой городской среды, привлекательной для жителей, туристов и бизнеса.

В рамках программы создаётся система пешеходных маршрутов, связывающих исторический центр, Воронцовский парк и побережье. Открыты Восточный и Воронцовский променады, туристический центр «Восточный», благоустроены общественные пространства. Обновлены пляжные зоны — Воронцовские купальни и Детский пляж, преобразована историческая территория «Порт Жорж».

Особое внимание уделяется развитию культурной жизни. В 2026 году состоялся первый Алупкинский симпозиум скульптуры с участием 12 художников, произведения которых интегрируются в городскую среду. Развивается событийная программа, объединяющая фестивали, исторические реконструкции и художественные инициативы.

За 2023–2025 годы туристический поток в Алупку увеличился на 80%, а число предпринимателей вдоль туристических маршрутов выросло с 70 до 500. Долгосрочная задача проекта — закрепить за Алупкой статус одного из ведущих культурных центров Крыма, где сохранение наследия становится основой устойчивого развития города.

paragraphs: Спектакль «Три сестры. Долой уныние» — лауреат премии «Сноба» «Сделано в России — 2026»

7 апреля 2026 года в Театре на Таганке состоялась премьера спектакля Саши Золотовицкого по пьесе Антона Чехова «Три сестры». В центре постановки — семья Прозоровых, которая пытается сохранить надежду на перемены, но постепенно оказывается в ловушке собственных ожиданий и иллюзий.

Режиссёр соединяет классический текст с современным культурным кодом, иронией и элементами гротеска. Спектакль исследует состояние героев, которые перестают действовать и передают управление собственной жизнью внешним обстоятельствам. В постановке также используются тексты современных авторов и музыка разных эпох.
