“I had become disenchanted with what we now call traditional Republicans,” she recalled.

Wiles’s relationship with Trump almost ended at his Miami golf club one night in the fall of 2016. Unhappy with a poll showing him doing worse than expected in Florida, Trump berated her in front of a gaggle of cronies. “It was a horrific hour-plus at midnight,” Wiles told me. “And I don’t think I’ve seen him that angry since. He was ranting and raving. And I didn’t know whether to argue back or whether to be stoic. What I really wanted to do was cry.”

Wiles steeled herself. “I finally said, ‘You know Mr. Trump, if you want somebody to set their hair on fire and be crazy, I’m not your girl. But if you want to win this state, I am. It’s your choice.’ ” Wiles walked out. Trump turned on a dime. “Lo and behold, he called me every day.” Wiles never looked back. Trump carried Florida, the first big prize in his stunning 2016 upset over Hillary Clinton.

Then, in a fateful turn of events, Wiles went to work in 2018 for an ambitious gubernatorial candidate named Ron DeSantis. (Trump urged DeSantis, then his protégé, to hire her.) She led the underdog candidate to victory. But afterward, DeSantis turned on her, denouncing Wiles publicly and bad-mouthing her privately. To this day, Wiles doesn’t know what triggered the governor’s vendetta. “I think he thought I was getting too much attention, which is ironic,” she told me. “I don’t ever seek attention.”

Wiles landed on her feet, organizing Florida for Trump’s 2020 reelection bid. Trump had rescued Wiles, recently divorced, at a dark moment in her life. (Wiles and her husband divorced in 2017—due, she has said, to his bad financial decisions.) Looking back on DeSantis’s behavior, Wiles reflected: “Had he said, ‘Look, thank you. I appreciate your help. We’re done here.’ I believe the course of his history would have been different. I might or might not have gone to work for Donald Trump.”

On Trump’s first day in office, the president signed a flurry of executive orders, 26 in all, withdrawing the US from the World Health Organization and the Paris climate agreement, rescinding birthright citizenship, sending troops to the southern border, freezing foreign aid, and stopping federal hiring. Then Trump issued pardons to almost everyone convicted in the bloody January 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol, in which nine people ultimately died and 150 were injured. Even rioters who’d beaten cops within an inch of their lives were set free. (Fourteen people convicted of seditious conspiracy had their sentences commuted.)
Did she ever ask the president, “ ‘Wait a minute, do you really want to pardon all 1,500 January 6 convicts, or should we be more selective?’ ”

“I did exactly that,” Wiles replied. “I said, ‘I am on board with the people that were happenstancers or didn’t do anything violent. And we certainly know what everybody did because the FBI has done such an incredible job.’ ” (Trump has said his FBI investigators were “corrupt” and part of a “deep state.”) But Trump argued that even the violent offenders had been unfairly treated. Wiles explained: “In every case, of the ones he was looking at, in every case, they had already served more time than the sentencing guidelines would have suggested. So given that, I sort of got on board.” (According to court records, many of the January 6 rioters pardoned by Trump had received sentences that were lighter than the guidelines.) “There have been a couple of times where I’ve been outvoted,” Wiles said. “And if there’s a tie, he wins.”

In the West Wing, Wiles is surrounded by young MAGA men. “She is a ‘go to church every Sunday, uses a swear word very, very rarely’ ” person, said James Blair, Wiles’s 36-year-old deputy chief of staff. “She doesn’t raise her voice. But she likes being around junkyard dogs.” Indeed, Wiles has seemed content to let her pit bulls—deputy chiefs of staff Miller, Blair, and Dan Scavino—run loose as she watches.

During Oval Office events, Wiles almost always sits just off camera. “There’s the president and then there’s whoever the three high-ranking people are on the sofa,” she said. “And then there’s a chair at the corner of the sofa, which is my chair, which means I’m the one that gets hit in the head with the boom mic.”

For all the chaos in the Cabinet, Wiles has kept palace intrigue and shivving to a minimum in the White House. Trump has empowered her; when Wiles weighs in, everyone knows she is speaking for him. She has in turn empowered her team: Blair, Miller, Scavino, and Taylor Budowich, who departed in September.

“First and foremost, she brings no ego,” says Blair. “And that is the starting point from which just an immense amount of power flows. There’s so much ego and testosterone around her, there wouldn’t be any room for hers anyway.”
From day one, Wiles had to grapple with another power center: Elon Musk.

“He is a complete solo actor,” said Wiles of Trump’s billionaire pal who led the scorched-earth blitz known as the Department of Government Efficiency. Wiles described Musk as something akin to a jacked-up Nosferatu. “The challenge with Elon is keeping up with him,” she told me. “He’s an avowed ketamine [user]. And he sleeps in a sleeping bag in the EOB [Executive Office Building] in the daytime. And he’s an odd, odd duck, as I think geniuses are. You know, it’s not helpful, but he is his own person.”

Musk triggered the first true crisis of the Trump presidency and an early test for Wiles. Trump’s chief was shocked when the SpaceX founder eviscerated USAID, the United States Agency for International Development. “I was initially aghast,” Wiles told me. “Because I think anybody that pays attention to government and has ever paid attention to USAID believed, as I did, that they do very good work.”

In his executive order freezing foreign aid, Trump had decreed that lifesaving programs should be spared. Instead, they were shuttered. “When Elon said, ‘We’re doing this,’ he was already into it,” said Wiles. “And that’s probably because he knew it would be horrifying to others. But he decided that it was a better approach to shut it down, fire everybody, shut them out, and then go rebuild. Not the way I would do it.”
Wiles knew that fixing this was on her. “The president doesn’t know and never will,” she told me. “He doesn’t know the details of these smallish agencies.”

Wiles says she called Musk on the carpet. “You can’t just lock people out of their offices,” she recalls telling him. At first, Wiles didn’t grasp the effect that slashing USAID programs would have on humanitarian aid. “I didn’t know a lot about the extent of their grant making.” But with immunizations halted in Africa, lives would be lost. Soon she was getting frantic calls from relief agency heads and former government officials with a dire message: Thousands of lives were in the balance.

Wiles continued: “So Marco is on his way to Panama. We call him and say, ‘You’re Senate-confirmed. You’re going to have to be the custodian, essentially, of [USAID].’ ‘Okay,’ he says.” But Musk forged ahead—all throttle, no brake. “Elon’s attitude is you have to get it done fast. If you’re an incrementalist, you just won’t get your rocket to the moon,” Wiles said. “And so with that attitude, you’re going to break some china. But no rational person could think the USAID process was a good one. Nobody.”

The shuttering of USAID crippled the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). The antiretroviral program, launched with $15 billion by George W. Bush in 2003, was credited with preventing millions of deaths. It depended on USAID grants. In an interview with The Financial Times, Bill Gates remarked: “The picture of the world’s richest man killing the world’s poorest children is not a pretty one.”
Privately, another drama was playing out.

Bush himself had gotten wind of the gutting of PEPFAR. He called Rubio to express alarm, according to a former aide close to Bush. “He’s been appalled by Trump from the beginning and he’s determined not to weigh in,” the aide said. But Musk’s attack on one of his legacy achievements was too much. Bush, said that person, “cares deeply about the PEPFAR program. That and Wounded Warriors are the two things where he will weigh in, not publicly, but with intention.”

Did Rubio have any regrets about the untold number of lives that PEPFAR’s evisceration might cost? “No. First of all, whoever says that, it’s just not being accurate,” he told me. “We are not eviscerating PEPFAR. PEPFAR has been rearranged and reorganized in such a way where we’re now going to be able to deliver aid in a way that has a goal. The goal is to help countries become self-sustaining.” With a note of “America First,” he added: “Let’s begin with the premise: Is it the United States’ fault? Why isn’t China paying for more immunizations? Why isn’t the UK or Canada or any of the G7 countries?” (The UK, following in the footsteps of the US, slashed foreign aid in 2025. In November, China, which funded the Africa CDC, pledged $3.5 million in AIDS prevention in South Africa alone.)
When I repeated Rubio’s comment to a former GOP White House chief of staff, he remarked: “I find that immoral.”
“Our job is lethality and readiness and war fighting.” —Pete Hegseth on his first day at the Pentagon, days after Vance cast the tiebreaking vote in his Senate confirmation

For Trump, Wiles has helped pick a Cabinet of MAGA hard-liners: Pete Hegseth, secretary of war (formerly defense); Kash Patel, FBI director; John Ratcliffe, CIA director; Pam Bondi, attorney general; Tulsi Gabbard, director of national intelligence; and Kristi Noem, head of Homeland Security. Wiles calls them “a world-class Cabinet, better than anything I could have conceived of.” Trump’s Cabinet members are either one of the least qualified presidential teams in history or, to hear Wiles tell it, disrupters—the only people with the balls to take on an entrenched deep state.

“People talk about the deep state being at the State Department,” Wiles said. “It’s not. It’s the military-industrial complex.” Hegseth, in her view, is just the guy to take on the powers that be. She referred to Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., another world-class disrupter, as “my Bobby” and “quirky Bobby.” In Wiles’s view, RFK Jr.’s shock treatment of HHS is warranted. “He pushes the envelope—some would say too far. But I say in order to get back to the middle, you have to push it too far.” (In December, Kennedy’s federal vaccine panel voted to end the decades-long recommendation for newborn vaccinations against hepatitis B, which is highly infectious and causes liver failure.)
“US deports hundreds of Venezuelans to El Salvador, despite court order.” —NPR

In mid-March, after Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents (ICE) shackled and herded 238 immigrants onto transport planes and flew them to a notoriously brutal Salvadoran prison. According to Trump, the men were members of Tren de Aragua, a violent Venezuelan gang, but the evidence was sketchy (often based on tattoos alone). Most had committed no serious crimes; one, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, was deported by mistake, the Trump administration admitted.
“I will concede that we’ve got to look harder at our process for deportation,” Wiles told me at the time.

When we spoke again in April, in cities across the country, masked ICE agents were snatching people off the street, throwing them in vans, and zip-tying and frog-marching them into makeshift deportation camps. Many were US citizens or entitled to be here. (ProPublica documented 170 cases in the first nine months of 2025 of US citizens being caught up in ICE’s dragnet.)

“If somebody is a known gang member who has a criminal past, and you’re sure, and you can demonstrate it, it’s probably fine to send them to El Salvador or whatever,” Wiles told me. “But if there is a question, I think our process has to lean toward a double-check.” But as the usa.gov site itself notes, “In some cases, a noncitizen is subject to expedited removal without being able to attend a hearing in immigration court.” Not long after the El Salvador deportation fiasco, in Louisiana, ICE agents arrested and deported two mothers, along with their children, ages seven, four, and two, to Honduras. The children were US citizens and the four-year-old was being treated for stage 4 cancer. Wiles couldn’t explain it.

“It could be an overzealous Border Patrol agent, I don’t know,” she said of the case, in which both mothers had reportedly been arrested after voluntarily attending routine immigration meetings. “I can’t understand how you make that mistake, but somebody did.”
“Long-threatened tariffs from U.S. President Donald Trump have plunged the country into trade wars abroad….” —PBS News
The president declared April 2 “Liberation Day,” bragging about billions of dollars that would flow into US coffers from tariffs, refusing to acknowledge that the levies were a tax on consumers.

“So much thinking out loud is what I would call it,” said Wiles of Trump’s chaotic tariff rollout. “There was a huge disagreement over whether [tariffs were] a good idea.” Trump’s advisers were sharply divided, some believing tariffs were a panacea and others predicting disaster. Wiles told them to get with Trump’s program. “I said, ‘This is where we’re going to end up. So figure out how you can work into what he’s already thinking.’ Well, they couldn’t get there.”

Wiles recruited Vance to help tap the brakes. “We told Donald Trump, ‘Hey, let’s not talk about tariffs today. Let’s wait until we have the team in complete unity and then we’ll do it,’ ” she said. But Trump barreled ahead, announcing sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs, from 10 to 100 percent—which triggered panic in the bond market and a sell-off of stocks. Trump paused his policy for 90 days, but by that time the president’s helter-skelter levies had given rise to the TACO chant: “Trump Always Chickens Out.”
Wiles believed a middle ground on tariffs would ultimately succeed, she said, “but it’s been more painful than I expected.”
At the time this article went to press, shortly before the December holidays, a Harvard poll showed 56 percent of voters think Trump’s tariff policies have harmed the economy.
“National Guard mobilizes 800 troops in DC to Support Federal, Local Law Enforcement—Trump declared a crime emergency in the nation’s capital.” —US Department of War

During the summer, Trump ordered the National Guard into four Democratic-led cities, claiming the troops were needed to crack down on crime and protect federal immigration facilities. In June the president deployed some 4,000 guard troops to Los Angeles; later he sent them to Washington, describing the city’s crime rate as “out of control.” “This was like a vitamin boost of ICE, of the [National] Guard, of the Park Service police, who actually have more authority than the DC Metro Police,” Wiles said. “And the idea was to right the ship and then slowly back off. And that’s what we’re doing.”
Critics denounced the deployments as unconstitutional, performative, and ineffective, and many feared Trump had another, more sinister plan up his sleeve.
Will the president use the military to suppress or even prevent voting during the midterms and beyond?
“I say it is categorically false, will not happen, it’s just wrongheaded,” she snapped.
“Do you understand where people who think that are coming from?” I asked.
“I do a little bit, but not fully. I mean, I think they hate the president. They think he’s too wrapped up in what happened in 2020.”

The president and his team were pushing almost every legal and constitutional boundary and defying courts to stop them. But would Trump obey the Supreme Court? “Do you think he will adhere to whatever the courts decide in the end?” I asked Wiles. “I do,” she replied. But Wiles made a prediction: “The smart lawyers around us think that we will be slowed down, as we already have been, but we will ultimately prevail.”
Click here to read Part 2 of 2 from Vanity Fair’s portfolio of Trump’s inner circle.

items.title: A Blue Wave Rejected Trump. Will Democrats Confront His Racism?
items.description: This article was produced by Capital & Main. It is co-published by Rolling Stone with permission.
items.author: Erin Aubry Kaplan; Ryan Bort
paragraphs: This article was produced by Capital & Main. It is co-published by Rolling Stone with permission.

The historic shellacking voters delivered to President Donald Trump and the GOP Tuesday already has many names — stinging rebuke, rejection, repudiation, reset. Analysts’ consensus is that the blue wave was a response to what so many Americans could see and feel every day — soaring prices, the effects of a needless war, blatant corruption at the top, all led by an erratic and increasingly unpopular president who openly dismissed the concerns of average people. The message was: enough.

For anyone alarmed about the country’s Trump-led decline, the midterm results are beyond heartening, the best possible outcome. At the very least — and this is still huge — a Democratic takeover of Congress puts a serious check on the chaos. At most, it is a generational opportunity to change direction. But what remains undiscussed is what the election results will mean for the country’s most intractable and corrosive problem, what powered the rise of Trumpism 10 years ago and powers it still: racism.

Will Democrats insist the country re-embrace diversity? And if so, how? In the last two years, many norms have been degraded and discarded with astonishing speed, chief among them the ideal of racial equality that is at the heart of America itself. Undoing diversity, equity and inclusion programs was the first agenda item of Trump’s second term, because it was dear to his base, but more importantly, because he intuited that dividing the country racially would weaken it and make it vulnerable to his authoritarian ambitions.

In his overarching campaign against DEI, Trump crossed lines and broke norms in ways detrimental and devastating for people of color, from sweeping federal job cuts that disproportionately hit Black workers to the targeting of Haitian immigrants for deportation to the recklessness and violence of ICE. It was the contempt and anything-goes lawlessness white authorities perpetrated on Black people during a century of Jim Crow segregation, but with the whole country drawn in this time.

Were the midterms a repudiation of this? Dorian Warren, co-president of the civil rights organization Community Change, is cautiously optimistic they might be. When we spoke in 2016 Warren told me that the crisis of Trump’s election was racial, a white problem that only white people could ultimately resolve. While that hasn’t happened, he now thinks the midterm results are a mark of notable progress.

“Though there were multiple motivations for voters, this was a definitely repudiation of Trump and MAGA,” Warren said in an interview on Thursday. “Think about it — now we have five Black governors. Keisha Lance Bottoms is the first Black female governor in history . . . It’s astounding.”
Warren said that this could be the moment that the Democratic Party finally realizes the magnitude of debt it owes to Black voters, who turned out in force, especially across the South.
“It’s like we’re saying, ‘Enough! We saved your butt many times,’” said Warren. “‘Stop running away from race.’”
In other words, Democrats need to unapologetically own the diversity of their party, and of America itself.

While it isn’t yet clear how much antiracism factored into the Democrats’ sweeping victory, there is no doubt about the role of Black Americans in pushing back. Black voters turned out in big numbers and shifted markedly to the left compared to 2024. That is at least in part an angry reaction to the GOP’s bald attempts to wipe out Black political representation with gerrymandering that disappeared Black-majority districts after the Supreme Court’s latest gutting of the Voting Rights Act.

That was perhaps the sweetest victory of all on Tuesday: that not only was a racist strategy ineffective, it backfired. Remarkable as that was, it’s also consistent with the resolve that has long characterized Black history.
“It’s amazing how resilient we are,” said Warren. “They tried to shut us down, and we said, ‘No, we’re not doing this.’”

Even if voters’ repudiation of Trump and the Republicans wasn’t chiefly about their racism, it was about morality. Candidates from Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico to Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton spoke about restoring decency, humanity and neighborliness to politics and American life. Talarico is a Presbyterian seminarian and Hamilton a Methodist pastor, but you didn’t have to be Christian to call out the moral rot of the Trump era, or to hear the message.

While few white candidates actually talked about racism — Talarico has called Christian nationalism “fundamentally un-Christian” and racism “immoral and wrong” — Democrats have generally been reluctant to talk in detail about spirituality or race. The moment demands they do both.
But even if the Democratic Party leaders don’t step up, Warren believes people of color will.

“My first thought after the election was, ‘This is a rainbow coalition,’” he said. “People are calling the increase of Black and Latino Democratic voters ‘blacklash’ and ‘brownlash.’ But that’s a coalition.”

While the Latino voters’ shift away from Trump was crucial, Warren said Black voters remain the anchor of the Democratic coalition. The question is whether their status within the party will change from being “captured” — taken for granted — to being “anchors” involved with directing the party and its mission.

The answer has great implications for the larger existential question about whether the U.S. will finally decide to champion its diversity as a permanent political and cultural good. Even at this moment of uncertainty and inflection, those answers are probably not coming anytime soon.
“As Black organizations and activists, we can’t wait around,” he said. “Now is the time we have to make demands and apply pressure. We have to get to work.”

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: The Price of Loyalty
items.description: Just when Henry and Julia think they have a little breathing room to figure out how to get back to the 1900s, a new wrinkle appears to blow up their plans. And this wrinkle, whether it actually happens or not, is surely going to have some major ramifications f
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Just when Henry and Julia think they have a little breathing room to figure out how to get back to the 1900s, a new wrinkle appears to blow up their plans. And this wrinkle, whether it actually happens or not, is surely going to have some major ramifications for Blood of My Blood going forward. Friends, Lord Lovat is totally going to try to kill Julia.

Let me back up a quick second: The lairds of loyalist clans — including Uncle Grant and Lovat — have gathered at the Duke of Sandringham’s Scottish Estate to meet with King George I. They are being celebrated and thanked for putting down the Jacobite rebellion. Lord Gerard Grey, who isn’t in attendance because he’s out hunting Dougal MacKenzie, gets elevated to Duke of Pardloe. Lovat gets his title and lands back and is named Governor of Inverness. Lovat could not be more smug about being the guest of honor. He’s especially thrilled to clock that Uncle Grant is bestowed with only a bronze medal, not a silver like him. And that’s not the only thing Lovat’s clocking: He meets Margaret Grant and is immediately taken by her.

You’d think this would be welcome news for Julia. It is initially, mainly because when Lovat makes up an excuse about Julia not feeling well to signal that he wants her to scram, it means she gets to sneak off with Henry. It does seem wild that everyone is cool with Julia being even remotely close to the dude they all think just tried to kidnap her, but I guess that just shows you how little Lovat actually cares about her. Sure, he makes a joke about demanding his head, and Henry gets big mad and begs him to try, which is objectively hot, but other than that, kidnapping, schmidnapping.

Julia and Henry do use Lovat’s fixation on Margaret and Uncle Grant’s fixation on Lovat’s fixation to their advantage. They sneak into a spare room so Julia can drop that bomb she discovered at the end of last week’s episode: According to Maisri, who has been right about everything else, Julia only traveled through the stones because she was pregnant with William, who does not have the power to travel. Leaving Julia behind is a nonstarter for Henry. It doesn’t take long before he’s like, Well, why don’t we just get you knocked up again? It sounds like an obvious conclusion to make, but Julia immediately shuts it down. She reasons that they shouldn’t have a child just to use it for their own needs, but I’d think a bigger reason is that there’s no guarantee the baby will be able to travel, and if not, they just brought another child into a very dangerous situation. But these two have never really concerned themselves with the nitty-gritty of time travel.

The next option they have is, of course, to grab William and run away together. But Lovat wants that baby — his future king — and if they run, he will never stop hunting them. Instead of feeling overwhelmed by the current situation, they take a moment to dance like they used to, remember how much they love each other, and remind themselves that for now, both of them are in safe situations and they have those gemstones ready to go in case of emergency. They have time to figure out what to do next.

Meanwhile, Lovat and Margaret have found a quiet place to make out. Uncle Grant bumps into them and is mostly disgusted by the whole thing, but it doesn’t take long for both Margaret and Grant to take control of the situation. Lovat wants to have sex with Margaret immediately, but she refuses to let Lovat do anything until he promises to marry her. She seems like the only woman he’s ever kowtowed to — and he likes it. God, he really is the worst.

We know that Uncle Grant has been looking to off-load his sister, so when Lovat sidles up to him, he starts talking about how Margaret would make a good wife, what with her sizable dowry and connections to some powerful people in London (she knows the king’s mistresses), but wow, isn’t it such a shame that Lovat’s already married … to his former maidservant. Whatever Grant is up to here, he’s good at it. Twisting the knife about how low-class Lovat’s wife is plays right into Lovat’s insecurities about his status. You see his wheels — okay, it’s like, one wheel — turning now. He wants Margaret, and he’s a man who gets what he wants. So he decides to build a little trust with Uncle Grant: He “lets” it slip that Ellen was handfasted to Brian before her wedding to Malcolm and the MacKenzies lied about it. Something tells me Uncle Grant isn’t just going to move on with his day after learning that piece of information.

Now that Lovat knows Grant is onboard with him marrying Margaret, he just starts spending time with her out in the middle of the room, for all to see. And “all” includes Julia. The moment she sees the two standing so close, she knows exactly what is happening here. Thankfully, Henry is nearby so she can tell him, too: Lovat wants to get rid of her, and the only way to do that and keep the baby without any type of scandal is for her to die. Seems like their whole plan to take a breath and figure things out, since they’re both safe for the moment, just got tossed out the window.

There are some death threats happening over at Castle Leoch, too. Lord Grey — now Duke, it seems — has arrived at Leoch looking for Dougal. (You’d think that would’ve been his first stop, but never mind me.) When Colum plays dumb about his brother’s whereabouts, Grey decides to arrest him. He doesn’t care that Colum stayed neutral in the rebellion — it’s still treason by omission and punishable by death. He agrees not to commandeer Leoch for the crown since the deed is under Ellen’s name and she had no power to fight for the king or stop Dougal from joining the Jacobites (Ellen’s plan worked!), but when Dougal rushes in to nobly save Colum from having to pay for crimes that aren’t his own, Grey takes it as an opportunity to kill two MacKenzie traitors.

Once again, Ellen has to clean up her brothers’ messes. At least this time, she’s going to take a little something for herself, too. She calmly gets Grey to agree to give Colum and Dougal time to pray before they’re taken off to be executed and then pays those boys a visit in the chapel. She will bargain for their lives — and she’ll get Grey to agree — but with a few conditions. First, Colum is going to be the sole laird of the clan. Dougal put them all at risk, and he can’t be trusted with any decision-making. Second, she’ll sign Leoch back over to Colum, but only if he agrees to give her the parcel of land that abuts Fraser land — the exact piece of Fraser land where Brian will be building their home. Colum and Dougal are livid that she’d even ask these things, which is especially rich because she could just let Grey take them, and Leoch and all the land and money that comes with it would be hers. These two are the biggest ding-dongs to ever ding-dong, and it is a wonder that they’re still around decades later in Outlander. Dougal can call his sister “a black-hearted bitch” all he wants, but they really have no choice but to agree to Ellen’s demands.

And Ellen makes good on her promise. She meets with Grey, and after flattering him for a bit, she reminds him that if he does go along with these executions, the story behind them will get out too. That story is, of course, that a rebel Highlander escaped Grey’s prison, killed a bunch of his men, and remained hidden and then gave himself up to save his family. Dougal will become a legend to the cause, and Grey will be humiliated. She also tosses in a bunch of money for good measure. It remains as true as ever: Ellen is the only MacKenzie really suited to be laird.

With Grey satisfied and Colum and Dougal saved, Ellen has one final condition for them: They are never, ever allowed to set foot on her and Brian’s land. At first, both of her brothers react to the rejection with anger. Colum refuses to pay her dowry, and Dougal makes a dig at Brian (who just saved his life, by the way) before storming out. But it becomes quite clear that they’re feeling more than anger, and if I had to guess, it would be that they’re embarrassed and heartbroken. Everyone on this show needs therapy, but especially the MacKenzie brothers.

You know what? There is one caveat to my previous statement. You know who is almost fully self-actualized? Ned. Sweet Ned! Colum may hide his tears when Ellen walks away from him, but not Ned. He finds Ellen one more time to say a real good-bye. He’s not afraid to tell her that he’ll miss her. The two used to sit by the fire and read and perform plays, and so, tearfully, he gives her a bit of Titania’s monologue from A Midsummer Night’s Dream — a bit in which he can tell her he loves her. “I do love thee,” she returns. She makes sure he knows he isn’t just the family lawyer and adviser to her. And hey, she never said Ned had to keep off her property. Fingers crossed these two best buds will get to perform Shakespeare again someday soon. Honestly, Brian would make a great Bottom.

• Have we been too hard on Colum? When Ellen tells him he’s not allowed to set foot in her home, he quietly tells her that she is always free to return to Leoch. When Ned remarks that he was actually worried Colum would turn Dougal over to Grey, he responds with a small but adamant “never.” Is he a secret softy inside, worried that he’s becoming a monster?

• Gah! John Cameron is headed to the West Indies (without Jocasta) to manage a sugarcane plantation he just bought, and he’s forcing Grace to go with him. Murtagh is beside himself when he finds out. He gets very Daniel Day-Lewis in The Last of Mohicans with his whole “I will board a ship! I will find you!” declaration. This can’t be the end for these two, can it?

• When Murtagh first goes to surprise Grace and she refuses to kiss him out of fear of them getting caught, he tells her that he’ll settle for his name on her lips. Murtagh is such a goddamned dreamboat. Nobody hurt him!!

items.title: Black Doves Season-Finale Recap: It’s So Hard to Find a Good Nanny
items.description: There’s a moment in “Murder Mix” that I barely noticed on my first watch and that I now think reveals a vital aspect of Laila’s character. She’s a mouthy smartass who amuses herself by launching peanuts into finance bros’ beers with stunning accuracy, sure. An
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: There’s a moment in “Murder Mix” that I barely noticed on my first watch and that I now think reveals a vital aspect of Laila’s character. She’s a mouthy smartass who amuses herself by launching peanuts into finance bros’ beers with stunning accuracy, sure. And yes, she can vanquish a van full of would-be kidnappers single-handedly. It’s likely Helen will be making choices to counteract the spy-wife label Laila slapped on her well into a hoped-for third season. But it’s the sincere “Mrs. Reed, are you okay?” when this teacup-size one-woman cavalry rolls up that points the way to Laila’s pivotal role in “Peace Summit.” It’s less of a softening detail — it does soften her a bit, but the character doesn’t need it — than a reminder of how focused Laila is on the purpose of the mission.

Everyone else is somewhere on the scale of checked out to what’s next. Helen’s locked in to being a supportive spy-wife for Wallace’s summit (and seemingly locked out of whatever he’s thinking — his face when she sees him in the kitchen the next morning, surrounded by the busy hive of his team, may as well be a closed door); Eleanor and Williams are figuring out what life after “I love you, too, you twat” looks like; having turned Reed over to Kestrel, Sam is doing penance by attending Jerry’s funeral. But Laila’s Spidey sense is tingling. She knows Sam didn’t walk Reed home, and she can feel something terrible is going to happen. Even if Sam had walked Reed home, I’m not convinced that home is safe anymore. What reason do we have to think the Black Doves are going to leave Reed alone now?

And Laila’s point about Reed’s safety and whereabouts is well taken. What was the point of all of them “risk[ing] our necks breaking her out of Downton fucking Abbey” if Sam was just going to put her right back into someone’s crosshairs? There’s not enough time, and goodness knows Sam doesn’t have the energy or inclination to explain the whole sordid story, but it turns out there’s no need to do so, anyway. Kestrel strikes on several fronts simultaneously with agents swooping into Wallace’s peace summit to kidnap Katya Chernov before she can deliver her late husband’s pre-opening remarks. They swarm his motorcade, snatching Cecile Mason and exploding her SUV (Helen has Wallace’s security team get them out of there immediately), and thanks to some very foolish IT assistance by Dani, they take over all of the security systems in the Black Doves’ main office.

It’s time to get the band back together! Yes, again! Laila explains she doesn’t just have a gut feeling that something is going down at the Black Doves’ offices; she knows because she has access to their computer network and saw the offices’ security system is down. And how does she know that? Well, remember how Laila was booted from active duty a few months back? It’s because she told her higher-ups their security system was inadequate and then hacked it after no steps were taken to improve it. So it took them three days to bring the system back up? Well, that only proves her point! The bosses do not like being made to look foolish (although right now would be a perfect time for a scathing “I told you so,” followed by a snotty, fully justified “Fuck around and find out”).

Meanwhile, Wallace and Helen are being whisked to a more secure location in a seemingly empty parking garage. This would be fine were it not for a couple of problems that make it completely not fine. Aside from the immediate threat of kidnapping, violence, and possibly death, I mean. Wallace can’t help but notice Helen’s effortless calm in a terrifying situation. She’s breathing normally and directing their team to contact the twins’ school so they can be secured as well, while Wallace is shaking like a leaf. Who is she? Who is Lily Morris? Why is the only photo of her as a girl the one Officer Perryman gave him? Helen puts in a decent performance with her usual lies, but it’s Katya, of all people, who provides the opportunity for Helen to start to come clean.

Katya was not kidnapped at all, as it turns out, because Katya is Vita. Storming the Black Doves’ offices was always the plan, as was having her mother frog-marched in and forced to sit through a very classic Bond-villain monologue about Franz eventually rescuing her from a Soviet orphanage and their pact to exact vengeance from everyone involved in the 1988 Berlin operation that nearly ruined their lives. She really shifts into high gear when she gets Helen on the line, taunting her about Nanny Marie’s years of service as a mole and current mission, having kidnapped Ollie and Jacqueline. Oh, dear. Katya, this is amateur-hour nonsense! I know you’ve spent years poring over the Black Doves and collecting details about Helen’s life and work; how are you going to stand there with all those hours of game tape under your belt and threaten her children to get her to convince her to shoot Wallace? Bush league!

Helen’s response is worth watching twice — first just to enjoy the scene in the flow of the episode as a whole, and then to see it through Wallace’s eyes. They’ve been together for over a decade, but in some ways, this is his first time seeing her. While she doesn’t confess any specific misdeed, she acknowledges the toll of the many secrets she’s kept from him and things she’s done, right alongside her love for him and their children. This may blow up their entire relationship and scuttle their planned future, but the score playing under this scene is the same bit of music that used to play under scenes of Helen’s reminiscences about Jason. It’s lovey-dovey and dreamy, and it could be a glimmer of hope. And then she pulls the trigger. Not on Wallace! Get real, this is a fake-out — she’s got children to rescue!

Chaos erupts immediately at Black Doves HQ once Eleanor, Williams, and Laila arrive. Kestrel is in immediate disarray, though Patrick manages to escape. Reed calmly grabs a gun and walks purposefully away, while Dani runs out of bullets and makes a run for the elevator, only to be blown to smithereens by the grenade Laila, Williams, and Eleanor relay to her. She really wasn’t going to get back to field work, was she? Reed finds an injured, bleeding-out Katya on one of the empty office floors below and confesses what we all knew: that she never went looking for her daughter because she didn’t want to find her. She was both selfish and generous in her restraint, expunging Vita from the mission records to save her own skin and to protect her child from any further fallout from the misfortune of being born to a Black Dove.

I can’t help thinking that this is a bit of a prelude to a similar conversation Helen must eventually have with her twins, not because she’s going to abandon them but because she’s murdered their nanny. What’s she going to tell them? Ollie and Jacqueline have known Marie their entire lives, then one day she takes them to the London Zoo for a treat and is never heard from again? They’re going to grieve and have all sorts of questions. They’re going to wonder if they’re to blame somehow! Therapy for all, stat.

So at the end of this mad week or so, where do we stand? Katya and most of her foot soldiers are dead, but Patrick survived and Kestrel is still well-funded. Black Doves have had to find new offices and deal with a staggering amount of paperwork, so they’re down but not out, and perhaps Reed will be able to bring Laila, Williams, and Eleanor on board. That might be over Helen’s objections: As Keira Knightley put it in our interview, Helen’s “whole life is about not knowing any of these people, and she really doesn’t want to have to be anywhere in such close proximity with them.” Then again, she may develop different notions about who should be on staff with the Black Doves because she finds herself needing their help. Regardless of future staffing issues, Knightley firmly believes that Helen is “going to take over the Black Doves, obviously,” reasoning that “if you are betraying your husband and the prime minister of your country, it is because you want to feel more powerful than them, right? I don’t think that kind of personality could just fade off into the distance.”

For now, Sam and Helen bid a loving, rueful good-bye as he heads back to that little town in Italy where it seemed like he’d found some peace (but he promises to come back if she sends up the Bat-signal). Most intriguing, Wallace does a bit of improvisational lying on Helen’s behalf in his follow-up meeting with Officer Perryman. There’s no CCTV footage from the parking garage or a several-block radius to compare to Wallace’s incredibly flimsy story about him and Helen dashing away to hide in a stairwell (where the armed men he references took their car but left them alone?) and Helen running off to some other hidey-hole until backup arrived. No mention here of Ollie and Jacqueline or of Sam. I assume all CCTV footage between the garage and the zoo is also gone. The real stars of this scene are the successive waves of micro-expressions crossing Adam Best’s face as Perryman is forced to perform calm acceptance of the obvious pack of lies that his prime minister is feeding him. I can’t wait to learn what Helen makes of Wallace’s freelancing, but first they’ll need to discuss her real name.
Strange Times to Be Nefarious

• So it turns out Cecile Mason was just there to be an insufferable American blowhard (fair, honestly) and then to get shot in the head? This piece of the story feels very rickety, though it does give us Reed’s “Well, you don’t hear much about Chechnya these days, do you? Thought it might be fun to bring them back,” so maybe it does balance out in the end.

• Jerry’s funeral was appropriately devastating and a vital reminder that, whatever assassins and their handlers tell themselves to justify their work, the grief and wreckage they leave behind in the lives of their victims’ loved ones is immense. Jerry’s best friend’s eulogy isn’t sad; she’s furious, and his murder will probably never be solved. The lavish, exuberant floral arrangement on top of his casket, reflecting his sunny personality and the way he made the world more colorful and beautiful, absolutely did not make me tear up.

items.title: David Walliams, Former ‘Britain’s Got Talent’ Judge, Accused of ‘Grooming Fans’ as Young as 15 After Failing to Get Injunction
items.description: David Walliams has been accused of “grooming fans” and “harassing” women by The Guardian newspaper after he failed to get an injunction to prevent them from publishing the story.
items.author: Ellise Shafer; K J Yossman
paragraphs: David Walliams has been accused of “grooming fans” and “harassing” women by The Guardian newspaper after he failed to get an injunction to prevent them from publishing the story.

“Comedian and former ‘Britain’s Got Talent’ judge alleged to have groomed fans he met when they were as young as 15 and harassed women in the workplace over a number of years,” the Guardian reports. “He denies the allegations.”

Among the allegations, which were made during a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News, is that Walliams was “predatory” and “pushy,” repeatedly contacting young women either via social media or modelling agencies, inviting them to his home or his dressing room at “Britain’s Got Talent.” One woman, who became friendly with the comedian after he contacted her, said he would “constantly pester her for sex.”
The report also alleges that Walliams would message “young female runners” who worked on his productions as well as staff at his publisher, HarperCollins.
Walliams has denied any wrongdoing, including any allegations of sexual harassment or inappropriate behavior.

Earlier this month, it was revealed that an anonymous celebrity had applied for a court injunction at the London High Court to try to prevent ITN and the Guardian from publishing a story about him containing allegations that he abused his power to engage in “inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women,” according to BBC News. He denies the allegations.

Walliams was not granted the injunction, meaning that these allegations may now be made public by the news organizations. He told the court that if the injunction was not granted and the stories were published, it was “highly likely” he would attempt to commit suicide. His lawyer told the court he had already attempted to do so twice before.

Walliams, known for the sketch series “Little Britain” and as a judge on “Britain’s Got Talent” as well as the author of bestselling children’s books, was first accused of inappropriate behavior in 2022 when it was alleged he had made sexually explicit and derogatory comments about contestants on “Britain’s Got Talent.” The revelations, in the Guardian newspaper, resulted in his exit from the show.
Walliams later sued “Britain’s Got Talent” producer Fremantle over data protection. The parties eventually settled out of court.

In 2025, HarperCollins ended its publishing contract with Walliams after an internal investigation regarding alleged inappropriate behavior and harassment toward junior female staff at the company. Earlier this year, the publisher said they would no longer sell or reprint his back catalogue of books.
Variety has contacted Walliams’ lawyers for comment.

items.description: Comedian, author and former “Britain’s Got Talent” judge David Walliams has denied that he is a sexual predator, following publication of allegations in the Guardian.
items.author: Leo Barraclough
paragraphs: Comedian, author and former “Britain’s Got Talent” judge David Walliams has denied that he is a sexual predator, following publication of allegations in the Guardian.
According to a statement published by the BBC, Walliams said, “Looking back, I realize that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
“I realize I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.
“And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”
He added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”
The Guardian on Tuesday alleged that Walliams “groomed fans he met when they were as young as 15 and harassed women in the workplace over a number of years.” He denies the allegations.

Walliams has denied any wrongdoing, including any allegations of sexual harassment or inappropriate behavior.

Walliams was not granted the injunction, meaning that these allegations may now be made public by the news organizations.
